# THE GHOST DANCE RELIGION
### AND THE
# SIOUX OUTBREAK OF 1890
### BY
## JAMES MOONEY

<vocab>Ghost Dance Religion, Sioux Outbreak of 1890, James Mooney</vocab>

<summary>This is the title page for James Mooney’s extensive study on the Ghost Dance religion and the associated Sioux Outbreak of 1890.</summary>
<keywords>Ghost Dance Religion, Sioux Outbreak, James Mooney, 1890, ethnology, Native American history</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page serves as a collection of introductory epigraphs for James Mooney’s study of the Ghost Dance, following the title page.</meta>

Say, shall I not at last attain
&nbsp;&nbsp;Some height, from where the Past is clear,
&nbsp;&nbsp;In whose immortal atmosphere
I shall behold my dead again?
->*Bayard Taylor.*<-

For the fires grow cold and the dances fail,
&nbsp;&nbsp;And the songs in their echoes die;
And what have we left but the graves beneath,
&nbsp;&nbsp;And, above, the waiting sky?
->*The Song of the Ancient People.*<-

My Father, have pity on me!
I have nothing to eat,
I am dying of thirst—
Everything is gone!
->*Arapaho Ghost Song.*<-

<summary>This page presents three introductory quotes and poems that establish the themes of loss, longing for the deceased, and spiritual desperation central to the Ghost Dance religion.</summary>
<keywords>Bayard Taylor, The Song of the Ancient People, Arapaho Ghost Song, epigraphs, poetry, mourning, Ghost Dance religion</keywords>

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION

->By JAMES MOONEY<-

### INTRODUCTION

In the fall of 1890, the author was preparing to go to Indian Territory, under the auspices of the Bureau of Ethnology, to continue research among the Cherokee, when the Ghost dance began to attract attention. Permission was asked and received to investigate that subject as well among the wilder tribes in the western part of the territory. Proceeding directly to the Cheyenne and Arapaho, it soon became evident that there was more to the Ghost dance than had been suspected. As a result, the investigation, which was intended to last only a few weeks, has extended over a period of more than three years and might be continued indefinitely, as the dance still exists (in 1896) and is developing new features at every performance. The uprising among the Sioux in the meantime also made it necessary to examine a mass of documentary material in the files of the Indian Office and the War Department bearing on the outbreak, in addition to the field study of the strictly religious features of the dance.

The first visit of about four months (December 1890—April 1891) was made to the Arapaho, Cheyenne, Kiowa, Comanche, Apache, Caddo, and Wichita, all living near together in the western part of what was then Indian Territory, but is now Oklahoma. These tribes were all more or less under the influence of the new religion. The principal study was made among the Arapaho, who were the most active propagators of the “Messiah” doctrine among the southern tribes and are especially friendly and cordial in disposition.

On returning to Washington, the author received a commission to make an ethnologic collection for the World’s Columbian Exposition, and, selecting the Kiowa for that purpose as a representative prairie tribe, started out again <gloss>underlined in ink</gloss>almost immediately to the same field. This trip, lasting three months, gave further opportunity for study of the Ghost dance among the same tribes. After returning and attending to the labeling and arranging of the collection, a study was made of all documents bearing on the subject in possession of the Indian Office and

<summary>James Mooney introduces his extensive multi-year investigation into the Ghost Dance religion, which began in 1890 among tribes in Oklahoma and the Indian Territory. The study combined direct field observations of tribes like the Arapaho and Kiowa with an analysis of government documents following the Sioux uprising.</summary>

<meta>This page continues James Mooney's introduction to his study of the Ghost dance, detailing his extensive field research and methodology between 1891 and 1894.</meta>

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION
[ETH. ANN. 14

the War Department. Another trip was then made to the field for the purpose of investigating the dance among the Sioux, where it had attracted the most attention, and among the Paiute, where it originated. On this journey, the author visited the Omaha, Winnebago, Sioux of Pine Ridge, Paiute, Cheyenne, and Arapaho; he met and talked with the messiah himself, and afterward, on the strength of this fact, obtained from the Cheyenne the original letter containing his message and instructions to the southern tribes. This trip lasted about three months.

A few months later, in the summer of 1892, another journey was made to the West, during which the southern tribes and the Sioux were revisited, and some time was spent in Wyoming with the Shoshoni and northern Arapaho; the latter were perhaps the most earnest followers of the messiah in the north. This trip took four months. After some time spent in Washington organizing the notes already obtained, a winter trip (1892–93) was made under another commission from the World’s Fair to the Navaho and the Hopi (or Moki) of New Mexico and Arizona. Although these tribes were not directly involved in the Ghost dance, they had been visited by apostles of the new doctrine and were able to give some account of the ceremony as it existed among the Havasupai (or Cohonino) and others farther to the west. On the return journey, another short stay was made among the Kiowa and Arapaho. In the summer of 1893, a final visit, covering a period of five months, was made to the western tribes of Oklahoma, bringing the personal observation and study of the Ghost dance down to the beginning of 1894.

The field investigation, therefore, occupied twenty-two months, involving nearly 32,000 miles of travel and a significant amount of time spent with about twenty tribes. To obtain exact knowledge of the ceremony, the author took part in the dance among the Arapaho and Cheyenne. He also carried a Kodak and a tripod camera, with which he made photographs of the dance and the trance both from outside and within the circle. Several months were spent consulting manuscript documents and printed sources of information in the departments and libraries at Washington, and correspondence was carried on with people in various parts of the country who might be able to provide additional facts. From the beginning, every effort was made to get a correct account of the subject. Beyond this, the work must speak for itself.

As the Ghost dance doctrine is only the latest of a series of Indian religious revivals, and as the idea on which it is founded is a hope common to all humanity, considerable space has been given to a discussion of the primitive messiah belief and of the teachings of the various Indian prophets who have preceded Wovoka, together with brief sketches of several Indian wars belonging to the same periods.

In the songs, the effort has been to give the spirit and exact translation, without going into analytical details. The main purpose of the work

MOONEY] INTRODUCTION

This study is not linguistic. Because nearly every tribe involved speaks a different language from all the others, any close linguistic study must be left to the philologist who can afford to devote a year or more to an individual tribe. The only one of these tribes of which the author claims intimate knowledge is the Kiowa.

# THE NARRATIVE

## CHAPTER I

### PARADISE LOST

> ->There are hours long past that memory recalls,<-
> ->Like blossoms of Eden that wind around the heart.<-
> ->Moore.<-

Wise men tell us that the world is growing happier—that we live longer than our ancestors did, have more comfort and less labor, fewer wars and conflicts, and higher hopes and goals. So say the wise men; but deep in our own hearts, we know they are wrong. For were we not also born in Arcadia? And have we not—every one of us—in the springtime of life when the world was young, started out lightly and cheerfully along the path that led through green meadows to the blue mountains on the distant horizon, beyond which lay the great world we were to conquer? And though others fell behind, have we not gone on through the brightness of morning and the heat of noon, with eyes always fixed forward, until the fresh grass began to be parched and withered, and the path grew hard and stony, and the blue mountains turned into gray rocks and thorny cliffs? And when at last we reached the exhausting summits, we found the glory that had lured us onward was only the sunset glow that fades into darkness while we watch, leaving us at the very goal to sink down, tired in body and sick at heart, with strength and courage gone, to close our eyes and dream again—not of the fame and fortune that were to be ours, but only of the old-time happiness that we have left so far behind.

As it is with individuals, so it is with nations. The lost paradise is the world’s dreamland of youth. What tribe or people has not had its golden age, before Pandora’s box was opened, when women were nymphs and nature spirits and men were gods and heroes? And when a race lies crushed and groaning under a foreign rule, how natural is the dream of a redeemer—an Arthur—who shall return from exile or awake from a long sleep to drive out the usurper and win back for his people what they have lost. This hope becomes a faith and the faith becomes the creed of priests and prophets, until the hero is seen as a god and the dream as a religion, looking toward some great miracle of nature for its fulfillment and completion. The doctrines of the Hindu avatar, the Hebrew Messiah, the Christian millennium, and the Hesûnanin of the Indian Ghost Dance are essentially the same and originate in a hope and longing common to all humanity.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Native American messiah concept, moving from a general reflection on the universal human longing for a "Golden Age" to the specific myths of hero-gods and deliverers among the tribes of North and South America.</meta>

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14]

Probably every Indian tribe, north and south, had its early hero-god—the great doer or teacher of all first things—from the <term>Iuskeha</term> and <term>Manabozho</term> of the primitive Iroquoian and Algonquian to the <term>Quetzalcoatl</term>, the <term>Bochica</term>, and the <term>Viracocha</term> of the more cultivated Aztecs, Muyscas, and Quichuas of the milder southland. Among the wandering tribes of the north, this hero is hardly more than an expert magician, frequently degraded to the level of a common trickster, who, after ridding the world of giants and monsters and teaching his people a few simple arts, retires to the upper world to rest and smoke until some urgent necessity again requires his presence below. Under softer southern skies, the myth takes a more poetic form and the hero becomes a person of dignified presence, a father and teacher of his children, a very Christ, worthy of all love and reverence, who gathers together the wandering nomads and leads them to their destined country. There, he instructs them in agriculture, house building, and the art of government; regulates authority; and encourages peaceful modes of life. “Under him, the earth teemed with fruits and flowers without the labor of cultivation. An ear of Indian corn was as much as a single man could carry. The cotton, as it grew, took of its own accord the rich dyes of human art. The air was filled with intoxicating perfumes and the sweet melody of birds. In short, these were the halcyon days, which find a place in the mythic systems of so many nations in the Old World. It was the golden age of Anahuac.” (*Prescott, 1.*)¹ When at last his work is well accomplished, he bids farewell to his sorrowing subjects, whom he consoles with the sacred promise that he will one day return and resume his kingdom, steps into his magic boat by the seashore, and sails away out of their sight to the distant land of the sunrise.

Such was Quetzalcoatl of the Aztecs, and such in all essential respects was the culture-god of the more southern semi-civilized races. Curiously enough, this god—at once a Moses and a messiah—is usually described as a white man with a flowing beard. From this and other circumstances, it has been argued that the whole story is only another form of the dawn myth; but whether the Indian god be an ancient deified lawgiver of their own race, or some nameless missionary who found his way across the trackless ocean in the early ages of Christianity, or whether we have here only a veiled parable of the morning light bringing life and joy to the world and then vanishing to return again from the east with the dawn, <note>penciled bracket begins</note> it is sufficient for our purpose that the belief in the coming of a messiah, who should restore them to their original happy condition, was nearly universal among the American tribes. <note>penciled bracket ends</note>

This faith in the return of a white deliverer from the east opened the gate to the Spaniards at their first coming alike in Haiti, Mexico, Yucatan, and Peru. (*Brinton, 1.*) The simple native welcomed the white strangers as the children or kindred of their long-lost benefactor,

PUEBLO REVOLT OF 1680

immortal beings whose coming had been foretold by oracles and omens, whose faces seemed to reflect the brightness of the dawn, whose glistening armor seemed woven from the rays of sunlight, and whose god-like weapons were the lightning and the thunderbolt. Their first overbearing demands awakened no resentment; for may not the gods claim their own, and is not resistance to the divine will a crime? Not until their most sacred things were trampled underfoot, and the streets of the holy city itself ran red with the blood of their slaughtered princes, did they correctly understand the awful prophecy by the light of their blazing temples, and know that instead of the children of an incarnate god, they had welcomed a horde of incarnate devils.

> “The light of civilization would be poured on their land. But it would be the light of a consuming fire, before which their barbaric glory, their institutions, their very existence and name as a nation, would wither and become extinct. Their doom was sealed when the white man had set his foot on their soil.” (Prescott, 2.)

<margin>*</margin>
The great revolt of the Pueblo Indians in August 1680 was one of the first determined efforts made by the natives on the northern continent to throw off the yoke of a foreign oppressor. The Pueblo tribes along the Rio Grande and farther to the west, a gentle, peaceful race, had early welcomed the coming of the Spaniards, with their soldiers and priests, as friends who would protect them against the wild marauding tribes around them and teach them the mysteries of a greater “medicine” than belonged to their own <term>kachinas</term>. The hope soon faded into bitter disappointment. The soldiers, while rough and overbearing toward their brown-skinned allies, were yet unable to protect them from the raids of their enemies. The priests prohibited their dances and simple amusements, yet all their ringing of bells and chanting of hymns did not help to bring more rain for the crops or to turn aside the vengeful Apache.

> “What have we gained by all this?” said the Pueblos to one another; “not peace and not happiness, for these new rulers will not protect us from our enemies, and they take from us all the enjoyments we once knew.”

<margin>*</margin>
The time was ripe. Popé, a medicine man of the Tewa, had come back from a pilgrimage to the far north, where he claimed to have visited the magic lagoon of <term>Shipapu</term>, from where his people traced their origin and to which the souls of their dead returned after leaving this life. By these ancestral spirits, he had been endowed with occult powers and commanded to go back and rouse the Pueblos to a united effort for freedom from the foreign yoke of the strangers.

These spirit messengers were wonderful beings. Swift as light and impalpable as thought, they passed under the earth from the magic lake to the secret subterranean chamber of the oracle and stood before him as shapes of fire. They spoke, telling him to prepare the strings of yucca knots and send them with the message to all the Pueblos far and near, so that in every village the chiefs might untie one knot from the string each day, and know when they came to the last knot that it was then the time to strike.

<summary>This page describes the shift in Pueblo perception of Spanish colonizers from gods to oppressors, leading to the 1680 revolt organized by the Tewa leader Popé. Popé claimed spiritual authority from ancestral spirits at Shipapu to unite the tribes using yucca-knot strings as a countdown for the uprising.</summary>

--- Page 30 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, documenting the expulsion of the Spaniards from New Mexico, and then broadens the scope to discuss similar messianic hopes for an indigenous redeemer in Mexico and Peru, specifically highlighting the 18th-century rebellion of Tupac Amaru II.</meta>

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14

From the Pecos River, across the Rio Grande to Zuñi and the far-distant Hopi mesas, every Pueblo village accepted the yucca string and began secret preparations for the uprising. The time chosen was the new moon of August 1680, but, because the plot was partially discovered, the outbreak was triggered early on the 10th. The surprise was so sudden and complete that many Spaniards in the Pueblo country—priests, soldiers, and civilians—were killed. The survivors, after holding out for a time under Governor Otermin at Santa Fe, fled to El Paso, and by October, not a single Spaniard remained in all of New Mexico. (*Bandelier, 1 a, 1 b.*)

Despite their bitter disappointment, the southern nations continued to cherish the hope of a coming redeemer, who now took on the character of a terrible avenger of their wrongs. The white-skinned conqueror has had bloody cause to remember that his silent laborer, as he toils by blue Lake Chapala or sits among the ruins of his former grandeur in the dark forests of Yucatan, still waits ever and always for the coming of the day that shall break the power of the foreign Spaniard and restore the children of Anahuac and Mayapan to their inheritance. In Peru, the natives refused to believe that the last of the Incas had died as a wanderer in the forests of the eastern Cordilleras. For more than two centuries, they cherished the tradition that he had only retired to another kingdom beyond the mountains, from which he would return in his own time to sweep their arrogant oppressors from the land. In 1781, this simmering hope found expression in a terrible insurrection under the leadership of the <term>mestizo</term> Condorcanqui, a descendant of the ancient royal family, who boldly proclaimed himself the long-lost Tupac Amaru, child of the sun and Inca of Peru. With wild enthusiasm, the Quichua highlanders hailed him as their destined deliverer and rightful sovereign. Binding the imperial headband of the Incas around his forehead, he advanced at the head of an immense army to the walls of Cuzco, declaring his purpose to erase the very memory of the white man and reestablish the Indian empire in the City of the Sun. Inspired by the hope of vengeance against the conqueror, even boys became leaders of their people. It was only after a bloody struggle lasting two years that the Spaniards were able to regain control and condemned the captured Inca, along with his entire family, to a shameful and barbaric death. Even then, the feeling of veneration he had inspired in the hearts of the Indians was so great that, "notwithstanding their fear of the Spaniards, and though they were surrounded by soldiers of the victorious army, they prostrated themselves at the sight of the last of the children of the sun, as he passed through the streets to the place of execution." (*Humboldt, 1.*)

<insert>J</insert> In the New World, as in the Old, the coming of the deliverer was to be signaled by signs and wonders. Thus in Mexico, a mysterious rising of the waters of Lake Tezcuco, three comets blazing in the sky, and a strange light in the east prepared the minds of the people for the approaching

MOONEY] A WINNEBAGO PROPHECY

...the coming of the Spaniards. (*Prescott, 3.*) In this connection as well, there was usually a belief in a series of previous destructions by flood, fire, famine, or pestilence, followed by a renewal through the all-powerful strength of the savior. The doctrine that the world is old and worn out, and that the time for its renewal is near at hand, is an essential part of the Ghost dance’s teaching. The number of these cycles of destruction was stated differently among various tribes, but perhaps the most sadly prophetic version of the myth was found among the Winnebago. Forty years ago, they believed that the tenth generation of their people was nearing its end, and that at the end of the thirteenth generation, the red race would be destroyed. Through prayers and ceremonies, they were then attempting to appease their angry gods and postpone the doom that now seems to be rapidly closing in on them. (*Schoolcraft, Ind. Tribes, 1.*)

## CHAPTER II

# THE DELAWARE PROPHET AND PONTIAC

> Hear what the Great Spirit has ordered me to tell you: Put off entirely the customs which you have adopted since the white people came among us.—*The Delaware Prophet.*

> This is our land, and not yours.—*The Confederate Tribes, 1752.*

The English advances were slow and halting, and for a long period almost imperceptible, while the establishment of a few small garrisons and isolated trading stations by the French hardly deserved to be called an occupation of the country. As a consequence, the warlike northern tribes were slow to realize that an empire was slipping from their grasp, and it was not until the two great nations prepared for the final struggle in the New World that the native proprietors began to read the stars correctly. Then it was, in 1752, that the Lenape chiefs sent to the British agent the pointed question: “The English claim all on one side of the river, the French claim all on the other—where is the land of the Indians?” (*Bancroft, 1.*) Then, as they saw the French strengthening themselves along the lakes, there came a stronger protest from the council ground of the confederate tribes of the west: “This is our land and not yours. Fathers, both you and the English are white; the land belongs to neither the one nor the other of you, but the Great Being above allotted it to be a dwelling place for us; so, fathers, I desire you to withdraw, as I have desired our brothers, the English.” A wampum belt gave weight to the words. (*Bancroft, 2.*) The French commander’s reply was blunt, but more practiced diplomats assured the Indians that all belonged to them, and that the great king of the French desired only to set up a boundary against the further encroachments of the English, who would otherwise sweep the native tribes from the Ohio as they had already driven them from the Atlantic. The argument was plausible. In every tribe were French missionaries, whose fearless courage and devotion had won the admiration and love of the Indians; in every village lived a hardy voyageur, with his Indian wife and family of children, in whose veins mixed the blood of the two races and whose ears <gloss>his</gloss> were attuned alike to the wild songs of the forest and the songs of Normandy or Provence. It was no common tie that bound together the Indians and the French, and when a governor of Canada and the general of his army stepped into the circle of braves to dance the war dance and sing the war song with their native allies, thirty-three wild tribes declared on the wampum belt, “The French are our brothers and their king is our father. We

<summary>This page describes the growing realization among Native American tribes in the mid-1700s that their lands were being seized by the British and French, leading to early diplomatic protests and a preference for the French due to closer cultural and familial ties.</summary>

will try his hatchet upon the English" (*Bancroft, 3*), and through seven years of blood and death the lily and the totem were carried side by side until the flag of France fell forever on the heights of Quebec.

For some time after the surrender, the unrest of the native tribes was calmed into a semblance of quiet by the belief, artfully taught by their old allies, that the king of France, exhausted by his great efforts, had fallen asleep for a little while, but would soon wake to take vengeance on the English for the wrongs they had inflicted on his red children. Then, as they saw English garrisons occupying the abandoned posts and English traders passing up the lakes even to the sacred island of the Great Turtle, the despairing warriors said to one another, "We have been deceived. English and French alike are white men and liars. We must turn from both and seek help from our Indian gods."

<margin>✓</margin>
<margin>*</margin>
<margin>✓</margin>
In 1762, a prophet appeared among the Delawares, at Tuscarawas, on the Muskingum, who preached a union of all the red tribes and a return to the traditional Indian life, which he declared to be the divine command, as revealed to himself in a wonderful vision. From an old French manuscript, written by an anonymous eyewitness of the scene which he describes, we have the details of this vision, as related by Pontiac to his native audience at the great council of the tribes held near Detroit in April 1763. Parkman gives the story on the authority of this manuscript, which he refers to as the "Pontiac manuscript," and states that it was long preserved in a Canadian family at Detroit, and afterward deposited with the Historical Society of Michigan. It bears internal evidence of being genuine, and is supposed to have been written by a French priest. (*Parkman, 1.*) The vision, from the same manuscript, is related at length in Schoolcraft's *Algic Researches*.

<margin>[</margin>
<margin>chief of world</margin>
According to the prophet's story, being anxious to know the "Master of Life," he determined, without mentioning his desire to anyone, to undertake a journey to the spirit world. Ignorant of the way, and not knowing any person who, having been there, could direct him, he performed a mystic rite in the hope of receiving some light as to the course he should pursue. He then fell into a deep sleep, in which he dreamed that it was only necessary to begin his journey and that by continuing to walk forward he would at last arrive at his destination.

Early the next morning, taking his gun, ammunition, and kettle, he started off, firmly convinced that by pressing onward without discouragement he should accomplish his object. Day after day he proceeded without incident, until at sunset of the eighth day, while preparing to camp for the night by the side of a small stream in a little opening in the forest, he noticed, running out from the edge of the prairie, three wide and well-trodden paths. Wondering somewhat why they should be there, he finished his temporary shelter and, lighting a fire, began to prepare his supper. While thus engaged, he observed with astonishment that the paths became more distinct as the night grew darker.

<summary>Following the French defeat at Quebec, indigenous tribes turned away from European alliances toward a spiritual revival led by the Delaware Prophet. # THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14

Alarmed by the strange sight, he was about to abandon his camp and look for another at a safer distance, when he remembered his dream and the purpose of his journey. It seemed to him that one of these roads must lead to the place he was looking for, and he decided, therefore, to stay where he was until morning, and then take one of the three paths and follow it to the end. Accordingly, the next morning, after a quick meal, he left his camp and, burning with the passion of discovery, took the widest path. He followed it until noon, when he suddenly saw a large fire apparently coming out of the earth. His curiosity was sparked, and he went toward it, but the fire grew to such an extent that he became frightened and turned back.

He then took the next widest of the three paths, which he followed as before until noon, when a similar fire again drove him back and forced him to take the third road. He traveled on this one for a whole day without meeting anything unusual, when suddenly he saw a steep mountain of dazzling brightness directly in his path. Recovering from his amazement, he drew near and examined it, but could see no sign of a road to the top. He was about to give in to disappointment when, looking up, he saw a beautiful woman sitting a short distance up the mountain. She was dressed in snow-white clothes and spoke to him in his own language, telling him that on the summit of the mountain was the home of the Master of Life, whom he had traveled so far to meet. “But to reach it,” she said, “you must leave all your heavy clothing and equipment at the base, then go and wash in the river that I show you, and afterward climb the mountain.”

He followed her instructions, and when he asked how he could hope to climb the mountain, which was steep and slippery as glass, she replied that in order to climb he must use only his left hand and foot. This seemed almost impossible to him, but, encouraged by the woman, he began to climb and at length, after much difficulty, reached the top. There the woman suddenly disappeared, and he found himself alone without a guide. Looking around, he saw a plain before him, in the middle of which were three villages with well-built houses arranged in an orderly way. He headed toward the main village, but after going a short distance he remembered that he was naked and was about to turn back when a voice told him that as he had washed himself in the river, he could go on without fear. Thus commanded, he walked without hesitation to the village gate, where he was admitted and saw a handsome man in white clothes approaching, who offered to lead him into the presence of the Master of Life. Admiring the beauty of everything around him, he was then led to the Master of Life, who took him by the hand and gave him a gold-trimmed hat to sit on. Afraid of ruining the hat, he hesitated to sit down until told to do so again, when he obeyed, and the Master of Life spoke to him as follows:

> I am the Master of Life, whom you wish to see and with whom you wish to speak. Listen to what I shall tell you for yourself and for all the Indians.

He then commanded him to urge his people to stop their drunkenness, wars, polygamy, and the medicine song, and continued: <note>Pencil checkmark and slash follow this line.</note>

> The land on which you are, I have made for you, not for others. Why do you allow the white people to live upon your lands? Can you not do without them? I know that those whom you call the children of your Great Father <note>the King of France</note> supply your needs; but if you were not as wicked as you are, you would not need them. You might live as you did before you knew them. Before those whom you call your brothers <note>the French</note> had arrived, did not your bow and arrow maintain you? You needed neither gun, powder, nor any other object. The flesh of animals was your food; their skins were your clothing. But when I saw you inclined toward evil, I moved the animals into the depths of the forest so that you might depend on your brothers for your necessities and for your clothing. Become good again and do my will, and I will send animals for your sustenance. I do not, however, forbid providing for your Father’s children among you. I love them; they know me; they pray to me. I supply their own needs and give them that which they bring to you. It is not so with those who have come to trouble your possessions <note>the English</note>. Let them remain there. (Schoolcraft, *Alg. Res.*, 1.)

The Master of Life then gave him a prayer, carved in <term>Indian hieroglyphics</term> upon a wooden stick, which he was told to deliver to his chief upon returning to earth. (Parkman, 2.) His instructor continued: <note>Pencil checkmark follows this line.</note>

> Learn it by heart, and teach it to all the Indians and children. It must be repeated morning and evening. Do all that I have told you, and announce it to all the Indians as coming from the Master of Life. Let them drink but one drink, or two at most, in one day. Let them have but one wife, and stop running after other people’s wives and daughters. Let them not fight one another. Let them not sing the medicine song, for in singing the medicine song they speak to the evil spirit. Drive from your lands those dogs in red clothing; they are only an injury to you. When you want anything, ask me, as your brothers do, and I will give to both. Do not sell to your brothers that which I have placed on the earth as food. In short, become good, and you shall want for nothing. When you meet one another, bow and give one another the <note>left</note> hand of the heart. Above all, I command you to repeat morning and evening the prayer which I have given you.

The Indian received the prayer, promising to do as he had been commanded and to recommend the same course to others. His former guide then came and, leading him to the foot of the mountain, told him to put his clothes back on and go back to his village. His return excited much surprise among his friends, who had thought he was lost. They asked him where he had been, but as he had been commanded to speak to no one until he had seen the chief, he motioned with his hand to signify that he had come from above. On entering the village, he went at once to the wigwam of the chief, to whom he delivered the prayer and the message which he had received from the Master of Life. (*Schoolcraft, Alg. Res.*, 2.) <note>Pencil underlining appears under the citation.</note>

Since the author of the manuscript was a Frenchman, it is more probable that we have here only the well-known preference of the wild tribes. English occupation of a region always meant the rapid expulsion of the natives. The French, on the contrary, lived side by side with the Indians, joining in their dances and simple amusements, and sympathizing fully with their wild life. As a result, they were regarded more as brothers from an allied tribe than as intruders from a foreign race. This feeling is clearly shown in the prophet’s narrative, where the Indians, while urged to discard everything they have adopted from the whites, are nonetheless permitted to let the French remain among them, even while being urged to wage relentless war on the English. This difference was tragically demonstrated at Michilimackinac a year later, when a few French traders looked on, unarmed and unharmed, while a crew of maddened warriors butchered, scalped, and drank the blood of British soldiers. The inclusion of the trivial incident involving the hat is typically Indian, and the mixing of dreams and visions with actual events is a frequent result of the mental state commonly found in the history of religious enthusiasts. The Delaware prophet considers the entire experience an actual fact rather than a fevered vision caused by long fasting and vigils; to him, the hieroglyphic prayer—undoubtedly carved by himself while in a state of ecstasy—is a genuine gift from heaven. The entire story is a striking parallel to the miraculous experiences described by the modern apostles of the Ghost Dance. The prayer-stick and the heavenly map, described and illustrated later, reappear in the account of Känakûk, the Kickapoo prophet, seventy years later, showing in a remarkable way the continuity of aboriginal ideas and methods.

The famous missionary Heckewelder, who spent fifty years among the Delawares, was personally acquainted with this prophet and provides a detailed account of his teachings and his symbolic parchments. He says:

> In the year 1762, there was a famous preacher of the Delaware nation who lived at Cayahaga, near Lake Erie. He traveled about the country among the Indians, trying to persuade them that he had been appointed by the Great Spirit to instruct them in those things that pleased Him. He pointed out to them the offenses by which they had drawn His displeasure upon themselves, and the means by which they might regain His favor in the future. He had drawn—as he claimed, by the direction of the Great Spirit—a kind of map on a piece of deerskin, prepared somewhat like parchment, which he called “the great Book or Writing.” He said he had been ordered to show this to the Indians so that they might see the situation in which the <term>Mannitto</term> <note>Manitou or Great Spirit</note> had originally placed them, the misery they had brought upon themselves by neglecting their duty, and the only way that was now left for them to regain what they had lost. He held this map before him while preaching, frequently pointing to specific marks and spots on it and giving explanations as he went along.

The size of this map was about fifteen inches square, or perhaps a bit more. An inner square was formed by lines drawn within it, measuring about eight inches on each side; however, two of these lines did not meet at the corners, leaving a gap of about half an inch.

<header>HECKEWELDER ON THE PROPHET</header>
<sig>MOONEY</sig>
Across these inner lines, other lines about an inch in length were drawn, along with various other lines and marks. All of this was intended to represent a strong, inaccessible barrier to prevent those outside from entering the space within, except at the place appointed for that purpose. When the map was held as he directed, the corners that were not closed lay on the left-hand side, directly opposite each other; one was at the southeast-by-south, and the nearest was at the northeast-by-north. In explaining or describing the specific points on this map, while always pointing his fingers to the place he was describing, he called the space within the inner lines “the heavenly regions,” or the place destined by the Great Spirit for the Indians to live in the afterlife. The space left open at the southeast corner he called the “avenue,” which had been intended for the Indians to enter this heaven, but which was now in the possession of the white people. Therefore, the Great Spirit had since caused another “avenue” to be made on the opposite side; however, it was both difficult and dangerous for them to enter it, as there were many obstacles in their way, including a large ditch leading to a gulf below which they had to leap across. Furthermore, the evil spirit kept a constant watch for Indians at this very spot, and whoever he seized could never escape him again but was carried to his regions. In those regions, there was nothing but extreme poverty; the ground was parched by the heat for lack of rain, no fruit ever ripened, the game animals were nearly starved for lack of pasture, and the evil spirit transformed men at his whim into horses and dogs to be ridden by him and to follow him in his hunts and wherever he went.

The space on the outside of this inner square was intended to represent the country given to the Indians to hunt, fish, and live in while in this world; the east side of it was called the ocean or the “great salt-water lake.” Then the preacher, drawing the attention of his listeners particularly to the southeast avenue, would say to them, “Look here! See what we have lost by neglect and disobedience; by being negligent in expressing our gratitude to the Great Spirit for what he has bestowed upon us; by neglecting to make sufficient sacrifices to him; by looking upon a people of a different color from our own, who had come across a great lake, as if they were a part of ourselves; by allowing them to sit down by our side and looking at them with indifference while they were not only taking our country from us, but this (pointing to the spot)—this, our own avenue leading into those beautiful regions which were destined for us. Such is the sad condition to which we are reduced. What is now to be done, and what remedy is to be applied? I will tell you, my friends. Hear what the Great Spirit has ordered me to tell you! You are to make sacrifices in the manner that I shall direct; to discard entirely the customs which you have adopted since the white people came among us. You are to return to that former happy state in which we lived in peace and plenty before these strangers came to disturb us; and, above all, you must abstain from drinking their deadly <term>beson</term>, which they have forced upon us for the sake of increasing their gains and diminishing our numbers. Then the Great Spirit will give us strength to conquer our enemies, to drive them from here, and to recover the passage to the heavenly regions which they have taken from us.”

This was, in general, the substance of his discourses. After having spoken at greater or lesser length on the various topics I have mentioned, he usually concluded in this way: “And now, my friends, so that what I have told you may remain firmly impressed on your minds, and to refresh your memories from time to time, I advise you to keep, in every family at least, such a book or writing as this, which I will finish for you, provided you bring me the price, which is only one buckskin or two doeskins each.” The price was, of course, paid <note>the original text reads “bought”</note>, and the book purchased. In some of these maps, the figure of a deer or turkey, or both, was placed in the heavenly regions and also in the dreary region of the evil spirit. The former animals, however, appeared fat and plump, while the latter seemed to be nothing but skin and bones. (*Heckewelder, I.*)

From the narrative of John McCullough, who was captured by the Indians when he was a child of 8 and lived for several years as an adopted son in a Delaware family in northeastern Ohio, we gather some additional details concerning this prophet, whose name seems to have been lost to history. McCullough himself, who was then only a boy, never met the prophet, but he obtained his information from others who had, especially from his Indian brother, who went to Tuscarawas (or Tuscalaways) to see and hear the new apostle during his first appearance.

Those who went to see him said that he had certain hieroglyphics marked on a piece of parchment, representing the testing that human beings were subjected to while they lived on earth, and also representing something of a future state. They informed me that he was crying almost constantly while he was preaching to them. I saw a copy of his hieroglyphics, as many of the people had made copies of them and began to preach or instruct others. The first or main doctrine they taught was to purify themselves from sin, which they believed they could do by using emetics and abstaining from sexual relations; to stop the use of firearms, and to live entirely in the original state they were in before the white people discovered their country. Indeed, they taught that fire made by steel and flint was not pure, but that they should make it by rubbing two sticks together. . . . It was said that their prophet taught them, or made them believe, that he received his instructions directly from *Keesh-she-la-mil-lang-up*, or a being that thought us into existence, and that by following his instructions they would, in a few years, be able to drive the white people out of their country.

I knew a group of them who had secluded themselves for the purpose of purifying themselves from sin, as they believed they could do. I believe they made no use of firearms. They had been away for more than two years before I left them. . . . It was said that they used no other weapons than their bows and arrows. They also taught that, when shaking hands, one should give the left hand as a sign of friendship, as it signified that they gave the heart along with the hand. (*Pritts, 1.*)

The religious excitement produced by the preaching of the Delaware prophet spread rapidly from tribe to tribe, until, under the leadership of the great mind of the celebrated chief, Pontiac, it took the form of a grand confederacy of all the northwestern tribes to oppose the further progress of the English. The coastal lands were lost to the Indians. The Ohio region and the lakes were still theirs, and the Alleghenies marked a natural boundary between the two sections. Pontiac determined to make his stand behind this mountain barrier. Although the possibility of restoring French power might have helped him rally a following, he knew himself that he could expect no help from the French, for their armies had been defeated and their garrisons were already being withdrawn; but, relying on the patriotism of his own red warriors, when told that the English were on their way to take possession of the abandoned forts, he sent back the defiant challenge, "I stand in the path."

The highest position among the leaders of the Algonquian race must be attributed to Pontiac. Born the son of a chief, he became in turn the chief of his own people, the *Ottawa*, whom it is said he commanded during *Braddock's* defeat. For this or other services on behalf of the French, he had received marks of distinguished respect from

<header>MOONEY] PONTIAC'S PLAN OF CONFEDERATION</header>

Montcalm himself. Due to his natural ability, his influence was felt and respected wherever the name of his tribe was spoken; to his dignity as chief, he added the sacred character of high priest of the powerful secret order of the Midé. (*Parkman, 3.*) Now, in the prime of his manhood, he originated and formulated the policy of a confederation of all the tribes—an idea later taken up and carried almost to a successful conclusion by the great Tecumtha. As the principal chief of the lake tribes, he summoned them to the great council near Detroit in April 1763. As high priest and keeper of the faith, he announced to them the will of the Master of Life, as revealed to the Delaware prophet, and called on them to unite to recover their ancient territories and preserve their national life. Under the spell of his passionate words, the chiefs listened as if to an oracle and cried out that he had only to declare his will to be obeyed. (*Parkman, 4.*) Once his project was unanimously approved, messengers were sent out to secure the cooperation of more remote nations, and in a short time the confederation embraced every important tribe of Algonquian lineage, along with the Wyandot, Seneca, Winnebago, and some of those to the south. (*Parkman, 5.*)

Only a genius like Pontiac could have molded such a collection of diverse elements of savagery into a working unit. His executive ability is sufficiently proven by his creation of a regular supply department based on promissory notes—hieroglyphics carved on birch bark and signed with the otter, the totem of his tribe. His diplomatic talent appeared in his employment of two secretaries to attend to this unique correspondence, each of whom he managed to keep ignorant of the business handled by the other (*Parkman, 6*); meanwhile, his military capacity was soon to be shown in the carefully laid plan which enabled his warriors to strike a crushing blow simultaneously at every British post scattered throughout the 500 miles of wilderness from Pittsburgh to the straits of Mackinaw.

The history of this war, so eloquently told by Parkman, reads like an old romance of knighthood. The warning from the Indian girl; the coordinated attack on the garrisons; the ball game at Mackinac on the king's birthday and the massacre that followed; the siege of Fort Pitt and the heroic defense of Detroit; the bloody Battle of Bushy Run, where the painted savage retreated before the kilted Highlander, who was as brave and almost as wild; Bouquet's march into the forests of the Ohio and the submission of the defeated tribes—all these things must be passed over here. They have already been told by a master of language. But the struggle of savagery against civilization has only one ending, and the scene closes with the death of Pontiac, a broken-spirited wanderer, finally killed by a hired assassin of his own race. For this crime, the blood of entire tribes was shed in atonement. (*Parkman, 7.*)

Forty years had passed, and changes had come to the Western Territory. The Cross of Saint George <note>the British flag</note>, which had been erected in place of the lilies of France <note>the French royal standard</note>, had been replaced by the flag of the young republic. In one generation, this republic had extended its authority from the Great Lakes to the

The Canadian boundary had been established along the lakes; the Ohio country was lost to the Indians; for them, there remained only extermination or removal to the west. Their bravest warriors were slain. Their ablest chieftain, who had led them to victory against St. Clair, had yielded to the inevitable and was now regarded as having a white man's heart and being a traitor to his race. A brooding dissatisfaction settled over the tribes. Who would deliver them from the desolation that had come upon them?

Now another prophet arose among the Shawano to point out to his people the "open door" leading to happiness. In November 1805, a young man named Laulewasikaw (Lalawe'thika, a rattle or similar instrument—Gatschet), then hardly more than 30 years of age, gathered his tribesmen and their allies at their ancient capital of Wapakoneta, within the present limits of Ohio. There, he announced himself as the bearer of a new revelation from the Master of Life, who had taken pity on his red children and wished to save them from threatened destruction. He declared that he had been taken up to the spirit world and had been permitted to lift the veil of the past and the future. He claimed to have seen the misery of evildoers and learned of the happiness that awaited those who followed the precepts of the Indian god. He then began an earnest exhortation, denouncing the witchcraft practices and medicine trickery of the tribe, and solemnly warning his hearers that no one who took part in such things would ever taste future happiness. The "firewater" of the whites was poisonous and accursed; those who continued to use it would be tormented after death with all the pains of fire, while flames would continually come out of their mouths.

This idea may have been derived from the teachings of white men or from the Indian practice of torture by fire. The young must cherish and respect the aged and infirm. All property must be held in common, according to the ancient law of their ancestors. Indian women must stop intermarrying with white men; the two races were distinct and must remain so. The white man's dress, along with his flint-and-steel, must be discarded for traditional buckskin and the fire-stick. More than this, every tool and every custom derived from the whites must be cast aside, and they must return to the methods that the Master of Life had taught them. When they did all this, he promised they would again be taken into divine favor and find the happiness their fathers had known before the arrival of the whites. Finally, in proof of his divine mission, he announced that he had received the power to cure all diseases and to stop the hand of death in sickness or on the battlefield. (*Drake, Tecumseh, 1. To avoid repetition, it should be stated that, except when otherwise noted, the principal facts concerning Tecumtha and the prophet are taken from Drake's work, the most...*)

The prophet and his doctrines are also discussed at some length by Tanner, Kendall, Warren, and Catlin, as quoted hereafter, while the history of Tecumtha is a part of the history of the Ohio Valley, to be found in any work treating of that region and period.

In an account quoted by Drake, probably from an English writer, it is stated that the prophet was noted for his stupidity and intoxication until his fiftieth (?) year. One day, while lighting his pipe in his cabin, he suddenly fell back apparently lifeless and remained in that condition until his friends had assembled for his funeral. He then revived from his trance, and after quieting their alarm, announced that he had been to the spirit world and commanded them to call the people together so that he might tell them what he had seen. When they had assembled, he declared that he had been conducted to the border of the spirit world by <gloss>underlined</gloss> **two young men**, who had permitted him to look in upon its pleasures but not to enter. After charging him with the message to his people already noted, they left him, promising to visit him again in the future. (*Drake, Aboriginal Races, 1.*)

<margin>✓ 4</margin>
Although the language of this account is somewhat exaggerated, the main statements are probably correct, <gloss>underlined</gloss> **as it is in complete accordance with the Indian system by which all truth has been revealed in dreams and trances from the first dawn of tradition down to Smohalla and the messiah of the Ghost Dance.**

<margin>|</margin>
His words aroused intense excitement among his hearers, and the impression deepened as the news of the new gospel was carried from camp to camp. Those who were addicted to drunkenness—the most common sin of the Indians since their acquaintance with white people—were so thoroughly alarmed at the prospect of fiery punishment in the spirit world that for a long time intoxication became practically unknown among the western tribes. Their zeal also led to the start of a <gloss>underlined</gloss> **crusade** against all who were suspected of practicing witchcraft or magic arts; however, the prophet took advantage of this feeling to effectively rid himself of all who opposed his sacred claims. He only had to denounce a person as a witch for them to lose their reputation, if not their life.

Among the first of his victims were several Delawares—<gloss>underlined</gloss> **Tatepocoshe** (more generally known as Teteboxti), Patterson, his nephew, Coltos, an old woman, and an aged man called Joshua. These were successively marked by the prophet and doomed to be burned alive. The tragedy began with the old woman. The Indians roasted her slowly over a fire for four days, frequently calling upon her to give up her charm and medicine bag. Just as she was dying, she exclaimed that her grandson, who was then out hunting, had it in his possession. Messengers were sent after him, and when found, he was tied and brought into camp. He acknowledged that on one occasion he had borrowed his grandmother's charm, by which he had flown through the air over Kentucky to the banks of the Mississippi and back again between twilight and bedtime; but he insisted that he had returned the charm to its owner, and after some consultation, he was set free. The respect due to his white hair led his executioners to treat him with mercy. He was deliberately killed with a tomahawk by a young man, and his body was then placed upon the blazing firewood and consumed. The next day, the old preacher Joshua met a similar fate. The wife of Tatepocoshe and his nephew Billy Patterson were then brought into the council house and seated side by side. The latter had led a blameless life and died like a Christian, singing and praying amid the flames that destroyed his body. While preparations were being made for the burning of Tatepocoshe's wife, her brother—a youth of twenty years old—suddenly stood up, took her by the hand, and, to the amazement of the council, led her out of the house. He soon returned and, exclaiming, "The devil has come among us (referring to the prophet), and we are killing each other," he sat down again in the middle of the crowd. This bold step checked the wild frenzy of the Indians, put an end to these cruel scenes, and for a time greatly weakened the impostor's influence among the Delawares. (Drake, *Tecumseh*, 2.)

The prophet now changed his name to Tenskwatawa, "The Open Door" (from *skwa'te*, a door, and *the'nui*, to be open; frequently spelled *Elskwatawa*). This name was symbolic of the new way of life which he had come to show his people. He established his headquarters at Greenville, Ohio, where representatives from the various scattered tribes of the Northwest gathered around him to learn the new doctrines. Some, especially the Kickapoo, embraced his spirit fervently, while others were inclined to oppose him. The Miami, who regarded the Shawano as intruders, were jealous of his influence, and the chiefs of his own tribe were somewhat inclined to view him as a rival. To establish his sacred character and to dispel the doubts of the unbelievers, he continued to have dreams and announce wonderful revelations from time to time, until an event occurred which effectively silenced opposition and marked him as one truly inspired.

By some means, he had learned that an eclipse of the sun was to take place in the summer of 1806. As the time drew near, he called the scoffers to him and boldly announced that on a certain day he would prove his supernatural authority to them by causing the sun to go dark. When the day and hour arrived and the earth at midday was enveloped in the gloom of twilight, Tenskwatawa, standing in the midst of the terrified Indians, pointed to the sky and cried, "Did I not speak the truth? See, the sun is dark!" There were no more doubters now. Everyone proclaimed him a true prophet and the messenger of the Master of Life. His fame spread far and wide, and apostles began to carry his revelations to the most distant tribes.

We have only fragmentary information regarding the details of the doctrine and ceremonies of this religious revival, as well as of the one that preceded it. There were then no railroads, no newspaper correspondents to record each day's events, and no telegraph to flash the news across the continent before nightfall; no reservation system with its accompanying army of employees—each a spy when an emergency arose—and no investigators to go among the tribes and study the

<header>MOONEY] DISSEMINATION OF THE DOCTRINE 675</header>

The matter is best understood from an ethnological point of view. Our information is derived chiefly from military officers, who knew these events only as vague rumors of Indian unrest stirred up by British agents; from the statements of a few illiterate interpreters or captives among the Indians; and from the hazy recollections of old men long after the excitement had passed away. We know nothing of the dances that are a part of every important Indian ceremony, the songs they chanted, or the peculiar dress and adornments that likely distinguished the believers. However, we may well assume that the entire elaborate 
<margin>✓</margin>
system of Indian mythology and ceremony was utilized to give weight to the prophet's words. Enough is known to show that, in its leading features, the movement closely resembled the modern Ghost Dance.

It is impossible to know how far the prophet was responsible for the final shaping of the doctrine. Like all such movements, it undoubtedly grew and took a more definite form in the hands of the apostles who went out from the presence of its originator to preach to the various tribes. A religion that found followers from the everglades of Florida to the plains of the Saskatchewan must necessarily have undergone local modifications. By comparing various accounts, we can arrive at a general statement of the belief.

The prophet was considered to be an incarnation of Manabozho, the great "first doer" of the Algonquian tradition. His words were believed to be the direct utterances of a deity. Manabozho had taught his people certain ways of living best suited to their condition and capacity. 
<margin>+</margin>
A new race had come upon them, and the Indians had discarded their primitive purity of life to adopt the innovations of the whites. These changes had now brought them to degradation and misery, threatening them with swift and total destruction. To punish them for their disobedience and bring them back to their duty, Manabozho had called the wild game from the forests and sealed it away under the earth; as a result, the tribes were now on the verge of starvation and forced to eat the meat of filthy hogs. They had also lost their former love for one another and had become addicted to the secret practices of poisoners and wizards, along with the offensive ceremonies of the calumet dance. They were now told to set aside all these things, throw away the weapons and clothing of the white man, pluck out their hair as in ancient times, wear eagle feathers on their heads, and clothe themselves again in breechcloths and the skins of animals slain with the bows and arrows that Manabozho had given them. (*Kendall, 1.*) They had to abandon the white man's flint-and-steel and cook their food over a fire made by rubbing two sticks together. This fire was to be kept burning constantly in their lodges as a symbol of eternal life, and their care for it was evidence that they heeded divine commands. Alcohol was to be given up forever, along with medicine bags, poisons, and the wicked sorcery that had corrupted the ancient traditions.

<summary>This page describes the lack of detailed historical records regarding the Prophet's ceremonies while outlining the core tenets of his doctrine, which called for a return to traditional Indian life and the rejection of white influence. The doctrine identified the Prophet as an incarnation of Manabozho and demanded a revival of ancient customs to restore the favor of the divine.</summary>

purity of the Midé rites. Instead of these, the prophet gave them new songs and new medicines. Their women had to stop having any relationships with white men. They were to love one another and end their constant wars, be kind to their children, keep only one dog per family, and avoid lying and stealing. If they would listen to his voice and follow his instructions, the incarnate <term>Manabozho</term> promised that at the end of four years (meaning in 1811) he would bring two days of darkness. During this time, he would travel invisibly throughout the land and cause the animals he had created to emerge from the earth once more. (*Kendall, 2.*) They were also promised that their deceased friends would be returned to them.

The ideas regarding the catastrophe that was to start the new era seem to have varied according to those who interpreted the belief. Among the Ottawa, and perhaps among the lake tribes in general, there was to be a period of darkness, as already mentioned. Among the Cherokee, and likely also among the Creek, it was believed that there would be a terrible hailstorm. This storm would destroy both the white people and the non-believers of the Indian race, while the chosen followers would be warned in time to save themselves by fleeing to the high mountain peaks. The idea of any hostile alliance against the white race seems to have been no part of the doctrine. In the north, however, there is always a clear prejudice against the Americans. The Great Father, through his prophet, is depicted as declaring himself to be the common parent of Indians, English, French, and Spaniards alike; while the Americans, on the contrary, “are not my children, but the children of the evil spirit. They grew from the scum of the great water when it was stirred by an evil spirit, and the foam was driven into the woods by a strong east wind. They are numerous, but I hate them. They are unjust; they have taken away your lands, which were not made for them.” (*Kendall, 3.*)

From the respected James Wafford of the Cherokee nation, the author obtained some interesting details in 1891 regarding the excitement among the Cherokee. According to his statement, the doctrine first reached them through the Creek around 1812 or 1813. It was likely shared with the Creek by <term>Tecumtha</term> and his group during their visit to that tribe in the fall of 1811, as will be described later. The Creek were taught by their prophets that the old Indian way of life was soon to return, when “instead of beef and bacon, they would have venison, and instead of chickens, they would have turkeys.” Great sacred dances were established, and the people were urged to be ready for what was coming. From the south, the movement spread to the Cherokee, and one of their priests, living in what is now northern Georgia, began to preach that on a day soon to come, there would be a terrible storm with a mighty wind and hailstones as large as hominy mortars. This storm would wipe from the face of the earth everyone except the true believers who had already taken refuge on the highest summits of the Great Smoky [Mountains]

Full of this belief, many members of the tribe in Alabama and Georgia abandoned their beehives, their orchards, their slaves, and everything else they might have acquired through the white man. Despite the pleas and protests of friends who had no faith in the prediction, they began their difficult journey toward the mountains of North Carolina. Wafford, who was about 10 years old at the time, lived with his mother and stepfather on the Valley River and vividly remembers the groups of pilgrims with their packs on their backs, fleeing from the lower country to escape the coming destruction. Many of them stopped at the house of his stepfather, who, being a white man, was somewhat better prepared than his neighbors to host travelers. He took the opportunity to try to convince them to turn back, telling them that their hopes and fears alike were unfounded. Some listened to him and returned to their homes, but others went on and climbed the mountain, where they waited until the appointed day arrived, only to find themselves disappointed. Slowly and sadly, they picked up their packs once more and turned back toward home, dreading the ridicule they were sure to meet there, yet still believing in their hearts that the glorious arrival was only postponed for a time. This excitement among the Cherokee is noted at some length in the *Cherokee Advocate* of November 16, 1844, published at Tahlequah, in the Cherokee Nation. Among the Creek, the excitement—intensified by reports of the struggle currently occurring in the north and fostered and encouraged by agents of Spain and England—grew and spread until it resulted in the terrible Creek War in the summer of 1813.

<margin><unclear>See Dan</unclear></margin>
Enough is known of the ceremonies of this religion to show that it must have had an elaborate ritual. We learn from Warren that the followers of the prophet were accustomed to perform certain ceremonies in solemn councils, and that, after he had forbidden the corrupt secret rites, he introduced new medicines and songs instead. At the ancient capital of the Ojibwa on Lake Superior, the Indians gathered in great numbers and performed these dances and ceremonies day and night. (*Warren, 1.*) They were also instructed to dance naked, with their bodies painted and with war clubs in their hands. (*Kendall, 4.*) The solemn rite of confirmation, known as “shaking hands with the prophet,” was particularly impressive. From the narrative of John Tanner—a white man captured as a child from his home in Kentucky and raised among the wild Ojibwa—we get the best contemporary account of the arrival of the new doctrine in the north and its effect on the Great Lakes tribes. He says:

> It was while I was living here at Great Wood River that news arrived of a great man among the Shawnee who had been favored by a revelation of the mind and will of the Great Spirit. I was hunting on the prairie, at a great distance from my lodge, when I saw a stranger approaching. At first, I was worried about an enemy, but as he drew nearer, his dress showed him to be an Ojibwa; however, when he reached me, there was something very strange and peculiar in his manner. He indicated to me that I must go home, but gave no explanation of the cause. He refused to look at

"From now on," said he, "the fire must never be allowed to go out in your lodge. Summer and winter, day and night, in the storm, or when it is calm, you must remember that the life in your body and the fire in your lodge are <margin>$\checkmark$</margin>the same and of the same age. If you allow your fire to be extinguished, at that moment your life will end. You must not allow a dog to live; you must never strike a man, a woman, a child, or a dog. The prophet himself is coming to shake hands with you; but I have come ahead of him so that you may know the will of the Great Spirit, as communicated to us by him, and to inform you that the preservation of your life, for even a single moment, depends on your complete obedience. From this time forward we are not to get drunk, steal, lie, or go against our enemies. While we yield complete obedience to these commands of the Great Spirit, the Sioux, even if they come to our country, will not be able to see us; we shall be protected and made happy." I listened to all he had to say, but I told him in response that I could not believe we would all die if our fire went out; furthermore, in many cases, it would be difficult to avoid punishing our children; our dogs were useful in helping us hunt and catch animals, so I could not believe the Great Spirit had any desire to take them from us. He continued talking to us until late at night; then he lay down to sleep in my lodge. I happened to wake first in the morning, and, seeing that the fire had gone out, I called him to get up and see how many of us were alive and how many were dead. He was prepared for the ridicule I attempted to cast on his doctrine, and told me that I had not yet shaken hands with the prophet. His visit was meant to prepare me for this important event and to make me aware of the obligations and risks I would incur by entering into the agreement implied by taking the prophet's message into my hand. I did not feel entirely at ease in my unbelief. The Indians, generally, received this man's doctrine with great humility and fear. Distress and anxiety were visible on every face. Many killed their dogs and endeavored to practice obedience to all the commands of this new preacher, who remained among us. But, as was usual for me in any emergency of this kind, I went to the traders, firmly believing that if the Deity had any communications to make to men, they would be given first to white men. The traders ridiculed and despised the idea of a new revelation of the Divine will, and the thought that it should be given to a poor Shawnee. Thus, I was confirmed in my disbelief. Nevertheless, I did not openly declare my unbelief to the Indians; I only refused to kill my dogs and showed no great desire to comply with his other requirements. As long as I remained among the Indians, I made it my business to conform to all their customs, so far as it seemed consistent with my immediate convenience and comfort. I have adopted many of their ideas, but I always found among them opinions that I could not hold. The Ojibwa whom I mentioned remained for some time among the Indians in my neighborhood and gained the attention of the leading men so effectively that a time was appointed and a lodge prepared for the solemn and public adoption of the prophet's doctrines. Four strings of moldy and discolored beans were the only remaining visible symbols of this important mission. After a long speech in which the main features of the new revelation were stated and urged upon everyone's attention, the four strings of beans—which we were told were made of the very flesh of the prophet—were carried with great solemnity to each man in the lodge. We had now been gathered in large numbers for some time. Great agitation and terror had prevailed among us, and now famine began to be felt. The faces of men wore an aspect of unusual gloom; the active became idle, and the spirits of the bravest seemed to be subdued. I went out to hunt with my dogs, which I had constantly refused to kill or allow to be killed. With their help, I found and killed a bear. Upon returning home, I said to some of the Indians, "Has the Great Spirit not given us our dogs to help us in obtaining what is necessary to support our lives? Can you believe he now wishes to deprive us of their service? The prophet, we are told, has forbidden us from allowing our fires to be extinguished in our lodges; and when we travel or hunt, he will not allow us to use a flint and steel, and we are told he requires that no man should give fire to another. Is it pleasing to the Great Spirit that we should lie in our hunting camps without fire, or is it more agreeable to him that we should make fire by rubbing two sticks together rather than with a flint and a piece of steel?" But they would not listen to me; and the intense fervor that prevailed among them affected me so much that I threw away my flint and steel, laid aside my medicine bag, and, in many details, complied with the new doctrines; but I would not kill my dogs. I soon learned to light a fire by rubbing dry cedar, which I was careful to carry with me always, but stopping the use of flint and steel caused many of the Indians much inconvenience and suffering. The influence of the Shawnee Prophet was very clearly and painfully felt by the most distant Ojibbeways of whom I had any knowledge, but it was not the general impression among them that his doctrines had any tendency to unite them for any human purpose. For two or three years, drunkenness was much less frequent than before, war was less thought of, and the entire state of affairs among them was somewhat changed by the influence of one man. But gradually the impression was erased; medicine bags, flints, and steels were used again; dogs were raised, women and children were beaten as before, and the Shawnee Prophet was despised. Today, he is looked upon by the Indians as an impostor and a bad man. (*Tanner, 1.*)

<margin>✓</margin>
Tanner’s account is confirmed by Warren, based on the statements of old men among the Ojibwa who had taken part in the revival. According to their story, the messengers of the new revelation appeared at the
<margin>✓</margin>
different villages, acting strangely and with their faces painted black—perhaps to signify their status as messengers from the world of the dead. They told the people that they must light a fire with two dry sticks in each of their principal settlements, and that this fire must always be kept sacred and burning. They predicted the speedy return of the old Indian life and asserted that the prophet would cause the dead to rise from the grave. The new belief took sudden and complete possession of the minds of the Ojibwa and spread “like wildfire” from one end of their vast territory to the other, even reaching the remote northern tribes allied with the Cree and Asiniboin. The strongest evidence of their absolute obedience to the new revelation was shown by their compliance with the command to throw away their medicine bags—the one item that every Indian considers most sacred. It is said that the shores of Lake Superior, near the great village of Shagawaumikong (Bayfield, Wisconsin), were covered with these medicine bags, which had been thrown into the water. <margin>Start of the revolt</margin>
The Ojibwa tribe gathered in great numbers to dance the dances and sing the songs of the new ritual, until a message was received from the prophet inviting them to come to him at Detroit, where he would explain in person the will of the Master of Life. This was in 1808. The excitement was now at fever heat, and it was determined to go in a body to Detroit. It is said that 150 canoe-loads of Ojibwa actually started on this pilgrimage, and one family even brought with them a dead child to be restored to life by the prophet. They had proceeded a considerable distance when they were met by an influential French trader, who reported, on the word of some who had already visited the prophet’s camp and returned, that the devotees were on the brink of starvation—which was true, as the great multitude had consumed their entire supply of provisions, and had been so occupied with religious ceremonies that they had neglected to plant their corn. It was also asserted that during the prophet’s frequent periods of absence from the camp, when he would disappear for several days, claiming on his return that he had been to the spirit world in conversation with the Master of Life, that he was really concealed in a hollow log in the woods. This is quite probable, and entirely consistent with the Indian theory of trances and soul pilgrimages while the body remains unconscious in one spot. These reports, however, put such a damper on the ardor of the Ojibwa that they returned to their homes and gradually ceased to think about the new revelation. As time went on a reaction set in, and those who had been most active evangelists of the doctrine among the tribe became most anxious to efface the remembrance of it. One good, however, resulted to the Ojibwa from the throwing away of the poisonous compounds formerly in common use by the lower order of doctors, and secret poisoning became almost unknown. (*Warren, 2.*)

<margin>*</margin>
When the celebrated traveler Catlin went among the prairie tribes some thirty years later, he found that the prophet’s emissaries—he says the prophet himself, which is certainly a mistake—had carried the living fire, the sacred image, and the mystic strings (see portrait and description) even to the Blackfeet on the plains of the Saskatchewan, going without hindrance among warring tribes where the name of the Shawano had never been spoken, protected only by the reverence that attached to their priestly character. There seems no doubt that by this time they had developed the plan of a confederacy for driving back the whites, and Catlin asserts that thousands of warriors among those remote tribes had pledged themselves to fight under the lead of Tecumtha at the proper time. His account of the prophet’s methods in the extreme northwest agrees with what Tanner has reported from the Ojibwa country. (*Catlin, 1.*) But disaster followed him like a shadow. Rivals, jealous of his success, came after him to denounce his plans as visionary and himself as an impostor. The ambassadors were obliged to turn back to save their lives and retrace their way in haste to the far distant Wabash, where the fatal battle of Tippecanoe and the death of his great brother, Tecumtha, put an end to all his splendid dreams.

Despite initial fervor and plans for a pan-Indian confederacy, the movement collapsed due to internal skepticism, starvation, and the defeat at the Battle of Tippecanoe.</summary>
