<page-num>681</page-num>

# CHAPTER IV

## TECUMTHA AND TIPPECANOE

> These lands are ours. No one has a right to remove us, because we were the first owners. — *Tecumtha to Wells, 1807.*

> The Great Spirit gave this great island to his red children. He placed the whites on the other side of the big water. They were not contented with their own, but came to take ours from us. They have driven us from the sea to the lakes—we can go no farther. — *Tecumtha, 1810.*

> The President may sit still in his town and drink his wine, while you and I will have to fight it out. — *Tecumtha to Harrison, 1810.*

And now we begin to hear of the prophet's brother, Tecumtha, the most heroic character in Native American history. Tecumtha, "The Meteor," was the son of a chief and the worthy descendant of a warrior race. His tribe, the Shawano, made it their proud boast that they, of all tribes, had offered the most determined resistance to the encroachments of the whites. His father had fallen under the bullets of the Virginians while leading his warriors at the bloody battle of Point Pleasant in 1774. His eldest and dearest brother had lost his life in an attack on a southern frontier post, and another had been killed fighting by his side at Wayne's victory in 1794. It is no wonder that the young Tecumtha declared that his flesh crawled at the sight of a white man!

But his was no mean spirit of personal revenge; his mind was too noble for that. He hated the whites as the destroyers of his race, but prisoners and the defenseless knew well that they could rely on his honor and humanity and were safe under his protection. When he was only a boy—for his military career began in childhood—he had witnessed the burning of a prisoner, and the spectacle was so abhorrent to his feelings that by an earnest and eloquent speech, he induced the party to give up the practice forever. In later years, his name was accepted by helpless women and children as a guarantee of protection even in the midst of hostile Indians. Of commanding figure, nearly six feet in height and compactly built; of dignified bearing and piercing eye, before whose lightning even a British general flinched; with the fiery eloquence of a Clay and the clear-cut logic of a Webster; temperate in habit, charitable in thought and action, brave as a lion, but humane and generous nonetheless—in a word, an Indigenous American knight—his life was given to his people. He fell at last, like his father and his brothers before him, in battle with the destroyers of his nation, the champion of a lost cause and a dying race.

His name has been translated as "The Shooting Star" and "The Panther Crouching, or Lying in Wait." From a reply to a letter of inquiry

Shawano personal names are nearly all clan names, and by their interpretation, the clan to which the individual or his father or mother belongs may be discovered. Thus, when a man is called "tight fitting" or "good fit," he is of the *Rabbit* clan, because the fur fits the rabbit very tightly and closely. The name of Tecumtha is

This indicates that the one so named belongs to the clan of the round-foot or claw-foot animals, such as the panther, lion, or even raccoon. Tecumtha and his brother belonged to the clan of the <term>manetuwi msipessi</term> or "miraculous panther" (<term>msi</term>, great, big; <term>pishiwi</term>, abbreviated <term>pessi</term>, cat; both combined meaning the American lion). So the translations "panther lying in wait," or "crouching lion," give only the sense of the name, and no animal is actually named in it. But the <term>msi-pessi</term>, when the epithet miraculous (<term>manetuwi</term>) is added to it, means a "celestial tiger," that is, a meteor or shooting star. ### EXPLANATION OF FIGURE 58

This portrait is a copy of the one provided by Lossing in his *American Revolution and the War of 1812*, volume III (1875), page 283. He quotes a description of Tecumtha's personal appearance by a British officer who saw him in 1812, and then continues to give the history of the portrait.

> "Captain J. B. Glegg, Brock's aide-de-camp, has recorded the following description of Tecumtha at that interview: 'Tecumseh's appearance was very prepossessing; his figure was light and finely proportioned; I imagined his age to be about thirty-five <note>he was about forty</note>; in height, 5 feet 9 or 10 inches; his complexion was light copper; his face was oval, with bright hazel eyes, showing cheerfulness, energy, and determination. Three small silver crosses or coronets were suspended from the lower cartilage of his aquiline nose, and a large silver medallion of George III—which I believe his ancestor had received from Lord Dorchester when he was Governor-General of Canada—was attached to a multicolored wampum string and hung around his neck. His dress consisted of a plain, neat uniform: a tanned deerskin jacket with long trousers of the same material, the seams of both being covered with neatly cut fringe, and he wore on his feet leather moccasins, highly ornamented with work made from the dyed quills of the porcupine.' The portrait of Tecumtha provided above is from a pencil sketch by Pierre Le Dru. . . . In this, I have included only the head by Le Dru. The cap was red, and in front was a single black eagle's feather with a white tip. The sketch of his dress (and the medal described above), in which he appears as a brigadier-general of the British army, is from a rough drawing that I saw in Montreal in the summer of 1858. It was made at Malden soon after the surrender of Detroit, where the Indians celebrated that event with a grand feast. It was only on festive occasions that Tecumtha was seen in full dress. The sketch did not claim to give a true likeness of the chief and was valuable only as a depiction of his costume. From these two sources, we are able to provide a fairly faithful picture of the great Shawnee warrior and statesman as he appeared in his best mood. When in full dress, he wore a cocked hat and plume, but he would not give up his blue breechcloth, red leggings fringed with buckskin, and buckskin moccasins."

<header>MOONEY] TECUMTHA AT GREENVILLE</header>

animal, but as a shooting star that was larger than other shooting stars. This legendary creature gave its name to a Shawano clan, and this clan—to which Tecumtha belonged—was also categorized among the claw-footed animals. The rapid motion of the shooting star was rightly compared to that of a tiger or wildcat pouncing on its prey. Throughout America, shooting stars are believed to be the souls of great men. The home of the dead is always in the west, where the celestial bodies set; because meteors travel westward, they were thought to be returning to their western home.

Tecumtha was now in the prime of his life, being about 40 years old. He had already devised his plan to unite all the tribes into one great confederation to resist the further expansion of the whites. This was based on the principle that the Indians shared common interests and that what affected one tribe affected all. Since the tribes were constantly moving to follow migrating game, he argued that no single tribe held more than a right of possession to the land while they actually occupied it. He maintained that for any land sale to be valid, it had to be approved by all the tribes involved. His claim was certainly based on justice, but the government refused to acknowledge the principle in theory, even though they repeatedly acted on it in practice. Every important treaty made afterward in the Mississippi Valley was a joint treaty, as it proved impossible to assign the ownership of any large area to a single tribe. The Shawano themselves hunted from the Cumberland to the Susquehanna. As a fundamental premise, Tecumtha claimed that the Treaty of Greenville was invalid because it had been forced upon the Indians. He argued that the only legitimate boundary was the Ohio River, as established in 1768, and that all future land cessions must have the approval of all the tribes claiming rights in that region.

By this time, hundreds of Indians had gathered at Greenville to listen to the Prophet's teachings. They represented all the widespread tribes of the Great Lakes region and the great Northwest, and they were all highly excited by the prospect of reviving the traditional Indian way of life and preserving native sovereignty. This was Tecumtha's opportunity, and he was quick to take advantage of it. Even those who were skeptical of the spiritual revelations could see the danger posed by the continued expansion of the white settlers. They were easily convinced that their safety required them to unite as one people to protect a common boundary. The pilgrims carried these ideas back to their various tribes, and so what began as a simple religious revival soon turned into political activism. Both movements were equally patriotic from the Indian perspective, and under the circumstances, one was almost the natural complement of the other. All evidence suggests that the movement was purely religious and peaceful at its start; however, Tecumtha’s military spirit later gave it a warlike and even aggressive character. From then on, the Prophet's messengers also became recruiting agents for his brother. Tecumtha himself was too practical to think that the whites would be destroyed by divine intervention or that they could be driven out by any Indian alliance alone, but he did believe it was possible

...that the westward advance of the Americans could be stopped at the Ohio River, leaving his people in undisturbed possession of what lay beyond. In this hope, he was encouraged by British officials in Canada, and it is doubtful whether the movement would ever have become so formidable if it had not been incited and assisted from across the border.

In the spring of 1807, it was estimated that fifteen hundred Indians had recently passed Fort Wayne on their way to visit the Prophet, while councils were constantly being held and messengers were traveling from tribe to tribe with pipes and belts of wampum. It was plain that some unusual movement was occurring among them, and it was also evident that British agents were involved in maintaining the excitement. The government became alarmed, and the crisis arrived when an order was sent from the President to Tecumtha at Greenville to move his party beyond the 1795 boundary (the Treaty of Greenville).

Trembling with excitement, Tecumtha rose and addressed his followers in a passionate speech, dwelling on the wrongs done to the Indians and the continued encroachments of the white settlers. Then, turning to the messenger, he said:

> “These lands are ours. No one has a right to remove us, because we were the first owners. The Great Spirit above has appointed this place for us on which to light our fires, and here we will remain. As for boundaries, the Great Spirit above knows no boundaries, nor will his red children acknowledge any.” (Drake, *Tecumseh*, 3.)

<margin>x</margin>
From this time on, it was understood that the Indians were preparing to make a final stand for the Ohio Valley. The Prophet continued to arouse their enthusiasm with his inspired utterances, while Tecumtha became the general and active organizer of the warriors. At a conference with the governor of Ohio in the autumn of 1807, he fearlessly denied the validity of previous treaties and declared his intention to resist the further extension of white settlements on Indian lands.

The following spring, large numbers of Indians came down from the lakes to visit Tecumtha and his brother. Finding their following increasing so rapidly, they accepted an invitation from the Potawatomi and Kickapoo and moved their headquarters to a more central location on the Wabash River. The Delaware and Miami, who claimed precedence in that region and who had opposed the Prophet and Tecumtha all along, protested against this move, but to no effect. The new settlement, which was on the western bank of the river just below the mouth of the Tippecanoe, was known to the Indians as Kehtipaquononk, “the great clearing,” and was an old and favorite location for them. It had been the site of a large Shawano village that had been destroyed by the Americans in 1791, and some years later the Potawatomi had rebuilt upon the same place, to which they now invited the disciples of the new religion. The white settlers had corrupted the name to Tippecanoe, and it now generally became known as the Prophet’s Town.

Nothing else of importance occurred during this year, but it was learned that Tecumtha contemplated visiting the southern tribes in the near

future to enlist them in his confederacy as well. In 1809, however, rumors of an approaching conflict began to spread, and it was evident that the British were inciting the Indians to hostility in anticipation of a war between England and the United States. Just at this moment, the anger of Tecumtha's party was further inflamed by the negotiation of treaties with four tribes in which additional large areas of land were surrendered in Indiana and Illinois. The Indians now refused to buy ammunition from American traders, saying that they could obtain all they needed for free from another source. In view of the signs of increasing hostility, Governor Harrison was authorized to take any steps necessary to protect the frontier. Tecumtha had now won over the Wyandot, the most influential tribe of the Ohio region, who were the keepers of the great wampum belt of union and the lighters of the council fire of the allied tribes. Their example was quickly followed by the Miami, whose support made the tribes of the Ohio and the Great Lakes practically unanimous. The Prophet now declared that he would follow in the footsteps of Pontiac, and he called on distant tribes to assist those on the border to push back the tide that would otherwise overwhelm them all. In response, the Sauk and Fox sent word that they were ready whenever he gave the command.

In the summer of 1810, according to a previous arrangement, Tecumtha, accompanied by several hundred warriors, traveled down the river to Vincennes to confer with Governor Harrison about the situation. The conference began on the 15th of August and lasted three days. Tecumtha repeated his previous claims, saying that by uniting the tribes he was trying to dam the mighty flood that was ready to overwhelm his people. The Americans had driven the Indians from the sea and threatened to push them into the Great Lakes; and, although he denied any intention of making war against the United States, he declared his firm resolution to insist on the old boundary, to oppose further intrusion by whites on Indian lands, and to resist the survey of the lands recently surrendered. He was followed by chiefs of five different tribes, each of whom in turn declared that he would support Tecumtha’s principles. Harrison replied that the government would never admit that any region belonged to all the Indians in common, and that, having purchased the surrendered lands from the tribes who were first found in possession of them, it would defend its title by force of arms. To this, Tecumtha said that he preferred to be on the side of the Americans, and that if his terms were granted, he would bring his forces to aid the United States in the war which he knew would soon break out with England; otherwise, he would be forced to join the British. The governor replied that he would present the case to the President, but that it was completely unlikely he would agree to the conditions. Recognizing the inevitable, Tecumtha expressed the hope that, as the President was to decide the matter, the Great Spirit would put sense into his head to persuade him to give up the lands, adding,

To this he readily agreed, and the promise was faithfully kept. (*Drake, Tecumseh, 4.*)

The conference had ended with a silent understanding that war was inevitable, and both sides began to prepare for the struggle. Soon after, it was learned that the Prophet had sent belts to the tribes west of the Mississippi, inviting them to join in a war against the United States. Outrages committed against the Indians by settlers intensified the hostile feeling, and the Delawares refused to hand over a murderer until some of the white people who had killed their people were first punished. Harrison himself states that the Indians could rarely obtain justice for even the most unprovoked wrongs. In another letter he says that Tecumtha "has taken the celebrated Pontiac as his model, and I am convinced he will compare favorably in every respect with that far-famed warrior."

In July 1811, Tecumtha visited Harrison again at Vincennes. In the course of his talk, he said that the white people were unnecessarily alarmed, as the Indians were only following the example set for them by the colonies in uniting for the promotion of common interests. He added that he was now on his way to the southern tribes to obtain their support for the league as well, and that on his return in the spring he intended to visit the President to explain his purposes fully and to clear away all difficulties. In the meantime, he expected that a large number of Indians would join his colony on the Wabash during the winter; to avoid any danger of conflict between them and the whites, he requested that no settlements be made on the disputed lands until he had an opportunity to see the President. To this Harrison replied that the President would never give up a country which he had bought from its rightful owners, nor would he allow his people to be harmed with impunity. This concluded the interview, and the next day Tecumtha started with his party for the south to visit the Creek and Choctaw. Around the same time, it was learned that the British had sent a message to the Prophet, telling him that the time had now come for him to take up the hatchet, and inviting him to send a party to their headquarters at Malden (now Amherstburg, Ontario) to receive the necessary supplies. In view of these things, Harrison suggested to the War Department that they take the opportunity of Tecumtha's absence in the south to strike a blow against his confederacy. Continuing in the same letter, he says of the great Indian leader:

> The absolute obedience and respect which the followers of Tecumseh show to him is really astonishing, and more than any other circumstance proves him to be one of

...those rare geniuses who arise occasionally to cause revolutions and overturn the established order of things. If it were not for the nearby presence of the United States, he would perhaps be the founder of an empire that would rival Mexico or Peru in glory. No difficulties deter him. For four years he has been in constant motion. You see him today on the Wabash, and in a short time hear of him on the shores of Lake Erie or Michigan or on the banks of the Mississippi; and wherever he goes, he makes an impression favorable to his purposes. He is now on his final tour, to put a finishing touch to his work. I hope, however, before his return that the part of the structure which he considered complete will be demolished, and even its foundations rooted up. (*Drake, Tecumseh, 5.*)

On this trip Tecumtha went as far as Florida and recruited the Seminole for his confederacy. Then, retracing his steps into Alabama, he came to the ancient Creek town of Tukabachi, on the Tallapoosa, near the present site of Montgomery. What happened here is best told in the words of McKenney and Hall, who derived their information from Indians at the same town a few years later:

<margin>?</margin>
> He made his way to the lodge of the chief called the Big Warrior. He explained his object, delivered his war speech, presented a bundle of sticks, gave a piece of wampum and a war hatchet—all of which the Big Warrior took—when Tecumthé, reading the spirit and intentions of the Big Warrior, looked him in the eye and, pointing his finger toward his face, said: “Your blood is white. You have accepted my message, and the sticks, and the wampum, and the hatchet, but you do not mean to fight. I know the reason. You do not believe the Great Spirit has sent me. You shall know. I am leaving Tuckhabatchee immediately and shall go straight to Detroit. When I arrive there, I will stamp on the ground with my foot and shake down every house in Tuckhabatchee.” So saying, he turned and left the Big Warrior in utter amazement at both his manner and his threat, and continued his journey. The Indians were no less struck by his conduct than was the Big Warrior, and began to dread the arrival of the day when the threatened calamity would befall them. They met often and talked over this matter, and counted the days carefully to know the day when Tecumthé would reach Detroit. The morning they had designated as the day of his arrival finally came. A mighty rumbling was heard—the Indians all ran out of their houses—the earth began to shake; when at last, sure enough, every house in Tuckhabatchee was shaken down. The cry was on every lip, “Tecumthé has reached Detroit!” The effect was electric. The message he had delivered to the Big Warrior was believed, and many of the Indians took their rifles and prepared for the war. The reader will not be surprised to learn that an earthquake had produced all this; but he will be, undoubtedly, that it should happen on the very day on which Tecumthé arrived at Detroit, and in exact fulfillment of his threat. <margin>|</margin>It was the famous New Madrid earthquake on the Mississippi. (*McKenney and Hall, 1.*)

The fire thus kindled among the Creek by Tecumtha was fanned into a blaze by the British and Spanish traders until the opening of the War of 1812 provided the opportunity for the terrible outbreak known in history as the Creek War.

<margin>7.</margin>Prophet himself announced that he had now taken up the tomahawk against the United States and would only lay it down with his life, unless the wrongs against the Indians were corrected. Harrison now decided to break up the Prophet’s camp. Accordingly, at the head of about 900 men, including about 250 regular soldiers, he marched from Vincennes, and on November 5, 1811, set up camp within a few miles of the Prophet’s town. The Indians had fortified the place with great care and effort. It was sacred to them as the spot where the rituals of the new religion had been performed for so long, and through these rituals, they believed it had been made unconquerable by the attacks of the white man. The next day, he approached even closer and was met by messengers from the town, who stated that the Prophet was anxious to avoid war and had already sent a peaceful message through several chiefs, who had unfortunately gone down the other side of the river and so had failed to find the general. A truce was therefore agreed upon until the next day, when peace terms were to be negotiated between the governor and the chiefs. The army set up camp on a spot pointed out by the Indians: a high piece of ground rising out of a marshy prairie, within a mile of the town. Although Harrison did not believe the Indians would attack at night, as a precaution, he had the troops sleep with their weapons ready in battle formation.

At 4 o'clock on the morning of the 7th, Governor Harrison, as was his custom, had risen to prepare for waking the troops. While putting on his boots by the fire, he was talking with General Wells, Colonel Owen, and Majors Taylor and Hurst. The drummer had been awakened to give the signal for the troops to assemble, when the Indian attack suddenly began on the left side of the camp. The entire army was immediately on its feet, the campfires were put out, and the governor mounted his horse and headed toward the point of attack. Several companies had taken their positions in line within forty seconds of the first gunshot, and all the troops were ready for action in the course

<header>MOONEY] THE BATTLE OF PROPHET'S TOWN</header>

within two minutes—a fact as much a credit to their own activity and bravery as to the skill and bravery of their officers. The battle soon became general and was maintained on both sides with remarkable and even desperate courage. The Indians advanced and retreated with the aid of a rattling noise made with deer hooves, and they persisted in their treacherous attack with an apparent determination to conquer or die on the spot. The battle raged with unabated fury and mutual slaughter until daylight, when a brave and successful charge by our troops drove the enemy into the swamp and put an end to the conflict.

Prior to the assault, the Prophet had given assurances to his followers that in the coming contest, the Great Spirit would make the weapons of the Americans ineffective; that their bullets would fall harmlessly at the feet of the Indians; and that the latter would have light in abundance, while the former would be shrouded in thick darkness. Taking advantage of the privilege granted by his unique office—and perhaps unwilling to personally witness the competing powers of a false prophecy and a real American bullet—he prudently took a position on a nearby hill. When the action began, he started performing certain mystical rituals, while at the same time singing a war song. In the course of the engagement, he was informed that his men were falling. He told them to fight on—it would soon be as he had predicted. And then, in louder and wilder tones, his inspiring battle song was heard mixing with the sharp crack of the rifle and the shrill war cry of his brave but deceived followers. (Drake, *Tecumseh*, 6.)

<margin>X</margin>
Drake estimates the total number of Indians involved in the battle at between 800 and 1,000, representing all the major tribes of the region, and places the number of killed at probably no less than 50, with an unusually large proportion of wounded. Harrison’s estimate would seem to place the numbers much higher. The Americans lost 60 killed or mortally wounded, and 188 in all. (Drake, *Tecumseh*, 7.) In their hurried retreat, the Indians left a large number of dead on the field. Believing the word of the Prophet that they would receive supernatural aid from above, they had fought with desperate bravery, and their defeat completely disheartened them. They at once abandoned their town and dispersed, each returning to his own tribe. Tecumtha’s great structure<gloss>12</gloss> was indeed demolished, and even its foundations<gloss>13</gloss> were torn up.

The night before the engagement, the Prophet had performed some spiritual rituals, by which he had assured his followers that half of the soldiers were already dead and the other half were deprived of their senses, so that the Indians would have little to do but rush into their camp and finish them with the hatchet.<gloss>14</gloss> The result infuriated the warriors. They refused to listen to the excuses that are always ready on the tongue of the unsuccessful medicine man; they denounced him as a liar and even threatened him with death. Deserted by all but a few of his own tribe and turned away from several villages where he sought help, he finally found refuge among a small band of Wyandot. However, his influence and his sacred status were gone forever, and he lived out his remaining days in the shadows of obscurity.

<margin>|</margin>
From the south, Tecumtha returned through Missouri, Iowa, and Illinois, gaining additions to his cause everywhere, but he reached the Wabash at last, just a few days after the battle, only to find his followers scattered to the four winds, his brother a refugee, and the great

# 690 THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14

The goal of his life—a confederation of all the tribes—was ruined. His grief and disappointment were bitter. He reproached his brother in severe terms for disobeying his instructions to maintain peace in his absence. When the prophet attempted to reply, it is said that Tecumtha so far forgot his dignity that he seized his brother by the hair and gave him a violent shaking, threatening to kill him.

Early in 1812, Tecumtha sent a message to Governor Harrison, informing him of his return from the south and stating that he was now ready for the proposed visit to the President. To this, Harrison replied by giving his permission, but refusing to allow any group to accompany him. This condition did not please the great leader, who had been accustomed to the attendance of a retinue of warriors wherever he went. He declined the terms, and thus ended his interactions with the governor. In June 1812, he visited the agent at Fort Wayne and there reaffirmed the justice of his position regarding the ownership of the Indian lands. He again denied having had any intention of making war against the United States and reproached Harrison for marching against his people in his absence. In return, the agent tried to persuade him to join forces with the United States in the upcoming conflict with England. 

<margin>/</margin>
“Tecumtha listened with cold indifference, made a few general remarks in reply, and then with an arrogant air left the council house and took his departure for Malden, where he joined the British forces.” (Drake, *Tecumseh*, 8.) His later career is a part of the history of the War of 1812.

The United States made a formal declaration of war against Great Britain on June 18, 1812. Tecumtha was already at Malden, the British headquarters on the Canadian side. When invited by some friendly Indians to attend a council near Detroit to make arrangements for remaining neutral, he sent back word that he had taken sides with the king, and that his bones would bleach on the Canadian shore before he would cross the river again to join in any council of neutrality. A few days later, he led his Indians into battle on the British side. For his services at Maguaga, he was soon afterward officially commissioned as a brigadier general in the British army.

We skip over the numerous events of this war—Maguaga, the Raisin, Fort Meigs, Perry’s victory—as they are beyond the focus of our story, and come to the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813, the last ever fought by Tecumtha. After Perry’s decisive victory on the lake, Proctor hastily prepared to retreat into the interior, despite the earnest protests of Tecumtha, who accused him of cowardice—an accusation that the British general did not dare to challenge. The retreat began with Harrison in close pursuit until the British and Indians reached a spot on the north bank of the Thames, near present-day Chatham, Ontario. Here, finding the ground favorable for defense, Tecumtha resolved to retreat no further and essentially forced Proctor to stand and fight. The Indian leader had no hope of

triumph in the outcome. His sun had gone down, and he felt himself already standing in the shadow of death. He was done with life and desired only to end it, as became a warrior, striking a last blow against the hereditary enemy of his race. When he had positioned his men, he called his chiefs about him and calmly said, "Brother warriors, we are now about to enter into a battle from which I shall never return—my body will remain on the field of battle." He then unbuckled his sword, and, placing it in the hands of one of them, said, "When my son becomes a noted warrior and is able to wield a sword, give this to him." He then laid aside his British military dress and took his place in the line, clothed only in an ordinary deerskin hunting shirt. *(Drake, Tecumseh, 9.)* When the battle began, his voice was heard encouraging his men until he fell under the cavalry charge of the Americans, who had already broken the ranks of the British regulars and forced them to surrender. Deprived of their leader and deserted by their white allies, the Indians gave up the unequal contest and fled from the field. Tecumtha died in his forty-fourth year.

After the close of the war, the prophet returned from Canada by permission of this government and rejoined his tribe in Ohio, with whom he moved to the west in 1827. *(Schoolcraft, Ind. Tribes, 2.)* Catlin, who met and talked with him in 1832, speaks of him this way:

> This has undoubtedly been a very shrewd and influential man, but circumstances have destroyed him, as they have many other great men before him, and he now lives respected, but silent and melancholy, within his tribe. I conversed with him a great deal about his brother Tecumseh, of whom he spoke frankly, and seemingly with great pleasure; but of himself and his own great schemes he would say nothing. He told me that Tecumseh’s plans were to unite all the Indian tribes in a grand confederacy, from the province of Mexico to the Great Lakes, to unite their forces in an army that would be able to meet and drive back the white people, who were continually advancing on the Indian tribes and forcing them from their lands toward the Rocky mountains; that Tecumseh was a great general, and that nothing but his premature death defeated his grand plan. *(Catlin, 2.)*

## CHAPTER V
# KÄNAKÛK AND MINOR PROPHETS
### KÄNAKÛK

> My father, the Great Spirit holds all the world in his hands. I pray to him that we may not be removed from our lands. . . . Take pity on us and let us remain where we are.—*Känakûk*.

> I was remarkably struck by the noble efforts of this champion of the mere remnant of a poisoned race, who is working so hard to rescue the remainder of his people from the deadly poison that has been brought among them by enlightened Christians.—*Catlin*.

The scene now shifts to the west of the Mississippi. With the death of Tecumtha, the confederacy of the northwestern tribes fell to pieces. At the closing of the War of 1812, the government initiated a series of treaties that resulted, within twenty years, in the removal of almost every tribe beyond the Mississippi and the taking over of their former lands by white settlers. Among others, the Kickapoo, through the Treaty of Edwardsville in 1819, had given up all of their ancient territory in Illinois—comprising nearly half the area of the state—in exchange for a much smaller piece of land on the Osage River in Missouri and $3,000 in goods. (*Treaties, 1.*) The government also agreed to provide two boats to take them up the river to their new home, where “the United States promise to guarantee to the said tribe the peaceful possession of the piece of land given up here to them, and to restrain and prevent all white persons from hunting, settling, or otherwise trespassing on it.”

For some reason, however, the Kickapoo showed no great desire to move from their villages and cornfields on the wide prairies of Illinois to the rugged hills of Missouri. This may have been due to the natural stubbornness of the savage, or possibly to the fact that the new country guaranteed to them was already occupied by their traditional enemies, the Osage, who outnumbered the Kickapoo three to one. To be sure, these original native owners had agreed to surrender the territory to the United States, but they were still there to meet all visitors, as the migrating Cherokee had learned to their regret. Regardless, several years passed and people began to suspect that the Kickapoo were not eager to go west and “grow up with the country.” An investigation revealed the fact that, instead of moving to the reservation on the Osage River, half of the tribe had gone southward as a group and crossed over to the Spanish side of the Red River (now Texas), where they might reasonably hope to be safe from the further advance of the Americans. Others were preparing to follow, and the govern-

> This man has acquired influence over his people through supposed revelations from God, which he urges upon them with an eloquence, mildness, and firmness of manner that convinces their believing ears of his communications with God. To give a favorable turn to his mind, I apparently believed his statements of these revelations and attempted to interpret them for him. He listened to me with great attention, and, after I had finished, said I might be right; that God would talk to him again and he would let me know what He said. In the meantime, he would use his influence to get his people to move, but he could not come over himself until everyone had relocated; he said there were many bad men still among them whom he hoped to convert to the ways of God, and then everyone would come over. He would preach to his men and warn them against taking or damaging the property of white people, and if any white man struck them—to use his own expression—he would bow his head and not complain; he would stop any attempt to take revenge. He seems to have a wonderful influence over those Indians who accompanied him. They neither drank nor painted themselves; they were serious, though not gloomy. (*Ind. Off.*, 1.)

In the same month, Känakûk himself visited General Clark at Saint Louis. In the course of a long talk, he explained the origin of his divine mission and the nature of his doctrine, illustrating the subject by using a unique diagram (figure 61) and closing with an earnest appeal on behalf of his people that they should be allowed to remain undisturbed. Although traders said that he had stolen his inspiration from a Methodist preacher, it is plain from an examination of his doctrine that he was the direct spiritual successor of *Tenskwatawa* and the Delaware prophet, who in their generation had preached to the same tribe. Like his predecessors, he also condemned the use of "medicine bags" and medicine songs; although these were universal among the tribes, they seem to have been regarded by the more principled Indians much as witchcraft was in former days among white people.

After the usual preliminary expressions of mutual friendship and goodwill, *Känakûk* stated that all his people were united in their feelings, and then proceeded to explain his religious views as follows:

> My father, the Great Spirit has placed us all on this earth; he has given our nation a piece of land. Why do you want to take it away and give us so much trouble? We ought to live in peace and happiness among ourselves and with you. We have heard of some trouble about our land. I have come down to see you and have it all explained.

My father, the Great Spirit appeared to me; he saw my heart was in sorrow about our land; he told me not to give up this matter, but to go to my Great Father <note>the President</note> and he would listen to me. My father, when I talked to the Great Spirit, I saw the chiefs holding the land fast. He told me the life of our children was short and that the earth would sink.

My father, I will explain to you what the Great Spirit said to me—to do so, I must make some marks. The Great Spirit says: My father, we started from this point (A, figure 61). We are here now (B). When we get here (C), the Great Spirit will appear to me again. Here (B) the Great Spirit gave his blessings to the Native people and told them to tell his people to throw away their medicine bags and not to steal, not to tell lies, not to murder, not to quarrel, and to burn their medicine bags. If they did not, they could not get on the straight way, but would have to go the crooked path of the wicked here (D); that when we got to this place (the curved line, E), we would not be able to cross it unless we were all good. It was fire. That we should go to this place (E), where all the Native chiefs would be gathered and there would be a great preaching. That if we had not thrown away all our bad deeds, these two points would meet (D and E), and then the Great Spirit would destroy everything and the world would be turned over. That if we would be good and throw away all our bad deeds, we would cross this fire, and then we would come to water (second line), which we would cross. There we would come to a country where there was nothing but a prairie and nothing grew upon it. There the sun would be hidden from us by four black clouds. When we get here (C), the Great Spirit will explain these round marks.

My father, I have now explained our situation as well as I can, with great effort. I wish you to tell me the truth and hide nothing from me. I have heard that some of your warriors are going to take up the tomahawk. I explained to you last fall our situation. We are now here (B), where we are in great trouble. I told you of all our troubles. I asked you to reflect on our situation and said that we would come back to see you.

The Great Spirit told me that no people owned the lands—that all was his, and not to forget to tell the white people that when we went into council. When I saw the Great Spirit, he told me, “Mention all this to your Great Father. I expect, my father, that God has put me in a good way—that our children shall see their sisters and brothers and our women see their children. They will grow up and travel and see their totems. A few years later, in 1831, Catlin visited Känakûk, who was still living with the survivors of his people in Illinois and was then regarded as their chief. He still preached the same doctrine, which the artist incorrectly assumed was the Christian religion—probably because the meetings were held on Sunday in imitation of the white people—and he especially was constantly and earnestly urging his tribesmen to stop drinking whiskey, which threatened to destroy their race. His influence had extended into Michigan, and many of the Potawatomi

were counted among his disciples. Catlin, who painted his portrait (reproduced in figure 60), heard him preach and expressed surprise and admiration at his easy and graceful manner and his clearly eloquent command of language. The traveler continues:

<margin>*</margin>
> I was remarkably struck by the noble efforts of this champion of the small remnant of a poisoned race, who labored so strenuously to rescue the rest of his people from the deadly curse brought among them by enlightened Christians. I cannot say how far this zealous man’s efforts have succeeded in Christianizing them, but it is quite certain that his constant and exemplary efforts have completely abolished the practice of drinking whiskey in his tribe. This alone is a very praiseworthy achievement and the first indispensable step toward all other improvements. I spent some time among these people and was also exceedingly pleased and surprised to witness their sobriety and peaceful conduct; I did not see a single instance of drunkenness, nor did I see or hear of any use of alcoholic liquors while I was with the tribe. (*Catlin, 3.*)

After mentioning—though apparently not believing the traders' claims—that the prophet had borrowed his doctrines from a white man, Catlin goes on to describe a peculiar prayer-stick which Känakûk had given to his followers. This immediately reminds us of a similar device used by the Delaware prophet in 1764 and aligns with the entire system of birchbark pictographs used among the northern tribes. These sticks were made of maple, engraved with hieroglyphic prayers and other religious symbols. The prophet himself carved them and distributed them to every family in the tribe, earning a significant income from their sale and thereby increasing his influence as both a priest and a man of property. At this time, apparently every man, woman, and child in the tribe was in the habit of reciting the prayers from these sticks upon waking in the morning and before going to bed at night. This was done by placing the right index finger first under the top character while repeating a short prayer it suggested, then under the next, and the next, and so on to the bottom. The entire prayer, which was sung as a type of chant, took about ten minutes.

Without attempting to judge the purity of the prophet’s motives, Catlin strongly asserts that his influence and example were good and had effectively turned his people from vice and indulgence toward temperance and hard work, despite the degrading influence of associating with the white population on the frontier.

The veteran missionary Allis also noted the use of this prayer-stick as he observed it in 1834 among the Kickapoo, who were then living near Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. The prophet’s followers used to meet for worship on Sundays, where Känakûk delivered a sermon in their own language. Afterward, they formed a line and marched around several times in single file, reciting the chant from their prayer-sticks and shaking hands with bystanders as they passed. As they left, they continued to chant until they arrived at the “father’s house” or heaven, which was indicated by the figure of a horn at the top of the prayer-stick. The worshipers also met on Fridays and made confessions

<header>MOONEY] THE PRAYER-STICK</header>

the surface of the wood, polished from long use. One side is carved with the symbolic figures already mentioned, while the other is smooth. In all its details, it is a fine specimen of Indian craftsmanship. According to the tradition of the Armstrong family, its former owners, the small square in the lower left-hand corner represents hell or the final home of the wicked, while the house with the four pine (?) trees at the top symbolizes the spiritual home of the devout followers of the prophet. As is well known, four is the sacred number of many Indian tribes. The meaning of several other lines above and below is unknown. Along the shaft of the stick from bottom to top are the prayer characters, arranged in three groups of five each; one group is near the bottom, while the others are along the upper portion of the shaft and are separated from one another by a small circle. The characters bear some resemblance to the old black-letter type of a missal, while the unique arrangement is strongly suggestive of the Catholic rosary with its fifteen "mysteries" in three groups of five each. It will be remembered that the earliest and most frequent missionaries among the Kickapoo and other Great Lakes tribes were Catholic, and we can easily see that their teachings and ceremonies influenced this native religion, as was later the case with the religions of Smohalla and the Ghost Dance. Neither three nor five are commonly known as sacred numbers among the Indians, while three is distinctly Christian in its symbolism.
<margin>✓</margin>
It is perhaps unnecessary to state that the ideas of heaven and hell are not indigenous, but were among the first concepts incorporated from the teachings of the white missionaries. The characters resembling letters may be from the alphabetic system of sixteen characters which it is said the Ojibwa invented for recording their own language, and taught to the Kickapoo and Sauk, and which resembled somewhat the letters of the Roman alphabet, from which they apparently were derived. (*Hamilton, 1.*)

This prayer-stick or "bible," as it has been called, was obtained by Mr. Bartlett from Mr. R. V. Armstrong, of Mill Creek, Indiana, who stated that it was the only remaining one of a large number that had been in the possession of the family for many years. The story of how it was originally obtained, as told by Mr. Armstrong, is interesting. 

> "His father, Reverend James Armstrong, was a Methodist minister and missionary who had been sent to northern Indiana in the early nineteenth century. In 1830, while living on Shawnee prairie, 3 miles from the present site of Attica, Indiana, a large group of Kickapoo Indians came to his house to visit the missionary, and apparently regarded the interview as very important to themselves. They declared that they were from beyond the Mississippi River, that they had heard of Mr. Armstrong and his missionary labors, and that they believed him to be the one for whom their people had long been looking. Each Indian held in his hand one of these wooden crosses, and as they knelt on the grass in front of the missionary's

<meta>This text continues the account of the Kickapoo prayer-sticks, describing how the prophet Känakûk’s followers used them as a substitute for the Bible and detailing the later life of the prophet and the emergence of a Winnebago prophet named Pa'thěskě.</meta>

house, they performed their devotions in their own language, moving their fingers over the inscription that ascends the shaft of the cross. The missionary understood them to say that this cross was their "bible," and that they knew it was not the true bible, but they had been told to use it until someone should come who would give them the genuine word of God in exchange. Thereupon the missionary collected their crosses—and there were more than a large basketful of them—and gave a copy of the New Testament to each person in exchange. The Indians received the books with many expressions of gratitude and apparently viewed them at once as sacred possessions. These wise men from the west then went away to their distant country."

Känakûk died of smallpox in 1852, in Kansas, where his people had been moved despite his eloquent appeals on their behalf. For many years he had been recognized as the chief of his tribe, and as such he exerted a very beneficial influence over the Kickapoo by restraining the introduction and use of liquor among them. At the same time, he staunchly upheld traditional Indian ideas and resisted every advance of the missionaries and civilization to the last. He was regarded as possessing supernatural powers, and during his last illness he asserted that he would rise again three days after death. In expectation that the prophecy would be fulfilled, a number of his followers remained watching near the corpse until they also contracted the disease and died likewise. <note>Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1</note> After his death, the decline of his tribe was rapid and unchecked. In 1894 there remained only 514 members, divided almost equally between Kansas and Oklahoma. These few survivors of a large tribe still hold the name of their chief and prophet in loving reverence.

### PA'THĚSKĚ

Recent personal investigation among the Winnebago failed to reveal any knowledge of a former doctrine concerning an approaching destruction of the world, as mentioned in a statement already quoted <note>see page 661</note>. It appeared, however, that at the time indicated, about 1852 or 1853, while the tribe was still living on the Turkey River in Iowa, a prophet known as Pa'thěskě, or Long Nose, announced that he had been instructed in a vision to teach his people a new dance, which he called the friendship dance (<term>chû'korăki'</term>). They were to perform this at intervals for one whole year, at the end of which time, in the spring, they were to take the warpath against their hereditary enemy, the Sioux, and would then reap a rich harvest of scalps. The dance, as he taught it to them, he claimed to have seen performed by a band of spirits in the other world, where he had been taken after a ceremonial fast of several days' duration. It differed from their other dances, and, although warlike in its ultimate purpose, it was not a war dance. It was performed by the men alone, circling around a fire within the lodge. He also designated a young man named <term>Sara'minûka</term>, or "Indistinct," as the proper person to lead the expedition at the appointed time.

<summary>The prophet Känakûk died of smallpox in 1852 after leading the Kickapoo and resisting assimilation, while a Winnebago prophet named Pa'thěskě later introduced a visionary "friendship dance" to prepare his people for war.</summary>
<keywords>Känakûk, Kickapoo, smallpox, Kansas, Oklahoma, Pa'thěskě, Winnebago, friendship dance, chû'korăki', Sioux, Sara'minûka, missionary influence</keywords>

--- Page 77 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of the Winnebago prophet Pa'thěskě, detailing the end of his movement, and begins the history of the Paiute prophet Tä'vibo, the father of the modern Ghost Dance messiah.</meta>

The friendship dance went on all through the summer and winter until spring, when the prophet announced that he had received a new revelation forbidding the proposed expedition. His disgusted followers at once denounced him as an impostor and abandoned the dance. Sara'minûka was soon afterward killed by an accident, which was considered by the Indians a direct retribution for his failure to carry out his part of the plan. The prophet died a few years later while on a visit to Washington with a delegation of his tribe.

Although the old men consulted on the subject seemed to know nothing of any predicted destruction of the world in this connection, it is probable that the statement given by Agent Fletcher at the time was correct, as such cycle myths are very common among the Indian and other primitive tribes. The Arapaho informed the author that we are now living in the sixth cycle, and that the final catastrophe will take place at the close of the seventh.

### TÄ'VIBO

About 1870 another prophet arose among the Paiute in Nevada. As most Indian movements are unknown to the whites at their beginning, the date is variously put from 1869 to 1872. He is said to have been the father of the present "messiah," who has unquestionably derived many of his ideas from him, and lived, as does his son, in Mason Valley, about 60 miles south of Virginia City, not far from the Walker River Reservation. In talking with his son, he said that his father's name was Tä'vibo or "White man," and that he was a *capita* (Spanish, *capitan*) or petty chief, but not a prophet or preacher, although he used to have visions and was invulnerable. From consistent testimony of Indians and white men, however, there seems to be no doubt that he did preach and prophesy and introduce a new religious dance among his people, and that the doctrine which he promulgated and the hopes which he held out twenty years ago were the foundation on which his son has built the structure of the present messiah religion. He was visited by Indians from Oregon and Idaho, and his teachings made their influence felt among the Bannock and Shoshoni, as well as among all the scattered bands of the Paiute, to whom he continued to preach until his death a year or two later. (*G. D., 1 and 2; A. G. O., 1; Phister, 1.*)

Captain J. M. Lee, Ninth Infantry, formerly on the staff of General Miles, was on duty in that neighborhood at the time and gives the following account of the prophet and his doctrines in a personal letter to the author:

> I was on Indian duty in Nevada in 1869, 1870, and 1871. When visiting Walker Lake Reservation in 1869-70, I became acquainted with several superstitious beliefs then prevailing among the Paiute Indians. It was a rough, mountainous region all around, and mysterious happenings, according to tradition, always occurred when the prophet or medicine-men went up into the mountains and there received their revelations from the divine spirits. In the earlier part of the sixties the whites

Tä'vibo, the father of the 1890 "messiah" Wovoka, is described as a visionary whose teachings reached several tribes in Nevada, Oregon, and Idaho.</summary>
<keywords>Pa'thěskě, Tä'vibo, Wovoka, Paiute, Ghost Dance, cycle myths, Arapaho, Mason Valley, Walker River Reservation, Captain J. M. Lee</keywords>

--- Page 78 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of Tävibo, a Paiute prophet who preceded the modern Ghost Dance movement, detailing his various revelations and the subsequent rise of his successor, Quoit-tsow.</meta>

began to come in and take over much of the Indian country in Nevada, and in the usual course of events, it turned out that the medicine men or prophets were looked to for relief. The most influential one went up alone into the mountain and there met the Great Spirit. He brought back with him no tablets of stone, but he was a messenger of good news to the effect that within a few months there was to be a great upheaval or earthquake. All the improvements of the whites—all their houses, their goods, stores, etc.—would remain, but the whites would be swallowed up, while the Indians would be saved and permitted to enjoy the earth and all its fullness, including anything left by the wicked whites. This revelation was duly proclaimed by the prophet and attracted a few believers, but the doubting skeptics were too many, and they ridiculed the idea that the white men would fall into the holes and be swallowed up while the Indians would not. As the prophet could not enforce his belief, he went up into the mountain again and came back with a second revelation, which was that when the great disaster came, everyone, both Indians and whites, would be swallowed up or overwhelmed, but that at the end of three days (or a few days) the Indians would be resurrected in the flesh and would live forever to enjoy the earth, with plenty of game, fish, and pine nuts, while their enemies, the whites, would be destroyed forever. There would thus be a final and eternal separation between Indians and whites.

This revelation, which seemed more reasonable, was rather popular for a while, but as time wore on, faith seemed to weaken and the prophet was without honor even in his own country. After much fasting and prayer, he made a third trip to the mountain, where he secured a final revelation or message to the people. The divine spirit had become so angered at the lack of faith in the prophecies that it was revealed to his chosen one that those Indians who believed in the prophecy would be resurrected and be happy, but those who did not believe in it would stay in the ground and be damned forever with the whites.

It was not long after this that the prophet died, and the poor, miserable Indians struggled along for nearly two decades, eating grasshoppers, lizards, and fish, and trying to be civilized until the appearance of this new prophet Quoit-tsow, who is said to be the son, either actual or spiritual, of the first one.

Additional details are given in the following interesting extract from a letter addressed to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, dated November 19, 1890, by Mr. Frank Campbell, who has an intimate acquaintance with the tribe and was employed in an official capacity on the reservation at the time when Tävibo first announced the new revelation. It would appear from Mr. Campbell’s statement that under the new system both races were to meet on a common level, and, as this agrees with what Professor Thompson (referred to later on) afterward found among the eastern Paiute, it is probable that the original doctrine had been significantly modified since its first announcement a few years before.

Eighteen years ago I was the resident farmer on the Walker Lake Indian reserve, Nevada. I had previously been connected with the Indian service at the reserve for ten years, was familiar with the Paiute customs, and was personally acquainted with all the Indians in that region. In 1872, an Indian began preaching a new religion at that reserve that caused a profound sensation among the Paiute. For several months I was kept in ignorance of the cause of the excitement—which was remarkable, considering the confidence they had always placed in me. They no doubt expected me to ridicule the sayings of the new messiah, as I had always labored among them to break down their superstitious beliefs. When finally I was made

acquainted with the true facts of the case, I told them the preachings of Waugh-zee-waugh-ber were good and no harm could come from them. Indian emissaries visited the reservation from Idaho, Oregon, and other places to investigate the new religion. I visited the Indian camp while the prophet was in a trance and remained until he regained consciousness. In accordance with instructions, the Indians gathered around him and joined in a song that was intended to guide the spirit back to the body. Upon his awakening, he gave a long account of his visit in spirit to the Supreme Ruler, who was then on his way with all the spirits of the deceased to reside once again upon this earth and change it into a paradise. Life was to be eternal, and no distinction was to exist between races.

This morning's press dispatches contain an account of Porcupine's visit to Walker Lake . . . that proves to me that the religion started at Walker Lake eighteen years ago is the same one that is now agitating the Indian world. There is nothing in it to cause trouble between whites and Indians unless the new Messiah is misquoted and his doctrine is misunderstood. I left the Walker Lake reservation in June 1873, and at the time I supposed this craze would die out, but I have several times since been reminded by Nevada papers and letters that it was gradually spreading. (*G. D., 3.*)

The name given by Campbell certainly does not much resemble Tä'vibo, but it is quite possible that the father, like the son, had more than one name. It is also possible that "Waughzeewaughber" was not the prophet described by Captain Lee, but one of his disciples who had taken up and modified the original doctrine. The name Tä'vibo refers to the east (*tävänagwat*) or the place where the sun (*täbi*) rises. Among the related Shoshoni and Comanche, white people are called *Taivo*.

From oral information provided by Professor A. H. Thompson of the United States Geological Survey, I have learned some details of the arrival of the new doctrine among the Paiute of southwestern Utah. While his party was engaged in that section in the spring of 1875, a great excitement was caused among the Indians by the report that two mysterious beings with white skins (it will be remembered that the father of Wovoka was named Tä'vibo or "white man") had appeared among the Paiute far to the west and announced a speedy resurrection of all the deceased Indians, the restoration of the game, and the return of the old-time primitive life. Under the new order of things, moreover, both races alike were to be white. A number of Indians from Utah went over into Nevada, where they met others who claimed to have seen these mysterious visitors farther in the west. On their return to Utah, they brought back with them the ceremony of the new belief, the chief part of the ritual being a dance performed at night in a circle, with no fire in the center, very much as in the modern Ghost Dance.

It is said that the Mormons, who hold the theory that the Indians are the descendants of the supposed "ten lost tribes," cherish, as a part of their faith, the tradition that some of the lost Hebrew emigrants are still ice-bound in the frozen north, from where they will one day emerge to rejoin their brothers in the south. When the news of this Indian revelation reached their ears, the Mormon priests accepted it as a prophecy of the speedy fulfillment of their own traditions, and Orson Pratt, one of the most prominent leaders, preached a sermon, which was extensively

According to the statement of the agent then in charge at Fort Hall, in Idaho, the Mormons at the same time—the early spring of 1875—sent emissaries to the Bannock, urging them to go to Salt Lake City to be baptized into the Mormon religion. A large number accepted the invitation without the knowledge of the agent, went down to Utah, and were baptized there, and then returned to work as missionaries of the new faith among their tribes. As an additional inducement, free rations were furnished by the Mormons to all who would come and be baptized, and "they were told that by being baptized and going to church the old men would all become young, the young men would never be sick, that the Lord had a work for them to do, and that they were the chosen people of God to establish his kingdom upon the earth," etc. It is also asserted that they were encouraged to resist the authority of the government. (*Comr., 2.*) However much truth there may be in these reports—and we must allow for considerable local prejudice—it is clear enough that the Mormons took an active interest in the religious ferment then existing among the neighboring tribes and helped to give shape to the doctrine which crystallized some years later in the Ghost Dance.

### NAKAI'-DOKLÏ'NI

Various other prophets of more or less local fame have arisen from time to time among the tribes, and the resurrection of the dead and the return of the old ways have usually figured prominently in their prophecies. In fact, this idea has probably been the daydream of every Indian medicine man since the whites first landed in America. Most of these, however, have been unknown to fame outside of their own narrow circles, except where chance or deliberate purpose has given a warlike meaning to their teachings and thus made them the subjects of official notice.

<image-desc>A diagram titled "Nakai'-doklï'ni's dance-wheel" consisting of a large central black dot from which eight spokes of smaller black dots radiate outwards in a circular pattern.</image-desc>
**Fig. 63—*Nakai'-doklï'ni's dance-wheel.***

Among these may be mentioned the Apache medicine man Nakai'-doklï'ni, who attracted some attention for a time in southern Arizona in 1881. (*Bourke, 1.*) In the early part of this year, he began to advertise his supernatural powers, claiming to be able to raise the dead and commune with spirits, and predicting that the whites would soon be driven from the land. He taught his followers a new and peculiar dance, in which the performers were arranged like the spokes of a wheel, all facing inward, while he, standing

<summary>This page details the Mormon influence on the religious beliefs of the Bannock tribe in 1875 and introduces the Apache medicine man Nakai'-doklï'ni, who preached the resurrection of the dead in Arizona.</summary>
<keywords>Mormons, Fort Hall, Bannock, Nakai'-doklï'ni, Apache, Ghost Dance, Arizona, baptism, medicine man, prophecy</keywords>

--- Page 81 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of the Apache prophet Nakai'-doklĭ'ni, describing his ritual practices, his promise to resurrect deceased chiefs, the subsequent military intervention at Cibicu Creek, and his death.</meta>

Standing in the center, he sprinkled them with the sacred <term>hoddentin</term><note>1</note> as they circled around him.

In June 1881, he announced to his people, the White Mountain band of Apache on the San Carlos reservation, that on the condition of receiving a sufficient number of horses and blankets for his trouble, he would bring back from the dead two chiefs who had been killed a few months before. This proposal naturally stirred great excitement among the Indians. Eager to have their beloved chiefs with them once again, they willingly produced the required ponies. When the agent protested, they replied that they would wait until the specified time for the fulfillment of the prediction; if the dead chiefs failed to appear, they would then demand the return of their property. (*Comr.*, 3.)

Accordingly, Nakai'-doklĭ'ni began his prayers and ceremonies, and the dance was held regularly at his camp on Cibicu Creek until August. At that time, it was reported to Colonel E. A. Carr, commander at Fort Apache, that the medicine man had announced that the dead chiefs refused to return because of the presence of the white people. He claimed that once the whites left, the dead would return, and that the whites would be out of the country by the time the corn was ripe.

As the situation seemed to be getting serious, the agent now called on the commanding officer to "arrest or kill him, or both." The officer prepared to make the arrest when Nakai'-doklĭ'ni was expected to come down to the post to lead a dance that had been arranged to take place in a few days. The prophet failed to appear, however, and messengers were sent to his camp to ask him to come to the fort the following Sunday. He returned an evasive reply to this message, whereupon Colonel Carr, with 85 white troops and 23 Apache scouts, started for his camp in Cibicu Canyon to place him under arrest. They arrived at the village on August 30. Nakai'-doklĭ'ni submitted quietly to the arrest, but as the troops were setting up camp for the night, their own scouts, joined by other Indians, opened fire on them. A sharp skirmish followed, in which several soldiers were killed or wounded, but the Indians were driven back with considerable losses, including the prophet himself, who was killed during the first exchange of fire. The result was another in the long series of Apache outbreaks. (*Comr.*, 4; *Sec. War*, 1; *A. G. O.*, 2.)

### THE POTAWATOMI PROPHET

In 1883, a new religion was introduced among the Potawatomi and Kickapoo of the Pottawotomie and Great Nemaha Agency in north—

---

<note>1 *Hadn-tin* or *hoddentin* (in Navajo, *tadatin*) is a sacred yellow powder made from the pollen of the tule rush or, among the Navajo, from corn. It is used in every important ceremonial performance of the Apache and Navajo. The Navajo always sprinkle some on the surface of the water before crossing a stream. The medicine man's name is also written as Nakay-doklunni or Nockay Delklinne, and white people commonly called him "Bobbydoklinny." Dr. Washington Matthews, the leading authority on the closely related Navajo dialect, believes the name might mean "spotted or freckled Mexican." *Nakai*, which literally means "white alien," is the word for Mexican in both dialects. The name would not necessarily indicate that the medicine man was of Mexican origin; instead, it might have been given, according to tribal custom, to commemorate the fact that he had killed a freckled Mexican.</note>

A new religious movement later emerged among the Potawatomi and Kickapoo tribes in 1883.</summary>

--- Page 82 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of indigenous religious movements, moving from the Apache prophet Nakai'-doklĭ'ni to a moralistic dance religion among the tribes of Kansas and Oklahoma, and the emergence of the Crow medicine man known as Sword-bearer.</meta>

eastern Kansas, by visiting Potawatomi, Winnebago, and Ojibwa from Wisconsin. As usual, the ritual part consists chiefly of a ceremonial dance. In doctrine, it teaches the same code of morality dictated by the Ten Commandments, and especially prohibits drinking alcohol, gambling, and horse racing. For this reason, the agents generally have not seen fit to interfere with it, and in some cases have even encouraged it as a civilizing influence among that portion of the tribes not yet enrolled in Christian denominations. The movement is entirely distinct from the Ghost Dance, and may perhaps be a revival of the system preached by Känakûk more than fifty years before. In 1891, the majority of the two tribes, numbering 749 in all, were reported as adherents of the doctrine. (*Comr., 5, 6, 7; also reports from the same agency for 1887 and 1889.*) A large number of the Sauk and Fox, Kickapoo, and Potawatomi of Oklahoma are also believers in the religion.

In 1885, Agent Patrick says on this subject:

> These Indians are virtuous, clean, and hardworking, and would be a valuable addition to the Prairie band if it were not for their intense devotion to a religious dance started among the northern Indians some years ago. This dance was introduced to the Prairie band about two years ago by the Absentee Potawatomi and Winnebago, and has spread throughout the tribes in the agency. They seem to have adopted the religion as a means of expressing their belief in the justice and mercy of the Great Spirit and of their devotion to him, and are so earnest in their convictions as to its affording them eternal happiness that I have thought it unwise so far to interfere with it any further than to advise as few meetings as possible and to discourage it in my interactions with the individuals practicing the religion. It is not an unmixed evil, as under its teaching drunkenness and gambling have been reduced 75 percent, and a departure from virtue on the part of its members meets with the severest condemnation. As some tenets of revealed religion are embraced in its doctrines, I do not consider it a step backward for the Indians who have not previously professed belief in any Christian religion, and believe its worst features are summed up in the loss of time it occasions and the fanatical train of thought involved in the constant contemplation of the subject. (*Comr., 6.*)

## CHEEZ-TAH-PAEZH THE SWORD-BEARER

It is probable that something of the messiah idea entered into the promises held out to his followers by Sword-bearer, a Crow medicine man in Montana in 1887. The official records are silent on this point, although it is definitely stated that he asserted his own invulnerability, and that his claims in this respect were implicitly believed by his people. Cheez-tah-paezh, literally "Wraps his tail" (also written Cheeschapahdisch, Cheschopah, Chese-cha-pahdish, and Chese-Topah), was without any special prominence in his tribe until the summer of 1887, when, in company with several other young men of the Crows, he participated in the sun dance of the Cheyenne, and showed such fortitude in enduring the dreadful torture that he was presented by the Cheyenne with a medicine saber painted red, in virtue of which he took the title of Sword-bearer. This naturally brought him into notice at home, and he soon aspired to become a chief and medicine man. Among other things, he asserted that no bullet or weapon had power to harm him.

<summary>This page describes a moralistic religious movement among the Potawatomi and nearby tribes that prohibited vice, as well as the rise of Cheez-tah-paezh (Sword-bearer), a Crow medicine man who claimed invulnerability.</summary>

# MOONEY] THE SWORD-BEARER AFFAIR

It is not known what other claims he made, but his words reportedly produced such an impression that, for a time, every full-blooded and mixed-race person among the Crows believed in him.

Within a few months, he had become one of the most influential leaders in the tribe. Taking advantage of some dissatisfaction toward the Indian agent, he led a demonstration against the agency on September 30. Troops under General Ruger were called upon to arrest him and the others involved. While attempting to do this on November 5, 1887, a skirmish broke out in which Sword-bearer was killed. His death convinced his followers that his claims were false, and the tribe, which until then had always been loyal to the government, soon returned to its friendly attitude. (*Secretary of War, 2; Adjutant General’s Office, 3; additional details from a personal letter by Colonel Simon Snyder, Fifteenth Infantry.*)

The event is vividly described by Theodore Roosevelt, based on the account of one of the officers involved. When the troops arrived, they found the Crow warriors waiting for them on a hill, mounted on their war ponies and dressed in full war paint and buckskin. In Roosevelt's words—

> The Crows on the hilltop presented a grim and threatening front. The troops advanced slowly toward them and then halted to negotiate. Meanwhile, a mass of black thunderclouds gathering on the horizon threatened one of those extremely severe and sudden cloudbursts so characteristic of the plains country. While they were still trying to make arrangements for a negotiation, a horseman charged out from the Crow ranks and galloped headlong toward the troops. It was the medicine chief Sword-bearer. He was in war paint and battle dress, wearing a war bonnet of floating, trailing eagle feathers, with plumes from the same bird braided into the mane and tail of his spirited little horse. On he came at a gallop, riding almost up to the troops, and then began to circle around them, shouting and singing while throwing his red sword into the air and catching it by the hilt as it fell. Twice he rode completely around the troops, who stood in uncertainty, not knowing what to make of his performance and being strictly forbidden to shoot at him. Then, paying them no further attention, he rode back toward the Crows. It appears that he had told the latter that he would ride twice around the hostile force and, through his incantations, would call down rain from heaven that would turn the hearts of the white men to water so that they would return to their homes. Sure enough, while the arrangements for the negotiation were still moving forward, the cloudburst hit, drenching the command and making the ground on the hills in front nearly impassable. Before it dried, a courier arrived with orders for the troops to return to camp.
>
> This fulfillment of Sword-bearer’s prophecy naturally raised his reputation to its peak, and the young men of the tribe prepared for war, while the older chiefs—who more fully realized the power of the white military—still hesitated. When the troops next appeared, they encountered the entire Crow force; the women and children with their teepees were off to one side beyond a small stream, while nearly all the warriors of the tribe were gathered in front. Sword-bearer started to repeat his previous ride, much to the intense irritation of the soldiers. Fortunately, however, this time some of his young men could not be restrained. They, too, began to ride near the troops, and one of them was unable to resist firing on Captain Edwards’s troop, which was in the lead. This gave the soldiers their opportunity. They instantly responded with a volley, and Edwards’s troop charged. The fight lasted only a minute or two, for Sword-bearer was struck by a bullet and fell. Since he had boasted that he was invincible and promised that his warriors would also be invincible if they followed him, the courage of his followers failed, and they scattered in every direction. (Roosevelt, 1.)
