# CHAPTER VI

## THE SMOHALLA RELIGION OF THE COLUMBIA REGION

### SMOHALLA

> I have only one heart. Although you say, "Go to another country," my heart does not feel that way. I do not want money for my land. I am here, and here is where I am going to stay. I will not part with my lands, and if you come again I will say the same thing. I will not part with my lands.—*Umatilla Chief*.

> We have never made any trade. The earth is part of my body, and I never gave up the earth. So long as the earth sustains me, I want to be left alone.—*Toohulhulsote*.

> Their only troubles arise from the attempts of white men to encroach upon the reservations. I truly believe that if the snow-crowned summits of Mount Rainier were set apart as an Indian reservation, white men would immediately begin trying to seize them.—*Superintendent Ross*.

Around the time the Paiute were preparing for the millennial dawn, reports began to circulate about a "dreamer prophet" on the Columbia River named Smohalla. He was becoming a source of constant trouble for the Indian agents in that region. He was reported to be organizing a new religion among the Indians that taught the destruction of white people and resistance to the government, and supposedly turned every crime in the book into a moral virtue. One agent, disregarding grammar if not truthfulness, solemnly reported that "the main object is to allow multiple wives, immunity from punishment for lawbreaking, and the permission of all vices—especially drinking and gambling—which are the chief virtues of the believers of this religion." (*Comr.*, 8.)

This was bad enough, but there was a deeper issue behind it. It appeared that Smohalla and his followers—numbering perhaps about 2,000 Indians from various tribes along the Columbia in eastern Washington and Oregon—had never signed treaties giving up any of their lands. Consequently, they claimed the right to catch salmon in the streams and dig <term>kamas</term> on the prairies of their ancestral country without being disturbed or harassed. They strongly objected to moving to any of the neighboring reservations at Yakima, Umatilla, or Warmspring. There is no doubt that justice and common sense were on the side of the Indians. The agents' own reports show that the people living on the reservations were generally neglected, poor, and miserable, and were subjected to constant encroachments by white settlers despite treaties and boundary lines. At the same time that agents and superintendents were calling for military help to force Smohalla’s followers onto a reservation, these same men were doing everything in their power to force the Indians already on reservations to give up their treaty rights and move to different, less valuable locations to begin their lives all over again.

<summary>This chapter introduces Smohalla, a prophet of the Columbia River region whose "Dreamer" religion resisted government control and land sessions. Despite accusations of promoting vice, the movement's primary focus was maintaining ancestral land rights and resisting the poor conditions found on official Indian reservations.</summary>

These matters are treated at length in the annual reports of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, along with the accompanying reports of superintendents and agents in charge of the reservations concerned, from 1870 to 1875. Regarding the Umatilla reservation, to which intense efforts were made to remove the "renegades," as they were called, Agent Boyle reports in 1870 *(Comr., 9)* that the Indians are "discouraged . . . as a result of the frequently repeated claim that their farms are to be taken from them and given to white settlers." He continues, "It is hardly to be expected that the Indians can keep this reservation much longer unless the strong arm of the government protects them. Daily I am called upon to notify the white settlers that they are trespassing upon the Indian lands." He advises their removal to a permanent reservation, "knowing as I do that they must leave sooner or later." Again, he states, "The agency has been established for ten years, and I regret exceedingly that I have been completely disappointed with what I see about me." In discussing the removal of the Indians to a new reservation, Superintendent Meacham says of a considerable portion of them that it "would suit them better to be set free to look out for themselves." *(Comr., 10.)*

In 1873, Agent Cornoyer reported that the Indians numbered 837 according to the census of 1870, which he believes was as accurate as could then be taken, but "this number I think is now too high." He continues<insert>red archival stamp</insert>

> Out of the appropriation of $4,000 per year for beneficial objects, not one single dollar of that fund has been turned over to me since September 1871; and out of the appropriation for incidental expenses of $40,000 per year for the Indian service in this state, only $200 of that appropriation has been turned over to me during the same period of two years. . . . I would also ask leave to call your attention to that portion of my last annual report where I directed the Department’s attention to the unfulfilled terms of the treaty of June 9, 1855, with these Indians. *(Comr., 11.)*

Commissioner Brunot, in 1871, stated that the estimated number of Indians coming under the provisions of the treaty at the time it was made in 1855 was 3,500, and "by the census taken in 1870 the number was 1,622"—a decrease of nearly half in fifteen years. Of these, only about half were on the reservation, with the rest being on the Columbia River, "never having shared in the benefits of the treaty." On the next page he tells us what some of these benefits are: "Mismanagement by agents, and the misuse of funds, the failure of the government to fulfill the promises of the treaty, and the fact that the Indians have been constantly unsettled by claims that the government intended to remove them, and that their removal was urged for several years in a row in the reports of a former agent, thus taking away from them all motivation to improve their lands." *(Comr., 12.)*

In 1871, a commission was sent to Umatilla and other reservations, which gave the Indians a chance to speak for themselves. The Cayuse

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14

A chief, described as a Catholic Indian, in dress, personal appearance, and bearing superior to the average American farmer, said:

> This reservation is marked out for us. We see it with our eyes and our hearts. We all hold it with our bodies and our souls. Right out here are my father and mother, and brothers and sisters and children, all buried. I am guarding their graves. My friend, this reservation, this small piece of land, we look upon it as our mother, as if she were raising us. You come to ask me for my land. It is as if we who are Indians were to be sent away and get lost. . . . What is the reason you white men who live near the reservation like my land and want to get it? You must not think this way. My friends, you must not talk too forcefully about getting my land. I like my land and will not let it go.

The Wallawalla chief said:

> I have tied all the reservation in my heart and it cannot be loosened. It is as dear to us as our own bodies.

The Umatilla chief said:

> Our red people were brought up here. . . . When my father and mother died, I was left here. They gave me rules and gave me their land to live upon. They left me to take care of them after they were buried. I was to watch over their graves. I do not wish to part with my land. I have felt tired working on my land, so tired that the sweat dropped off me onto the ground. Where is everything that Governor Stevens or General Palmer said <note>that is, that it was to be a reservation for the Indians forever</note>? I am very fond of this land that is marked out for me. . . . Should I take only a small piece of ground and a white man sit down beside me, I fear there would be trouble all the time.

An old man said:

> I am getting old now, and I want to die where my father and mother and children have died. I do not wish to leave this land and go off to some other land. . . . I see where I have sweat and worked in trying to get food. I love my church, my mills, my farm, and the graves of my parents and children. I do not wish to leave my land. That is my whole heart, and I show it to you.

A young chief said:

> I have only one heart, one tongue. Although you say, "Go to another country," my heart is not that way. I do not wish for any money for my land. I am here, and here is where I am going to be. . . . I will not part with lands, and if you come again I will say the same thing. I will not part with my lands.

The commissioner who was conducting the negotiations, after listing the promises made to the Indians in return for the lands which they had surrendered under the original treaty of 1855, tells how some of these promises have been fulfilled:

> . . . A miserably inadequate supply of worn-out farming tools. A group of eight or ten dilapidated shanties used for the agency buildings. The physician promised has never resided upon the reservation, but lives and practices his profession at Pendleton. The hospital promised (fifteen years ago) has not yet been built.

### JOSEPH AND THE NEZ PERCÉ WAR

We first hear officially of Smohalla and his people from A. B. Meacham, the superintendent of Indian affairs in Oregon, who stated in September 1870 that:

> ...One serious drawback [to the adoption of the white man’s road] is the existence among the Indians of Oregon of a peculiar religion called Smokeller or Dreamers, the chief doctrine of which is that the red man is again to rule the country, and this sometimes leads to rebellion against lawful authority.

A few pages further on, we learn the nature of this rebellion:

> The next largest band (not on a reservation) is Smokeller’s, at Priest Rapids, Washington Territory. They also refused to obey my order to come in, which was given to them during last February, and of which a full report was made. I would also recommend that the military remove them to Umatilla. (*Commissioner's Report, 15.*)

Three months before this report, Congress had passed a bill appointing commissioners to negotiate with the tribes of the Umatilla reservation “to ascertain upon what terms they would be willing to sell their lands and remove elsewhere,” and Meacham himself was the principal member of this commission. (*Commissioner's Report, 15.*)

In 1872, Smohalla’s followers along the Columbia were reported to number 2,000, and his apostles were described as constantly traveling from one reservation to another to win over new converts to his teachings. Repeated efforts had been made to induce them to go onto the reservations in eastern Oregon and Washington, but without success. We are told now that:

<margin>X</margin>
> They have a new and peculiar religion, by the doctrines of which they are taught that a new god is coming to their rescue; that all the Indians who have died previously, and who shall die hereafter, are to be resurrected; that as they will then be very numerous and powerful, they will be able to conquer the whites, recover their lands, and live as free and unrestrained as their fathers lived in olden times. Their model of a man is an Indian. They aspire to be Indians and nothing else. . . . It is thought by those who know them best that they cannot be made to go upon their reservations without at least being intimidated by the presence of a military force. (*Commissioner's Report, 17.*)

We hear very little more of Smohalla and his doctrines for several years, until attention was again attracted to Indian affairs in the Northwest by the growing dissatisfaction which culminated in the Nez Percé war of 1877. The Nez Percés, especially those who acknowledged the leadership of Chief Joseph, were largely under the influence of the Dreamer prophets, and there was reason to believe that an uprising started by such a prominent tribe would involve all the smaller tribes in sympathy with the general Indian belief. Therefore, as soon as it became evident that matters were approaching a crisis, a commission—of which General O. O. Howard was chief—was appointed to make some peaceful arrangement with the so-called “renegades” on the upper Columbia. The commissioners met Smohalla and his principal men

These spiritual beliefs were seen by government officials as a catalyst for resistance and were closely linked to the tensions leading to the Nez Percé War of 1877.</summary>

at Wallula, Washington Territory, on April 23, 1877, and as a result of the council then held, these non-treaty tribes, although they insisted as strongly as ever on their right to live undisturbed in their own country, yet refrained from taking part in the war which broke out a few weeks later.

It is not our purpose to recount the history of the *Nez Percé* war of 1877. As is generally the case with Indian wars, it originated in the unauthorized intrusion of lawless whites onto lands which the Indians claimed as theirs by right of occupancy since time immemorial. The *Nez Percés*, whom all authorities agree in representing as a superior tribe of Indians, originally inhabited the valleys of the Clearwater and Salmon rivers in Idaho, with the territory extending west of the Snake River into Washington and Oregon as far as the Blue Mountains. They are first officially mentioned in the report of the Indian Commissioner for 1843, where they are described as “noble, industrious, sensible,” and well-disposed toward the whites, while “though brave as Caesar, the whites have nothing to fear from them as long as they are dealt with in a way they consider right and fair.” (<note>Commissioner's Report</note>, 18.) Since it was considered advisable to bring them into more direct relations with the United States, the agent who made the report called the chiefs together in that year and “assured them of the kind intentions of our government, and of the sad consequences that would follow for any white man, from that time forward, who should invade their rights.” (<note>Commissioner's Report</note>, 19.) On the strength of these fair promises, a portion of the tribe, in 1855, entered into a treaty by which they ceded a large part of their territory and were guaranteed possession of the rest. In 1860, however, gold was discovered in the country, and the usual result followed. “In defiance of law, and despite the protests of the Indian agent, a townsite was laid out in October 1861 on the reservation, and Lewiston, with a population of 1,200, sprang into existence.” (<note>Commissioner's Report</note>, 20.) A new treaty was then made in 1863, by which the intruders were secured in the possession of what they had thus seized, and the *Nez Percés* were restricted within much narrower limits. By this treaty, the Wallowa Valley in northeastern Oregon, the ancestral home of that part of the tribe under the leadership of Chief Joseph, was taken from the Indians. This portion of the tribe, however, had refused to take part in the negotiations, and “Chief Joseph and his band, utterly ignoring the treaty of 1863, continued to claim the Wallowa Valley, where he was quietly allowed to travel without restraint until the encroachments of white settlers induced the government to take some definite action regarding this band of non-treaty *Nez Percés*.” (<note>Commissioner's Report</note>, 21.) At this time, the tribe numbered about 2,800, of whom about 500 recognized Joseph as their chief.

Conflicts between the whites and Indians in the valley became more frequent, and one of Joseph’s band had been killed, when a commission was appointed in 1876 to persuade the Indians to give up the Wallowa Valley and move to the Lapwai reservation in Idaho. Joseph still refused—

<header>MOONEY] CAUSE OF THE NEZ PERCÉ WAR</header>

Refusing to remove, the matter was turned over to General Howard. On May 3, 1877, he held the first council with Joseph and his followers at Fort Lapwai. Their ceremonial approach, which was probably in accordance with the ritual teachings of the Dreamer religion, is described by the general in this way:

> A long line of men, followed by women and children, with faces painted—the red paint extending back into the partings of the hair—the men's hair braided and tied with showy strings—decorated in dress, in hats, in blankets with various colors, in buckskin leggings and both beaded and plain moccasins; women with bright shawls or blankets, and skirts reaching to the ankle and high moccasins. All were mounted on Indian ponies as varied in color as the riders' clothing. These picturesque people, after keeping us waiting long enough for effect, came into sight from up the valley from the direction of their temporary camp just above the company gardens. They drew near to the hollow square of the post and in front of the small company to be interviewed. Then they struck up their song. They were not armed except with a few tomahawk pipes that could be smoked with peaceful tobacco or penetrate the skull of an enemy at the holder's will. Yet somehow this wild sound produced a strange effect. It made one feel glad that there were only fifty of them, and not five hundred. It was shrill and piercing; sad, like a wail, and yet defiant at its close. The Indians swept around outside the fence and made a full circuit, still keeping up the song as they rode. The buildings broke the refrain into irregular bursts of sound until the ceremony was completed. (*Howard, 1.*)

At this conference, Toohulhulsote, the principal Dreamer priest of Joseph's band, acted as spokesman for the Indians. He insisted, according to the Smohalla doctrine, that the earth was his mother, that she should not be disturbed by hoe or plow, that men should live off the natural products of nature, and that the sovereignty of the earth could not be sold or given away. Continuing, he asserted, "We never have made any trade. Part of the Indians gave up their land. I never did. The earth is part of my body, and I never gave up the earth. So long as the earth keeps me, I want to be left alone." General Howard finally ordered him under arrest, after which the Indians at last agreed to go on a reservation by June 14. (*Howard, 2.*) A few days later, councils were held with Smohalla and his people, and with Moses, another noted "renegade" chief with a considerable following further up the Columbia. Both chiefs, representing at least 500 warriors, denied any hostile intentions and agreed to go on reservations. Smohalla said, "Your law is my law. I say to you, yes. I will be on a reservation by September." (*Howard, 3.*) Groups under Joseph and other leading chiefs then went out to select suitable locations for reservations, with Joseph and his band deciding in favor of Lapwai valley. Everything was moving smoothly toward a quick and peaceful settlement of all difficulties, and the commission had already reported the successful completion of the work, when a single act of lawless violence undid the labor of weeks and triggered a bloody war. (*Comr., 22.*)

One of Joseph's band had been murdered by white men some time before, but the Indians had remained quiet. (*Comr., 23.*) Now, while the Nez Percés were gathering their livestock to move to the selected reservation, a band of white robbers attacked them, drove off the cattle, and

...killed one of the party in charge. Joseph could no longer hold back his warriors, and on June 13, 1877—one day before the date that had been set for moving onto the reservation—the enraged Nez Percé attacked the neighboring settlement on White Bird Creek, Idaho, and killed 21 people.^1^ The war began. The troops under Howard were ordered to move out. The first battle occurred on June 17 at Hangman's Creek and resulted in the loss of 34 soldiers. Then came another on July 4 with a loss of 13 more. Then, on July 12, there was another encounter by troops under General Howard himself, in which 11 soldiers were killed and 26 wounded. *(<note>Commissioner's Report, 24</note>)*

Then began one of the most remarkable displays of military leadership in the history of the Indian wars—a retreat worthy of being remembered alongside the famous "ten thousand." With barely a hundred warriors, and slowed by more than 350 vulnerable women and children—with General Howard behind him, Colonel (General) Miles in front, and Colonel Sturgis and the Crow scouts descending upon his flank—Chief Joseph led his small band up the Clearwater River and across the mountains into Montana. He turned at Big Hole Pass long enough to fight back his pursuers, causing them a loss of 60 men. He then continued by winding mountain trails southeast into Yellowstone Park, where he again turned on Howard and drove him back with additional losses of men and horses. Then he moved out of Wyoming and north into Montana again, hoping to find safety on Canadian soil, until he was intercepted near the Yellowstone by Colonel Sturgis in front with fresh troops and a detachment of Crow scouts. They fought two more battles with these forces, this time with heavy losses of men and horses themselves. Then, escaping their pursuers once more, this handful of starving and exhausted warriors—now reduced to barely fifty able-bodied men, carrying their wounded and their vulnerable families—crossed the Missouri and entered the Bear Paw Mountains. But new enemies were on their trail, and at last, when within 50 miles of the land of refuge, Miles, with a fresh army, cut off their retreat with a decisive strike, capturing more than half their horses, killing a number of the group (including Joseph's brother and the noted chief Looking Glass), and wounding 40 others. *(<note>Commissioner's Report, 25</note>)*

Forced either to surrender or to abandon the wounded, the women, and the children, Joseph chose to surrender to Colonel Miles on October 5, 1877, after a masterful retreat of more than a thousand miles. He claimed that this was “a conditional surrender, with a distinct promise that he should go back to Idaho in the spring.” *(<note>Commissioner's Report, 26</note>)* The statement of General Howard’s aide-de-camp is clear on this point:

> It was promised Joseph that he would be taken to Tongue River and kept there until spring, and then be returned to Idaho. General Sheridan, disregarding the promises made

# MOONEY] CHARACTER OF THE NEZ PERCÉS

On the battlefield, supposedly because of the difficulty of getting supplies there from Fort Buford, the commanding officer ordered the hostile warriors to Leavenworth... but a different treatment had been promised to them when they still held rifles in their hands. (*Sutherland, 1.*)

Seven years passed before that promise was kept, and in the meantime, the band had been reduced by disease and death in Indian Territory from about 450 people to about 280.

This strong testimony to the high character of Joseph and his people, and the justice of their cause, comes from the commissioner at the head of Indian affairs during and immediately after the outbreak:

> I traveled with him in Kansas and the Indian Territory for nearly a week and found him to be one of the most gentlemanly and well-behaved Indians that I ever met. He is bright and intelligent, and is anxious for the welfare of his people. . . . The Nez Percés are very much superior to the Osages and Pawnees in the Indian Territory; they are even brighter than the Poncas, and care should be taken to place them where they will thrive. . . . It will be borne in mind that Joseph has never made a treaty with the United States, and that he has never surrendered to the government the lands he claimed to own in Idaho. . . . I had occasion in my last annual report to say that “Joseph and his followers have shown themselves to be brave men and skilled soldiers, who, with one exception, have observed the rules of civilized warfare, and have not mutilated their dead enemies.” These Indians were encroached upon by white settlers on soil they believed to be their own, and when these encroachments became intolerable they were compelled, in their own estimation, to take up arms. (*Comr., 27a.*)

In all our sad Indian history, there is nothing to surpass the poignant eloquence of the surrender speech of the Nez Percé chief:

> I am tired of fighting. Our chiefs are killed. Looking Glass is dead. Toohulhulsote is dead. The old men are all dead. It is the young men who say yes or no. He who led the young men is dead. It is cold and we have no blankets. The little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills and have no blankets, no food. No one knows where they are—perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired. My heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever. (*Sec. War, 3.*)

## CHAPTER VII

# SMOHALLA AND HIS DOCTRINE

<margin>red ink bracket</margin>
->My young men shall never work. Men who work cannot dream, and wisdom comes to us in dreams. . . . You ask me to plow the ground. Shall I take a knife and tear my mother’s bosom? You ask me to dig for stone. Shall I dig under her skin for her bones? You ask me to cut grass and make hay and sell it and be rich like white men. But how dare I cut off my mother’s hair?—*<term>Smohalla</term>*.<—

We hear little of <term>Smohalla</term> for several years after the <term>Nez Percé</term> War until the opening of the Northern Pacific Railroad in 1883 once again brought the land grievances of the Indians in that region into focus. Along the <term>Yakima</term> Valley, the railroad "was located through Indian fields and orchards, with little respect for individual rights," while the crowd of prospective settlers who immediately swarmed into the country showed the typical white man's lack of consideration for the native owners. Some of the Indians, breaking away from their old traditions in order to secure permanent homes before everything was taken by the whites, had gone out and selected homesteads according to the law. However, the agent was now using the Indian police to force them to return to the reservation, "and a strange contradiction arose: the United States Indian agent on the one hand was requesting troops to drive the Indians from their homestead settlements to the reservation a hundred miles away, while on the other hand, the Indians were telegraphing military authorities to send troops to protect them from the Indian police." (*MacMurray MS.*) In addition to their land troubles, the <term>Yakima</term> and their confederated tribes—among whom were many progressive and even prosperous Indians—were restless because of constant interference with their religious ceremonies (pertaining to <term>Smohalla</term>), which a large portion of them still practiced.

To understand the nature of the Indians' dissatisfaction and, if possible, remove the cause, General Miles—then commanding the military department of the Columbia—sent Major J. W. MacMurray to the site of the disturbance in June 1884. He spent about a year on this task, visiting various villages of the upper Columbia, especially <term>P nä</term> at Priest Rapids. There he met <term>Smohalla</term>, the high priest of the <term>Dreamer theology</term>, and MacMurray's report on the subject is invaluable.

<term>Smohalla</term> is the chief of the <term>Wa'napûm</term>, a small tribe in Washington numbering probably fewer than 200 people. They are commonly known, rather vaguely, as "<term>Columbia River Indians</term>" and roam along both banks of the Columbia from the area around Priest Rapids down to the mouth of the Snake River. They are of <term>Shahaptian</term> stock and are closely related to the <term>Yakima</term> and <term>Nez Percé</term>, and they have never made a treaty with

the government. Among his own people and his disciples in the neighboring tribes, he is known as <term>Shmóqûla</term>, "The Preacher."<note>Bureau of Ethnology alphabet. Like most Native American names, it appears in a variety of forms. Other spellings are: Imoholla (misprint), Smawhola, Smohaller, Smohallow, Smohanlee, Smohollie, Smokeholer, Smokeller, Smuxale, Snohollie, Snooholler, and Somahallie. As the correct pronunciation is difficult for English speakers, I have chosen the popular form. In one official report he is mentioned as "Smohal-ler, or Big-talk, or Four Mountains"; in another, probably by misprint, as "Big talk on four mountains."</note> He is also frequently called <term>Yu’yunipí'tqana</term>, "The Shouting Mountain," based on a belief among his followers that a part of his revelation came to him from a mountain which became alive and spoke into his soul while he lay dreaming upon it. Still another name by which he is sometimes known is <term>Waip-shwa</term>, or "Rock Carrier," though the reason for this is not clear. The name that belonged to him in his youth, before he took on his priestly role, is now forgotten. For more than forty years, he has lived at the <term>Wanapûm</term> village of <term>P’nä</term> on the west bank of the Columbia River, at the foot of Priest Rapids, in what is now Yakima County, Washington. The name <term>P’nä</term> signifies "a fish weir," as this location was a major gathering place for the neighboring tribes during the salmon-fishing season. These frequent gatherings provide many opportunities for the teaching and spreading of his unique doctrines, which is clear from the fact that, while his own tribe numbers hardly forty families, his followers along the river are counted by the thousands.

<term>Smohalla</term> was born around 1815 or 1820 and is consequently now an old man, although he is still well-preserved, with his few thinning locks of hair unchanged in color. At the time of the <term>Nez Percé</term> War, he was in the full vigor of manhood. His appearance in 1884 is described by Major MacMurray in this way: "In person, <term>Smohalla</term> is unique. Short, thick-set, bald-headed, and almost hunch-backed, he is not attractive at first sight, but he has a head like Daniel Webster’s, with a deep brow over bright, intelligent eyes. He is a skilled orator. His manner is mostly of the mild, persuasive, and subtle style, but when provoked, he is full of fire and seems to use strong language effectively. His audience seemed spellbound under his magical manner, and it never lost my interest, even though he spoke in a language understood by few white men and translated for me by several different people." By another writer who met him a year later, he is described as rather small and tending toward obesity, with "a reserved and cunning but not unkind expression, and a large, well-shaped head. His manners were more polite and persuasive than is typical for Indians." He had a comfortable appearance; his moccasins and leggings were new, and he rode a fine pinto pony. (*Huggins, 1.*)

In his youth, he had frequently visited the Catholic mission of <term>Atahnam</term> among the <term>Yakima</term>, where he became familiar with the rituals of that service and also acquired a slight knowledge of French. Whether or not he was a regular member of the mission school is a disputed point, as some assert that he has never worn the white man’s dress

or had his hair cut. The influence of Catholic ceremonies is plainly visible in his own ritual performances. In his early manhood, he distinguished himself as a warrior and had already come to be regarded as a prominent man when he first began to preach his unique theology around the year 1850. There can be no question that the rapid spread of his doctrines among the tribes of the Columbia River significantly aided their confederation in the Yakima War of 1855–56. It is said that he aspired to be the leader in this war and that, to achieve this goal, he invited all the neighboring bands to attend a council at his village of <term>P’nä</term>, but he failed to accomplish his objective.

Shortly after the end of the war, probably around 1860, an incident occurred that caused a complete change in his life, establishing him as an oracle and prophet beyond any doubt and giving his religious system the authority it has retained ever since. He had already established a reputation as a medicine man and was believed to be "making medicine" against the life of Moses, the famous chief of a tribe further up the river. Moses greatly feared Smohalla’s occult powers and forced a quarrel to rid himself of his rival forever. A fight resulted, and Smohalla was nearly killed. It is reported that he was left on the ground as dead but revived enough to crawl away and get into a boat on the bank of the nearby Columbia River. Bleeding and disabled, he was carried down by the current until he was finally rescued from his dangerous position by some white men far downstream. His recovery was slow. When it was complete, being unwilling to return in disgrace to his own country and probably still fearing the anger of Moses, he decided to become a wanderer.

Then began one of the most remarkable series of journeys ever undertaken by a Native American. Traveling down the Columbia to Portland and the coast, he turned south and, stopping at various points in Oregon and California along the way, continued past San Diego into Mexico. Then, turning back, he returned through Arizona, Utah, and Nevada to his former home on the Columbia. There, he announced that he had died and been in the spirit world, and had now returned by divine command to guide his people. Since he was thought to have been killed in the encounter with Moses and had disappeared so completely until then, his awe-stricken audience readily believed they were in the presence of someone who had been taken bodily into the spirit world, from which he was now sent back as a teacher.

On the occasion of MacMurray's visit, that authority says, "Smohalla asked me many geographic questions, and I spread out a railroad map, marking the locations of Priest Rapids, Portland, and Vancouver Barracks; he traced with a straw down the coastline to below San Diego. He asked where San Bernardino was and paused long over this. He recognized the ocean, or '<term>salt chuck</term>,' along with many other geographic features and locations, but he would neither admit nor deny having been to Salt Lake City, although he admitted having been in Utah,"

<summary>Following a near-fatal conflict with Chief Moses around 1860, Smohalla undertook an extensive journey through the American West and Mexico. Upon his return, he claimed to have visited the spirit world, a revelation that solidified his authority as a prophet among the Columbia River tribes.</summary>

knew the lake and adjacent mountain chains, and said that he had seen Mormon priests getting commands directly from heaven. He spoke at length about Arizona and remarked, ‘bad Indian.’”

<margin>*</margin>
Smohalla now declared to his people that the Sa’ghalee Tyee, the Great Chief Above, was angry at their abandonment of their faith and commanded them through him to return to their original ways. He explained that their current miserable condition in the presence of the invading race was due to their having abandoned their own religion and violated the laws of nature and the teachings of their ancestors. He then explained in detail the system they must follow in the future if they wished to conform to the expressed will of the higher power. It was a system based on original indigenous mythology and customs, featuring an elaborate ritual that combined genuine Indian elements with much of what he had seen and remembered of Catholic ceremonies and military parades, along with perhaps some additions from Mormon practices.

His words made a deep impression on his listeners. They had indeed abandoned their original simplicity to a great extent and were now suffering the penalty through all the misery that had come to them with the arrival of the white race, which threatened to wipe them out from the earth. The voice of the prophet was accepted as a voice from the other world, for they knew that he had been dead and was now alive. What he said must be true and wise, for he had been everywhere and knew tribes and countries they had never heard of. Even the white men confirmed his words in this regard. He could even control the sun and the moon, for he had predicted when they would be dark, and they were dark.

If genius is a form of insanity, as has been claimed, intense religious enthusiasm would seem to have a close connection with physical as well as mental disease. Like Muhammad and Joan of Arc, and like the Shaker prophet of Puget Sound, Smohalla is subject to cataleptic trances, and it is while in this unconscious condition that he is believed to receive his revelations. MacMurray says:

> He falls into trances and lies rigid for long periods. Unbelievers have experimented by sticking needles through his flesh, cutting him with knives, and otherwise testing his sensitivity to pain, without provoking any response. It was asserted that he was surely dead because blood did not flow from the wounds. These trances always excite great interest and often alarm, as he threatens to abandon his earthly body altogether because of the disobedience of his people; on each occasion, they are in a state of suspense as to whether the Sa’ghalee Tyee will send his soul back to earth to reoccupy his body or will, on the contrary, abandon it and leave them without his guidance. It is this practice of going into long trances—out of which he comes as if from a heavy sleep and almost immediately relates his experiences in the spirit land—that gave rise to the title of “Dreamers,” or believers in dreams, commonly given to his followers by the neighboring white people. His actions are similar to those of a trance medium, and if self-hypnosis is possible, that would seem to explain it. I questioned him about his trances and hoped to have him explain them to me, but he avoided the subject and was angered when I pressed him. He clearly believes all he says about what occurs to him in this trance state. As we

...have hundreds of thousands of educated white people who believe in similar fallacies, this is no more unlikely in an Indian subjected to such influence.

In studying Smohalla, we have to deal with the same curious mixture of honest conviction and cunning deception that runs through the history of the priesthood in all ages. Like some other prophets before him, he seeks to convey the idea that he is in control of the elements and the heavenly bodies, and he has added greatly to his reputation by predicting several eclipses. This he was enabled to do by the help of an almanac and some little explanation from a party of surveyors. In this matter, however, he was soon made to realize that a little knowledge is a dangerous thing. He could not get another almanac, and his astronomical prophecies came to an abrupt end at the end of the first year. Concerning this, Major MacMurray says:

> He showed me an almanac of a preceding year and asked me to readjust it for eclipses, as it did not work as it had formerly done. I explained that Washington (the Naval Observatory) made new ones every year, and that old ones could not be fixed up to date. He had probably obtained this one from the station agent at the railroad, now superseded by a new agent, who had cut off Smohalla's supply of astronomical data. My inability to repair the 1882 almanac for use in predicting in 1884 cost me much of his respect as a wise man from the east. (*MacMurray MS.*)

Smohalla also had a blank book containing mysterious characters, some of which resembled letters of the alphabet, and which he said were records of events and prophecies. MacMurray was unable to decide whether they were mnemonic symbols <note>symbols used as memory aids</note> or were simply meaningless marks intended to foster among his followers the impression of his superior wisdom. It is probable that they were genuine mnemonic symbols invented by himself for his own purposes, as such systems, devised and used by single individuals or families and unintelligible to others, are by no means rare among those who may be called the literary men of our indigenous tribes.

As their principal troubles arose out of the disputed title to their lands, Major MacMurray was asked by the Indians to explain the Indian homestead law and how white men divided land. This was carefully done with the aid of a checkerboard, and they were shown how the land was mapped out into equal squares arranged on straight lines so that every man could find his own. They were then urged by the officer to apply for homesteads and settle upon them so as to avoid further trouble with the new settlers who were pouring into the country. Smohalla replied that he knew all this, but he did not like the new law, as it was against nature. He then went on to expound in detail the Indian <term>cosmogony</term>. Said he:

> I will tell you about it. Once the world was all water and God lived alone. He was lonely; he had no place to put his foot, so he scratched the sand up from the bottom and made the land, and he made the rocks, and he made trees, and he made a man; and the man had wings and could go anywhere. The man was lonely, and God made a woman. They ate fish from the water, and God made the deer and other animals, and he sent the man to hunt and told the woman to cook the meat and to

<page-num>721</page-num>
# MOONEY] SMOHALLA ON THE COSMOS

They dressed the skins. Many more men and women grew up, and they lived on the banks of the great river whose waters were full of salmon. The mountains contained much game, and there were buffalo on the plains. There were so many people that the stronger ones sometimes oppressed the weak and drove them from the best fisheries, which they claimed as their own. They fought and nearly all were killed, and their bones can still be seen in the hills. God was very angry at this and he took away their wings and commanded that the lands and fisheries should be shared by all who lived upon them; that they were never to be marked off or divided, but that the people should enjoy the fruits that God planted in the land, the animals that lived upon it, and the fishes in the water. God said he was the father and the earth was the mother of mankind; that nature was the law; that the animals, fish, and plants obeyed nature, and that only man was sinful. This is the old law.

<margin>✓</margin>
I know all kinds of men. First there were my people (the Indians); God made them first. Then he made a Frenchman <note>referring to the Canadian voyagers of the Hudson Bay Company</note>, and then he made a priest <note>priests accompanied these expeditions of the Hudson Bay Company</note>. A long time after that came Boston men <note>Americans are called this in the Chinook jargon because the first of our nation arrived at the Columbia River in 1796 in a ship from Boston</note>, and then King George men <note>the English</note>. Later came black men, and last God made a Chinese man with a tail. He is of no importance and has to work all the time like a woman. All these are new people. Only the Indians are of the old stock. After a while, when God is ready, he will drive away all the people except those who have obeyed his laws.

Those who cut up the lands or sign papers for lands will be cheated of their rights and will be punished by God’s anger. Moses was bad. God did not love him. He sold his people's houses and the graves of their dead. It is a bad message that comes from Washington. It is not a good law that would take my people away from me to make them sin against the laws of God.

> You ask me to plow the ground! Shall I take a knife and tear my mother's bosom? Then when I die she will not take me to her bosom to rest.
> 
> You ask me to dig for stone! Shall I dig under her skin for her bones? Then when I die I cannot enter her body to be born again.
> 
> You ask me to cut grass and make hay and sell it, and be rich like white men! But how dare I cut off my mother's hair?
> 
> It is a bad law, and my people cannot obey it. I want my people to stay with me here. All the dead men will come to life again. Their spirits will come to their bodies again. We must wait here in the homes of our fathers and be ready to meet them in the bosom of our mother. (*MacMurray MS.*)

The idea that the earth is the mother of all created things lies at the base, not only of the Smohalla religion, but of the theology of the Indian tribes generally and of primitive races all over the world. This explains <term>Tecumtha</term>'s reply to Harrison: "The sun is my father and the earth is my mother. On her bosom I will rest." In the Indian mind the corn, fruits, and edible roots are the gifts which the earth-mother gives freely to her children. Lakes and ponds are her eyes, hills are her breasts, and streams are the milk flowing from her breasts. Earthquakes and underground noises are signs of her displeasure at the wrongdoing of her children. Especially are the malarial fevers, which often follow extensive disturbance of the surface by excavation or otherwise, held to be direct punishments for the crime of cutting into her bosom.

Smohalla's chief supporter and assistant at the ceremonies was <term>Kotai'aqan</term>, or Coteea'kun, as MacMurray spells it, of the <term>Yakima</term> tribe.

<summary>Smohalla explains the "old law" of communal land and the sacred nature of the Earth as a mother, rejecting agriculture and mining as desecrations. He outlines a racial hierarchy created by God and predicts a future restoration where only those faithful to the old laws will remain.</summary>

The name [Kotai'aqan] refers to a brood of young ducks scattering in alarm. He was the son of Kamai'äkan, the great war chief of the Yakima. He also gave MacMurray the story of the cosmos, which agrees with the one obtained from Smohalla but is more detailed:

> The world was all water, and Saghalee Tyee was above it. He threw up large quantities of mud from the water in shallow places, and that created the land. Some was piled so high that it froze hard, and the rains that fell turned into snow and ice. Some of the earth was made into hard rocks, and anyone could see that it had not changed—it was only harder. We have no records of the past, but we have heard from our ancestors from long ago that Saghalee Tyee threw down many of the mountains he had made. It is all as our fathers told us, and we can see that it is true when we are hunting for game or berries in the mountains. I did not see it happen. He made trees grow, and he made a man out of a ball of mud and instructed him on what he should do. When the man became lonely, he made a woman as his companion and taught her how to dress skins, gather berries, and make baskets from the bark of roots, which he taught her how to find.
> 
> She was asleep and dreaming about her lack of knowledge on how to please man, and she prayed to Saghalee Tyee to help her. He breathed on her and gave her something that she could not see, hear, smell, or touch; it was preserved in a little basket, and through it, all the arts of design and skilled handiwork were passed down to her descendants.
> 
> Despite all the benefits they enjoyed, there was quarreling among the people, and the Earth Mother was angry. The mountains that overhung the river at the Cascades were thrown down, damming the stream and destroying forests and whole tribes, burying them under the rocks. (*MacMurray MS.*)

Regarding the wonderful little basket, MacMurray states that Kotai'aqan gave him a very ancient drum-shaped basket, about 2 ½ inches in diameter, to give to his wife so that she might also be inspired. Concerning the catastrophe mentioned in the last paragraph, he goes on to say:

> The Cascade Range, where it crosses the Columbia River, shows enormous cross-sections of lava, and at its base are petrified tree trunks that have been covered and hidden from view, except where the flow of the mighty stream has exposed them. Indians have told me from their own knowledge that bones of animals from *siah*, or the long ago, are buried deep under these flows of basalt or volcanic tufa. Traditions of the great landslide at the Cascades are numerous but vary little in form. According to one account, the mountain tops fell together and formed a kind of arch under which the water flowed, until the overhanging rocks finally fell into the stream and created a dam or gorge. Since the rock is columnar basalt, which is very brittle and easily crumbled, this was not impossible, and the landscape suggests such a massive avalanche. The submerged trees are clearly visible near this location. I have not seen animal remains, but these salmon-eating Indians have lived on the river's bank for countless ages and know every feature of their surroundings through constant association over generations; they naturally connect these facts with their religious theories. (*MacMurray MS.*)

In an article titled “The submerged trees of the Columbia River,” in *Science* from February 18, 1887, the geologist Major Clarence E. Dutton also notes the peculiar formation at the Cascades and mentions the Indian tradition of a natural bridge over the river at this point.

<meta>This page continues the account of Kotai'aqan (referred to here as Coteeakun) regarding the spiritual beliefs of the Yakima people, specifically the return of spirits to the earth and his views on peaceful coexistence with white men, contrasted with the more isolationist views of the prophet Smohalla.</meta>

at a certain time, would be reoccupied by the spirits which now live on the mountaintops, watching their descendants on earth and waiting for the resurrection to come. The voices of these spirits of the dead can be heard at all times in the mountains, and they often answer back when spoken to. Mourners who wail for their dead hear spirit voices replying, and know they will always remain near them. No man knows when it will come, and only those who have observed nature's laws and adhered to the faith of their ancestors will have their bones preserved and be certain of an earthly home for their spirits. He wanted me to confirm this.

Coteeakun was peaceful and gentle. He said all men were like brothers to him and he hoped all would live together. He had been told that white, black, and all other kinds of men originally lived in tents, as the red men always have done, and that God in former times came to communicate with white men. He thought there could be only one Saghalee Tyee <note>The Great Spirit or Chief Above</note>, in which case white and red men would live on a common level. We came from one source of life and in time would "grow from one stem again. It would be like a stick that the whites held by one end and the Indians by the other until it was broken, and it would be made again into one stick."

Some of the wilder Indians to the north have more aggressive ideas regarding the final cataclysm which is to overturn the mountains again and bring back the peaceful days of the long past. As the whites and the others arrived only within the lifetime of the fathers of these Indians, they are not to be included in the benefits of the resurrection, but are to be overturned along with everything that the white man's civilization has placed upon the current surface of the land.

Coteeakun was for progress—limited progress, it is true—to the extent of permanent homes and agriculture, but he did not want his people to leave their villages or to abandon their religious faith. They were nearly all inclined to work for wages among the farmers, and had orchards and some domestic animals upon whose produce they lived, besides the fish from the rivers. Smohalla opposed anything that related to civilization, and had neither cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, nor chickens, and not a single tree or vegetable was grown anywhere in his neighborhood. Kowse (*Peucedanum cous*), kamas (*Camassia esculenta*), berries, fish, and the game of the mountains alone provided food to his people, whom he advised to resist every advance of civilization as improper for a true Indian and in violation of the faith of their ancestors. I found, however, that he was willing to advise his people to take up lands and adopt the white man's way if the government would pension him as it had pensioned Chief Moses; so, while I thought he believed in his religion as much as other religious leaders do in theirs, he was tainted by the mercenary desire to live off his followers unless otherwise provided for by the government.

From Captain E. L. Huggins, Second Cavalry, who visited Smohalla about the same time, we obtain further information concerning the prophet's personality and doctrines. When Smohalla was urged to follow the example of other Indians who had adopted the white man's way, he replied, "No one has any respect for these book Indians. Even the white men like me better and treat me better than they do the book Indians. My young men shall never work. Men who work cannot dream, and wisdom comes to us in dreams."

When it was argued that the whites worked and yet knew more than the Indians, he replied that the white man's wisdom was poor and weak and of no value to Indians, who must learn the highest wisdom from dreams and from participating in the Dreamer ceremonies. Being pressured to explain the nature of this higher knowledge, he replied, "Each person must learn the highest wisdom for himself. It cannot be taught. You have the wisdom of your race. Be content."

When the officer argued that even the Indians had to work hard during the fishing season to gather food for winter, the prophet answered:

<margin>*</margin>
> “This work lasts only for a few weeks. Besides, it is natural work and does them no harm. But the work of the white man hardens the soul and body. Nor is it right to tear up and mutilate the earth as white men do.”

In response to the officer’s assertion that the Indians also dug roots and were even then digging <term>kamas</term> in the mountains, he replied:

> “We simply take the gifts that are freely offered. We harm the earth no more than an infant’s fingers would harm its mother’s breast. But the white man tears up large tracts of land, digs deep ditches, cuts down forests, and changes the whole face of the earth. You know very well this is not right. Every honest man,” he said, looking at me searchingly, “knows in his heart that this is all wrong. But the white men are so greedy they do not consider these things.”

He asserted that the Indians were now so helpless before the white men that they would cease to exist unless they had assistance from a higher power, but that if they heeded the sacred message, they would receive strong and sudden help as surely as the spring comes after winter. When some doubt was expressed regarding his own faith in these things, he asked pointedly:

> “Do the white teachers believe what they teach?”

“It is said, Smohalla, that you hate all white men.”

> “It is not true. But the whites have caused us great suffering. Many years ago, Dr. Whitman made a long journey to the east to get a bottle of poison for us. He was gone about a year, and after he came back, strong and terrible diseases broke out among us. The Indians killed Dr. Whitman, but it was too late. He had uncorked his bottle and all the air was poisoned. Before that, there was little sickness among us, but since then many of us have died. I have had children and grandchildren, but they are all dead. My last grandchild, a young woman of 16, died last month. If only her infant could have lived”— his voice faltered slightly, but with scarcely a pause he continued in his former tone, “I worked hard to save them, but my medicine would not work as it used to.”

He rejected the idea that the Indians had benefited from the coming of the whites, and especially denied that they had obtained ponies from that source. His statement on this point may be of interest to those who believe that the horse is native to America:

> “What! The white man gave us ponies? Oh, no; we had ponies long before we ever saw white people. The Great Spirit gave them to us. Our horses were swifter and more enduring, too, in those days, before they were mixed with the white man’s horses.”

He went on to tell how the Indians had befriended the first explorers who came among them and how ungrateful their later reward had been, saying: “We are now so few and weak that we can offer no resistance, and their preachers have persuaded them to let a few of us

Our knowledge of the Smohalla ritual is derived from the account given by Major MacMurray and from the statements of Yakima and Pälus informants. The officer’s account is that of an intelligent observer who noted ceremonies closely, but without fully understanding their meaning. The Indian account is that of initiates and true believers, one of them being the regular interpreter for the Smohalla services on the Yakima reservation.

The officer had already seen the ceremonial performances at the Indian villages at Celilo and Umatilla in Oregon, and at Tumwater and Yakima Gap in Washington, but he found its greatest development at the source: the home of Smohalla at Priest Rapids. His account is so full of interest that we give it almost in its entirety.

*While still several miles away, his party discovered the village, the houses extending along the bank of the river, with several flags attached to long poles fluttering in the wind. The trail from the mountains was winding and difficult, but at last—*

> We reached the plain and were met by a procession, headed by Smohalla in person, all dressed in gorgeous clothing and mounted on their best horses. We made our way through sagebrush and sand dunes to the village street; not a soul was visible, but from the mat-roofed salmon houses there came an indescribable chorus of bell ringing, drum beating, and screeching. I noticed that the street was neatly swept and well sprinkled—an unusual thing in any Indian village. This, Smohalla said, was in my honor and to show that his people had clean tastes. Our procession passed on beyond the village to a new canvas tent, which had a brush shade to keep off the sun and was lined and carpeted with new and very pretty matting. Smohalla said this had been prepared especially for me, and was to be my house as long as I should stay with him. To top it all off, he had built a bench for me, having sent more than 90 miles for the nails. Fresh salmon, caught in a unique trap among the rocks and broiled on a plank, were regularly provided to my party, and with hardtack and coffee of our own supplying we had enough to eat and drink. Our own blankets provided sleeping arrangements. The river was within two yards of our tent door and served as a spacious washroom.
> 
> When I awoke the next morning, the sound of drums was heard again, and for days it continued. I do not remember that there was any pause except for a few minutes at a time. Seven bass drums were used for the purpose. I was invited to be present, and took great interest in the ceremonies, which I shall try to describe.
> 
> There was a small open space to the north of the larger house, which was Smohalla’s residence and the village assembly room as well. This space was enclosed by a whitewashed fence made of boards that had drifted down the river. In the middle was a flagstaff with a rectangular flag resembling a target. In the center of the flag was a round red patch. The background was yellow, representing grass, which has a yellow hue there in summer. A green border indicated the boundary of the world, the hills being moist and green near their tops. At the top of the flag was a small extension of blue color, with a white star in the center. Smohalla explained: “This is my flag, and it represents the world. God told me to look after my people—all are my people. There are four directions in the world—north and south and

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION
## THE SMOHALLA RITUAL

“East and west—I have traveled all those ways. This is the center. I live here. The red spot is my heart; everyone can see it. The yellow grass grows everywhere around this place. The green mountains are far away, surrounding the whole world. Beyond them, there is only water—salt water. The blue <note>referring to the blue cloth strip</note> is the sky, and the star is the North Star. That star never changes; it is always in the same place. I keep my heart fixed on that star. I never change.”

There are frequent services, including a sort of procession around the outside of the fence. The prophet and a small boy with a bell enter the enclosure where, after raising the flag, the prophet delivers a type of sermon. Captains or class leaders give instructions to the ranks; the men and women, divided into different classes, march in single file to the sound of drums. There seems to be a regular system of signals given at the prophet’s command by the boy with the bell, at which the people chant loudly or softly, quickly or slowly, or remain silent. These outdoor services occurred several times each day.

Smohalla invited me to participate in what he considered a grand ceremonial service within the larger house. This house was built with a framework of sturdy logs placed upright in the ground and roofed over with brush, or with canvas in rainy weather.

<image-desc>A rectangular heraldic flag (Figure 64) with a dark, horizontally-lined field. In the upper center is a white five-pointed star. In the lower center is a large white circle containing a smaller, thick black ring. The caption below the image reads: "FIG. 64—Smohalla's flag (heraldic)."</image-desc>

->FIG. 64—Smohalla's flag (heraldic).<-

The sides of the building consisted of bark and rush matting. It was about 75 feet long by 25 feet wide. Singing and drumming had been going on for some time when I arrived. The air echoed with the voices of hundreds of Indians, both male and female, and the beating of drums. Inside, the room was dimly lit. Smoke curled from a fire on the floor at the far end and filled the atmosphere. The ceiling was hung with hundreds of salmon, split and drying in the smoke.

The scene was a strange one. On either side of the room stood a row of twelve women, standing straight with their arms crossed and hands extended so that their fingertips touched their shoulders. They kept time with the drums and their own voices by balancing on the balls of their feet and tapping their heels on the floor, while they chanted with varying pitch and tempo. The excitement and constant repetition exhausted them, and I heard that others besides Smohalla had seen visions during their trances, though I saw no one who would admit to it or explain anything about it. I suspected they feared their own actions, and that real death might come to them during this imitation of death.

Those on the right side were dressed in red garments, in an attempt at uniformity. Those on the left wore costumes of white buckskin, said to be very ancient ceremonial outfits, decorated with red and blue trimmings. All wore large, round silver plates or whatever other glittering ornaments they owned. A canvas covered the floor, and on it knelt the men and boys in lines of seven. As a rule, each group of seven wore shirts of the same color. The tallest stood in front, with their size decreasing steadily toward the rear. Children and elderly women filled in any remaining space. In front, on a mattress, knelt Smohalla with his left hand covering his heart. To his right was the boy bell-ringer in a similar pose. Smohalla wore a white garment which he chose to call a priest’s gown, but it was simply a white cloth shirt with a colored stripe down the back.

The ceremony took place in a large longhouse at Priest Rapids, with participants arranged strictly by gender, height, and costume color.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the Smohalla religion, detailing the observers and participants in the ritual, the lineage of its leaders, and the geographic spread of the faith among the tribes of the Columbia River region.</meta>

MOONEY] SMOHALLA RITUAL

My two assistants and I were seated on a mattress about 10 feet in front of the prophet, which fortunately placed us near the door and, incidentally, near fresh air. There were two other witnesses, Indians from distant villages, who sat at one side with Smohalla's son looking on.

Smohalla's son was said to be in training as his successor. He was a young man, apparently about 23 years old, tall, slender, and active in movement, and he commonly kept himself apart from the body of the people. He was much darker than his father. His dress was brilliant in style and color. He ordinarily wore a short gown or surplice, sometimes yellow and at other times sky blue, with ornate decorations of appliqué stars or moons, cut from bright-colored cloths. The sleeves were extravagantly trimmed with beads and silver ornaments. He knelt at the right of the group as the place of honor. On his left was Coteeakun, the head man of the Indian village at Union Gap, on the Yakima reservation. The third man was Coteeakun's brother, a most intelligent and progressive Indian. (*MacMurray MS.*)

From Charles Ike, an intelligent half-blood interpreter on the Yakima reservation, who is also the regular interpreter of the Smohalla ritual services at the Yakima village of Pa'kiut, we obtain additional interesting details concerning the ceremony as performed there, along with the underlying religious teachings.

As it is currently taught, the religion finds adherents among probably all the tribes along the Columbia from near the British border down to the Wushqûm tribe at The Dalles, with the exception, perhaps, of the Klikatat, who are nearly all Catholics. The two chief centers are at P'nä or Priest Rapids, where Smohalla in person regularly preaches to about 120 hearers, and at Pa'kiut, at Union Gap on the Yakima reservation, where, until his death a short time ago, Tianä'ni regularly conducted the services for about 300 of his tribe. At each place is a church or meeting house built as already described.

The former high priest of the doctrine among the Yakima, and the right-hand man of Smohalla himself, was Kotai'aqan, already mentioned, the son of the great war chief Kamai'äkan. It is even asserted that he was the originator of the system. However this may be, it is certain that he had much to do with formulating both the dogmas and the ritual. In temper, he was more gentle than Smohalla and more disposed to meet civilization halfway. Upon his death, about 1890, he was succeeded by his stepson, Tianä'ni, or "Many Wounds," who filled the office until about October 1892, when he was murdered near his home by two drunken Indians. He was succeeded in the chieftainship by a younger son of Kotai'aqan named Sha'awě (or Shaw-wawa Kootiacan), and in his priestly functions by a man known to the whites as Billy John.

The regular services take place on Sunday, in the morning, afternoon, and evening. Sunday has been held sacred among the Nez Percés and neighboring tribes for more than sixty years, as the result of the teachings of the Hudson Bay officers. The prairie tribes also, having learned that Sunday is the great "medicine day" of the whites, now select it by preference for their own religious ceremonies of the Ghost dance and the mescal. There are also services during the week, besides special

MOONEY] SMOHALLA FORM OF WORSHIP 729

At the eastern end of the building at Pa'kiut are the flags: the center one is blue, representing the sky; another is white, representing the earthly light; and the third is yellow, representing the heavenly light of the spirit world. Blue, white, and yellow are the sacred colors of this system, as well as those of the Shakers, who will be described later. Upon entering, the worshippers arrange themselves in two lines along the sides of the building. The men and boys stand along the northern wall, while the women and girls stand along the southern wall, and all face toward the center. The first man to enter takes his place on the north side nearest the door; the next one stands just beyond him, and so on. When their turn comes, the women and girls make the full circuit along the northern side, then, turning at the far end, take their places in reverse order along the southern wall. In the open space between the rows is a floor-walker, whose duty is to see that everyone is in the right place. All are dressed as much as possible in the finest style of the traditional Indian costume, including buckskin and shell ornaments. Their faces are painted yellow, white, or red with Indian paints, and they carry eagle feathers in their right hands (plates XC, XCI; figure 66).

<image-desc>Figure 66 is a technical diagram depicting the arrangement of worshippers inside a building during a Smohalla service. A corresponding row of circles representing "WOMEN AND GIRLS" lines the southern wall. In the center of the room is a solid black dot representing the "FLOOR-WALKER," and near the entrance on the right is the "DOORKEEPER."</image-desc>

->FIG. 66—Diagram showing the arrangement of worshippers at a Smohalla service.<-

At the far end, facing the door, sits the high priest, while his "interpreter" stands just behind him. To his left, the three drummers sit on the ground with their large drums in front of them. The high priest carries a large bell in his left hand and a smaller one in his right.

Dishes of freshly cooked salmon and jars of water, along with a plentiful supply of other food, are arranged in front of the devotees. After a preliminary ceremony resembling a litany—in which the principal articles of their theology are recited in a question-and-answer format by the entire body of worshippers—the high priest gives the command, "Take water," at which point everyone raises a cup of water to their lips. Next comes the command, "Now drink," and each person takes a sip. At the words, "Now the salmon," each person picks up a portion of fish, which they put into their mouth at the next command, "Now eat." Finally, the command, "Now help yourselves," serves as the signal for everyone to begin eating the provisions.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Smohalla ritual, moving from the setup and costume to the specific choreography of the dance and the structure of the liturgical songs.</meta>

<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

When everyone has satisfied their hunger, the remains of the feast are cleared away and the "dance" begins. At a signal given by a single stroke of the bell in the high priest's left hand, everyone stands up in line on either side of the building. At another stroke of the bell, everyone puts their right hand on their chest. Another tap of the bell, and they bring their right hand out in front of the body. With another tap, they begin to move their right hands backward and forward like fans in front of their chests; they continue this throughout the dance, also keeping time to the singing by balancing alternately upon their toes and heels, as previously described, without moving from their places. Ritual songs are sung throughout the rest of the service, in time with the movements of the dancers and the sounds of the drums, all regulated by the strokes of the bell.

Between songs, anyone who wishes to speak steps out into the open space. With a single tap of the bell, the high priest then summons his "interpreter" who stands behind him. The interpreter comes forward and stands beside the speaker, a few feet in front and to the right of the high priest. The speaker then tells their story in a low tone—usually a trance vision of the spirit world—to the interpreter, who repeats it in a loud voice to the company. At the end of the recital, the high priest gives the signal with the bell, and then everyone raises their right hand with a loud "Ai!" (Yes!). The high priest himself sometimes speaks to the people through the interpreter as well; at other times, he speaks to them directly.

Each song is repeated until the high priest gives the signal with the bell to stop. In the native language, most of the songs consist of seven lines. At the end of the first line, the high priest taps the bell once; at the end of the second line, he taps it twice, and so on until the end of the song, when he rings the bell loudly and continuously, and everyone raises their hands with a loud "Ai!" Then the song leader, who stands with a feather fan between the high priest and the drummers, starts the next song.

The first song is performed by everyone standing motionless, with their right hand on their chest and their eyes cast down. It may be translated as:

> Truly, truly, Our Brother made the body.
> He gave it a spirit, and the body moved.
> Then he counted out the words for us to speak.

Another begins:

> Truly, Our Brother put salmon in the water to be our food.

Another begins:

> Oh, brothers! Oh, sisters!
> When the light first struck this world, it lit the world forever.

<term>Our Brother</term> (<term>Nämi Piäp</term>) is the term used when referring to the creating spirit, instead of "our father," as we might expect them to say.

On leaving, at the close of the ceremony, the person nearest the high priest passes around in front of him and down along in front of the

### *Tribes of the Columbia region*

The following overview will give a good general idea of the location and numbers of the tribes in the Columbia region, from the Canadian border down to the Cascades, including all those under the influence of the Smohalla religion. Except when taken from well-known authorities such as Lewis and Clark, Stevens, Gibbs, etc., the information provided is the result of personal investigation and work with the Yakima and Palus Indians. The general boundaries of the tribes west of the Cascade range, including those who follow the Shaker religion, are also shown on the accompanying map (plate LXXXVIII), but our information regarding this region is too thin to be certain.

**KUTENAI** (Kitunahan stock).—*Synonyms:* Arcs Plats, Cotonné, Cottonoi, Coutanie, Flatbow, Kitunaha, Kootenai, Koutaine, Kutneha, Skalzi, Tushepaw (Lewis and Clark, 1805), White-tailed Deer People (Clark, Indian Sign Language). The Kutenai, properly Kituna'qa, form a distinct linguistic stock and live primarily on the Canadian side around the Kutenai river and lake, but they also extend across the border into northern Idaho and northwestern Montana. Their expansion southward dates back to their peace treaty with the Flatheads about ninety years ago. Together with the Flatheads, they used to come down from the mountains in the autumn to hunt buffalo at the headwaters of the Missouri. They are mentioned by Lewis and Clark in 1805 under the name of Tushepaw, with bands identified as Ootlashoot, Micksucksealton (?), and Hohilpo living in the mountains and on Clark Fork within United States territory. According to Gatschet, Tu'shipa is a collective term used by the Shoshoni for the tribes living north of them, including the Nez Percés and others, as well as the Kutenai. Some of the Kutenai joined the Flatheads and Upper Pend d’Oreilles in a treaty with the government in 1855 and are now on the Flathead (Jocko) reservation in Montana. They are probably all Catholics. Others, living in northern Idaho, have never entered into treaty agreements and may be followers of Smohalla. The best estimates from the last fifty years place the population of those within the United States between 400 and 450.

**PEND D'OREILLE** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Calispel, Coospellar (Lewis and Clark), Kahlispelm, Kalispelines, Kalispelusses, Kellespem, Kullas-Palus, Ku'shpĕlu (a Yakima or Palus form), Papshpûn-lĕma or "people of the great fir trees" (Yakima name), Pend d'Oreilles or

“ear-rings” (French name), Ponderas. The Pend d’Oreilles occupied the territory along the river and lake of the same name in Idaho and Washington, directly southwest of the Kutenai. They are commonly distinguished as the Upper Pend d’Oreilles, located on the lake, and the Lower Pend d’Oreilles, on both banks of the river. They are the Coospellar mentioned by Lewis and Clark in 1805. They used to cross the mountains every year to hunt buffalo on the Missouri River. Since 1844, they and most of the other Salishan tribes of this region have been under the influence of Catholic missionaries. The Upper Pend d’Oreilles joined with the Flatheads and Kutenai in a treaty with the government in 1855 and are now on the Flathead reservation in Montana. Some of the Lower band joined them there in 1887. Others are on the Cœur d’Alêne reservation in Idaho, a few are with Moses <note>Chief Moses of the Sinkiuse-Columbia</note> on the Columbia in Washington, and the rest are still in their original territory, never having entered into treaty agreements. The entire tribe numbers about 1,000 people.

**Colville** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Chaudière (French name), Chualpay, Kettle Falls, Quiarlpi or “basket people” (Hale), Schrooyelpi, Schwogelpi, Schwoyelpi, Swielpee, Wheelpoo (Lewis and Clark). They originally occupied the territory on the Colville and Kettle rivers and on both sides of the Columbia from Kettle Falls down to the Spokane River in Washington, extending north into British territory to about the lower Arrow Lake. They are mentioned by Lewis and Clark under the name of Wheelpoo. Kettle Falls on the Columbia, within their territory, was the major salmon fishing resort for all the tribes of this region, and here, in 1846, the Catholic mission of Saint Paul was established. As a result of this missionary work, all of these Salishan tribes, except for the Sanpoil, Nespelim, Mitaui, and a part of the Spokan, are now Catholics. In 1854, according to Stevens, the original Shwoyelpi were nearly extinct and their places had been filled by Indians from neighboring tribes. Without ever having entered into any treaty with the government, they were assigned in 1872 to the Colville reservation in Washington, which had been set apart for the tribes of that section. They were reported to number 616 in 1870 and only 301 in 1892.

**Lake** or **Senijextee** (Salishan stock).—These owned the territory on both sides of the Columbia in Washington, from about Kettle Falls northward into British Columbia to the vicinity of Arrow Lake. They are now on the Colville reservation in Washington and number about 350, with perhaps a few others across the boundary. They may be identical with the Lahannas mentioned by Lewis and Clark.

**Spokan** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Lartielo (Lewis and Clark), Sarlilso (Gibbs), Sinhumanish, Sinkoman (Kutenai name), Spokihnish, Spokomish, Zingomenes. They are commonly distinguished as the Upper Spokan or Sineeguomenah, the Middle or Sintootoo, and the Lower or Chekis-schee (Winans, Commissioner, 1870). Spokan is the name given to them by the Cœur d’Alênes; Sinkoman is their Kutenai name, while the Lartielo or Sarlilso of Lewis and Clark is simply a bad misprint for Sintootoo, the

They formerly owned the entire basin of the Spokane River in Washington, extending into Idaho.
