**CŒUR D'ALÊNE** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms*: Pointed Hearts, Q’ma’shpăl or “kamas people” (so called by the Yakima), Skeechaway, Skeetsomish (Lewis and Clark), Skitsămŭq (Pälus name), Skitswish, Stietshoi. They occupied the lake and river bearing their name in Idaho and the adjacent headwaters of the Spokane. A part of this territory they held jointly with the Spokan, whose language they speak. In 1892, they numbered 427 on the Cœur d'Alêne reservation in Idaho.

**SANPOIL** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms*: Hai-ai’nĭma (Yakima name), Hihighenimmo (Lewis and Clark), Ipoilq (another Yakima name), N’pochle (Stevens), Sans Puelles, Sinapoils, Sinipouals, Sinpaivelish, Sinpohellechach, Sinpoilschne, Siur Poils. The name by which this tribe is commonly known is sometimes written in the French form *Sans Poils*, meaning “without bristles” or “hairless,” but it is more probably an Indian word. They occupy the country on the Sanpoil River in Washington, now included within the Colville reservation, and are closely allied with the Nespelim. These two tribes are the most aboriginal in eastern Washington and adhere strictly to their primitive customs and religion. The two tribes were described as follows by Winans, the government farmer, in 1870:

> They have never received any presents from the government, although they have frequently been asked to do so. They seem suspicious of the whites and are the least civilized and most independent of any of the tribes of the territory. They are rich in horses and cattle, possessing all the comforts they know how to enjoy, and it appears their only fear is that they will be interfered with by the government. They are perfectly contented with their condition and would not accept anything from the government if offered, except a religious instructor and a doctor.

Some years later, they were brought under the reservation system, and a change came over the spirit of their dream. In 1892, we are told officially that “the Sanpuell Indians are the worst people that I have anything to do with. . . . They are surly, ignorant, and filthy,” notwithstanding which they still “have the same religious prejudice as the Nespelims about receiving aid from the government.” Regarding the Nespelim, the same intelligent witness tells us that “they are a peculiar class of Indians, having a religion of their own.” The religion of the two tribes is aboriginal and is similar to the Smohalla doctrine in principle, although not in ceremony. In 1892, the Sanpoil were estimated at 300.

**NESPELIM** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms*: Inspellum, Sinspeelish. They live on the north bank of the Columbia in Washington, along the Nespelim River and down to the junction of the Okinagan, and on the opposite side of

**OKANAGAN** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Oakinacken, Okinakane, Okiwahkine. They occupy the whole basin of the Okanagan River in Washington, extending north into British Columbia, and including the Similkameen River. The Okanagan were an important tribe or confederacy divided into a number of bands, some of which have also at times been considered as belonging to the Spokan, while others are commonly recognized as distinct tribes. Ross lists their "twelve tribes" as follows: Skamoynumach, Kewaughtchenunaugh, Pisscow (Piskwaus), Incomecane'took, Tsillane (Chelan), Intie'took (Entiatook), Battlelemuleemauch or Meatwho (Mitaui), Inspellum (Nespelim), Sinpohellechach (Sanpoil), Sinwhoyelppetook (Colville), Samilkanuigh (Similkameen), and Oakinacken (Okanagan). They are now included within the Colville agency and are Catholics. They were estimated at 340 in 1870 and reported as numbering 405 in 1892.

**MITAUI** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Battlelemuleemauch, Meatwho, Meshons, Meteowwee (Lewis and Clark), Methows, Mithouies. They formerly lived on the west side of the Columbia, including the basins of the Methow, Lake Chelan, and Entiatook River. Lewis and Clark met some of them in 1805 below the mouth of the Walla Walla. They are closely connected with the Piskwaus and Isle de Pierres. They now reside in the Nespelim Valley on the Colville reservation, confederated with the Isle de Pierres under Chief Moses. The two tribes were reported at 390 in 1892. A few others live in the neighborhood of Kittitas near the Yakima tribe. See *Piskwaus*.

**ISLE DE PIERRE** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Columbias, Linkinse, Sinkiuse. They originally occupied the country in Washington from the Columbia eastward to the Grande Coulée, extending from about the mouth of the Grande Coulée down nearly to Crab Creek. *Isle de Pierre* is the French name of Rock Island in the Columbia at the mouth of the Wenatchee. For a long time, under their noted chief Moses, they refused to recognize the authority of the government or to go on a reservation. Now, however, they are settled in the Nespelim Valley, on the Colville reservation. They were reported to number 390 in 1892 and are described as "true, genuine Indians in every sense of the word." Their chief, Moses, the enemy and rival of Smohalla, was described in 1870 as follows:

> "Moses, the head chief, has been a great warrior. He was foremost in the fights of 1858 with Colonels Steptoe and Wright, and was severely wounded a number of times; however, because he did not die, the Indians believe he has a charmed life. He is medium-sized, about 45 years old, noble-looking, straight as an arrow, and never breaks his word. He has more influence than any other chief east of the Cascade Mountains in the territory. He comes closer to being the kind of chief one reads about."

**WA'NAPÛM** (Shahaptian stock).---*Synonyms*: Columbia River Indians, Sokulks. This is the tribe for which Smohalla is the chief and high priest. They are a small band, likely numbering fewer than 200 people, and are closely connected linguistically and politically with the Yakima, Pä'lus, and Nez Percés. Wanapûm is the name by which they are known to these related tribes and means "river people"; it is derived from *wana* or *wala*, "river" (particularly the Columbia River), and *pûm* or *pam*, "people or tribal country." Along with the other non-treaty tribes of this region, they are known to white settlers by the vague name "Columbia River Indians." They are the same as the Sokulk encountered by Lewis and Clark at the mouth of the Snake River and described as living further up the Columbia. The name Sokulk seems to be entirely unknown among the Yakima and Pä'lus of today. The Wa'napûm range along both banks of the Columbia, in Washington, from above Crab Creek down to the mouth of the Snake River. Their village, where Smohalla lives, is on the west bank of the Columbia at the foot of Priest Rapids in the Yakima country. It is called P'nä, meaning "a fish weir," and is a major gathering place for neighboring tribes during the salmon fishing season. Because they have never made a treaty or moved onto a reservation, they are not officially recognized by the government.

**PÄ'LUS** (Shahaptian stock).---*Synonyms*: Palouse, Pelloatpallah Chopunnish (Lewis and Clark), Peloose, Polonches, Sewatpalla. The Pä'lus owned the entire basin of the Palouse River in Washington and Idaho, and also extended along the north bank of the Snake River to its junction with the Columbia. They were, and remain, closely connected with the Wanapûm and the Nez Percés. Pä'lus, the name by which the tribe is commonly known, is actually the name for Standing Rock at the junction of the Palouse and Snake rivers. They cannot explain the meaning of the word. They have four villages: Almotu, on the north bank of the Snake River in Washington, about 30 miles above the mouth of the Palouse River; Pä'lus, on the north bank of the Snake River just below the junction with the Palouse; Ta'sawîks, on the north bank of the Snake River about 15 miles above its mouth; and Kasî'spä or Cosispa (meaning "at the point," from *kasî's*, a point, and *pä*, the locative suffix), at Ainsworth at the junction of the Snake and Columbia. This last village has a slight difference in dialect and is sometimes considered to belong to the Wa'napûm. Although the Pä'lus are mentioned as parties to the Yakima Treaty of 1855, they have never, as a tribe, recognized any treaty restrictions or moved onto a reservation. They hold traditional beliefs and are among the most devoted followers of the Smohalla religion. They were estimated to number 500 in 1854, but since they are not officially recognized, it is impossible to provide their current population.

**PISKWAUS** or **WINÄTSHIPÛM** (Salishan stock).—*Synonyms:* Piskaous, Piscous, Pisquose. The name by which this tribe is commonly known is actually the name of a fishing place on the Wenatchee River; it is probably Salishan, but may come from the Yakima word *pĭsko*, meaning "a bend in the river." The Yakima call the river *Winätshi*, meaning a "river issuing from a canyon," and call the tribe Winätshipûm. The Piskwaus proper, located on the Wenatchee River, along with their connected bands or tribes living in the same neighborhood west of the Columbia in Kittitas and Okanogan counties, Washington, are a southern extension of the Mitaui and speak the same language. Under the name of Piskwaus, Stevens includes "the Indians on the Columbia between the Priest and Ross rapids, on the Pisquose or Winatshapam river; the Enteatkeon, Chelaun lake, and the Mithaw on Barrier river. The name of Pisquouse, however, properly refers to a single locality on the river known to the Yakamas as Winatshapam. The Pisquouse themselves, as has before been remarked, are so much intermarried with the Yakamas that they have almost lost their distinct identity. These bands were formerly all united under one principal chief, Stalkoosum, who is said to have been a man of great reputation among them. He was killed a few years ago in a fight with the Blackfeet; since then, there has been no head of the tribe." (*Stevens, Commissioner's Report, 1854.*) The Piskwaus and smaller connected tribes took part in the Yakima treaty of 1855, but they do not live on the reservation. Most of them live on the Wenatchee and the north branch of the Yakima River in Kittitas County. They are all Catholics. There is no official statement regarding their population size. Smaller tribes or bands connected with the Piskwaus proper and speaking the same language are:

1. **K'TÄTÄS**, K'tätäs-lĕ'ma, Ketetas (Stevens), Pshwa'năpûm (Yakima name), Shanwappoms (Lewis and Clark). K'tätäs means "a shoal," *lĕ'ma* being a tribal suffix, and Pshwană-pûm in the Yakima language means "shoal people," the name referring to a shoal in the Yakima River at Ellensburg.

2. **SKA'UTĂL**, or Skaddal (of Lewis and Clark). Located near Boston Creek and Kahchass Lake, at the head of the Yakima River.

3. **W'SHÄ'NĂTU**, or Shallattoos (of Lewis and Clark). The word means "huckleberry" in Yakima and is applied to a site on the Yakima River just above Ellensburg.

4. **SKWA'NĂNĂ**, or Squannaroos (of Lewis and Clark). A Yakima word meaning "whirlpool," applied to a point on the Yakima River approximately opposite the entrance of Selah Creek; the village is on the west bank of the river. This band may possibly speak the language of the Ätanûm, a Shahaptian tribe whose territory adjoins theirs.

5. **QAMÎL-LĔMA** or Kahmiltpah. The name is Yakima and means "people of Qamî'lh." Qamî'lh, or "Watching for Fish," was a chief who formerly lived with his band around Saddle Mountain, on the east side of the Columbia, above Priest Rapids. They are called Kahmiltpah in

6. SǏ’ĂPKAT or Seapcat. They reside now in Kittitas County, but probably lived originally at a place of the same name on the east bank of the Columbia River, near Bishop Rock and Milk Creek, below the Wenatchee River. They are called Seapcat in the Yakima treaty of 1855. The word belongs to the Piskwaus language.

**YÄ'KĬMÂ** (Shahaptian stock).—*Synonyms*: Cutsahnim (Lewis and Clark), Eyackimah, Pa'kiut-lĕ'ma, Stobshaddat (by Puget Sound tribes, Tolmie), Waptai'lmĭm, Yackamans, Yookoomans. The Yakima are the most important tribe of the Shahaptian stock, excluding the Nez Percés. They occupied the country of the Naches and middle Yakima rivers, in present-day Yakima County, Washington, and are now on a reservation within the same county. Stevens says the name signifies "black bear" in the Walla Walla language, but Yakima informants state that it is a nickname signifying "coward" or "runaway," and say that the proper name of the tribe is Waptai'lmĭm, "people of the narrow river," or Pa'kiut-lĕ'ma, "people of the gap," both names referring to the narrows in the Yakima River at Union Gap, near Yakima Bridge. Their old village was on the west side of the river, just below the gap. They are the Cutsahnim mentioned by Lewis and Clark. This name may possibly come from the same root as Kû'tsano't, "Lying Alongside," the name of an old Yakima chief who died about 1880. In 1854, according to Stevens, they were "divided into two principal bands, each made up of a number of villages and very closely connected, the one owning the country on the Naches and lower Yakima, the other on the Wenas and its main branch above the forks." These latter people, however, were primarily of the Piskwaus connection. They had several chiefs at that time, of whom Kamaiakan was the most important. Like all the other Columbia tribes east of the Cascade Range, they formerly crossed the Rocky Mountains annually to hunt buffalo on the waters of the Missouri River. In 1855, the government made a treaty with the Yakima, Piskwaus, Pälus, and other tribes by which they were to cede territory on both sides of the Columbia River, extending generally from the Cascade Range eastward to the Palouse and Snake rivers, and southward from above Lake Chelan to the Columbia, except for a small portion between the Columbia and the lower Yakima. At the same time, the Yakima Reservation was established and an arrangement was made by which all the tribes and bands concerned were to be confederated under the title of the "Yakama Nation," with Kamaiakan as head chief. Shortly afterward, the Yakima War broke out, and the treaty remained unratified until 1859. As already stated, the Pälus and several other tribes have never recognized it or come to the reservation, and their objection to such removal has become a religious principle of the Smohalla doctrine. In the original treaty of 1855, fourteen tribes are named as participating, as follows: Yakama (Yäkima), Palouse (Pä'lus), Pis-

Among these groups, at least six languages and three linguistic stocks were represented. The majority of these Indians west of the Columbia River, including the Yakima proper and others on the reservation, are Catholics; there are also a number of followers of the Shaker and Smohalla doctrines. Those on the reservation numbered 1,200 in 1892, with an estimated 1,500 living outside the boundaries. Besides the principal band of Yakima, the Waptailmĭm already mentioned, there are also the Sĕ'tăs-lĕma, or "people of the rye prairie," on Setass Creek (a western tributary of the Yakima in the eastern part of the reservation), and the Pĭsko, or "people of the river bend," in a village also on the south side of the Yakima, between Topinish and Setass creeks. (See Pishquitpah.) Their dialects are said to differ slightly from that of the Waptailmĭm.

**Ä'TĂNÛM-LĚMA** (Shahaptian stock) or "people (*lĕma*) of Ätanûm Creek."—A small tribe on Atahnum Creek in Yakima County, Washington, on the northern boundary of the reservation. They are said to speak a language distinct from Yakima or Klûkatät, but related to them. They have no official recognition now, nor were they recognized in the treaty of 1855. The name Ä'tănûm is Yakima and refers to a stream "ascended" (by salmon).

**KLÛ'KĂTÄT** (Shahaptian stock).—*Synonyms:* Clickahut, Clickitat, Klikatat, Qwû'lh-hwai-pûm, Weyehhoo, Whulwhypum. The name by which this tribe is commonly known is from the Wasko language and signifies "beyond (the mountain)"—that is, east of the Cascade Range—with reference to the Chinookan tribes on the lower Columbia. The same name was also at times applied to the Yakima. They call themselves Qwûlh-hwai-pûm, "prairie people," from *qwûlh-hwai*, "prairie," and *pûm*, "people," referring particularly to their occupancy of Camass Prairie. They formerly occupied the southern slopes of Mount Adams and Mount Saint Helens, along with the country of the Klickitat and Lewis rivers in the present Klickitat and Skamania counties, Washington. East of them were the Yakima, and to the west were the Salishan and Chinookan tribes. At one time they lived farther east but were driven west by the Cayuse. (*Stevens.*) About sixty years ago, they crossed the Columbia and overran the Willamette country, even penetrating as far south as the Umpqua, but they afterward withdrew again to their own territory. Although only a small tribe, they were aggressive and enterprising, serving as the trade medium between the tribes west of the mountains and those to the east. They joined in the Yakima treaty of 1855 and are now located chiefly on the Yakima reservation, though a few are still on the White Salmon River in Klickitat County. Their total number is unknown. The Taitinapam and Topinish speak the same language and may be considered branches of this tribe.

**QA'PNĬSH-'LĚMA or TOPINISH** (Shahaptian stock).——A small tribe on the Topinish River in Yakima County, Washington, within the current boundaries of the reservation. They speak the Klûkatät language. The name means "people (*lěma*) of the trail coming from the foot of the hill."

**TAITINAPAM** (Shahaptian stock).——*Synonym*: Tai-kie-a-pain (a misprint). A small tribe speaking the Klûkatät language, who formerly lived on the western slopes of the Cascade Mountains, between the headwaters of the Lewis and Cowlitz rivers in Skamania County, Washington, being the westernmost tribe of the Shahaptian stock. If any survivors remain, they are probably incorporated with the Klûkatät on the Yakima reservation. They never received official recognition.

**CHÄMNÄ'PÛM** (Shahaptian stock).——*Synonyms*: Chimnahpum, Chimnapoos, Cuimnapum. A tribe that occupied the bend of the Columbia River below the Yakima River, along with the territory on the lower Yakima, primarily in the current Yakima County, Washington. They are the Chimnahpum mentioned by Lewis and Clark and speak a dialect of the language of the Pä'lus and Wanapûm, the tribes with which the few survivors are now merged. A few are also still living on the west side of the Columbia, opposite Pasco. The name is from their own language and means "people (*pûm*) of Chämnä'," their old village which was located roughly opposite Wallula.

**PISHQUITPAH** (Shahaptian stock).——This name appears only in the narrative of Lewis and Clark as that of a tribe in 1805, "living at the Muscleshell Rapid and on the north side of the Columbia to the beginning of the high country, spending the winter on the borders of the Tapteal." The Tapteal (properly Waptail or Waptailmĭm) is the Yakima River. This would place them in eastern Klickitat and Yakima counties, Washington. They are probably identical to the Pĭsko band of the Yakima. In the name Pishquitpah, the final *pah* is the Yakima or Pä'lus locative suffix *pä*, meaning "at."

**K'KA'SĂWI or KOWWASSAYEE** (Shahaptian stock).——A small tribe speaking the Tenino language that formerly occupied a village of the same name, K'ka'săwi, on the north bank of the Columbia in Klickitat County, Washington, roughly opposite the mouth of the Umatilla. The full name is K'ka'săwi-lě'ma, "*people (lěma) of the arrow-making place,*" with the local form derived from *k'ka'so*, meaning "arrow." They took part in the Yakima treaty of 1855 under the name of Kowwassayee and are now on the Yakima reservation.

**HĂHAU'PÛM or WAHOWPUM** (Shahaptian stock).——A small tribe speaking the Tenino language and occupying a village, Hăhau'u, on the north bank of the Columbia, near the mouth of Olive Creek in Klickitat County, Washington. The word means "willow people," from *hăhau'u*, a species of willow, and *pûm*, meaning "people." They are the Wahowpum of Lewis and Clark. They have never received official recognition.

**UCHI'CHOL or OCHECHOTES** (Shahaptian stock).——A small tribe speaking the Tenino language, living now, or formerly, on the north bank of the Columbia in Klickitat County, Washington. They are mentioned as Ochechotes in the Yakima Treaty of 1855 and may now be incorporated with other tribes on the Yakima reservation. The name, from the Tenino language, signifies the "hind dorsal fin" (of a salmon) and is the name of a rock on the north side of the Columbia, opposite the upper end of the island at the mouth of the Des Chutes. See *Tapänäsh*.

**SKI'NPÄ** (Shahaptian stock).——*Synonyms:* Sawpaw (?), Skien, Skin, Skinpah. A small tribe speaking the Tenino language and formerly having a village on the north bank of the Columbia in Klickitat County, Washington, at the falls opposite Celilo. They took part in the Yakima Treaty of 1855 under the name of Skinpah and are now incorporated with the other tribes on the Yakima reservation. The name is Tenino and means "cradle place" or "at the cradle," from *skin*, "cradle," and *pä*, the locative; it refers to a prominent rock at the site of their former village that has some resemblance to an Indian cradle. See *Tapänäsh*.

**TAPÄNÄ'SH or ENEESHUR** (Shahaptian stock).——A small tribe speaking the Tenino language, having a village on the north bank of the Columbia in Klickitat County, Washington, roughly opposite the mouth of the Des Chutes River and a little above Celilo. The name is identical to the Eneeshur mentioned by Lewis and Clark; in 1805, these explorers also included under this name the various bands speaking the Tenino language on both sides of the Columbia near the mouth of the Des Chutes. The Tapänäsh have no official recognition. See *Tenino*.

**TLAQLUIT or WŬSHQÛM** (Chinookan stock).——*Synonyms:* Echebool, Echeloot, Eloot, Helwit, Niculuita, Ouichram, Tchilouit, Tilhulhwit, Wisham, Wishham, Wishram, Wisswham. The Tlaqluit, along with the Wasko, are the easternmost tribes of Chinookan stock on the Columbia, having the Shahaptian tribes who speak the Tenino language immediately above them. The Tlaqluit territory lies along the north bank of the Columbia in Klickitat County, Washington, from Tenino—about 6 miles above The Dalles—down to the neighborhood of the White Salmon River. They call themselves Tlaqluit (the Echeloot of Lewis and Clark) and are called Wŭshqûmă-pûm, or "Wŭshqûm people," by the tribes speaking the Tenino language. *Wŭshqûm* is the name of their chief village near the South Side at The Dalles, which was the great fishing and trading center for the tribes of this region. The name also appears as *Wishram*. Both *Tlaqluit* and *Wŭshqûm* refer to a species of louse or flea that is abundant in that neighborhood. They participated in the Yakima Treaty of 1855 under the name of Wishham, but most of them have probably never moved to the reservation. See *Wasko*.

**CHILÛ'KTKWA** or **CHILLUCKITTEQUAWS** (Chinookan stock).—A tribe that formerly extended along the north bank of the Columbia in Klickitat and Skamania counties, Washington, from about the White Salmon River down to some distance below the Cascades. They are called Chilluck-ittequaws in 1805 by Lewis and Clark, who also speak of a separate band of the same tribe under the name of Smackshop, a name which cannot now be identified. The tribe now numbers fewer than 100 people. Until recently, the remnant lived about the mouth of the White Salmon River, but moved about thirteen years ago to the Cascades. Their language is nearly the same as that of the Wasko. They have never had official recognition.

**KWIKWÛ'LIT** or **DOG RIVER** (Chinookan stock).—*Synonyms*: Cascade Indians, Kigaltwalla, Upper Chinook, Wahclellah, Watlala. A small tribe that formerly lived at the Cascades and around Dog River, a small stream flowing into the Columbia about halfway between the Cascades and The Dalles, in Wasco County, Oregon. They are identical, at least in part, with the Wahclellahs of Lewis and Clark (mentioned as a part of the "Shahala nation"), and are the "Ki-gal-twal-la band of the Wascoes" and the "Dog River band of the Wascoes" of the Wasco treaty of 1855. The "Dog River or Cascade Indians" were reported to number 80 people in 1854. In the following year, they, along with other tribes, entered into the Wasco treaty, by which they agreed to move to the Warm Springs reservation, where some of them now reside, while others are still around the Cascades. Their language is nearly the same as that of the Wasko.

**WASKO** (Chinookan stock).—*Synonyms*: Dalles Indians, Wascopum. A tribe that formerly claimed the country around The Dalles, on the south bank of the Columbia, in Wasco County, Oregon. They, along with the Tlaqluit on the opposite bank, are the easternmost extent of the Chinookan stock and speak the same language. The name is said to be a Tenino word meaning "grass" or "grass people." It has sometimes been used to include several related bands around The Dalles and Cascades on both sides of the Columbia. Under the name of "The Dalles band of the Wascoes," they entered into the Wasco treaty of 1855 and are now on the Warm Springs reservation in Oregon. They numbered 260 in 1892.

**WAIÄM** (Shahaptian stock).—*Synonyms*: (Lower) Des Chutes, Waiäm-lĕma, Wayyampa, Wyam. A tribe speaking the Tenino language and formerly living around the mouth of the Des Chutes River, in the present Wasco and Sherman counties, Oregon. Their chief village was on the Columbia where Celilo is now located and was called Waiäm, from which their name of Waiäm-lĕma or "people of Waiäm" is derived. They joined in

**TAI′-ĂQ** (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).--*Synonyms:* Taigh, Ta-ih, Tairtla, Tyich. A tribe speaking the Tenino language that formerly occupied the territory around the Tygh and White rivers in Wasco County, Oregon. The name Tai′-ăq refers to the stream and means "muddy, white water." They took part in the Wasco treaty of 1855 under the name of "Ta-ih or Upper Deschutes band of Walla-Wallas," and are now on the Warm Springs reservation, Oregon. Their number is not reported.

**TÍLQÛNI** (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).--A tribe formerly claiming the country between Tygh Valley and the Warm Springs River, west of the Deschutes River, in the present Wasco County, Oregon. They are now on the Warm Springs reservation in the same neighborhood. They have never been officially mentioned by their Indian name and may be considered the Warm Springs proper, although this name is local rather than tribal. They speak the Tenino language. See *Tenino*.

**TENINO** or **MĚLI′-LĚMA** (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).--The most important <term>Shahaptian</term> tribe of western Oregon. They formerly occupied the middle Deschutes River and conquered the current Warm Springs reservation from the <term>Paiute</term> or Snake tribes, but they never occupied it until they were placed there by the Wasco treaty of 1855. Since then, they have been known interchangeably as Tenino or Warm Springs Indians, although this latter designation is commonly used to include other related tribes on the same reservation. For this reason, it is impossible to give their population numbers definitely. The Tenino language, in various dialects, is spoken (except by the Lohim) by all the tribes formerly living on both banks of the Columbia and on its tributaries from the territory of the Wasco near The Dalles up to about the mouth of the Umatilla.

Most of this region, on the south or Oregon side of the Columbia, was formerly held by <term>Shoshonean</term> tribes related to the <term>Paiute</term>, who were driven out by the <term>Shahaptian</term> tribes and forced further back to the south. The only <term>Shoshonean</term> tribe that maintained its place on the Columbia was the Lohim, on Willow Creek. The Tenino themselves conquered the present Warm Springs reservation from the Snakes. This expulsion was in full progress when Lewis and Clark traveled down the Columbia in 1805, but it had been practically completed when the first treaties were made with these tribes fifty years later. Lewis and Clark state that "on that (the south) side of the river, none of the tribes have any permanent dwellings, and upon inquiry, we were confirmed in our belief that this was due to the fear of being attacked by the Snake Indians, with whom they are constantly at war. This nation they represent as being very numerous and residing in a great many villages on the Towahnahioooks (Wanwaui or Deschutes), where they live principally on salmon, . . . the first villages of the Snake Indians being twelve days' journey on a course about southeast of this

**TÛKSPÛ'SH or JOHN DAY INDIANS (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).**—*Synonyms*: Dock-spus, John Day Rivers, Tûkspû'sh-lĕma. A tribe speaking the <term>Tenino language</term> and formerly living along the lower part of the John Day River in Oregon; their principal village was at the falls about 4 miles above the river's mouth. They are now on the Warm Springs reservation and numbered 59 in 1892, with perhaps others living off the reservation. <term>Tûkspû'sh</term> is the name of the John Day River in the <term>Tenino language</term>.

**LOHIM or WILLOW CREEK INDIANS (<term>Shoshonean stock</term>).**—A tribe living on Willow Creek in Gilliam and Morrow counties, Oregon. They are of <term>Shoshonean</term> connection, being the only Indians of this stock who have been able to maintain their position on the Columbia against the encroachments of the <term>Shahaptian</term> tribes. They have never made a treaty with the government and are generally described as renegades belonging to the Umatilla reservation. In 1870, they were reported to number 114, but they are not mentioned in recent official reports.

**CAYUSE or WAILĔ'TPU (<term>Waiilatpuan stock</term>).**—*Synonyms*: Cailloux, Kayuse, Shiwanish, Skyuse, Wailetma, Yeletpo Chopunnish (of Lewis and Clark). The <term>Cayuse</term> are a warlike tribe of a distinct stock who formerly occupied the mountain country at the headwaters of the Walla Walla, Umatilla, and Grande Ronde rivers in Oregon and Washington, including the present Umatilla reservation. Further investigation may yet establish a linguistic connection with the <term>Shahaptian</term> tribes. The <term>Molala</term>, formerly on Molalla Creek west of the Cascades, are a separate band whose westward migration is still remembered in the traditions of the <term>Cayuse</term> and their neighbors. The <term>Cayuse</term> formerly held a high reputation for intelligence and bravery; however, because of their fighting tendencies, which led them to wage constant war on the Snake and other tribes to the west, they were never very numerous. In 1838, a Presbyterian mission called <term>Waiilatpu</term> was established among the <term>Cayuse</term> by Dr. Whitman at the site of the current town of Whitman in Walla Walla County, Washington. In 1847, smallpox—previously unknown among them—wiped out a large portion of the tribe. The <term>Cayuse</term>, believing that the missionaries were the cause of the disease, attacked the mission on November 29, 1847, killed Dr. Whitman and thirteen others, and destroyed the mission. In reality, there seems to be little question that the infection was brought into the country in supplies intended for the mission's use.

In 1854, according to Stevens, "the tribe, though still feared by their neighbors because of their courage and warlike spirit, is only a small one, numbering 126 according to the census of 1851. Of these, individuals of unmixed ancestry are few, as the majority are intermingled with the Nez Percés and the Wallawallas—particularly with the former—to such an extent that their own language has fallen into disuse." In 1855, they joined in the treaty by which the Umatilla reservation in Oregon was established; most of those remaining are now there, while a few others are with the Nez Percés at Lapwai. Joseph, the famous Nez Percé chief, is himself the son of a Cayuse father. The name Cayuse comes from the <term>Nez Percé language</term>. They call themselves <term>Wailětpu</term>. **UMATILLA (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).**—*Synonym:* Utilla. A tribe formerly occupying the lower portion of the river of the same name, along with the nearby bank of the Columbia in Oregon. They speak a distinct language of the <term>Shahaptian stock</term>. By the treaty of 1855, they agreed to move to the Umatilla reservation in Oregon, where in 1892 they were reported to number 216. A large proportion of those now called Cayuse on the same reservation are actually of Umatilla mixed ancestry.

**WALLAWALLA (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).**—*Synonyms:* Oualla-Oualla, Walawaltz, Wollawollah, Wollaw-Wollah. A tribe formerly occupying the country around the lower portion of the river of the same name and along the east bank of the Columbia from the Snake River down nearly to the Umatilla, in Washington and Oregon. They take their name from the river, and the word is said to refer to "rushing water." Their language is said to closely resemble that of the Nez Percés. By the treaty of 1855, they agreed to move to the Umatilla reservation in Oregon, where in 1892 they were reported to number 474.

A small band of the same tribe, known to the Yakima as <term>Walu'la-pûm</term>, formerly lived on the west bank of the Columbia opposite the present Wallula. Their dialect is said to have been more closely related to the <term>Pä'lus language</term>.

**SAHAPTIN or NEZ PERCÉS (<term>Shahaptian stock</term>).**—*Synonyms:* Chohoptins, Chopunnish <note>Lewis and Clark</note>, Copunnish, Laaptin <note>misprint</note>, Â'dal-k'ato'igo, "people with hair cut across the forehead" <note>Kiowa name</note>, Shi'wanĭsh <note>Tenino name, also applied to the Cayuse</note>, Wa'pamětănt <note>Yakima name for the language</note>. The Nez Percés are said to call themselves <term>Sahaptin</term>, and they were named Nez Percés, or "pierced noses," by the French because of their former custom of wearing nose pendants. <meta>This page continues the ethnographic description of the tribes along the Columbia River, shifting from the Umatilla and Cayuse to the Nez Percé (Shahaptian stock), detailing their historical territory, their interaction with the Lewis and Clark expedition, and the events leading to the Nez Percé War.</meta>

<header>MOONEY] TRIBES OF THE COLUMBIA</header>

They formerly occupied a large territory in eastern Washington and Oregon and central Idaho, bounded on the east by the main divide of the Bitterroot Mountains, and including the lower Grande Ronde and Salmon Rivers, along with a large part of the Snake River and all of the Clearwater River. The Wallowa Valley, the disputed ownership of which led to the Nez Percé War, lies on a branch of the Grande Ronde in Oregon. They were bordered by the Salishan tribes to the northeast, the Shoshonean tribes to the south, and the Cayuse, Wallawalla, and Pälus—with all of whom they are much intermarried—on the west and northwest. Almost all authorities credit them with a high character for bravery, intelligence, and honorable conduct—traits which were strikingly displayed in the Nez Percé War.

Lewis and Clark traveled through their country in 1805 and speak of them and some connected tribes under the name of Chopunnish, distinguished as follows: the Chopunnish nation (located around the current Lapwai reservation); the Pelloatpallah band (the Pälus); the Kimooenim band (on the Snake River, between the Salmon and the Clearwater); the Yeletpo band (the Cayuse); the Willewah band (in Wallowa Valley, later Joseph's band); the Soyennom band (on the north side of the upper Clearwater in Idaho; these were actually a part of the Pälus—the proper form is Tätqu'nma, from which the Thatuna Hills are named, referring to "a fawn" in the Pälus language, and was the name applied to their camas ground around Camass Creek); and the Chopunnish of the Lewis River (on the Snake River, below the Clearwater). In response to a request from the Nez Percés, who sent a delegation all the way to Saint Louis for that purpose in 1832, the first Protestant mission was established among them at Lapwai, Idaho, in 1837. Soon afterward, they entered into relations with the government and made their first treaty with the United States in 1855. By this treaty, they ceded the greater portion of their territory and were confirmed in the possession of a reservation including the Wallowa Valley. Upon the discovery of gold in the country, however, miners rushed in, and as a consequence, a new treaty was made in 1863, by which they surrendered all but the current Lapwai reservation in Idaho. Joseph, who occupied the Wallowa Valley with his band, refused to recognize this treaty or move to Lapwai. This refusal finally led to the Nez Percé War in 1877, as already related. The main body of the tribe took no part in the war. After Joseph surrendered, his band was moved to Indian Territory, where the mortality rate among them was so high that in 1884 they were returned to the Northwest. For several reasons, however, it was considered inadvisable to settle them near their old home, and a place was finally found for them in 1887 on the Colville reservation in northern Washington. In 1892, there were 1,828 on the Lapwai reservation and 138 on the Colville reservation, a total population of 1,966.

### CHAPTER VIII
## THE SHAKERS OF PUGET SOUND

> My breath was gone and I died. All at once I saw a great shining light. Angels told me to look back. I did, and saw my own body lying dead. It had no soul. My soul left my body and went up to the judgment place of God. . . . My soul was told that I must come back and live on earth. When I came back, I told my friends, “There is a God. My good friends, be Christians. If you all try hard and help me, we shall be better men on earth.” — *John Slocum.*

In 1881, a new religion began among the tribes of Puget Sound in Washington. Although it was apparently not founded on any doctrinal prophecy, it deserves special attention because of the prominent role that hypnotism plays in its ceremonies. Indeed, there is good reason to believe that the Paiute Messiah himself, and through him all the apostles of the Ghost Dance, obtained their knowledge of hypnotic secrets from the “Shakers” of Puget Sound.

<meta>This page continues the account of John Slocum’s apparent death and the resulting birth of the Shaker religion, transitioning from the general description to a detailed report by Reverend Myron Eells.</meta>

[He remained in this] condition until the middle of the afternoon, when he awoke and announced that he had been to heaven, but had been met at the entrance by angels. They forbade him from entering because of his wickedness and gave him a choice: either go to hell or return to earth to teach his people what they must do to reach heaven. Consequently, he returned to earth and began his divinely appointed mission, incorporating much of what he had learned from white missionaries into the new doctrine and ritual. Because of the nervous twitching that so uniquely distinguished them, his followers soon became known as "Shakers." Although strongly opposed by the agent—who arrested and imprisoned the leaders and imposed various minor penalties on their followers—the Shaker religion grew and flourished. It now has a formal organization with several houses of worship and has received the official endorsement of the Presbyterian Church.

The following account of the system, written in response to a letter of inquiry, was obtained from the missionary Reverend Myron Eells, the agent’s brother:

> A curious religious phase emerged in the fall of 1882 among some Indians in the southern part of Puget Sound. It has prevailed mainly among the Squaxon, Nisqually, Skokomish, and Chehalis Indians. It has been called the "Shake religion" by its opponents, and its followers have been called "Shakers" due to the significant amount of nervous shaking that is part of their rituals. It is clearly based on the same psychological principles as the "jerks" and shouting seen at camp meetings among white people in the southern and western states fifty years ago, when they were more ignorant and less acquainted with genuine religion than they are now. When superstition, ignorance, dreams, imagination, and religion are all mixed together—whether among white people, Indians, or any other race—they produce a strange combination. This has proven to be the case here.
> 
> In the fall of 1882, an Indian named John Slocum, who lived on Skookum Bay in Mason County, apparently died. Some years earlier, he had lived on the Skokomish reservation, where he had attended a Protestant church and learned about the white man’s religion, God, Jesus Christ, and the morality taught there. In his early life, he had also learned something of the Catholic religion and its forms and ceremonies. Many Indians were present when he fell ill and apparently died. They said his neck was broken and that he remained dead for about six hours; then he returned to life, jumped up, ran a short distance, and soon began to talk with the people. Whether it was actually a case of suspended animation is a question. A white neighbor who saw him before his apparent death, while he lay still, and after his revival, said he believed the Indian was "playing possum." However, the Indians believed that he truly died and rose again.
> 
> Slocum stated that he died and tried to enter heaven, but could not because he was so wicked. He was told the way of life there, however, and that he must return to this earth to teach his people the way and persuade them to become Christians. He gained a small group of followers; a church was built for him, and he preached steadily to the people.
> 
> Matters continued this way until the following August. Then, after consulting with other Indians who supported him—especially on the Skokomish reservation—it was decided to hold a large meeting. The Indians of the surrounding region were summoned to attend. They were told they would be lost if they did not; that four women would be turned into angels; that people would die and be raised to life again, and that other miraculous things would occur.

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14]

Many went—about half of those on the Skokomish reservation were among the number—and they did hold a large meeting. Women went around trying to fly like angels; four persons are said to have died, and, with the power that was supposedly given to them from above, others were said to have brought them back to life again. This was a mixture of trying to perform miracles, as in Bible times, to prove the divinity of their religion, and some of the ceremonies of their old *black tomahnous*. This was a secret society from their days of traditional culture, in which persons entered a hypnotic condition, became very rigid, and recovered after some time. The followers of this new religion dreamed dreams, saw visions, performed some unpleasant ceremonies in the style of the *black tomahnous*, and were overtaken by a kind of shaking. With their arms at full length, their hands and arms would shake so fast that an ordinary person not under that excitement could hardly shake half as fast. Gazing into the heavens, their heads would also shake very fast, sometimes for a few minutes and sometimes for hours, or half the night. They would also brush each other with their hands, as they said, to brush off their sins; for they said they were much worse than white people, as the latter were bad only in their hearts, while the Indians were so bad that the badness came to the surface of their bodies and the ends of their fingernails, so that it could be picked off. They sometimes brushed each other lightly, and sometimes so roughly that the person brushed was left bruised for a week, or even made sick.

In connection with this, they held church services, prayed to God, believed in Christ as a savior, spoke much about his death, and used the cross. Their services were a combination of Protestant and Catholic rituals, though at first they almost totally rejected the Bible, for they said they had direct revelations from Christ and were more fortunate than the whites, who had an old, antiquated book.

After having kept up this meeting for about a week, they disbanded and went to their homes, but did not stop their shaking or services. They sometimes held meetings from 6 o’clock in the evening until about midnight, lighting candles and putting them on their heads for a long time. They became very particular about making the sign of the cross many times a day: when they began to eat as they asked a blessing, and when they finished their meal and returned thanks; when they shook hands with anyone—and they shook hands very often—when they went to church and prayer meetings on Thursday evening, and at many other times, far more often than the Catholics do.

On the Skokomish reservation, their lack of caution caused the death of a mother and her child, and an additional loss of time and property to the amount of $600 or $800 in a few weeks. It also became a serious question whether the constant shaking of their heads would drive some of them insane, and based on symptoms and indications, it was the opinion of the agency physician, J. T. Martin, that it would do so. Accordingly, on the reservation, the authority of the agent was brought to bear, and to a great extent the shaking was stopped, though they were encouraged to keep up some good habits which they had begun, such as ceasing gambling and drunkenness, and ending their old-style incantations over the sick, and the like. Some at first said they could not stop shaking, and that at their prayer meetings and church services on the Sabbath, their hands and heads would continue to shake in spite of themselves; but after a short time, when the excitement had died away, they found that they could stop.

But around Skookum Bay, Mud Bay, and Squaxon, the shaking continued, and it spread to the Nisqually and Chehalis Indians. It seemed to be as "catching," to use the expression of the Indians, as the measles. Many who at first ridiculed it and fought against it, and invoked the aid of the agent to stop it, were drawn into it after a little while, and then they became its strong supporters. This was especially true of the medicine-men, or Indian doctors, and those who had the strongest faith in them. The Shakers declared that all the old Indian religion, and especially the cure of the sick by the medicine-men, was from the devil, and they would have nothing to do with it. Those who at first originated and propagated it had been among the...

more intelligent and progressive of the uneducated Indians. Very few of those who had learned to read and had been in Sabbath school for a considerable length of time were drawn into it. It was the class between the most educated and the most superstitious who at first upheld it. They seemed to know too much to continue in the old-style religious ceremonies, but not to know enough, and to be too superstitious, to fully believe the Bible. Consequently, the medicine-men were at first bitterly opposed to it. About this time, however, an order came from the Indian Department to stop all medicine-men from practicing their incantations over the sick. As a respectable number of the Indians had declared against the old style of curing the sick, it seemed to be a good time to enforce this order, as there was sufficient popular opinion in connection with the authority of the agent to enforce it. This was done, and then the medicine-men almost entirely joined the Shakers, as their style was more nearly in accordance with the old style than with the religion of the Bible.

As it spread, one Indian went so far as to declare himself to be Christ come to earth again, and rode through the streets of Olympia at the head of several dozens of his followers with his hands outstretched as Christ was when he was crucified. But he was so ridiculed by other Indians and by the whites that he gave up this idea and simply declared himself to be a prophet who had received revelations from heaven.

For several years there has been very little of the shaking or this mode of worship among the Indians on the reservation, except secretly when persons were sick. Still, their native superstition and their interaction with those off the reservation—who sometimes hold a special gathering and meeting when their followers grow cold and careless—has kept the belief in it as a religion firm in their hearts. Thus, lately, since they have become citizens and are therefore more free from the authority of the agent, the practice of it has become more common, especially when persons are sick.

In fact, while it is a religion for use at all times, it is practiced especially over the sick, and in this way takes the place of the medicine-men and their methods. Unlike the system of the medicine-men, it has no single performer. Although they often select for a leader one who can pray the best, in his absence another may take the lead. Like the old system, it involves much noise. They especially use bells, which are rung over the person where the sickness is supposed to be. The others present use their influence to help in curing the sick one, and so imitate the attendants of an Indian doctor, getting down upon their knees on the floor and holding up their hands, with a candle in each hand, sometimes for an hour. They believe that by so holding up their hands, the man who is ringing the bell will get the sickness out more easily than he otherwise would. They use candles both when they attempt to cure the sick and in their general service, avoiding lamps for fear of being easily tempted, as they believe coal-oil lights are from Satan.

In another point also, this resembles their old religion very closely. For a long time before a person is taken sick, they foretell that his spirit is gone to heaven and profess to be able to bring it back and restore it to him, so that he will not die as soon as he otherwise would. This was also a part of the old <term>tomahnous</term> belief.

<margin>Sweeny</margin> They have also prophesied very much. Several times when a person has died, they have told me that someone had foretold this event, but they have never told me this until after the event happened, except in one case. They have prophesied much regarding the end of the world and the day of judgment. Generally, the time set has been on a Fourth of July, and many have been frightened as the time drew near, but, alas, in every instance the prophecy failed. Like Christians, they believe in a Supreme Being, in prayer, the Sabbath, in heaven and hell, in man as a sinner, and Christ as a savior; and the system led its followers to stop drinking, gambling, betting, horse racing, the use of tobacco, and the old-style incantations over the sick. In recent years, however, some of them have fallen from grace.

It has been a somewhat strange turn of human nature, a combination of morals and immorals, of Protestantism, Catholicism, and old Indian practices, of dreams

and visions—a study in mental philosophy, showing what the mind can do under certain circumstances. Yet it is all easily explained. These Indians have interacted with white people for a long time, nearly since most of them were children. All classes of white people have mocked their religion—the non-believer, the profane man, the immoral one, the moral one, and the Christian—and they have been told that God and the Bible were against it; consequently, they lost faith in it. But the Indian must have some religion. He cannot do without one. They were not ready to accept the Bible in all its purity. They wanted more excitement. Like the Dakota Indians more recently, they saw that Christ was the great center of the most powerful religion of the most powerful, intelligent, successful, and wisest nations with whom they came in contact. Therefore, they formulated a system for themselves that would meet all their requirements. Once a few leaders had originated it, a large portion of the rest were ready to accept it. However, because they had received more Christian teaching than the wild Dakotas, it took a somewhat different form, with no thought of war and with more of real Christianity.

James Wickersham, Esquire, of Tacoma, Washington—the well-known historian of that region—is the regular attorney for these people as a religious organization, and is consequently in a position to speak with authority concerning them. In reply to a letter of inquiry, he states that the Shakers believe in an actual, localized heaven and hell, and they revere the Bible but regard John Slocum’s revelations as having more authority. “They practice the strictest morality, sobriety, and honesty. Their 500 or 600 members are models, and it is beyond question that they do not drink whiskey, gamble, or race, and they are more free from vice than any other church. They practice a mixture of Catholic, Presbyterian, and old Indian ceremonies, and allow only Indians in the church. They have five churches, built by themselves, and the sect is growing quite rapidly.” From all this, it would appear that the Shaker religion is a distinct advance compared to the old Indian system.

Under the date of December 5, 1892, Mr. Wickersham wrote again on this subject, as follows:

> I read your letter to my Indian friends, and they beg me to write to you and explain that they are not Ghost Dancers and have no sympathy with that ceremony or any other founded on the Dreamer religion. They believe in heaven as do the orthodox Christians; they also believe in Christ, and God, the Father of all; they believe in future rewards and punishments, but not in the Bible particularly. They do believe in it as a history, but they do not value it as a book of revelation. They do not need it, for John Slocum personally came back from a conference with the angels at the gates of heaven and has imparted to them the actual facts and the angelic words concerning the means of salvation.
>
> This testimony is even better than the words of Christ contained in the Bible, for John Slocum comes 1,800 years closer; he is an Indian, and he personally appears to them and reports the facts in an Indian language. These people believe Slocum as firmly as the martyr at the stake believed in that for which he offered up his life; but it is the Christian religion which they believe, and not the Ghost Dance or Dreamer religion.
>
> In short, they have a mixture of Catholic, Protestant, and Indian ceremonies, with a thorough belief in John Slocum’s personal visit to heaven and his return with a mission to save the Indians and so guide them that they, too, shall reach the realms of bliss. Personally, I think they are honest but mistaken; however, the belief certainly has a beneficial effect and has reduced drinking and crime to a minimum among the members of the “Shaker” or “Tschaddam” church.

<header>MOONEY] SKETCH OF WOVOKA</header>

is a narrow strip of level sage prairie some 30 miles in length, walled in by the giant Sierras, their sides torn and gashed by volcanic convulsions and dark with gloomy forests of pine, their towering summits white with everlasting snows, and roofed over by a cloudless sky whose blue infinity the mind instinctively seeks to penetrate to far-off worlds beyond. Away to the south the view is closed in by the sacred mountain of the Paiute, where their Father gave them the first fire and taught them their few simple arts before leaving for his home in the upper regions of the Sun-land. Like the valley of Rasselas, it seems set apart from the great world to be the home of a dreamer.

The greater portion of Nevada is an arid desert of rugged mountains and alkali plains, the little available land being confined to narrow mountain valleys and the borders of a few large lakes. These tracts are occupied by scattered ranchmen engaged in stock raising, and as the white population is sparse, Indian labor is largely utilized, the Paiute being very good workers. The causes which in other parts of the country have conspired to sweep the Indian from the path of the white man seem inoperative here, where the original indigenous owners are regarded more like peons under the protection of the dominant race, and are allowed to set up their small camps of tule lodges in convenient out-of-the-way places. There they spend the autumn and winter in hunting, fishing, and gathering seeds and piñon nuts, working at fair wages on ranches through the spring and summer. In this way, young Wovoka became attached to the family of a ranchman in Mason Valley named David Wilson, who took an interest in him and gave him the name of Jack Wilson, by which he is commonly known among the whites. From his association with this family, he gained some knowledge of English, together with a confused idea of the white man's theology. On growing up, he married and continued to work for Mr. Wilson, earning a reputation for industry and reliability, but attracting no special notice until nearly 30 years of age, when he announced the revelation that has made him famous among the tribes of the West.

Following are the various forms of his name which I have noticed: Wo'voka, or Wü'voka, which I have provisionally translated as "Cutter," derived from a verb signifying "to cut;" Wevokar, Wopokahte, Kwohitsauq, Cowejo, Koit-tsow, Kvit-Tsow, Quoitze Ow, Jack Wilson, Jackson Wilson, Jack Winson, John Johnson. He has also been confused with Bannock Jim, a Mormon Bannock of Fort Hall reservation, Idaho, and with Johnson Sides, a Paiute living near Reno, Nevada, who is bitterly opposed to Wovoka. His father's name, Tävibo, has been given also as Waughzeewaughber. It is not quite certain that the Paiute prophet of 1870 was the father of Wovoka. This is stated to have been the case by one of Captain Lee's informants (A. G. O., 4) and by Lieutenant Phister (*Phister, 2*). Wovoka himself says that his father did not preach, but was a "dreamer" with supernatural powers. Certain it is that a similar doctrine was taught by an Indian living in

In proportion as Wovoka and his doctrines have become subjects of widespread curiosity, they have also become subjects of ignorant misrepresentation and deliberate lies. Different writers have claimed he is a <term>Paiute</term>, a person of mixed race, and a Mormon white man. Countless stories have been told of the origin and nature of his mission and the day predicted for its final accomplishment. The most harmful and persistent of these stories has been the one that represents him as preaching a violent campaign against white people, whereas his doctrine is one of peace, and he himself is a mild-tempered member of a small and peaceful tribe. His own good name has been stolen from him, and he has been made to appear under a dozen different names, including that of his greatest enemy, <term>Johnson Sides</term>. He has been denounced as a fraud, mocked as a madman, and ridiculed as a self-proclaimed Christ, while the Indians revere him as a direct messenger from the Other World. Among many of the remote tribes, he is believed to be all-knowing, to speak all languages, and to be invisible to white men. We shall give his own story as told by himself, with such additional information as seems to come from reliable sources.

Despite all that had been said and written by newspaper correspondents about the Messiah, not one of them had undertaken to find the man himself and to learn from his own lips what he really taught. It is almost equally certain that none of them had even seen a Ghost Dance at close range—certainly none of them understood its meaning. The Messiah was regarded almost as a myth, something abstract, to be talked about but not to be seen. The first reliable information as to his personality was shared by the scout, <term>Arthur Chapman</term>, who, under instructions from the <term>War Department</term>, visited the <term>Paiute</term> country in December 1890 and spent four days at Walker Lake and Mason Valley. In the course of an interview with Wovoka, he obtained from him a detailed statement similar in all essentials to the one I obtained later. <note>See Secretary of War Report, page 3.</note>

After having spent seven months in the field investigating the new religion among the prairie tribes, particularly the <term>Arapaho</term>, and after having examined all the documents bearing on the subject in the files of the <term>Indian Office</term> and <term>War Department</term>, the author left Washington in November 1891 to find and talk with the Messiah and to gather additional material concerning the Ghost Dance. Before starting, I had written to the agent in charge of the reservation to which he was attached for information regarding the Messiah (<term>Jack Wilson</term>) and the dance, and learned in reply, with some surprise, that the agent had never seen him. The surprise grew into amazement when I was further informed that there were “neither Ghost songs, dances, nor ceremonies—”

<header>MOONEY] SPEECH OF YOWALUCH</header>

> "A good Christian man prayed with me for four days. After four days, a voice said to me, 'You shall live on earth for four weeks.' My soul was told that they must build a church for me in four weeks. I had lumber for a house, and my friends built the church. They had it all done in four weeks, except for six feet of the roof, and they spread a mat over that. As soon as the church was finished, the people came and filled the house and began to worship God. I felt strong—stronger than I do today—and all these men know this. My friends worked hard, and I am here because they finished the house in four weeks. My soul was told to remain on earth for four weeks more. All my friends came, and every Saturday we worshiped God. In four more weeks, my soul was told that I should live on earth for four years if I did right and preached for God. Everyone felt thankful, and people joined the church—about fifty people. I was promised more time if we worshiped God.

> "A bad man cannot reach heaven. I believe in God. I saw how bad I used to be. God sends us light so we can see. They know in heaven what we think. When people are sick, we pray to God to cure us. We pray that he takes the evil away and leaves the good. If a man is not a Christian, he will suffer and see what is bad. When we remember Jesus Christ's name, we always feel happy in our hearts. This is a good road for us to travel if we hold on. If we do, God's angels are near to our souls. Power comes from this to help us. When we pray, it helps us a great deal in our hearts. Sometimes we do not do good because our hearts are not right. When our bodies and hearts feel warm, we do good and sing good songs. As Christ said, he sends power to every believing soul on earth.

> "While one man can try to start a religion here on earth, it does not do much good; they will not believe him much. That is why we join together to worship. Now we are preparing ourselves for judgment. For it is said, it does not make any difference if he prays well and does good. God gives him help and words to speak. It makes no difference if one is a <term>'Boston'</term> or an Indian; if God helps, we know it. These things are what we learned. We learn good things while we pray—a voice says, 'Do good.'

> "It has been ten years now since we began, and we have good things. We all love these things and will follow them all the time. We learn to help ourselves when we are sick. When our friend is sick, we kneel and ask for help to cure him. We learn something once in a while to cure him. Then we do what we know to help him and cure him. If we do not learn how to help him, we generally lose him."

This is a fairly accurate synopsis of the speech delivered to me by <term>Slocum</term> and translated by another Indian who spoke fairly good English. However, so that a more thorough knowledge of their religious belief may be given, I also provide a brief synopsis of another speech made at the same meeting by <term>Louis Yowaluch</term>, a full-blooded Indian who is the legal head of this church. It is approximately as follows:

> "Well, my friend, we were about the poorest tribe on earth. We were the only tribe now that was full-blooded and nothing else. We would not believe anything. A minister came here, but we laughed at him. We loved bad habits—stealing—and then <term>John Slocum</term> died. He was not a religious man—he knew nothing of God—and all of us were the same. We heard there was a God from Slocum; we could see it was true. At the same time we heard of God, we believed it. I was the worst of the lot. I was a drunkard—I was half-starving—and I spent every cent on whiskey. I gambled, raced horses, and bet my shirt, money, and blankets; I did not know any better.

> "John Slocum brought good to us; his words civilized us. We could see. We all felt blind in those times. We lost people by drowning—our friends would drink whiskey and the canoes would overturn—we died out in the bay. Today, who stopped us from these things?

> "John Slocum came back to life, and I remembered God and felt frightened. We never heard of such a thing as a man dying and bringing back word that there was a God. I became sick for three or four weeks. I heard a voice saying to my soul, 'Tomorrow they will be coming to fix you up.' I had just heard about John Slocum, and I knew it was punishment for my bad habits. My heart was black—it was a bad thing."

“Now I have quit swearing—my heart is upside down—it has changed. After I heard the voice, I heard another say: ‘There it is now—someone to fix you up. Have you prepared your heart? If you do not believe in Christ, you will go into a great fire and burn forever.’ I saw a man’s hand coming toward my heart. That day I got up—I was well—and I talked to my friends, advising them. I will remain a follower of Christ as long as I live.

“A long time ago, we knew nothing at all. When Slocum came back from God, we found out there was a God. From that time on, we have prayed for anything we want. We follow God’s way. God teaches us that if we do bad things, we will go to hell. That is why we pray and avoid bad habits. If we do not ask for grace, bad things happen while we are eating. When we drink water, we think about God before drinking. If we do not think of him, maybe we will get sick from the water. If traveling, maybe we will die if we do not think of God. We are afraid to do wrong against God. A long time ago, we worked on Sundays, but not anymore. Our brother Christ has given us six days to work. On Sunday, we pray to God. God put people here to grow—he puts our souls in our bodies. That is why we pray so much. If we quit, just as a man might quit his job, he gets no pay. We would go to the fire in hell. We have no power to put out hellfire.

“Louis Yowaluch is the strong man of the Shaker church. He is six feet tall, rawboned, muscular, and rather slow. While he may once have been, as he says, a drunkard, he is now a Christian man. His conservative nature makes him a fine leader for the organization, while all the Indians respect him for his humanity and charity, for his honesty and uprightness, and for his fearlessness and love of right. He fully and freely places John Slocum at the head of the church, as the man who ascended to heaven and brought back personal knowledge of the path, but at the same time, he takes the lead in organizing work, building churches, and sending out preachers to new tribes.

“A new feature of this religion is found in Sam Yowaluch, the brother of Louis. He is younger than Louis and has more of the native superstition in his character. He has, by common consent, been placed at the head of the faith-cure branch of the church. The following summary of his ‘talk’ will explain his position:

“Among the Shakers, John Slocum is first. Louis is next. I take the power and cure people when they are sick. A long time ago, I knew nothing—I was just like an animal. No healing, no medicine—nothing was good. I was a drunkard, a thief, and a robber. When I joined this religion, I was told to be good. When John Slocum was preaching, I heard that if I prayed, I would have power and be a medicine man, and could cure the sick. From the time John Slocum preached, I tried to be a good Christian man. I prayed and was sick—my soul was sick. I prayed to God, and he rewards me for that. There is a great difference between this power and the old Indian doctoring. This is not the old power. I can cure people now. I have cured some white men and women, but they are ashamed to admit it. I cure without money. One prominent, wealthy man, Henry Walker, was sick—he had great pains in his ear and leg. The doctor at Olympia failed to cure him, and he came to John Slocum and me. We worked for him and prayed; then he lay down, slept, and was cured. He offered us twenty dollars—but no, we refused it. God will pay us when we die. This is our religion. When we die, we receive our reward from God.

“No, we do not believe the Bible. We believe in God, and in Jesus Christ as the Son of God, and we believe in a hell. In these matters, we believe the same as the Presbyterians. We think deeply of God today. A good Christian man is a good medicine man. A good Christian man sees a light toward God in the dark. God makes a fog—a good Christian man goes straight through it to the end, like a good

<header>MOONEY] SHAKER FORM OF CEREMONY</header>

medicine. I believe in this religion. It helps poor people. A bad man cannot see good—a bad man cannot get to heaven—he cannot find his way. We were sent to jail for this religion, but we will never give up. We all believe that John Slocum died and went to heaven, and was sent back to preach to the people. We all talk about that and believe it.

“The Shakers use candles, bells, crucifixes, Catholic pictures, etc., in their church and other ceremonies. As Mr. Ellis says, they use the paraphernalia of the Catholic, Presbyterian, and even some of the Indian religions. They cross themselves as the Catholics do; they say grace before and after meals; they stand and pray and chant in unison; they set candles around the dead as the Catholics do, and believe in the cure of the sick by faith and prayer. In times of excitement many of them twitch and shake, but in no instance do they conduct themselves in so nervous a manner as I have seen orthodox Christians do at the old Sandy Branch camp-meeting in Illinois. They believe that by praying with a man or woman and rubbing the person, they could induce them to join their church and could rub away their sins; but they have no rite, no ceremony, no belief, no policy, no form of religion that is not in use by some one or another of our orthodox people.

“Their religion, in brief, is a belief in God as the father and ruler of all, and in Jesus Christ as the Son of God and the Savior of mankind. They know there is a heaven, for John Slocum was there, and they believe in a hell of fire for the punishment of sinners, because the angels in heaven told John Slocum about it. They do not care for the Bible. It is of no use to them, for they have a distinct revelation direct from heaven. This is the only practical difference between them and the orthodox believers, and this they do not care for.”

Mr. Wickersham then gives an account of the persecutions to which the rising sect was subjected for a long time, chiefly at the hands of agent Edwin Eells and his brother, Reverend Myron Eells (already quoted at length), who was at that time the missionary on the Skokomish reservation. Since Mr. Wickersham's statements in this regard are mainly in the form of extended quotations from *Ten Years' Missionary Work at Skokomish*, written by the Reverend Mr. Eells himself, they may be regarded as conclusive. It is clear that at least part of this persecution—which took the form of banishment, chains, and imprisonment, and even the forceful seizure of a dead body from grieving relatives—was due to the fact that the Shakers, who considered themselves a genuine branch of the Christian church, were inclined toward Catholicism rather than toward the denominational form upheld by the agent and his brother.

However, religious persecution failed as completely in its purpose in this case as it has and must in all others. Quoting from Mr. Eells, "The chiefs did not care if they were deposed, were about to resign, and did not wish to have anything more to do with the 'Boston' religion <note>A term often used by Northwestern tribes to refer to American Protestantism or Americans in general.</note> or the agent. Billy Clams was ready, if need be, to suffer as Christ did. He was willing to be a martyr."

Mr. Wickersham continues:
> "While Billy Clams and some of his people publicly abandoned the forms of Shaker religion rather than be banished, John Slocum and his people refused to surrender in that way. The agent sent out his police and arrested John Slocum, Louis Yowaluch, and two or three more of these people—good, true men—and, loading their limbs with chains, confined them for several weeks in the dirty little single room of a jail at the Puyallup agency, near Tacoma. Their only offense was worshiping in a different form from that adopted by the agent and his brother. They had broken no law and created no disorder, and yet they suffered shameful incarceration in a vile dungeon, loaded with chains, at the pleasure of the agent. The Shakers believed in God, in Jesus Christ, in heaven and hell, in temperance, sobriety, and a virtuous life. They

<header>MOONEY] EFFECT OF LAND-SEVERALTY LAW</header>

They abandoned the old Indian religion with all its vices and rituals, including the influence of the doctors or medicine-men. These medicine-men held a great hold over the Indian mind, and they joined the minister and the agent in their fight against the Shakers because the Shakers opposed them. Thus, one could see the unique spectacle of the traditional shamanism of the American Indian and the supposedly orthodox religion of civilization working hand in hand to fight the followers of Jesus Christ.

> "Imprisonment, banishment, threats, chains, and the general hostility of the agent and all his employees were inflicted on those Shakers who continued to practice their forms of worship, and yet they did continue. Despite the fact that they occupied a status halfway between slaves and freemen—being under the orders of the agent and subject to constant harassment and annoyance from him—they persisted nobly and fearlessly in practicing their religion and worshiping God and Jesus Christ as they saw fit. To do so, however, they were forced to stay away from the reservations where most of the employees were located; their churches were built at Mud Bay and Oyster Bay, far away from the reservations.

> "But a brighter day arrived for these people, a day when they could stand up and defy every form or force of persecution. In 1886, Congress passed the Indian Land Severalty Act <note>Also known as the Dawes Act of 1887; it authorized the federal government to break up tribal lands into individual plots.</note>, a law providing for the division of lands in severalty to Indians. It provided that those who took land and adopted the habits of civilized life should be American citizens, with all the rights, privileges, and immunities of any other citizen. In 1892, I was appointed by Judge Hanford to defend a prisoner in the United States District Court at Tacoma. The prisoner was accused of selling liquor to a Puyallup Indian, but it appeared during cross-examination that this Indian owned land in severalty, voted, paid taxes, and exercised other rights of citizenship. I then raised the question on a motion to dismiss, arguing that these land-holding, tax-paying Indians were free and independent citizens of the United States. The United States prosecuting attorney appeared to contest the claim, but after an extended argument, Judge Hanford ruled in my favor, and the prisoner was discharged.

> "The effect of this decision was far-reaching. It meant that all land-holding Indians were no longer wards of the government but free citizens, and no longer under the control of the Indian agent. When the Shaker people heard this, they sent a delegation to see me. I held a long consultation with them, assuring them that they were as free as the agent himself and could establish their own church, own and build houses of worship, and conduct themselves in both religious and worldly matters as other citizens of the United States could. This was glorious news to them. It meant freedom; it meant the end of persecution and annoyance by the agency employees, and they were jubilant.

> "Accordingly, they met on June 6, 1892, at Mud Bay, at Louis Yowaluch's house, and organized their church on a regular business basis.

<summary>A landmark 1892 legal decision confirmed that Indians holding land under the Severalty Act were American citizens, exempting them from the authority of Indian agents. This legal victory allowed the Indian Shaker Church to finally organize openly and escape years of official persecution.</summary>
