<header>MOONEY] GROWTH OF THE SHAKER CHURCH</header>

and their religion, or at least to leave them alone. They now feel quite confident of their position and are acting much like the average citizen. Even the persons who persecuted them for eleven years now felt obligated to retire from the conflict, and a day of peace is reached at last.

“The Shaker church now reaches over nearly the whole of western Washington. The story of Slocum’s death, his visit to heaven, and his return to preach to the Indians is accepted by them as a direct revelation of the will of God. They say that they do not need to read the Bible, for do they not have better and more recent testimony of the existence of heaven and of the way to that celestial home than is contained in the Bible? Here is John Slocum, alive, and has he not been to heaven? Then, why read the Bible to learn the road, when John can so easily tell them all about it? The Bible says there are many roads; the Catholics have one, the Presbyterians another, and the Congregationalists a third; but John Slocum gives a short, straight road—and they choose that.

“The Shaker church now has a building for church purposes at Mud Bay, at Oyster Bay, at Cowlitz, Chehalis, and Puyallup. They have about a dozen regularly licensed ministers and about 500 members. Most of the Indians at Skokomish belong, while the Squaxins, Chehalis, Nisqually, Cowlitz, and Columbia River Indians—and in fact the majority of the Indians of western Washington—either belong or are in sympathy with its teachings, so that it is now the strongest church among them. They are sending out runners to the Yakimas east of the Cascade mountains and expect before long to make an effort to convert that tribe.

“The Indian is inclined to be weak and to adopt the vices of the white man, but not his virtues. However, this is not true of the Shakers. They do not drink intoxicants of any kind and make a special effort at all times to banish liquor. This is the strong element in their faith, and the one for which they fight hardest. They feel their honor is at stake in the matter and contrast the members of their church in every place with those belonging to other denominations—and it is too true that an Indian does not seem at all to be restrained from drinking by belonging to the other churches as he is in the Shaker church. In the others, he feels no personal interest. The honor of neither himself nor his people is involved, and if he disgraces himself, it reflects, in his opinion, rather on the white man’s church. Not so with the Shakers. No white man belongs to their church, and it is their boast that no white preacher can keep his Indian members from drinking as they can—and it is true. After their opposition to liquor, next comes gambling. From these two vices flow nearly all troubles for the Indian, and the Shakers are certainly successful in stopping their spread among the Indians. They make special war on drunkenness, gambling, and horse racing, and preach honesty, sobriety, temperance, and right living.

> "The Presbyterian church occupies an unusual position regarding these people. The Reverend M. G. Mann has been the missionary to the Indians of Puget Sound for many years and has succeeded in making a very favorable impression upon them. He has been especially attentive to the Shakers and, to his credit, has never tried to coerce them, only dealing with them kindly. This has gone so far that Louis Yowaluch was long ago taken into the Presbyterian church and is now an accredited elder there. Louis seemingly does not know how to escape from his dual position, or rather does not seem to think that he needs to escape. It all seems to be for the best interest of his people, so he continues to occupy the position of elder in the Presbyterian church and headman of the Shaker church.
>
> "At a recent meeting of Presbyterian ministers, the position of these Shaker people was fully discussed. The strongest language was used to say only good things about them, and every effort seems to be made by the Presbyterians to claim the Shakers as a body belonging to the Presbyterian church. If this account were not already too long, the church reports on the subject would be quoted, but the fact speaks volumes for the character of the Shakers and their teaching.

> "In conclusion: I have now known the Shaker people intimately as their attorney for more than a year, and out of the many drunken Indians I have seen in that time, not one was a Shaker. Not one of their people has been arrested for a crime in that time. They are good citizens and are far more temperate and peaceable than those Indians belonging to other churches. I feel that their church is a grand success in that it prevents idleness and vice, drunkenness and disorder, and tends to produce quiet, peaceable citizens and good Christian people. I think the Presbyterians make a mistake in trying to bring the Shakers into their fold—they ought rather to protect them and give them every assistance in their autonomy. It adds the greatest incentive to their labors and makes them feel as if they were of some importance. It lets them labor for themselves instead of feeling, as they always have before, that someone else—they hardly knew who—was responsible. Their forms of Christianity are not very unorthodox—their Christianity is quite orthodox; it is not exactly because they take Slocum’s revelation instead of the Bible, but the result is the same—a Christian.

### MOONEY] SHAKER CEREMONIAL SYMBOLISM

the Yakima, from the fact that on meeting a stranger, instead of at once shaking hands with him in the usual manner, they first wave the hand gently in front of his face like a fan, and blow on him, in order to “blow away the badness” from him. They first appeared among the Yakima and other eastern tribes about six years ago, and are gradually gaining adherents, although as yet they have no regular time or place of assembly. They frequently make the sign of the cross—the cross, it is hardly necessary to state, being as much an Indian as a Christian symbol—and are highly respected as doctors. Their treatment consists chiefly of hypnotic performances over the patient, resulting in the spasmodic shaking already described. In treating a patient, the “blowers” usually gather around him in a circle numbering about twelve, dressed in a very attractive ceremonial costume. Each wears on his head a sort of crown of woven cedar bark, in which two lighted candles are fixed, while in his right hand he carries a small cloth, and in the left another lighted candle. By fastening screens of colored cloth over the candles, the light is made to appear yellow, white, or blue. The candle upon the forehead is yellow, representing celestial glory; that at the back of the head is white, typical of earthly light, while the third is blue, the color of the sky.

They also frequently carry in their hands or wear on their heads garlands of roses and other flowers of various colors—yellow, white, and blue being the favorites—which they say represent the colors of objects in the celestial world. While the leader is performing his hypnotic ritual over the patient, the others wave the cloths and swing the candles held in their hands in circles. In all this, it is easy to see the influence of Catholic ritual, with its censers, tapers, and flowers, with which these tribes have been more or less familiar for the last fifty years.

A single instance will suffice to show the methods of the blower doctors. The story is told from the Indian point of view, as related by the half-blood interpreter, who believed it all. About six years ago, two of these doctors from the north, while visiting near Woodland on the Columbia, were called to assist a woman who was seriously ill and had received no benefit from the treatment of the native doctors. They came, and almost immediately upon seeing the patient, announced to the relatives that the sickness had been put into her by the evil magic of a neighboring medicine-man, whom they then summoned into their presence. When the messenger arrived for him, the medicine-man refused to go, saying that the doctors were liars and that he had not made the woman ill. By their <term>clairaudient</term> power—or possibly by a shrewd anticipation of probabilities—the doctors in the other house knew of his refusal and sent another messenger to tell him that concealment or denial would not help him, and that if he refused to come they would proceed to blow the sickness into his own body. Without further

argument, he accompanied the messengers to the sick woman’s house. As he entered, the chief doctor stepped up to him and, looking intently into his face, said, “I can see your heart inside your body, and it is black with evil things. You are not fit to live. You are making this woman sick, but we shall take out the badness from her body.” With the cloths and lighted candles, the two doctors then approached the sick woman and commanded her to arise, which she did, although she had been thought to be too weak to stand. Waving the cloths in front of her with a gentle fanning motion and blowing on her at the same time, they proceeded to drive the disease out of her body, beginning at the feet and working upward until, as they approached the head, the principal doctor changed the movement to a rapid fanning and corresponding blowing, while the assistant stood ready with his cloth to seize the disease when it was driven out. All this time, the medicine man standing a few feet away was shaking and quivering like someone in a fit, and the trembling became more violent and spasmodic as the doctors increased the speed of their motions. Finally, the leader brought his hands together over the woman’s head, where, just as the disease attempted to escape, it was caught and imprisoned in the cloth held by his assistant. Then, going up to the medicine man, with a few rapid passes they fanned the disease into his body and he fell down dead. The woman recovered, and with her sister has recently come up to the Yakima country as an apostle of the new religion, preaching the doctrines and performing the wonders which she was taught by the Nisqually doctors.

<note>A blue ink bracket marks the left margin of the following paragraph. A blue underline emphasizes the text from "means of bringing them" to "magnetic doctors," followed by a diagonal slash.</note>

This is the Indian story as told by a man of mixed heritage, who did not claim to have been an eyewitness but spoke of it as a matter of common knowledge and beyond question. It is likely substantially correct. The hypnotic action described is the same which the author has repeatedly seen employed in the Ghost Dance, resulting successively in involuntary trembling, violent spasmodic action, rigidity, and final deathlike unconsciousness. The Ghost Dancers regard the process not only as a means of bringing them into trance communication with their departed friends, but also as a preventive and cure of disease, just as we have our faith healers and magnetic doctors. With the Indians' implicit faith in the supernatural ability of the doctor, it is easy to suppose that the mental effect on the woman—who was told and believed that she was to be cured—would aid recovery if recovery was possible. It is unlikely that death actually resulted for the medicine man. It is more probable that under the hypnotic spell of the doctors he fell unconscious and apparently lifeless and remained so perhaps for a considerable time, as frequently happens with sensitive subjects in the Ghost Dance. The fact that the same process should produce exactly opposite effects in the two subjects is easily explainable. The object of the hypnotic performance was simply to bring the mind of the subject under the control of the operator. This accomplished, the mental, and ultimately the

<header>MOONEY] SHAKER CONTACT WITH WOVOKA 763</header>

The physical effect on either subject was whatever the practitioner intended it to be. After bringing both under mental control in the manner described, he suggested recovery to the woman and sickness or death to the medicine man, and the result followed.

Until the arrival of these women from beyond the mountains, such hypnotic performances seem to have been unknown among the Yakima and other eastern tribes of the Columbia region. The trance condition in the followers of Smohalla was apparently caused entirely by the effect of rhythmic dances and songs acting on excited imaginations, without the aid of blowing or hand gestures.

Hypnotism and so-called magnetism, however, appear to have been used by the medicine men of the Chinook tribes of the lower Columbia since ancient times. The stories told about one of these men residing at Wushqûm or Wisham, near The Dalles, are especially wonderful in this regard.

Around the time the two blower doctors appeared at Woodland, other apostles of the same doctrine—or perhaps the same two men—went up the Willamette river into central Oregon, teaching the same system and performing the same wonders among the tribes of that region. And here a remarkable coincidence occurs, if it is nothing more. It is said among the northern Indians that on this journey these apostles met, somewhere in the south, a young man to whom they taught their mysteries. He became such a talented pupil that he soon outstripped his teachers, and is now performing even greater wonders among his own people. This young man can be none other than Wovoka, the messiah of the Ghost dance, living among the Paiute in western Nevada. The only question is whether the story told among the Columbia tribes is a myth based on vague rumors of the southern messiah and his hypnotic performances—so similar to those of the blower doctors—or whether Wovoka actually derived his knowledge of such things from these northern apostles. The latter theory is entirely within the bounds of possibility. The time corresponds with the date of his original revelations, as he himself stated to the author. He is a young man, and, although he has never been far from home, the tribe to which he belongs roams in scattered bands over the whole country to the Willamette and the watershed of the Columbia, so that communication with the north is by no means difficult. He himself stated that Indians from the Warmspring reservation, in northern Oregon, have attended his dances near Walker lake.

The author notes that the timing of Wovoka's revelations and the migratory patterns of the Paiute make this direct influence highly plausible.</summary>

In conclusion, let me say that the general assembly of the Presbyterian church in this state has examined the religion and character of the Shaker (or Slocum) church several times and has highly endorsed its people, their character, and their actions. Yowaluch is currently their leader and the most intellectually capable man among them.

Some months later, Mr. Wickersham forwarded a detailed and carefully written statement regarding the history and current condition of the movement. At his request, we are publishing it exactly as written, omitting only those paragraphs that do not directly relate to the general subject. It may be considered an official statement on the Shaker case by their legally appointed representative. As might be expected, it directly disagrees with those who have opposed the new religion. The reader will notice the repeated use of the Indian sacred number, four, in Slocum's speech, as well as the fact that his first trance was the result of a serious illness.

->*Tschaddam or Shaker religion*<-

> "On Christmas Day, 1854, a treaty was signed at the mouth of Shenahnam (or Medicine Creek), on the south side of Puget Sound, Washington, between Isaac I. Stevens, governor and <term>ex officio</term> superintendent of Indian affairs for the United States, and the chiefs and leaders of the Nisqually, Puyallup, and other small Indian tribes living around the southern shores of Puget Sound.
> "One of these small tribes was the Squaxin, located on the southwestern branch or arm of Puget Sound, now known as Little Skookum Bay, in Mason County, Washington, near Olympia. The surviving members of this tribe still live in their ancestral homelands, having purchased small plots of their old hunting grounds from the first settlers; they now earn a living by fishing and gathering oysters, just as they did in the old days. From the fishing tribe of Squaxin, John Slocum was born; he is known by this name to the <term>Boston man</term> <note>A term used by Northwest Indians to refer to white Americans.</note>, but to his native friends, he is known as Squ-sacht-un.
> "John Slocum (Squ-sacht-un) is now (in 1893) about 51 years of age, about 5 feet 8 inches tall, and weighs about 160 pounds. He is somewhat stoop-shouldered, with a thin beard and a head of long black hair. He has a flat head (fashionably flattened by pressure during infancy), bright eyes, but generally a common facial expression. He is modest and somewhat retiring, but he has unquestioned confidence in himself and his mission. He is married, and until the time of his spiritual transformation, he was viewed as an ordinary Indian with a slight inclination toward alcohol and pony racing, as well as a known fondness for Indian gambling.
> "In October 1881, Slocum was unexpectedly moved to reflect on his immoral behavior. While in the woods, he knelt and prayed to God and began to think seriously about the error of his ways and the hard times that had befallen his few remaining native friends. Whiskey, gambling, laziness, and general vice had almost wiped out his people. His eyes were opened to the foolishness of these facts, and he

He, however, became sick; and as his sickness increased, these ideas became brighter in his mind and his duty became clearer. He grew worse, and one day he died. He was pronounced dead by everyone present and was laid out for burial. His brother went to Olympia for a coffin, and a grave was prepared. He died at 4 o'clock in the morning, and late in the afternoon, he returned to life and regained consciousness.

“His recovery was rapid, and he immediately told those present that during the time he was dead, his soul had been to heaven. There, he was met by angels who, after a proper inquiry as to his name and other details, told him that he had been a bad man on earth. They reminded him very forcefully of his shortcomings while there and finally informed him that he could not enter heaven, but that he could either go to hell or return to the earth to preach to the Indians and tell them the way to heaven. He accepted this latter offer, and the result was that his soul returned to earth, reentered its old body, and from that day to this has filled Slocum with the spirit of a crusader against gambling, whiskey drinking, and other ‘Boston’ <note>In the Pacific Northwest, "Boston" was a common term used by Indigenous people to refer to white Americans or their customs.</note> vices.

“About a year ago, I was employed by these people as their attorney and, at their request, attended the meetings in Mason County and had a long conference with them. As a practical person would, Slocum undertook to demonstrate to me his honesty and the divine character of their religion. At a large meeting composed only of Indians who were members of his church, he gave me a long public statement of facts and explained, through an interpreter, the character of their religion and of their belief. I wrote down a summary of what was said to me at the time, and I now quote it at some length as being the exact words of Slocum and the best explanation of their religion.

“Standing before all his people in the most solemn and impressive manner in their church, he said in substance:

> “The witnesses have spoken the truth. I was sick for about two weeks and had five Indian doctors. I grew very weak and frail. Dr. Jim was there, but he could not cure me. They wanted to save me, but my soul would die for two or three hours at a time. At night my breath was gone, and I died. All at once I saw a shining light—a great light—testing my soul. I looked and saw my body had no soul—I looked at my own body—it was dead.
>
> “I regained consciousness the first time and told my friends, ‘When I die, do not cry,’ and then I died again. Before this, I shook hands and told my friends I was going to die. Angels told me to look back and see my body. I did, and I saw it lying there. When I saw it, it looked very frail. My soul left my body and went up to God’s place of judgment. I do not know what happened to my body after 4 o'clock.
> 
> “I have seen a great light in my soul from that good land; I have understood all that Christ wants us to do. Before I came back to life, I saw I was a sinner. An angel in heaven said to me, ‘You must go back and become alive again on earth.’ I learned that I must be a good Christian man on earth, or I will be punished. My soul was told that I must come back and live four days on earth. When I returned, I told my friends, ‘There is a God—there is a Christian people. My good friends, be Christians.’
> 
> “When I came back to life, I told my friends, ‘There are good things in heaven. God is kind to us. If you all try hard and help me, we will be better men on earth.’ And now we all feel that it is so.

->“UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE,<-
->“Pyramid Lake, Nevada Agency, October 12, 1891.<-
“JAMES MOONEY, Esq.,
“*Bureau of Ethnology.*
“MY DEAR SIR: Your letter of September 24 regarding Jack Wilson, the ‘Messiah,’ has been received and noted. In reply, I will say that his Indian name is Ko-wee-jow (‘Big Belly’). I do not know if it will be possible to get a photo of him. I have never seen him or a photo of him. He works among the white people about 40 miles from my Walker Lake reserve and never comes near the agency when I visit it. My headquarters are at Pyramid Lake, about 70 miles north of Walker. I am pursuing the course with him of non-attention or silent ignoring. He seems to think, so I hear, that I will arrest him should he come within my reach. I would give him no such notoriety. He, like all other prophets, has but little honor in his own country. He has been visited by delegations from various and many Indian tribes, which I think should be discouraged as much as possible. I do not know what the ‘Smoholler’ <note>Smohalla</note> religion you speak of is. He speaks English well, but is not educated. He gained his doctrine in part from contact with, and living in, a religious family. There are neither ghost songs, dances, nor ceremonies among the Indians at my agencies. They would not be allowed. I think they died out with ‘Sitting Bull.’ This is the extent of the information I can give you.
“Very respectfully yours,
->C. C. WARNER, *United States Indian Agent.*”<-

Here is an agent who has under his special charge, and within a few miles of his agency, the man who has created the greatest religious ferment known to the Indians of this generation—a movement that has been occupying the attention of the newspaper and magazine press for a year—yet he has never seen him. While the Indian Office, from which he receives his commission, is sending circular letters everywhere to the western agencies in a praiseworthy effort to understand the matter, calling for all obtainable information regarding the Messiah and his doctrines, he “pursues the course of non-attention.” He has never heard of the Smohalla religion of the neighboring northern tribes, although the subject is repeatedly mentioned in the volumes of the Indian Commissioner’s report from 1870 to 1879, which were—or should have been—on a shelf in the office where this letter was written. He asserts that there are no ghost songs, dances, or ceremonies among his Indians, even though these things were happening constantly and had been for at least three years; only a short time before, a large delegation from beyond the mountains had attended a Ghost Dance near Walker Lake that lasted four days and nights. Chapman in 1890, and I in 1891, saw the cleared grounds with the willow frames where these dances were being held regularly at short intervals. I found the ghost songs familiar to all the Indians with whom I talked and had no special trouble finding the Messiah and obtaining his picture. The peaceful character of the movement is sufficiently shown by the fact that while the eastern papers are full of rumors of uprisings and massacres, and troops are being hurried to the front, the agent at the central point of the disturbance seems unaware that anything special is happening around him and can “silently ignore” the whole matter.

In a casual way, I then offered to show him the pictures of some of my Indian friends from across the mountains, and I brought out the photos of several Arapaho and Cheyenne whom I knew had recently come as delegates to the Messiah. This convinced him that I was trustworthy, and he became communicative. The result was that we spent about a week together in the <term>wikiups</term> (lodges made of tule rushes), always surrounded by a crowd of interested Paiute, discussing the old stories and games, singing Paiute songs, and sampling the seed mush and roasted piñon nuts. On one of these occasions, at night, a medicine man was performing his incantations over a sick child on one side of the fire while we were talking on the other. When the ice was well thawed, I cautiously approached the subject of the Ghost songs and dance. As confidence was now established, I found no difficulty in obtaining a number of the songs, along with a description of the ceremony. I then told Charley that, as I had taken part in the dance, I was anxious to see the Messiah and get from him some medicine paint to bring back to his friends among the eastern tribes. He readily agreed to go with me and promised to use his influence with his nephew to obtain what was wanted.

<margin>247</margin>
It is 20 miles north by railroad from the Walker River Agency to Wabuska, and 12 miles more in a southwesterly direction from there to the Mason Valley settlement. There we met a young white man named Dyer, who was well acquainted with Jack Wilson and who also spoke the Paiute language. We learned from him that the Messiah was about 12 miles further up the valley, near a place called Pine Grove. Enlisting his services, along with a team and driver—making four of us in all—we started up toward the mountain. It was New Year’s Day of 1892, and there was deep snow on the ground, a very unusual thing in this part of the country, which was due in this instance—as Charley assured us—to the direct influence of Jack Wilson. It is hard to imagine anything more monotonously unattractive than a sage prairie under ordinary circumstances, unless it is the same prairie when covered by a heavy fall of snow, under which the smaller clumps of sagebrush look like prairie-dog mounds, while the larger ones can hardly be distinguished at a short distance from <term>wikiups</term>. However, the mountains were bright in front of us, the sky was blue overhead, and the road was good under foot.

Soon after leaving the settlement, we passed the dance ground with the brush shelters still standing. We met only a few Indians on the way. After several miles, we noticed a man at some distance from the road with a gun across his shoulder. Dyer looked for a moment and then exclaimed, “I believe that’s Jack now!” The Indian thought so, too, and pulling up our horses, he shouted some words in the Paiute language. The man replied, and sure enough, it was the Messiah, hunting jackrabbits. At his uncle’s call, he soon came over.

As he approached, I saw that he was a young man, a dark full-blood, compactly built, and taller than the Paiute generally, being nearly 6

... feet tall. He was well-dressed in white man’s clothes, with the broad-brimmed white felt hat common in the West, secured to his head by a beaded ribbon under his chin. This, along with a blanket or a robe of rabbit skins, is now the standard Paiute dress. He wore a good pair of boots. His hair was cut straight across at the base of his ears, according to the custom of his tribe. His expression was open and showed firmness and decisiveness, but without any marked intellectual look. His features were broad and heavy, very different from the thin, clear-cut features of the prairie tribes.

As he approached, he shook my hand with a strong, hearty grip and asked what we wanted. His uncle explained the situation, adding that I was well-acquainted with some of his Indian friends who had visited him a short time before and that I was returning to those same people. After some consideration, he said that the white people had lied about him and he did not like to talk to them; some of the Indians had disobeyed his instructions and trouble had come of it, but because I was sent by Washington and was a friend of his friends, he would talk with me. He was hunting then, but if we would come to his camp that night, he would tell us about his mission.

With another handshake, he left us, and we drove on to the nearest ranch, arriving around dark. After supper, we got ready and started across the country through the sagebrush for the Paiute camp, which was several miles away, guided by our Indian companion. It was already night, with nothing to be seen but the clumps of snow-covered sagebrush stretching away in every direction. After traveling for an hour or more without reaching the camp, our guide had to admit that he had lost the trail. It had been two years since he had been there, his eyesight was failing, and, between the snow and the darkness, he was completely unsure of his location.

To be lost on a sagebrush plain on a freezing night in January is not a pleasant experience. There was no road and no house except for the one we had left miles behind, and it would be almost impossible to find our way back to it through the darkness. Except for a lantern, there was no light other than the glare from the snow and a few stars in the frosty sky above. To add to our difficulty, the snow was crisscrossed in every direction by cattle trails, which looked like Indian trails and kept us doubling back and circling pointlessly. In the uncertain gloom, every large clump of sagebrush looked like a wikiup <note>A traditional circular dwelling used by the Paiute and other Great Basin tribes, typically made of a frame of poles covered with brush or mats.</note>, only to disappoint us as we drew closer. On top of it all, the night was bitterly cold, and we were half-frozen. After unsuccessfully following a dozen false trails and shouting repeatedly in the hope of hearing an answering cry, we decided on the plan of leaving the Indian guide with the wagon—as he was the oldest man in the party—while the rest of us each went in a different direction from that central point. We followed the cattle tracks in the snow and called out to each other at short intervals so that we would not get lost from one another. After going

Once we were far enough to know that none of us had yet found the right trail, the wagon was moved forward a short distance and the same process was repeated. Finally, a shout from our driver brought us all together. He claimed that he had heard sounds ahead, and after listening for a few minutes in tense suspense, we saw a shower of sparks rise into the darkness and knew that we had reached the camp. Returning to the wagon, we climbed in and drove straight to the spot, where we found three or four small wikiups. In one of them, we were told, the messiah was waiting for us.

Entering through the low doorway, we found ourselves in a circular lodge made of bundles of tule rushes laid over a framework of poles, similar to the thatched roofs of Europe and very like the grass lodges of the Wichita. The lodge was only about 10 feet in diameter and 8 feet high, with sloping sides. It was almost entirely open at the top, like a cone with the top cut off, because rain or snow is rare in this part of the country. As mentioned before, the deep snow at the time was unusual. In the center, built directly on the ground, was a blazing sagebrush fire; fresh stalks were thrown onto it from time to time, sending a shower of sparks into the open air. This was how we had been guided to the camp. Sitting or lying around the fire were half a dozen Paiute, including the messiah and his family: his young wife, a boy about 4 years old whom he seemed very fond of, and an infant. It was clear that he was a kind husband and father, which matched his reputation among the white people for being hardworking and reliable. 

The only furniture consisted of a few grass-woven bowls and baskets of various sizes and patterns. There were no Indian beds or seats like those found in every prairie tipi—no rawhide boxes, no toiletry pouches, not even a pit dug in the ground for the fire. Although everyone wore white men’s clothing, there were no pots, pans, or other manufactured goods like those now used by even the most primitive prairie tribes. Strangely, although these Paiute are essentially farm laborers and tenants for the white people around them and earn good wages, they seem to desire nothing belonging to the white man. Instead, they spend their money on clothing, small trinkets, and ammunition for hunting. They continue to live on seeds, piñon nuts, and small game, sleeping at night on the dusty ground in their cramped wikiups, lacking even the most ordinary conveniences used by other tribes. It is a curious example of a people accepting the inevitable while still resisting innovation.

Wovoka welcomed us cordially and then asked more specifically about my purpose for wanting an interview. His uncle gave a detailed explanation that lasted an absurdly long time because of a unique Paiute conversational style. Every statement made by the older man was repeated at its conclusion, word for word and sentence by sentence, by the other, with the same monotonous inflec-

# MOONEY] WOVOKA'S REVELATION

Once this was done, the first speaker indicated with a grunt of approval that the message had been correctly repeated, and then proceeded with the next statement, which was repeated in the same way. The first time I had heard two old men talking together in this fashion on the reservation, I had supposed they were reciting some sort of Indian litany, and it took several such experiences and some patience to get used to it.

Finally, he indicated that he understood and was satisfied. Then, in answer to my questions, he gave an account of himself and his doctrine; much of the interpretation was provided by Dyer, with whom he seemed to be on intimate terms. He said he was about 35 years old, fixing the date based on a well-known battle<note>This battle, probably the most important conflict that ever occurred between the Paiute and the whites, was fought in April 1860 near the current agency at Pyramid Lake and about 8 miles from Wadsworth, Nevada. After some miners kidnapped and forcibly held a couple of Indian women, their husbands gathered a party and rescued them, without, however, inflicting any punishment on the guilty men. This was considered an "Indian outrage," and a large group of miners gathered and marched toward Pyramid Lake to destroy the Indian camp. The Paiute, armed almost entirely with bows and arrows, surprised them in a narrow pass at the spot indicated. As a result, the whites were defeated and fled in disorder, leaving nearly fifty dead on the field. The entire affair, in its causes and results, was most disgraceful to the whites.</note> between the Paiute and the whites near Pyramid Lake in 1860. At that time, he said he was about the size of his little boy, who appeared to be about 4 years old. His father, Tävibo ("White Man"), was not a preacher, but was a *capita* (from the Spanish *capitan*) or petty chief, and was a dreamer and invulnerable. His own proper name from boyhood was Wovoka or Wüvoka, "The Cutter," but a few years ago he had taken the name of his paternal grandfather, Kwohitsauq, or "Big Rumbling Belly." After the death of his father, he had been taken into the family of a white farmer, David Wilson, who had given him the name of Jack Wilson, by which he is commonly known among the white people. He thus has three distinct names: Wovoka, Kwohitsauq, and Jack Wilson. He stated positively that he was a full-blooded Indian, a statement supported by his appearance. The impression that he is of mixed race may have arisen because his father's name was "White Man" and because he uses a white man's name. His followers, both in his own and in all other tribes, commonly refer to him as "our father." He has never been away from Mason Valley and speaks only his own Paiute language, with some little knowledge of English. He is not acquainted with the sign language, which is hardly known west of the mountains.

<margin>Sten</margin>
When he was about 20 years old, he married and continued to work for Mr. Wilson. He had given the dance to his people about four years earlier, but had received his great revelation about two years previously. On this occasion "the sun died" (was eclipsed), and he fell asleep during the daytime and was taken up to the other world. There he saw God, along with all the people who had died long ago, engaged in their old-fashioned sports and occupations, all happy and forever young. It was a pleasant land, full of game. After showing him everything, God told him he must go—

THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14

...back and tell his people they must be good and love one another, have no quarreling, and live in peace with the whites; that they must work, and not lie or steal; that they must put away all the old practices that suggested war; that if they faithfully obeyed his instructions they would at last be reunited with their friends in this other world, where there would be no more death, sickness, or old age. He was then given the dance, which he was commanded to bring back to his people. By performing this dance at intervals, for five consecutive days each time, they would secure this happiness for themselves and speed up the event. Finally, God gave him control over the elements so that he could make it rain or snow or be dry at will, and appointed him as his deputy to take charge of affairs in the West, while "Governor Harrison" would attend to matters in the East, and he, God, would look after the world above. He then returned to earth and began to preach as he was directed, convincing the people by exercising the wonderful powers that had been given to him.

In 1890 Josephus, a Paiute informant, thus described the occasion of Wovoka's first inspiration to the scout Chapman: "About three years ago, Jack Wilson took his family and went into the mountains to cut wood for Mr. Dave Wilson. One day while at work, he heard a great noise which appeared to be above him on the mountain. He laid down his axe and started to go in the direction of the noise, when he fell down dead, and God came and took him to heaven." Afterward, on one or two other occasions, "God came and took him to heaven again." Wovoka also told Chapman that he had then been preaching to the Indians for about three years. In our conversation, he said nothing about a mysterious noise and stated that it was about two years since he had visited heaven and received his great revelation, but that it was about four years since he had first taught the dance to his people. The fact that he has different revelations from time to time would account for the discrepancy in his statements.

<margin>X</margin>
He denied all responsibility for the ghost shirt, which formed such an important part of the dance costume among the Sioux; he said that there were no trances in the dance as performed among his people—a statement confirmed by eyewitnesses among the neighboring ranchmen—and earnestly rejected any idea of hostility toward the whites, asserting that his religion was one of universal peace. When questioned directly, he said he believed it was better for the Indians to follow the white man's path and to adopt the habits of civilization. If appearances are anything to go by, he is sincere in this, for he was dressed in a good suit of white man's clothing and works regularly on a ranch, although living in a <term>wikiup</term>. While he rejected almost everything for which he had been held responsible in the East, he asserted positively that he had been to the spirit world and had been given a revelation and message from God himself, with full control over the elements. From his uncle, I learned that Wovoka has five songs for making it

### MOONEY] WOVOKA’S VISION

rain, the first of which brings on a mist or cloud, the second a snowfall, the third a shower, and the fourth a hard rain or storm, while when he sings the fifth song the weather again becomes clear.

I knew that he was holding something in reserve, as no Indian would reveal his private thoughts on religious matters to a white man with whom he had not had a long and intimate acquaintance. This was especially true in view of the warlike turn affairs had taken across the mountains. Consequently, I accepted his statements with several grains of salt, but on the whole, he seemed to be honest in his belief and his supernatural claims, although, like others of the priestly profession, he occasionally resorts to cheap trickery to maintain the impression of his miraculous powers. Based on some of the reports, he is evidently an expert sleight-of-hand performer. He makes no claim to be Christ, the Son of God, as has been so often asserted in print. He does claim to be a prophet who has received a divine revelation. I could not help feeling that he was sincere in his denial of a number of the wonderful things attributed to him, for the reason that he insisted so strongly on other things that were just as trying to the faith of a white man. He made no argument and offered no proofs, but said simply that he had been with God, as though the statement no more allowed for controversy than the proposition that 2 and 2 are 4. From Mr. J. O. Gregory, formerly employed at the agency and well acquainted with the prophet, I learned that Wovoka had once requested him to write and send a statement of his supernatural claims to the President, with a proposal that if he could receive a small regular salary, he would take up his residence on the reservation and agree to keep the people of Nevada informed of all the latest news from heaven and to provide rain whenever it was wanted. The letter was never sent.

From a neighboring ranchman, who knew Wovoka well and sometimes employed him during the working season, I obtained a statement which seems to explain the whole matter. It appears that a short time before the prophet began to preach, he was stricken down by a severe fever; during this illness, the ranchman frequently visited and cared for him. While he was still sick, an eclipse of the sun occurred, a phenomenon which always causes great alarm among primitive peoples. In their belief system, the sun is a living being of great power and kindness, and the temporary darkness is caused by an attack on him by some supernatural monster that tries to devour him. It will succeed, and thus plunge the world into eternal night, unless it is driven off by incantations and loud noises. On this occasion, the Paiute were frantic with excitement, and the air was filled with the noise of shouts, wailings, and the firing of guns for the purpose of frightening off the monster that threatened the life of their god. It was at this time, as Wovoka stated, "when the sun died," that he went to sleep during the daytime and was taken up to heaven. This means simply that the excitement and alarm produced by the eclipse, acting on a mind and body

already weakened by sickness, resulted in delirium, in which he imagined himself entering the portals of the spirit world. Constantly dwelling on the subject in his thoughts by day and in his dreams by night would create and sustain the heightened mental state in which imaginary visions would have all the appearance of real events. To those familiar with the spiritual nature of Indians and their absolute faith in dreams, all of this is perfectly understandable. His frequent trances would also indicate that, like so many other religious ecstatics, he is prone to cataleptic seizures.

I have not been able to determine the date of this eclipse satisfactorily. From inquiries at the Nautical Almanac office, I learned that solar eclipses visible in Nevada and the neighboring territory from 1884 to 1890 occurred as follows: 1884, October 18, partial; 1885, March 16, partial; 1886, March 5, partial; 1887, none; 1888, none; 1889, January 1, total or partial; 1890, none. The total eclipse of January 1, 1889, fits best with his statement to me on New Year’s night in 1892, when he said it had been about two years since he went up to heaven when the sun died. It should be noted that Indians generally count years by winters instead of by twelve-month calendar cycles, a difference which sometimes causes an apparent discrepancy of nearly a year.

In later conversations, he added a few minor details regarding his vision and his doctrine. He asked many questions about the eastern tribes whose delegates had visited him and was pleased to learn that the delegates from several of these tribes were my friends. He spoke particularly of the large delegation—about twelve people—from the Cheyenne and Arapaho who had visited him the previous summer and participated in the dance with his people. Nearly all the members of this party were known to me personally, and the leader, Black Coyote—whose picture I had with me and showed to him—had been my main instructor in the Ghost Dance among the Arapaho. While this fact placed me on a more confidential footing with Wovoka, it also greatly assisted my further investigation upon my return to the prairie tribes; once they were satisfied by my statements and the items I brought back that I had indeed seen and spoken with the messiah, they were convinced that I sincerely desired to understand their religion correctly, and from then on, they spoke freely and without reservation.

I had my camera and was eager to get Wovoka’s picture. When the subject was brought up, he replied that his picture had never been taken; he said a white man had offered him five dollars for permission to take his photograph, but he had refused. However, because I had been sent from Washington specifically to learn and tell white people all about him and his doctrine, and because he was satisfied from my friendship with his friends in the other tribes that I must be a good man, he would allow me to take his picture. As is common when dealing with Indians, he wanted to make the most of his bargain and demanded two dollars

MOONEY] WOVOKA'S LEGERDEMAIN

...and a half for the privilege of taking his picture and a like sum for each one of his family. I was prepared for this, however, and refused to pay any such charges, but agreed to give him my regular price per day for his services as an informant and to send him a copy of the picture when finished. After some hesitation he consented and got ready for the operation by knotting a handkerchief about his neck, fastening an eagle feather at his right elbow, and taking a wide-brimmed sombrero upon his knee. I afterward learned that the feather and sombrero were important parts of his spiritual stock in trade. After taking his picture, I obtained from him—as souvenirs to bring back and show to my Indian friends in Indian Territory—a blanket of rabbit skins, some piñon nuts, some tail feathers of the magpie (highly prized by the Paiute for ornamentation), and some of the sacred red paint, endowed with most miraculous powers, which plays so important a part in the ritual of the Ghost-dance religion. Then, with mutual expressions of good will, we parted, his uncle going back to the reservation, while I took the train for Indian Territory.

As soon as the news of my arrival spread among the Cheyenne and Arapaho on my return, my friends of both tribes came in, eager to hear all the details of my visit to the messiah and to get my own impressions of the man. In comparing notes with some of the recent delegates, I discovered something of Wovoka's hypnotic methods, and incidentally learned how much of a miracle depends on the mental receptivity of the observer.

The Cheyenne and Arapaho, although for generations associated in the most intimate manner, are of very different characters. In religious matters it may be said briefly that the Arapaho are devotees and prophets, continually seeing signs and wonders, while the Cheyenne are more skeptical. In talking with Tall Bull, one of the Cheyenne delegates and then captain of the Indian police, he said that before leaving they had asked Wovoka to give them some proof of his supernatural powers. Accordingly, he had arranged them in front of him, seated on the ground, while he sat facing them with his sombrero between them and his eagle feathers in his hand. Then with a quick movement he had put his hand into the empty hat and drawn out from it “something black.” Tall Bull would not admit that anything more had happened, and did not seem to be very profoundly impressed by the occurrence, saying that he thought there were medicine-men of equal capacity among the Cheyenne. In talking soon afterward with Black Coyote, one of the Arapaho delegates and also a police officer, the same incident came up, but with a very different sequel. Black Coyote told how they had seated themselves on the ground in front of Wovoka, as described by Tall Bull, and went on to tell how the messiah had waved his feathers over his hat, and then, when he withdrew his hand, Black Coyote looked into the hat and there “saw the whole world.” The explanation is simple. [Tall Bull, despite his partial] paralysis, was a jovial, light-hearted fellow, fond of joking and playing tricks on his associates, but nevertheless a man of good hard sense and inclined to be skeptical in regard to all medicine-men outside of his own tribe. Black Coyote, on the contrary, is a man of a contemplative nature, much given to speculation on the unseen world. His body and arms are covered with the scars of wounds which he has inflicted on himself in obedience to commands received in dreams. When the first news of the new religion reached the southern tribes, he had made a long journey, at his own expense, to his relatives in Wyoming to learn the doctrine and the songs, and since his return had been drilling his people day and night in both. Now, on his visit to the fountainhead of inspiration, he was prepared for great things, and when the messiah performed his hypnotic gestures with the eagle feather, as I have so often witnessed in the Ghost Dance, Black Coyote saw the whole spirit world where Tall Bull saw only an empty hat. From my knowledge of the men, I believe both were honest in their statements.

As a result of the confidence established between the Indians and myself following my visit to the messiah, one of the Cheyenne delegates named Black Sharp Nose, a prominent man in his tribe, soon after voluntarily brought me the written statement of the doctrine obtained from the messiah himself, and requested me to take it back and show it to Washington, to convince the white people that there was nothing bad or hostile in the new religion. The paper had been written by a young Arapaho of the same delegation who had learned some English at the Carlisle Indian School, and it had been taken down on the spot from the dictation of the messiah as his message to be carried to the prairie tribes. On the reverse page of the paper the daughter of Black Sharp Nose, a young woman who also had some school education, had written out the same thing in somewhat better English from her father’s dictation on his return. No white man had any part, directly or indirectly, in its production, nor was it originally intended to be seen by white men. In fact, in one part the messiah himself expressly warns the delegates to tell no white man.

# CHAPTER X

## THE DOCTRINE OF THE GHOST DANCE

> ->You must not fight. Do no harm to anyone. Do right always.—*Wovoka*.<-

The primary underlying principle of the Ghost Dance doctrine is that a time will come when the entire Indian race, both living and dead, will be reunited on a regenerated earth to live a life of indigenous happiness, forever free from death, disease, and misery. On this foundation, each tribe has built a structure from its own mythology, and every apostle and believer has filled in the details according to his own mental capacity or ideas of happiness, along with additions that come to him through trances. Some changes have also undoubtedly resulted from the transmission of the doctrine through the imperfect medium of sign language. These differences in interpretation are exactly like those found in Christianity, with its hundreds of sects and countless shades of individual opinion. The white race—being alien, secondary, and hardly real—has no part in this plan of indigenous regeneration and will be left behind with the other earthly things that have served their temporary purpose, or else will cease to exist entirely.

All this is to be achieved by a supreme spiritual power that requires no help from human beings. Although certain medicine men were inclined to anticipate the Indian millennium by preaching resistance to the further encroachments of white people, such teachings are not part of the true doctrine. It was only where long-standing dissatisfaction was worsened by recent grievances, as among the Sioux, that the movement took on a hostile tone. On the contrary, all believers were urged to make themselves worthy of the predicted happiness by setting aside everything warlike and practicing honesty, peace, and goodwill—not only among themselves, but also toward white people as long as they lived together. Some apostles have even thought that all racial distinctions will be erased and that white people will share in the coming happiness with the Indians; however, it seems certain that this is also contrary to the doctrine as it was originally preached.

Different dates have been set at various times for the fulfillment of the prophecy. Regardless of the year, it has generally been believed—for very natural reasons—that the regeneration of the earth and the renewal of all life would occur in the early spring. In some cases, July, and particularly the 4th of July, was the expected time. This, it should be noted, was around the season when the great annual ceremony of the

The sun dance used to take place among the prairie tribes. The messiah himself has set several dates from time to time, as one prediction after another failed to materialize, and in his message to the Cheyenne and Arapaho in August 1891, he leaves the whole matter as an open question. The date universally recognized among all the tribes immediately before the Sioux outbreak was the spring of 1891. As springtime came and passed, and summer grew and waned, and autumn faded again into winter without the realization of their hopes and longings, the doctrine gradually took its present form—that at some time in the unknown future, the Indian people will be united with their friends who have died, to be forever supremely happy, and that this happiness may be anticipated in dreams, if not actually hastened in reality, by earnest and frequent attendance at the sacred dance.

On returning to the Cheyenne and Arapaho in Oklahoma, after my visit to Wovoka in January 1892, I was at once sought out by my friends from both tribes, who were anxious to hear the report of my journey and see the sacred things I had brought back from the messiah. The Arapaho especially, who are of a more spiritual nature than any of the other tribes, showed a deep interest and followed every detail of the narrative intently. As soon as the news of my return was spread abroad, men and women, in groups and individually, would come to me; after grasping my hand, they would repeat a long and earnest prayer, sometimes aloud and sometimes with their lips moving silently, and frequently with tears rolling down their cheeks and their whole bodies trembling violently from the stress of emotion. Often, before the prayer was ended, the devotee's condition bordered on hysteria, very little less than in the Ghost Dance itself. The substance of the prayer was usually an appeal to the messiah to hasten the coming of the promised happiness, with a petition that—since the speaker was unable to make the long journey themselves—they might, by grasping the hand of one who had seen and talked with the messiah face-to-face, be enabled in their trance visions to catch a glimpse of the coming glory. During all of this performance, the bystanders awaiting their turn kept a reverent silence. In a short time, it became very embarrassing, but until the story had been told over and over again, there was no way of escape without wounding their feelings. The same thing afterward happened among the northern Arapaho in Wyoming; one chief even held out his hands toward me with short exclamations of *hŭ! hŭ! hŭ!*, as is sometimes done by the devotees around a priest in the Ghost Dance, in the hope, as he himself explained, that he might thus be enabled to go into a trance then and there. That hope, however, was not realized.

After this preliminary ordeal, my visitors would ask to see the things I had brought back from the messiah—the rabbit-skin robes, the piñon nuts, the gaming sticks, the sacred magpie feathers, and, above all, the sacred red paint. This is a bright-red ocher, about the color of brick dust, which the Paiute procure from the neighborhood

It is the principal paint used by the Paiute in the Ghost Dance, and small portions of it are given by the messiah to all the delegates and are carried back by them to their respective tribes. On the battlefield of Wounded Knee, I have seen this paint smeared on the posts of the enclosure around the trench in which the Indians killed in the fight are buried. I found it very hard to refuse the numerous requests for some of the paint, but as I had only one cake myself, I could not afford to be too generous. My friends were very anxious to touch it, however; but when I found that every man tried to rub off as much of it as possible on the palms of his hands, afterward smearing this dust on the faces of himself and his family, I was obliged in self-defense to put it away entirely.

The piñon nuts, although not considered quite as sacred, were also the subject of reverent curiosity. One evening, by invitation from Left Hand, the principal chief of the Arapaho, I went over to his tipi to talk with him about the messiah and his country, and I brought a quantity of the nuts for distribution. Upon entering, I found the chief and a number of the principal men arranged on one side of the fire, while his wife and several other women, with his young grandchildren, completed the circle on the other. Each of the adults in turn took my hand with a prayer, as described before, varying in length and earnestness according to the devotion of the speaker. This ceremony took a considerable amount of time. I then produced the piñon nuts and gave them to Left Hand, telling him how they were used as food by the Paiute. He handed a portion to his wife, and before I knew what was coming, the two arose in their places and, stretching out their hands toward the northwest—the country of the messiah—made a long and earnest prayer aloud that <term>*Hesûnanin*</term>, "Our Father," would bless them and their children through the sacred food, and hasten the time of his coming. The others, men and women, listened with bowed heads, breaking in from time to time with similar appeals to "the Father." The scene was deeply affecting. It was another of those impressive exhibitions of natural religion which it has been my fortune to witness among the Indians, and which throw light on a side of their character of which the ordinary white observer never dreams. After the prayer, the nuts were carefully divided among those present, down to the youngest infant, so that all might taste of what to them was the true bread of life.

After considerable difficulty and hardship, the Indians were at last fully satisfied that I truly desired to learn the truth concerning their new religion. A few days after my visit to Left Hand, several of the delegates who had been sent out in the previous August came down to see me, led by Black Short Nose, a Cheyenne. After preliminary greetings, he stated that the Cheyenne and Arapaho were now convinced that I would tell the truth about their religion. As they loved their religion and were anxious to have the whites know that it was all good and contained nothing bad or hostile, they would now give me the message which the Messiah himself had given to them, so that I might take it back to show to Washington. He then took from a beaded pouch and gave to me a letter, which proved to be the message or statement of the doctrine delivered by Wovoka to the Cheyenne and Arapaho delegates—of whom Black Short Nose was one—on the occasion of their last visit to Nevada in August 1891. It had been written down on the spot in broken English by one of the Arapaho delegates, Casper Edson, a young man who had acquired some English education by several years’ attendance at the government Indian school at Carlisle, Pennsylvania. On the reverse page of the paper was a duplicate in somewhat better English, written out by a daughter of Black Short Nose, a schoolgirl, as dictated by her father upon his return. These letters contained the message to be delivered to the two tribes and, as is expressly stated in the text, were not intended to be seen by a white man. The daughter of Black Short Nose had attempted to erase this clause before her father brought the letter down to me, but the lines were still plainly visible. It is the genuine official statement of the Ghost Dance doctrine as given by the Messiah himself to his disciples. It is reproduced here in duplicate and word-for-word, just as received, with a translation for the benefit of those not accustomed to "Carlisle English." In accordance with the request of the Indians, I brought the original to Washington, where it was read by the Indian Commissioner, the Honorable T. J. Morgan. Afterward, I had two copies made, giving one to the commissioner and retaining the other myself, before returning the original to its owner, Black Short Nose.

And he will give you a good spirit. And he will give you <gloss>all</gloss> good paint.

<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

Every organized religion has a system of ethics, a system of mythology, and a system of ritual observance. In this message from the high priest of the Ghost Dance, we have a summary of all three. Regarding the ritual part, ceremonial purification and bathing have been a part of every great religion in some form or another since the beginning of history, while the religious dance dates back far beyond the day when the daughter of Saul “looked through a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord.” The feasting required is a part of every Indian ceremonial gathering—whether religious, political, or social. The dance is to continue for four successive nights, in accordance with the regular Indian system, in which *four* is the sacred number, just as *three* is in Christianity. In obedience to this message, the southern prairie tribes—after the return of the delegation in August 1891—stopped holding frequent one-night dances at irregular intervals as they had previously without ceremonial bathing. Instead, they adopted a system of four-night dances at regular intervals of six weeks, followed by ceremonial bathing on the morning of the fifth day.

The mythology of the doctrine is only briefly mentioned, but the main points are provided. The dead have all arisen and the spirit hosts are advancing; they have already arrived at the boundaries of this earth, led forward by the regenerator in a cloud-like, indistinct form. The spirit captain of the dead is always represented in this shadowy appearance. The great change will be ushered in by a trembling of the earth, which the faithful are urged not to fear. The hope offered is the same that has inspired Christians for nineteen centuries—a happy immortality in eternal youth. As for setting a date, the Messiah is as cautious as his predecessor in prophecy, who declared that “no man knows the time, not even the angels of God.” His weather predictions are also about as definite as the inspired utterances of the Delphian oracle <note>The Delphian oracle refers to the priestess of Apollo in ancient Greece, famous for giving vague or ambiguous prophecies.</note>.

The moral code taught is as pure and comprehensive in its simplicity as anything found in religious systems from the days of Gautama Buddha <note>Gautama Buddha was the spiritual teacher from ancient India who founded Buddhism.</note> to the time of Jesus Christ. “*Do no harm to anyone. Do right always.*” Could anything be more simple, and yet more precise and demanding? It teaches honesty—“*Do not tell lies.*” It preaches goodwill—“*Do no harm to anyone.*” It forbids the extreme mourning customs formerly common among the tribes—“*When your friends die, you must not cry,*” which is interpreted by the prairie tribes as a ban on killing horses, burning tipis, destroying property, cutting off hair, and slashing the body with knives. All of these were previously the distressing rule at every death until forbidden by the new doctrine. As an Arapaho man said to me when his little boy died, “I shall not shoot any ponies, and my wife will not slash her arms. We used to do this when our friends died because we thought we would never see them again, and it made us feel bad. But now we know we shall all be united again.” If the Kiowa had held to

<header>MOONEY] THE DOCTRINE OF THE DANCE</header>

If they had followed the Ghost Dance doctrine instead of abandoning it as they had done, they would have been spared the loss of thousands of dollars in horses, tipis, wagons, and other destroyed property. They would also have been spared much of the mental suffering and all the physical scarring that resulted from the recent fatal epidemic in the tribe. For weeks and months, the sound of wailing rose every night and morning; in every camp, men and women could be seen daily with disheveled clothing and hair cut close to the scalp, with blood hardened in clots upon the skin or streaming from mutilated fingers and fresh gashes on their faces, arms, and legs. <insert>(</insert>It preaches peace with the whites and obedience to authority until the day of deliverance comes. Above all, it forbids war—"*You must not fight.*"<insert>)</insert> It is hardly possible for us to realize the tremendous and radical change this doctrine works in the entire spirit of tribal life. The career of every Indian has been the war-path. <margin>No! No! No! It is not true.</margin> His proudest title has been that of warrior. His conversation by day and his dreams by night have been of bloody deeds against the enemies of his tribe. His highest boast was the number of his scalp trophies, and his chief delight at home was the war dance and the scalp dance. The thirst for blood and massacre seemed inborn in every man, woman, and child of every tribe. Now comes a prophet as a messenger from God to forbid not only war, but everything that suggests war—the war dance, the scalp dance, and even the bloody torture of the Sun Dance—and his teaching is accepted and his words obeyed by four-fifths of all the warlike, predatory tribes of the mountains and the Great Plains. <insert>(</insert>Only those who have known the deadly hatred that once drove the Ute, Cheyenne, and Pawnee against one another, and are able to contrast it with their current spirit of mutual brotherly love, can know what the Ghost Dance religion has accomplished in bringing these people toward civilization. It is a revolution that happens only once in the life of a race.<insert>)</insert>

The beliefs held among the various tribes regarding the final apocalypse are as probable as some held on the same subject by more orthodox authorities. As for the dance itself, with its scenes of intense excitement, spasmodic action, and physical exhaustion leading even to unconsciousness, such manifestations have always accompanied religious upheavals among primitive peoples and are not entirely unknown among ourselves. In a country that produces magnetic healers, Shakers, trance mediums, and the like, all these things can very easily be found without going far from home.

In conclusion, we may say of the prophet and his doctrine what a careful and competent investigator said of one of his apostles: 

> “He has given these people a better religion than they ever had before, taught them precepts which, if faithfully carried out, will bring them into better accord with their white neighbors, and has prepared the way for their final Christianization.” (*G. D.*, 4, and *A. G. O.*, 5.)

<margin>1.</margin>
We may now consider the details of the doctrine as held by different tribes, beginning with the <term>Paiute</term>, among whom it originated. The best account of the <term>Paiute</term> belief is contained in a report to the War Department by Captain J. M. Lee, who was sent out in the autumn of 1890 to investigate the mood and fighting strength of the <term>Paiute</term> and other Indians in the vicinity of Fort Bidwell in northeastern California. We provide the statement obtained by him from Captain Dick, a <term>Paiute</term>, as delivered one day in a conversational way and apparently without reserve, after nearly all the Indians had left the room:

> A long time ago, twenty years ago, an Indian medicine man in Mason Valley at Walker Lake spoke the same way, just as you hear now. In maybe one year after he began to talk, he died. Three years ago, another medicine man began the same talk. There has been a lot of talk all the time. Indians hear all about it everywhere. Indians came from a long way off to hear him. They came from the east; they made signs. Two years ago, I went to Winnemucca and Pyramid Lake; I saw Indian Sam, a leader, and Johnson Sides. Sam told me he had just been to see the Indian medicine man to hear him talk. Sam said the medicine man spoke this way:
> “All Indians must dance, everywhere, and keep on dancing. Very soon, in the next spring, the Big Man [Great Spirit] will come. He will bring back all game of every kind. The game will be plentiful everywhere. All dead Indians will come back and live again. They will all be strong, just like young men; they will be young again. The old, blind Indian will see again, become young, and have a fine time. When the Old Man [God] comes this way, then all the Indians will go to the mountains, high up and away from the white people. The whites cannot hurt the Indians then. Then, while the Indians are far up high, a big flood will come like water and all the white people will die; they will be drowned. After that, the water will go away, and then there will be nobody but Indians everywhere, and all kinds of game will be plentiful. Then the medicine man told the Indians to send word to all Indians to keep up the dancing and the good times would come. Indians who do not dance, and who do not believe in this word, will grow small, only about a foot high, and stay that way. Some of them will be turned into wood and be burned in the fire.” That is the way Sam told me the medicine man spoke. (A. G. O., 6.)

Lieutenant N. P. Phister, who gathered part of the material included in Captain Lee’s report, confirms this general statement and gives a few additional details. The flood is to consist of mixed mud and water, and when the faithful go up into the mountains, the skeptics will be left behind and will be turned to stone. The prophet claims to receive these revelations directly from God and the spirits of the dead Indians during his trances. He also asserts that he is invulnerable, and that if soldiers should attempt to kill him, they would fall down as if they had no bones and die, while he would still live, even though cut into small pieces. (*Phister, 3.*)

One of the first and most prominent of those who brought the doctrine to the prairie tribes was <term>Porcupine</term>, a <term>Cheyenne</term>, who crossed the mountains with several companions in the fall of 1889, visited <term>Wovoka</term>, and attended the dance near Walker Lake, Nevada. In his report of his experiences, made some months later to a military officer, he states that <term>Wovoka</term> claimed to be Christ himself, who had come back again many centuries after his first rejection, out of pity to teach his children. He quotes the prophet as saying:

> I found my children were bad, so I went back to heaven and left them. I told them that in so many hundred years I would come back to see my children. At the

MOONEY] THE DOCTRINE OF THE DANCE 785

At the end of this time, I was sent back to try to teach them. My father told me the earth was getting old and worn out and the people were becoming bad, and that I was to renew everything as it used to be and make it better.

He also told us that all our dead were to be resurrected; that they were all to come back to earth, and that, as the earth was too small for them and us, he would get rid of heaven and make the earth itself large enough to contain us all; he said that we must tell all the people we met about these things. He spoke to us about fighting and said that it was bad and we must keep from it; that the earth was to be entirely good from now on, and we must all be friends with one another. He said that in the autumn, the youth of all good people would be renewed so that nobody would be more than forty years old, and that if they behaved themselves well after this, the youth of everyone would be renewed in the spring. He said if we were all good, he would send people among us who could heal all our wounds and sickness by a mere touch and that we would live forever. He told us not to quarrel or fight or strike each other, or shoot one another; that the whites and Indians were to be all one people. He said if any man disobeyed what he ordered, his tribe would be wiped from the face of the earth; that we must believe everything he said, and we must not doubt him or say he lied; that if we did, he would know it; that he would know our thoughts and actions no matter what part of the world we might be in. (*G. D., 5.*)

Here we have the statement that both races are to live together as one. We also have the doctrine of healing by touch. Whether or not this is an essential part of the system is questionable, but it is certain that the faithful believe that great physical good comes to them, to their children, and to the sick from the laying on of hands by the priests of the dance, in addition to the ability this grants them to see the things of the spiritual world.

Another idea presented here—namely, that the earth becomes old and decrepit and requires that its youth be renewed at the end of certain great cycles—is common to a number of tribes and has an important place in the oldest religions of the world. As an Arapaho who spoke English expressed it, "This earth is too old, the grass is too old, the trees are too old, our lives are too old. Then all will be new again." Captain H. L. Scott also found among the southern plains tribes the same belief that the rivers, the mountains, and the earth itself are worn out and must be renewed, along with an indefinite idea that both races alike must die at the same time, to be resurrected in new but separate worlds.

The Washo, Pit River, Bannock, and other tribes adjoining the Paiute on the north and west hold the doctrine substantially as taught by the messiah himself. We have very little light regarding the belief as held by the Walapai, Cohonino, Mohave, and Navaho to the south, beyond the general fact that the resurrection and return of the dead formed the principal tenet. As these tribes received their knowledge of the new religion directly from Paiute apostles, it is quite probable that they made but few changes in or additions to the original gospel.
