THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14

with the dance. At that time, they were expecting the Indian redeemer to appear on earth within three or four years. They were particularly anxious to make it understood that their intentions were not hostile toward white people, and that they desired to live in peace with them until the redeemer arrived. However, they believed that once he came, they would be unable to prevent the destruction of the whites, even if they wanted to. (J. F. L., 3.)

The nature of the final change and the destruction of the white people has been interpreted in various ways as the doctrine spread from its original center. East of the mountains, it is commonly believed that a deep sleep will come over the believers, during which the great catastrophe will occur, and the faithful will awake to immortality on a new earth. The Shoshoni of Wyoming say this sleep will last four days and nights, and that on the morning of the fifth day, everyone will open their eyes in a new world where both races will live together forever. The Cheyenne, Arapaho, Kiowa, and others in Oklahoma say that the new earth—along with all the resurrected dead from the beginning, and the buffalo, elk, and other game—will come from the west and slide over the surface of the present earth, just as a right hand might slide over a left hand. As it approaches, the Indians will be carried upward and land on it with the help of the sacred dance feathers they wear in their hair, which will act as wings to carry them up. They will then become unconscious for four days, and upon waking from their trance, they will find themselves with their former friends in the midst of all their old-time surroundings. 

Sitting Bull, the Arapaho apostle, believes that this advancing new earth will be preceded by a wall of fire that will drive white people across the water back to their original and proper country, while the Indians will be able to use their sacred feathers to fly over the flames and reach the promised land. Once the expulsion of the whites is complete, the fire will be extinguished by a rain lasting twelve days. A few believe that a hurricane with thunder and lightning will come to destroy only the whites. This last idea is reportedly also held by the Walapai of Arizona, who include unbelieving Indians in this destruction as well. (G. D., 6.) The doctrine held by the Caddo, Wichita, and Delaware of Oklahoma is practically the same as that of the Arapaho and Cheyenne from whom they received it. All these tribes believe that the destruction or removal of the whites is to be achieved entirely by supernatural means; they severely blame the Sioux for provoking a physical conflict out of impatience, instead of waiting for their God to deliver them in his own time.

Among all the tribes that have accepted the new faith, it is believed that frequent, devout attendance at the dance helps to ward off disease and restore the sick to health. This applies not only to the actual participants but also to their children and friends. The idea of obtaining worldly blessings as the reward for a faithful performance

<page-num>787</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] SIOUX VERSION OF THE DANCE</header>

The fulfillment of religious duties is too natural and universal to require comment. The purification through the sweat-bath, which serves as an important preliminary to the dance among the Sioux, while devotional in its purpose, is probably also sanitary in its effect.

Among the powerful and warlike Sioux of the Dakotas—who were already restless due to both old and recent grievances, and more recently brought to the brink of starvation by a reduction of rations—the doctrine quickly took on a hostile meaning and developed some peculiar features. For this reason, it deserves particular notice regarding this tribe. The earliest rumors of the new messiah reached the Sioux from more western tribes in the winter of 1888-89, but the first definite account was brought by a delegation that crossed the mountains to visit the messiah in the fall of 1889, returning in the spring of 1890. Following the report of these delegates, the dance was immediately inaugurated and spread so rapidly that, within a few months, the new religion had been accepted by the majority of the tribe.

Perhaps the best statement of the Sioux version is given by the veteran agent, James McLaughlin, of the Standing Rock agency. In an official letter dated October 17, 1890, he writes that the Sioux, under the influence of Sitting Bull, were greatly excited over the approaching "Indian millennium" or "return of the ghosts." In this predicted event, the white man would be annihilated and the Indian would again be supreme; the medicine-men promised this would occur as soon as the grass turned green in the spring. They were told that the Great Spirit had sent the dominant race to punish them for their sins, but that their sins were now forgiven and the time of deliverance was at hand. Their diminished numbers were to be reinforced by all the Indians who had ever died. These spirits were already on their way to inhabit the earth again—which had originally belonged to the Indians—and were driving immense herds of buffalo and fine ponies ahead of them as they advanced. The Great Spirit, who had so long deserted his red children, was now once more with them and against the whites, and the white man's gunpowder would no longer have the power to drive a bullet through the skin of an Indian. The whites themselves would soon be overwhelmed and smothered under a deep landslide, held down by sod and timber, and the few who might escape would become small fish in the rivers. In order to bring about this happy result, the Indians had to believe in and organize the Ghost Dance.

The agent continues:

> It would seem impossible that any person, no matter how ignorant, could be brought to believe such absurd nonsense; but as a matter of fact, a great many Indians at this agency actually believe it. Since this new doctrine was grafted here from the more southern Sioux agencies, the infection has been wonderful—and so harmful that it now includes some of the Indians who were formerly numbered among the progressive and more intelligent. Many of our very best Indians appear dazed and undecided when talking about it, as their inherent superstition has been thoroughly aroused. (*G. D.*, 7.)

<page-num>788</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14]</header>

The following extract is from a translation of a letter dated March 30, 1891, written in Sioux by a Native American at Pine Ridge to a friend at the Rosebud agency:

> And now I will tell another thing. Recently, a man died and came back to life, and he says he has been to the Indian nation of ghosts; he tells us the dead Indian nation is all coming home. The Indian ghost told him to come for his war bonnet. The Indian (not the ghost Indian) gave him his war bonnet, and he died again. (*G. D., 8.*)

The Sioux, like other tribes, believed that at the moment of the catastrophe, the earth would tremble. According to one version, the landslide was to be accompanied by a flood of water, which would flow into the mouths of the whites and cause them to choke with mud. Storms and whirlwinds were also to assist in their destruction. The Indians were to rise above the avalanche—likely in the manner described when speaking of the southern tribes—and upon reaching the surface of the new earth, they would behold boundless prairies covered with long grass and filled with great herds of buffalo and other game. When the time was near at hand, they had to assemble at certain meeting places and prepare for the final abandonment of all earthly things by stripping off their clothing. In accordance with the general idea of a return to traditional habits, the believers, as far as possible, discarded the white man’s dress and utensils. Those who could obtain buckskin—which is now very scarce in the Sioux country—resumed wearing buckskin dress, while the dancers put on “ghost shirts” made of cloth, but cut and ornamented in the Indian fashion. No metal of any kind was allowed in the dance, no knives, and not even the earrings or belts of imitation silver which form such an important part of prairie Indian costume. This contradicted the custom among the Cheyenne and other southern tribes, where the women always wear their finest belts studded with large disks of German silver <note>A white alloy of nickel, copper, and zinc.</note> during the dance. The beads used so freely on moccasins and leggings seem to have been regarded as a substitute for the old-time <term>wampum</term> and porcupine quill work, and were therefore not included in the prohibition. No weapon of any kind was allowed to be carried in the Ghost Dance by any tribe, north or south—a fact which effectively refutes the assertion that this was another variety of war dance. At certain Sioux dances, however, sacred arrows and a sacred bow, along with other items, were tied to the tree in the center of the circle.

Significant insight regarding the Sioux version of the doctrine is obtained from the sermon delivered at Red Leaf camp, on the Pine Ridge reservation, October 31, 1890, by Short Bull, one of those who had been selected to visit the messiah, and who afterward became one of the primary leaders in the dance:

> My friends and relations: I will soon get this movement fully underway. I have told you that this would come to pass in two seasons, but since the whites are interfering so much, I will move up the time from what my father above told me to do, so the time will be shorter. Therefore, you must not be afraid of anything. Some of my relations have no ears <note>Meaning they refuse to listen or follow the doctrine.</note>, so I will have them blown away.

### EXPLANATION OF PLATE XCIII

The original ghost shirts, now held in the National Museum, were taken from the bodies of Indians killed at Wounded Knee by scouts who were present during the fight. They were obtained by the author at Pine Ridge from Philip Wells and Louis Menard, mixed-blood interpreters; Wells had also been present as an interpreter for the Indian scouts during the battle. They are made of coarse white cloth sewn with sinew. One of the shirts is partially burned, having likely been taken out of one of the tipis that was overturned and set on fire during the action. Two other ghost shirts, said to be from the same battlefield, are also in the National Museum.

# MOONEY] SHORT BULL'S SERMON

> Now, a tree will sprout up, and there all the members of our religion and the tribe must gather together. That will be the place where we will see our dead relatives. But before this time, we must dance for the remainder of this moon, at the end of which time the earth will shake very violently. Whenever this occurs, I will cause the wind to blow. We are the ones who will then see our fathers, mothers, and everyone. We, the tribe of Indians, are the ones who are living a sacred life. God, our father himself, has told, commanded, and shown me to do these things.
> 
> Our father in heaven has placed a mark at each point of the four winds. First, a clay pipe, which lies at the setting of the sun and represents the Sioux tribe. Second, there is a holy arrow lying at the north, which represents the Cheyenne tribe. Third, at the rising of the sun, there lies hail, representing the Arapaho tribe. Fourth, there lies a pipe and a nice feather at the south, which represents the Crow tribe. My father has shown me these things; therefore, we must continue this dance. If the soldiers surround you four deep, three of you, on whom I have put holy shirts, will sing a song that I have taught you around them, and then some of them will drop dead. Then the rest will start to run, but their horses will sink into the earth. The riders will jump from their horses, but they will sink into the earth also. Then you can do as you desire with them. Now, you must know this: all the soldiers and that race will be dead. There will be only five thousand of them left living on the earth. My friends and relations, this is straight and true.
> 
> Now, we must gather at Pass Creek where the tree is sprouting. There we will go among our dead relations. You must not take any earthly things with you. Then the men must take off all their clothing, and the women must do the same. No one shall be ashamed of exposing their bodies. My father above has told us to do this, and we must do as he says. You must not be afraid of anything. The guns are the only things we are afraid of, but they belong to our father in heaven. He will see that they do no harm. Whatever white men may tell you, do not listen to them, my relations. This is all. I will now raise my hand up to my father and close what he has said to you through me. (*Short Bull; War, 4.*)

The pipe referred to here is the most sacred object in Sioux mythology and will be discussed more fully when dealing with the Sioux songs. The sacred object of the Cheyenne is the "medicine arrow," which is now in the keeping of the band living near Cantonment, Oklahoma. The Crow and Arapaho references are not as clear. The Arapaho are called the "Blue Cloud" people by the Sioux, a name which may possibly have some connection with hail. The sprouting tree where all the believers must gather refers to the tree or pole that the Sioux planted in the center of the dance circle. The cardinal directions assigned here to the other tribes may refer to their former locations in relation to the Sioux. The Cheyenne and Arapaho, who now live far west and south of the Sioux, originally lived north and east of them, around the Red River and the Saskatchewan.

The most noted thing connected with the Ghost Dance among the Sioux is the "ghost shirt," which was worn by all adherents of the doctrine—men, women, and children alike. It is described by Captain Sword in his account of the Ghost Dance, given in the appendix to this chapter, and will be discussed in detail later when dealing with the ceremony of the dance. During the dance, it was worn as an outer garment, but it was said to be worn at other times under ordinary dress. Although the shape, fringing, and feather adornment were practically the same in every case, considerable variation existed in

...regarding the painting, the designs on some were very simple, while others were practically covered with representations of the sun, moon, stars, sacred mythological figures, and visions seen during trances. The feathers attached to the garment were always from an eagle, and the thread used for sewing was always traditional sinew. In some cases, the fringe or other parts were painted with the messiah's sacred red paint. It was firmly believed that the shirt was impenetrable to bullets or any kind of weapon. When one of the women shot in the Wounded Knee massacre was approached while lying in the church and told that her ghost shirt must be removed to better treat her wound, she replied: "Yes, take it off. They told me a bullet would not go through. Now I don't want it anymore."

The idea of protection associated with the ghost shirt does not seem to be indigenous. Indian warriors usually went into battle naked above the waist. Their protective "medicine" was a feather, a small bag of sacred powder, an animal's claw, a bird's head, or some other small object that could be easily twisted into the hair or hidden behind a shield without attracting attention. Its power depended entirely on the consecration ceremony and not on its size or material. War paint carried the same magical power of protection. Covering the body in battle was not a traditional Indian custom, which required a warrior to be as free and unhindered in movement as possible. The so-called "war shirt" was worn mainly for ceremonial parades and only rarely on the warpath.

Dreams are merely disorganized combinations of waking ideas, and even the wildest visions of sleep contain hints of memory. The ghost shirt may easily have been inspired by a trance, while the trance vision itself resulted from ideas gathered through previous observation or reports. The author strongly suspects that the idea of an invulnerable sacred garment did not originate with the Indians. Instead, like several other significant points of the Ghost Dance doctrine, it is a practical adaptation of ideas encountered through contact with white sectarian groups. It may have been suggested by the "endowment robe" of the Mormons—a seamless white muslin garment decorated with symbolic figures. This is worn by initiates as the most sacred badge of their faith and is believed by many followers to make the wearer invulnerable. The Mormons have always shown a particular interest in the Indians, whom they consider to be the "Lamanites" of their sacred writings; consequently, they have made special efforts to convert them. This has resulted in a considerable number of the neighboring Ute, Paiute, Bannock, and Shoshoni tribes being received into the Mormon church and invested with the endowment robe. (See the appendix to this chapter: "The Mormons and the Indians"; also "Tell It All" by Mrs. T. B. H. Stenhouse.) The Shoshoni and northern Arapaho occupy the same

MOONEY] THE GHOST SHIRT 791

The reservation is in Wyoming, and anything that concerns one tribe is more or less discussed by the others. Since the Sioux, Cheyenne, and other eastern tribes frequently visit the Arapaho, and because these Arapaho have been the primary apostles of the Ghost Dance, it is easy to see how an idea borrowed by the Shoshoni from the Mormons could find its way through the Arapaho first to the Sioux and Cheyenne, and afterward to more distant tribes. Wovoka himself explicitly denied any responsibility for the ghost shirt, and both white people and Indians agreed that it was not part of the dance costume in Mason Valley. When I first went among the Cheyenne and neighboring tribes of Oklahoma in January 1891, the ghost shirt had not yet reached them. Soon afterward, the first one was brought down from the Sioux country by a Cheyenne named White Buffalo, who had been a Carlisle student. However, the Arapaho and Cheyenne, after debating the matter, refused to allow it to be worn in the dance, on the grounds that the Ghost Dance doctrine was one of peace, whereas the Sioux had turned the ghost shirt into an instrument of war. As a result of this decision, such shirts have never been worn by dancers among the southern tribes. Instead, they wear their finest buckskin shirts and dresses in the dance, covered with painted and beaded figures from Ghost Dance mythology and trance visions.

The Ghost Dance is named differently among the various tribes. In its original home among the Paiute, it is called *Nänigükwa*, "dance in a circle" (*nüka*, dance), to distinguish it from the tribe's other dances, which use only the ordinary up-and-down step without the circular movement. The Shoshoni call it *Tänä'räyün* or *Tämanä'rayära*, which may be translated as "everybody dragging," referring to the way the dancers move around the circle holding hands, like children do in ring games. They insist that it is a revival of a similar dance that existed among them fifty years ago. The Comanche call it *A'p-anĕka'ra*, "the Father's dance," or sometimes the dance "with joined hands." The Kiowa call it *Mânposo'ti guan*, "dance with clasped hands," and refer to the frenzy as *guan â'dalka-i*, "dance craziness." The Caddo know it as *Ă'ă kakĭ'mbawi'ut*, "the prayer of all to the Father," or as the *Nänisana ka au'-shan*, "nänisana dance," from *nänisana*, meaning "my children." This phrase forms the refrain of many ghost songs in the Arapaho language, from whom the Caddo obtained the dance. Among the Sioux, Arapaho, and most other prairie tribes, it is called the "spirit" or "ghost" dance (Sioux, *Wana'ghi wa'chipi*; Arapaho, *Thigû'nawat*), because everything connected with it relates to the return of the spirits of the dead from the spirit world; it is by this name that it has become known among white people.

# APPENDIX

## THE MORMONS AND THE INDIANS

While Indian excitement was at its height in 1892, a curious pamphlet was published anonymously in Salt Lake City in connection with a proposed series of lectures. We provide some extracts from it for the light they shed on the Mormon attitude toward the Indians. ### PORCUPINE’S ACCOUNT OF THE MESSIAH

The following statement was made to Major Carroll, in command of Camp Crook, at Tongue River agency, Montana, June 15, 1890, and transmitted through the War Department to the Indian Office:

> In November of last year <note>1889</note>, I left the reservation with two other Cheyennes. I went through <note>Fort</note> Washakie and took the Union Pacific railroad at Rawlins. We boarded early in the morning around breakfast time, rode the train all day, and reached a fort <note>Bridger?</note> around dark. I stayed there for two days, and then took a passenger train, and the next morning arrived at Fort Hall. I found some lodges of Snakes <note>Shoshone</note> and Bannocks there. I saw the agent here, and he told me I could stay at the agency, but the chief of the Bannocks who was there took me to his camp nearby. The Bannocks told me they were glad to see a Cheyenne and that we should make a treaty with the Bannocks.
>
> The chief told me he had been to Washington and had seen the President, and that we should all be friends with the white people and live at peace with them and

We took the railroad to a little town nearby, and then took a narrow-gauge road. We stayed there one day, taking the train at night, rode all night, and the next morning about 9 o'clock saw a settlement of Indians. We traveled south on a narrow-gauge road. We got off at this Indian town. The Indians here were different from any Indians I ever saw. The women and men were dressed in white people’s clothes, and the women had their hair in bangs. These Indians had their faces painted white with black spots. We stayed with these people all day. We took the same road at night and kept going. We traveled all night, and around daylight we saw a lot of houses, and they told us there were many more Indians there; so we got off, and that is where we saw Indians living in huts made of grass [<gloss>tule?</gloss>]. We stopped here and got something to eat. There were white people living nearby. We got on the train again at night, and during the night we got off among some Indians who were fish-eaters [<gloss>Paiute</gloss>]. We stayed among the Fish-eaters until morning, and then got into a wagon with the son of the chief of the Fish-eaters; we arrived about noon at an agency on a big river. There was also a big lake near the agency.

The agent asked us where we were from and said we were a long way from home, and that he would write to our agent and let him know we were all right. From this agency, we went back to the station, and they told us there were more Indians to the south. One of the chiefs of the Fish-eaters then provided us with four wagons. We traveled all day and then came to another railroad. We left our wagons here and took the train, as the Fish-eaters told us there were more Indians along the railroad who wanted to see us. We took this train about 2 o'clock and reached another agency by sunset, where there were more Fish-eaters. They told us they had heard from the Shoshone agency that the people in this country were all bad people, but that they were good people there. All the Indians from the Bannock agency down to where I finally stopped danced this dance [<gloss>referring to the recent religious dances at the Cheyenne agency</gloss>], and the whites often danced it themselves. [<gloss>It should be remembered that he traveled constantly through Mormon country.</gloss>] I knew nothing about this dance before going. I happened to come across it; that is all. I will tell you about it. [<gloss>At this point, all the Indian listeners removed their hats as a sign that the following talk would be on a religious subject.</gloss>] I want you all to listen to this, so that there will be no mistake. There is no harm in what I am going to say to anyone. I heard this where I met my friends in Nevada. It is a wonder you people never heard this before. In the dance we had there [<gloss>Nevada</gloss>], the whites and Indians danced together. I met many different kinds of people there, but they all seemed to know all about this religion. The people there all seemed to be good. I never saw any drinking, fighting, or bad behavior among them. They treated me well on the trains without charge. They gave me food for free, and I found that this was their habit toward their neighbors. I thought it strange that the people there were so good, so different from the people here.

What I am going to say is the truth. The two men sitting near me were with me and will testify that I speak the truth. I and my people have been living in ignorance until I went and found out the truth. I was told there that all whites and Indians are brothers. I never knew this before.

# MOONEY] PORCUPINE'S VISIT TO WOVOKA

The Fish-eaters near Pyramid Lake told me that Christ had appeared on earth again. They said Christ knew he was coming and that eleven of his children were also coming from a far land. It appeared that Christ had sent for me to go there, and that was why I had unconsciously begun my journey. It had been foreordained. Christ had summoned me and others from all the heathen tribes—two, three, or four people from each of fifteen or sixteen different tribes. There were more different languages than I had ever heard before, and I did not understand any of them. When I arrived, they told me that my Great Father was there as well, but I did not know who he was. The assembled people called a council, and the chief's son went to see the Great Father <note>messiah</note>, who sent word to us to remain in that camp for fourteen days, after which he would come to see us. He sent me a small package of something white to eat, the name of which I did not know. There were a great many people in the council, and this white food was divided among them. The food was a large white nut. Then I went to the agency at Walker Lake, and they told us Christ would be there in two days. At the end of two days, on the third morning, hundreds of people gathered at this place. They cleared a space near the agency in the shape of a circus ring, and we all gathered there. This space was perfectly cleared of grass and debris. We waited there until late in the evening, anxious to see Christ. Just before sundown, I saw a great many people, mostly Indians, approaching dressed in white men's clothes. The Christ was with them. They all formed a ring around him. They put up sheets all around the circle, as they had no tents. Just after dark, some of the Indians told me that the Christ <note>Father</note> had arrived. I looked around to find him and finally saw him sitting on one side of the ring. Everyone started toward him to see him. They built a large fire to cast light on him. I did not look around but went forward, and when I saw him, I bowed my head. I had always thought the Great Father was a white man, but this man looked like an Indian. He sat there for a long time, and no one went up to speak to him. He sat with his head bowed the entire time. After a while, he rose and said he was very glad to see his children. "I have sent for you and am glad to see you. I am going to talk to you in a while about your relatives who are dead and gone. My children, I want you to listen to all I have to say to you. I will also teach you how to perform a dance, and I want you to dance it. Get ready for your dance, and then, when the dance is over, I will talk to you." He was dressed in a striped white coat. The rest of his clothing was like a white man's, except that he wore a pair of moccasins. Then he began our dance, and everyone joined in; the Christ sang while we danced. We danced until late in the night, when he told us we had danced enough.

The next morning, after breakfast was finished, we went into the circle and spread canvas over the ground; the Christ stood in the midst of us. He told us he was going away that day but would be back the next morning to talk to us.

In the night when I first saw him, I thought he was an Indian, but the next day, when I could see better, he looked different. He was not as dark as an Indian, nor as light as a white man. He had no beard or whiskers but had very heavy eyebrows. He was a good-looking man. We were crowded very close together. We had been told that no one was to talk, and that even if we whispered, the Christ would know it. I had heard that Christ had been crucified, and I looked to see; I saw a scar on his wrist and one on his face, and he seemed to be the man. I could not see his feet. He would talk to us all day.

That evening we all assembled again to see him depart. When we were gathered, he began to sing; he started to tremble violently all over for a while and then sat down. We danced all night while the Christ lay down beside us, apparently dead.

The next morning when we went to eat breakfast, the Christ was with us. After breakfast, four heralds went around and called out that the Christ was back with us and wanted to talk with us. The circle was prepared once more. The people assembled, and Christ came among us and sat down. He said he wanted to talk to us again and wanted us to listen. He said: "I am the man who made everything you see around you. I am not lying to you, my children. I made this earth and everything on it. I have

I talked to them for four nights and five days. I told them exactly what I have told you here today. I told them what I said were the words of God Almighty, who was looking down on them. I wish some of you had been in our camp here to have heard my words to the Cheyennes. The only bad thing that there has been in it at all was this: I had just told my people that the Christ would punish the sins of any Indian upon the whole tribe, when the recent trouble <note>the killing of Ferguson</note> occurred. If any one of you thinks I am not telling the truth, you can go and see this man I speak of for yourselves. I will go with you, and I would like one or two of my people who doubt me to go with me.
> 
> The Christ talked to us all in our own languages. You can see this man in your sleep any time you want after you have seen him and shaken hands with him once. Through him, you can go to heaven and meet your friends. Since my return, I have seen him often in my sleep. Around the time the soldiers went up the Rosebud, I was lying in my lodge asleep when this man appeared and told me that the Indians had gotten into trouble, and I was frightened. The next night he appeared to me and told me that everything would turn out all right.

<header>MOONEY] THE DANCE AMONG THE SIOUX</header>

The following was translated by a Native American for Miss Emma C. Sickels and is published through her courtesy. The copy of the original Sioux manuscript is in the archives of the Bureau of Ethnology:

In the history of ghost dancing, the Oglala heard that the Son of God was truly on earth in the west, far from their country. This was in the year 1889. The first people to know that the messiah was on earth were the Shoshoni and Arapaho. So, in 1889, Good Thunder and four or five others visited the place where the Son of God was said to be. These people went there without permission. They said the messiah was at that place, but that he was there to help the Indians and not the whites; the Indians were happy to find this out. Good Thunder, Cloud Horse, Yellow Knife, and Short Bull visited the place again in 1890 and saw the messiah. Their story of the visit to the messiah is as follows:

> "From the country of the Arapaho and Shoshoni, we started in a northwesterly direction by train for five nights and arrived at the foot of the Rocky Mountains. Here we saw him and also several tribes of Indians. The people said that the messiah would come to a place in the woods that had been prepared for him. When we went to the place, smoke descended from heaven to the spot where he was to appear. When the smoke disappeared, there was a man of about forty, who was the Son of God. The man said:
> 
> "'My grandchildren! I am glad you have come from far away to see your relatives. These are your people who have come back from your country.' When he said he wanted us to go with him, we looked and saw a land created across the ocean on which all the nations of Indians were coming home; but, as the messiah looked at the land that was created and reached across the ocean, it disappeared again, and he said that it was not yet time for that to take place. The messiah then gave Good Thunder some paints—Indian paint and a white paint—and some green grass <note>sagebrush twigs?</note>; and he said, 'My grandchildren, when you get home, take up farming and send all your children to school. And on your way home, if you kill any buffalo, cut off the head, the tail, and the four feet and leave them, and that buffalo will come back to life. When the soldiers of the white people's chief want to arrest me, I shall stretch out my arms, which will knock them into nothingness; or, if not that, the earth will open and swallow them up. My father commanded me to visit the Indians for a purpose. I came to the white people first, but they were not good. They killed me, and you can see the marks of my wounds on my feet, my hands, and on my back. My father has given you life—your old life—and you have come to see your friends, but you will not take me home with you at this time. I want you to tell your people when you get home to follow my examples. Any Indian who does not obey me and tries to take the white people's side will be covered over by a new land that is to come over this old one. All of you people shall use the paints and grass I give you. In the spring, when the green grass comes, your people who have gone before you will return, and you shall see your friends then, for you have come at my call.'"

People from every tipi sent for us to visit them. They are people who died many years ago. Chasing Hawk, who died not long ago, was there, and we went to his tipi. He was living with his wife, who was killed in war long ago. They live in a buffalo skin tipi—a very large one—and he wanted all his friends to go there to live. A son of Good Thunder, who died in war long ago, was also one who took us to his tipi so that his father could see him. On our return journey, we came across a herd of buffalo. We killed one and took everything except the four feet, head, and tail, and when we had gone a little way from it, the buffalo came back to life and went off. This was one instance where the messiah's word proved true. The messiah said, "I will shorten your journey when you feel tired of the long way, if you call upon me." This we did when we were tired. When night fell, we stopped at a place and called upon the messiah to help us because we were tired from the long journey. We went to sleep, and in the morning, we found ourselves a great distance from where we had stopped.

The people returned here and gathered those loyal to the government, while those who did not favor the whites held a council. The agent’s soldiers were sent after them and brought Good Thunder and two others to the agency, where they were confined in prison. They were asked by the agent and Captain Sword whether they had seen the Son of God and whether they were holding councils regarding their return from their visit, but Good Thunder refused to say "yes." They were held in prison for two days and were released only after promising not to hold councils about their visit. They went back to the people and told them about their trouble with the agent. Then they dispersed without holding a council.

In the following spring, the people at the Pine Ridge agency began to gather at White Clay Creek for councils. At this time, Kicking Bear, from the Cheyenne River agency, visited the Arapaho and reported that the Arapaho there were practicing the Ghost Dance. He said that people participating in the dance would become delirious and die, at which point the Messiah and all the ghosts would be seen. When they die, they see strange things; they see their relatives who died long ago. They saw these things when they died during the Ghost Dance and then returned to life. The dancer becomes dizzy and finally drops as if dead, and the first thing they see is an eagle that comes to them and carries them to where the Messiah stays with his ghosts. The man said this:

The people in the Ghost Dance all join hands. A man stands, then a woman, forming a very large circle in that way. They dance around in the circle continuously until some of them become so exhausted that they become delirious and finally drop as if dead, foaming at the mouth and drenched in sweat. All the men and women made holy shirts and dresses to wear during the dance. The people who collapsed during the dance would lie in the thick dust kicked up by the dancing. They painted the white muslin used for the holy shirts and dresses with a blue line across the back, alongside a line of yellow paint. They also painted the front of the shirts and dresses. A picture of an eagle was made on the back of every shirt and dress. They tied eagle feathers to the shoulders and sleeves. They said that bullets would not penetrate these shirts and dresses, so they used them for war. Their enemies' weapons would not pierce these garments. The Ghost Dancers all had to wear an eagle feather on their heads. It was said that any man could be made delirious if fanned with this feather. In the Ghost Dance, no person was allowed to wear anything made of metal, except for the metal guns carried by some of the dancers. When they returned from the ghosts or recovered from their delirium, they brought meat from the ghosts or from the supposed Messiah. They also brought water, fire, and wind to kill all the white people or the Indians who helped the leader of the white people. They built a sweat house and made holes in the middle of it, from which they said water would flow. Before beginning the dance, they all raised their hands toward the northwest and cried out in supplication to the Messiah, then began the dance with the song, "*Ate misunkala ceya omani-ye*," and so on.

### SELWYN’S INTERVIEW WITH KUWAPI

On November 21, 1890, it was reported to Agent E. W. Foster, in charge of the Yankton agency in South Dakota, that a Native American named Kuwapi, from the Rosebud agency, was on the reservation teaching the doctrine and ceremony of the Ghost Dance. He immediately had the man arrested by a force led by William T. Selwyn, a full-blooded Yankton Sioux. Selwyn had received a good education through the patronage of a gentleman in Philadelphia and had been employed in various roles at different Sioux agencies for several years. Selwyn had recently arrived from Pine Ridge, where he had learned of and reported to Agent Gallagher the religious excitement among the

> During a quiet interval in one of the kivas, I found the Hopi who brought the news of the resurrection to his people. His name is Pütci, and his story is very sparse and confused. When the Hopi returned home, they shared these wonders, but it apparently made little impression, and it was only with difficulty that I could gather these few details.

Beyond the Cohonino, and extending for about 200 miles along the Colorado River on the Arizona side, are the associated tribes of the Mohave, Walapai, and Chemehuevi, numbering in total about 2,800 people, of whom only about one-third are on a reservation. The Chemehuevi, being a branch of the Paiute and in constant communication with them, undoubtedly practiced the dance and the doctrine. The Mohave also have much to do with the Paiute, the two tribes exchanging visits and mutually borrowing songs and games. They sent delegates to the Messiah and in all probability took up the Ghost Dance, despite the agent's statement to the contrary. As only 660 of more than 2,000 Mohave are reported to be on the reservation, the agent may have a good reason for not being fully informed about them.

Concerning the Walapai, we have positive information. In September 1890, the commanding officer at Fort Whipple was informed that a Paiute from southern Utah was among the Walapai, inciting them to dance for the purpose of causing hurricanes and storms to destroy the white people and any Indians who would not participate in the dances. It was stated also that these dances had then been going on for several months and were participated in by a large portion of the tribe, and that each dance lasted four or five nights in succession. Upon investigation, it appeared that this Paiute was one of a party who had come down and introduced the Ghost Dance among the Walapai the previous year. (G. D., 17.)

Q. Do you intend to introduce the doctrines of the <term>new messiah</term> from Rosebud to this agency as a missionary of the gospel? — A. No, I did not.
Q. What brings you here, then? — A. I have some relatives here that I wanted to see, and this was the reason why I came here.
Q. Where does this <term>new messiah</term> question originate? I mean, from its very beginning. — A. This originated in the White Mountains.
Q. Where are these White Mountains? — A. Close to the big Rocky Mountains, near the country that belongs to the Mexicans.
Q. Do you think that there will be trouble in the West by next spring? — A. Yes.
Q. What makes you think so? — A. Because that is what I have heard people talk about.

This is all that I have questioned Kuwapi on regarding the subject of the <term>new messiah</term>.

Respectfully, your obedient servant,
William T. Selwyn.

## CHAPTER XI

### THE GHOST DANCE WEST OF THE ROCKIES

<margin>|</margin>The first Ghost Dance on the Walker Lake reservation took place in January 1889, about a mile above the railroad bridge near the agency. Wovoka's preaching had already been attracting general attention among his own people for several months. It is said that six Apaches attended this first dance, but that statement is improbable, as it would imply they had made a journey of 600 miles through a desert country to see a man who was yet unknown outside of his own tribe. From this time, however, his fame spread abroad, and another large dance in the same vicinity soon after was attended by a number of Utes from Utah. The Utes are neighbors of the Paiutes to the east, just as the Bannocks are to the north; these tribes were naturally the first to hear of the new prophet and to send delegates to attend the dance. The doctrine spread almost simultaneously to all the scattered bands of Paiutes in Nevada, Oregon, and adjacent areas.

<margin>(</margin>In its essential features, the Ghost Dance among the Paiutes, as conducted by the messiah himself, was practically the same as among the majority of the prairie tribes, as will be described later. (The Sioux, Kiowa, and perhaps some other tribes, however, danced around a tree or pole set up in the center of the ring, differing in this respect from the Paiutes, as well as from the Cheyennes, Arapahos, Caddos, and others. No fire was allowed within the ring by any of the prairie tribes among whom the subject was investigated, but among the Paiutes, it seems that fires were built either within the circle or close to it. When I visited the messiah in January 1892, deep snow was on the ground, which had caused the temporary suspension of dancing, so I had no opportunity of seeing the performance there for myself. I saw, however, the place cleared for the dance ground—the same spot at the upper end of Mason Valley where the large delegation from Oklahoma had attended the dance the preceding summer. A large circular space had been cleared of sagebrush and leveled, and around the circumference were the remains of the low, round structures of willow branches which had sheltered those in attendance. At one side, within the circle, was a larger structure of branches where the messiah gave audience to the delegates from distant tribes and, according to their statements, showed them the glories of the spirit world through the medium of hypnotic trances. (The Paiutes always dance for five nights, or perhaps more accurately, four nights and the morning of the fifth day.<margin>)</margin>

as instructed by the messiah to the visiting delegates, ending the performance with a general shaking and waving of blankets, as is done among the prairie tribes, after which all go down and bathe in the nearest stream. The shaking of the blankets removes all evil influences and drives sickness and disease away from the dancers. There is no prior consecration of the ground, as seen among the Arapaho, and no preliminary sweat bath, as seen among the Sioux. The sweat bath seems to be unknown to the Paiute, who are predominantly a dirty people, and I saw no trace of sweat-house frames at any of their camps. Nakash, the Arapaho who visited the messiah in 1889 and first brought the dance to the eastern tribes, confirmed the statements of the Paiute and ranchmen that there were no trances in the Paiute Ghost dance.

Besides the dance ground in Mason Valley, where the messiah himself generally presided, there were several others on the Walker River reservation, although, if we are to believe the agent, no Ghost dances were ever held on either reservation.

The following extract from Porcupine’s account of his visit to the messiah in the fall of 1889 (see page 793) gives some idea of the Paiute Ghost dance and throws light on the cataleptic peculiarities of the messiah:

> I went to the agency at Walker Lake, and they told us Christ would be there in two days. At the end of two days, on the third morning, hundreds of people gathered at this place. They cleared a space near the agency in the shape of a circus ring, and we all gathered there. This area was completely cleared of grass and other debris. We waited there until late in the evening, anxious to see Christ. Just before sundown, I saw many people, mostly Indians, arriving dressed in white men’s clothing. The Christ was among them. They all formed a circle around him within this ring. They put up sheets all around the circle, as they had no tents. Just after dark, some of the Indians told me that the Christ (father) had arrived. I looked around to find him and finally saw him sitting on one side of the ring. They all started toward him to see him. They built a large fire to illuminate him. I did not look around but went forward, and when I saw him, I bowed my head. . . . He sat there for a long time, and nobody went up to speak to him. He sat with his head bowed the whole time. After a while, he rose and said he was very glad to see his children. “I have sent for you and am glad to see you. I am going to talk to you after a while about your relatives who are dead and gone. My children, I want you to listen to all I have to say to you. I will teach you, too, how to perform a dance, and I want you to dance it. Get ready for your dance, and then when the dance is over, I will talk to you.” He was dressed in a white coat with stripes. The rest of his clothing was like a white man’s, except that he wore a pair of moccasins. Then he began our dance, with everyone joining in; the Christ sang while we danced. We danced until late in the night; then he told us we had danced enough.
>
> The next morning, after breakfast was over, we went into the circle and spread canvas over the ground, the Christ standing in the midst of us. He told us he was going away that day but would be back the next morning to talk to us. . . . He had no beard or whiskers, but very heavy eyebrows. He was a good-looking man. We were crowded very close together. We had been told that nobody was to talk, and that even if we whispered, the Christ would know it. . . . He would talk to us all day.

> That evening, we all assembled again to see him depart. When we were assembled, he began to sing, and he started to tremble violently all over for a while

We come now to the other tribes bordering the Paiute. First in order are the Washo, a small band living on the slopes of the Sierras near Carson, Nevada, and speaking a unique language of unknown origin. They are completely under the influence of the Paiute. They had no separate dance but joined in with the nearest Paiute camps and sang the same songs. Occupying practically the same territory as the Paiute, they were among the first to receive the new doctrine.

</margin>
Farther to the south, in California, around Bridgeport and Mono Lake and extending across to the western slope of the Sierras, are several small Shoshonean bands closely related to the Paiute and known locally as the “Diggers.” The Paiute state that bands of these Indians frequently came up and participated in the dance on the reservation. They undoubtedly had their own dances at home as well.

According to the statement of the agent in charge of the Mission Indians in southern California in 1891, the doctrine reached them as well, and the medicine men of Potrero began to prophesy the destruction of the whites and the return of Indian supremacy. Few believed their predictions, however, until rumors brought news of the overflow of the Colorado River and the creation of the “Salton Sea” in the summer of 1891. Never doubting that the great change was near at hand, the frightened Indians fled to the mountains to await developments. However, after going hungry for several days, the dawn of the millennium seemed as far away as ever, and they returned to their homes with disappointment in their hearts. Although the agent specifically mentions only the Indians of Potrero, there can be no doubt that the inhabitants of the other Mission *rancherias* in the area were also affected; we are thus able to fix the boundary of the messiah excitement in this direction at the Pacific Ocean. (*Comr., 27.*)

In northern California, the new doctrine was adopted late in 1890 by the Pit River Indians, a group of tribes forming a distinct linguistic family and scattered throughout the entire basin of the Pit River, from Goose Lake to the Sacramento River, which may have formed the boundary of the Ghost Dance movement in this direction. (*A. G. O., 7.*) As a number of these Indians also live on the Round Valley reservation in California, it is possible that the doctrine reached there as well. Having obtained the dance ritual directly from the Paiute, their neighbors to the east, the ceremony and belief were likely the same for both tribes.

A single Nez Percé visited the messiah, but the visit had no effect on his tribe at home. In a general way, it may be stated that the doctrine of the Ghost Dance was never taken up by any tribes of the Salishan or Shahaptian stocks, which occupy practically the whole of the great Columbia basin. This is probably due to the fact that the more important of these tribes have been for a long time under the influence of Catholic or other Christian missionaries, while most of the others are adherents of the Smohalla or the Shaker doctrine.

Of the tribes southward from the Paiute, according to the best information available, the Ghost Dance never reached the Yuma, Pima, Papago, Maricopa, or any of the Apache bands in Arizona or New Mexico; neither did it affect any of the Pueblo tribes except the Taos, who performed the dance merely as a pastime. As previously stated, it is said that six Apache attended the first large dance at Walker Lake in 1889. This seems improbable, but if true, it produced no effect on any part of the tribe at large. Later on, the Jicarilla Apache in northern New Mexico may have heard of it through the southern Ute, but, so far as is known officially, neither of these tribes ever engaged in the dance. The agent of the Jicarilla states that the tribe knew nothing of the doctrine until he informed them of it himself. (*G. D.*, 10.) It seems never to have been taken up by the Mescalero Apache in southern New Mexico, although they are in the habit of making frequent visits to the Kiowa, Comanche, Apache, and other Ghost-dancing tribes of Oklahoma. The agent of the Mohave states officially that these Indians knew nothing about it, but this must be a mistake, as there is constant communication between the Mohave and the southern Paiute. According to Wovoka's statement, Mohave delegates attended the dance in 1890, while the 700 Walapai and Chemehuevi associated with the Mohave are known to have been devoted adherents of the doctrine.

The dance was adopted almost simultaneously by the Bannock, Shoshoni, Gosiute, and Ute in the early part of 1889. All these tribes are neighbors (to the east) of the Paiute and closely related to them; the Bannock particularly have only a slight dialect difference in language, so that communication between them is an easy matter. <margin>†</margin> In regard to the dance among the Shoshoni and Paiute on the Western Shoshone reservation, in Nevada and Idaho, their agent writes, under the date of November 8, 1890:

<margin>|</margin>
> The Indians of this reservation and vicinity have just concluded their second medicine dance, the previous one having taken place last August. They are looking for the coming of the Indian Christ, the resurrection of the dead Indians, and the resulting supremacy of the Indian race. Fully one thousand people took part in the dance. While the best order prevailed, the excitement was very great as morning approached. When the dancers were worn out mentally and physically, the medicine men would shout that they could see the faces of departed friends and relatives moving about the circle. No pen can paint the picture of wild excitement that followed. Everyone shouted in a chorus, "Christ has come," and then danced and sang until they fell in a confused and exhausted mass on the ground. . . . I expect no trouble beyond the loss of time and the general demoralizing effect of these large gatherings of people. Several of the leading men have gone to Walker Lake to confer with a man who calls himself Christ. Others have gone to Fort Hall to meet Indians from Montana and Dakota to get the news from that section. In fact, the astonishing part of the business is the fact that all the Indians in the country seem to possess practically the same ideas and expect about the same result. (*G. D., 12.*)

On December 6, he writes that another Ghost Dance had then been in progress for six days, and that the Indians had announced their intention to dance one week in each month until the grass grew, at which time the medicine men had told them the messiah would come, bringing all their dead friends with him. (*G. D., 13.*) This dance, however, was attended by a much smaller number of Indians, and skeptics had already arisen among them to scoff at the new believers. The influence was working, and only a little shrewd diplomacy was needed to turn the religious scale, as is shown by an extract from a third letter, dated January 10, 1891. From this, it would seem that Agent Plumb is a man of practical common sense, and also that Esau was not the only one who would sell his birthright for a bowl of stew:

> Christmas Day was the day set for commencing another dance. I told them they could play all of their usual games—in fact, have a good time—but that dancing was forbidden. I showed them how continued dancing at various Sioux agencies had ended in soldiers being sent to stop them. I stated the case as clearly as I could; the Indians debated it for two days, and then

Up to this date, they have kept their word. I have no hope of stopping their dances altogether, but I have strong hopes of controlling <margin>boo!</margin> them. (*G. D., 14.*)

Arapaho
Disciples
</margin>
The Bannock and Shoshoni of the Fort Hall reservation in Idaho **have served as the primary messengers of the doctrine between the tribes west of the mountains and those of the plains.** Situated almost on the summit of the Great Divide, they are within easy reach of the Paiute to the west—among whom the dance originated and whose language the Bannock speak. Meanwhile, at no great distance to the east on the Wind River reservation in Wyoming, **the remaining Shoshoni are allied with the Arapaho, who have been from the beginning the great apostles of the doctrine among the prairie tribes.** There is constant visiting back and forth between the tribes of these two reservations. The four railroads coming into Fort Hall, combined with its close proximity to the main line of the Union Pacific, make it a major hub and stopping point for Indian travel. Almost every delegation from the tribes east of the mountains stopped at this agency to get the latest news from the messiah and to find interpreters among the Bannock to accompany them to Nevada. In a letter dated November 26, 1890, to the Indian Commissioner, the agent in charge states that during the previous spring and summer, his Indians had been visited by representatives from about a dozen different reservations. Regarding the dance and the doctrine at Fort Hall, he also says that the "extermination and resurrection business" was not a new thing with his tribes by any means; rather, it had been quite a craze with them every few years for the last twenty years or more, varying only slightly according to the whims of particular medicine men. (*G. D., 15.*) This may have referred to the doctrine already mentioned as having been taught by *Tävi-bo*.

Early in 1889, a Bannock from Fort Hall visited the Shoshoni and Arapaho of the Wind River reservation in Wyoming and brought them the first knowledge of the new religion. He had just returned from a visit to the Paiute country, where he said he had met messengers who told him that the dead were coming back and who commanded him to go and tell all the tribes. “And so,” said the Shoshoni, “he came here and told us all about it.” Accordingly, in the summer of that year, a delegation of five Shoshoni led by *Täbinshi*, along with *Nakash* (“*Sage*”), an Arapaho, visited the messiah of Mason Valley. They traveled most of the way by railroad, and the journey took several days. They attended a Ghost Dance which, according to their accounts, was a very large one. After dancing all night, they were told by the messiah that they would meet all their dead relatives in two years from that time, at the turning of the leaves—that is, in the autumn of 1891. They were urged to dance frequently, “because the

<page-num>808</page-num>

dance moves the dead.” One of the Shoshoni delegates understood the Bannock and Paiute languages and interpreted for the rest. The information was probably conveyed by the Shoshoni to the Arapaho through the use of sign language.

In accordance with the report of the delegates, the Shoshoni and Arapaho began to dance immediately upon their return home. A year later, in the fall of 1890, dense smoke from forest fires in the mountains drifted down and obscured the air in the lower country to such an extent that horses were lost in the haze. This was regarded by the Indians as an indication of the approach of the great change, and the dance was continued with increased fervor; but at last, the atmosphere began to clear and the phenomenon ended as it had begun—in smoke. The dance was kept up, however, without stop for another year, until the predicted time had come and gone. At that point the Shoshoni—who seem to share the skeptical nature of their southern kinsmen, the Comanche—concluded that they had been deceived and abandoned the dance. The Arapaho, who have greater faith in the unseen things of the spirit world, kept it up and were still dancing when I visited them in the summer of 1892. A part of the Arapaho, headed by their chief, Black Coal, and encouraged by Catholic missionaries, had steadily opposed the dance from the first. After considerable discussion of the matter, it was decided, on Black Coal’s proposal, to send another delegation to the messiah under the guidance of Yellow Eagle, a graduate of a government Indian school, to learn the truth or falsity of the new doctrine. They returned early in 1891 and reported against the movement. Their report confirmed the doubters in their skepticism but produced little effect on the rest of the tribe.

When I visited the Wind River reservation in Wyoming in June 1892, the agent in charge informed me that there was no Ghost dancing on his reservation; he said he had explained how foolish it was and had strictly forbidden it, and that as a result, the Indians had abandoned it. However, he expressed interest in my investigation, and as the Arapaho, with whom I had most to do, were then camped together a few miles up in the mountains cutting wood, he very kindly furnished a vehicle and camping outfit, along with two of the agency employees—a clerk and an interpreter—to take me out. It appeared afterward that the escort had received instructions of their own before starting. Having reached the camp and set up our tent, the Arapaho soon came around to get acquainted over a pipe and a cup of coffee; but, in answer to questions put by one of my companions, a white man who assumed the burden of the conversation, it seemed that the Indians had lost all interest in the dance. In fact, some of them acted so ignorant on the subject that they wanted to know what it meant.

After trying in vain to convince me that it was useless to waste further time with the Indians, the clerk started back again after supper, satisfied that that part of the country was safe as far as the Ghost

<header>MOONEY] SACRED REGARD FOR THE CEDAR</header>

dance was concerned. By this time it was dark, and the Indians invited the interpreter and me to come over to a tipi about half a mile away, where we could meet all the old men. We started, and had gone but a short distance when we heard from a neighboring hill the familiar measured rhythm of the ghost songs. Turning with a questioning look to my interpreter—who was himself of mixed heritage—he quietly said: “Yes; they are dancing the Ghost Dance. That is something I have never reported, and I never will. It is their religion and they have a right to it.” Not wishing to be an accomplice in a crime, I did not go over to the dance; but it is unnecessary to state that the old men in the tipi that night, and for several successive nights thereafter, knew all about the songs and ceremonies of the new religion. As already stated, the Shoshoni had really lost faith and abandoned the dance.

<margin>Pencil bracket in left margin alongside this paragraph</margin>
Among the Shoshoni, the dance was performed around a small cedar tree, planted in the ground for that purpose. Unlike the Sioux, they hung nothing on this tree. The men did not clasp each other’s hands, but held onto their blankets instead; however, a woman standing between two men took hold of their hands. There was no preliminary medicine ceremony. The dance usually took place in the morning, and at its close, the performers shook their blankets in the air, as among the Paiute and other tribes, before dispersing. However new the doctrine may have been, the Shoshoni claim that the Ghost Dance itself as performed by them was a revival of an old dance which they had used fully fifty years before.

<margin>Pencil bracket in left margin alongside this paragraph</margin>
The selection of the cedar in this connection aligns with the general Indian idea, which has always attributed a mystic sacredness to that tree: from its evergreen foliage, which makes it such a conspicuous feature of the desert landscape; from the aromatic fragrance of its twigs, which are burned as incense in sacred ceremonies; from the durability and fine texture of its wood, which makes it particularly appropriate for tipi poles and spear shafts; and from the dark-red color of its heartwood, which appears as if dyed in blood. In Cherokee myth, the cedar was originally a pole to the top of which they fastened the fresh scalps of their enemies, and the wood was thus stained by the blood that trickled slowly down along it to the ground. The Kiowa also selected a cedar for the center of their Ghost Dance circle.

<margin>Handwritten note in right margin: Southern</margin>
We return now to the southern tribes west of the mountains. Sometime in the winter of 1889-90, Paiute runners brought news of the near arrival of the messiah and the resurrection of the dead to the powerful Navaho tribe, living in northern New Mexico and Arizona. They preached and prophesied for a considerable time, but the Navaho were skeptical, laughed at the prophets, and paid very little attention to the prophecies. (*Matthews, 1.*) According to the official report for 1892, these Indians, numbering somewhat over 16,000 souls, have, in round numbers, 9,000 cattle, 119,000 horses, and 1,600,000

<page-num>811</page-num>
# MOONEY] THE MESSIAH AND THE NAVAHO

Keams Canyon is about 125 miles northwest of Fort Wingate, the point from which Dr. Matthews writes, and is that much closer to the *Paiute*, *Cohonino*, and *Walapai*, all of whom have accepted the new religion. Mr. Stephen states that sometime in February or March 1890, he first heard rumors among the Navaho that “the old men long dead” had returned to some foreign tribes in the north or east—the vague far away. The news was brought to the Navaho either by the *Ute* or *Paiute*, or both. (The rumor grew and the idea became commonly current among the Navaho that the mythic heroes were to return and that under their direction they were to expel Americans and Mexicans and restrict the *Zuñi* and *Hopi* close to their villages, and, in fact, to reestablish their old domain from the San Francisco mountains to Santa Fe.) (*Stephen, 1.*) On November 22, 1891, he further wrote:

> While out this last time, I camped overnight with some Navaho friends and, over a pipe, brought up the messiah topic. This family belongs to the Bitter-Water gens, and this is the gist of what I got from them: A *Pah-ute* came to a family of their gens living near Navaho Mountain and told them that *Na'-Keh-tkla-ĭ* was to return from the underworld and bring back all the *Tinneh* (Navaho) he had killed. *Na'-keh-tkla-ĭ* (meaning “foreigner with white foot sole”) in the long ago had a puma and a bear. These were his pets. He would call the puma from the east and the bear from the west, and just before dawn they met in the center. Thus they met four times. On the fourth meeting, the puma reached back with his forepaw and plucked his mane, tossing the hair into the air; and for every hair, a *Tinneh* died. This deadly sorcery continued for a long time, and great numbers were killed. Now, the *Pah-ute* said, this sorcerer was to return and would call his pets, and they would come from the east and west, and following their trail would be all the people whose deaths they had caused. These Navaho said they had heard of other *Pah-ute* prophecies a year or more ago, all to the effect that long-dead people were to return alive from the underworld. These resurrected ones were also to bring back the departed game, and the *Tinneh* would again dominate the region. But, said my informant, *datsaigi yelti*, “it is worthless talk.” (*Stephen, 2.*)

In connection with hypnotism as seen in the Ghost Dance, Dr. Matthews states that in one curious Navaho ceremony, he has several times seen the patient hypnotized or pretending to be hypnotized by a character dressed in evergreens. The occurrence of the hypnotic trance is regarded as a sign that the ceremony has been effective. If the trance does not occur, some other ceremony must be tried. (*Matthews, 2.*)

West of the Navaho in northeastern Arizona live the Hopi, or Moki, a Pueblo tribe occupying several villages on the tops of nearly inaccessible mesas. In July 1891, four of these Indians, while on a visit to the *Cohonino*, living farther to the west, first heard of the new doctrine and witnessed a Ghost Dance, as will be described hereafter. They brought back the news to their people, but it made no impression on them and the matter was soon forgotten. (*Stephen, 3.*) In this connection Mr. Stephen states, in response to a letter of inquiry, that although he does not recollect any Hopi myth concerning the rejuvenation of the world and reunion with the resurrected dead on this earth, yet the doctrine of a reunion with the revived dead in the underworld is a commonly accepted belief of the Hopi. They also have a curious myth

western Sioux, and had afterward repeated this information to the agent at Yankton. While Kuwapi was in his custody, Selwyn questioned him at length concerning the new doctrine and forwarded the following report (*G. D., Document 36861—1890*) of the interview to Agent Foster:

->YANKTON AGENCY, SOUTH DAKOTA,<-
->*November 22, 1890.*<-

Colonel E. W. FOSTER,
*United States Indian Agent, Yankton Agency, South Dakota.*

DEAR SIR: It was reported here a few days ago that there was an Indian visitor at White Swan from the Rosebud agency who has been telling or teaching the doctrines of the new messiah, and has caused some unrest among the people there. At the request of Captain Conrad, United States Army, of Fort Randall, South Dakota, and by your order of the 21st of this month, I went to White Swan and arrested the man we were seeking (Kuwapi, or "One they chased after"). On my way to the agency with the prisoner, I conducted a brief interview with him on the subject of the new messiah. The following are the facts which he confirmed concerning the new messiah and his laws and doctrines for the Indians of this continent:

Q. Do you believe in the new messiah?—A. I believe it to some extent.

Q. What made you believe it?—A. Because I ate some of the buffalo meat that he (the new messiah) sent to the Rosebud Indians through Short Bull.

Q. Did Short Bull say that he saw the living herd of roaming buffaloes while he was with the son of the Great Spirit?—A. Short Bull told the Indians at Rosebud that the buffalo and other wild game will be restored to the Indians at the same time the general resurrection for the benefit of the Indians takes place.

Q. You said a “general resurrection for the benefit of the Indians takes place;” when or how soon will this be?—A. The father sends word to us that he will cause all these things to happen in the spring, when the grass is knee-high.

Q. You said “father;” who is this father?—A. It is the new messiah. He has ordered his children (the Indians) to call him “father.”

Q. You said the father is not going to send the buffalo until the resurrection takes place. Would he be able to send a few buffaloes over this way as a sample, so that his children (the Indians) could taste the meat?—A. The father wishes to do everything all at once, including the destruction of the white race.

Q. You said something about the destruction of the white race. Do you mean to say that all mankind except the Indians will be killed?—A. Yes.

Q. How, and who is going to kill the white people?—A. The father is going to cause a great cyclone or whirlwind, by which he will cause all the white people to perish.

Q. If it should be a cyclone or whirlwind, what are we going to do to protect ourselves?—A. The father will make some kind of provisions by which we will be saved.

Q. You said something about the coming destruction of the white people by your father. Supposing your father is sick, tired out, forgets, or some other accident occurs that prevents him from accomplishing his purpose, what would happen regarding the destruction of the white people?—A. There is no doubt about these things, as the miracle worker or the father is going to do exactly what he said he would do.

Q. What other evidence has led you to believe that there is such a new messiah on earth at present?—A. The Ghost Dancers faint whenever the dance takes place.

Q. Do you believe that they have really fainted?—A. Yes.

Q. What makes you believe that the dancers have really fainted?—A. Because when they wake up or regain consciousness, they sometimes bring back news from the unknown world and some little trinkets, such as a buffalo tail, buffalo meat, etc.

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14]

Q. What did those who fainted see when they lost consciousness?—A. They visited the happy hunting grounds, the camps, multitudes of people, and many strangers.

Q. What did the spirits or the strangers tell the person or people who fainted?—A. When the person who fainted reaches the camp, he is welcomed by his relatives, and he is also invited to several feasts.

Q. Were the people at the Rosebud Agency anxiously waiting or expecting to see all of their dead relatives who died several years ago?—A. Yes.

Q. We would have a great many elderly people when all the dead return, wouldn't we?—A. The visitors all say that there is not a single old man or woman in the other world—everyone has been made young again.

Q. Are we going to die when the dead return?—A. No; we will be just as we are today.

Q. Did the visitor say that there are any white men in the other world?—A. No; no white people.

Q. If there are no white people in the other world, where did they get their supplies and clothing?—A. The messenger tells us that in the other world, they have depended entirely for their food on the meat of buffalo and other wild game; also, they were all dressed in the skins of wild animals.

Q. Did the Indians at the Rosebud Agency believe in the new messiah, or the son of the Great Spirit?—A. Yes.

Q. How do they show that they have a belief in the new messiah?—A. They show it by praying to the father while looking up to heaven and calling him "father," just as you would in a church.

Q. Have you ever been in a church?—A. No.

Q. Do you truly believe in the new messiah?—A. I did not at first, but as I became more familiar with the doctrines of the new messiah, I came to truly believe in him.

Q. In your opinion, how many people at Rosebud believe in this new messiah?—A. Nearly everyone.

Q. Didn't the Rosebud people prepare to attack the white people this summer? While I was at the Pine Ridge Agency this summer, the Oglalla Sioux Indians said they would resist the government if it should try to put a stop to the messiah movement. Did your people at Rosebud say the same thing?—A. Yes.

Q. Are they still preparing and planning to attack the white people if the government sends our soldiers with orders to stop these new messiah activities?—A. I do not know, but I think that the Wojaji band at the Rosebud Agency will cause some harm at any time.

Q. You do not mean to say that the Rosebud Indians will try to cause an uprising?—A. That seems to be the case.

Q. You mentioned the "son of the Great Spirit" or "the father." What do you mean by the son of the Great Spirit?—A. This "father," as he is called, said himself that he is the son of the Great Spirit.

Q. Have you talked with any Indian at White Swan about the new messiah, his laws and doctrines, or have you mentioned this to anyone while there?—A. I have told a few of them. I did not go out of my way to tell them to follow the doctrines of the new messiah.

Q. Yes, but you did explain the matter to the Indians, didn't you?—A. Yes, I did.

Q. Do the Yankton Indians at White Swan believe in your teaching of the new messiah?—A. I did not intend to teach them, but since I have been questioned on the subject, I have said something about it.

Q. Did any of them believe you?—A. Some have already believed it, and some did not.

Q. Those who have believed you must be better men than the others, aren't they?—A. I do not know.

->MOONEY] AMONG THE WALAPAI<-

with the expected god, and on coming down again delivered his message to the people. The dance was held at irregular intervals, according to the instructions received on the butte by the medicine men. The dance place was a circular piece of ground a hundred feet in diameter, enclosed by a fence of poles and bushes, and surrounded by high mountain walls of granite, which reflected the light from half a dozen fires blazing within the circle. The dancers, numbering 200, dressed in white robes with decorative trimmings, their faces and hair painted white in various decorative designs, moved slowly around in a circle, keeping time with a wild chant, while 200 more stood or crouched around the fires, awaiting their turn to participate. The dancers faced toward the center, each holding the hands of those next to him and joining in the chant in unison. The dust rose in clouds from beneath their feet, and with the dust and exertion combined, the performers were soon exhausted and dropped out, at which point others took their places. After each circuit they rested a few minutes and then started around again. At each circuit a different chant was sung, and thus the dance continued until midnight, when, with a loud clapping of hands, it ended, and the people separated and went to their homes. Throughout the performance, two or three chiefs or medicine men were constantly moving about on the outside of the circle to preserve order and reprimand any laughter, one of them explaining to the visitors that, as this was a religious ceremony, proper solemnity must be observed. (*F. L. J., 2.*)
