# CHAPTER XII

## THE GHOST DANCE EAST OF THE ROCKIES—AMONG THE SIOUX

> In 1889 the Ogalala heard that the Son of God had come to earth in the west. They said the Messiah was there, but he had come to help the Indians and not the whites, and it made the Indians happy to hear this.—*George Sword*.

> They signed away a valuable portion of their reservation, and it is now occupied by white people, for which they have received nothing. They understood that ample provision would be made for their support; instead, their supplies have been reduced, and much of the time they have been living on half and two-thirds rations. Their crops, as well as the crops of white people, have been almost a total failure for two years. The dissatisfaction is widespread, especially among the Sioux, while the Cheyenne have been on the verge of starvation and were forced to commit depredations to sustain life. These facts are beyond question, and the evidence is positive and supported by thousands of witnesses.—*General Miles*.

Among the tribes east of the mountains and north of Oklahoma, it appears from official documents in the Indian Office and from other obtainable information that the Ghost Dance and its doctrine, if known at all, were never accepted by the Blackfeet of Montana; the Ojibwa of Turtle Mountain and Devils Lake in North Dakota, or by the rest of the tribe further east in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan; the Omaha, Winnebago, and Ponca in Nebraska; the small band of Sauk and Fox in Iowa; the still smaller band of Sauk and Fox, the Potawatomi, Kickapoo, Iowa, and Ojibwa in northeastern Kansas; or by the Sioux of Devils Lake in North Dakota, Lake Traverse (Sisseton Agency) and Flandreau in South Dakota, and Santee Agency in Nebraska. All or most of these Sioux belong to the Santee or eastern division of the tribe, and have long been under civilizing influences. According to official statements, the dance was not taken up by any of the Sioux of the Crow Creek or Yankton agencies in South Dakota, but they were certainly more or less affected by it, as they knew all about it and were in constant communication with the wilder bands of Sioux who were involved in the outbreak. I was informed by the Omaha and Winnebago in 1891 that they had been told of the new Messiah by visiting Sioux from Pine Ridge Agency in April 1890, and later by other Sioux from Yankton Agency, but they did not believe the story and never organized a Ghost Dance. According to the agent in charge, the Crow of Montana were not affected. If true, this is remarkable, considering that the Crow are a large and relatively primitive tribe and live near the wildest of the Ghost-dancing tribes, particularly the Northern Cheyenne, who occupy practically the same reservation. It is possible that their experience in the Sword-bearer affair in 1887, already mentioned, had a tendency

MOONEY] DELEGATES TO THE MESSIAH

...to weaken their faith in later prophets. Dr. George Bird Grinnell, a competent authority, states, in reply to a personal letter, that nothing was known about the dance by the Blackfeet of Montana or by the Blackfeet, Sarsi, or Plains Cree on the Canadian side of the boundary line.

Within the same general region, east of the Rocky Mountains and north of Oklahoma, the doctrine and the dance were accepted by the Asiniboin (Fort Belknap and Fort Peck agencies), Grosventres (Arapaho subtribe, Fort Belknap agency), northern Cheyenne of Montana; the Arikara, Grosventres (Minitari), and Mandan of Fort Berthold agency, North Dakota; the Shoshoni and northern Arapaho on Wind River reservation in Wyoming, as already mentioned; and by the great body of the Sioux, at Fort Peck agency (Yanktonais), Montana, and at Standing Rock, Cheyenne River, Lower Brulé, Pine Ridge, and Rosebud agencies in North Dakota and South Dakota. The whole number of Sioux involved was about 20,000, of whom 16,000 belonged to the Teton division—among the wildest and most warlike of all the western tribes. A few Cheyenne are also associated with the Sioux at Pine Ridge.

<margin>Redman</margin>
The northern Arapaho and the Shoshoni of Wyoming were the means by which the doctrine of the new messiah was originally communicated to all these tribes. In the spring of 1889, Nakash, “Sage,” the Arapaho chief already mentioned, crossed the mountains to investigate the reports of the new religion and brought back a full confirmation of all that had been told to them from the west. A visiting Grosventre, then among the Arapaho, heard the story and brought the wonderful news back to the Grosventres and Asiniboin of Fort Belknap; however, although some received his account with unquestioning faith, the excitement was not of a dangerous character. (*G. D.*, 18.)

In a short time, the news spread to the Cheyenne in Montana and the Sioux of the Dakotas, and in the fall of 1889, delegates from these two tribes arrived at Fort Washakie to learn more about the messiah in the west. The principal Cheyenne delegate was Porcupine, while Short Bull and Kicking Bear were the leaders of the Sioux party. After hearing the statements of the Arapaho and Shoshoni, it was decided that some of the Cheyenne should return and report to their tribe, while Porcupine and one or two others—along with the Sioux delegates, several Shoshoni, and the Arapaho, Sitting Bull, and Friday—should go to Nevada, interview the messiah himself, and learn the whole truth of the matter. Accordingly, about November 1889, Porcupine and his companions left Fort Washakie in Wyoming for the Fort Hall reservation in Idaho, where they met the Shoshoni and Bannock and were well received and entertained by them. The tribes at this place were firm believers in the new doctrine, and Porcupine states that from there to the end of the journey, all the Indians they met were dancing...

After staying a few days at Fort Hall, they went on again, accompanied by several Bannock and Shoshoni, and traveling rapidly by railroad, they soon found themselves in the territory of the Paiute. After stopping at one or two camps, they arrived at the agency at Pyramid Lake. Here, the Paiute provided them with transportation and guides to the other agency further south at Walker River. Porcupine is our main authority for the events of the trip, and although he claims that he undertook this journey of a thousand miles without any definite purpose or destination in mind, it is clear enough from his own narrative that he left Wyoming with the fixed intention of confirming the rumors of a messiah. He has much to say about the kindness of the white people they met west of the mountains, who, it should be remembered, were largely Mormons, who have always shown a special interest in the Indians. He also states that many of the white people took part with the Indians in the dance.

They were now in the messiah’s country. 

> “The Fisheaters, near Pyramid Lake, told me that Christ had appeared on earth again. They said Christ knew he was coming; that eleven of his children were also coming from a distant land. It appeared that Christ had sent for me to go there, and that was why, unconsciously, I began my journey. It had been predestined. Christ had summoned me and others from all the various tribes. There were more different languages than I had ever heard before, and I did not understand any of them.” 

The delegation Porcupine belonged to was likely the one mentioned by the agent in charge at Pyramid Lake as having arrived in the spring of 1890, consisting of thirty-four Indians from different tribes. (*G. D., 19.*)

In a few days, preparations were made for a great dance near Walker Lake, with all the delegates from various tribes and hundreds of Indians attending. They danced for two nights or longer; the messiah himself—Wovoka—came down from his home in Mason Valley to lead the ceremony. After the dance, Wovoka went into a trance, and on awaking, announced to those assembled that he had been to the other world and had seen the spirits of their dead friends and of his own father and mother, and had been sent back to teach the people. According to Porcupine, he claimed to be the returned Christ and bore on his body the scars of the crucifixion. He told them that the dead were to be resurrected, and that as the earth was old and worn out, it would be renewed as it used to be and improved; that when this happened, everyone’s youth would be renewed with each return of spring, and they would live forever; that there would be universal peace, and that any tribe that rejected his message would be wiped from the face of the earth.

In June, the matter came to the attention of the military officer on the reservation, who summoned Porcupine before him and obtained from him a full account of the journey and the doctrine. He claimed also that the messiah could speak all languages. As a matter of fact, Wovoka speaks only his native Paiute and a little English, but due allowance must be made for the mental excitement of the narrator.

Grinnell states that the failure of certain things to happen according to the predictions of the messiah, in September 1890, caused a temporary loss of faith on the part of the Cheyenne, but that shortly afterward some visiting Shoshoni and Arapaho from Wyoming reported that in their journey as they came over, they had met a party of Indians who had been dead thirty or forty years, but had been resurrected by the messiah, and were now going about as if they had never died. It is useless to speculate on the mental condition of men who could seriously report or believe such things; but, however that may be, the result was that the Cheyenne returned to the dance with redoubled fervor. (J. F. L., 5.)

The Sioux first heard of the messiah in 1889. According to the statement of Captain George Sword, of that tribe, the information came to the Oglala (Sioux of Pine Ridge) in that year, through the Shoshoni and Arapaho. Later in the same year, a delegation consisting of Good Thunder and several others started out to the west to find the messiah and to investigate the truth of the rumor. On their return, they announced that the messiah had indeed come to help the Indians, but not the whites. Their report aroused a fervor of joyful excitement among the Indians and a second delegation was sent out in 1890, consisting of Good Thunder, Cloud Horse, Yellow Knife, and Short Bull. They confirmed the report of the first delegation, and on this assurance the Ghost dance was inaugurated among the Sioux at Pine Ridge in the spring of 1890.

The matter is stated differently and more correctly by William Selwyn, an educated Sioux, at that time employed as postmaster at Pine Ridge. He says there was some talk on the subject by Indians from western tribes who visited the agency in the fall of 1888 (?), but that it did not excite much attention until 1889, when numerous letters concerning the new messiah were received by the Indians at Pine Ridge from tribes in Utah, Wyoming, Montana, Dakota, and Oklahoma. As Selwyn was postmaster, the Indians who could not read usually brought their letters to him to read for them, so that he was thus in

In a position to gain accurate knowledge of the extent and nature of the excitement, it is worth noting that, under present conditions—where the various tribes are isolated on widely separated reservations—the Ghost Dance could never have become so widespread and would probably have died out within a year of its beginning. This is because it would not have had the efficient aid it received from the returned students of various eastern government schools. These students handled the sacred correspondence for their friends at the different agencies, acted as interpreters for the delegates visiting the messiah, and in various ways assumed the leadership and management of the dance.

In the fall of 1889, at a council held at Pine Ridge by Red Cloud, Young Man Afraid, Little Wound, American Horse, and other Sioux chiefs, a delegation was appointed to visit the western agencies to learn more about the new messiah. The chosen delegates were Good Thunder, Flat Iron, Yellow Breast, and Broken Arm from Pine Ridge; Short Bull and another from Rosebud; and Kicking Bear from the Cheyenne River agency. They began their journey to the west and soon started writing from Wyoming, Utah, and beyond the mountains, confirming everything that had been said about the coming of a redeemer. They were gone all winter, and their return in the spring of 1890 caused intense excitement among the Sioux, who had been anxiously awaiting their report. All the delegates agreed that there was a man near the base of the Sierras who said that he was the son of God, who had once been killed by the whites, and who bore the scars of the crucifixion on his body. He had now returned to punish the white people for their wickedness, especially for their injustice toward the Indians. With the coming of the next spring (1891), he would wipe the whites from the face of the earth and would then resurrect all the dead Indians, bring back the buffalo and other game, and restore the supremacy of the Indigenous race. He had come to the white people before, but they had rejected him. He was now the God of the Indians, and they must pray to him, call him “father,” and prepare for his fearsome arrival. Selwyn’s account of this delegation, which was accompanied by representatives of several other tribes—including Porcupine the Cheyenne and Sitting Bull the Arapaho—matches the statements of the Arapaho as given in chapter XIV. Three of the Sioux delegates found their way to the Umatilla reservation in Oregon and remained there several days discussing the new doctrine. (*Comr., 30—Dorchester, 529.*)

The delegates made their report at Pine Ridge in April 1890. A council was immediately called to discuss the matter, but Selwyn informed the agent, Colonel Gallagher, who had Good Thunder and two others arrested and imprisoned. They were held in confinement for two days but refused to talk when questioned. The intended council was not held, but soon afterward, Kicking Bear returned from a visit to the northern Arapaho in Wyoming with the news that those Indians were already dancing and could see and talk with their dead relatives.

...in the trance. The excitement, which the agent had thought to suppress by arresting the leaders, broke out again with renewed strength. Red Cloud himself, the great chief of the Ogalala, declared his support for the new doctrine and said his people must do as the messiah had commanded. Another council was called at White Clay Creek, a few miles from the Pine Ridge agency, and the Ghost Dance was formally started among the Sioux, with the recent delegates acting as priests and leaders of the ceremony.

Based on everything he could learn, Selwyn, in November 1890, warned the agent in charge of the Yankton agency that the Indians intended a general uprising in the spring. Six months earlier, and before Porcupine's statement had been made to the officer at Camp Crook, a letter dated May 29, 1890, had been sent to the Department of the Interior from a citizen of Pierre, South Dakota, stating that the Sioux, or at least some of them, were secretly planning for an uprising in the near future. This was the first sign of trouble ahead. (*G. D., 20.*)

The returned delegates said miraculous things about the messiah. It was claimed that he could make animals talk and make distant objects appear close at hand, and that he came down from heaven in a cloud. He conjured a vision of the spirit world before their eyes, so that when they looked, they saw an ocean, and beyond it a land where they saw "all the nations of Indians coming home"; however, as they looked, the vision faded away, and the messiah said that the time had not yet come. Interestingly enough, although he came to restore the traditional way of life, he advised his listeners to work and to send their children to school. If soldiers tried to harm him, he said he only had to stretch out his arms and his enemies would become powerless, or the ground would open and swallow them. If they killed a buffalo on their way home—the messiah had evidently not read Allen's monograph <note>A reference to Joel Asaph Allen’s 1876 work, "The American Bisons, Living and Extinct," which documented the animal's near-extinction.</note>—they were to cut off its head, tail, and feet and leave them on the ground, and the buffalo would come back to life. They were told to tell their people to follow his instructions. Unbelievers and disloyal Indians would be buried under the new earth that was to cover the old. They were to use the sacred red and white paint and the sacred grass (possibly sagebrush) that he gave them, and in the spring, when the green grass grew, their ancestors would return, and they would see their friends again.

The <term>Messiah</term> said, “I will shorten your journey when you feel tired of the long way, if you call upon me.” This we did when we were tired. It is useless to assert that these men—who had been selected by the chiefs of their tribe to investigate and report upon the truth or falsity of the <term>Messiah</term> rumors—were all liars, and that all the <term>Cheyenne</term>, <term>Arapaho</term>, and other delegates who reported equally wonderful things were liars as well. They were simply laboring under some strange psychological influence as yet unexplained. The story of the restored buffalo became so widely known that it became the subject of a <term>Kiowa</term> <term>Ghost Dance</term> song.

Having mentioned some characteristics of the <term>Ghost Dance</term> west of the Rockies, we shall now note some of the peculiar features of the dance as it existed among the <term>Sioux</term>. The ceremony will be described in detail later on.

Before participating in the dance the men, or at least the leaders, fasted for twenty-four hours, and then at sunrise entered the <term>sweat-house</term> for the religious rite of purification preliminary to painting themselves for the dance. The <term>sweat-house</term> is a small circular framework of willow branches driven into the ground, bent over, and joined at the top in such a way that when covered with blankets or buffalo robes the structure forms a tiny round-top <term>tipi</term> just high enough to enable several persons to sit or to stand in a stooping posture inside. The doorway faces the east, as is the rule in Indian structures, and at a distance of a few feet in front of the doorway is a small mound of earth, on which is placed a <term>buffalo skull</term>, with the head turned as if looking into the lodge. The earth of which the mound is formed is taken from a hole dug in the center of the lodge. Near the <term>sweat-house</term>, on the outside, there is frequently a tall <term>sacrifice pole</term>, from the top of which are hung strips of bright-colored cloth, packages of tobacco, or other offerings to the deity invoked by the worshiper on any particular occasion.

The sweat bath is in frequent use, both as a religious rite of purification and as a hygienic treatment. Like everything else in Indian life, even the sanitary application is attended with much religious ceremony. Fresh bundles of the fragrant wild sage are strewn upon the ground inside of the <term>sweat-house</term>, and a fire is kindled a short distance away outside. In this fire, stones are heated by the <term>medicine-men</term>, and when all is ready the patient or worshiper, stripped to the <term>breech-cloth</term>, enters the <term>sweat-house</term>. The stones are then handed in to him by the priests using two forked sticks, cut especially for the purpose, and with two other forked sticks he puts the stones into the hole already mentioned as having been dug in the center of the lodge. Water is then passed in to him, which he pours over the hot stones until the whole interior is filled with steam; the blankets are pulled

<header>MOONEY] THE SWEAT BATH</header>

tight to close every opening, and he sits in this indigenous Turkish bath until his naked body is dripping with perspiration. During this time, the doctors outside perform their part by praying to the gods and maintaining the supply of hot stones and water until, in their judgment, he has been sufficiently purified, physically or morally. At that point, he emerges and puts his clothes back on, sometimes first stopping the perspiration and stimulating a reaction by plunging into a nearby stream. The sweat bath, in one form or another, was common to almost every tribe in the United States, but as an accompaniment to the Ghost Dance, it seems to have been used only by the Sioux. It may have been used in this way among the Shoshone or Northern Cheyenne, but it was not used among any of the tribes of the southern plains. The Ghost Dance sweat-house of the Sioux was often made large enough to accommodate a significant number of people standing inside at the same time.

After the sweating ceremony, the dancer was painted by the medicine men who acted as leaders, among whom Sitting Bull was considered the greatest of the Sioux. The design and color varied with the individual, often being determined by a previous trance vision of the subject; however, circles, crescents, and crosses—representing the sun, the moon, and the morning star, respectively—were always favorite figures on the forehead, face, and cheeks. Since this was not a naked dance, the rest of the body was not usually painted. After the painting, the dancer was dressed in the sacred ghost shirt already described. This was also painted with symbolic figures, which usually included representations of the sun, moon, or stars, the eagle, magpie, crow, or sage hen—all sacred to the Ghost Dance among the Sioux. Along with the painting, the face and body were rubbed with the sweet-smelling vernal grass (*Hierochloe*), which was used for this purpose by many of the prairie tribes. It was also sometimes burned as incense in their sacred ceremonies or carried as a perfume in small pouches attached to their clothing.

The painting took up most of the morning, so it was about noon before the participants formed the circle for the dance. Among the Sioux, unlike the southern and western tribes generally, a small tree was planted in the center of the circle, with an American flag or colored streamers flying from the top. The priests sat around the base of this tree. During a great dance at No Water’s camp on the White River near Pine Ridge, shortly before the arrival of the troops, a young woman standing within the circle gave the signal for the performance by shooting four sacred arrows into the air toward the cardinal directions. These arrows were made in the old primitive style with bone heads and were dipped in the blood of a steer before being brought to the dance. These were then gathered up and tied to the branches of the tree, along with the bow, a gaming wheel and sticks, and a peculiar staff or wand with horns. (See plates XC, XCI.) Another young woman, or perhaps the same one, remained standing near the tree throughout the dance, holding a sacred redstone pipe

At the beginning, the performers—both men and women—sat on the ground in a large circle around the tree. A mournful chant was then sung, after which a vessel of sacred food was passed around the circle until everyone had shared it. Then, at a signal from the priests, the dancers stood up, joined hands, and began to chant the opening song, moving slowly around the circle from right to left. The rest of the performance, including its frenzies, trances, and recitals of visions, was the same as that of the southern tribes, which will be described in detail later. Like those tribes, the Sioux usually chose Sunday—the white man’s "great medicine day"—for the ceremony.

We come now to the Sioux outbreak of 1890, but before discussing the history of this short but costly war, it is appropriate to briefly state the causes of the conflict. In the documentary appendix to this chapter, these causes are fully explained by competent authorities—including civilian, military, missionary, and Indian sources. They may be summarized as: (1) unrest among the conservative members of the tribe due to the decline of their traditional way of life; (2) repeated neglect of promises made by the government; and (3) hunger.

The Sioux are the largest and strongest tribe in the United States. Despite wars, forced removals, and a diminished food supply since the arrival of the white man, they still number nearly 26,000. In addition to these, there are about 600 more living in Canada. They formerly controlled the headwaters of the Mississippi, extending eastward almost to Lake Superior, but were driven onto the prairies about two centuries ago by their enemies, the Ojibwa, after the latter had obtained firearms from the French. Upon reaching the buffalo plains, they acquired horses. By using this advantage to reinforce their own overwhelming numbers, the Sioux were soon able to take the offensive; in a short time, they became the undisputed masters of an immense territory extending, generally, from Minnesota to the Rocky Mountains and from the Yellowstone River to the Platte River. A few small tribes managed to maintain their positions within these limits, but only by staying close to their strongly built permanent villages on the Missouri River. With millions of buffalo providing an unlimited food supply, thousands of horses, and hundreds of miles of free range, the Sioux were, until the year 1868, the richest and most prosperous, the proudest, and perhaps the wildest of all the Plains tribes.

In that year, following a policy established to bring all the Plains tribes under the direct control of the government, a treaty was negotiated with the Sioux living west of the Missouri. By this treaty, they renounced their claims to a large portion of their territory and had "set apart for their absolute and undisturbed use and occupation"—as the treaty states—a reservation that included all of the present state of South Dakota west of the Missouri River. At the same time, agents were appointed and agencies established for them; annuities and rations,

<header>MOONEY] DEVELOPMENT OF THE SIOUX TROUBLE</header>

Cattle, physicians, farmers, teachers, and other benefits were promised to them, and they agreed to allow railroad routes to be surveyed and built and military posts to be established in their territory and neighborhood. In a single stroke, they were reduced from a free nation to dependent wards of the government. It was also stipulated that they should be allowed to hunt within their old range, outside the limits of the reservation, as long as the buffalo remained—a provision which, to the Indians, must have seemed like it would last forever.

The reservation established this way was immense and would have been enough for all the Sioux while they were being gradually educated toward civilization, if the buffalo could have remained and the white man had stayed away. But times were changing. The building of the railroads brought swarms of hunters and emigrants onto the plains, who began to exterminate the buffalo at such a rate that in a few years the Sioux, along with all the other hunting tribes of the plains, realized that their food supply was rapidly disappearing. Then gold was discovered in the Black Hills, within the reservation, and thousands of miners and thousands more lawless desperadoes immediately rushed into the country in defiance of the Indians' protests and the government's pledges. The Sioux saw their last remaining hunting ground taken from them. The result was the Custer war and massacre, and a new agreement in 1876 by which the Sioux were stripped of one-third of their guaranteed reservation, including the Black Hills. This led to deep and widespread dissatisfaction throughout the tribe. The conservatives brooded over the past and planned opposition to further changes which they felt unable to meet. The progressives felt that the white man’s promises meant nothing.

On this point, Commissioner Morgan says in his statement regarding the causes of the outbreak:

> Prior to the agreement of 1876, buffalo and deer were the main support of the Sioux. Food, tents, and bedding were the direct result of hunting, and with furs and pelts as items for barter or exchange, it was easy for the Sioux to obtain whatever constituted the necessities, comforts, or even luxuries of life for them. Within eight years of the 1876 agreement, the buffalo had gone, and the Sioux were left with alkali land and government rations. It is hard to overestimate the magnitude of the calamity, as they viewed it, which happened to these people by the sudden disappearance of the buffalo and the large decrease in the number of deer and other wild animals. Suddenly, and almost without warning, they were expected at once and without previous training to settle down to farming in a land largely unfit for such use. The freedom of the hunt was to be exchanged for the idleness of the camp. The boundless range was to be abandoned for the restricted reservation, and an abundance of plenty was to be replaced by limited and decreasing government subsistence and supplies. Under these circumstances, it is not in human nature not to be discontented and restless, even turbulent and violent. (Commissioner, 28.)

It took our own <term>Aryan</term> <note>In the 19th century, "Aryan" was a common anthropological term for Indo-European peoples.</note> ancestors untold centuries to develop from savagery into civilization. Was it reasonable to expect that the Sioux could do the same in fourteen years?

The white population in the Black Hills had rapidly increased, and it had become desirable to open communication between eastern and western Dakota. To accomplish this, it was proposed to cut out the heart of the Sioux reservation, and in 1882, only six years after the Black Hills had been seized, the Sioux were called on to surrender more territory. A commission was sent out to negotiate with them, but the price offered—only about 8 cents per acre—was so absurdly small, and the methods used so clearly unjust, that friends of the Indians intervened and succeeded in defeating the measure in Congress. Another agreement was prepared, but experience had made the Indians suspicious, and it was not until a third commission went out, under the chairmanship of General Crook—known to the Indians as a brave soldier and an honorable man—that the Sioux consented to negotiate. (*Welsh, 1.*) The result, after much effort on the part of the commission and determined opposition by the conservatives, was another agreement in 1889. By this agreement, the Sioux surrendered half (about 11,000,000 acres) of their remaining territory, and the great reservation was cut up into five smaller ones; the northern and southern reservations were separated by a strip 60 miles wide.

Then came a swift accumulation of miseries. Dakota is an arid country with thin soil and short seasons. Although well adapted to grazing, it is not suited to agriculture, as is sufficiently proven by the fact that the white settlers in that and the adjoining state of Nebraska have several times been obliged to call for state or federal assistance on account of the failure of crops. To wild Indians recently coming from the warpath, the problem was much more serious. As General Miles points out in his official report, thousands of white settlers, after years of successive failures, had given up the struggle and left the country; however, the Indians, confined to reservations, were unable to emigrate and were also generally unable to find employment, as the whites might, by which they could earn a living. The buffalo was gone. They had to depend on their cattle, their crops, and the government rations issued in return for the lands they had surrendered. If these failed, they would starve. The highest official authorities concur in the statement that all of these did fail, and that the Indians were driven to an outbreak by starvation. (See the appendix to this chapter.)

In 1888, their cattle had been diminished by disease. In 1889, their crops were a failure, owing largely to the fact that the Indians had been called into the agency in the middle of the farming season and kept there to negotiate with the commission, only to return afterward to find their fields trampled and torn up by livestock during their absence. Then followed epidemics of measles, influenza <note>Originally "grippe"</note>, and whooping cough in rapid succession and with terribly fatal results. Anyone who understands the Indian character does not need the testimony of witnesses to know the mental effect produced this way. Sullenness and gloom, amounting almost to despair, settled down on the Sioux, especially among the wilder—

<summary>Following the forced surrender of half their remaining land in 1889, the Sioux faced a devastating combination of crop failures, livestock disease, and deadly epidemics. These hardships, exacerbated by government mismanagement and the loss of the buffalo, reduced the tribe to a state of starvation and profound despair.</summary>

Then another total crop failure occurred in 1890, along with an unexpected reduction in rations, and the Indians were brought face to face with starvation. They had been explicitly and repeatedly told by the commission that their rations would not be affected by signing the treaty; however, immediately after the agreement was finalized, Congress cut their beef rations by 2,000,000 pounds at Rosebud, 1,000,000 pounds at Pine Ridge, and by smaller proportions at other agencies. Earnest protests against this reduction were made by the commission that had negotiated the treaty, by Commissioner Morgan, and by General Miles, but Congress still failed to remedy the matter until the Sioux had actually been driven to rebellion. As Commissioner Morgan states, "It was not until January 1891, *after the troubles*, that Congress made an appropriation of $100,000 for additional beef for the Sioux." The commission's protest, made a full year before the outbreak and quoted by Commissioner Morgan (see page 829), is strong and definite on this point.

Commissioner Morgan, while claiming that the Sioux had previously been receiving more rations than they were justly entitled to according to their census numbers, and denying that the reduction was enough to cause even extreme suffering, nevertheless states that the reduction was especially unwise at this time. It was a direct violation of the promises made to the Indians and would be used as an argument by those opposed to the treaty to show that the government cared nothing for the Indians once it had obtained their lands. It is quite possible that the previous number of rations was greater than the actual number of people, as it is always difficult to count nomadic Indians, and the difficulties were even greater when the old census was taken. The census is taken at long intervals, and the tendency is nearly always toward a decrease. Furthermore, it has usually been the policy of agents to keep their Indians quiet by keeping them as well-fed as possible. On the other hand, it must be remembered that the distribution is based on the weight of the cattle as delivered at the agency in the fall, and that months of exposure to a Dakota winter will reduce an animal's weight by several hundred pounds. The official investigation by Captain Hurst at the Cheyenne River agency shows conclusively that the essential food items of meat, flour, and coffee were far below the amount stipulated by the treaty. (See page 837.)

In regard to the effect of this food deficiency, Bishop Hare says: "The people were often hungry and, as the physicians said in many cases, died when taken sick not so much from disease as for want of food." General Miles says: "The fact that they had not received sufficient food is admitted by the agents and the government officers who have had opportunities to know," and in another place he states that despite crop failures and other difficulties, after the sale of the reser—

vation, "instead of an increase, or even a reasonable supply for their support, they have been compelled to live on half and two-thirds rations and received nothing for the surrender of their lands." The testimony from every agency is all to the same effect.

There were other causes of dissatisfaction, some local and others general and chronic, which do not need to be detailed here. Some of these are treated in the documents appended to this chapter. Prominent among them were the failure of Congress to make payment of the money due to the Sioux for the lands recently ceded, or to have the new boundary lines surveyed promptly so that the Indians might know what was still theirs and select their allotments accordingly; the failure to reimburse the friendly Indians for horses confiscated fourteen years earlier; the late arrival of annuities, consisting largely of winter clothing, which according to the treaty were due by the 1st of August, but which seldom arrived until the middle of winter; the sweeping and frequent changes of agency employees from the agent down, preventing anything like a systematic working out of any consistent policy, and almost always operating against the good of the service—especially at Pine Ridge, where a man as brave and efficient as McGillycuddy was followed by someone like Royer—and, finally, the Ghost dance.

The Ghost dance itself, in the form which it assumed among the Sioux, was only a symptom and expression of the real causes of dissatisfaction. With a man like McGillycuddy or McLaughlin in charge at Pine Ridge, there would have been no outbreak, in spite of broken promises and starvation, and the Indians could have been controlled until Congress had afforded relief. That it was not the cause of the outbreak is sufficiently proved by the fact that there was no serious trouble on any other of the Sioux reservations (excepting on the occasion of the attempt to arrest Sitting Bull) and none at all among any of the other Ghost-dancing tribes from the Missouri to the Sierras, although the doctrine and the dance were held by nearly every tribe within that area and are still held by the more important ones. Among the Paiute, where the doctrine originated and the messiah has his home, there was never the slightest trouble. It is significant that Commissioner Morgan, in his official statement of the causes of the outbreak, places the "messiah craze" eleventh in a list of twelve—the twelfth being the alarm created by the appearance of troops. The Sioux outbreak of 1890 was due entirely to local grievances, whether recent or long-standing. The remedy and prevention for similar trouble in the future is sufficiently indicated in the appended statements of competent authorities.

# APPENDIX—CAUSES OF THE OUTBREAK

## COMMISSIONER MORGAN’S STATEMENT

->*[From the Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1891, Vol. I, 132-135.]*<-

In stating the events which led to this outbreak among the Sioux, the effort too often has been merely to find some opportunity to assign blame. The causes are complex, and many are hidden and distant. Among them may be named the following:

First. A feeling of unrest and concern in the minds of the Indians has naturally grown out of the rapid advance of civilization and the great changes which this progress has required in their habits and way of life.

Second. Before the agreement of 1876, buffalo and deer were the main support of the Sioux. Food, tents, and bedding were the direct result of hunting; with furs and hides used as articles of trade or exchange, it was easy for the Sioux to obtain whatever they considered the necessities, comforts, or even luxuries of life. Within eight years of the agreement of 1876, the buffalo had disappeared, and the Sioux were left with alkali-rich land and government rations. It is hard to overestimate the size of the disaster, as they viewed it, which happened to these people because of the sudden disappearance of the buffalo and the large decrease in the numbers of deer and other wild animals. Suddenly, almost without warning, they were expected to settle down immediately to the pursuit of agriculture in a land largely unfit for such use, and without previous training. The freedom of the hunt was to be exchanged for the boredom of the camp. The boundless range was to be abandoned for the restricted reservation, and a life of plenty was to be replaced by limited and decreasing government support and supplies. Under these circumstances, it is only human nature to be discontented and restless, or even rebellious and violent.

Third. During a long series of years, treaties, agreements, surrenders of land and privileges, and the relocation of bands and agencies have kept many of the Sioux—particularly those at Pine Ridge and Rosebud—in an unsettled condition, especially as some of the promises made to them were fulfilled late or not at all. (A brief history of negotiations with the Sioux was given in my letter of December 24, 1890, to the Department, which can be found in the appendix, page 182.)

Fourth. The very large reduction of the Great Sioux Reservation, brought about by the Sioux Commission through the consent of the large majority of the adult males, was bitterly opposed by a large, influential minority. For various reasons, they regarded the land surrender as unwise and did all in their power to prevent its completion, and afterward were constant in expressing their dissatisfaction and in their efforts to stir up similar feelings in the minds of those who had signed the agreement.

Fifth. There was a reduction and partial failure of the crops for 1889, because the Indians neglected them while gathered in large numbers for the meeting with the Sioux Commission, and a further reduction of ordinary crops by the drought of 1890. Also, in 1888, the disease known as "black leg" appeared among the cattle of the Indians.

Sixth. At this time, due to delayed and reduced funding, the Sioux rations were temporarily cut back. Rations were not reduced to such an extent as to bring the Indians to starvation or even extreme suffering, as has been often reported; but short rations came just after the Sioux Commission had negotiated the agreement for the surrender of lands and, as a condition of securing the signatures of the majority, had assured the Indians that their rations would be continued unchanged. To this matter, the Sioux Commission called special attention in their report dated December 24, 1889, as follows:

> "During our conference at the different agencies we were repeatedly asked whether the acceptance or rejection of the act of Congress would influence the action of the

government with reference to their rations, and in every instance the Indians were assured that subsistence was provided in accordance with former treaties, and that signing would not affect their rations, and that they would continue to receive them as provided in former treaties. Without our assurances to this effect, it would have been impossible to secure their consent to the cession of their lands. Since our visit to the agencies, it appears that large reductions have been made in the amounts of beef provided for distribution, amounting at Rosebud to 2,000,000 pounds and at Pine Ridge to 1,000,000 pounds, with lesser amounts at the other agencies. This action of the Department, following immediately after the successful conclusion of our negotiations, cannot fail to have a harmful effect. It will be impossible to convince the Indians that the reduction is not due to the fact that the government, having obtained their land, has less concern for their material interests than before. It will be viewed as a breach of faith and especially as a violation of the explicit statements of the commissioners. Already this action is being used by the Indians opposed to the bill, especially at Pine Ridge, as an argument in support of the wisdom of their opposition."

In forwarding this report to Congress, the Department called special attention to the above-quoted statements of the commission and said: "The commission further remarks that, regarding the quality of the rations provided, there seems to be no just cause for complaint. However, it was particularly important to avoid any reduction of the rations promised under the former treaties at this time, as the Indians would attribute it to their agreement to the bill. Such a reduction certainly should not be allowed, as the government is bound in good faith to carry out the former treaties where they are not directly and positively affected by the act. If, under the provisions of the treaty itself, the ration is at any time reduced, the commissioners recommend that the Indians should be notified before spring opens, so that crops may be cultivated. It is desirable that the recent reduction made should be restored, as it is now impossible to convince the Indians that it was not due to the fact that the government, having obtained their lands, had less concern for their material interests."

Despite this plea from the commission and the Department, the appropriation made for the subsistence and civilization of the Sioux for 1890 was only $950,000, which was $50,000 less than the amount estimated and appropriated for 1888 and 1889. Because the appropriation was not made until August 19, rations had to be temporarily purchased and distributed in limited quantities while waiting for the arrival of new supplies to be secured from that appropriation. It was not until January 1891, after the troubles, that an appropriation of $100,000 was made by Congress for additional beef for the Sioux.

Seventh. Other promises made by the Sioux commission and the agreement were not promptly fulfilled. Among them were an increase in appropriations for education, for which this office had asked $150,000; the payment of $200,000 in compensation for ponies taken from the Sioux in 1876 and 1877; and the reimbursement of the Crow Creek Indians for a reduction made in their per person allowance of land, as compared with the amount allowed other Sioux, which required an appropriation of $187,039. The fulfillment of all these promises, except for the last one mentioned, was included in the act of January 19, 1891.

Eighth. In 1889 and 1890, epidemics of *la grippe*, measles, and whooping cough, followed by many deaths, added to the gloom and misfortune which seemed to surround the Indians.

Ninth. The wording of the agreement changed the boundary line between the Rosebud and Pine Ridge diminished reservations. This required the removal of a portion of the Rosebud Indians from the lands which, by the agreement, were included in the Pine Ridge reservation to lands offered them in exchange on the diminished Rosebud reserve. While this involved no great hardship to any significant number of people, it added to the general discontent.

Tenth. Some of the Indians were strongly opposed to the census that Congress ordered to be taken. The census at Rosebud, as reported by Special Agent Lea and confirmed by a special census taken by Agent Wright, revealed the somewhat startling fact that rations had been issued to a far greater number of Indians than were actually present. This reduction in numbers shown by the census required a reduction in rations, which were, of course, based upon the census.

Eleventh. The Messiah craze—which promoted the belief that "ghost shirts" would be bulletproof and that the supremacy of the Indian race was guaranteed—added the passion of fanaticism to their discontent. This brought those who accepted the new faith into an attitude of sullen defiance, though it was defensive rather than aggressive.

Twelfth. The sudden appearance of the military on their reservation gave rise to the wildest rumors of danger and disaster among the Indians. These were eagerly spread by dissatisfied Indians and supported by exaggerated accounts in the newspapers. These and other influences, which are inseparable from military movements, frightened many Indians away from their agencies and into the Badlands, greatly intensifying whatever spirit of opposition to the government already existed.

## EX-AGENT McGILLYCUDDY'S STATEMENT

[*Letter from Dr. V. T. McGillycuddy, formerly an agent at Pine Ridge, written in reply to an inquiry from General L. W. Colby, commander of the Nebraska state troops during the outbreak, dated January 15, 1891. From an article on "The Sioux Indian War of 1890-91," by General L. W. Colby, in Transactions and Reports of the Nebraska State Historical Society, III, 1892, pages 176-180.*]

SIR: In answer to your recent inquiry, I would state that, in my opinion, the recent so-called outbreak by the Sioux cannot be attributed to any single cause. Instead, it resulted from a combination of causes that built up over many years—stretching back, in fact, to the beginning of our clearly flawed Indian policy.

There can be no question that many of the treaties, agreements, or formal promises made by our government with these Indians have been broken. Many of them have been kept by us in a technical sense, but the Indians have misunderstood them due to a lack of proper explanation at the time of signing; consequently, they consider them broken.

It must also be remembered that in all the treaties made by the government with the Indians, a large portion of them did not agree to or sign the documents. This was notably the case in the agreement we secured the summer before last, by which we acquired one-half of the remaining Sioux reservation, amounting to about 16,000 square miles. This agreement barely passed among the Sioux nation as a whole and did not pass at Pine Ridge or Rosebud, where a strong majority opposed it. It should be noted that wherever the strongest opposition to the recent treaty was shown, the elements opposed to the government have been found during the current trouble.

The Sioux nation—which at one time, along with the allied bands of Cheyennes and Arapahos, controlled a region bounded on the north by the Yellowstone, on the south by the Arkansas, and reaching from the Missouri River to the Rocky Mountains—has seen this vast domain dwindle under various treaties to their current limited reservation of less than 16,000 square miles. Along with the land, the buffalo and other game have disappeared. The memory of this, for which they blame the white man, naturally irritates them.

Behind all of this is the natural racial antagonism which our dealings with the original inhabitants <note>The original text uses the term "aborigine."</note>, combined with the inevitable onward march of civilization, has not lessened in the slightest. It has been our experience, and the experience of other nations, that defeat in war is soon forgotten by the coming generation. As a result, we see a tendency for outbreaks to recur constantly on the part

...of the weaker race. It has now been sixteen years since our last war with the Sioux in 1876—a time when our current Sioux warriors were mostly children and therefore have no memory of feeling the power of the government. It is only natural that these young warriors, lacking experience, would require very little incentive to induce them to test the bravery of the white man on the warpath, which the traditions of their people teach them is the only path to glory and a chosen seat in the "happy hunting grounds." For these reasons, every precaution should be taken by the government to guard against trouble and its disastrous results. Have such precautions been taken? An investigation of the current trouble does not suggest so.

Sitting Bull and other unyielding remnants of the 1876 campaign were allowed to remain among their people and stir up discord. The staple food supply at Pine Ridge and some of the other agencies had been reduced below the level of survival; most notably the beef at Pine Ridge, which was cut from an annual treaty allowance of 6,250,000 pounds gross weight to 4,000,000 pounds. The contract for that beef was violated because the contract called for northern ranch beef, but <term>through beef</term> <note>Cattle driven from the south, typically Texas, which were less hardy in northern winters.</note> from Texas was substituted instead. This resulted in an unparalleled loss of weight during the winter, so the Indians did not actually receive even a half-ration of this food in winter—the very time when the largest food allowance is required. Through the fortunes of political conflict, weak agents were put in charge of some of the agencies at the very time that trouble was known to be brewing. This was especially true at Pine Ridge, where a notoriously weak and unfit man was placed in charge. His flight, his abandonment of his agency, and his request for troops—along with the horrible results of those actions—have become facts in history.

Now, regarding the facts about Pine Ridge—the agency that has unfortunately become the stage for the current "war"—was there a necessity for troops? My past experience with those Indians does not suggest so. For seven long years, from 1879 to 1886, I, as agent, managed this agency without a single soldier on the reservation and none closer than 60 miles, even though the Indians were naturally much wilder in those times than they are today. To be sure, during those seven years, we occasionally had tense moments when the only thing missing to cause an outbreak was the agent calling for troops or their actual presence. In fact, however, no matter how disturbed affairs were or how imminent an outbreak seemed, the progressive chiefs and their followers stepped forward in sufficient numbers, along with the fifty Indian policemen, to immediately crush all attempts at rebellion against the authority of the agent and the government.

Why was this? Because in those days, we believed in trusting the Indians and in establishing, as far as possible, a local self-government on the reservation. We established local courts presided over by Indians with Indian juries; in fact, we believed in having the Indians help work out their own salvation. We sought and secured the friendship and support of the progressive and orderly group, as opposed to the unruly mob. Whether the system we started was practical or successful can be decided by comparing it with recent events.

When my Democratic successor took charge in 1886, he felt it was necessary to make sweeping changes to the system at Pine Ridge—that is, the Republican system. All white men, people of mixed ancestry, or Indians who had supported the agent under the previous administration were labeled Republicans and had to leave. Progressive chiefs, such as Young Man Afraid, Little Wound, and White Bird, were ignored, and the support of the group favoring order and progress was alienated from the agent and the government. In place of this strong support that had maintained order for seven years, Red Cloud and other non-progressive chiefs, who supported the ancient tribal system, were substituted.

If my successor had been anything other than an amateur, or if he had any knowledge or experience with the internal politics of an Indian tribe, he would have known that if the group he was trying to push aside had not held the balance of power, I could not have held out for seven years against the unruly element he now tried to put in power. In other words, he unintentionally threw the

The Democratic agent was succeeded last October by the recently removed Republican agent, a man completely ignorant of Indians and their unique traits. He lacked any qualification in his character that would fit him for the position of agent at one of the largest and most difficult agencies in the service to manage; he was a man selected solely as a reward for political favors. He might possibly have been an average success as an Indian agent at a small, well-regulated agency. He tried to tighten control, but the chiefs and leaders who could have assisted him in doing so had been alienated by the previous agent. They essentially said among themselves, "After making enemies of the bad elements among our people by supporting the government, we have been ignored and mistreated by that government; therefore, this is not our business." Being ignorant of the situation, the agent had no one to rely on. In his first clash with the unruly element, he discovered that the Pine Ridge police—formerly the finest in the service—lacked discipline and courage. Not having much of those necessary qualities himself, he mistook the bluff of a crowd for a declaration of war, fled from his agency, and returned with troops—and you see the result.

As for the ghost dance, too much attention has been paid to it. It was only the symptom or outward sign of a deep-rooted, long-existing problem; it is as useless as treating a smallpox rash as the disease itself while ignoring the underlying illness.

Regarding the disarming of the Sioux, as desirable as it might seem, I consider it neither advisable nor practical. I fear it will result in the same way as the attempted enforcement of prohibition in Kansas, Iowa, and Dakota; you will succeed in disarming the friendly Indians because you can, but you will not succeed with the hostile element because you cannot. If I were to be an Indian agent again and had my choice, I would prefer to take charge of 10,000 armed Sioux rather than the same number of disarmed ones. Furthermore, I would agree to handle that number, or the entire Sioux nation, without a single white soldier.

Respectfully, etc., V. T. McGILLYCUDDY.

P. S.—I neglected to state that up to this date, there has been neither a Sioux outbreak nor a war. No citizen in Nebraska or Dakota has been killed, harassed, or even scratched by a pin, and no property has been destroyed outside the reservation.

### STATEMENT OF GENERAL MILES

<note>From the Report of the Secretary of War for 1891, Vol. I, pp. 133, 134, and 149. He lists specific causes of complaint at each of the main Sioux agencies; all of these causes may be summarized as hunger and unfulfilled promises.</note>

**Causes of Indian dissatisfaction.**—The causes that led to the serious disturbance of the peace in the Northwest last autumn and winter were so remarkable that an explanation of them is necessary in order to understand the seriousness of the situation. The Indians taking the most threatening stance of hostility were the Cheyennes and Sioux. Their condition may be described as follows: For several years following their defeat in 1877, 1878, and 1879, the most dangerous elements of the Cheyennes and the Sioux were under military control. Many of them were disarmed and their horses taken away; their war ponies were sold, and the proceeds were returned to them in the form of livestock, farm tools, wagons, and so on. Many of the Cheyennes, under the supervision of military officers, were settled on land in accordance with the laws of Congress. However, after they were turned over to civil agents and the vast herds of buffalo and large game had been destroyed, their supplies were insufficient, and they were forced to kill cattle belonging to white people to survive.

The fact that they had not received enough food is admitted by the agents and the officers of the government who have had opportunities to know the truth. The majority of the Sioux were under the charge of civil agents, who were frequently changed and often

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION
[ETH. ANN. 14

inexperienced. Many of the tribes were rearmed and remounted. They claimed that the government had not fulfilled its treaties and had failed to make large enough appropriations for their support; they suffered for want of food, and the evidence of this is beyond question and sufficient to satisfy any unprejudiced, intelligent mind. The statements of officers and inspectors from both the military and the Interior departments, as well as agents, missionaries, and civilians familiar with their condition, leave no room for reasonable doubt that this was one of the principal causes. While statements may be made as to the amount of money that has been expended by the government to feed the different tribes, the manner of distributing those appropriations will furnish one reason for the deficit.

The unfortunate failure of the crops in the plains country during the years 1889 and 1890 added to the distress and suffering of the Indians, and it was possible for them to raise very little from the ground for self-support; in fact, white settlers have been most unfortunate, and their losses have been serious and universal throughout a large section of that country. They have struggled on from year to year; occasionally they would raise good crops, which they were compelled to sell at low prices, while in seasons of drought their labor was almost entirely lost. So serious have been their misfortunes that thousands have left that country within the last few years, crossing over the mountains to the Pacific slope or returning east of the Missouri or the Mississippi.

The Indians, however, could not migrate from one part of the United States to another; neither could they obtain employment as readily as white people, either upon or beyond the Indian reservations. They had to remain in relative idleness and accept the results of the drought—an insufficient supply of food. This created a feeling of discontent even among the loyal and well-disposed and added to the feeling of hostility from the element opposed to every process of civilization.

Reports forwarded by Brigadier-General Ruger, commanding the Department of Dakota, contained the following:

The commanding officer at Fort Yates, North Dakota, under the date of December 7, 1890—at the time the "Messiah delusion" was approaching a climax—says, in reference to the dissatisfaction of the Sioux Indians at the Standing Rock agency, that it is due to the following causes:

(1) Failure of the government to establish a fair southern boundary for the Standing Rock agency reservation.

(2) Failure of the government to spend a just proportion of the money received from the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad Company for right-of-way privileges for the benefit of the Indians of said agency. Official notice was received October 18, 1881, by the Indian agent at the Standing Rock agency, that the said railroad company had paid the government the sum of $13,911 under its agreement with the Sioux Indians for right-of-way privileges. What additional payments, if any, have been made by the said railroad company, and what payments have been made by the Dakota Central Railroad Company, the records of the agency do not show. In 1883, and again in 1885, the agent, upon complaints made by the Indians, wrote to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, making certain recommendations regarding the expenditure of the money received from the railroad company, but was in each instance informed that until Congress took action with respect to the funds referred to, nothing could be done. No portion of the money had been spent up to that time (December 1890) for the benefit of the Indians of the agency, and frequent complaints had been made to the agent by the Indians because they had received no benefits from their concessions to the railroad companies.

(3) Failure of the government to issue the certificates of title to allotments, as required by Article 6 of the Treaty of 1868.

(4) Failure of the government to provide the full allowance of seeds and agricultural implements to Indians engaged in farming, as required in Article 8 of the Treaty of 1868.

(5) Failure of the government to provide the Indians with the full number of cows and oxen promised in Article 10 of the Treaty of 1876.

(7) Failure of the government to provide the Indians with the full rations promised in Article 5 of the Treaty of 1876. (For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 1890, the following shortages in rations were found to exist: 485,275 pounds of beef [gross weight], 761,212 pounds of corn, 11,937 pounds of coffee, 281,712 pounds of flour, 26,234 pounds of sugar, and 39,852 pounds of beans. Although the government's obligations only extend to furnishing as much of the ration prescribed in Article 5 as is necessary for the support of the Indians, it seems that—due to the almost total failure of crops on the Standing Rock reservation for the past four years and the lack of wild game—the need to issue the full ration to the Indians here was never greater than at the present time, December 1890.)

(8) Failure of the government to issue to the Indians the full amount of yearly annuity supplies to which they were entitled under the provisions of Article 10 of the Treaty of 1868.

(9) Failure of the government to have the clothing and other yearly supplies ready for distribution on the first day of August each year. As a rule, these supplies have not been ready for distribution to the Indians until the winter season is well underway. (After a careful examination at this agency, the commanding officer is convinced that no more than two-thirds of the supplies provided for in Article 10 have been issued there. Furthermore, the government has never complied with the provision of Article 10 that requires the supplies listed in paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 to be delivered on or before the first day of August each year. Such supplies for the current fiscal year, beginning July 1, 1890, had still not reached the nearest railway station—about 60 miles away—by December 1890. From that point, at this time of year, they must be transported to this agency by wagons. It is now certain that the winter will be well advanced before the Indians at this agency receive their annual allowance of clothing and other yearly supplies.)

(10) Failure of the government to set aside money to pay the Indians for the ponies taken from them by government authority in 1876.

In conclusion, the commanding officer says: “It appears from the facts above that the government has failed to fulfill its obligations. In order to make the Indians law-abiding, peaceful, satisfied, and prosperous, it is strongly recommended that the treaties be carried out promptly and fully, and that the promises made by the commission in 1889 be faithfully kept.”

->RAPID CITY, SOUTH DAKOTA, *December 19, 1890.*<-

Senator DAWES,
   *Washington, District of Columbia:*
You may be assured of the following facts, which cannot be denied:
First. The forced process of attempting to make large groups of Indians self-sufficient while the government was cutting their rations and their crops were failing is one cause of the difficulty.
Second. While the Indians were pressured and nearly forced to sign a treaty presented to them by the commission authorized by Congress—in which they gave up a valuable portion of their reservation that is now occupied by white people—the government has failed to fulfill its part of the agreement. Instead of an increase or even a reasonable supply for their support, they have been compelled to live on half and two-thirds rations and have received nothing for the surrender of their lands. Neither has the government given any definite guarantee that they intend to treat them any differently in the future.
Congress has been in session for several weeks and could, if it were willing, confirm the treaties that its commissioners have made with these Indians in a few hours and

RAPID CITY, SOUTH DAKOTA, December 19, 1890.
General **JOHN M. SCHOFIELD**,
*Commanding the Army, Washington, District of Columbia:*

In response to your long telegram, one point is of vital importance—the difficult Indian problem cannot be solved permanently from this end of the line. It requires Congress to fulfill the treaty obligations which the Indians were urged and forced to sign. They ceded a valuable portion of their reservation, and it is now occupied by white people, for which they have received nothing. They understood that ample provision would be made for their support; instead, their supplies have been reduced, and for much of the time they have been living on half and two-thirds <term>rations</term>. Their crops, as well as the crops of the white people, have been almost a total failure for two years. Dissatisfaction is widespread, especially among the Sioux, while the Cheyennes have been on the verge of starvation and were forced to commit depredations to stay alive. These facts are beyond question, and the evidence is certain and supported by thousands of witnesses. Serious difficulty has been building for years. Congress has been in session for several weeks and could, in a single hour, confirm the treaties and allocate the necessary funds for their fulfillment, which their commissioners and the highest officials of the government have guaranteed to these people. Unless the officers of the army can give some positive assurance that the government intends to act in good faith with these people, the loyal group will decrease and the hostile group will increase. If the government will give some positive assurance that it will fulfill its part of the agreement with these 20,000 Sioux Indians, they can safely trust the military authorities to subjugate, control, and govern these turbulent people, and I hope that you will ask the Secretary of War and the President to bring this matter directly to the attention of Congress.

### REPORT OF CAPTAIN HURST

->(A. G. O. Doc. 6266—1891.)<-

FORT BENNETT, SOUTH DAKOTA, January 9, 1891.
ASSISTANT ADJUTANT-GENERAL,
*Department of Dakota, Saint Paul, Minnesota.*

SIR: In compliance with instructions from the department commander—copy attached marked A—I have the honor to submit the following report as the result of my investigations into the matters referred to there.

I have been at this post continuously since August 6, 1887, and have been the inspector of Indian supplies at the Cheyenne River Indian agency, located here, during that period and at the present time.

The Indians of this agency have an ongoing list of grievances which they present at every opportunity and talk about in council when they assemble for every monthly <term>ration</term> issue. The Indians most persistent in recounting and proclaiming their grievances are those least willing to help in bettering their condition, and who are opposed to any change or improvement of their old habits and customs, and oppose all progress. Of this class I cite Big Foot's band of irreconcilables—who have now ceased to complain—and those in agreement with them. Except in the matter of short rations, the story of their wrongs needs no attention. It begins with a recital of the wrong done to them by the white race sharing the earth with them.

[837]

->MOONEY] CAUSES OF THE OUTBREAK<-

The other class, comprising a large majority of Indians on the reservation, have accepted the situation forced upon them, and have been for years bravely struggling in the effort to reconcile themselves to the ways of civilization and moral progress, with a gratifying degree of success. It is this class whose complaints and grievances demand considerate attention. They complain in true Indian style that they alone have kept faith in all treaties made with them, and that somehow the treaties, when they appeared in print, were not in many respects the treaties which they signed.

They complain principally—

(1) That the boundaries of the reservation in the treaty of 1877 are not what they agreed to and thought they were signing on the paper, and they especially emphasize the point that the line of the western boundary should be a straight line at the Black Hills, instead of how it appears on the maps.

(2) That they have never received full compensation for the ponies taken from them in 1876.

(3) That the game has been destroyed and driven out of the country by the white people.

(4) That their children are taken from them to eastern schools and kept for years, instead of being educated among them.

(5) That when these eastern graduates return to them with civilized habits, education, and trades, there is no provision made on the reservation for their employment and improvement for the benefit of themselves and their people.

(6) That the agents and employees sent out to them have not all been "good men" or considerate of the Indians' interests and welfare.

(7) That the distribution of their annuity goods is delayed so late into the winter that it causes them much suffering.

(8) That they are expected to plow the land and raise grain when the climate will not permit them to reap a crop. They think cattle should be issued to them for breeding purposes instead of farming implements for useless labor.

(9) That the <term>rations</term> issued to them are insufficient in quantity and frequently (especially beef and flour) very poor in quality.

Complaints 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9 are all well-founded and justified by the facts in each case; number 9 is especially so, and this is through no fault or negligence of the agent. The agent makes his annual estimate for provisions for the number of people listed on his rolls, based on the stipulated ration in the treaty of 1877. This estimate is modified or cut down in the Indian Commissioner's office to meet the requirements of a limited or reduced Congressional appropriation. When it returns to the agent's hands approved, he finds that he has only a certain number of pounds of beef and flour, etc., placed to his credit for the year, without regard to whether they constitute the full number of treaty rations or not. There is no allowance given to him for loss by shrinkage, wastage, or other unavoidable loss. Even with the very best efforts and care in the distribution of this usually reduced allowance throughout the year, he cannot issue to each Indian his treaty ration nor enough to properly sustain life. As a general rule, the Indians of this reservation have been compelled to purchase food according to their means between ration distributions. Those having no means to purchase have suffered.

The half pound of flour called for by the treaty ration could not be issued in full, and the half pound of corn required has never been issued, nor has anything been given instead of it. Regarding the beef, only 1 pound was issued instead of the pound and a half called for in the treaty. During the early spring months, when the cattle on the range are thin and lean, the pound of beef issued to the Indian is only a fraction of the pound recorded on the agent's returns; under the system of purchase in practice until the present fiscal year, this must necessarily be the case. The agent's purchase of the beef supply "on the hoof" (live cattle) for the year, under contract, is closed in the month of November, from which time he has to herd them for the rest of the year as best he can. He is responsible for the weight they show on the scales when they are fat and in prime condition, so that a steer weighing 1,200 pounds in the fall must represent 1,200 pounds...

### APPENDIX C.—EXTRACT COPY—TREATIES OF 1877 AND 1868

#### TREATY OF 1877

**ARTICLE 3.** The said Indians also agree that they will hereafter receive all annuities provided by the said treaty of 1868, and all subsistence and supplies which may be provided for them under the present or any future act of Congress, at such points and places on the said reservation and in the vicinity of the Missouri River as the President of the United States shall designate.

**ARTICLE 5.** In consideration of the previously mentioned surrender of territory and rights, and upon full compliance with each and every obligation assumed by the said Indians, the United States agrees to provide all necessary aid to assist the said Indians in the work of civilization; to furnish them with schools and instruction in mechanical and agricultural arts, as provided for by the treaty of 1868. Also to provide the said Indians with subsistence consisting of a ration for each individual of a pound and a half of beef (or in place of that, one-half pound of bacon), one-half pound of flour, and one-half pound of corn; and for every one hundred rations, four pounds of coffee, eight pounds of sugar, and three pounds of beans, or the equivalent of those articles, at the discretion of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Such rations, or as much of them as may be necessary, shall be continued until the Indians are able to support themselves. Rations shall in all cases be issued to the head of each separate family; and whenever schools have been provided by the government for said Indians, no rations shall be issued for children between the ages of six and fourteen years (excepting the sick and infirm), unless such children regularly attend school. Whenever the said Indians are located upon lands which are suitable for cultivation, rations shall be issued only to the persons and families of those who work (excepting the aged, sick, and infirm); and as an incentive to industrious habits, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs may provide that persons be furnished, in payment for their labor, other necessary articles required for civilized life. . . .

**ARTICLE 8.** The provisions of the treaty of 1868, except as modified here, shall continue in full force. . . .

### TREATY OF 1868

ARTICLE 8. When the head of a family or lodge has selected lands in good faith and received a certificate for them and commenced farming in good faith, he is to receive no more than one hundred dollars for the first year in seeds and agricultural implements, and for a period of three years more, no more than twenty-five dollars in seeds and implements.

ARTICLE 10. Instead of all sums of money or other annuities provided to be paid to the Indians named here under any treaty or treaties made before this, the United States agrees to deliver at the agency house on the reservation named here on (or before) the first day of August of each year for thirty years, the following articles, namely:

For each male person over fourteen years of age, a suit of good, substantial woolen clothing, consisting of a coat, pants, flannel shirt, hat, and a pair of homemade socks.

For each female over twelve years of age, a flannel skirt or the goods necessary to make it, a pair of woolen stockings, twelve yards of calico, and twelve yards of <term>cotton domestics</term>.

For the boys and girls under the ages named, such flannel and cotton goods as may be needed to make each a suit as described above, with a pair of stockings for each. And in addition to the clothing named here, the sum of ten dollars for each person entitled to the benefits of this treaty shall be annually appropriated for a period of thirty years while such persons roam and hunt, and twenty dollars for each person who engages in farming, to be used by the Secretary of the Interior in the purchase of such articles as the condition and necessities of the Indians may indicate to be proper from time to time. And if at any time within thirty years it appears that the amount of money needed for clothing under this article can be applied to better uses for the Indians named here, Congress may, by law, change the appropriation to other purposes; but in no event shall the amount of the appropriation be withdrawn or discontinued for the period named.

Article 10 further stipulates that each lodge or family who begins farming shall receive, within sixty days after starting, one good American cow and one good, well-broken pair of American oxen.
