### STATEMENT OF AMERICAN HORSE

-><note>Delivered in council at the Pine Ridge agency to Agent Royer, and forwarded to the Indian Office, November 27, 1890. G. D. Doc. 37002—1890.</note><-

American Horse, Fast Thunder, Spotted Horse, Pretty Back, and Good Lance present, with American Horse as spokesman:

> "I think the recent Sioux commissioners (General Crook, Major Warner, and Governor Foster) had something to do with starting this trouble. I was the speaker for the whole tribe. In a general council, I signed the bill (the recent Sioux bill) and 580 signed with me. The other members of my band withdrew, and it divided us, and ever since"

these two parties have been divided. The non-progressives started the Ghost Dance to draw people away from us. Many promises were made to us, but we have never heard anything about them since. The Great Father says that if we do what he directs, it will be to our benefit; but instead of this, they are cutting down our rations every year, and we do not receive enough to keep us from suffering. General Crook spoke kindly to us; but after we signed the bill, they took our land and reduced our food allowance. The commission made us believe that we would receive full sacks if we signed the bill, but instead, our sacks are empty. We lost a considerable amount of property by being here with the commissioners last year, and we have never received anything for it. Our chickens were all stolen, some of our cattle were killed, and our crops were entirely lost because we were away here with the Sioux commission; we have not benefited one bit from the bill. In fact, we are worse off than we were before we signed it. We are told that if we live as white men do, we will be better off, but we are becoming worse off every year.

“The commissioners promised the Indians living on Black Pipe and Pass creeks that if they signed the bill, they could remain where they were and receive their rations at this agency. They showed them the boundary line on the map, and our people want them here, but they have been ordered to move back to the Rosebud Agency. This is one of the broken promises. The commission promised to survey the boundary line and appropriate $1,000 for that purpose, but it has not been done. When we were at Washington, the President, the Secretary of the Interior, and the Commissioner all promised us that we would receive the million pounds of beef that were taken from us, and I heard the bill appropriating the money passed Congress, but we never received the beef. The Commissioner refused to give it to us. American Horse, Fast Thunder, and Spotted Horse were each promised a spring wagon, but they have never heard anything about them. This is another broken promise.”

In forwarding the report of the council, the agent says: “After American Horse had finished speaking, I asked the other men present if his statement expressed their feelings, and they all answered, 'Yes.'”

->STATEMENT OF BISHOP HARE<-

[*Bishop W. H. Hare is the veteran Episcopal missionary bishop among the Sioux. The following extracts are from a communication by him to Secretary Noble, dated January 7, 1891. G. D. Doc. 2440—1891.*]

The evidence compels the conclusion that, among the Pine Ridge Indians at least, hunger has been a significant factor in the causes of discontent and insubordination. In the farming season of 1889 (July), the Indians were all called to the agency and kept there for a month by the Sioux commission. During their absence, their cattle broke into their fields and trampled or ate their crops. The Indians harvested practically nothing. In 1890, a drought—the worst known for many years—afflicted the western part of South Dakota, and the Indian crops were a total failure. There is ample evidence that during this period, the issued rations lasted—even when used carefully—for only two-thirds of the time for which they were intended. To add to their distress, the years 1889 and 1890 were marked by extraordinary misfortune. Measles was highly virulent in 1889, and the <term>grippe</term> <note>influenza</note> followed in 1890. Whooping cough also attacked the children. The sick died from deprivation. Inspector Gardiner, Dr. McGillycuddy (the former agent), Miss Elaine Goodale (who has spent a great deal of time in the camps), the missionary force, and many others all agree with this statement; their testimony is of the highest value because of their character and knowledge of the situation. . . .

The time seemed now to have come to take a further step and divide the Great Sioux Reservation into separate reserves for each major tribe, and to open the surplus land for settlement. The needs of the white population, with their businesses and railroads, and the welfare of the Indians, seemed to equally demand this. Commissioners were therefore sent out to negotiate with the people to accomplish

# MOONEY] CAUSES OF THE OUTBREAK

of this end, and an agreement which, after much debate, had won general approval was committed to them for presentation to the Indians. The objections of the Indians to the bill, however, were many and they were ardently pressed. Some preferred their old life, the more earnestly because schools and churches were sapping and undermining it. Some wished delay. All complained that many of the engagements solemnly made with them in former years, when they had surrendered valued rights, had been broken—and here they were right. They suspected that present promises of pay for their lands would prove to be only old ones in a new shape (when milk cows were promised, cows having been promised in previous agreements, the Indians exclaimed, “There’s that same old cow”), and demanded that no further surrender should be expected until former promises had been fulfilled. They were assured that a new era had dawned, and that all past promises would be kept. So we all thought. The benefits of the proposed agreement were set before them, and verbal promises, over and above the stipulations of the bill, were made that special requests of the Indians would be met. The Indians have no competent representative body. The commissioners had to treat at each agency with a crowd—a crowd composed of full-bloods, half-breeds, and <term>squaw men</term>, a crowd among whom all sorts of sinister influences and brute force were at work. Commissioners with such a business in hand have the devil to fight, and can fight him, so it often seems, only with fire; and many friends of the Indians think that in this case the commission, convinced that the acceptance of the bill was essential, carried persuasion to the verge of intimidation. I do not blame them if they sometimes did. The wit and patience of an angel would fail often in such a task.

But the requisite number, three-fourths of the Indians, signed the bill, and expectation of rich and prompt rewards ran high. The Indians understand little of the complex forms and delays of our government. Six months passed, and nothing came. Three months more, and nothing came. A bill was drawn up in the Senate under General Crook’s eye and passed, providing for the fulfillment of the promises of the commission, but it was pigeon-holed in the House. But in the midst of the winter’s pinching cold, the Indians learned that the transaction had been declared complete and half of their land proclaimed as thrown open to the whites. Surveys were not promptly made—perhaps they could not be—and no one knew what land was theirs and what was not. The very earth seemed sliding from beneath their feet. Other misfortunes seemed to be crowding on them. On some reserves their rations were being reduced, and lasted, even when carefully managed, but one-half the period for which they were issued. (The amount of beef bought for the Indians is not a fair criterion of the amount they receive. A steer will lose 200 pounds or more of its flesh during the course of the winter.) In the summer of 1889, all the people on the Pine Ridge reserve—men, women, and children—were called in from their farms to the agency to treat with the commissioners and were kept there a whole month; on returning to their homes, they found that their cattle had broken into their fields and trampled down or eaten up all their crops. This was true to a degree elsewhere. In 1890 the crops, which promised splendidly early in July, failed entirely later because of a severe drought. The people were often hungry, and the physicians in many cases said they died when taken sick, not so much from disease as for want of food. (This is doubtless true of all the poor—the poor in our cities and the poor settlers in the West.)

No doubt the people could have saved themselves from suffering if industry, economy, and thrift had abounded; but these are just the virtues which a people emerging from barbarism lack. The measles prevailed in 1889 and were exceedingly fatal. Next year the <term>grippe</term> <note>influenza</note> swept over the people with appalling results. Whooping cough followed among the children. Sullenness and gloom began to gather, especially among the non-Christian and wilder Indians. A witness of high character told me that a marked discontent amounting almost to despair prevailed in many quarters. The people said their children were all dying from diseases brought by the whites, their race was perishing from the face of the earth, and they might as well be killed

In a word, everything was against them, and to add to the calamity, many Indians, especially the more traditional element, had nothing to do but brood over their misfortunes. While in this unhappy state, the story of a coming messiah, with its ghost dance and strange hallucinations, spread among the traditional part of the people. . . .

But we do want these things. First, a profound conviction in the minds of the *people*, not just a few, that the Indian problem is worth attending to. Next, that the officials placed in charge of the difficult Indian problem should be protected from the harassment of hungry politicians, and that the employees in the Indian country—agents, teachers, farmers, and carpenters—should not be changed with every political reshuffling. The abuse here has been shameful. Next, that Congress, especially the House of Representatives, shall consider itself bound in honor to provide for the fulfillment of promises made to the Indians by commissioners who were duly appointed and sent to the Indians by another branch of the government. The evils which have arisen from a violation of this cooperation have been most serious. Next, that testimony regarding Indian affairs should not be accepted until a careful inquiry has been made as to the objectivity of the witness. An honest man out here burns with indignation when he reads in the papers that so-and-so, represented as being fully informed on the whole question, affirms that Indians have no grievances and ought to receive no mercy, when he knows that the property lots which the witness owns in a town near the Indian country would no longer be stagnant on the market if the Indians could be removed. Next, let it be remembered that the crisis has brought the evils in the Indian country into the light and left the good things in the shade. But the good things are *real* and have shown their strength under trial. There is no reason for losing faith or courage. Let all kind and honest men unite with the higher officials of the government—all of whom, I believe, mean well—in a spirit of tolerance toward each other, a willingness to learn, and mutual helpfulness, to accomplish the results which they all desire.

## CHAPTER XIII

### THE SIOUX OUTBREAK—SITTING BULL AND WOUNDED KNEE

> We were made many promises, but have never heard from them since. — *American Horse.*

> Congress has been in session for several weeks and could, if it were so inclined, confirm the treaty that its commissioners have made with these Indians in a few hours. It could also appropriate the necessary funds for their fulfillment, and thereby show an act of good faith or intention to fulfill their part of the agreement. In my judgment, such action is essential to restore confidence among the Indians and provide peace and protection to the settlements. — *General Miles.*

Approximate cost of the outbreak in one month: Forty-nine whites and others on the government side, and three hundred Indians killed; $1,200,000 in expenses to the government and individuals.

Short Bull and the other Sioux delegates who had gone to see the messiah in the fall of 1889 returned in March 1890. Short Bull, on the Rosebud reservation, immediately began to preach the doctrine and arrival of the messiah to his people, but he stopped after being warned to do so by Agent Wright. <note>Comr., 29.</note> However, the strange hope had taken hold of the Indians, and the influence spread rapidly, though quietly, among all the more traditional portions of the tribe. The first warning of trouble ahead came in the form of a letter addressed to Secretary Noble by Charles L. Hyde, a citizen of Pierre, South Dakota, dated May 29, 1890. In it, he stated that he had trustworthy information that the Sioux, or a part of them, were secretly planning an outbreak in the near future. His informant appears to have been a young person of mixed heritage from Pine Ridge, who was attending school in Pierre at the time and was in correspondence with his Indian relatives at home. <note>G. D., 20.</note> The letter was referred to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, who forwarded a copy of it to the agents of the several western Sioux reservations with a request for further information. They promptly and unanimously replied that there was no reason for alarm, that the Indians were peaceably inclined, and that there was no unusual excitement beyond what was caused by the rumors of a messiah in the west. They thought this excitement would continue to increase as the predicted time drew near and would fade away naturally when the prophecy failed to come true.

All the agents were certain in their opinion that at this time, about the middle of June 1890, the Indians had no hostile intentions. McLaughlin, the veteran agent of Standing Rock, who probably knew the Sioux better than any other white man having official relations with them, states that among his people there was nothing in word or action to jus-

It is the most remote agency from the white settlements along the Missouri River and borders the Rosebud reservation, which has 4,000 more Sioux in about the same condition and temperament. This created a concentrated group of 10,000 of the most warlike Indians on the plains. Of all the reservations in the United States, this was the one where efficient and vigorous administration, as well as the prompt and honest fulfillment of promises, was most urgent and necessary.

From 1879 to 1886, this agency was managed by Dr. V. T. McGillycuddy, a man of unwavering courage, strong will, and excellent administrative skills. Taking charge of these Indians when they had just come off the warpath, he managed them—as he himself states—for seven years without a single soldier present on the reservation, and with none closer than 60 miles. Relying on the Indians themselves, he introduced the principle of home rule by organizing a force of 50 Indian police, trained in regular cavalry and infantry tactics. With these men, he was able to block all the troublesome schemes of Red Cloud, maintain authority, and start the Indians well on the path toward civilization.

Then a political change in administration occurred, resulting in a series of changes throughout the entire service. Out of 58 Indian agents, more than 50 were removed and replaced with new appointees. While some of these appointments were improvements, the general result was poor, mainly due to the inexperience of the new officials. Meanwhile, commissioners were negotiating with the Sioux for more land, which was eventually secured despite opposition from a large part of the tribe—especially those influenced by Red Cloud and Sitting Bull at Pine Ridge and Standing Rock. Then food rations were reduced, and the Indians began to suffer and, consequently, become restless. This unrest was intensified, though not caused, by rumors that a messiah would soon appear to restore their former way of life. According to the official statement of General Brooke, the beef supply at Pine Ridge was cut from 8,125,000 pounds in 1886 to 4,000,000 pounds in 1889—a reduction of more than half in three years. (*War, 5.*) In April 1890, Gallagher, the agent then in charge, informed the Department that the monthly beef issue was only 205,000 pounds, even though the treaty required 470,400 pounds. He was told it was better to issue half-rations year-round than to give three-quarter or full rations for two months and nothing for the rest of the year. Warnings also came from other sources to the Department that the Sioux at Pine Ridge were becoming restless because of hunger. (*G. D., 22.*) Repeated reports failed to secure more beef, and finally, in the summer of 1890, the Indians at Pine Ridge made their first actual protest by refusing to accept the insufficient rations and making threats against the agent. They were eventually persuaded to take the beef, but Agent Gallagher, seeing that dissatisfaction was growing and apparently without

Under these circumstances, the agent, although known to be a brave man, decided it was best to withdraw, and the dance continued. (*Comr., 31; G. D., 23.*)

On the Rosebud Reservation, which borders Pine Ridge to the east and is inhabited by the restless and warlike Brulé Sioux, the warning given to Short Bull had such an effect that there was no public display until September. At that time, the Ghost Dance was started at the various camps under the leadership of Short Bull the <term>medicine-man</term>, Crow Dog, and Two Strike. Agent Wright, who was then in charge, went out to the Indians and told them the dance must be stopped, which was done accordingly. He clearly stated that no violence was intended by the Indians and that no weapons were carried during the dance, but that he forbade it because of its physical and mental effect on the participants and its tendency to draw them away from their homes. Somehow, a rumor spread among the Indians at this time that troops had arrived on the reservation to attack them, and in an incredibly short time, every Indian had left the area near the agency and was making preparations to meet the enemy. It was with some difficulty that Agent Wright was able to convince them that the report was false and persuade them to return to their homes. Soon afterward, circumstances forced him to be away temporarily, leaving affairs in the meantime in the care of a special agent. The Indians took advantage of his absence to restart the Ghost Dance and soon were beyond control. The agent stated, however, that no Indians left the agency until the troops arrived, at which point the leaders immediately departed for Pine Ridge along with 1,800 of their followers. (*G. D., 24; Comr., 32.*)

On October 9, Kicking Bear of the Cheyenne River Agency, the chief high priest of the Ghost Dance among the Sioux, went to Standing Rock at the invitation of Sitting Bull and started the dance on that reservation at Sitting Bull's camp on the Grand River. This is evident in every letter and telegram he sent during his short time in office, and is further proven by the name the Sioux soon gave him: <term>Lakota Kokipa-Koshkala</term>, or “Young-man-afraid-of-Indians.” Before he had been in charge for even a week, he had lost so much control over the Indians that he allowed half a dozen of them to release and take away a prisoner named Little, whom the police had arrested and brought to the agency. On October 12, he reported that more than half of his 6,000 Indians were dancing and were entirely beyond the control of the police; he suggested that calling out the military would be necessary. (G. Instructions were also sent to agents in Nevada to warn the dance leaders in that region to stop. The next day the general had a talk with the Indians, who informed him that they intended to continue the dance. He gave them some good advice and told them that they must stop. Had the matter rested here until the words of the commanding officer could have been considered in their minds—for the mental process of an Indian cannot easily be rushed—all might have been well. Unfortunately, however, the agent, now thoroughly frightened, wrote a long letter to the Department on October 30, stating that the only remedy for the matter was the use of the military, and that about 600 or 700 troops would be necessary. On November 11 he telegraphed for permission to come to Washington to "explain," and was refused. Then came other telegraphic requests, at the rate of one every day, for the same permission, all of which were refused, with a clear indication that the interests of the service required that the agent should remain at his post of duty. Finally, the matter was reported by the Indian Office to the War Department, and on November 15 Royer was instructed to report the state of affairs to the commander of the nearest military post, Fort Robinson, Nebraska. On the same day, he had telegraphed that the Indians were wild and crazy and that at least a thousand soldiers were needed. The agent at Rosebud also now reported that his Indians were beyond the control of the police. Special agents were sent to both agencies and confirmed the reports regarding the alarming state of affairs. The agent at Crow Creek and Lower Brulé agency reported at the same time that his Indians were under good control and that the police were sufficient for all purposes. (*G. D., 28; L. B., 2.*)

On the last day of October, Short Bull, one of those who had been to see the messiah, made an address to a large gathering of Indians near Pine Ridge, in which he said that as the whites were interfering so much in the religious affairs of the Indians, he would advance the time for the great change and make it sooner, even within the next month. He urged them all to gather in one place and prepare for the coming messiah, and told them they must dance even though troops should surround them, as the guns of the soldiers would be made harmless and the white race itself would soon be annihilated. (See his speech, page 788.)

Soon afterward, McLaughlin personally visited Sitting Bull at his camp on Grand River and attempted to reason with the Indians on the absurdity of their belief. In reply, Sitting Bull proposed that they should both go with competent attendants to the country of the messiah and see and question him for themselves, and let the truth or falsity of the new doctrine rest on the result. The proposition was not accepted. (*G. D., 29.*) There can be no question that the leaders of the Ghost Dance among the Sioux were just as much deceived as their followers.

As the local agents had declared the situation beyond their control, the War Department was finally called upon and responded. On November 13, the President had directed the Secretary of War to assume military responsibility to prevent an outbreak (*G. D., 30*), and on November 17, troops under the command of General John R. Brooke were ordered to the front. The general plan of the campaign was under the direction of General Nelson A. Miles, who was in command of the military department of the Missouri. On November 19, the first troops arrived at Pine Ridge from Fort Robinson, Nebraska, and were quickly reinforced by others. Within a few days, at the Pine Ridge agency, under General Brooke’s immediate command, there were eight troops of the Seventh Cavalry under Colonel Forsyth; a battalion of the Ninth Cavalry (composed of Black soldiers) under Major Henry; a battalion of the Fifth Artillery under Captain Capron; and one company of the Eighth Infantry and eight companies of the Second Infantry under Colonel Wheaton. At Rosebud, there were two troops of the Ninth Cavalry, along with portions of the Eighth and Twenty-first Infantry, under Lieutenant-Colonel Poland. Between Rosebud and Pine Ridge, seven companies of the First Infantry were stationed under Colonel Shafter. West and north of Pine Ridge, portions of the First, Second, and Ninth Cavalry were stationed under the command of Colonel Tilford and Lieutenant-Colonel Sanford. Farther west, at Buffalo Gap on the railroad, three troops from the Fifth and Eighth Cavalry were stationed under Captain Wells. Farther north on the railroad, at Rapid City, was Colonel Carr with six troops of the Sixth Cavalry. Along the south fork of the Cheyenne River, Lieutenant-Colonel Offley took a position with seven companies of the Seventeenth Infantry; east of him was stationed Lieutenant-Colonel Sumner with three troops of the Eighth Cavalry, two companies of the Third Infantry, and Lieutenant Robinson’s company of Crow Indian scouts. Small garrisons were also stationed at Forts Meade, Bennett, and Sully. Most of the force was positioned between the Indians now gathering in the Bad Lands, led by Short Bull and Kicking Bear, and the nearest scattered settlements. Seven companies of the Seventh Infantry, under Colonel Merriam, were also placed along the Cheyenne River to restrain the Indians from the Cheyenne River and Standing Rock reservations. In a short time, there were nearly 3,000 troops in the field within the Sioux country. General Miles established his headquarters at Rapid City, South Dakota, near the center of the disturbance (*War, 6*). On December 1, the Secretary of the Interior directed that agents be instructed to obey and cooperate with military officers in all matters regarding the suppression of an outbreak (*G. D., 31*).

Upon the first appearance of the troops, a large number of Indians from Rosebud and Pine Ridge, led by Short Bull, Kicking Bear, and others, left their homes and fled to the rough, broken country known as the Bad Lands, northwest of the White River in South Dakota, on the edge

<summary>Following the agents' loss of control, the War Department deployed nearly 3,000 troops under General Miles to the Sioux reservations to prevent an uprising. This military presence prompted many Indians, led by Short Bull and Kicking Bear, to retreat into the Bad Lands.</summary>

<page-num>852</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

The retreat to the Bad Lands was not properly a hostile movement, but was a stampede caused by panic at the appearance of the troops. In his official report, Commissioner Morgan says:

> When the troops reached Rosebud, about 1,800 Indians—men, women, and children—fled in a stampede toward Pine Ridge and the Bad Lands, destroying their own property and that of others along the way before they left.

After the death of Sitting Bull, he says:

> Groups of Indians from the various reservations had begun gathering in the Bad Lands, either on or near the Pine Ridge reservation. These Indians killed cattle and destroyed other property, almost entirely within the boundaries of the Pine Ridge and Rosebud reservations. However, no signal fires were lit, no warlike demonstrations were made, no violence was committed against any white settlers, and there was no coordination or organization among the Indians themselves. Many of them were friendly Indians who had never taken part in the ghost dance, but had fled there out of fear of the soldiers, as a result of the Sitting Bull incident, or because of the strong persuasion of their friends. The military gradually began to close in around them, and they offered no resistance; a quick and quiet surrender of everyone was confidently expected. (*Comr., 33.*)

The Sioux nation totals over 25,000 people, with between 6,000 and 7,000 warriors. Barely more than 700 warriors were involved in the trouble altogether, including those from Big Foot’s band and those who fled to the Bad Lands. None of the Christian Indians took any part in the disturbance.

<margin><unclear>in law</unclear></margin>
While it is certain that the movement toward the Bad Lands and the events that followed resulted from panic at the arrival of the troops, it is equally true that the troops were only sent at the request of the civilian authorities. On this point, General Miles says: "Not until the civil agents had lost control of the Indians and declared themselves powerless to preserve peace, and the Indians were in armed hostility and defiance of the civil authorities, was a single soldier moved from his garrison to suppress the general revolt." (*War, 7.*) Throughout the entire trouble, McGillycuddy <note>This likely refers to former agent Valentine McGillycuddy, though James McLaughlin was the agent at Standing Rock at this time.</note> at Standing Rock consistently declared his ability to control his Indians without the presence of troops.

In accordance with instructions from the Indian Office, the several agents in charge of the Sioux had submitted lists of agitators whom it would be advisable to arrest and remove from among the Indians, using the military for that purpose if necessary. The agents at the other reservations sent in a combined total of about fifteen names for removal, while Royer, at Pine Ridge, submitted a "conservative estimate" of sixty-four names. Since Short Bull and Kicking Bear were in the Bad Lands, and Red Cloud was now an old man and too cautious to make much of an open demonstration, the primary leader among the offenders was Sitting Bull, the irreconcilable; but McLaughlin, who had jurisdiction over him, advised in a letter on November 22 that the arrest should not be attempted until later in the season, as at the date of writing the weather was warm and pleasant—in other words, favorable to the Indians in case they should offer opposition. (*G. D., 32.*) The worst

(G. D., 33; L. B., 3.) These were the conditions at the beginning of December 1890. Everything seemed to be calming down, and it was now considered a favorable time to prevent future disturbances by removing the ringleaders.

Agent McLaughlin at Standing Rock had notified the Department some weeks earlier that it would be necessary to remove Sitting Bull and several others in the near future to end their harmful influence among the Sioux. However, he also stated that the matter should not be rushed, and that when the proper time arrived, he could carry out the task with his Indian police without the help of troops. As soon as the War Department took control of the Sioux agencies, it was determined to attempt to secure Sitting Bull through military power. Accordingly, orders were given to the famous scout William F. Cody—better known as Buffalo Bill—who was well acquainted with Sitting Bull and was believed to have influence over him. He was to go to the Standing Rock agency to persuade him to come in, with the authority to make whatever terms might seem necessary; if he were unsuccessful, he was to arrest him and move him from his camp to the nearest post, Fort Yates. Cody arrived at Fort Yates on November 28 and was about to carry out the arrest when his orders were canceled due to the urgent protests of Agent McLaughlin. McLaughlin argued that such a step at that particular time was unwise, as military interference was likely to provoke a conflict in which the Indians would have the advantage, since the warm weather favored them. He insisted that there was no immediate danger from the dancing, and that at the proper time—when the weather grew colder—he could handle Sitting Bull and the other agitators whose removal he recommended using the Indian police, whom he had always found capable of handling emergencies throughout his years of service. Consequently, the attempt was postponed. In the meantime, Sitting Bull had promised to come to the agency to discuss the situation with the agent, but he failed to keep his appointment. A close watch was kept on his movements, and the agent was instructed not to make any arrests except by the authority of the military or the Secretary of the Interior. (*G. D., 34.*)

There is no question that Sitting Bull was plotting trouble. His previous record was one of uncompromising hostility toward the government, and in every disturbance on the reservation, his camp had been the center of unrest. It was at his camp and by his invitation that Kicking Bear had organized the first Ghost Dance on the reservation, and the dance had been continued by Sitting Bull ever since, despite the repeated protests of the agent. At the same time, the unruly followers of the medicine man took every opportunity to insult and annoy the peaceful and progressive Indians who refused to join them, until the latter were forced to complain to the agent. In October, while the dance was being organized at his camp, Sitting Bull had deliberately broken the "peace pipe" which he had kept

<page-num>855</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] SITTING BULL'S ARREST ORDERED</header>

He had remained in his house since his surrender in 1881. When asked why he had broken his word, he replied that he wanted to die and wanted to fight. From that time on, he stopped his regular visits to the agency. It became known that he intended to leave the reservation to visit other leaders of the unrest at the southern Sioux agencies. To prevent such an attempt, the agent gradually increased the number of police near his camp and arranged for quick information and prompt action in case of any sudden move on his part. (G. D., 35.)

Foreseeing from the active military movements that Sitting Bull’s arrest might be ordered at any moment, and fearing that such action might occur at an inconvenient time and result in trouble, McLaughlin arranged to have him and several other agitators arrested by the Indian police on the night of December 6. In his opinion, the weather and other conditions were most favorable for the attempt at that time. However, upon telegraphing the Indian Department for authority, he was directed to make no arrests except by order of the military authorities or the Secretary of the Interior. In reply to a telegram from General Ruger, McLaughlin stated there was no immediate need for haste and that a delay was preferable, as the winter weather was cooling the enthusiasm of the dancers.

On December 12, the military order arrived for Sitting Bull’s arrest. Colonel Drum, commanding at Fort Yates, was directed to personally ensure his capture and to ask the agent for assistance and cooperation in the matter. After a consultation between the commandant and the agent, who were in full agreement, they decided to make the arrest on the 20th, when most of the Indians would be at the agency for rations. Consequently, there would be less danger of a conflict at the camp. However, late on Sunday afternoon, December 14, a courier arrived from Grand River with a message from Mr. Carignan, the teacher of the Indian school. The message, based on information from the police, stated that Sitting Bull had just received an invitation from Pine Ridge to go there because God was about to appear. Sitting Bull was determined to go and sent a request to the agent for permission; meanwhile, he had already completed his preparations to go regardless of whether permission was refused. With this intention, it was further stated that he had already selected his horses for a long, difficult ride, and the police urgently asked for permission to arrest him immediately, as it would be difficult to catch him once he had started.

Immediate action was necessary, and Colonel Drum and Agent McLaughlin arranged to attempt the arrest at dawn the next morning, December 15. The Indian police were to make the arrest, assisted if necessary by a detachment of troops who were to follow within supporting distance. There were already twenty-eight police under the command of Lieutenant Bull Head in the immediate vicinity of Sitting Bull’s camp on Grand River, about 40

<page-num>857</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] DEATH OF SITTING BULL</header>

The Indians had been dancing until nearly morning, and the house was consequently left unguarded.

At daybreak on Monday morning, December 15, 1890, the police and volunteers, 43 in number, under the command of Lieutenant Bull Head—a calm and reliable man—surrounded Sitting Bull's house. He had two log cabins, a few rods <note>A rod is a unit of length equal to 16.5 feet.</note> apart, and to make sure of their man, eight of the police entered one house and ten went into the other, while the rest remained on guard outside. They found him asleep on the floor in the larger house. He was awakened and told that he was a prisoner and must go to the agency. He did not object, but said, "All right; I will dress and go with you." He then sent one of his wives to the other house for some clothes he wanted to wear and asked to have his favorite horse saddled for him to ride, which was done by one of the police. While looking around the room, the police found and took two rifles and several knives. While dressing, he apparently changed his mind and began insulting the police for disturbing him, to which they made no reply. While this was going on inside, his followers, numbering perhaps 150, were gathering around the house outside, and by the time he was dressed, an excited crowd of Indians had the police entirely surrounded and were pressing them against the wall. Upon being brought out, Sitting Bull became greatly excited and refused to go, calling on his followers to rescue him. Lieutenant Bull Head and Sergeant Shave Head were standing on either side of him, with Second Sergeant Red Tomahawk guarding from behind, while the rest of the police were trying to clear the way in front. At that moment, one of Sitting Bull's followers, Catch-the-Bear, fired and shot Lieutenant Bull Head in the side. Bull Head at once turned and fired a bullet into the body of Sitting Bull, who was also shot through the head at the same moment by Red Tomahawk. Sergeant Shave Head was shot by another person in the crowd and fell to the ground along with Bull Head and Sitting Bull. Catch-the-Bear, who fired the first shot, was immediately shot and killed by Alone Man, one of the police, and the situation became a desperate hand-to-hand fight of fewer than 43 men against more than a hundred. The trained police soon drove their attackers into the nearby timber, then returned and carried their dead and wounded into the house, holding it for about two hours until the arrival of the troops under Captain Fechét at about half past seven. The troops had been notified of the dangerous situation of the police by Hawk Man, who had volunteered to carry the information from Sitting Bull's camp. He succeeded in getting away with the help of Red Tomahawk, although he was pursued so closely that several bullets passed through his clothing. Despite the efforts of the <term>hostiles</term>, the police also maintained control of the corral, which Sitting Bull had filled with horses in preparation for his flight. When the cavalry came into sight over a hill about 1,500 yards away from the camp, the police at the corral raised a white flag to show where they were; however, the troops, mistaking them for hostiles, fired two shells at them from

They had offered no resistance to the troops, but fled immediately upon their appearance.

Those most qualified to judge give the highest praise to the Indian police for their conduct on this occasion. Some of those who faced death in obedience to orders had close relatives among those opposed to them. In one official letter, Agent McLaughlin says that he

[Agent McLaughlin] cannot too strongly commend their splendid courage and ability in the action, and in another letter says: “The details of the battle show that the Indian police behaved nobly and exhibited the best judgment and bravery, and a recognition by the government for their services on this occasion is richly deserved. . . . I respectfully urge that the Interior Department cooperate with the War Department in obtaining Congressional action which will secure to these brave survivors and to the families of the dead a full and generous reward.” Colonel Drum, under whose orders the arrest was made, after stating that Sitting Bull was not hurt until he began struggling to escape and until one of the police had been shot, adds: “It is also remarkable that no women or children were hurt. The police appear to have constantly warned the other Indians to keep away, until they were forced to fight in self-defense. It is hardly possible to praise their conduct too highly.” Despite the recommendation of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Congress has taken no action in recognition of their services on this occasion.

Before the action, orders had been sent to the police to have a wagon with them in order to convey Sitting Bull quickly away from the camp to avoid trouble, but in the excitement of preparation, this was overlooked. The police returned to the agency late in the afternoon, bringing with them their dead and wounded, together with two prisoners and the body of Sitting Bull, which was turned over to the military authorities at Fort Yates. The four dead policemen were buried at the agency the next day with military honors. Bull Head and Shave Head died in the hospital soon afterward, with the consolation of having their friends around them in their last moments. The agent states that the large majority of the Indians were loyal to the government and expressed satisfaction at what they considered the end of the disturbance. McLaughlin again sent couriers after the fleeing Indians, warning them to return to the agency where they would be safe, or suffer the consequences if found outside the reservation. Within a few days, nearly 250 had come in and surrendered, leaving only about one-third still out. Most of these soon afterward surrendered with Hump on Cherry Creek, while the remainder, about 50, joined Big Foot or went on to Pine Ridge. (*G. D., 36; War, 8.*)

<margin>+</margin>
Thus died *Tata'nka I'yota'nke*, Sitting Bull, the great medicine man of the Sioux, on the morning of December 15, 1890, at about 56 years of age. He belonged to the *Uncpapa* <note>Modernly spelled Hunkpapa</note> division of the *Teton Sioux*. Although a priest rather than a chief, he had gained a reputation in his early years by organizing and leading war parties, and became prominent by his participation in the Battle of the Little Bighorn, in Montana, on June 25, 1876, by which Custer’s command was wiped out of existence. Being pursued by General Terry, Sitting Bull and his band made their escape northward into Canada, where they remained until 1881, when he surrendered, through the mediation of the Canadian authorities, on a

<header>MOONEY] SITTING BULL</header>

...promise of pardon. To obtain food and supplies while in Canada, his people had been forced to sell almost everything they owned, including their firearms, so they returned to their old homes in a state of poverty. After being held as a prisoner of war until 1883, Sitting Bull lived on the Grand River until his death. Here, he continued to lead the opposition against white civilization, and his camp became a gathering point for the dissatisfied, conservative members of the tribe who clung to the old ways and felt that any change meant the destruction of their race. For seven years, he had steadily opposed the treaty by which the great Sioux reservation was finally broken up in 1889. After the treaty had been signed by the necessary number of people to make it law, a white man asked him what the Indians thought about it. With a burst of passionate anger, he replied, "Indians! There are no Indians left now but me." However mistaken he may have been in continuing a losing fight against the inevitable, it is possible that from the Indian perspective, he was their patriot just as he was their high priest. He has been mercilessly condemned as a bad man and a liar; but there can be no doubt that he was honest in his hatred of the white people. His breaking of the peace pipe, while saying that he "wanted to fight and wanted to die," showed that he was no coward. But he represented the past. His influence was at odds with progress, and his death marks the end of an era in the civilization of the Sioux. In the words of General Miles, "His tragic fate was only the conclusion of a tragic life. Since the days of Pontiac, Tecumseh, and Red Jacket, no Indian has had the power to attract such a large following of his people and to shape and direct it against the authority of the United States, or to inspire it with greater hostility against the white race and civilization." (*War, 9.*)

On December 18, the Indians who had already fled to the Bad Lands attacked a small party of men at Spring Creek on the Cheyenne River. Major Tupper, with 100 men from Carr's division, was sent to rescue them. A skirmish followed with the Indians, who were hidden in the bushes along the creek. The government wagons were also attacked by the hostiles while crossing the creek, but they were eventually driven off by cavalry reinforcements under Captain Wells. On the same date, over a thousand Indians returned to Pine Ridge. News arrived that there were still about 1,500 fugitives camped on the Cheyenne River near Spring Creek. (*Colby, 1.*)

After the death of Sitting Bull, the most dangerous leader of the dissatisfied Indians in the north was considered to be Hump, on the Cheyenne River reservation. The agent in charge had recommended his removal long before, but it was thought that it would now be almost impossible to arrest him. Hump and his band of about 400 people, along with Big Foot and nearly as many followers, had their camps near the junction of Cherry Creek and the Cheyenne River. For several weeks, they had been dancing

P. Ewers of the Fifth Infantry, who had been in charge of this chief and his band for seven years and held their full confidence and respect. He was then on duty in Texas but was ordered forward and reported soon after at Fort Bennett on the border of the reservation. Hump was considered to be so dangerous that the civilian agents did not think it was possible for even the officer to communicate with him. However, Captain Ewers, without troops and accompanied only by Lieutenant Hale, immediately left the fort and rode 60 miles to Hump's camp. 

"Hump was 20 miles away at the time, and a runner was sent for him. Immediately upon hearing that Captain Ewers was in the vicinity, he came to him and was told that the division commander desired him to take his people away from the hostiles and bring them to the nearest military post. He replied that if General Miles sent for him, he would do whatever the general desired. He immediately brought his people into Fort Bennett and complied with all the orders and instructions given him, and subsequently rendered valuable service for peace. Thus, an element regarded as among the most dangerous was removed." 

After coming into the fort, Hump enlisted as a scout under Captain Ewers, and soon afterward, in connection with the same Lieutenant Hale, proved his loyalty by bringing about the surrender of the Sitting Bull fugitives. Subsequently, Captain Ewers further distinguished himself by conducting the Northern Cheyenne—who were considered particularly dangerous, but who regarded Captain Ewers with absolute affection—from Pine Ridge to Tongue River, Montana, a distance of 300 miles. This was done during the most rigorous part of the winter season, without an escort of troops and without the loss of a single life or the commission of a single unlawful act by an Indian. (*War, 10.*)

The Sitting Bull fugitives who had not come in at once had fled southward toward their friends and close relatives of the Cheyenne River reservation and were camped on Cherry Creek, a few miles above its junction with the Cheyenne River at Cheyenne City. As their presence there could only serve to increase the unrest among the other Indians in that vicinity, and as there was great danger that they might attempt to join those already in the Bad Lands, Captain Hurst of the Twelfth Infantry, commanding at Fort Bennett, directed Lieutenant H. E. Hale on December 18 to go out and bring them in. Upon arriving at Cheyenne City, the officer found it deserted; all the citizens except for one man had fled in alarm a short time before following the report of a mixed-blood that the Sitting Bull Indians were coming and had sworn to kill the first white man they met. Having succeeded in frightening the entire population, the mixed-blood himself, Narcisse Narcelle, left at once for the fort.

Knowing the importance of haste, they started out on this winter ride of 40 miles without blankets or rations.

On arriving, Captain Hurst told them briefly why he had come, and then—being exhausted from the rapid ride and knowing that an Indian must not be hurried—he ordered some beef and a plentiful supply of tobacco for them. After the death of Sitting Bull and the enlistment of Hump into government service, the only prominent leader outside of the Bad Lands who was considered potentially dangerous was Sitanka, or Big Foot, whose village was at the mouth of Deep Creek, a few miles below the forks of the Cheyenne River. The duty of watching him was assigned to Lieutenant-Colonel E. V. Sumner of the Eighth Cavalry, who had his camp just above the forks. There, Big Foot and his head men visited him, assuring the officer that they were peaceful and intended to remain quietly at home. Friendly relations continued until the middle of December, when Big Foot came to say goodbye, telling Sumner that all of his people were going to the agency to receive their annuities. A day or two later, the order arrived to arrest Big Foot and send him as a prisoner to Fort Meade. Believing that the chief was acting in good faith to control his warriors—who might easily go beyond control if he were taken from them—Colonel Sumner informed General Miles that the Indians were already on their way to the agency; that if Big Foot should return, he (Sumner) would try to capture him, and that otherwise he could be arrested at the agency, if necessary. Soon after, however, a report arrived that Big Foot had stopped at Hump’s camp on the way to the agency to meet the fugitives fleeing south from Sitting Bull’s camp.

Upon receiving this information, Sumner immediately marched down the river with the intention of stopping Big Foot. When they were about halfway to Hump’s camp, Big Foot himself came up to meet him, saying that he was friendly and that he and his men would obey any orders the officer might give. He stated that he had with him 100 of his own Indians and 38 from Standing Rock (Sitting Bull’s band). Sumner then directed one of his officers, Captain Hennisee, to go to the Indian camp with Big Foot and bring in all the Indians. They went into camp as directed, turned out their ponies to graze, and were fed, and on the next morning all started quietly back with the troops. As they had appeared perfectly friendly and compliant with every order all along, no attempt was made to disarm them. On arriving near their own village, however, it became apparent that Big Foot could not control their desire to go to their homes. The chief came frankly to Sumner and said that he himself would go wherever wanted, but that there would be trouble in forcing the women and children, who were cold and hungry, away from their village. He also protested that they were now at home, where they had been ordered by the government to stay, and that none of them had done anything to justify their removal. As it was evident that they would not go peaceably, Colonel Sumner determined to bring his entire force the next day to compel them. In the meantime, he sent a white man named Dunn, who was on friendly terms with Big Foot, to tell him that the Indians must obey the order to move. Dunn delivered the message and returned; he was followed later by the interpreter, who stated that the Indians had consented to go to the agency and would start the next morning, December 23. That evening, however, scouts arrived with the news that the Indians had left their village and were going southward. It was at first thought that they intended to turn onto another trail to the agency, but instead they continued in the direction of Pine Ridge and the refugees in the Bad Lands, taking with them only their ponies and tipi poles.

The cause of this sudden flight after the promise given by Big Foot is somewhat uncertain. The statement of the interpreter, Felix Benoit, suggests that the Indians were frightened by Dunn, who told them that the soldiers were coming in the morning to take them away and would shoot them if they refused to go. While this undoubtedly alarmed them, the real cause of their flight was probably the fact that, at this critical moment, Colonel Merriam was ordered to move his command up the Cheyenne River to join forces with Sumner to compel their surrender. Such is the opinion of General Ruger, who states officially that “Big Foot and the followers who had joined him, probably becoming alarmed by the movement of Colonel Merriam’s command from Fort Bennett and a rumor that Colonel Sumner would capture them, eluded Colonel Sumner’s command and started for the Pine Ridge reservation.” This agrees with

Sumner, in his report, calls attention to the fact that they committed no raids in their flight, although they passed several ranches and at one time even went through a pasture filled with horses and cattle without attempting to take them. Immediately on learning of their flight, Colonel Sumner notified General Carr, who was commanding in the direction of the Bad Lands. (*War, 12.*)

The situation at this crisis is thus summed up by Indian Commissioner Morgan:

> Groups of Indians from the different reservations had begun concentrating in the Bad Lands upon or in the vicinity of the Pine Ridge reservation. The killing of cattle and destruction of other property by these Indians, almost entirely within the limits of the Pine Ridge and Rosebud reservations, occurred, but no signal fires were built, no warlike demonstrations were made, no violence was done to any white settler, nor was there cohesion or organization among the Indians themselves. Many of them were friendly Indians who had never participated in the ghost dance, but had fled there from fear of soldiers, as a consequence of the Sitting Bull affair or through the persuasion of friends. The military gradually began to close in around them and they offered no resistance, and a speedy and quiet surrender of all was confidently expected. (*Comr., 34.*)

Nearly 3,000 troops were now in the field in the Sioux country. This force was fully sufficient to have engaged the Indians successfully, but as such action would have inevitably resulted in mass killings on both sides—with the prospect of triggering a raiding war unless the hostiles were completely destroyed—it was thought best to bring about a surrender by peaceful means.

The refugees in the Bad Lands who had fled from Pine Ridge and Rosebud had been surrounded on the west and north by a strong line of troops operating under General Brooke, which had the effect of gradually forcing them back toward the agency. At the same time, that officer made every effort to speed up the process by creating divisions in the Indian camp and trying in various ways to persuade them to come in by small parties at a time. To this end, the Indians were promised that if they complied with the orders of the military, their rights and interests would be protected as far as it was within the power of the military department to accomplish that result. Although they had almost lost confidence in the government, these assurances had a good effect. This was further emphasized by the news of the death of Sitting Bull, the arrest of Big Foot, the return of Hump to his agency, and the steady pressure of the troops from behind. On December 27, 1890, the entire force broke camp, left their stronghold in the Bad Lands, and began moving in toward the agency at Pine Ridge. The several detachments of troops followed behind,

As early as December 6, a conference was arranged at Pine Ridge through the efforts of Father Jutz, the priest of the Catholic mission, between General Brooke and the leading chiefs of both the "friendlies" and "hostiles." Although no definite conclusion was reached, the meeting was friendly, ending with a feast and an Indian dance. The immediate effect was a division in the hostile camp, culminating in a quarrel between the two factions. As a result, Two Strike and his party left the others and moved toward the agency, while Short Bull and Kicking Bear retreated farther into the Bad Lands. Upon learning of this state of affairs, General Brooke sent out American Horse and Big Road with a large party of warriors to meet Two Strike and return with him to persuade the others, if possible, to come in. At the same time, the troops were moved up to intercept the flight of the hostiles. (*Colby, 2; G. D., 37.*)

On Christmas Day, the Cheyenne scouts, camped on Battle Creek north of the Bad Lands, were attacked by a party of hostiles led by Kicking Bear in person. The fight continued until after dark, with several killed or wounded on both sides, but the hostiles were finally driven off. (*Colby, 3.*)

But the tragedy was near at hand. Orders had been given to intercept Big Foot’s party in its flight from the Cheyenne River toward the Bad Lands. This was accomplished on December 28, 1890, by Major Whitside of the Seventh Cavalry, who encountered him a short distance west of the Bad Lands. Because he had not succeeded in communicating with the refugees who had fled there and who were already on their way to the agency, Big Foot had not stopped, but continued also toward Pine Ridge. Upon sighting the troops, he raised a white flag, advanced into the open country, and asked for a parley. This was refused by Major Whitside, who demanded an unconditional surrender, which was immediately given. The Indians then moved with the troops to Wounded Knee Creek, about 20 miles northeast of the Pine Ridge agency, where they camped as directed by Major Whitside. To ensure complete security, General Brooke sent Colonel Forsyth to join Major Whitside with four additional troops of the Seventh Cavalry. This, along with the scouts under Lieutenant Taylor, constituted a force of eight troops of cavalry, one company of scouts, and four pieces of light artillery (Hotchkiss guns), totaling 470 men, compared to the 106 warriors then present in Big Foot’s band. A scouting party from Big Foot’s band was out looking for the camp under Kicking Bear and Short Bull; however, since these chiefs and their followers were already on their way to the agency, the scouting party was returning to rejoin Big Foot when the fight occurred the next morning. At this time there were no Indians in the Bad Lands. Two Strike and Crow Dog had come in about a week before and were now camped close to the agency. Kicking Bear and Short Bull, with their followers, had yielded to the friendly persuasions of American Horse, Little Wound, Standing Bear, and others who had gone out to them in the interests of peace, and both parties were now coming in together and had arrived at the Catholic mission, 5 miles from the agency, when the battle occurred.

On the morning of December 29, 1890, preparations were made to disarm the Indians before taking them to the agency and then to the railroad. In obedience to instructions, the Indians had pitched their tipis on the open plain a short distance west of the creek, surrounded on all sides by the soldiers. In the center of the camp, the Indians had raised a white flag as a sign of peace and a guarantee of safety. Behind them was a dry ravine running into the creek, and on a slight rise in the front was posted the battery of four Hotchkiss machine guns, aimed directly at the Indian camp. In front, behind, and on both flanks of the camp were posted the various troops of cavalry; a portion of two troops, together with the Indian scouts, were dismounted and drawn up in front of the Indians at a distance of only a few yards from them. Big Foot himself was ill with pneumonia in his tipi, and Colonel Forsyth, who had taken command as the senior officer, had provided a tent warmed with a camp stove for his reception.

Shortly after 8 o'clock in the morning, the warriors were ordered to come out from the tipis and deliver their arms. They came forward and seated themselves on the ground in front of the troops. They were then ordered to go by themselves into their tipis and bring out and surrender their guns. The first twenty went and returned in a short time with only two guns. It seemed evident that they were unwilling to give them up, and after consultation among the officers, part of the soldiers were ordered up to within ten yards of the group of warriors, while another detachment of troops was ordered to search the tipis. After a thorough search, these last returned with about forty rifles, most of which, however, were old and of little value. The search had taken considerable time and created a great deal of excitement among the women and children, as the soldiers found it necessary during the process to overturn the beds and other furniture in the tipis and, in some instances, drove out the occupants. All this had its effect on their husbands and brothers, who were already strained by high nervous tension and did not know what might happen next. While the soldiers had been looking for the guns, Yellow Bird, a medicine man, had been walking about among the warriors, blowing on an eagle-bone whistle and urging them to resist, telling them that the soldiers would become weak and powerless and that the bullets would be

<summary>On the morning of December 29, 1890, U.S. troops surrounded Big Foot’s camp at Wounded Knee to disarm the Indians, leading to high tensions as soldiers searched tipis and the medicine man Yellow Bird urged resistance.</summary>

At this time, there were no Indians in the Bad Lands. Two Strike and Crow Dog had arrived about a week earlier and were now camped close to the agency. Kicking Bear and Short Bull, along with their followers, had yielded to the friendly persuasion of American Horse, Little Wound, Standing Bear, and others who had gone out to meet them in the interest of peace. Both parties were now coming in together and had arrived at the Catholic mission, five miles from the agency, when the battle occurred.

On the morning of December 29, 1890, preparations were made to disarm the Indians before taking them to the agency and then to the railroad. In obedience to instructions, the Indians had pitched their tipis on the open plain a short distance west of the creek, surrounded on all sides by the soldiers. In the center of the camp, the Indians had raised a white flag as a sign of peace and a guarantee of safety. Behind them was a dry ravine running into the creek, and on a slight rise in front was positioned a battery of four Hotchkiss machine guns, aimed directly at the Indian camp. In front, behind, and on both flanks of the camp, various troops of cavalry were stationed; a portion of two troops, together with the Indian scouts, were dismounted and drawn up in front of the Indians at a distance of only a few yards from them. Big Foot himself was ill with pneumonia in his tipi, and Colonel Forsyth, who had taken command as the senior officer, had provided a tent warmed with a camp stove for his reception.

MOONEY] THE WOUNDED KNEE BATTLE

ineffective against the sacred "ghost shirts" that almost every one of the Indians wore. Since he spoke in the Sioux language, the officers did not immediately realize the dangerous direction of his talk, and the climax happened too quickly for them to intervene. It is said that one of the searchers then attempted to lift a warrior's blanket. Suddenly, Yellow Bird stooped down and threw a handful of dust into the air. As if this were the signal, a young Indian, said to be Black Fox from the Cheyenne River, pulled a rifle from under his blanket and fired at the soldiers. They instantly responded with a volley directly into the crowd of warriors, so close that their guns were almost touching. Based on the number of sticks the Indians set up to mark where the dead fell—as seen by the author a year later—this single volley must have killed nearly half of the warriors (plate XCIX). The survivors jumped to their feet, throwing their blankets from their shoulders as they rose. For a few minutes, there was a terrible hand-to-hand struggle where every man’s only thought was to kill. Although many of the warriors had no guns, nearly all had revolvers and knives in their belts under their blankets, along with some of the deadly war clubs still carried by the Sioux. The lack of guns actually made the fight bloodier, as it forced the combatants into closer quarters.

At the first volley, the Hotchkiss guns aimed at the camp opened fire and sent a storm of shells and bullets among the women and children, who had gathered in front of the tipis to watch the unusual military display. The guns fired 2-pound explosive shells at a rate of nearly fifty per minute, mowing down every living thing. The terrible effect can be judged by the fact that one survivor, a woman named Blue Whirlwind whom the author interviewed, received fourteen wounds, while each of her two young sons at her side was also wounded. Within a few minutes, 200 Indian men, women, and children, along with 60 soldiers, lay dead or wounded on the ground. The tipis had been torn down by the shells, and some were burning over the helpless wounded. The surviving handful of Indians fled in wild panic toward the shelter of the ravine, pursued by hundreds of enraged soldiers and followed by raking fire from the Hotchkiss guns, which had been moved into position to sweep the ravine.

There can be no question that the pursuit was simply a massacre, where fleeing women with infants in their arms were shot down after resistance had ended and when almost every warrior lay dead or dying on the ground. On this point, the careful writer Herbert Welsh says:

> "Because so many women and children were killed, and their bodies were found far from the scene of action—as if they were shot down while fleeing—it appears that blind rage was at work. This is in striking contrast to the moderation shown by the Indian police during the fight with Sitting Bull, when they were attacked by women." (Welsh, 3.)

The testimony of American Horse and other friendly Indians strongly supports this view. (See page

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14]

839.) Commissioner Morgan says in his official report that “Most of the men, including Big Foot, were killed around his tent, where he lay sick. The bodies of the women and children were scattered along a distance of two miles from the scene of the encounter.” (*Comr., 35.*)

This is no reflection on the humanity of the officer in charge. On the contrary, Colonel Forsyth had taken measures to guard against such an occurrence by separating the women and children, as already stated, and had also endeavored to make the sick chief, Big Foot, as comfortable as possible, even to the extent of sending his own surgeon, Dr. Glennan, to attend to him on the night of the surrender. Strict orders had also been issued to the troops that women and children were not to be hurt. The butchery was the work of infuriated soldiers whose comrades had just been shot down without cause or warning. In justice to a brave regiment, it must be said that a number of the men were new recruits fresh from eastern recruiting stations who had never before been under fire, were not yet filled with military discipline, and were probably unable in the confusion to distinguish between men and women by their clothing.

After examining all the official papers bearing on the subject in the files of the War Department and the Indian Office, together with the official reports of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, the Secretary of War, and the several officers involved; after gathering all that might be obtained from unofficial printed sources and from conversations with survivors and participants in the engagement on both sides, and after going over the battleground in company with the interpreter of the scouts involved, the author arrives at the conclusion that when the sun rose on Wounded Knee on the fatal morning of December 29, 1890, no trouble was anticipated or planned by either the Indians or the troops; that the Indians in good faith desired to surrender and be at peace, and that the officers in the same good faith had made preparations to receive their surrender and escort them quietly to the reservation; that in spite of the peaceful intent of Big Foot and his band, the medicine man, Yellow Bird, at the critical moment urged the warriors to resistance and gave the signal for the attack; that the first shot was fired by an Indian, and that the Indians were responsible for the engagement; that the answering volley and attack by the troops was right and justifiable, but that the wholesale slaughter of women and children was unnecessary and inexcusable.

Authorities differ as to the number of Indians present and killed at Wounded Knee. General Ruger states that the band numbered about 340, including about 100 warriors, but Major Whitside, to whom they surrendered, reported them officially as numbering 120 men and 250 women and children, a total of 370. (*War, 15; G. D., 38.*) This agrees almost exactly with the statement made to the author by Mr. Asay, a trader who was present at the surrender. General Miles says that there were present 106 warriors, a few others being absent at the time in

D., 39.*) No exact account of the dead could be made immediately after the fight because of a second attack by another party of Indians coming up from the agency. Some of the dead and wounded left on the field were undoubtedly carried off by their friends before the burial party came out three days later; of those brought in alive, a number afterwards died of wounds and exposure but received no notice in the official reports. The Adjutant-General, in response to a letter of inquiry, states that 128 Indians were killed and 33 wounded. Commissioner Morgan, in his official report, puts the number killed at 146. (*Comr., 36.*) Both these estimates are clearly too low. General Miles, in his final report, states that about 200 men, women, and children were killed. (*War, 17.*) General Colby, who commanded the Nebraska state troops, says that about 100 men and over 120 women and children were found dead on the field, a total of about 220. (*Colby, 4.*) Agent Royer telegraphed immediately after the fight that about 300 Indians had been killed, and General Miles, telegraphing on the same day, says, "I think very few Indians have escaped." (*G. D., 40.*) Fifty-one Indians were brought in the same day by the troops, and a few others were found still alive by the burial party three days later. A number of these later died. No significant number escaped, as they were unable to reach their ponies after the fight began. General Miles states that 98 warriors were killed on the field. (*War, 18.*) The total number killed on the field, or who later died from wounds and exposure, was probably very nearly 300.

According to an official statement from the Adjutant-General, 31 soldiers were killed in the battle. About as many more were wounded, one or two of whom afterwards died. All of those killed, except for Hospital Steward Pollock and an Indian scout named High Backbone, belonged to the Seventh Cavalry, as did probably nearly all of the wounded. The only commissioned officer killed was Captain Wallace. He received four bullet wounds in his body and finally succumbed to a hatchet stroke to the head. Lieutenant E. A. Garlington of the Seventh Cavalry and Lieutenant H. L. Hawthorne of the Second Artillery were wounded. (*War, 19.*) The last-named officer owed his life to his watch, which deflected the bullet that otherwise would have passed through his body.

The heroic missionary priest, Father Craft, had dedicated a large part of his life to working among the Sioux, who loved and respected him. At the beginning of the trouble, he had attempted to persuade the panicked Indians to come into the agency, but he was unsuccessful. The Indians claimed that not a single treaty ever made with them had been fulfilled in all its terms. Since many of the soldiers shared his faith, he accompanied the detachment that received Big Foot’s surrender to provide whatever help he could to either side. In the desperate fight, he was stabbed through the lungs; yet, with bullets flying around him and hatchets and war clubs swinging through the air, he continued his work, administering last rites to the dying until he fell unconscious from loss of blood. He was brought back to the agency along with the other wounded, and although his life was in danger for some time, he finally recovered. In talking about Wounded Knee with one of the friendly warriors who had gone into the Bad Lands to urge the holdouts to come in, he spoke with warm admiration of Father Craft. I asked why it was, then, that the Indians had tried to kill him. He replied, "They did not recognize him. Father Jutz <note>the priest at the Drexel Catholic mission, mentioned previously</note> always wears his black robe, but Father Craft wore a soldier's cap and overcoat that day. If he had worn his black robe, no Indian would have hurt him." On

<header>MOONEY] THE NEWS AT PINE RIDGE</header>

Upon inquiring afterward, I learned that this was not correct, as Father Craft was indeed wearing his priestly robes. From the Indian statement, however, and the well-known affection in which he was held by the Sioux, it is probable that the Indian who stabbed him was too excited at the moment to recognize him.

The news of the battle was brought to the agency by Lieutenant Guy Preston of the Ninth Cavalry, who, in company with a soldier and an Indian scout, made the ride of 16 or 18 miles in a little over an hour; one horse fell dead of exhaustion on the way. There were then at the agency, under the command of General Brooke, about 300 men of the Second Infantry and 50 Indian police.

The firing at Wounded Knee was plainly heard by the thousands of Indians camped about the agency at Pine Ridge, who had come in from the Bad Lands to surrender. They were at once thrown into great excitement, undoubtedly believing that there was a deliberate purpose afoot to disarm and massacre them all. When the fugitives—mostly women and children—began to come in, telling the story of the terrible slaughter of their friends and showing their bleeding wounds as evidence, the camp was divided between panic and desperation. A number of warriors mounted in haste and made all speed to the battleground, only about two hours distant. There they met the troops, who were now scattered about, hunting down the fugitives who might have escaped the first killing and picking up the dead and wounded. The soldiers were driven in toward the center, where they threw up entrenchments by means of which they were finally able to repel the attacking party. With the assistance of a body of Indian scouts and police, they then gathered up the dead and wounded soldiers, along with some of the wounded Indians and a few other prisoners to the number of 51, and returned to the agency.

In the meantime, the hostiles under Two Strike had opened fire on the agency from the neighboring hills and endeavored to approach, by way of a deep ravine, near enough to set fire to the buildings. General Brooke, desiring to avoid a general engagement, ordered out the Indian police—a splendidly drilled body of 50 brave men—who gallantly took their stand in the center of the agency enclosure, in full view of the hostiles, some of whom were their own relatives, and kept them off. They returned the fire of the besiegers with such good effect as to kill two and wound several others. The attacking party, as well as those who rode out to help their kinsmen at Wounded Knee, were not the Pine Ridge Indians (Oglala) but the Brulé from Rosebud under the leadership of Two Strike, Kicking Bear, and Short Bull. On the approach of the detachment returning from Wounded Knee, almost the entire body that had come in to surrender broke away and fell back to a position on White Clay Creek, where the next day found a camp of 4,000 Indians, including more than a thousand warriors who were now thoroughly hostile. On the evening of the battle, General Miles telegraphed to military headquarters,
