<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

"Last night everything looked favorable for getting all the Indians under control; since the report from Forsyth, it looks more serious than at any other time." *(G. D., 41.)* It seemed that all the careful work of the last month had been undone.

At the first indication of coming trouble in November, all the remote schools and mission stations on the Pine Ridge Reservation had been abandoned. The teachers, farmers, and missionaries had fled to the agency to seek the protection of the troops—all except for the members of the Drexel Catholic Mission, 5 miles northwest of the agency. Here, the two or three priests and five Franciscan sisters remained quietly at their post, with a hundred little children around them, safe in the assurance of the "hostiles" that they would not be harmed. While the fighting was going on at Wounded Knee and hundreds of furious warriors were firing into the agency—where the handful of whites were shivering in fear despite the presence of troops and police—these gentle women and the kindly old German priest were looking after the children, feeding the frightened fugitive women, and tenderly caring for the wounded Indians who were being brought in from Wounded Knee and the agency. Throughout all these weeks of terror, they went calmly about the duties to which they had dedicated their lives, and kept their little flock together and their school in operation. They did this without the presence of a single soldier, completely cut off from the troops and the agency and surrounded by thousands of wild Indians.

Some time afterward, in talking with the Indians about the events of the campaign, the warrior who had spoken with such admiration of Father Craft referred with the same affectionate enthusiasm to Father Jutz. He said that when the infuriated Indians attacked the agency upon hearing of the slaughter at Wounded Knee, they had sent word to the mission that no one there need be afraid. "We told him to stay where he was and no Indian would disturb him," said the warrior. He told how the priest and the sisters had fed the starving refugees and bound up the wounds of the survivors who escaped the slaughter, and then after a pause he said: "He is a brave man; braver than any Indian." Curious to know why this man had not joined the hostiles, among whom were several of his near relatives, I asked him the question. His reply was simple: "I had a little boy at the Drexel mission. He died and Father Jutz put a white stone over him. That is why I did not join the hostiles."

While visiting Pine Ridge in 1891, I went out to see the Drexel school and found Father John Jutz, a simple, kindly old German from the Tyrol, with one or two other German lay brothers and five Franciscan sisters, who were Americans. Although it was only a recent establishment, the school was in a flourishing condition, showing everywhere the evidence of orderly industry. Like a true German of the Alps, Father Jutz had already devised a way to make jelly from the wild plums and excellent wine from the chokecherry. While we were talking, the recess hour arrived and

<page-num>875</page-num>
MOONEY] HOSTILITY RENEWED.

A group of small children came trooping in, pushing over one another in an effort to grab a finger of the good father, or at least to hold onto his robe while he led them into another room where one of the sisters gave each of them a ginger cake, hot from the oven. The room was filled with the children's shouts and laughter, and the father explained, "Children get hungry, and we always have some cakes for the little ones at recess. I let the boys be noisy in the playroom as long as they don't fight. It is good for them." Looking at the happy, noisy crowd around the missionary in his black gown and the sister, it was easy to see how they had felt safe in the affection of the Indians throughout all the days and nights when others were trembling behind fortifications and lines of soldiers. Referring to what the Indians had told me, I asked Father Jutz if it was true that the hostiles had sent word to them not to be afraid. He replied, "Yes; they had sent word that no one in the mission need be alarmed," and then, with a gentle smile, he added, "But it was never our intention to leave." It was clear enough that beneath the quiet exterior burned the old missionary fire of Jogues and Marquette.

The conflict at Wounded Knee quickly bore fruit. On the same day, as has been mentioned, a portion of the Indians under Two Strike attacked the agency, and the entire body of nearly 4,000 who had come in to surrender retreated again to entrench themselves in preparation for renewed hostilities. On the morning of December 30, the day after the fight, the wagon train of the Ninth Cavalry <note>A regiment composed of Black soldiers, known as Buffalo Soldiers.</note> was attacked within two miles of the agency while arriving with supplies. One soldier was killed, but the Indians were driven back with the loss of several of their own men.

On the same day, news reached the agency that the hostiles had attacked the Catholic mission five miles away. General Brooke ordered Colonel Forsyth, with eight troops of the Seventh Cavalry and one piece of artillery, to go out and drive them off. It turned out that the hostiles had set fire to several houses between the mission and the agency, but the mission itself had not been disturbed. As the troops approached, the hostiles retreated, but Forsyth failed to occupy the commanding hills and was consequently surrounded by the Indians. They tried to draw him into a canyon and pressed him so closely that he was forced to send back for reinforcements three times. Major Henry had just arrived at the agency with a detachment of the Ninth Cavalry, and upon hearing the sound of the firing, he immediately set out to relieve Forsyth with four troops of cavalry and a Hotchkiss gun. Upon arriving at the scene, he occupied the hills and thus succeeded in driving off the hostiles without further casualties, rescuing the Seventh Cavalry from its dangerous position. In this skirmish, known as the "mission fight," the Seventh lost one officer, Lieutenant Mann, and a private, Dominic Francischetti, who were killed, and seven others who were wounded. ( *War, 20; G. D., 42.* )

Father Jutz reflects on the safety of the mission, which was maintained through the mutual affection between the missionaries and the Indian community.</summary>

The conduct of the Black troops of the Ninth <term>cavalry</term> on this occasion deserves the highest praise. At the time of the battle at Wounded Knee the day before, they were in the Bad Lands, about 80 or 90 miles from Pine Ridge, when the order was sent for them to come in to help repel the attack on the agency. By riding all night, they arrived at the agency at dawn, along with two <term>Hotchkiss guns</term> under the command of Lieutenant John Hayden of the First Artillery. They had barely dismounted when word arrived that their wagon train, following behind, was being attacked, and they were forced to go out again to rescue it, as previously described. Upon returning again, they lay down to rest after their long night ride, but they were once more called out to assist the Seventh Cavalry at the mission. Jumping into their saddles, they rode at full speed to the mission, five miles away, drove back the hostile forces and saved the command, and returned to the agency. They had ridden over 100 miles and fought in two engagements within thirty hours. Lieutenant Hayden, with his Hotchkiss guns, who had arrived with them from the Bad Lands, also took part with them in the fight at the mission.

On the same evening, Standing Soldier, an Indian scout, arrived at the agency with a party of 65 Indians, including 18 men. These were part of Big Foot’s or Short Bull’s followers who had lost their way during the flight from the Cheyenne River and were searching for the rest of the band when they were captured by the scouts. They were not aware of the death of Big Foot and the total destruction of his band. After being disarmed and placed under guard, they were informed of it, but only in a gentle manner so as not to cause unnecessary distress. (G. D., 43.)

Immediately after the battle of Wounded Knee, because of the panic among the frontier settlers of Nebraska, the Nebraska state troops were called out under the command of General L. W. Colby. They were stationed at the most vulnerable points between the settlements and the reservation and remained in the field until the surrender of the hostile forces two weeks later. The only casualty among them was the death of Private George Wilhauer, who was accidentally shot by a sentry. (Colby, 5.)

On New Year’s Day of 1891, three days after the battle, a detachment of troops was sent out to Wounded Knee to gather and bury the Indian dead and to bring in any wounded who might still be alive on the field. In the meantime, there had been a heavy snowstorm, ending in a blizzard. The bodies of the slaughtered men, women, and children were found lying under the snow, frozen stiff and covered with blood (plate XCVIII). Almost all the dead warriors were found lying near where the fight began, around Big Foot’s <term>tipi</term>, but the bodies of the women and children were found scattered for two miles from the scene of the encounter, showing that they had been killed while trying to escape. (Comr., 37; Colby, 6.) A number of women and children were found still alive, but all were badly wounded or frozen, or both, and most of them died after being brought in. Four babies were found

<header>MOONEY] LOYALTY OF THE SCOUTS</header>

family before the trouble began. She had already given him his name, Herbert Zitkalazi, the last word being the Sioux form of his father’s name, “Yellow Bird.” She brought him back with her to Washington, where he soon learned English and became a general favorite of all who knew him for his affectionate nature and unusual intelligence, showing genuine boyish enthusiasm in all he undertook. His picture provided here (figure 82) is from a photograph made in Lafayette Park, Washington, in 1892. Since his adopted mother has resumed her school work among his tribe, he is now back with her, attending school under her supervision at Standing Rock. There, as in Washington, he seems to be a natural leader among those of his own age. When we think of these children and consider that only by the narrowest of accidents they escaped the death that overtook a hundred other children at Wounded Knee—who might all have possessed the same potential for affection, education, and happy usefulness—we can understand the sickening meaning of such events as the Chivington massacre <note>Also known as the Sand Creek massacre of 1864.</note> in Colorado and the Custer fight on the Washita, where the newspaper reports merely stated that “the enemy was surprised and the Indian camp destroyed.”

The Indian scouts at Wounded Knee, like the Indian police at Grand River and Pine Ridge, were brave and loyal, as has been the almost universal rule with Indians when enlisted in the government service—even when called on, as these were, to serve against their own tribe and relatives. The prairie Indian is a born soldier, with all the soldier’s pride in loyalty to duty, and may be trusted implicitly once he has consented to enter the service. The scouts at Wounded Knee were Sioux, with Philip Wells as interpreter. Other Sioux scouts were ranging the country between the agency and the hostile camp in the Bad Lands, acting as mediators in the peace negotiations which led to the final surrender. Fifty Cheyenne and about as many Crow scouts were also employed in the same region. Throughout the entire campaign, the Indian scouts and police were faithful and received the warmest praise from their officers.

On New Year’s Day, 1891, Henry Miller, a herder, was killed by Indians a few miles from the agency. This was the only noncombatant killed by the Indians during the entire campaign, and during the same period no raid or act of destruction was committed by them outside of the reservation. On the next day, the agent reported that the school buildings and Episcopal church on White Clay Creek had been burned by hostiles, who were then camped—numbering about 3,000—on Grass Creek, 15 miles northeast of the agency. They had captured the government beef herd and were depending on it for food. Red Cloud, Little Wound, and their people were with them and were reported to be anxious to return, but were prevented by the hostile leaders, Two Strike, Short Bull, and Kicking Bear, who threatened to kill the first person who made a move to come in. (G. D., 44.) A few days later a number of

Red Cloud’s men came in and surrendered and reported that the old chief was practically a prisoner and wanted the soldiers to come and rescue him from the hostiles, who were trying to force him into the war. They reported further that there was much suffering from cold and hunger in the Indian camp, and that all the Ogalala (Red Cloud’s people of Pine Ridge) were intending to come in at once in a body.

On the 3rd of January, General Miles took up his headquarters at Pine Ridge and directed General Brooke to assume immediate command of the troops surrounding the hostile camp. Brooke’s men swung out to form the western and northern part of a circle around the hostiles, cutting them off from the Bad Lands, while the troops under General Carr closed in on the east and northeast in such a way that the Indians were hemmed in and unable to move in any direction except toward the agency.

On January 3, a party of hostiles attacked a detachment of the Sixth cavalry under Captain Kerr on Grass creek, a few miles north of the agency, but were quickly repulsed with the loss of four of their number, the troops having been reinforced by other detachments in the vicinity. In this engagement the Indian scouts again distinguished themselves. *(War, 21.)* The effect of this repulse was to check the westward movement of the hostiles and hold them in their position along White Clay creek until their passion had somewhat abated.

On January 5, there was another encounter on Wounded Knee creek. A small detachment which had been sent out to meet a supply train coming into the agency found the wagons drawn up in a square to resist an attack made by a band of about 50 Indians. The soldiers joined forces with the teamsters, and by firing from behind the protection of the wagons succeeded in driving off the Indians and killing a number of their horses. The hostiles were reinforced, however, and a hard skirmish was kept up for several hours until more troops arrived from the agency about dark, having been sent in answer to a courier who managed to elude the attacking party. The troops charged on a gallop and the Indians retreated, having lost several killed and wounded, besides a number of their horses. *(Colby, 7.)*

Amid all these warlike alarms, the gentle muse Calliope hovered over the field and inspired W. H. Prather, a Black private of troop I of the Ninth cavalry, to the production of the ballad given below, one of the few good specimens of American ballad poetry, and worthy of equal place with “Captain Lovewell’s Fight,” “Old Quebec,” or anything that originated in the late rebellion <note>The American Civil War.</note>. It became a favorite among the troops in camp and with the scattered frontiersmen of Dakota and Nebraska, being sung to a simple air with vigor and expression and a particularly rousing chorus, and is probably by this time a classic of the barracks. It is here reproduced verbatim from the printed slip published for distribution among the soldiers during the campaign.

<header>MOONEY] A GHOST-DANCE BALLAD</header>

# THE INDIAN GHOST DANCE AND WAR

The Redskins left their agency, the soldiers left their post,
All on the strength of an Indian tale about the Messiah's ghost,
Started by savage chieftains to lead their tribes astray;
But Uncle Sam wouldn't have it so, for he isn't built that way.
They swore that this Messiah came to them in a vision's sleep,
And promised to restore their game and buffaloes a heap,
So they must start a big Ghost Dance, then all would join their band,
And maybe so we lead the way into the great Badlands.
*Chorus:*
They claimed the shirt the Messiah gave, no bullet could go through,
But when the soldiers fired at them they saw this was not true.
The medicine man supplied them with their great Messiah's grace,
And he, too, hurried away and swore the 7th was hard to face.

About their tents the soldiers stood, awaiting one and all,
That they might hear the trumpet clear when sounding the general call
Or "Boots and Saddles" in a rush, so that each and every man
Might mount in haste, ride soon and fast to stop this devilish band.
But great generals like Miles and Brooke don't do things that way,
For they know an Indian like a book, and let him have his sway
Until they think him far enough and then to John they'll say,
"You had better stop your fooling or we'll bring our guns to play."
*Chorus.—They claimed the shirt, etc.*

The 9th marched out with splendid cheer the Badlands to explore—
With Colonel Henry at their head they never fear the foe;
So on they rode from Christmas Eve until the dawn of Christmas Day;
The Redskins heard the 9th was near and fled in great dismay;
The 7th is of courage bold, both officers and men,
But bad luck seems to follow them and twice has taken them in;
They came in contact with Big Foot's warriors in their fierce might;
This chief made sure he had a chance of advantage in the fight.
*Chorus.—They claimed the shirt, etc.*

A fight took place, it was hand to hand, unwarned by trumpet call,
While the Sioux were dropping man by man—the 7th killed them all,
And to that regiment let it be said, "You noble braves, well done,
Although you lost some gallant men, a glorious fight you've won."
The 8th was there, the 6th rode miles to swell that great command
And waited for orders night and day to round up Short Bull's band.
The infantry marched up in mass as the cavalry's support,
And while the latter rounded up, the former held the fort.
*Chorus.—They claimed the shirt, etc.*

E Battery of the 1st stood by and did their duty well,
For every time the Hotchkiss barked they say a hostile fell.
Some Indian soldiers joined in too and helped to quell the fray,
And now the campaign's ended and the soldiers have marched away.
So all have done their share, you see, whether it was thick or thin,
And all helped break the Ghost Dance up and drive the hostiles in.
The settlers in that region now can breathe with better grace;
They only ask and pray to God to make John hold his base.
*Chorus.—They claimed the shirt, etc.*

(W. H. Prather, I, 9th Cavalry).

The song recounts the military's efforts to suppress the Ghost Dance movement, highlighting the roles of various regiments and leaders during the 1890-1891 conflict.</summary>

# APPENDIX—THE INDIAN STORY OF WOUNDED KNEE

*[*From the Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1891, volume 1, pages 179-181. Extracts from a verbatim stenographic report of a council held by delegations of Sioux with the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, at Washington, February 11, 1891.*]*

<term>TURNING HAWK</term>, Pine Ridge (Mr. Cook, interpreter). Mr. Commissioner, my purpose today is to tell you what I know of the condition of affairs at the agency where I live. A certain lie came to our agency from the west which acted like a fire upon the Indians; and when this fire reached our people, those who had foresight and could see into the matter decided to stand against it and fight it. The reason we took this hostile stance toward this fire was because we believed that you yourself would not favor this particular mischief-making thing. Just as we expected, the authorities did not like this movement, and we were quietly told that we must give it up or have nothing to do with it. Although this was the advice from our good friends in the east, there were, of course, many foolish young men who were longing to be identified with the movement, even though they did not know if there was anything absolutely bad or absolutely good associated with it.

In the course of time, we heard that the soldiers were moving toward the scene of trouble. After a while, some of the soldiers finally reached our place, and we heard that a number of them also reached our friends at Rosebud. Of course, when a large body of soldiers moves in a certain direction, they inspire a certain amount of awe; it is natural that the women and children who see this large moving mass are made afraid of it and are put in a condition that makes them run away. At first, we thought that Pine Ridge and Rosebud were the only two agencies where soldiers were sent, but finally, we heard that the other agencies fared the same. We heard and saw that about half of our friends at the Rosebud agency, out of fear from seeing the soldiers, began to run away from their agency toward ours (Pine Ridge). When they had gotten inside our reservation, they learned that right ahead of them at our agency was another large crowd of soldiers. While the soldiers were there, there were constantly many false rumors flying back and forth. The specific rumor I have in mind is the threat that the soldiers had come there to disarm the Indians entirely and to take all their horses away from them. That was the oft-repeated story.

This story was so constantly repeated that our friends from Rosebud, instead of going to Pine Ridge, their intended destination, veered off and went in another direction toward the “Bad Lands.” We did not know definitely how many there were, but we understood there were 300 lodges, about 1,700 people. Eagle Pipe, Turning Bear, High Hawk, Short Bull, Lance, No Flesh, Pine Bird, Crow Dog, Two Strike, and White Horse were the leaders.

Well, after the people veered off in this way, many of those at our agency who believe in peace and order were very anxious that some influence should be brought to bear upon them. In addition to our love of peace, we remembered that many of these people were related to us by blood. So, we sent out peace commissioners to the people who were thus running away from their agency.

I understood at the time that they were simply going away out of fear because of so many soldiers. The word of these good men from the Pine Ridge agency was so constant that they finally succeeded in persuading half of the party from Rosebud to leave the place where they had taken refuge, and they were finally brought to the agency at Pine Ridge. Young-Man-Afraid-of-his-Horses, Little Wound, Fast Thunder, Louis Shangreau, John Grass, Jack Red Cloud, and I were some of these peacemakers.

The remnant of the party from Rosebud that was not taken to the agency finally reached the wilds of the Bad Lands. Seeing that we had succeeded so well, we once more sent word to the same party in the Bad Lands and succeeded in bringing these very Indians

...out of the depths of the Bad Lands and were being brought toward the agency. When we were about a day's journey from our agency, we heard that a certain party of Indians (Big Foot's band) from the Cheyenne River agency was fleeing toward Pine Ridge.

**CAPTAIN SWORD.** Those who actually left the Cheyenne River agency probably numbered 303, and there were a few from the Standing Rock reservation with them, though I do not know their exact number. There were a number of Oglalas—old men and several schoolboys—returning with that same party. One of the very seriously wounded boys was a member of the Oglala boarding school at the Pine Ridge agency. He was not on the warpath; he was simply returning home to his agency and to his school after a summer visit to relatives on the Cheyenne River.

**TURNING HAWK.** When we heard that these people were coming toward our agency, we also heard this: these people were approaching the Pine Ridge agency, and when they were almost at the agency, they were met by the soldiers, surrounded, and finally taken to Wounded Knee Creek. There, at a designated time, their guns were demanded. When they had surrendered them, the men were separated from their families and their tipis and taken to a certain spot. When the guns were thus taken and the men thus separated, a crazy man—a young man of very bad influence and in fact a nobody—among that group of Indians fired his gun. Of course, the firing of a gun must have been the breaking of some sort of military rule, because the soldiers immediately returned fire and indiscriminate killing followed.

**SPOTTED HORSE.** This man shot an officer in the army; the first shot killed this officer. I was a voluntary scout at that encounter and I saw exactly what happened; that was what I noticed: that the first shot killed an officer. As soon as this shot was fired, the Indians immediately began drawing their knives. They were urged from all sides to stop, but they did not obey. Consequently, the firing began immediately on the part of the soldiers.

**TURNING HAWK.** All the men who were bunched together were killed right there, and those who escaped that first fire fled into the ravine. As they went a long distance up the ravine, they were pursued on both sides by the soldiers and shot down, as the dead bodies showed afterward. The women were standing in a different place from where the men were stationed, and when the firing began, those men who escaped the first onslaught went in one direction up the ravine. Then the women, who were gathered together at another place, went in an entirely different direction through an open field, and the women met the same fate as the men who went up the deep ravine.

**AMERICAN HORSE.** The men were separated, as has already been said, from the women, and they were surrounded by the soldiers. Next came the Indian village, and that was also entirely surrounded by the soldiers. When the firing began, of course, the people who were standing immediately around the young man who fired the first shot were killed instantly. Then they turned their guns—Hotchkiss guns, and so on—upon the women who were in the lodges standing there under a flag of truce. Of course, as soon as they were fired upon, they fled; the men fled in one direction and the women ran in two different directions. So, there were three general directions in which they took flight.

There was a woman with an infant in her arms who was killed just as she almost touched the flag of truce, and the women and children, of course, were strewn all along the circular village until they were killed. Right near the flag of truce, a mother was shot down with her infant; the child, not knowing its mother was dead, was still nursing, and that especially was a very sad sight. The women were killed together with their babies as they fled, shot right through, and women who were very heavy with child were also killed. All the Indians fled in these three directions, and after almost all of them had been killed, a cry was made that all those who were not killed or wounded should come forward and they would be safe. Little boys who were not wounded came out of their places of refuge, and

as soon as they came in sight, a number of soldiers surrounded them and butchered them there.

Of course, we all feel very sad about this affair. I remained very loyal to the government throughout those troublesome days, and believing so much in the government and being so loyal to it, my disappointment was very strong, and I have come to Washington with a heavy burden of blame in my heart. Of course, it would have been all right if only the men were killed; we would feel almost grateful for it. But the fact of the killing of the women, and more especially the killing of the young boys and girls who are to go on to make up the future strength of the Indian people, is the saddest part of the whole affair, and we feel it very deeply.

I was not there at the time before the burial of the bodies, but I did go there with some of the police and the Indian doctor and a great many of the people—men from the agency—and we went through the battlefield and saw where the bodies were from the tracks of the blood.

**TURNING HAWK.** I had just reached the point where I said that the women were killed. We heard, besides the killing of the men, of the onslaught also made upon the women and children, and they were treated as roughly and indiscriminately as the men and boys were.

Of course, this affair brought a great deal of distress upon all the people, but especially upon the minds of those who stood loyal to the government and who did all they were able to do in the matter of bringing about peace. They especially have suffered much distress and are very much hurt at heart. These peacemakers continued in their good work, but there were a great many fickle young men who were ready to be moved by the change in the events there; consequently, in spite of the great fire that was brought upon everyone, they were ready to assume a hostile attitude. These young men prepared themselves and went in the direction of the scene of battle so they might be of service there. They arrived there and finally exchanged shots with the soldiers. This party of young men was made up from Rosebud, Ogalalla (Pine Ridge), and members of any other agencies that happened to be there at the time. While this was going on in the neighborhood of Wounded Knee—the Indians and soldiers exchanging shots—the agency, our home, was also fired into by the Indians. Matters continued in this strain until the evening came on, and then the Indians went off down by White Clay Creek. When the agency was fired upon by the Indians from the hillside, of course, the shots were returned by the Indian police who were guarding the agency buildings.

Although fighting seemed to have been in the air, yet those who believed in peace were still constant at their work. Young-Man-Afraid-of-his-Horses, who had been on a visit to some other agency in the north or northwest, returned and immediately went out to the people living about White Clay Creek, on the border of the Bad Lands, and brought his people out. He succeeded in obtaining the consent of the people to leave their place of refuge and return to the agency. Thus, the remaining portion of the Indians who started from Rosebud were brought back into the agency. Mr. Commissioner, during the days of the great whirlwind out there, those good men tried to maintain a counteracting power, and that was "Peace." We have now come to realize that peace has prevailed and won the day. While we were engaged in bringing about peace, our property was left behind, of course, and most of us have lost everything, even down to the matter of guns with which to kill ducks, rabbits, etc.—shotguns and guns of that kind. When Young-Man-Afraid brought the people in and their guns were requested, both men who were called hostile and men who stood loyal to the government delivered up their guns.

## CHAPTER XIV

## CLOSE OF THE OUTBREAK—THE GHOST DANCE IN THE SOUTH

In the meantime, peace overtures had been made by General Miles to the hostiles, most of whose leaders he knew personally, having received their surrender on the Yellowstone ten years earlier at the close of the Custer war. Upon the urgent representations of himself and others, Congress had also appropriated the necessary funds to carry out the terms of the recent treaty. Most of the trouble had been caused by the neglect of this treaty, so the commander was now able to assure the Indians that their rights and needs would receive attention. They were urged to come in and surrender, with a guarantee that the general himself would represent their case to the government. At the same time, they were informed that their retreat was cut off and that further resistance would be useless. As an additional step toward regaining their confidence, the civilian agents were removed from the various disturbed agencies, which were then put in charge of military officers well known and respected by the Indians. Cheyenne River agency was assigned to Captain J. H. Hurst, and Rosebud agency to Captain J. M. Lee, while Royer, at Pine Ridge, was replaced on January 8 by Captain F. E. Pierce. The last-named officer was later relieved by Captain Charles G. Penney, who is currently in charge. <note>War Department Reports, 22; Commissioner of Indian Affairs Report, 38; Ghost Dance, 45.</note>

The friendly overtures made by General Miles—along with evidence that the government desired to remedy their grievances and that longer resistance was hopeless—had an effect on the hostiles. Little Wound, Young-Man-Afraid-of-His-Horses (more accurately, “Young-Man-of-Whose-Horses-They-Are-Afraid”), Big Road, and other friendly chiefs also used their persuasion with such success that by January 12 the entire body of nearly 4,000 Indians had moved to within sight of the agency and expressed their desire for peace. The troops closed in around them, and on January 16, 1891, the hostiles surrendered, and the outbreak was at an end. They complied with every order and direction given by the commander and gave up nearly 200 rifles. Including other arms already surrendered, this made a total of between 600 and 700 guns—more than had ever before been surrendered by the Sioux at one time. As a further guarantee of good faith, the commander demanded the surrender of Kicking Bear and Short Bull, the principal leaders, along with about twenty other prominent warriors, as

<summary>General Miles ended the Sioux outbreak in January 1891 by addressing treaty grievances and replacing civilian agents with military officers. Following these overtures and the mediation of friendly chiefs, nearly 4,000 Indians surrendered at the Pine Ridge Agency.</summary>

hostages. The demand was readily complied with, and the designated men came forward voluntarily and gave themselves up as sureties for the good conduct of their people. They were sent to Fort Sheridan, Illinois, near Chicago, where they were kept until there was no further fear of trouble, and were then returned to their homes. (*War, 23; Colby, 8.*) After the surrender, the former hostiles pitched their camp, numbering 742 tipis in total, in the lowlands along White Clay Creek, just west of the agency. There, General Miles had supplies of beef, coffee, and sugar issued to them from the supply department, and that night they enjoyed the first full meal they had known in several weeks.

Thus ended the so-called Sioux outbreak of 1890-91. It might be better described, however, as a Sioux panic and stampede; for, to quote the expressive letter of McGillycuddy, writing on January 15, 1891, "Up to date there has been neither a Sioux outbreak nor war. No citizen in Nebraska or Dakota has been killed, molested, or can show the scratch of a pin, and no property has been destroyed off the reservation." (*Colby, 9.*) Only a single noncombatant was killed by the Indians, and that was close to the agency. The entire time occupied by the campaign, from the killing of Sitting Bull to the surrender at Pine Ridge, was only thirty-two days. The former hostiles were returned to their homes as quickly as possible. The Brulé of Rosebud, regarded as the most unruly of the hostiles, were taken back to the agency by Captain Lee—for whom they had respect based on an acquaintance of several years—without an escort and during the most intense cold of winter, yet without any trouble or dissatisfaction whatever. The military units were returned to their usual stations, and within a few weeks after the surrender, affairs at the various agencies were moving again in their usual course.

An unfortunate event occurred just before the surrender: the killing of Lieutenant E. W. Casey of the Twenty-second Infantry by Plenty Horses, a young Brulé, on January 7. Lieutenant Casey was in command of a troop of Cheyenne scouts and was stationed at the mouth of White Clay Creek, charged with the special duty of watching the hostile camp, which was located 8 miles further up the creek at No Water's place. On the day before his death, several of the hostiles had visited him and held a friendly conference. The next morning, in company with two scouts, he went out expressly for the purpose of observing the hostile camp more closely. He rode up to within a short distance of the camp, meeting and talking with several of the Indians on the way, and had stopped to talk with a mixed-blood relative of Red Cloud, when Plenty Horses, a short distance away, deliberately shot him through the head, and he fell from his horse dead. His body was not disturbed by the Indians but was brought in by some of the Cheyenne scouts soon after. Plenty Horses was brought before a United States court but was acquitted on the grounds that as the Sioux were then at war and the officer was practically a spy upon the Indian camp, the act

<header>MOONEY] THE FEW-TAILS AFFAIR</header>

...was not murder in the legal sense of the word. Lieutenant Casey had been in charge of the Cheyenne scouts for a year and had taken great interest in their welfare and proficiency; the Indians greatly mourned his death, viewing it as the insane act of a boy overwhelmed by the excitement of the times. (*War, 24; Commissioner, 39; Colby, 10; Ghost Dance, 46.*)

On January 11, an unprovoked murder was committed against a small party of peaceful Indians on the Belle Fourche, or the North Fork of the Cheyenne River. Because of this, the Indians who had come in to surrender were once again thrown into such alarm that, for a time, it seemed as if serious trouble might result. A group of Ogalala from Pine Ridge—consisting of Few Tails, a kind and peaceful old man, with his wife, an elderly woman, and One Feather, with his wife and two children (one a girl about thirteen years old and the other an infant)—had been hunting in the Black Hills with a pass from the agency. They had had a successful hunt and were returning with their two wagons heavily loaded with meat when they camped for the night at the mouth of Alkali Creek. During the evening, they were visited by some soldiers staying at a ranch a few miles away, who examined their pass and pronounced it valid. In the morning, after breakfast, the Indians started toward the agency again, but they had gone only a few hundred yards when they were fired upon by a group of white men hidden near the road. The leaders of the white men were three brothers named Culbertson, one of whom had only recently returned from prison. One of the murderers had visited the Indians in their camp the night before, and even that very morning. At the first shots, Few Tails was killed, along with both ponies hitched to the wagon. His wife jumped out and was hit by two bullets, which brought her to the ground. However, the murderers rode past her to get to the other Indian, who was following behind in the other wagon with his wife and two children. As soon as he saw his companion killed, One Feather turned his wagon in the opposite direction. Telling his wife—who had also been shot—to drive as fast as she could to save the children, he jumped onto one of the extra ponies and held off the murderers until his family had time to gain some distance. He then turned and joined his family and drove for about eight or ten miles until the pursuers caught up again; he then turned once more and fought them off while his wife went ahead with the wagon and the children. The wounded woman bravely drove on while the two small children lay down in the wagon with their heads covered by blankets. As they drove, they passed near a house from which several other shots were fired at the fleeing mother; her husband again rode up and held off the entire party until the wagon could get ahead. Finally, as the ponies were exhausted, this heroic man abandoned the wagon. He placed the two children on one of the spare ponies and put his wounded wife and himself on another, continuing to retreat until the white men gave up the pursuit. He finally reached the agency with his wife and children.

The wife of Few Tails, after being wounded by two bullets and falling beside the wagon where her dead husband lay, remained helpless and likely unconscious on the ground throughout the long winter night. When she revived in the morning, she found one of the horses still alive, mounted it, and managed to reach a settler’s house about 15 miles away by nightfall. Instead of finding help and sympathy, however, she was driven away by two men armed with loaded rifles. Frightened, she abandoned her horse and hurried away as best she could, despite having a bullet in her leg and another in her breast. She passed the trail of One Feather’s wagon, seeing the fresh tracks of his pursuers behind it, until she neared a trader’s store about 20 miles further south. Afraid to approach it because of her previous experience, the poor woman circled around it and continued—wounded, cold, and starving—to travel by night and hide by day until she reached the Bad Lands. The rest may be told in her own words:

> After that I traveled every night and rested during the day until I arrived here at the beef corral. By then I was very tired and was near the military camp. Early in the morning, a soldier came out and shouted something back, and in a few minutes, fifty men were there; they brought a blanket and took me to a tent. I had no blanket and my feet were swollen, and I was nearly dead. After I reached the tent, a doctor came in—a soldier doctor, because he had straps <note>rank insignia</note> on his shoulders—and he washed me and treated me well.

A few of the soldiers camped near the scene of the attack had joined the pursuit at the beginning, based on the claims of some of the murderers, but they abandoned it as soon as they realized their mistake. According to all the evidence, the killing was a wanton, unprovoked, and deliberate murder, yet the criminals were acquitted in the local courts. The apathy shown by the authorities of Meade County, South Dakota, where the murder was committed, sparked several vigorous protests. Colonel Shafter, in his statement on the case, concluded by referring to the recent killing of Lieutenant Casey: "As long as Indians are being arrested and held for killing armed men under conditions of war, it seems to me that the white murderers of a peaceful band of Indians should not be permitted to escape punishment." The Indians held the same view of the case. When General Miles demanded that Young-man-afraid-of-his-horses surrender the killers of Casey and the herder Miller, the old chief indignantly replied: "No; I will not surrender them, but if you will bring the white men who killed Few Tails, I will bring the Indians who killed the white soldier and the herder; and right out here in front of your tipi, I will have my young men shoot the Indians and you have your soldiers shoot the white men, and then we will be done with the whole business."

Regarding the heroic conduct of One Feather, the officer then in charge of the agency says: "The determination and genuine courage, as well as the leadership he showed in keeping the six pursuing men at a distance, and the devotion he showed toward his family by risking his life against great odds, make him worthy of a place on the list of heroes." (*War, 25; Comr., 40; G. D., 47.*)

<page-num>891</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE RESULTS OF THE TROUBLE</header>

On the recommendation of General Miles, a large delegation of the primary leaders from both the friendly and hostile Sioux factions was permitted to visit Washington in February 1891. Their goal was to present their grievances and suggest ways to prevent dissatisfaction in the future. Among the principal speakers were: from Pine Ridge, American Horse, Captain George Sword, Big Road, and He Dog; from Rosebud, White Bird and Turning Hawk; from Cheyenne River, Little No Heart and Straight Head; and from Standing Rock, John Grass and Mad Bear. The interpreters were Reverend C. S. Cook, David Zephier, Louis Primeau, Louis Richard, Clarence Three Stars, and Louis Shangreau. Their visit was highly successful and resulted in the start of a more effective administration of Sioux affairs. Steps were taken to repay those whose ponies had been seized during the Custer war in 1876, and extra funding was provided for food rations. As a result, before the end of the year, the Indians were receiving fifty percent more than they had before the conflict began. (*War, 26.*) After returning to their homes, the Indians of the various Sioux agencies began working in good faith, planting their crops and tending to their livestock. Within a short time, all further fears of conflict were over.

The discussion of Indian affairs following the outbreak led Congress to pass a bill. It mandated that all future vacancies for the position of Indian agent be filled by military officers chosen by the Indian Office and assigned for that purpose from the army. At the same time, a plan was developed to enlist Indians as a formal part of the regular army. Small groups from various tribes had long been attached to different posts and commands as informal scouts. These groups of scouts were now reduced in number or disbanded entirely, and in their place, Indian troops or companies were organized to be formally attached to various cavalry or infantry regiments. In the spring of 1891, officers were sent to several western reservations and succeeded in recruiting a number of regular troops from the most combative tribes; a significant number of these recruits came from the recently hostile Sioux.

Although the campaign lasted only about a month, the loss of life was high for an Indian war, and the financial cost to the government and to individuals was massive. Three officers and 28 privates were killed or fatally wounded during the campaign, and 4 officers and 38 privates were less severely wounded, though several of these died later. (*War, 27.*) The number of Indian casualties cannot be stated exactly. During the arrest of Sitting Bull, eight members of Sitting Bull's party and six police officers were killed or fatally wounded, totaling 14 deaths. Those killed in the Wounded Knee fight, or who afterward died of wounds or exposure, numbered at least 250 according to the best estimates. Those killed later in various small skirmishes, including the Few Tails incident, may have numbered 20 or 30. In total, the campaign cost the lives of 49 people on the government side and approximately 300 or more Indians.

<summary>Following the conflict, a Sioux delegation visited Washington to negotiate better conditions, leading to increased rations and the enlistment of Indians into the regular army. The brief campaign resulted in significant casualties, including approximately 300 Indians and 49 government-affiliated individuals.</summary>

<page-num>892</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

The direct or incidental expenses of the campaign were as follows: Expenses of the Department of Justice for defending Plenty Horses and prosecuting the murderers of Few Tails, unknown; appropriation by Congress to reimburse the Nebraska National Guard for the expense of service during the campaign, $43,000; paid out under an act of Congress to reimburse friendly Indians and other legal residents on the reservations for property destroyed by hostiles, $97,646.85 (*Comr., 41*); extra expense of the Commissary Department of the army, $37,764.69; extra expense of the Medical Department of the army, $1,164, besides extra supplies purchased by individuals; extra expenses of the Ordnance Department of the army for ammunition, not accounted for; total extra expense of the Quartermaster’s Department of the army, $915,078.81, including $120,634.17 for the transportation of troops over bonded railroads. (*A. G. O., 8.*) The total expense, public or private, was probably just under $1,200,000, or nearly $40,000 per day—a significant commentary on the bad policy of breaking faith with Indians.

According to the report of the agency farmer sent out after the trouble to learn the extent of the property of friendly Indians destroyed by the hostiles on the Pine Ridge Agency, 53 Indian dwellings, 1 church, 2 schoolhouses, and a bridge were burned, all on White Clay Creek, while nearly every remaining house along the creek had the windows broken out. A great deal of farming machinery and nearly all of the hay were burned, while stoves were broken to pieces and livestock killed. A few of the friendly Indians had been so overcome by the excitement that they had burned their own houses and run their machinery down high hills into the river, where it was found frozen in the ice several months later. (*G. D., 48.*)

In view of the fact that only one noncombatant was killed and no raids were committed off the reservation, the panic among the frontier settlers of both Dakotas, Nebraska, and Iowa was something ludicrous. The inhabitants worked themselves into such a high state of panic that ranches and even whole villages were temporarily abandoned, and the people flocked into the railroad cities with vivid stories of murder, scalping, and desolation that had no foundation whatever in fact. A reliable authority who was on the ground shortly after the scare had subsided gives this characteristic instance among others:

> In another city, a place of 3,000 inhabitants, 75 miles from any Indians and 150 miles from any hostiles, word came about 2 o’clock Sunday morning for the militia to be in readiness. The company promptly assembled and were instructed and drilled. In an evening church service, one of the pastors broke out in prayer: “O Lord, prepare us for what awaits us. We have just been listening to the sweet sounds of praise, but before the morning sun, we may hear the war whoop of the red man.” The effect on children and nervous persons may be imagined. The legislature was in session, and the impression upon that body was such as to lead it to make an appropriation for the benefit of the state militia at the expense of one for the state agricultural fair. (*Comr., 42.*)

The crisis produced the usual crop of patriots, all ready to serve their country—usually for a fee. Among these was a lady of Utica,

<page-num>893</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] PATRIOTIC OFFERS OF AID</header>

A woman in New York, claiming to be of the renowned Iroquois blood and calling herself the “Doctor Princess Viroqua,” wrote to the Indian Office with her sister “Wynima.” They requested a commission to go out and try the effect of moral persuasion on the warring Sioux, representing that by virtue of her descent from a long line of aboriginal princes, she would be welcomed with enthusiasm and accomplish her mission of peace. (*G. D., 49.*) As a matter of fact, neither of the names Viroqua or Wynima could be pronounced by a genuine Iroquois person knowing only their own language, and the second name, Wynima, is borrowed from Meacham’s sensational history of the Modoc war in California.

The proprietor of a “wild west” show in New York, signing himself Texas Ben, also wrote to volunteer his services, submitting his museum letterhead as credentials; it stated that he had served with Quantrell and had the written endorsement of Cole Younger. An old veteran from the Iowa soldiers’ home wrote to Secretary Noble with an excess of capital letters and much bad spelling, offering his help against the hostiles. He stated that he had been “raised” among them, could “talk the tongue,” and was ready to “do anything for my country.” (*G. D., 50.*)

A band of patriots in Minnesota, whose early education appears to have been somewhat neglected, wrote to the Secretary of the Interior offering to organize a company of 50 men to put down the outbreak, provided the government would look after a few items which they listed:
> “The government is to furnish each of us with two good horses, a good Winchester rifle, two good coats, and revolvers. Give us a $300.00 bounty and, say, a salary of fifty per month each, and our own judgment, and we will settle this Indian question forever, along with rations and ammunition. We should have, in addition to this, say, five dollars a head.” (*G. D., 51.*)

A man named Albert Hopkins appeared at Pine Ridge in December 1890, wearing a blanket and claiming to be the Indian Messiah. He announced his intention of going alone into the Bad Lands to the Indians, who were expecting his arrival with the “Pansy Banner of Peace.” His claims were ridiculed by Red Cloud and others, and he was promptly arrested and removed from the reservation. However, he was not dead, but only sleeping; in March 1893, having come to Washington, he addressed an urgent letter to Secretary Noble requesting official authority to visit the Sioux reservations to preach to the Indians. He stated that “with the help of the Pansy and its motto and manifest teaching, ‘Union, Culture, and Peace,’ and the star-pansy banner, of which I enclose an illustration, I hope to establish the permanent peace of the border.” He signed himself “Albert C. Hopkins, President Pro Tempore of The Pansy Society of America.”

The letter was referred to the Indian Office, which refused permission. This brought a reply from Hopkins, who this time signed himself “The Indian Messiah,” in which he states that as the Indians were expecting the Messiah in the spring, “in accordance with the prophecy of Sitting Bull...

Receiving no answer, he wrote again around the end of March to both the Secretary and the Indian Commissioner. He stated that messiahs, being human, were subject to human limitations—a fact the Indians were well aware of. However, he warned these officials that if the government imposed these limitations, it would be held responsible for his failure to appear to the Indians as he had promised, "before the native pansies blossom on the prairies." He ends by stating that he would leave for the Sioux country on Easter Sunday, but as nothing was heard of him later, it is presumed that he succumbed to those limitations. (*G. D., 52.*)

The first direct knowledge of the messiah and the Ghost Dance reached the northern Arapaho in Wyoming through Nakash, known as "Sage." In the early spring of 1889, Sage and several Shoshone visited the messiah; upon his return, he brought the first songs of the dance back to his people. These were probably some of the original Paiute songs of the messiah himself. The Ghost Dance was immediately inaugurated among the Shoshone and northern Arapaho. In the summer of the same year, the first rumors of the new redeemer reached the southern Arapaho and Cheyenne in Oklahoma through letters written by students who had returned from eastern government schools.

New reports of wonderful things beyond the mountains were constantly reaching the northern prairie tribes, and the excitement grew until the end of 1889. At that time, a large delegation—including Sioux, northern Cheyenne, and northern Arapaho—crossed the mountains to the Paiute country to see and talk with the messiah. Among the Sioux delegates were Short Bull, Fire Thunder, and Kicking Bear, as previously stated. Among the Cheyenne were Porcupine and several others, including one woman. The Arapaho representatives were Sitting Bull (Hänä'chä-thi'ăk) and Friday. The delegates from the different tribes met at the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming, which they left around Christmas. After stopping for a short time among the Bannock and Shoshone at Fort Hall, they went on to Walker Lake in Nevada. They were away for some time and returned to Wyoming in March 1890, while the Sioux and Cheyenne continued to their homes further east. According to Nakash’s statement, they had a five-day conference with the messiah, who at one time entered a trance, though his visitors did not.

Before their return, the southern Arapaho in Oklahoma had sent Wa'tän-ga'a ("Black Coyote"), an officer of the Indian police, and Washee, a scout at Fort Reno, to their relatives in Wyoming to learn definitely whether the rumors were true or false. Washee went as far as Fort Hall, where his faith failed him, and he returned with the report that the messiah was only a half-blood <note>A person of mixed-race ancestry.</note>. based on hearsay. Black Coyote stayed until the other delegates returned from the Paiute country with the announcement that everything said about the messiah and the arrival of a new earth was true. He listened eagerly to all they had to tell, participated with the others in the dance, learned the songs, and returned in April 1890 to start the first Ghost Dance in the south among the Arapaho.

The Cheyenne, being naturally skeptical, were unwilling to trust Black Coyote’s report entirely, and so they sent two of their own delegates, Little Chief and Bark, to investigate the story in the north. Sometime later, White Shield, another Cheyenne, went north alone on the same mission. Since their report was favorable, the Cheyenne also began practicing the Ghost Dance in the summer of 1890. However, they never participated with the same intensity. Although they had their own separate dance with songs in their own language, they more commonly danced together with the Arapaho and sang the Arapaho songs with them. For several years, the old Indian dances had been nearly out of use among these tribes; but since the new religion meant a revival of Indian traditions, these dances soon became common again—with the exception of the war dance and others of that kind, which were strictly prohibited by the messiah.

From this time on, the Ghost Dance grew in intensity and frequency among the Arapaho and Cheyenne. In almost every camp, the dance would be held two or three times a week, beginning around sunset and often continuing until daylight. The excitement reached a fever pitch in September 1890, when Sitting Bull <note>This refers to the Arapaho leader, not the famous Sioux chief of the same name.</note> came down from the northern Arapaho to instruct the southern tribes in the doctrine and ceremony.

At a great Ghost Dance held on the South Canadian River, about two miles below the agency at Darlington, Oklahoma, it was estimated that 3,000 Indians were present. This included nearly all of the Arapaho and Cheyenne, along with a number of Caddo, Wichita, Kiowa, and others. The first trances of the Ghost Dance among the southern tribes occurred at this time through the influence of Sitting Bull. One informant states that a leader named Howling Bull had produced trances at a dance on the Washita some time before, but the statement has not been confirmed.

Because Sitting Bull was the great advocate of the Ghost Dance among the southern tribes—being regarded almost in the same light as the messiah himself—he deserves special attention. He is now about 42 years of age, and at the start of his leadership in 1890, he was only 36. He is a full-blood Arapaho, although he has a rather light complexion and eye color. He speaks only his native language but converses with ease using the universal sign language of the plains. It was chiefly by means of this sign language that he instructed his followers among the Caddo, Wichita, and Kiowa. He is about 5 feet 8 inches tall, dignified but humble in his manner, and has a particularly winning smile. For this, he is entitled to no little credit. (G. D., 54.)

He made no claim to be a regular <term>medicine-man</term>, and so far as known never went into a trance himself. Since the failure of his predictions, especially regarding the recovery of the ceded reservation, he has fallen from his high status. Truth compels us also to state that, in spite of his role as an apostle, he is about as unpredictable in his movements as the "average" Indian.

After Sitting Bull, the principal leader of the Ghost dance among the southern Arapaho is <term>Wa'täñ-ga'a</term> or Black Coyote, from whom the town of Watonga, in Canadian County, derives its name. Black Coyote is a man of considerable importance both in his tribe and in his own estimation, and aspires to be a leader in anything that concerns his people. With a natural inclination toward religious things, it is the dream of his life to be a great priest and <term>medicine-man</term>. At the same time, he keeps a sharp lookout for his worldly affairs and has managed to accumulate considerable property in wagons and livestock, including three wives. Although still a young man, being but little more than 40 years of age, he has had his share of the world's honors, being not only a leader in the Ghost dance and other Indian ceremonies, a tribal delegate to Washington, and captain of the Indian police, but also, in his new character as an American citizen, a deputy sheriff of Canadian County. He is a good-natured fellow and proud of his possessions and titles, but at the same time thoroughly loyal and reliable in the discharge of his duties, and always ready to carry out his orders at whatever personal risk. He has repeatedly asked me to obtain a permanent license for him from the government to enable him to visit the various reservations at will as a general evangelist of Indian medicine and ceremony. Black Coyote in full uniform, with an official badge, a Harrison medal, and an immense police overcoat which he procured in Washington, and riding with his three wives in his own double-seated coach, is a magnificent and impressive spectacle. Black Coyote in a breechcloth, paint, and feathers, leading the Ghost Dance, or sitting flat on the ground and beating the earth with his hand in an excess of religious fervor, is equally impressive. It was this combination of leadership vanity and a sense of duty as a government officer that made him my first and most willing informant on the Ghost Dance, and enabled me, through him, to do so much with the Arapaho.

In his portrait (Plate CV), a number of scars will be noticed on his chest and arms. The full number of these scars is seventy, arranged in various patterns of lines, circles, crosses, etc., with a long figure of the sacred pipe on one arm. According to his own statement, they were made in obedience to a dream as a sacrifice to save the lives of his children. Several of his children had died in rapid succession, and in accordance with Indian custom, he undertook a fast of four days as an atonement to the presiding spirit. During this time, while lying on his bed, he heard a voice somewhat resembling the cry of an owl or the subdued bark of a dog. The voice told him that if he wished to save his other children, he must cut out seventy pieces of skin and offer them to the sun. He at once cut out seven pieces, held them out to the sun and prayed, and then buried them. But the sun was not satisfied, and soon after, he was warned in a vision that the full number of seventy must be sacrificed if he would save his children. He then did as directed, cutting out the pieces of skin in the various patterns indicated, offering each in turn to the sun with a prayer for the health of his family, and then burying them. Since then, there has been no death in his family. In cutting out the larger pieces, some of which were several inches long and nearly half an inch wide, the skin was first lifted up with an awl and then sliced away with a knife. This had to be done by an assistant, and Black Coyote was particular to show me by signs, sitting very erect and bracing himself firmly, that he had not flinched during the process.

As has been stated, the first trances in the southern Ghost Dance occurred at the great dance held near the Cheyenne and Arapaho agency under the auspices of <term>Sitting Bull</term> <note>This refers to the Arapaho Ghost Dance leader and apostle, not the Hunkpapa Lakota chief of the same name.</note> in September 1890. On this occasion, Cheyenne and Arapaho, Caddo, Wichita, Kiowa, and Apache, numbering perhaps 3,000, assembled and remained together for about two weeks, dancing every night until daylight. This was the largest Ghost Dance ever held in the south. After dances had been held for two or three nights, Sitting Bull announced that at the next one he would perform a great wonder in the sight of all the people, after

<header>MOONEY] HYPNOTISM IN THE DANCE</header>
<meta>The page contains minor pencil markings, including a vertical line along the right margin of the first paragraph and small checkmarks near names and specific terms.</meta>

...through which they would be able to make songs for themselves. He said no more, but dismissed them to their tipis, wondering what this miracle could be. On the next night he appeared wearing a wide-brimmed hat with a single eagle feather—the same hat in which he is generally seen. Nearly all of the two tribes of Cheyenne and Arapaho were present, and probably 600 or 800 were in the dance circle at one time. Nothing unusual occurred for several hours until the dancers had gradually worked themselves up to a high state of excitement, when Sitting Bull stepped into the circle. Going up close in front of a young Arapaho woman, he began to make hypnotic passes before her face with the eagle feather. In a few seconds she became rigid and then fell to the ground unconscious. Sitting Bull then turned his attention to another and another, and the same thing happened to each in turn until nearly a hundred were stretched out on the ground at once. As usual in the trances, some lay this way for a long time, while others recovered sooner; however, none were disturbed, as Sitting Bull told the dancers that these people were now seeing happy visions of the spirit world. When they next came together, those who had been in the trance related their experiences in the other world, telling how they had met and talked with their departed friends and joined in their old-time amusements. Many of them embodied their visions in songs, which were sung that night and afterward in the dance, and from that time the Ghost Dance was established in the south and developed rapidly along new lines. Each succeeding dance resulted in other visions and new songs, and from time to time other hypnotists arose, until almost every camp had its own.

About this time a commission arrived to negotiate with the Cheyenne and Arapaho for the sale of their reservation. The Indians were much divided in opinion, with the great majority opposing any sale whatsoever, even of their claim in the Cherokee strip, which they believed was all that the agreement was intended to cover. While the debate was in progress, Left Hand, chief of the Arapaho, went to Sitting Bull and asked his opinion on the matter. Sitting Bull advised him to sell for what they could get, as they had need of the money, and in a short time the Messiah would come and restore the land to them. On this advice Left Hand signed the agreement, in the face of threats from those opposed to it, and his example was followed by nearly all of his tribe. This incident shows how thoroughly Sitting Bull and the other Arapaho believed in the new doctrine. In view of the misery that has come upon these tribes from the sale of their reservation, it is sad to think that they could have so deceived themselves by false hopes of divine intervention. A large party of the Cheyenne refused to have anything to do with the sale or to support the transaction by accepting their share of the purchase money, even after the whites had taken possession of the lands.

The troubles in the Sioux country now began to attract public attention, and there was a suggestion of military interference. The news—

<margin>|</margin>The newspaper liar has reached an abnormal level of development in Oklahoma, and reports from Guthrie, El Reno, and Oklahoma City were filled with vivid accounts of war dances, scalping parties, and imminent uprisings, mingled with frantic appeals for troops. A typical report stated that a thousand Kickapoo were dancing, whereas in fact the entire tribe numbers only 325, very few of whom were in any way involved with the Ghost Dance. Indian Commissioner Morgan was at this time (November 1890) on a tour of inspection among the western tribes of Oklahoma, and he convinced himself that all such sensational reports were false, and that there was no danger to be feared from the dance. (*G. D.*, 55.) At the same time, the War Department assigned Lieutenant (now Captain) H. L. Scott of the Seventh Cavalry, then and now stationed at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, to investigate the meaning of the excitement and the possibility of an outbreak. Captain Scott was exceptionally well-qualified for the work due to his close relationship with the Indians and his perfect knowledge of the sign language. During December 1890, and January and February 1891, he visited the various camps of the western tribes in the territory, attended a number of dances, and talked with the leaders. His reports on the Ghost Dance are most valuable, and they confirmed the War Department's previous opinion that no danger was to be expected, and that the correct policy was one of non-interference.

The dance constantly grew stronger among the Arapaho and Cheyenne, despite the failure of the first prophecy, and it spread rapidly to the neighboring tribes, with Sitting Bull himself serving as the high priest and chief promoter. The negative report brought back by Ä'piatañ, the Kiowa, in the spring of 1891 had no effect outside of his own tribe. In the early part of that year, the Arapaho and Cheyenne sent a group of representatives, including one woman, to visit the Messiah in Nevada and bring back the latest news from heaven. They were gone for a considerable time and returned with some of the sacred ceremonial paint given to them by Wovoka, after having participated with the Paiute in a Ghost Dance under his leadership at the regular dance ground near Mason Valley. Tall Bull, captain of the Cheyenne police, was a member of this party, and Arnold Woolworth, a Carlisle student, served as the translator.

<margin>short</margin>In August 1891, another group went out, consisting of Black Coyote, Little Raven, Red Wolf, Grant Left Hand, and Casper Edson (Arapaho), and Black Sharp<insert>/</insert> Nose and Standing Bull (Cheyenne). Grant Left Hand and Casper Edson, who were Carlisle students, acted as translators, recorded the words of the Messiah, and delivered his message to their people upon their return. This message, as recorded at the time by Casper Edson, is given in the previous chapter on the doctrine of the Ghost Dance. In accordance with the Messiah's instructions, the two tribes now changed their manner of dancing from frequent small dances at each camp at irregular intervals to larger dances involving several camps together at regular intervals of six weeks, each dance

Sitting Bull and some others opposed the change, but the delegates, having the messiah's authority for the innovation, succeeded in winning their argument. From then on, they assumed a leadership role equal to Sitting Bull, who lost much of his interest in the dance from that time forward. They were gone for about two weeks and brought back a quantity of the sacred paint and many magpie feathers, the kind commonly worn by the Paiute in the Ghost Dance. This started a demand for magpie feathers, and shrewd traders soon took advantage of this fact by importing selected crow feathers, which they sold to the unsuspecting Indians as the genuine article at a rate of two feathers for a quarter. While in the land of the Paiute, the delegates took part in the Ghost Dance at Mason Valley and were thrown into a trance by Wovoka, as related in chapter IX. <note>1</note>

The Ghost Dance practically replaced all other dances among the Cheyenne and Arapaho and constantly developed new features, notably the auxiliary "<term>crow dance</term>," which was organized by Grant Left Hand. This was claimed to be a dance seen in a trance vision of the spirit world, but it is really only a modification of the "<term>Omaha dance</term>," common to the northern prairie tribes. The opening of the reservation and the arrival of white settlers served to intensify the religious fervor of the Indians, who now felt their dependent and helpless condition more than ever. However, it was impossible for the intense mental strain to last forever, and after the failure of the predictions on the appointed dates, the wild excitement gradually cooled. It crystallized into a fixed but tranquil expectation of ultimate happiness under the old conditions in another world.

In October 1892, another delegation, consisting of Sitting Bull and his wife, along with Washee, two other Arapaho, and Edward Guerrier, a Cheyenne of mixed heritage, visited the messiah. They brought back a very discouraging report; essentially, the messiah was tired of so many visitors and wanted them to go home and tell their tribes to stop dancing. Although the Indians generally refused to accept the message as genuine, the effect was naturally depressing. A year later, in October 1893, Black Coyote and several others dictated a letter to Wovoka through me, asking him to send them some of the sacred paint or anything else that would make them think of him, with "some good words to help us and our children." They also requested to know whether he had been truthfully reported by the delegates of the previous year. To one who knows these people, their simple religious faith is too touching to be a subject of amusement.

on the Little Washita and other streams on the northern boundary of the reservation, adjoining the tribes most interested in the Ghost Dance. These Comanche held a few Ghost Dances and made a few songs, but the body of the tribe would have nothing to do with it. This lack of interest was due partly to the general skeptical temperament of the Comanche, shown in their carelessness regarding ceremonial forms, and partly to their tribal pride, which forbade them from following the strange gods of another people, as they considered their own mescal rite sufficient for all their needs. Quanah Parker, their head chief, a shrewd man of mixed heritage, opposed the new doctrine and prevented its spread among his tribe.

The Ghost Dance was brought to the Pawnee, Ponca, Oto, Missouri, Kansa, Iowa, Osage, and other tribes in central Oklahoma by delegates from the Arapaho and Cheyenne in the west. The doctrine made slow progress for some time, but by February 1892, the majority of the Pawnee were dancing in confident expectation of the speedy coming of the messiah and the buffalo. Of all these tribes, the Pawnee took the most interest in the new doctrine, becoming as devoted to the Ghost Dance as the Arapaho themselves. The leader among the Pawnee was Frank White, and among the Oto was Buffalo Black. The agent in charge took strict measures against the dance and had the Oto prophet arrested and confined in the Wichita jail, threatening at the same time to cut off supplies from the tribe. As the united Oto and Missouri number only 362 in total, they were easily brought under control, and the dance was abandoned. The same method was pursued with the Pawnee prophet and his people, but as they are stronger in number than the Oto, they were proportionately harder to deal with, though the final result was the same. (*Comr., 43.*) The Osage paid very little attention to the story, perhaps because they are the wealthiest tribe in the country and feel no such urgent need for a redeemer as their less fortunate brothers. The Sauk, Fox, Kickapoo, and Potawatomi engaged in the dance only to a limited extent, because a number of the natives of these tribes, particularly the Potawatomi, are under Catholic influence, while most of the others adhere to the doctrine of Känakûk, the Potawatomi prophet mentioned in chapter V.

The Ghost Dance doctrine was communicated directly to the Caddo, Wichita, Kichai, Delaware, and Kiowa by the Arapaho and Cheyenne, their neighbors to the north. We shall speak now of the tribes first mentioned, leaving the Kiowa until last. The Caddo, Wichita, Kichai, and several remnants of related tribes, with a small band of the Delaware, numbering in all about a thousand Indians, occupy a reservation between the Washita and the South Canadian in western Oklahoma, having the Arapaho and Cheyenne on the north and west, the Kiowa on the south, and the white settlers of Oklahoma and the Chickasaw nation on the east. ...more than half of the whole group. They were the first of these tribes to take up the dance and have shown the greatest interest in it since the time it was introduced among them.

A group of Caddo first attended the great Ghost Dance held by the Cheyenne and Arapaho on the South Canadian River in the fall of 1890, during the time when Sitting Bull came down from the north and initiated the trances. After returning to their homes, they started the Ghost Dance and kept it up, singing the Arapaho songs as they had heard them on the Canadian, until Sitting Bull arrived around December 1890. He came to give them further instruction in the doctrine and to “give the feather” to the seven people selected to lead the ceremony. From this time on, the Caddo had songs and trances of their own; the chief priest and hypnotist of the dance was Nĭshkû'ntŭ, known as “Moon Head,” or John Wilson. The Caddo and the Delaware usually danced together on Boggy Creek. The Wichita and the Kichai, who adopted the doctrine from the Caddo, usually danced together on Sugar Creek, about 15 miles from the agency at Anadarko, but they showed less interest in the matter until Sitting Bull arrived around the beginning of February 1891 and “gave the feather” to their leaders. From this time, all these tribes participated in the dance wholeheartedly, sometimes dancing for days and nights together from mid-afternoon until the sun was well up in the morning. The usual custom was to continue until about midnight. Cold weather did not stop them, and they kept up the dance in the snow; those in trances sometimes lay unconscious in the snow for half an hour at a time. At this time, it was confidently expected that the “great change” would occur in the spring, and as that time drew near, the excitement became most intense. The return of the Kiowa delegate, Ä'piatañ, in mid-February 1891, with a negative report about the messiah, had no effect on the Caddo and their allies. They refused to believe his statements, claiming either that he had not seen the real messiah or that he had been bribed by the white people to make a false report.

Around the time that Black Coyote and the others went out to see the messiah in the fall of 1891, the Caddo and their allies sent out a delegation for the same purpose. The delegates were Billy Wilson and Squirrel (Caddo), Nashtowi and Lawrie Tatum (Wichita), and Jack Harry (Delaware). Tatum was a schoolboy and served as the interpreter for the party. Like the Arapaho, they came back filled with reverence for the messiah and immediately changed the time and method of the dancing, according to his instructions, to periodic dances at intervals of six weeks. These dances lasted for five consecutive days, with the dance on the last night continuing until daylight, when all the participants went down to bathe in the stream and then returned to their homes. They were dancing in this fashion when last visited in the fall of 1893.
