He is of mixed heritage, being half Delaware, one-fourth Caddo, and one-fourth French. One of his grandfathers was a Frenchman. As the Caddo lived originally in Louisiana, there is a considerable mixture of French blood among them, which is visible in his case by a fairly heavy beard. He is about 50 years of age, rather tall and well built, and wears his hair at full length, flowing loosely over his shoulders. With a good head and strong, intelligent features, he has the appearance of a natural leader. He is also prominent in the <term>mescal rite</term>, which has recently come to his tribe from the Kiowa and Comanche. He was one of the first Caddo to go into a trance, the occasion being the great Ghost Dance held by the Arapaho and Cheyenne near the Darlington agency, at which Sitting Bull presided, in the fall of 1890. Upon regaining consciousness, he had wonderful things to tell of his experiences in the spirit world, composed a new song, and from that time became the high priest of the Caddo dance. Since then his trances have been frequent, both in and out of the Ghost Dance, and in addition to his leadership in this connection, he assumes the occult powers and authority of a great medicine-man; all the powers he claims are freely acknowledged by his people.

When Captain Scott was investigating the Ghost Dance among the Caddo and other tribes of that section, during the period of greatest excitement in the winter of 1890-91, he met Wilson, of whom he has this to say:

> John Wilson, a Caddo man of much prominence, was especially affected, performing a series of gyrations that were most remarkable. At all hours of the day and night his cry could be heard all over camp, and when found he would be dancing in the ring, possibly upon one foot, with his eyes closed and the forefinger of his right hand pointed upward, or in some other ridiculous posture. Upon being asked his reasons for taking these positions, he replied that he could not help it; that it came over him just like cramps.

Somewhat later Captain Scott says:

> John Wilson had progressed finely, and was now a fully qualified doctor, a healer of diseases, and a discoverer of stolen property through supernatural means. One day, while we were in his tent, a Wichita woman entered, guided by the spirit. It was explained to us that she did not even know who lived there, but some force she could not account for brought her. Having stated her case to John, he went into a fit of the jerks, in which his spirit went up and saw “his father” <note>that is, God</note>, who directed him how to cure this woman. When he regained consciousness, he explained the cure to her and sent her away rejoicing. Soon afterward a Keechei man came in, who was blind in one eye, and who desired to have his vision restored. John again consulted his father, who informed him that nothing could be done for that eye because that man stayed away from the dance.

While the author was visiting the Caddo on Sugar Creek in the fall of 1893, John Wilson came down from his own camp to explain his part in the Ghost Dance. He wore a wide-brimmed hat, with his hair flowing down to his shoulders, and on his breast, suspended from a cord about his neck, was a curious amulet consisting of the polished end of a buffalo horn, surrounded by a circle of downy red feathers, within another circle of badger and owl claws. <header>MOONEY] A NATIVE BLESSING</header>

...the source of his prophetic and clairvoyant inspiration. The buffalo horn was “God’s heart,” the red feathers contained his own heart, and the circle of claws represented the world. When he prayed for help, his heart communed with “God’s heart,” and he learned what he wished to know. He also had much to say about the moon. Sometimes during his trances, he went to the moon, and the moon taught him secrets. It must be remembered that the sun, moon, stars, and almost every other thing in nature are considered by the Indians to be endowed with life and spirit. He claimed an intimate acquaintance with the other world and asserted positively that he could tell me “exactly what heaven is like.” Another man who accompanied him had a yellow sun with green rays painted on his forehead, with an elaborate rayed crescent in green, red, and yellow on his chin; he wore a necklace from which hung a crucifix and a brass clock-wheel—the latter, as he stated, representing the sun.

On entering the room where I sat awaiting him, Nishkû'ntŭ came forward and performed mystical motions in front of my face with his hands, in the manner of the hypnotist priests in the Ghost Dance, blowing on me at the same time. He later explained that this was to blow evil things away from me before beginning to talk about religious subjects. He was also kind enough to say that he had prayed for enlightenment before coming and had found that my heart was good. Laying one hand on my head and grasping my hand with the other, he prayed silently for some time with a bowed head. Then, lifting his hand from my head, he passed it over my face, down my shoulder and arm to my hand, which he grasped and pressed slightly, and then released the fingers with a graceful upward sweep, as if in a minuet. The first part of this—the laying of the hands upon the head, then drawing them down along the face and chest or arms—is the standard Indian form of blessing, reverential gratitude, or prayerful entreaty. It occurs frequently in connection with the Ghost Dance, when the believers ask for help from the priests or beg for the prayers of the older people.

The next day, about twenty or more Caddo people passed by on their way to the agency, all dressed and painted for a dance that was to be held that night. They stopped for a while to see us. On entering the room where we were, the whole company—men, women, and children—performed the same ceremony with each of the occupants in turn, beginning with Wilson and myself and ending with the members of the family. The ceremony took a considerable amount of time and was both beautiful and impressive. Not a word was said by either party during this time, except when someone in an outpouring of devotion would utter prayerful exclamations aloud, like the undertone of a litany. Every face wore a look of reverent solemnity, from the old men and women down to little children of six and eight years. Several of them, especially the women, trembled while praying, as if under the excitement of the Ghost Dance. Once the religious greeting was over, the women of the family and those of the party went out to prepare dinner, while the rest remained to listen to the doctrinal discussion.

<summary>Nishkû'ntŭ describes the spiritual symbolism of his sacred objects and his visions of the moon, followed by a detailed account of a traditional Caddo blessing ritual. The author observes a group ceremony involving over twenty people, noting the profound solemnity and physical devotion shared by all participants.</summary>

<page-num>906</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

The Kiowa were predisposed to accept the doctrine of the Ghost Dance. No tribe had made a more desperate resistance to the encroachment of the white people upon their hunting grounds, and even after the failure of the last effort of the confederated tribes in 1874–75, the Kiowa were slow to accept the reality of defeat. The result of this unsuccessful struggle was the end of the boundless freedom of the prairie, where they had roamed without question from Dakota almost to central Mexico; from then on, the tribes were confined within the narrow limits of reservations. Within five years, the great southern buffalo herd was extinct, and the Indians suddenly found themselves both prisoners and paupers. The change was so swift and terrible in its effects that they could not believe it was real and final. It seemed to them like a dream of sorrow, a supernatural cloud of darkness sent to punish their failings, but one that could be lifted from them by prayer and sacrifice. Their old men spoke of years when the buffalo were scarce or had moved far away, but never since the beginning of the world had there been a time when there were no buffalo. They believed the buffalo still lived beyond their horizon or in caves under the earth, and that with its return, prosperity and freedom would also come back. Before we wonder at their faith, we must remember that the disappearance of these millions of buffalo in the space of just a few years has no parallel in the records of natural history.

In 1881, a young Kiowa named *Da'tekañ*, "Keeps-his-name-always," began to "make medicine" to bring back the buffalo. He set up a sacred tipi, in front of which he erected a pole with a buffalo skin at the top, and made for himself a red priestly robe trimmed with rows of eagle feathers. Then, standing in front of his tipi, he called the people around him and told them that he had been commanded and empowered in a dream to bring back the buffalo. He told them that if they strictly observed the prayers and ceremonies he commanded, the great herds would once more cover the prairie. His listeners believed his words, promised strict obedience, and gave freely of their blankets and other property to reward his efforts on their behalf. *Da'tekañ* retired to his sacred tipi where, in his feathered robe of office, he continued to prophesy and make buffalo medicine for a year, until he died without seeing the realization of his hopes. The excitement caused by his predictions came to the notice of the agent then in charge, who mentions it in his annual report without understanding the cause. On a Kiowa calendar obtained by the author, the event is recorded in a pictograph representing the medicine man in his tipi, with his scarlet robe over his shoulders and a buffalo beneath his feet (figure 84).

About six years later, in 1887, another prophet named *Pa'-íñgya*, "In the Middle," revived the prophecy, claiming to be the heir to all the supernatural powers of his late predecessor. He expanded the doctrine by asserting, logically enough, that since the white people were responsible for the disappearance of the buffalo, the white people themselves would be destroyed by the gods when the time was near for the return of

These earlier movements laid the groundwork for the Kiowa's eventual acceptance of the Ghost Dance religion.</summary>

In October 1890, shortly after Ä'piatañ's departure, Sitting Bull, the Arapaho prophet of the Ghost Dance, came down from his tribe and gave new momentum to the excitement among the Kiowa. This event is also recorded on the same Kiowa calendar in a well-drawn picture representing a buffalo standing beside the figure of a man (Figure 86). It is also indicated less clearly on another calendar obtained from the tribe. Sitting Bull confirmed, as if from personal knowledge, everything that had been told about the Messiah, and predicted that the new earth would arrive in the following spring, 1891. The Kiowa gathered on the Washita, at the mouth of Rainy Mountain Creek, and here, at the largest Ghost Dance ever held by the tribe, Sitting Bull consecrated seven men and women as leaders of the dance and teachers of the doctrine by giving each one a sacred feather to be worn in the dance as the badge of priesthood.

Until the Ghost Dance reached the prairie tribes, their women had never before been elevated to such dignity as to be allowed to wear feathers in their hair. After "giving the feather" to the chosen leaders, they were taught the songs and ritual of the dance. At first, the songs were all in the Arapaho language, but after the trances, which now began to occur frequently, the Kiowa composed their own songs.

Among the dreamers and prophets who now rose to prominence was one who deserves more than a brief mention. Frequently, these vigils were undertaken at the request of friends of sick people to obtain spiritual knowledge of the proper remedies to be applied, or at the request of surviving relatives who wished to hear from their departed friends in the other world. He is now about 55 years of age, quiet and dignified in manner, with a thoughtful facial expression which fits well with his character as a priest and seer. His intellectual nature is further shown by the fact that he has invented a system of <term>ideographic writing</term> which is nearly as distinct from the ordinary Indian pictograph system as it is from our own alphabet. It is based on the sign language of the plains tribes, with the primary effort being to convey an idea through a pictured representation of the gesture sign; but, as in the evolution of the alphabet, a part is frequently used to represent the whole, and numerous arbitrary or extra characters are added, until the result is a well-developed seed of an alphabetic system. He has taught the system to his sons, and by this means was able to keep up a correspondence with them while they were attending Carlisle school. It is incomprehensible to the rest of the tribe. I have specimens of this curious writing method, obtained from the father and his sons, which may be discussed at length at a future time. In the picture of Äsa'tito'la (*Plate CVI*), he holds in one hand a paper on which is depicted one of his visions, while in the other is the pointer with which he explains its meaning.

*Plate CVII* herewith represents this vision. On this occasion, after reaching the spirit world, he found himself on a vast prairie covered with herds of buffalo and ponies, represented respectively in the picture by short black and green lines at the top. He went on through the buffalo, the way being indicated by the dotted green lines, until he came to a large Kiowa camp, in which, according to their old custom, nearly every tipi had its distinctive style of painting or decoration to show which family it belonged to; all these families are still represented in the tribe. He went on to the point indicated by the first heavy blue mark, where he met four young women, whom he knew as having died years before, returning on horseback with their saddle-pouches filled with wild plums. After some conversation, he asked them about two brothers, his relatives, who had died some time ago. He went in the direction pointed out by the young women and soon met the two young men coming into camp with a load of fresh buffalo meat hanging at their saddles. Their names were Emanki'na, "Can't-hold-it," a policeman, and E'pea, "Afraid-of-him," who had died while held as a prisoner of war in Florida about fifteen years before. It will be noted that they are represented in the picture as armed only with bows and arrows, in agreement with the Ghost-dance doctrine of a return to traditional ways. # MOONEY] Ä’PIATAÑ’S PILGRIMAGE

to continue, and as he did, he came to an immense circle of Kiowa dancing the Ghost Dance around a cedar tree, indicated by the black circle with a green figure resembling a tree in the center. He stood for a while near the tree, shown by another blue mark, when he saw a woman he knew leave the dance. He hurried after her until she reached her own tipi and entered it—shown by the blue mark beside the red tipi with red flags on the ends of the tipi poles—at which point he turned around and came back. She belonged to the family of the great chief Set-t’aiñti, "White Bear," as indicated by the red tipi with red flags; no other warrior in the tribe had such a tipi. When he asked about his own relatives, he was directed to the other side of the camp, where he met a man—represented by the heavy black mark—who told him his own people were inside the next tipi. Upon entering, he found the whole family, consisting of his father, two brothers, two sisters, and several children, feasting on fresh buffalo beef from a kettle hung over the fire. They welcomed him and offered him some of the meat, which for some reason he was afraid to taste. To convince him it was good, they held it up for him to smell, at which point he woke up and found himself lying alone on the mountain.

Ä’piatañ traveled first to Pine Ridge, where he was welcomed by the Sioux, who had much to say about the new messiah in the west. They encouraged him to stay and join them in the Ghost Dance, but he refused and hurried on to Fort Washakie, where he met the northern Arapaho and the Shoshoni, whom he called the "northern Comanches." There, the new prophecy was the main subject of conversation. After stopping only long enough to learn the proper route to the Paiute country, he traveled over the Union Pacific railroad to Nevada. Upon arriving at the agency at Pyramid Lake, the Paiute provided him with a wagon and an Indian guide to travel across the country to the home of Wovoka in the upper end of Mason Valley. The next day, he was allowed to meet him. The result was a complete disappointment. A single interview convinced him of the total falsity of the messiah's claims and the deceptive nature of the hopes offered to believers.

Saddened and disgusted, Ä’piatañ did not stay, but started at once on his return home. On his way back, he stopped at the Bannock agency at Fort Hall, Idaho, and from there sent a letter to his people, stating briefly that he had seen the messiah and that the messiah was a fraud. This was the first indication the Kiowa had received from an Indian source that their hopes were not well-founded. The author was present when the letter was received at Anadarko and read to the assembled Indians by Ä’piatañ’s sister, an educated woman named Laura Dunmoi, formerly of the Carlisle school. The result was a division of opinion. Some of the Indians, feeling that the ground had been pulled out from under them, at once gave up all hope and accepted the inevitability of despair. Others were inclined to doubt the genuineness of the letter, as it had come through the medium of a white man, and decided

<header>MOONEY] Ä'PIATAÑ'S RETURN</header>

The council was held at the agency at Anadarko, Oklahoma, on February 19, 1891; the author was among those present on the occasion. It was a great gathering, representing every tribe on the reservation; there were also a number of Arapaho in attendance who had accompanied Sitting Bull from the other agency. Everything said was interpreted in turn into English, Kiowa, Comanche, Caddo, Wichita, and Arapaho. This was a slow process and necessitated frequent repetition, so that the talk occupied the entire day. Ä'piatañ first made his report, which was interpreted into the various languages. Questions were asked by the agent, Mr. Adams, and by leading Indians, and after the full details had been obtained in this manner, Sitting Bull, the Arapaho, was called on to make his statement. The scene was dramatic in the highest degree. Although in a certain sense Sitting Bull himself was on trial, it meant more than that to the assembled tribes. Their power, prosperity, and happiness had declined; their very race was withering away before the white man. The messiah doctrine promised a restoration of the old conditions through supernatural assistance. If this hope was without foundation, the Indian had no future and his day was forever past.

After some preliminaries, Ä'piatañ arose and told his story. He had traveled as previously related until he arrived at the home of Wovoka in Mason Valley. There, he was told that the messiah could not be seen until the next day. Upon finally being admitted to his presence, he found him lying down, his face covered with a blanket, and singing to himself. When he had finished the song, the messiah uncovered his face and asked Ä'piatañ, through an interpreter, what he wanted. Since Ä'piatañ had approached with great reverence, fully believing that the messiah was omniscient, able to read his secret thoughts and to speak all languages, this question was a great surprise to him, and his faith at once began to waver. However, he told who he was and why he had come, and then asked that he be permitted to see some of his dead relatives, particularly his little child. Wovoka replied that this was impossible, and that there were no spirits there to be seen. With their mixture of Christian and aboriginal ideas, many of the Indians had claimed that this messiah was the actual Christ and bore the scars of the crucifixion upon his hands and feet. Not seeing these scars, Ä'piatañ expressed some doubt as to whether Wovoka was really the messiah he had come so far to see. To this, Wovoka replied that he need go no farther, for there was no other messiah. He went on to say that he had preached to Sitting Bull and the others and had given them a new dance, but that some of them, especially the Sioux, had twisted things and made trouble, and now Ä'piatañ had better go home and tell his people to stop the whole business. Discouraged and sick at heart, Ä'piatañ left his presence, convinced that there was no longer a god in Israel.

After the story had been told and interpreted to each of the tribes, Sitting Bull was called on for his statement. He told how he had visited the messiah a year before and what the messiah had said to—

him. The two versions were widely different, and there can be little doubt that Wovoka made claims and prophecies, supported by hypnotic performances, which he afterward retracted when he found that the excitement had grown beyond his control and resulted in an Indian outbreak. Sitting Bull insisted on the truth of his own statements, and when accused by Ä'piatañ of deceiving the Indians in order to obtain their property, he replied that he had never asked them for the ponies which they had given him, and that if they did not believe what he had told them, they could come and take their ponies back. Ä'piatañ replied that such was not the Kiowa way; what had once been given was not taken back. Sitting Bull spoke in a low, musical voice, and the soft Arapaho syllables contrasted pleasantly with the choking sounds of the Kiowa and the boisterous loudness of the Wichita. I could not help feeling pity for him when, at the close of the council, he drew his blanket around him and left the gathering to cross the river to the Caddo camp, attended only by his faithful Arapaho followers. For his services in reporting against the dance, Ä'piatañ received a medal from President Harrison.

<margin>||</margin>
For some time, this marked the end of the Ghost Dance among the Kiowa; while a few of the tribes were inclined to doubt the honesty or accuracy of the report, the majority accepted it as final, and from that time on, the dance became a mere amusement for children. The other tribes, however—the Caddo, Wichita, and their allies—refused to accept the report, claiming that white men had hired Ä'piatañ to lie to the Indians and that he had never actually seen the messiah as he claimed. Even the Apache, despite their close tribal connection with the Kiowa, continued to follow the doctrine and the dance.

**Note.**—Since the above was written and while awaiting publication, there has been a revival of the Ghost Dance among the Kiowa, brought about chiefly through the efforts of Bi'äñk'i, Pa'tadal, and others of its former priests. After several times dispersing the dancers and threatening them with severe penalties if they persisted, the Indian agent was finally obliged to grant permission at the earnest request of a delegation of chiefs and leading men of the tribe. As a result, in September 1894, the Kiowa publicly revived the ceremony in a great dance on the Washita River, which lasted four days and was attended by several thousand Indians from all the surrounding tribes.

<summary>Following Ä'piatañ's report, the Kiowa generally abandoned the Ghost Dance as a religious practice, though other tribes like the Caddo and Wichita continued to believe in the messiah. A later note records a significant revival of the dance among the Kiowa in 1894 led by former priests.</summary>

### EXPLANATION OF PLATE CIX

The original of this picture was drawn in colored inks on buckskin by Yellow Nose, a Ute captive living among the Cheyenne, in 1891. It was obtained from him by the author and is now kept in the National Museum in Washington. In addition to being a particularly fine specimen of Indian pictography, it provides an excellent idea of the Ghost Dance as it existed at that time among the Cheyenne and Arapaho. The dancers are in full costume, adorned with paint and feathers. The women of the two tribes are clearly distinguished by their hairstyles; the Cheyenne women have their hair braided at the sides, while the Arapaho women wear theirs hanging loosely. Two of the women carry children on their backs. One of the men carries the <term>bä'qati wheel</term>, another a <term>shinny stick</term>, and a woman holds out the <term>sacred crow</term>, while several wave handkerchiefs that help produce the hypnotic effect. In the center are several people with their arms outstretched and rigid, while at one side, the medicine man is seen hypnotizing a subject who holds out a blue handkerchief toward him. The spotted object on the ground behind the medicine man is a shawl that has fallen from the shoulders of the woman standing nearby.

# CHAPTER XV

## THE CEREMONY OF THE GHOST DANCE

In chapter <term>xi</term>, we spoke of the Ghost Dance as it existed among the <term>Paiute</term>, <term>Shoshoni</term>, <term>Walapai</term>, and <term>Cohonino</term>, west of the mountains. We shall now give a more detailed account of the ceremony and the connected ritual among the prairie tribes.

### AMONG THE NORTHERN CHEYENNE

<insert>(</insert>According to <term>Dr Grinnell</term>, the Ghost Dance among the northern <term>Cheyenne</term> had several features not found in the south. Four fires were built outside of the dance circle and about 20 yards back from it, toward each of the cardinal points. These fires were built of long poles set up on end, so as to form a simple cone, much like how the poles of a tipi are erected. The fires were lighted at the bottom, and thus made high bonfires, which were kept burning as long as the dance continued.<insert>)</insert>
(J. F. L., 5.)

### AMONG THE SIOUX

<insert>(</insert>Perhaps the most important feature in connection with the dance among the <term>Sioux</term> was the “<insert>(</insert>ghost shirt,”<insert>)</insert> already noticed and <insert>(</insert>to be described more fully hereafter.<insert>)</insert> <insert>(</insert>On account of the scarcity of buckskin, these shirts were almost always made of white cloth cut and decorated in the Indian fashion. The <term>Sioux</term> wore no metal of any kind in the dance, differing in this respect from the southern tribes, who wore on such occasions all their finery of German silver ornaments. The <term>Sioux</term> also sometimes began the dance in the morning, as well as in the afternoon or evening. Another important feature not found among the southern tribes, except for the <term>Kiowa</term>, was the tree planted in the center of the circle and decorated with feathers, stuffed animals, and strips of cloth.<insert>)</insert>

At a Ghost Dance at <term>No Water's</term> camp, near <term>Pine Ridge</term>, as described by <term>J. F. Asay</term>, formerly a trader at the agency, the dancers first stood in line facing the sun, while the leader, standing and facing them, made a prayer and waved the “ghost stick” over their heads—a staff about 6 feet long, trimmed with red cloth and feathers of the same color. After waving the stick over them in this way, he faced the sun and made another prayer, after which the line closed up to form a circle around the tree and the dance began. During the prayer, a woman standing near the tree held out a pipe toward the sun, while another beside her held out several (four?) arrows from which the points had been removed. On

On another occasion, at a <term>Ghost Dance</term> at the same camp, four arrows, headed with bone in the old-fashioned way, were shot up into the air from the center of the circle and afterward gathered up and hung upon the tree, together with the bow, a gaming wheel and sticks, and a staff of peculiar shape (<term>ghost stick</term>?). See <term>plate CXI</term>. The ceremonies of fasting, painting, and the sweat-bath in connection with the <term>Ghost Dance</term> among the <term>Sioux</term> have been already described.

The best account of the dance itself and of the <term>ghost shirt</term> is given by <term>Mrs. Z. A. Parker</term>, who was a teacher on the <term>Pine Ridge reservation</term> at that time, writing of a <term>Ghost Dance</term> observed by her on <term>White Clay Creek</term>, on June 20, 1890. We quote at length from her description:

> We drove to this spot about 10:30 o'clock on a delightful October day. We came upon tents scattered here and there in low, sheltered places long before reaching the dance ground. Presently we saw over three hundred tents placed in a circle, with a large pine tree in the center, which was covered with strips of cloth of various colors, eagle feathers, stuffed birds, claws, and horns—all offerings to the <term>Great Spirit</term>. The ceremonies had just begun. In the center, around the tree, were gathered their <term>medicine men</term>; also those who had been so fortunate as to have had visions and in them had seen and talked with friends who had died. A company of fifteen had started a chant and were marching abreast, others coming in behind as they marched. After marching around the circle of tents they turned to the center, where many had gathered and were seated on the ground.
> I think they wore the <term>ghost shirt</term> or ghost dress for the first time that day. I noticed that these were all new and were worn by about seventy men and forty women. The wife of a man called <term>Return-from-scout</term> had seen in a vision that her friends all wore a similar robe, and on reviving from her trance she called the women together and they made a great number of the sacred garments. They were of white cotton cloth. The women’s dress was cut like their ordinary dress, a loose robe with wide, flowing sleeves, painted blue at the neck, in the shape of a three-cornered handkerchief, with the moon, stars, birds, etc., interspersed with real feathers, painted on the waist and sleeves. While dancing they wound their shawls about their waists, letting them fall to within 3 inches of the ground, with the fringe at the bottom. In the hair, near the crown, a feather was tied. I noticed an absence of any manner of bead ornaments, and, as I knew their vanity and fondness for them, wondered why it was. Upon making inquiries I found they discarded everything they could which was made by white men.
> The <term>ghost shirt</term> for the men was made of the same material—shirts and leggings painted in red. Some of the leggings were painted in stripes running up and down, others running around. The shirt was painted blue around the neck, and the whole garment was fantastically sprinkled with figures of birds, bows and arrows, the sun, moon, and stars, and everything they saw in nature. Down the outside of the sleeve were rows of feathers tied by the quill ends and left to fly in the breeze, and also a row around the neck and up and down the outside of the leggings. I noticed that a number had stuffed birds, squirrel heads, etc., tied in their long hair. The faces of all were painted red with a black half-moon on the forehead or on one cheek.
> As the crowd gathered about the tree the high priest, or master of ceremonies, began his address, giving them directions as to the chant and other matters. After he had spoken for about fifteen minutes they arose and formed in a circle. As nearly as I could count, there were between three and four hundred persons. One stood directly behind another, each with his hands on his neighbor’s shoulders. After walking about a few times, chanting, “Father, I come,” they stopped marching, but

She describes the construction and symbolic decoration of the ghost shirts and dresses, noting the intentional exclusion of all white-made ornaments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the eyewitness account by Mrs. Z. A. Parker of a Sioux Ghost Dance on White Clay Creek in 1890, describing the physical intensity of the dance, the participants' emotional distress, and the trances that followed.</meta>

They remained in the circle and set up the most fearful, heart-piercing wails I ever heard—crying, moaning, groaning, and shrieking out their grief, and naming their departed friends and relatives. At the same time, they took up handfuls of dust from at their feet, washing their hands in it and throwing it over their heads. Finally, they raised their eyes to heaven, their hands clasped high above their heads, and stood straight and perfectly still, invoking the power of the <term>Great Spirit</term> to allow them to see and talk with their people who had died. This ceremony lasted about fifteen minutes, when they all sat down where they were and listened to another address, which I did not understand, but which I later learned were words of encouragement and assurance of the coming messiah.

When they stood up again, they enlarged the circle by facing toward the center, taking hold of hands, and moving around in the manner of school children in their play of "needle's eye." And now the most intense excitement began. They would go as fast as they could, their hands moving from side to side, their bodies swaying, and their arms—with hands gripped tightly in their neighbors'—swinging back and forth with all their might. If someone, more weak and frail, came near to falling, he would be jerked up and into position until exhausted nature gave way. The ground had been worked and worn by many feet until the fine, flour-like dust lay light and loose to the depth of two or three inches. The wind, which had increased, would sometimes pick it up, enveloping the dancers and hiding them from view. In the ring were men, women, and children; the strong and the robust, the weak consumptive, and those near to death's door. They believed those who were sick would be cured by joining in the dance and losing consciousness. From the beginning they chanted, to a monotonous tune, the words—

> Father, I come;
> Mother, I come;
> Brother, I come;
> Father, give us back our arrows.

They would repeat all of this over and over again until first one and then another would break from the ring, stagger away, and fall down. One woman fell a few feet from me. She came toward us, her hair flying over her face, which was purple, looking as if the blood would burst through; her hands and arms moved wildly; every breath was a pant and a groan; and she fell on her back and went down like a log. I stepped up to her as she lay there motionless, but with every muscle twitching and quivering. She seemed to be perfectly unconscious. Some of the men and a few of the women would run, stepping high and pawing the air in a frightening manner. Some told me later that they had a sensation as if the ground were rising toward them and would strike them in the face. Others would drop where they stood. One woman fell directly into the ring, and her husband stepped out and stood over her to prevent them from trampling on her. No one ever disturbed those who fell or took any notice of them except to keep the crowd away.

<margin>✓</margin>
They kept up the dancing until fully 100 persons were lying unconscious. Then they stopped and seated themselves in a circle, and as each one recovered from his <term>trance</term>, he was brought to the center of the ring to relate his experience. Each told his story to the <term>medicine-man</term>, and he shouted it to the crowd. Not one in ten claimed that he saw anything. I asked one Indian—a tall, strong fellow, straight as an arrow—what his experience was. He said he saw an eagle coming toward him. It flew round and round, drawing nearer and nearer until he put out his hand to take it, and then it was gone. I asked him what he thought of it. "Big lie," he replied. I found by talking to them that not one in twenty believed it. After resting for a time, they would go through the same performance, perhaps three times a day. They practiced fasting, and every morning those who joined in the dance were obliged to immerse themselves in the creek. (*Comr., 44.*)

<summary>This page provides a firsthand account of the Sioux Ghost Dance, detailing the participants' extreme physical exertion, the onset of trances, and the subsequent sharing of visions. The observer notes the skepticism of some participants despite the communal rituals of fasting, chanting, and dancing.</summary>

## SONG REHEARSALS

Just like church choirs, the leaders—both men and women—frequently gathered privately in a tipi to rehearse new or old songs for the next dance. During the first winter I spent among the Arapaho, I had frequent opportunities to be present at these rehearsals, as the snow was too deep for a long time to allow dancing outside. After I had gained their confidence, the Arapaho police invited me to their camp at night to hear them practice the songs in anticipation of better weather for dancing. From then on, rehearsals were held in Black Coyote’s tipi almost every night until the snow melted, with each session usually lasting about three hours.

On these occasions, eight to twelve people were present, sitting in a circle on the low beds around the fire in the center. Black Coyote acted as the master of ceremonies and opened the proceedings by filling and lighting the redstone pipe. He offered the first puff to the sun, then reversed the stem in an offering to the earth, next presented the pipe to the fire, and then to each of the four cardinal points. He then took a few puffs himself before passing the pipe to his neighbor, who performed the same rituals before smoking. In this way, the pipe went around the circle, with each person taking only a few puffs before passing it on. The pipe was then returned to its pouch, and Black Coyote—standing with his face toward the northwest, the messiah’s country, with eyes closed and arms outstretched—offered a fervent prayer for the help and prosperity of his tribe, closing with an earnest petition to the messiah to hasten his coming. The others listened in silence with bowed heads. 

After the prayer ended, they consulted about which song to sing first, which Black Coyote then started in a clear, musical bass, while the others joined in. From time to time, they offered explanations when the meaning of a song was unclear. They invited me to ask for any songs I wished to hear, and these songs were repeated over and over again to give me the opportunity to write them down, though they postponed detailed discussion for another time. Usually, the men alone were the singers, but sometimes Black Coyote’s wives or other women present joined in the songs. It was noticeable that even in these rehearsals, the women easily became caught up in the excitement of the dance. Finally, around 10 o'clock, everyone rose together and sang the closing song, *Ni’ninitubi’na Huhu*, “The Crow has given the signal,” and the rehearsal concluded. On one occasion, before I had transcribed this song, I asked for it so that I might write it down; however, they explained that we must wait, as it was the closing song, and if they sang it then, they would have to stop for the night.

## PREPARATIONS FOR THE DANCE

On several occasions, the dance ground was consecrated before the performance. One of the leaders would walk all around the area, sprinkling a type of sacred powder over the ground while praying.

## SONG REHEARSALS

Just like church choirs, the leaders—both men and women—frequently gathered privately in a tipi to rehearse new or old songs for the next dance. During the first winter I spent among the Arapaho, I had frequent opportunities to be present at these rehearsals, as the snow was too deep for a long time to allow dancing outside. After I had gained their confidence, the Arapaho police invited me to their camp at night to hear them practice the songs in anticipation of better weather for dancing. From then on, rehearsals were held in Black Coyote’s tipi almost every night until the snow melted, with each session usually lasting about three hours.

On these occasions, eight to twelve people were present, sitting in a circle on the low beds around the fire in the center. Black Coyote acted as the master of ceremonies and opened the proceedings by filling and lighting the redstone pipe. He offered the first puff to the sun, then reversed the stem in an offering to the earth, next presented the pipe to the fire, and then to each of the four cardinal points. He then took a few puffs himself before passing the pipe to his neighbor, who performed the same rituals before smoking. In this way, the pipe went around the circle, with each person taking only a few puffs before passing it on. The pipe was then returned to its pouch, and Black Coyote—standing with his face toward the northwest, the messiah’s country, with eyes closed and arms outstretched—offered a fervent prayer for the help and prosperity of his tribe, closing with an earnest petition to the messiah to hasten his coming. Frequently in the dance, one or more of the leaders, while sitting within the circle, would beat upon the earth with his extended palm, then lay his hand upon his head, afterward blow into his hand, and then repeat the operation, praying all the time. Sometimes the hypnotist would beat the ground in the same way and then lay his hand on the head of the subject (plate cxv). No satisfactory explanation of this ceremony was obtained, beyond the general idea that the earth, like the sun, the fire, and the water, is sacred.

<insert>(</insert>
### GIVING THE FEATHER
<insert>)</insert>

The ceremony of “giving the feather” has been already mentioned. <insert>(</insert>(This was an official ordination of the priests in the dance, conferred on them by the apostle who first brought the ceremony to the tribe.)<insert>)</insert> Among the Arapaho, Caddo, Kiowa, and adjoining tribes in the south, the feather was conferred by Sitting Bull himself. The feather was thus given to seven leaders, or sometimes to fourteen—that is, seven men and seven women—the number seven being sacred with most tribes <insert>✓</insert>and more particularly in the Ghost Dance. The feather, which was worn upon the head of the dancers, was either that of the crow, the sacred bird of the Ghost Dance, or of the eagle, which is sacred in all Indian religions. If from the crow, two feathers were used, being attached at a slight angle to a small stick which was thrust into the hair. (See Arapaho song 8.) The feathers were previously consecrated by the priest with prayer and ceremony. The chosen ones usually reciprocated with presents of ponies, blankets, or other property. After having thus received the feather, the tribe began to make songs of its own, having previously used those taught them by the apostle from his own language.

Besides the seven leaders who wear the sacred crow feathers as emblems of their leadership, nearly all the dancers wear feathers variously painted and ornamented, and the preparation of these is a matter of much concern. The dancer who desires instruction on this point usually takes with him six friends, so as to make up the sacred number of seven, and goes with them to one who has been in a trance and has thus learned the exact method in vogue in the spirit world. At their request, this man prepares for each one a feather, according to what he has seen in some trance vision, for which they return thanks, usually with a small present. The feathers are painted in several colors, each larger feather usually being tipped with a small down feather painted in a different color. On certain occasions, a special day is set apart for publicly painting and preparing the feathers for all the dancers, the work being done by the appointed leaders of the ceremony.

In making the request, the dancer lays his hands upon the head of the leader and says, "My father, I have come to be painted, so that I may see my friends; have pity on me and paint me," as the sacred paint is believed to sharpen spiritual vision as well as be beneficial to physical health. The painting consists of elaborate designs in red, yellow, green, and blue upon the face, with a red or yellow line along the parting of the hair. Suns, crescents, stars, crosses, and birds (crows) are the designs in most common use.

### ( THE CEREMONY )

The dance commonly begins about the middle of the afternoon or later, after sundown. When it begins in the afternoon, there is always an intermission of an hour or two for supper. The announcement is made by the criers—old men who assume this office apparently by tacit understanding—who go about the camp shouting in a loud voice for the people to prepare for the dance. The preliminary painting and dressing is usually a work of about two hours. When all is ready, the leaders walk out to the dance place, and facing inward, join hands so as to form a small circle. Then, without moving from their places, they sing the opening song, according to a previous agreement, in a soft undertone. Having sung it through once, they raise their voices to their full strength and repeat it, this time slowly circling around in the dance. The step is different from that of most other Indian dances, but very simple: the dancers move from right to left, following the course of the sun, advancing the left foot and following it with the right, hardly lifting the feet from the ground. For this reason, it is called by the Shoshoni the <gloss>ga-ut-la-ti-ga</gloss>, or "dragging dance." All the songs are adapted to the simple measure of the dance step. As the song rises and swells, the people come singly and in groups from the various tipis, and one after another joins the circle until any number from fifty to five hundred men, women, and children are in the dance. When the circle is small, each song is repeated through a number of circuits. If large, it is repeated only through one circuit, measured by the return of the leaders to the starting point. Each song is started in the same manner: first in an undertone while the singers stand still in their places, and then with full voice as they begin to circle around. At intervals between the songs, and more especially after the trances have begun, the dancers unclasp hands and sit down to smoke or talk for a few minutes. At such times, the leaders sometimes deliver short addresses or sermons, or relate the recent trance experience of a dancer. In holding each other’s hands, the dancers usually intertwine their fingers instead of grasping the hand as we do. Only an Indian could keep a blanket in place as they do under such circumstances. Old people hobbling along with sticks, and little children hardly past the toddling period, sometimes form a part of the circle, the more vigorous dancers...

Dogs are driven off from the neighborhood of the circle lest they should run against any of those who have fallen into a trance and thus awaken them. The dancers themselves are careful not to disturb the trance subjects while their souls are in the spirit world. Full Indian dress is worn, with buckskin, paint, and feathers, but among the Sioux, the women discarded the belts ornamented with disks of German silver because the metal had come from the white man. Among the southern tribes, on the contrary, hats were sometimes worn in the dance, although this was not considered in strict accordance with the doctrine.)

<margin>✓ X</margin>
(No drum, rattle, or other musical instrument is used in the dance, except sometimes by an individual dancer in imitation of a trance vision. In this respect particularly, the Ghost dance differs from every other Indian dance. Neither are any fires built within the circle, so far as is known, with any tribe except the Walapai. The northern Cheyenne, however, built four fires in a peculiar fashion outside of the circle, as already described. With most tribes, the dance was performed around a tree or pole planted in the center and variously decorated. In the southern plains, however, only the Kiowa seem ever to have followed this method, as they sometimes danced around a cedar tree. On breaking the circle at the end of the dance, the performers shook their blankets or shawls in the air with the idea of driving away all evil influences. On later instructions from the messiah, all then went down to bathe in the stream—the men in one place and the women in another—before going to their tipis. The idea of washing away evil things, spiritual as well as earthly, by bathing in running water is too natural and universal to need comment.)

The peculiar ceremonies of prayer and invocation, with the laying on of hands and the stroking of the face and body, have several times been described and need only be mentioned here. (As trance visions became frequent, the subjects strove to imitate what they had seen in the spirit world, especially where they had taken part with their departed friends in some of the old-time games. In this way, gaming wheels, shinny sticks, hummers, and other toys or implements would be made and carried in future dances, accompanied with appropriate songs, until the dance sometimes took on the appearance of an exhibition of Indian curios on a small scale.)

Since these two tribes are involved, it does not require an extensive description here. Although claimed by its inventors as a direct inspiration from the other world—where they saw it performed by "crows," or the spirits of departed friends—it is really only a modification of the picturesque <term>Omaha dance</term> of the prairie tribes, with the addition of religious features borrowed from the new doctrine. The men who participate are stripped to their breechcloths, with their whole bodies painted as in the <term>Omaha dance</term>, and they wear elaborate pendants of multicolored feathers hanging down behind from the waist. A massive drum is an important feature. Men and women take part, and the songs refer to the general subject of the crow and the <term>messiah</term>, but they are set to a variety of dance steps and movements performed by the dancers. As the leaders, who are mostly young men, are constantly studying new features, the <term>crow dance</term> has become one of the most attractive ceremonies among the prairie tribes. <term>Hypnotism</term> and <term>trances</term> form an essential feature of this, as they do in the <term>Ghost dance</term> proper. (See plate CXIX.)

### THE HYPNOTIC PROCESS

(The most important feature of the <term>Ghost dance</term>, and the secret of the <term>trances</term>, is <term>hypnotism</term>.) It has been hastily assumed that hypnotic knowledge and ability belong only to a highly developed civilization, such as that of India and ancient Egypt, or to the most modern period of scientific investigation. However, the fact is that practical knowledge—if not a full understanding—of such things belongs to people who live close to nature, and many of the stories told by reliable travelers about the strange performances of indigenous <term>shamans</term> can be explained only by this theory. Numerous references in the works of the early Jesuit missionaries, the Puritan writers of New England, and English explorers further to the south indicate that hypnotic ability, no less than dexterity in sleight of hand, formed part of the <term>medicine-man's</term> equipment from the St. Lawrence to the Gulf. Enough has been said in the chapters on <term>Smoholla</term> and the <term>Shakers</term> to show that <term>hypnotism</term> exists among the tribes of the Columbia River, and the author has had frequent opportunity to observe and study it in the <term>Ghost dance</term> on the plains. It cannot be said that the Indian priests understand the phenomenon, for they attribute it to a supernatural cause, but they know how to produce the effect, as I have witnessed hundreds of times. In treating the subject in connection with the <term>Ghost dance</term>, the author must be understood as speaking from the point of view of an observer and not as a psychological expert.

Immediately after arriving among the <term>Arapaho</term> and <term>Cheyenne</term> in 1890, I heard numerous stories of wonderful things that occurred in the <term>Ghost dance</term>—how people died, went to heaven and came back again, and how they talked with dead friends and brought back messages from the other world. Quite a number who had "died" in this way were mentioned, and their adventures in the spirit land were related with great detail...

detail, but since most of the testimony came from white men, none of whom had seen the dance for themselves, I maintained a scientific attitude of skepticism. As far as could be determined, none of the educated people at the agency had considered the subject worthy of serious consideration or attempted to learn whether the reports were true or false. In talking with the Indians, however, I found them unanimous in their statements about the visions, until I began to think there might be something to it.

The first clue to the explanation came from Paul Boynton's account of his own experience in a trance. Paul was an exceptionally bright student from the <term>Carlisle Indian Industrial School</term> who acted as my interpreter. His brother had died some time before, and since Paul was anxious to see and talk with him—which the new doctrine taught was possible—he attended the next <term>Ghost dance</term>. Following the regular formula, he placed his hands upon the head of <term>Sitting Bull</term> and asked for help to see his dead brother. Paul has an inquiring mind, and besides his natural longing to see his brother again, he was motivated, as he said himself, by a desire to try “every Indian trick.” He then described how <term>Sitting Bull</term> had hypnotized him with an eagle feather and the motion of his hands, until he fell unconscious and actually saw his brother. He woke up just as he was about to speak to him, probably because one of the dancers had accidentally brushed against him as he lay on the ground. He later composed a song about his experience, which was afterward sung during the dance. From his account, it seemed almost certain that the secret was <term>hypnotism</term>. This explanation might have occurred to me sooner, but my previous Indian informants, like some other witnesses, had only described their trance visions and forgotten to mention how those visions were induced.
<margin>x</margin>

This occurred in winter, and the ground was covered deeply with snow, which stopped the dancing for several weeks. In the meantime, I took the opportunity to visit the tipis every night to learn the songs and talk about the new religion. When the snow melted, the dances were renewed. Because I had gained the confidence of the Indians by this time, I was invited to be present, and thereafter, on numerous occasions, I was able to watch the whole process by which the trances were produced. From the outside, hardly anything can be seen of what goes on within the circle. However, because I was a part of the circle myself, I was able to see everything that occurred inside. By focusing on one subject at a time, I was able to note all the stages of the phenomenon: from the moment the subject first attracted the notice of the <term>medicine man</term>, through the staggering, the rigidity, and the unconsciousness, and finally back to wakefulness. On two occasions, my partner in the dance—a woman both times—came under the influence. This allowed me to notice the very first nervous tremor of her hand and track it as it increased in violence until she broke away and staggered toward the <term>medicine man</term> within the circle.

Young women are usually the first to be affected, followed by older women, and finally men. Sometimes, however, a man proves as sensitive as the

average woman. In particular, I have seen one young Arapaho man become rigid in a trance night after night. He was a Carlisle student who spoke good English and was employed as a clerk in a store. He afterward took part in the sun dance, dancing for three days and nights without food, drink, or sleep. He is of a quiet, religious disposition, and if he were of white parentage, he would perhaps have become a minister; but being an Indian, the same tendency leads him into the Ghost Dance and the sun dance. The fact that he could endure the terrible ordeal of the sun dance goes to show that his physical constitution is not frail, as is frequently the case with hypnotic or trance subjects. So far as personal observation goes, the hypnotic subjects are usually as strong and healthy as the average member of their tribe. It seems to be a question more of temperament than of bodily condition or physique. After having observed the Ghost Dance among the southern tribes at intervals during a period of about four years, it is apparent that the hypnotic tendency is growing, although the original religious excitement is dying out. The trances are now more numerous among the same number of dancers. Some begin to tremble and stagger almost at the beginning of the dance, without any effort on the part of the medicine man, while formerly it was usually late in the night before the trances began, although the medicine men were constantly at work to produce such a result. In many, if not in most cases, the medicine men themselves have been in trances produced in the same fashion, and must thus be considered "sensitives" as well as those hypnotized by them.

<insert>A pencil bracket appears in the left margin encompassing the text from "(Not every" to "responsible.)"</insert>
(Not every leader in the Ghost Dance is able to bring about the hypnotic sleep, but anyone may try who feels so inspired. Excepting the seven chosen ones who start the songs, there is no priesthood in the dance; the authority of <gloss>certain men</gloss> ~~such~~ men as Sitting Bull and Black Coyote is due to the voluntary recognition of their superior ability or interest in the matter. Any man or woman who has been in a trance, and has thus derived inspiration from the other world, is at liberty to go within the circle and endeavor to bring others into a trance. Even when the result is unsatisfactory, there is no interference with the performer, as it is held that he is but the passive instrument of a higher power and therefore in no way responsible.) A marked instance of this is the case of Cedar Tree, an Arapaho policeman, who took much interest in the dance, attending nearly every performance in his neighborhood, consecrating the ground and working within the circle to hypnotize the dancers. He was in an advanced stage of consumption <note>tuberculosis</note>, and was nervous and excitable to an extreme degree; perhaps it was for this reason that those who came under his influence in the trance constantly complained that he led them on the "devil's road" instead of the "straight road." They said that he made them see monstrous and horrible shapes, but never the friends whom they wished to see. On this account, they all dreaded to see him at work within the circle, but no one commanded him to stop, as it was held that he was controlled by a stronger power and was to be pitied rather than blamed for his lack of success. We shall now describe the hypnotic process as used by the operators, along with the various stages of the trance. The hypnotist, usually a man, stands within the ring, holding in his hand an eagle feather or a scarf or handkerchief, which may be white, black, or any other color. Sometimes he holds the feather in one hand and the scarf in the other. As the dancers circle around singing the songs in time with the dance step, the excitement increases until the more sensitive participants are visibly affected. In order to hasten the result, certain songs are sung to a quicker tempo (notably the Arapaho song beginning *Nâ'nanû'naatani'na Hu'hu.* We shall assume that the subject is a woman). The first indication that <gloss>when</gloss> she is becoming affected is a slight muscular tremor, which is distinctly felt by <gloss>the</gloss> two partners who hold her hands on either side. The medicine man is on the watch, and as soon as he notices the woman's condition, he comes over and stands immediately in front of her. He looks intently into her face while whirling the feather or the handkerchief, or both, rapidly in front of her eyes, moving slowly around with the dancers at the same time but constantly facing the woman. Throughout this process, he keeps up a series of sharp exclamations, "Hu! Hu! Hu!" like the rapid breathing of an exhausted runner. (From time to time, he changes the motion of the feather or handkerchief from a whirling movement to a rapid up-and-down movement in front of her eyes. For a while, the woman continues to move around with the circle of dancers, singing the song with the others, but usually before the circuit is completed)
<margin>when</margin> <gloss>she</gloss> loses control of herself entirely and, breaking away from the partners who have hold of her hands on either side, she staggers into the ring while the circle at once closes up again be<gloss>hind</gloss> her. She is now standing before the medicine man, who gives hi<gloss>s</gloss> <gloss>w</gloss>hole attention to her, whirling the feather swiftly in front of her eyes, waving his hands before her face as though fanning her, and drawing his hand slowly from the level of her eyes away to one side or upward into the air while her gaze follows it with a fixed stare. All the while, he keeps up the "Hu! Hu! Hu!" as the song and the dance go on around them without a pause. For a few minutes, she continues to repeat the words of the song and keep time with the step, but in a staggering, drunken fashion. Then the words become unintelligible sounds and her movements become violently spasmodic, until at last she becomes rigid, with her eyes shut or fixed and staring, and stands there uttering low, pitiful moans (plate CXVII). If this occurs in the daytime, the operator tries to stand with his back to the sun so that the full sunlight shines into the woman's face (plate CXVI). The subject may retain this fixed, immovable posture for an indefinite time, but at last falls heavily to the ground, unconscious and motionless (plate CXVIII). The dance and the song never

stop, but as soon as the woman falls, the medicine man gives his attention to another person among the dancers. The first one may lie unconscious for ten or twenty minutes, or sometimes for hours, but no one goes near to disturb her, as her soul is now communing with the spirit world. At last, consciousness gradually returns. A violent tremor seizes her body, just as it did at the beginning of the fit. A low moan comes from her lips, and she sits up and looks about her like someone waking from sleep. Her whole form trembles violently, but at last she rises to her feet and staggers away from the dancers, who open the circle to let her pass. (All the symptoms of recovery, except for the stiffness, occur in the exact reverse order of those that precede unconsciousness.)

Sometimes before falling, the hypnotized subject runs wildly around the circle or out over the prairie, or goes through various wild movements like those of a lunatic. On one occasion—but only once—I saw the medicine man point his finger almost in the face of the hypnotized subject, and then, withdrawing his finger, describe a large circle with it around the tipis. The subject followed the direction indicated, sometimes being hidden from view by the crowd, and finally returned, with his eyes still fixed and staring, to the place where the medicine man was standing. (There is frequently a good deal of humbug mixed with these performances, with some evidently pretending to be hypnotized in order to attract notice or to bring about such a condition through the power of imitation; however, the greater portion is unquestionably genuine and beyond the control of the participants.) In many instances, the hypnotized person spins around for minutes at a time like a dervish, or whirls their arms with apparently impossible speed, or assumes and keeps most uncomfortable positions until the final fall, which would be impossible to maintain for any length of time under normal conditions. Frequently, a number of people are within the ring at once, in all the various stages of hypnotism. The proportion of women affected this way is about three times that of men.

### THE AREA COVERED BY THE DANCE

It is impossible to give more than an approximate statement regarding the geographic extent of the Ghost Dance and the messiah doctrine, or the number of Indians involved. According to the latest official report, there are about 146,000 Indians west of the Missouri River, excluding the Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory. Probably all these tribes heard of the new doctrine, but only a portion took any active interest in it. Generally speaking, it was never taken up by the great Navaho tribe, by any of the Pueblos except for the Taos, or by any of the numerous tribes of the Columbia region. The thirty or thirty-five tribes more or less involved with the dance have a total population of about 60,000 people. A number of these were practically unanimous in their acceptance of the new doctrine, notably the Paiute, Shoshoni, Arapaho, Cheyenne, Caddo, and Pawnee, while among others, such as the Comanche, only a

Only a small minority ever engaged in it. Only about one-half of the 26,000 Sioux took an active part in it. It may safely be said, however, that the doctrine and ceremony of the Ghost Dance found more followers among our tribes than any similar Indian religious movement within the historical period, with the single possible exception of the crusade started by Tenskwatawa, the Shawnee prophet, in 1805. (See plate LXXXV.)

### PRESENT CONDITION OF THE DANCE

Among most of these tribes, the movement is already extinct, having died a natural death, except in the case of the Sioux. The Shoshoni and some others lost faith in it after the failure of the first predictions. The Sioux probably discontinued the dance before their final surrender, as the Battle of Wounded Knee and the subsequent events convinced even the most fanatical believers that their expectations of invulnerability and supernatural assistance were false. The Paiute were still dancing a year ago, and as their dream has received no such harsh awakening as that of the Sioux, they are probably still patiently awaiting the great deliverance despite repeated postponements; however, the frenzied earnestness of the early period has long since faded. The Kiowa, who rejected the doctrine after the negative report of Ä'piatañ, have recently taken up the dance again and are now dancing as religiously as ever under the leadership of the old men, even though the progressive group within the tribe is strongly opposed to it. Among the other tribes in Oklahoma—especially the Arapaho, Cheyenne, Caddo, Wichita, Pawnee, and Oto—the Ghost Dance has become a part of tribal life and is still performed at frequent intervals. The feverish expectation of a few years ago has now settled into something closely approaching the Christian hope of a reunion with departed friends in a happier world at some point in the unknown future.

As for the great messiah himself, when last heard from, Wovoka was on exhibition as an attraction at the Midwinter Fair in San Francisco. By this time, he has undoubtedly retired into his original obscurity.

# CHAPTER XVI

## PARALLELS IN OTHER SYSTEMS

> I will pour out my spirit upon all people; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions.—*Joel*.
> 
> How is it then, brothers? When you come together every one of you has a doctrine, has a revelation.—*I Corinthians*.

### THE BIBLICAL PERIOD

The remote in time or distance is always strange. The familiar present is always natural and a matter of course. Beyond the narrow range of our horizon, imagination creates a new world, but as we advance in any direction, or as we go back over forgotten paths, we always find a continuity and a succession. The human race is one in thought and action. The systems of our highest modern civilizations have their counterparts among all the nations, and their chain of parallels stretches backward link by link until we find their origin and interpretation in the customs and rites of our own barbarian ancestors, or of our still-existing aboriginal tribes. There is nothing new under the sun.

The Indian messiah religion is the inspiration of a dream. Its ritual is the dance, the ecstasy, and the trance. Its priests are hypnotics and cataleptics. All these have formed a part of every great religious development of which we have knowledge from the beginning of history.

In the ancestors of the Hebrews, as described in the Old Testament, we have a pastoral people, living in tents, acquainted with metal working, but without letters, agriculture, or permanent habitations. They had reached about the level of our own Navaho, but were below that of the Pueblo. Their mythological and religious system was closely parallel. Their chiefs were priests who assumed power to govern by inspiration from God, communicated through frequent dreams and waking visions. Each of the patriarchs is the familiar confidant of God and his angels, ascending to heaven in dreams and receiving direct instructions in waking visits, and regulating his family and his tribe, and ordering their religious ritual, in accordance with these instructions. Jacob, alone in the desert, sleeps and dreams, and sees a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down upon it, and God himself, who tells him of the future greatness of the Jewish nation. So Wovoka, asleep on the mountain, goes up to the Indian heaven and is told by the Indian god of the coming restoration of his race. Abraham is “tempted” by God and commanded to sacrifice his son, and proceeds to carry out the supernatural injunction. So Black Coyote dreams and is commanded to sacrifice himself for the sake of his children.

<summary>This chapter establishes the Ghost Dance as part of a universal human religious tradition, drawing direct parallels between the experiences of Indian prophets and those of biblical patriarchs like Jacob and Abraham.</summary>

# MOONEY] DREAMS AND TRANCES 929

Coming down to a later period, we find the Chaldean Job declaring that God speaks “in a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls upon men; then he opens the ears of men and seals their instruction.” The whole of the prophecies are given as direct communications from the other world, with the greatest particularity of detail, as, for instance, in the beginning of the book of Ezekiel, where he says that “it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God.”

In the New Testament, representing the results of six centuries of development beyond the time of the prophets and in intimate contact with more advanced civilizations, we still have the dream as the controlling influence in religion. In the very beginning of the new dispensation we are told that, while Joseph slept, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, and as a result “Joseph, being raised from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him.” The most important events in the history of the infant redeemer are regulated, not in accordance with the ordinary manner of probabilities, but by dreams.

The four gospels are full of inspirational dreams and trances, such as the vision of Cornelius, and that of Peter, when he went up alone upon the housetop to pray and “fell into a trance and saw heaven opened,” and again when “a vision appeared to Paul in the night,” of a man who begged him to come over into Macedonia, so that “immediately we attempted to go into Macedonia, assuredly concluding that the Lord had called us.” In another place Paul—the same Paul who had that wonderful vision on the road to Damascus—declares that he knew a man who was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words. In Paul we have the typical religious evangelist, a young enthusiast, a man of sensibility and refinement above his fellows, so carried away by devotion to his ideal that he attaches himself to the most uncompromising sect among his own people. When it seems to be assailed by an alien force, not content simply to hold his own belief, he seeks and obtains official authority to root out the heresy. As he goes on this errand, “breathing out threats and slaughter,” the mental strain overcomes him. He falls down in the road, hears voices, and sees a strange light. His companions raise him up and lead him by the hand into the city, where for several days he remains sightless without food or drink. From this time he is a changed man. Without any previous knowledge or investigation of the new faith, he believes himself called by heaven to embrace it, and the same irrepressible enthusiasm which had made him its bitterest persecutor leads him now to defend it against all the world and even to cross the sea into a far country in obedience to a dream to spread the doctrine. In many respects he reminds us forcibly of such later evangelists as Fox and Wesley.

The cloudy indistinctness which Wovoka and his followers attribute to the Father as he appears to them in their trance visions has numerous parallels in both Testaments. At Sinai the Lord declares to Moses, “I

"I come to you in a thick cloud," and thereafter whenever Moses went up the mountain or entered into the tabernacle to receive revelations, "the Lord descended upon it in a cloudy pillar." Job also tells us that "thick clouds are a covering to him," and Isaiah says that he "rides upon a swift cloud," which reminds us of the Ghost song of the Arapaho representing the Indian redeemer as coming upon the whirlwind. Moses goes up a mountain to receive inspiration like Wovoka of the Paiute and Bi'äñk'i of the Kiowa. As Wovoka claims to bring rain or snow at will, so Elijah declares that "there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word," while of the Jewish Messiah himself his wondering disciples say that even the winds and the sea obey him.

Fasting and solitary contemplation in lonely places were as powerful aids to the trance condition in Bible days as they are now among the tribes of the plains. When Daniel had his great vision by the river Hiddekel, he tells us that he had been mourning for three full weeks, during which time he "ate no pleasant bread, neither did meat nor wine enter my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all." When the vision comes, all the strength and breath leave his body and he falls down, and "then I was in a deep sleep on his face, and my face toward the ground." Six hundred years later, Christ is "led by the spirit into the wilderness, being forty days tempted by the devil, and in those days he ate nothing." Another instance occurs at his baptism, when, as he was coming out of the water, he saw the heavens opened and the spirit like a dove, and heard a voice, and immediately was driven by the spirit into the wilderness. In the transfiguration on the mountain, when "his face did shine as the sun," and in the agony of Gethsemane, with its mental anguish and bloody sweat, we see the same phenomena that appear in the lives of religious enthusiasts from Mohammed and Joan of Arc down to George Fox and the prophets of the Ghost dance.

Dancing, which forms so important a part of primitive rituals, had a place among the forms of the ancient Hebrews and of their neighbors, although there are but few direct references to it in the Bible. The best example occurs in the account of the transfer of the ark to Zion, where there were processions and sacrifices, and King David himself "danced before the Lord with all his might."

### MOHAMMEDANISM

Six hundred years after the birth of Christianity another great religion, which numbers its adherents by the hundred million, had its origin in the same region and among a kindred Semitic race. Its prophet and high priest was the cataleptic Mohammed, who was born about the year 570 and died in 642. In infancy and all through life he was afflicted with epileptic attacks and fainting fits, during which he would lose all appearance of life without always losing inner consciousness. It was while in this condition that he received the visions and revelations on which he built his religious system. Frequently at such times it was necessary to wrap him up to preserve life in his body, and
