at other times he was revived by being drenched with cold water. For one two-year period, his mental state was such—marked by hallucinations—that he doubted his own sanity, believed he was possessed by evil spirits, and contemplated suicide. 

> “It is debated whether Mohammed was epileptic, cataleptic, hysterical, or something else. Sprenger seems to think that the answer to this medical question is the key to the entire problem of Islam.” (“Mohammedanism,” in *Encyclopedia Britannica*.) 

To how many other systems might such an answer be the key?

We are told that normally his body had little natural warmth, but whenever the angel appeared to him—as the Mohammedan biographers describe it—sweat broke out on his forehead, his eyes turned red, he trembled violently, and he would bellow like a young camel—all the symptoms of a severe epileptic seizure. Usually, the seizure ended in a faint. There is no doubt that he was sincere in his claim of divine inspiration. His final hours were serene and peaceful, and there is no evidence that he had the slightest doubt about the reality of his mission as a prophet sent by God. Some of his inspiration came in dreams, and he used to say that a prophet’s dream is a revelation. At times, the revelation came to him without any painful or strange symptoms.

The seizure during which he received the revelation of his religious mission is described this way, occurring after a long period of despondency and mental hallucinations: 

> “In this morbid emotional state, he is said to have heard a voice; upon raising his head, he saw Gabriel, who assured him he was the prophet of God. Frightened, he returned home and asked for a covering. He had a seizure, and they poured cold water on him; when he regained consciousness, he heard these words: ‘Oh, you covered one, arise, and preach, and magnify your Lord.’ From then on, we are told, he received revelations without interruption. Before this supposed revelation, he had been medically treated for the evil eye, and when the Koran first descended to him, he fell into fainting fits where, after violent shuddering, his eyes closed and his mouth foamed.” (*Gardner, Faiths of the World.*)

Solitude also played a large role in his visions, as a great part of his early life was spent in the lonely work of a shepherd among the Arabian mountains. Like other prophets, he asserted that various angels had offered him control over the stars, the sun, the mountains, and the sea. Furthermore, his followers claim most positively that his great ascent into the seven heavens was made physically and while fully awake, not merely in spirit while asleep. They supported this assertion with “the declarations of God and his prophet, the imâms of the truth, the verses of the Koran, and thousands of traditions,” as earnestly as religious enthusiasts the world over have ever supported the impossible.

This direct lineage becomes even clearer when we learn how Mohammed, upon his return from speaking with God in the seventh heaven, meets Moses again. Moses convinces him that the religious duties prescribed by God for the faithful are too burdensome and goes back with him to plead with the Lord to reduce the daily prayers from fifty to five, just as Abraham pleaded for Sodom.

The spirit world of our Indians is a place where death and old age are unknown, and where everyone is happy in the simple happiness they knew on earth—hunting, feasting, and playing the old-time games with former friends, but without war, for there everything is at peace. This ideal happiness is perhaps material, but it is the kind of happiness the world might long for, with nothing in it that is crude or beyond reasonable probability. The Semitic ideal, from which our own is derived, is very different. We see one conception in the book of Revelation and another, six hundred years later, in the vision of Mohammed, which is childish in the extreme. Among its wonders is a *houri* who comes out of a quince, and whose body is composed of camphor, amber, and musk. Then there is a rooster that stands with its feet on the lowest earth while its head reaches the highest heaven and its outstretched wings reach the limits of space; its task is to praise the Lord every morning and prompt all the roosters on earth to crow after him. There is an angel who bathes daily in a river, after which he flaps his wings, and from every drop that falls from them, an angel is created with 20,000 faces and 40,000 tongues, each of which speaks a distinct language that is unintelligible to the rest. But the masterpiece is the tree *tooba*, whose fruit is the food of the inhabitants of paradise. Every branch produces a hundred thousand different-colored fruits, while from its roots run rivers of water, milk, wine, and honey. As if this were not enough, the tree also produces ready-made clothing. "On the tree were baskets filled with garments made of the brocade and satin of paradise. A million baskets are allotted to each believer, each basket containing a hundred thousand garments, all of different classes and fashions"—and so on *ad nauseam*. (*Merrick's Mohammed*.) When we reflect that this is accepted by more than 150,000,000 civilized people of the East, from whom we have derived much of our own culture, we may, perhaps, be more tolerantly disposed toward the American Indian belief.

The spirit world of our Indians is a place where death and old age are unknown, and where everyone is happy in the simple happiness they knew on earth—hunting, feasting, and playing the traditional games with former friends, but without war, for there everything is at peace. This ideal happiness is perhaps material, but it is the kind of happiness the world might long for, with nothing in it that is crude or beyond reasonable probability. <header>MOONEY] JOAN OF ARC</header>

beatified as the patron saint of France. Naturally of a contemplative disposition, she was accustomed from earliest childhood to long fasts and solitary spiritual reflections, in which she brooded over the miserable condition of her country, which was then overrun by English armies. When she was 13 years old, she had a vision in which a voice spoke to her from out of a great light, telling her that God had chosen her to restore France. She immediately fell on her knees and made a vow of virginity and total devotion to the cause; from that day until the time of her cruel death, she believed herself inspired and guided by supernatural voices to lead her countrymen against the invader. A simple peasant girl, she sought out the royal court and boldly announced her divine mission to the king. Her manner made such an impression that she was assigned a command. Putting on a soldier's dress and carrying a sword which she claimed had come to her through miraculous means, she led the armies of France, performing superhuman feats of courage and endurance and winning victory after victory for three years until she was finally captured. After a long and harassing mockery of a trial, in which the entire machinery of the law and the church was brought into action for the destruction of one poor girl barely 19 years old, she was finally condemned and burned at Rouen, supposedly as a witch and a heretic, but in reality as the most dangerous enemy of English tyranny in France.

She was constantly hearing these spirit voices, which she called “her voices” or “her counsel.” They spoke to her with clear words in the ripple of the village fountain, in the evening bells, in the rustling of the leaves, and in the sighing of the wind. Sometimes it was the warlike archangel Michael, but more often it was the gentle Saint Katherine, who appeared to her as a beautiful woman wearing a crown. Her visions must be attributed to the influence of the troubled times in which she lived, acting on an enthusiastic, unquestioning religious temperament. She is described as physically robust and intellectually sharp, aside from her hallucinations, as was proven in her trial; there is no evidence that she was subject to epilepsy or other abnormal conditions such as those belonging to Mohammed and most others of the same class. Her long and frequent fasts undoubtedly aided the result. She claimed no supernatural powers outside of her specific mission, and in every public undertaking she relied entirely on the guidance of her voices.

Toward the end, these voices were accompanied by other hallucinations, together with premonitions of her coming death. On one occasion, while assaulting a garrison, her men fled, leaving her standing on the moat with only four or five soldiers. Seeing her danger, a French officer galloped up to rescue her and impatiently asked her why she stood there alone. Lifting her helmet from her face, she looked at him with astonishment and replied that she was not alone—that she had 50,000 men with her—and then, despite his pleas, she turned to her phantom army and shouted out her commands to bring logs to bridge the moat. It was in April, while standing alone on the ram-

I have seen them with my physical eyes, and I believe they are saints as firmly as I believe that God exists.”

It was in my father’s garden at noon in the summer. I had fasted the day before. The voice came from the right side, near the church, and there was a great light with it. When I came into France, I heard it frequently. I believe it was sent to me from God. After I heard it three times, I knew it was the voice of an angel. I understand perfectly what it says. It commanded me to be good and go to church often, and it told me I must go into France. Two or three times a week it said I must go into France, until I could no longer rest where I was. It told me I should lift the siege of Orleans, and that Robert de Baudricourt would give me people to escort me. Twice he rejected me, but the third time he received me and sent me on my way.”

The examiners were very curious to know by what sign she had recognized the king when she had first seen him among his courtiers. To this question, she said she must first consult with Saint Katherine before replying, and afterward continued: “The sign was a crown. The first time I saw the king, he had the sign, and it meant that he should hold the kingdom of France. I neither touched it nor kissed it. The angel came by the command of God and entered through the door of the room. I came with the angel up the steps to the king’s room, and the angel went before the king and bowed low before him, and said: ‘My lord, here is your sign; take it.’ He left the way he had come. There were a number of other angels with him, and Saint Katherine and Saint Margaret. He left me in the little chapel. I was neither glad nor afraid, but I was very sorrowful, and I wish he had taken my soul away with him.”

To another question she replied emphatically: “If I were at judgment, if I saw the fire kindled and the faggots ablaze and the executioner ready to stir the fire, and if I were in the fire, I would say no more, and to the death I would maintain what I have said in the trial.”

The end came at last in the marketplace of Rouen, when this young girl, whose name for years had been a terror to the whole English army, was dragged in her white shroud and bound to the stake, and saw the wood heaped up around her and the cruel fire lit under her feet. “Brother Martin, standing almost in the draft of the flames, heard her sob with a last sublime effort of faith, bearing witness to the God whom she trusted: ‘My voices have not deceived me!’ And then came death.” *(Parr, Jeanne d’Arc.)*

### DANCE OF SAINT JOHN

In 1374 an epidemic of maniacal religious dancing broke out on the lower Rhine and spread rapidly over Germany, the Netherlands, and into France. The victims of the mania claimed to dance in honor of Saint John. Men and women went about dancing hand in hand, in pairs, or in a circle, on the streets, in the churches, at their homes, or wherever they might be, hour after hour without rest until they fell into convulsions. While dancing they sang doggerel verses in honor of Saint John and uttered unintelligible cries. Of course they saw visions. At last whole companies of these crazy fanatics—men, women, and children—went dancing through the country, along the public roads, and into the cities, until the clergy felt compelled to interfere, and cured the dancers by exorcising the evil spirits that moved them. In the fifteenth century the epidemic broke out again. The dancers were now formed into divisions by the clergy and sent to the church of Saint Vitus at Rotestein, where prayers were said for them, and they were led in procession around the altar and dismissed cured. Hence the name of Saint Vitus’ dance given to one variety of abnormal muscular tremor. *(Schaff, Religious Encyclopedia.)*

### THE FLAGELLANTS

About the same time another strange religious extravagance spread over western Europe. Under the name of Flagellants, thousands of enthusiasts banded together with crosses, banners, hymns, and all the paraphernalia of religion, and went about in procession, publicly scourging one another as an atonement for their sins and the sins of mankind in general. They received their first impetus from the preaching of Saint Anthony of Padua in the thirteenth century. About the year 1260 the movement broke out nearly simultaneously in Italy, France, Germany, Austria, and Poland, and afterward spread into Denmark and England. It was at its height in the fourteenth century. In Germany in 1261 the devotees, preceded by banners and crosses, marched with faces veiled and bodies bared above the waist, and scourged themselves twice a day for thirty-three successive days in

The mania finally wore itself out, but reappeared in 1349 with a more systematic organization. According to Schaff, “When they came to towns, the groups marched in regular military order while singing hymns. At the time of flagellation, they selected a square, a churchyard, or a field. Taking off their shoes and stockings and forming a circle, they girded themselves with aprons and lay down flat on the ground. . . . The leader then stepped over each person, touched them with the whip, and told them to rise. As each person was touched, they followed the leader and imitated him. Once all were on their feet, the flagellation began. The brothers went two by two around the whole circle, striking their backs until the blood trickled down from the wounds. The whip consisted of three thongs, each with four iron teeth. During the flagellation, a hymn was sung. After everyone had gone around the circle, the whole group fell to the ground again, beating their breasts. On arising, they whipped themselves a second time. While the brothers were putting on their clothes, a collection was taken from the audience. The scene was concluded by the reading of a letter from Christ, which an angel had brought to earth and which commended the pilgrimages of the Flagellants. The fraternities never stayed longer than a single day in a town. They gained great popularity, and it was considered an honor to entertain them.” (*Schaff, Religious Encyclopedia.*) The society still exists among the Latin races, although it is banned by the church. As recently as 1820, a procession of Flagellants passed through the streets of Lisbon. Under the name of Penitentes, they have several organizations in the Mexican towns of our Southwest, where they periodically appear in processions, inflicting horrible self-torture on themselves. They even go to the extent of binding one of their members upon a cross, which is then set up in the ground, while the blood streams down the victim's body from wounds made by a crown of cactus thorns and from innumerable gashes caused by the thorny whips. Such things among people called civilized enable us to understand the feeling that leads the Indian to offer himself as a willing sacrifice in the sun dance and other propitiatory rites.

### RANTERS, QUAKERS, AND FIFTH-MONARCHY MEN

The middle of the seventeenth century was a time of great religious and political upheaval in England. Hatreds were intense and persecutions were cruel and bitter, until people’s minds gave way under the strain. “The air was thick with reports of prophecies and miracles, and there were people of all parties who lived on the borderland between sanity and insanity.” This was due chiefly to the long-continued mental tension that weighed on the whole population during this troubled period, and in particular cases to wholesale confiscations through which families were ruined, and to confinement in wretched prisons, suffering from

...insufficient food and brutal treatment. Individuals even within the established church began to assert supernatural power, while numerous new sects sprang up, incorporating prophecy, miracle-working, hypnotism, and convulsive ecstasy into their doctrine or ritual. Chief among these were the Ranters, the Quakers, and the Fifth-Monarchy Men. The first and last groups have disappeared along with the conditions that produced them; but the Quakers, being based on a principle, have outlasted persecution. By discarding the excesses that belonged to their early period, they are now established on a permanent foundation under the name of the "Society of Friends." One of the Ranter prophets, in 1650, claimed to be the reincarnation of Melchizedek and even declared his own divinity. He asserted that certain people then living were Cain, Judas, Jeremiah, and others, whom he had raised from the dead; the strangest part was that the people involved strongly affirmed the truth of his assertion. Others among them claimed to perform miracles and to produce lights and apparitions in the dark. In Barclay's opinion, all the evidence "supports the view that these people were mad, and had a unique power of producing a kind of sympathetic madness or temporary mental aberration in others."

<margin>//</margin>
We are more familiar with the Quakers (Friends), although it is not generally known that they were originally prone to similar practices. This is a fact, however, as is shown by the name itself. Their founder, George Fox, claimed and believed that he had the gift of prophecy and clairvoyance, and of healing by a mere word. His biographer, Janney, who belonged to the same denomination, apparently sees no reason to doubt that such was the case. As might be expected, he was also a believer in dreams.

We are told that on one occasion, upon entering the town of Lichfield, "a very remarkable <term>exercise</term> <note>a specific Quaker term for a spiritual burden or conviction</note> occupied his mind. Walking through the streets without his shoes, he cried, 'Woe to the bloody city of Lichfield!' His feelings were deeply affected, for there seemed to be a channel of blood running down the streets, and the market place appeared like a pool of blood." Upon inquiry, he learned that a large number of Christians had been put to death there during the reign of the Emperor Diocletian thirteen centuries earlier. "He therefore attributed the <term>exercise</term> <note>spiritual burden</note> that came upon him to the awareness he was given of the blood of the martyrs."

We are also told that he "received <term>evidence</term> <note>a spiritual premonition or intuitive sign</note>" of the Great Fire of London in 1666 before the event. Janney narrates at length a "still more remarkable vision" of the same fire by another Friend, "whose prophecy is well-attested." According to the account, this man rode into the city as if he had come in haste and went up and down the streets for two days, prophesying that the city would be destroyed by fire. To others of his own denomination, he declared that he had seen a vision of the event some time before, but had delayed declaring it as commanded until he felt the fire within his own chest.

When the fire occurred as he had predicted, he stood before the flames with arms outstretched, as if to stop their advance, until he was forcibly taken away by his friends.

In mental and physical temperament, Fox seems to have closely resembled Mohammed and the Indian prophets of the Ghost Dance. We are told that he suffered much mental distress and was often under great temptation. “He fasted much, and walked about in solitary places. Taking his Bible, he sat in hollow trees or secluded spots, and often at night he walked alone in silent meditation.” At one time “he fell into such a condition that he looked like a corpse, and many who came to see him supposed him to be really dead. In this trance he continued for fourteen days, after which his sorrow began to fade, and with humility and tears of joy he acknowledged the infinite love of God.” (*Janney, George Fox.*)

The sect obtained the name of Quakers from the violent tremblings which overcame the worshipers in the early days, and which they regarded as manifestations of divine power upon them. These convulsions were so violent that, as their own historian tells us, on one occasion the house itself seemed to be shaken. According to another authority, men and women sometimes fell down and lay upon the ground struggling as if for their lives. Their ministers, however, seem not to have encouraged such exhibitions, but tried to relieve the fit by putting the patient to bed and administering soothing medicines. (“*Quakers,*” *Encyclopedia Britannica.*)

The Fifth-Monarchy Men were a small group of religious followers who arose about the same time, proclaiming that the “Fifth Monarchy” prophesied by Daniel was near, when Christ would come down from heaven and reign visibly upon earth for a thousand years. In 1657 they formed a plot to kill Cromwell, and in 1661 they broke out in insurrection at night, parading the streets with a banner on which was depicted a lion, proclaiming that Christ had come and declaring that they were invulnerable and invincible, since “King Jesus” was their invisible leader. Troops were called out against them, but the Fifth-Monarchy Men, expecting supernatural assistance, refused to surrender, and fought until they were nearly all shot down. The leaders were afterward tried and executed. (*Janney’s George Fox and Schaff’s Religious Encyclopedia.*)

### FRENCH PROPHETS

Forty years later, about the end of the seventeenth century, another sect of convulsionists, being driven out of France, “found a refuge in Protestant countries [and] carried with them the disease, both of mind and body, which their long sufferings had produced.” They spread into Germany and Holland, and in 1706 reached England, where they became known as “French prophets.” Their meetings were characterized by such extravagant convulsions and trance performances that they became the wonder of the ignorant and the scandal of the more

They had visions and trances and were subject to violent physical agitations. Men and women, and even little children, were so moved that onlookers were struck with great wonder and amazement. Their powerful exhortations and prophetic warnings were heard and received with reverence and awe.”

At one time Charles Wesley had reason to stay overnight with a gentleman who belonged to the sect. Wesley was unaware of this fact until, as they were about to go to bed, his new friend suddenly fell into a violent fit and began to gobble like a turkey. Wesley was frightened and began exorcising him, so that he soon recovered from the fit; then they went to bed, although the evangelist confesses that he himself did not sleep very soundly with Satan so near him.

Some time later, Wesley and several companions visited a prophetess of the sect, as he says, to test whether the spirits came from God. She was a young woman of pleasant speech and manner. “Presently she leaned back in her chair and had strong heaving in her chest and uttered deep sighs. Her head, her hands, and in turn every part of her body were affected by convulsive motions. This continued for about ten minutes. Then she began to speak with a clear, strong voice, but so interrupted by the heaving, sighing, and contortions of her body that she seldom managed to finish half a sentence at a time. What she said was mostly in spiritual terms, and all spoken as if by God himself, as if it were the language of direct inspiration.” (*Southey’s Wesley, I, and Evans’ Shakers.*)

### JUMPERS

About 1740, a similarly radical sect known as the Jumpers arose in Wales. According to the description given by Wesley, their practices were a very precise parallel to the Ghost Dance. “After the preaching was over, anyone who wished gave out a verse of a hymn, and they sang this over and over again with all their might, thirty or forty times, until some of them worked themselves into a state of intoxication or madness; they were then violently agitated and leaped up and down in all sorts of positions, often for hours at a time.” A contemporary writer states that he had seen perhaps ten thousand people at a single meeting of the Jumpers, shouting in the middle of the sermon and ready to leap for joy. (*Southey’s Wesley, II.*)

### METHODISTS

Around the same time, the Methodists originated in England under Wesley and Whitefield. Their assemblies were characterized by all the hysterical and convulsive excesses which they brought with them to this country, and which are not yet extinct in the South.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of physical manifestations in religious movements, specifically focusing on the early Methodist revival led by John Wesley and George Whitefield, comparing their followers' "fits" and "convulsions" to the behaviors seen in the Ghost Dance.</meta>

The most remarkable of these displays took place during the preaching of Wesley, following him, as we are told, wherever he went. Whitefield, although more forceful and sensational in his preaching, did not at first produce the same effect on his listeners, and he considered such manifestations to be but doubtful signs of the presence of the Lord and by no means to be encouraged. However, while preaching to a congregation in which Wesley had already produced such convulsions—and where, consequently, there was a predisposition in this direction—several persons were thus seized and sank down upon the floor, and we are told by the biographer that “this was a great triumph for Wesley.”

Wesley himself describes several instances. At one time, he states, a physician suspecting fraud attended a meeting during which a woman was thrown into a fit, crying aloud and weeping violently, until large drops of sweat ran down her face and her whole body shook. The doctor stood close by, noting every symptom and not knowing what to think, being convinced that it was neither fraud nor any natural disorder. “But when both her soul and body were healed in a moment, he acknowledged the finger of God.” On another occasion, Wesley tells us, “While I was earnestly inviting all men to enter into the Holiest by this new and living way, many of those who heard began to call upon God with strong cries and tears. Some sank down, and no strength remained in them. Others trembled and quaked exceedingly. Some were racked with a kind of convulsive motion in every part of their bodies, and so violently that often four or five persons could not hold one of them. I have seen many hysterical and epileptic fits, but none of them were like these in many respects. I immediately prayed that God would not allow those who were weak to be offended; but one woman was greatly offended, being sure that they could help it if they wanted to, and no one could persuade her otherwise; and she had gone only three or four yards when she also dropped down in as violent an agony as the rest.”

At another time, “while he was speaking one of his listeners dropped down, and in the course of half an hour seven others followed in violent agonies. The pains as of hell, he says, surrounded them; but despite his own reasoning, neither he nor his audience questioned the divine origin of these emotions, and they went away rejoicing and praising God. . . . Sometimes he had scarcely begun to speak before some of his believers, overwrought with expectation, fell into the crisis—for so it may be called in this case, as properly as in <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>A 19th-century term for hypnotism or mesmerism.</note>. Sometimes his voice could scarcely be heard amid the groans and cries of these suffering and raving enthusiasts. It was not long before men, women, and children began to act like the demonically possessed as well as the convert. Wesley had seen many hysterical fits and many fits of epilepsy, but none that were like these, and he confirmed the patients in their belief that they were tormented by Satan. One or two indeed perplexed him a little, for they were tormented in such an unaccountable manner that they seemed to be lunatic, he says, as well as

### SHAKERS

About the year 1750, another peculiar group of sectarians originated in England, calling themselves the “<term>United Society of Believers in Christ’s Second Appearing</term>,” but commonly known, for obvious reasons, as <term>Shakers</term>. Their chief prophetess and founder was “Mother” Ann Lee, whom they claim as the actual reincarnation of Christ. They also claim the inspiration of prophecy, the gift of healing, and sometimes even the gift of tongues; they believe in the reality of constant communication with the spirit world through visions. Due to persecution in England because of their public dancing, shouting, and shaking, they moved to this country around 1780 and settled at New Lebanon, New York, where the society still maintains its organization.

The best understanding of the Shakers is given in a small volume by Evans, who was himself a member of the sect. Speaking of the convulsive manifestations among them, he says: “Sometimes, after sitting for a while in silent meditation, they were seized with a mighty trembling, during which they would often express the indignation of God against all sin. At other times, they practiced singing, shouting, and leaping for joy at the near prospect of salvation. They often experienced great agitation of body and limbs—shaking, running, and walking the floor—with a variety of other actions and signs, swiftly passing and repassing each other like clouds driven by a mighty wind. These exercises, so strange in the eyes of onlookers, gave them the name of Shakers, which has been their most common distinguishing name ever since.” With regard to their dancing, he says: “It is fairly well known that the Shakers serve God by singing and dancing; but why they practice this mode of worship is not as widely understood. . . . When sin is fully removed by confessing and forsaking it, the cause of heaviness, gloom, and sorrow is gone; joy, rejoicing, thanksgiving, and praise are then the spontaneous effects of a true spirit of devotion. And whatever manner the spirit may dictate, or whatever form the spirit may lead one into, it is acceptable to Him from whom the spirit proceeds.” On one particular occasion, “before our coming, we called a meeting, and there were <insert>[sic]</insert> so many gifts (such as prophecies, revelations, visions, and dreams) confirming a former revelation for us to come, that some could hardly wait for others to describe their gifts. We had a joyful meeting and danced until morning.”

Regarding Ann Lee, their founder, he asserts that she saw Jesus Christ in an open vision and received direct revelations from this source. On a certain occasion, she herself declared to her followers: "The room over your head is full of the angels of God. I see them, and you could see them too if you were redeemed. She then began to sing, and they praised the Lord in the dance. On another occasion she said: "The apostles, in their day, saw as through a glass darkly, but we see face to face; we see things as they are, converse with spirits, and see their conditions. The gospel is preached to souls who have left the body. I see thousands of the dead rising and coming to judgment, right now at this present time." At another time she declared that she had seen a certain young woman in the spirit world, "praising God in the dance;" and of a deceased man, "He has appeared to me again, and has arisen from the dead and come into the first heaven, and is traveling on to the second and third heaven."

Their dance is performed regularly at their religious gatherings at the New Lebanon settlement. The two sexes are arranged in ranks opposite and facing each other, in which position they listen to a sermon by one of the elders, after which a hymn is sung. They then form a circle around a party of singers, keeping time to the singing in the dance. At times the excitement and fervor of spirit become intense, and their bodily movements become as rapid as those of the dervishes, although they still preserve the order of the dance. <note>Evans' Shakers and encyclopedia articles on Shakers.</note>

->KENTUCKY REVIVAL<-

About the year 1800, an epidemic of religious frenzy known as the Kentucky Revival broke out in Kentucky and Tennessee, chiefly among the Methodists and Baptists, with accompaniments that far surpassed the wildest excesses of the Ghost Dance. Fanatic preachers taught their deluded followers that the spiritual arrival of the kingdom was near at hand, when Christ would reign on earth and there would be an end to all sin. The date generally fixed for this completion was the summer of 1805, and the excitement continued and grew in violence for several years until that time came and passed without any extraordinary event. Then, the frenzy gradually subsided, leaving the ignorant believers in a state of utter collapse. The performances at the meetings of these enthusiasts were of the most exaggerated camp-meeting variety, such as may still be witnessed in many parts of the South, especially among Black people. Evans, the Shaker historian, who is strong in the gift of faith, tells us that "the subjects of this work were greatly exercised in dreams, visions, revelations, and the spirit of prophecy. In these gifts of the spirit, they saw and testified that the great day of

From another authority, perhaps with less fervor but more common sense, we get a description of these “exercises” that has a familiar ring, making it seem very relevant to us.
> “The people stayed on the ground day and night, listening to the most exciting sermons and engaging in a form of worship that consisted of alternating crying, laughing, singing, and shouting, accompanied by extraordinary gestures. Often there would be an unusual outcry; some bursting out with loud exclamations of thanksgiving; others urging their indifferent friends to ‘turn to the Lord;’ some struck with terror and rushing to escape; others trembling, weeping, and fainting away until every sign of life was gone and the body's extremities became as cold as a corpse. At one meeting, no fewer than a thousand people fell to the ground, apparently without sense or motion. It was common to see them shed many tears about an hour before they fell. They were then seized with a general shaking, and sometimes they uttered one or two piercing screams at the moment of falling. This latter phenomenon was common to both sexes, all ages, and all kinds of people.” (*Caswall, The Prophet of the Nineteenth Century, quoted by Remy.*)

After a time, these wild performances in the sacred name of religion became so routine that they were regularly categorized into groups such as the *rolls*, the *jerks*, the *barks*, etc.
> “The rolling exercise was performed by doubling themselves up, then rolling from one side to the other like a hoop, or by extending the body horizontally and rolling over and over in the dirt like so many pigs. The jerk consisted of violent spasms and twistings of every part of the body. Sometimes the head was twisted around so that the face was turned to the back, and the features were so distorted that they could not be recognized. When attacked by the jerks, they sometimes hopped like frogs, and their faces and limbs underwent the most hideous contortions. The bark consisted of throwing themselves on all fours, growling, showing their teeth, and barking like dogs. Sometimes a group of people crouching down in front of the minister continued to bark as long as he preached. These last were supposed to be especially endowed with the gifts of prophecy, dreams, rhapsodies, and visions of angels.” (*Remy, Journey to Great Salt Lake City, I.*)

Twenty years later, the jerking epidemic broke out again in Tennessee, and is described in a letter by the famous visionary and revivalist Lorenzo Dow, who was then preaching in that same region. His description matches what was told to the author by old men who lived in eastern Tennessee at that time. We quote from Dow’s letter: “A trembling began among the wicked. One, and then a second, fell from their seats. I believe that for eleven hours there was no stop to the loud cries. Of

The wicked are more afraid of it than of smallpox or yellow fever."

It is worth noting that, according to his account, investigators who wished to study the phenomenon were unable to fall under its influence, even though they desired to do so.

### ADVENTISTS

Around 1831, William Miller, a licensed minister, began to preach about the coming of Christ and the destruction of the world, setting the date for the year 1843. Like most others of his kind who have achieved notoriety, he based his prediction on the prophecies of the Bible, which he calculated with mathematical exactness. He began preaching in New York and New England, but afterward traveled south, reportedly delivering over three thousand lectures in support of his theory. His predictions led to the formation of a new sect commonly known as

--- Page 389 ---

<page-num>945</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] ADVENTISTS</header>

Adventists, who are said at one time to have numbered over fifty thousand. Carried away by blind enthusiasm, they made their preparations for the end of all things, which they confidently expected in the summer of 1843. As the time drew near, the believers made all preparations for their final departure from the world; many of them sold their property and dressed themselves in white "ascension robes," which were actually put on sale by storekeepers for the occasion. But the day and the year went by without the fulfillment of the prophecy. Miller claimed to have discovered an error in his calculations and fixed one or two other dates later on, but as these also proved false, his followers lost faith and the delusion died out. The Adventists still number fifteen or twenty thousand, with the largest body being in southern Michigan; but although they hold the doctrine of the near advent of the final end and endeavor to be ready at all times, they no longer undertake to fix a specific date.

It may be noted here that the idea of a millennium—when the Messiah shall come in person upon the earth and reign with the righteous for a thousand years—was so firmly held by many of the early Christians that it may almost be said to have formed a part of the doctrinal tradition of the church. The belief was an inheritance from the Jews, many of whose sacred writers taught that time was to endure through seven great "years" of a thousand years each; the seventh and last being the Sabbatical year or millennium, when their Messiah would appear and make their kingdom the mistress of the world. For this materialistic view of the millennium, the Christian fathers substituted a belief in the spiritual triumph of religion, when the armies of the antichrist would be annihilated; but the expectation of the return of Christ to rule in person over his church before the last days was an essential part of the doctrine, founded on numerous prophecies of both the Old and the New Testament.

### OTHER PARALLELS

#### BEEKMANITES

It would require a volume to treat of the various religious abnormalities—based on hypnotism, trances, and the messiah idea—which have sprung up and flourished in different parts of our own country even within the last twenty years. Naturally, these delusions thrived best among the ignorant classes, but there were some notable exceptions, particularly in the case of the Beekmanites or "Church of the Redeemed." About 1875, Mrs. Dora Beekman, the wife of a Congregational minister in Rockford, Illinois, began preaching that she was the immortal reincarnation of Jesus Christ. Absurd as this claim may appear, she found those who believed her, and as her converts increased in numbers, they established their headquarters—which they called "heaven"—near Rockford, built a church, and went zealously to work to gather proselytes. Beekman refused to believe the new doctrine,

In the meantime, the female Christ found a capable disciple in the Reverend George Schweinfurth, a young Methodist minister of considerable education and ability, who was installed as bishop and apostle of the new sect. Mrs. Beekman died soon after, despite her claim to immortality, and Schweinfurth immediately stepped into her place, declaring that the Christly essence had passed from her into himself. His claim was accepted, and when last heard from, about three years ago, he was worshiped by hundreds of followers—drawn from the most prominent denominations in the area—as the risen Christ, the lord of heaven, and the immortal creator and ruler of the earth. (*J. F. L., 6, and current newspapers.*)

### PATTERSON AND BROWN’S MISSION

In 1888, a man named Patterson in Soddy, a small town in eastern Tennessee, began preaching that a wonderful event was about to occur. After the matter had been discussed enough for his purposes, he announced that Christ had come in the person of A. J. Brown, who had served as Patterson's assistant. Later on, Brown disappeared, and it was announced that he had gone up into the mountains to fast for forty days and nights to be properly prepared for his mission. At the end of this period, on a Sunday morning in June, his followers went out toward the hills, where he suddenly appeared before them, dressed in white with his hands uplifted. A great shout went up, and the people rushed toward him, falling to their knees and kissing his feet. Many who were ill declared themselves healed by his touch. So great was the fanaticism of these people that one girl declared she was ready to die to prove her faith. Nonbelievers became so fearful that a human life might be sacrificed that they sent for the sheriff at Chattanooga; it required all his authority to compel Patterson and Brown to leave the neighborhood so that peace could be restored. (*J. F. L., 6.*)

### WILDERNESS WORSHIPERS

In 1889 and 1890, a remarkable messianic excitement developed among the Black population along the Savannah River in Georgia and South Carolina. One man after another proclaimed himself to be Christ, promised miracles, and drew crowds of excited men and women away from their work, creating a general alarm among the white population of the entire region. The most prominent of these "Christs" was a man of mixed race named Bell, who went about preaching his own divinity and urging everyone who wanted to be saved to give up everything and follow him. Hundreds of people abandoned the cotton fields, the sawmills, and the turpentine woods to follow him, obeying his every word and ready to fall down and worship him. They took the name "Wilderness Worshipers,"

and set up a "temple" in the woods consisting of a series of circular seats around an oak tree. The excitement became so destabilizing and dangerous that Bell was finally arrested. His frenzied disciples would have resisted the officers, but he commanded them to be patient, declaring that he could not be harmed and that an angel would come and open his prison doors by night. Since no specific charge could be formulated against him, he was released after a short time and continued his preaching to even larger crowds than before. At last, he announced that the world would come to an end on August 16, 1890; that all the Black people would then turn white and all white men would turn black, and that everyone who wished to ascend on the last day must purchase wings from him. (J. F. L., 6.) He was finally judged insane and sent to an asylum. Successors rose in his place, however, and kept up the excitement for a year afterward, despite the efforts of the authorities to put a stop to it. One of these claimed to be King Solomon, while another asserted that he was Nebuchadnezzar, and he emphasized his claim by eating grass on all fours. In addition to the "temple" in the woods, they set up an "ark," and the leaders told the followers that any persecutors who sacrilegiously attempted to touch it would fall down dead. Despite this warning, the officers destroyed both the ark and the temple in their efforts to end the delusion. At last, a woman was killed by the enthusiasts, and a series of mass arrests followed. King Solomon, Nebuchadnezzar, and others who were clearly insane were sent to join Bell in the asylum, and the others were released from custody after the excitement had faded.

### HEAVENLY RECRUITS

Within the last five years, various local revivalists have attracted attention in different sections of Indiana, Illinois, and Missouri due to their extravagances, among which prophecies, visions, trances, and frenzied physical exercises were all prominent. Especially at the meetings of the "Heavenly Recruits" in central Indiana, and at other gatherings under the direction of Mrs. Woodworth, cataleptic trances occurred nightly. The physical and mental breakdown eventually became so great that the authorities suppressed the meetings.

From the beginning of history, dance and similar physical exercises have formed a part of the religious ritual of various eastern sects, while hypnotic powers and practices have been claimed for their priests. This is especially true of the Muslim sect or order of the Dervishes, of which some account is given in the appendix to this chapter.

# APPENDIX—HYPNOTISM AND THE DANCE AMONG THE DERVISHES

->[From Brown's Dervishes]<-

HYPNOTISM.—It is through the performance of the <term>Zikr</term>, by <term>khalvet</term> (pious retirement for purposes of deep devotion), by the <term>Tevejjuh</term> (or turning the face or mind devoutly toward God in prayer), by the <term>Murakebeh</term> (or awe-filled contemplation of God), the <term>Tesarruf</term> (or self-abandonment to pious reflection and inspiration), and the <term>Tesavvuf</term> (or mystical spiritualism), that the fervent <term>Dervish</term> attains unique spiritual powers called *<term>Kuvveh i roohee batinee</term>* (a mystical, internal, spiritual power). The life or biography of every eminent <term>sheikh</term> or <term>peer</term> provides countless examples of this power exercised in a strange and unique manner. This exercise is called the *<term>Kuvveh Iradat</term>*, or the “Power of the Will,” and, as a theory, may be traced historically to Divine Power—the soul of man being connected with the Divine Spirit—from which it emanates, and with which, through the means mentioned before, it begins. Some <term>sheikhs</term> are more celebrated than others for their unique and strange powers, and it is to their superiority that their reputation and reverence in the <term>Mussulman</term> world in general, and among <term>Dervishes</term> in particular, is attributed. Assuming that the details given of them by their biographers, disciples, or successors are not invented or even exaggerated, their powers are certainly very remarkable. While among them an implicit belief in these powers is firmly sustained, sultans and princes have evidently doubted them; being alarmed by the influence the possessors acquired and maintained among the public generally, they have often shown a dreadful exercise of their own arbitrary will and power, which resulted in the untimely end of the unfortunate <term>sheikh</term>. Many, on the other hand, have survived the frequent exercise of their “spiritual powers,” either because they acquired power and influence over the minds of their temporal rulers, or because they used them for their own private purposes to win over the more religious or fanatical, succeeding in reaching advanced ages and a peaceful end to their remarkable careers. When the ruler of the country did not care to order the execution of the <term>sheikh</term> who declared himself possessed of these spiritual powers, he simply exiled him from his capital or his territory and permitted him to freely exercise his powers and renown in some less objectionable location. These powers can only be acquired through the long instruction of a superior spiritual director, or <term>Murshid</term>, or *<term>As-hâb i Yekeen</term>*, for whom the disciples always retain a most grateful remembrance and attachment.

Among the practices of these powers is the faculty of foreseeing coming events; of predicting their occurrence; of preserving individuals from the harm and evil which would otherwise certainly result for them; of ensuring one person’s success over the schemes of another, so that he may freely attack him and prevail over him; of restoring harmony between those who would otherwise be relentless enemies; of knowing when others devised harm against them, and through certain spells preserving themselves and causing harm to befall the evil-minded, and even of causing the death of anyone against whom they wish to proceed. All this is done as well from a distance as when near.

In other parts of the world and among other people, these attainments would have been attributed to sorcery and witchcraft; in modern times they would be ascribed to spiritualism or magnetic influences, either of the spirit or of the body; but to the instructed <term>Dervish</term>, they all derive their origin in the spirit of the holy <term>sheikh</term>—the special gift of the great Spirit of God, which begins with the spirit of man, from which it directly emanated. The condition or disposition necessary for these effects is called the *<term>Hâl</term>* (state or frame of mind), and is much the same as that required by the person being hypnotized and the person performing the operation. The powers of the body are weakened by fasting and mental fatigue in prayer, and the imagination is kept in a fervent state, fully impressed with the conviction that such powers are really possessed by the <term>sheikh</term> and that he can readily exercise them over the

willing mind and body of the disciple. How the <term>sheikh</term> can produce such strange results on a distant and unconscious person is left to the admiration and imagination of the faithful disciple, as an incentive to labor in the same true path as that of his <term>sheikh</term>.

To exercise the power of the will, it is necessary to focus the thoughts suddenly upon the object intended to be affected so perfectly as to leave no room for the mind to dwell, possibly, upon any other. The mind must not doubt for an instant the success of this effort, nor the possibility of failure; it must, in fact, be completely absorbed by the single idea of carrying out the determination strongly made and firmly relied upon. People must practice this from time to time; and as they proceed, they will be able to see how much closeness exists between themselves and the <term>Hazret i Asmâ</term> <note>The Presence of the Names of God</note> and how much they are capable of exercising this power.

As an example, the author of the *Reshihât* narrates the following:

> In my youth, I was always with our Lord <term>Molânâ Sa'eed ed Deen Kâshgharee</term> at <term>Hereed</term>. It happened that we walked out together one day and came upon a gathering of the inhabitants of the place who were engaged in wrestling. To try our powers, we agreed to aid one of the wrestlers with our "powers of the will," so that the other should be overcome by him, and after doing so, to change our intention in favor of the defeated individual. So we stopped and, turning toward the parties, gave the full influence of our united wills to one, and he was immediately able to subdue his opponent. As the person we chose, each in turn, conquered the other, whichever we willed to prevail became the more powerful of the two; the power of our own wills was thus clearly demonstrated.
> 
> On another occasion two other persons possessed of these same powers came upon a gathering of people at a place occupied by prize fighters. "To prevent any of the crowd from passing between and separating us, we joined our hands together. Two persons were engaged in fighting; one was a powerful man, while the other was a lean and weak person. The former easily overcame the latter; and seeing this, I proposed to my companion to aid the weak one by the power of our wills. So he asked me to aid him in the project, while he concentrated his powers upon the weaker person. Immediately a wonderful occurrence took place; the thin, lean man seized his giant-like opponent and threw him on the ground with surprising force. The crowd cried out with astonishment as he turned him over on his back and held him down with apparent ease. No one present except ourselves knew the cause. Seeing that my companion was much affected by the effort which he had made, I told him to notice how perfectly successful we had been, and adding that there was no longer any necessity for us to remain there, we walked away." (Pages 129–132.)

---

Many individuals who seriously wronged and oppressed his friends received punishments through the powers of the <term>sheikh</term>. Several instances are related wherein some such even fell sick and died, or were only restored to health by open declarations of repentance and by imploring his prayerful intercession with God. His spirit seems to have accompanied those in whose welfare he took an active interest, and enabled them to commune with him, though far distant from him. His power of hearing them was well known to his friends, and several instances are cited to prove the fact. His power of affecting the health of those who injured him or his friends was greatly increased while he was excited by anger, and on such occasions his whole frame would be convulsed and his beard would move as if moved by electricity. On learning details of cruelty done to innocent individuals, the <term>sheikh</term> would be strangely affected—so much so that no one dared to speak to him until the fit had passed; and on such occasions he never failed to commune spiritually with the sovereign or prince in such a mysterious manner as to inspire him to deal justly with the guilty person and secure his deserved punishment.

Through his "mystical powers," many persons were impressed with the unrighteousness of their conduct, and, having repented of the same, became good, pious, and firm believers in his spiritual influences. These powers were always connected with his prayers, and it was during these that he was enabled to assure the parties interested of their beneficial results and the acceptance of their desires. It scarcely needs

Sometimes he would affect the mind of the individual upon whom he exercised his powers in such a manner as to throw him into a kind of trance, after which he could remember nothing that he had previously known, and he remained in this state until the sheikh chose to restore him to the enjoyment of his ordinary faculties. Despite all of these remarkable powers, this great sheikh is said to have spent the final days of his life at Herat in extreme poverty, much disregarded and neglected by those who had so admired him while in the vigor of his career. All fear of his mystical influences seems to have vanished, and it is narrated that these declined significantly along with his ordinary strength of mind and body. (Pages 137–139.)

DERVISH DANCE.—The exercises followed in these halls are of various kinds, according to the rules of each institution; but in nearly all of them, they begin with the recital, by the sheikh, of the seven mysterious words of which we have spoken. He next chants various passages of the Koran, and at each pause, the Dervishes, placed in a circle around the hall, respond in chorus with the word “Allah!” or “Hoo!” In some of the societies, they sit on their heels, their elbows close to one another, and all simultaneously making light movements of the head and the body. In others, the movement consists of balancing themselves slowly, from right to left and from left to right, or bowing the body methodically forward and backward. There are other societies in which these motions begin while seated, in measured cadences, with a solemn expression, the eyes closed or fixed upon the ground, and are continued on foot. These singular exercises are grouped under the name of <term>Murâkebeh</term> (exaltation of the Divine glory), and also under that of the <term>Tevheed</term> (celebration of the Divine unity), from which comes the name Tevheed Khâneh, given to all of the halls devoted to these religious exercises.

In some of these institutions—such as the <term>Kâdirees</term>, the <term>Rufâ'ees</term>, the <term>Khalwettees</term>, the <term>Bairâmees</term>, the <term>Gulshenees</term>, and the <term>Ushâkees</term>—the exercises are performed while each holds the other by the hand, stepping forward always with the right foot and increasing the strength of the body's movement at every step. This is called the <term>Devr</term>, which may be translated as the “dance” or “rotation.” The duration of these dances is flexible—each person is free to leave when he pleases. Everyone, however, makes it a point to remain as long as possible. The strongest and most robust among them, and the most enthusiastic, strive to persevere longer than the others; they uncover their heads, take off their turbans, form a second circle within the other, entwine their arms with those of their brothers, lean their shoulders against each other, gradually raise their voices, and without ceasing repeat “Yâ Allah!” or “Yâ Hoo!” increasing the movement of the body each time, and not stopping until their entire strength is exhausted.

Those of the order of the <term>Rufâ'ees</term> excel in these exercises. They are, moreover, the only ones who use fire in their devotions. Their practices embrace nearly all those of the other orders; they are ordinarily divided into five different scenes, which last more than three hours, and which are preceded, accompanied, and followed by certain ceremonies peculiar to this order. The first begins with praises which all the Dervishes offer to their sheikhs, who are seated before the altar. Four of the more senior members come forward first and approach their superior, embrace each other as if to give the kiss of peace, and next place themselves two to his right and two to his left. The rest of the Dervishes, as a group, press forward in a procession, all having their arms crossed and their heads bowed. Each one, at first, salutes with a profound bow the tablet on which the name of his founder is inscribed. Afterward, putting his two hands over his face and his beard, he kneels before the sheikh, kisses his hand respectfully, and then they all go on with a solemn step to take their places on the sheepskins, which are spread in a semicircle around the interior of the hall. As soon as a circle is formed, the Dervishes together chant the <term>Tekbeer</term> and

their breasts and their abdomens, and on their knees.
The second scene is opened by the <term>Hamdee Mohammedee</term>, a hymn in honor of the
prophet, chanted by one of the elders placed on the right of the sheikh. During this
chant the Dervishes continue to repeat the word “<term>Allah!</term>” moving, however, their
bodies forward and back. A quarter of an hour later they all rise up, approach each
other, and press their elbows against each other, balancing from right to left and
afterward in a reverse motion, the right foot always firm, and the left in a period-
ic movement, the opposite of that of the body, all observing great precision of rhyth-
m and cadence. In the midst of this exercise they cry out the words “<term>Yâ Allah!</term>”
followed by that of “<term>Yâ Hoo!</term>” Some of the performers sigh, others sob, some shed
tears, others perspire great drops, and all have their eyes closed, their faces pale, and
their eyes languid.
A pause of some minutes is followed by a third scene. It is performed in the mid-
dle of an <term>Ilahee</term>, chanted by the two elders on the right of the sheikh. The <term>Ilahees</term>, as
has already been said, are spiritual canticles, composed almost exclusively in Per-
sian by sheikhs who died in the odor of sanctity. The Dervishes then hasten their
movements, and, to prevent any relaxation, one of the first among them puts himself
in their center, and excites them by his example. If there are any
strange Dervishes in the assembly, which often happens, they give them, through politeness, this
place of honor; and all fill it successively, one after the other, shaking them-
selves as mentioned before. The only exception made is in favor of the <term>Mevevees</term>; these
never perform any other dance than that peculiar to their own order, which consists
in turning round on each heel in succession.
After a new pause the fourth scene commences. Now all the Dervishes take off
their turbans, form a circle, bear their arms and shoulders against each other, and
thus make the circuit of the hall at a measured pace, striking their feet at intervals
against the floor, and all springing up at once. This dance continues during the
<term>Ilahees</term> chanted alternately by the two elders to the left of the sheikh. In the midst
of this chant the cries of “<term>Yâ Allah!</term>” are redoubled, as also those of “<term>Yâ</term>
<term>Hoo!</term>” with terrible howlings shrieked by the Dervishes together in the dance.
At the moment that they would seem to stop from sheer exhaustion the sheikh makes
a point of urging them to new efforts by walking through their midst, making most 
violent movements himself as well. He is next replaced by the two elders, who double
the quickness of the step and the agitation of the body; they even straighten them-
selves up from time to time, and excite the envy or emulation of the others in their
astonishing efforts to continue the dance until their strength is entirely exhausted.
The fourth scene leads to the last, which is the most terrible of all, the wholly
prostrated condition of the actors becoming converted into a species of ecstasy which
they call <term>Halet</term>. It is in the midst of this abandonment of self, or rather of religious
delirium, that they make use of red-hot irons. Several cutlasses and other instru-
ments of sharp-pointed iron are suspended in the niches of the hall, and upon a part
of the wall to the right of the sheikh. Near the close of the fourth scene two Der-
vishes take down eight or nine of these instruments, heat them red hot, and present
them to the sheikh. He, after reciting some prayers over them, and invoking the
founder of the order, <term>Ahmed er Rufa’ee</term>, breathes over them, and raising them
slightly to the mouth, gives them to the Dervishes, who ask for them with the great-
est eagerness. Then it is that these fanatics, transported by frenzy, seize upon these
irons, gloat upon them tenderly, lick them, bite them, hold them between their teeth,
and end by cooling them in their mouths. Those who are unable to procure any
seize upon the cutlasses hanging on the wall with fury, and stick them into their
sides, arms, and legs.

a merit in the eyes of the Divinity, all stoically bear up against the pain which they

There was no regularity in their dancing, but each seemed to be performing the antics of a madman; now moving his body up and down; the next moment turning around, then using odd gestures with his arms, next jumping, and sometimes screaming; in short, if a stranger observing them was not told that this was the involuntary effect of enthusiastic excitement, he would certainly think that these <term>Dervishes</term> were merely striving to excel one another in playing the buffoon. ### THE FIT.
After this preface, the performers began the <term>Zikr</term>. Sitting in the manner described above, they chanted, in slow measure, <term>*Lá iláha illa 'lláh*</term> (there is no deity but God), to the following air: *Lá i-lá-ha ha illa-l-láh. Lá i-lá-ha-illa-l-lá-h*. Bowing the head twice on each repetition of “*Lá iláha illa 'lláh*.”
Thus they continued for about a quarter of an hour, and then, for about the same length of time, they repeated the same words to the same air, but in a quicker measure, and with correspondingly quicker motion.

They next rose, and, standing in the same order in which they had been sitting, repeated the same words to another air. During this stage of their performance, they were joined by a tall, well-dressed, black slave, whose appearance led me to inquire who he was. I was informed that he was a eunuch belonging to the pasha. The <term>Zikkirs</term>, still standing, next repeated the same words in a very deep and hoarse tone, laying the principal emphasis upon the word “*Lá*,” and the first syllable of the last word, *Alláh*, and uttering them, apparently, with a considerable effort. The sound much resembled that which is produced by beating the rim of a tambourine. Each <term>Zikkir</term> turned his head alternately to the right and left at each repetition of “*Lá iláha illa 'lláh*.” The eunuch mentioned above, during this part of the <term>Zikr</term>, became what is termed <term>*melboos*</term>, or “possessed.” Throwing his arms about, and looking up with a very wild expression of countenance, he exclaimed, in a very high tone and with great vehemence and rapidity, *Alláh! Alláh! Alláh! Alláh! la! la! la! la! la! la! la! la! la! la! láh! Yá 'ammee! Yá 'ammee! Yá 'ammee! Ashmáwee! Yá Ashmáwee! Yá Ashmáwee!* (<term>Yá 'ammee</term> signifies O, my uncle!) His voice gradually became faint, and when he had uttered those words, though he was held by a <term>Dervish</term> who was next to him, he fell on the ground, foaming at the mouth, his eyes closed, his limbs convulsed, and his fingers clenched over his thumbs. It was an epileptic fit. No one could see it and believe it to be the effect of feigned emotions; it was undoubtedly the result of a high state of religious excitement. Nobody seemed surprised at it, for occurrences of this kind at <term>Zikrs</term> are not uncommon. All the performers now appeared much excited, repeating their ejaculations with greater rapidity, violently turning their heads, and sinking the whole body at the same time, some of them jumping. The eunuch became <term>melboos</term> again several times, and I generally remarked that his fits happened after one of the <term>Munshids</term> had sung a line or two, and exerted himself more than usually to excite his hearers. The singing was, indeed, to my taste, very pleasing. Toward the close of the <term>Zikr</term> a private soldier, who had joined through the whole performance, also seemed several times to be <term>melboos</term>, growling in a horrible manner and violently shaking his head from side to side. The contrast presented by the vehement and distressing exertions of the performers at the close of the <term>Zikr</term>, and their calm gravity and solemnity of manner at the commencement, was particularly striking. Money was collected during the performance for the <term>Munshid</term>. The <term>Zikkirs</term> receive no pay. (Pages 252-255.)

# THE SONGS

## INTRODUCTORY

The Ghost Dance songs are of the utmost importance in connection with the study of the messiah religion, as we find much of the doctrine itself embodied within them. They also contain more of the specific tribal mythologies, along with so many references to old customs, ceremonies, and lifestyles that have long been obsolete that they form a comprehensive collection of Indigenous thought and practice. There is no limit to the number of these songs, as every trance at every dance produces a new one. After regaining consciousness, the person who experienced the trance expresses their experience in the spirit world in the form of a song, which is then sung at the next dance and subsequent performances until it is replaced by other songs originating in the same way. Thus, a single dance may easily result in twenty or thirty new songs. While songs are born and die in this manner, certain ones that especially appeal to the Indian heart—due to their mythology, pathos, or unique beauty—live on and are preserved. Each tribe also has certain songs that are a regular part of the ceremony, such as the opening and closing songs, which are repeated at every dance. Of these, the closing song is the most significant and permanent. In some cases, certain songs form a regular series, detailing the experiences of the same person in successive trance visions. The songs of the Arapaho are foremost in importance because of their quantity, rich references, beautiful sentiment, and rhythmic language.

## THE ARAPAHO

### TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*Ähyä'to*—Kiowa name; meaning unknown; the Kiowa call the wild plum by the same name.
*Ano's-anyotskano*—Kichai name.
*Ärä'päho*—popular name; derivation uncertain; but perhaps, as Dunbar suggests, from the Pawnee word *tirapihu* or *larapĭhu*, meaning "he buys or trades," in allusion to the Arapaho having formerly been the trading intermediary between the Pawnee, Osage, and others in the north, and the Kiowa, Comanche, and others to the southwest (Grinnell letter).
*Äräpäkata*—Crow name, derived from the word Arapaho.
*Bĕtiděě*—Kiowa Apache name.
*Detseka'yaa*—Caddo name, "dog eaters."
*Hitäniwo'ĭv*—Cheyenne name, "cloud men."
*Inûna-ina*—proper tribal name, "our people," or "people of our kind."
*Kaninahoic* or *Kaninä'vish*—Ojibwa name; meaning unknown.

### TRIBAL SIGNS

Southern Arapaho, "*rub noses;*" northern Arapaho, "*mother people;*" Gros Ventres of the Prairie, "*belly people.*"

### SKETCH OF THE TRIBE

The Arapaho, along with their subtribe, the Gros Ventres, are one of the westernmost tribes of the extensive Algonquian stock. According to their oldest traditions, they formerly lived in northeastern Minnesota and moved westward in the company of the Cheyenne, who at that time lived on the Cheyenne fork of the Red River. From the earliest times, the two tribes have always been closely confederated, so that they have no memory of a time when they were not allies. In the westward migration, the Cheyenne took a more southerly direction toward the country of the Black Hills, while the Arapaho continued nearly due west up the Missouri River. The Arapaho proper probably ascended the southern side of the river, while the Gros Ventres went up the northern bank and finally drifted toward the Blackfeet, with whom they have ever since been closely associated. However, they have on several occasions made long visits, extending sometimes over several years, to their southern relatives, by whom they are still regarded as part of the "Inûna-ina." The others continued to the Great Divide between the waters of the Missouri and those of the Columbia, then turning southward along the mountains, they finally separated into two main divisions. The northern Arapaho continued to occupy the headwaters of the Missouri and the Yellowstone in Montana and Wyoming, while the southern Arapaho made their camps on the headwaters of the Platte, the Arkansas, and the Canadian rivers in Colorado and adjacent states, frequently joining the Comanche and Kiowa in their raids far down into Mexico. From their earliest memory, until they were placed on reservations, they were at war with the Shoshoni, Ute, Pawnee, and Navajo, but have generally been friendly with their other neighbors. The southern Arapaho and Cheyenne have usually acted in concert with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Kiowa Apache.

They recognize among themselves five original divisions, each having a different dialect. They are listed here in order of their importance:
1. *Na'kasinĕ'na*, *Ba'achinĕna*, or Northern Arapaho. *Nakasinĕna*, "sagebrush men," is the original name of this portion of the tribe and the divisional name used by themselves. The name *Baachinĕna*, by which they are commonly known to the rest of the tribe, is more

<header>MOONEY] DIVISIONS OF THE ARAPAHO</header>

modern and may mean "red willow (that is, <term>kiñikinik</term>) men," or possibly "blood-pudding men." The latter meaning is said to have been a reference to a kind of sausage formerly made by this band. They are commonly known as the Northern Arapaho to distinguish them from the other large division now living in Oklahoma. The Kiowa distinguished them as <term>Tägyä'ko</term>, "sagebrush people," which is a translation of their proper name, <term>Baachiněna</term>. Although they are not the largest division, the <term>Baachiněna</term> claim to be the "mother people" of the Arapaho and are the keepers of the tribe's grand medicine, the <term>sěicha</term> or sacred pipe.

2. *<term>Na'wuněna</term>*, "southern men," or *Southern Arapaho*, called *<term>Nawa-thi'něha</term>*, "southerners," by the Northern Arapaho. This latter name is said to be the archaic form. The Southern Arapaho, who now live in Oklahoma, make up by far the larger division, although they are subordinate in tribal sociology to the Northern Arapaho. In addition to their everyday dialect, they are said to have an archaic dialect, some words of which closely resemble <term>Cheyenne</term>.

3. *<term>Aä'niněna</term>*, *<term>Hitu'něna</term>*, or *Gros Ventres of the Prairie*. The first name, said to mean "white clay people" (from <term>aäti</term>, "white clay"), is the name by which they call themselves. <term>Hituněna</term> or <term>Hituněnina</term>, "begging men," "beggars," or, more exactly, "spongers," is the name the other Arapaho call them. This is because, as the others claim, they have a tendency to fill their stomachs at someone else's expense. The same idea is meant to be conveyed by the tribal sign, which signifies "belly people," not "big bellies" (<term>Gros Ventres</term>), as translated by the French Canadian trappers. The Kiowa call them <term>Bot-k'iñ'ago</term>, "belly men." The Shoshoni also know them as <term>Sä'pani</term>, "bellies," while the Blackfeet call them <term>Atsina</term>, "gut people." The Ojibwa call them <term>Bahwetegow-ēninnewug</term>, "fall people," according to Tanner, which is why they have sometimes been called Fall Indians or Rapid Indians, due to their former residence near the rapids of the Saskatchewan River. The Sioux know them as <term>Sku'tani</term>. Lewis and Clark incorrectly call them "Minnetarees of Fort de Prairie." The Hidatsa or Minitari are sometimes known as the Gros Ventres of the Missouri.

4. *<term>Bä'sawuně'na</term>*, "wood lodge men," or, according to another authority, "big lodge people." These were formerly a distinct tribe and were at war with the other Arapaho. They are described as having been a very foolish people in the old times, and many absurd stories are told about them, in keeping with the general Indian practice of belittling conquered or subordinate tribes. They have been incorporated with the Northern Arapaho for at least 150 years, according to the statements of the oldest men of that band. Their dialect is said to have differed considerably from the other Arapaho dialects. There are still about one hundred people of this lineage among the Northern Arapaho, and perhaps a few others with the two other main divisions. Weasel Bear, the current keeper of the sacred pipe, is of the <term>Bäsawuněna</term>.

<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

5. *Ha'nahawuněna* or *Aanû'hawă* (meaning unknown). These, like the Bäsawuněna, lived with the northern Arapaho, but are now practically extinct.

<margin>✓</margin> There seems to be no possible trace of a clan or <term>gentile system</term> among the Arapaho, and the same remark holds true for the Cheyenne, Kiowa, and Comanche. It was once assumed that all Indian tribes had a clan system, but later research shows that it is lacking over wide areas in the western territory. It is very doubtful if it exists at all among the prairie tribes in general. Mr. Ben Clark, who has known and studied the Cheyenne for half a lifetime, states positively that they have no clans as the term is usually understood. This agrees with the result of personal investigations and the testimony of George Bent, a Cheyenne of mixed descent and the best living authority on all that relates to his tribe. With the eastern tribes, however, and those who have moved from the east or the timbered country, such as the Caddo, the <term>gentile system</term> is so much a part of their daily life that it is one of the first things to attract the attention of an observer.

In regard to the tribal camping circle, common to most of the prairie tribes, the Arapaho state that because they live in three main divisions, they have had no common camping circle within their recollection; however, each of these three divisions formed a single circle when encamped in one place.

Among the northern Arapaho, on the occasion of every grand gathering, the sacred pipe occupied a special large tipi in the center of the circle, and the taking down of this tipi by the medicine keeper was the signal to the rest of the camp to prepare to move. On the occasion of a visit of several hundred Cheyenne and Arapaho to the Kiowa and Comanche at Anadarko in the summer of 1892, each of the visiting tribes camped in a separate circle adjacent to the other. The opening of the circle, like the door of each tipi, always faces the east.

Under the name of Kanenăvish, the Arapaho proper are mentioned by Lewis and Clark in 1805 as living southwest of the Black Hills. As a tribe, they have not been at war with the whites since 1868 and took no part in the outbreak of the Cheyenne, Kiowa, and Comanche in 1874. At present, they are in three main divisions. First come the Gros Ventres, numbering 718 in 1892, associated with the Assiniboin on the Fort Belknap reservation in Montana. There are probably others of this band with the Blackfeet on the British side of the border. Next come the northern Arapaho, numbering 829, associated with the Shoshoni on the Wind River reservation in Wyoming. They were placed on this reservation in 1876, after having made peace with the Shoshoni, their hereditary enemy, in 1869. They are divided into three bands: the "Forks of the River Men" under Black Coal, the head chief of the whole division; the "Bad Pipes" under Short Nose; and the "Greasy Faces" under Spotted Horse. The third division, the southern Arapaho, associated with the Cheyenne in Oklahoma, constitute the main body
