They have five bands: 1, Wa'quithi, "bad faces," the principal band and the one to which the head chief, Left Hand, belongs; 2, Aqa'thinĕ'na, "pleasant men;" 3, Gawunĕ'na or Ga'wunĕhäna (Kawinahan, "black people"—Hayden), "Blackfeet," so called because they are said to be of partial Blackfoot blood, the same name being applied to the Blackfoot tribe; 4, Ha'qihana, "wolves," because they had a wolf (not a coyote) for medicine; 5, Säsa'bä-ithi, "looking up," or according to another authority, "looking around, that is, watchers or lookouts." Under the treaty of Medicine Lodge in 1867, they and the southern Cheyenne were placed on the reservation which they sold in 1890 to take allotments and become citizens. Their present

<image-desc>A black and white photograph of a traditional Arapaho tipi made of animal skins. Next to the tipi is a long, low windbreak structure made of vertical wooden posts and woven brush. A person stands in front of the tipi's entrance.</image-desc>

chief is Left Hand (Nawat), who succeeded the celebrated Little Raven (Hosa) a few years ago. The total number of the Arapaho and Gros Ventres, including a few in eastern schools, is about 2,700.

Until very recently the Arapaho have been a typical prairie tribe, living in skin tipis and following the buffalo in its migrations, yet they retain a tradition of a time when they were agricultural. They are of a friendly, accommodating disposition, religious and contemplative, without the aggressive, combative character that belongs to their confederates, the Cheyenne, although they have always proved themselves to be brave warriors. They are also less mercenary and more manageable than the prairie Indians generally, and having now recognized the inevitability of civilization, they have gone to work in good faith to make the best of it.

Their religious nature has led them to take a more active interest in the Ghost Dance, which, together with the rhythmic character of their language, has made Arapaho songs the favorites among all the tribes of Oklahoma. The primary study of the Ghost Dance was conducted among the Arapaho, whom the author visited six times for this purpose. One visit was made to those in Wyoming, while the remainder of the time was spent with the southern branch of the tribe.

### 2. SĚ'ICHA HEI'TA'WUNI'NA

<margin><note>Pencil checkmark and a small mark in the margin.</note></margin>
The <term>sěicha</term>, or flat pipe, is the sacred tribal medicine of the Arapaho. According to myth, it was given to their ancestors at the beginning of the world after the Turtle had brought the earth up from under the water. It was delivered to them by the Duck, which was discovered swimming about on the surface of the water after the land emerged. At the same time, they were given an ear of corn, from which all the corn in the world originates. The Arapaho lost the knowledge of agriculture when they moved onto the buffalo plains, but the sacred pipe—which the Turtle long ago changed to stone—and the first ear of corn, also transformed to stone, they have treasured to this day as their great medicine. The pipe, turtle, and ear of corn are preserved among the northern Arapaho in Wyoming, who claim to be the "mother people" of the tribe. These items are passed down through the care of a specific family from generation to generation; the current priestly guardian is *Se'hiwûq*, "Weasel Bear" (from *sea*, weasel, and *wûq*, bear; the name has also been translated as "Gray Bear," from *se*, gray, and *wûq*, bear), of the *Bäsawuně'na* division.

The three sacred objects are preserved carefully wrapped in deerskins and are displayed only on rare occasions, always within the sacred tipi.

<margin>✓</margin>
and in the presence of only a few witnesses, who take this opportunity to smoke the sacred pipe and pray for the things they desire most. The pipe itself is made of stone and is described as being made of two layers; one part is laid over the other like the bark of a tree. The outer part of both the bowl and stem is made of the usual red pipestone, while the inner part of both is made of white stone. The stem is only about 10 inches long, while the bowl is large and heavy, with the characteristic projection for resting the end on the ground. Both the bowl and stem are rounded, but have a flange about an inch wide along each side of the stem and up the bowl. This is the source of its name, <term>*sĕicha*</term>, or "flat pipe." When it is displayed on such occasions, the devotees sit around the fire in a circle. The bundle is opened on the ground so that everyone may see the sacred objects. The medicine keeper then lights the pipe and, after taking one or two puffs, passes it to the person next to him, who takes a single puff and passes it to the next. It thus goes clockwise (sunwise?) around the circle. When receiving the <term>*sĕicha*</term>, the devotees do not grasp the stem as they would when smoking on other occasions; instead, they receive it upon the outstretched palm of the right hand, smoke, and pass it around the circle. The flanges along the side of the pipe allow it to rest flat on the hand. After everyone has smoked, the priest recites the creation story of how the land began and how the pipe and corn were given to their ancestors. The corresponding Cheyenne myth takes "four smokes" (that is, four consecutive nights) to tell, but I cannot say if this is also true for the Arapaho. This tradition is held so sacredly that no one except the priest of the pipe dares to recite it, for fear of divine punishment if even the smallest error is made in the telling. At the end of the recitation, the devotees offer prayers for the blessings they need most, after which the priest carefully wraps the sacred objects in the skins again. Before leaving the lodge, the worshipers cover the bundle with offerings of blankets or other valuables, which the medicine keeper takes as his fee.

When camped in the tribal circle, the sacred pipe and its keeper occupied a large tipi reserved especially for this purpose. This tipi was set up within the circle near its western line, directly opposite the eastern entrance. In the center of the circle, between the entrance and the sacred tipi, the sweat-house of the <term>*Chi'nachichinĕ'na*</term>, or old men of the highest rank in the warrior order, was built. When the attendants of the pipe keeper took down the sacred tipi, it served as the signal for the entire camp to move; no other tipi was allowed to be taken down before it. While on the march, the pipe keeper traveled on foot—never on horseback—carrying the sacred bundle on his back and accompanied by a group of guards. Naturally, the sacred pipe was not carried by war parties or on other expeditions that required speed. In recent years, the rules have

### MOONEY] THE ARAPAHO SACRED PIPE

The rules have relaxed so much that its current guardian sometimes rides a horse while carrying the pipe; however, even then, he carries the bundle on his own back instead of on the saddle. He never rides in a wagon with it. Since the tribe is permanently divided under the modern reservation system, individuals or small groups of the Southern Arapaho frequently make the long journey by railroad and stagecoach to the reservation in Wyoming to see and pray over the <term>sĕicha</term>. This is because it is impossible, due to ceremonial regulations, for the keeper to bring it down to them in the south.

As far as is known, only one white man, Mr. J. Roberts—former superintendent of the Arapaho school in Wyoming—has ever seen the sacred pipe. It was shown to him on one occasion by Weasel Bear as a special sign of gratitude for some kindness. After spending several months among the Southern Arapaho, from whom I learned the songs of the pipe and much of its sacred history, I visited the Messiah in Nevada and then went to the Northern Arapaho in Wyoming. I had great hopes of seeing the <term>sĕicha</term> and hearing the full tradition. Because of my close acquaintance with their relatives in the south and with their great Messiah in the west, the chiefs and headmen favored my goal and encouraged my hopes. However, upon going out to the mountain camp where nearly the whole tribe was then gathered cutting wood, my hopes were crushed on the first night. I heard the old priest, Weasel Bear, making a loud public announcement throughout the camp that a white man was among them to learn about their sacred things, but that these belonged to the religion of the Indian and a white man had no business asking about them. The chief and those who had been delegates to the Messiah came to the tipi where I was staying soon after to express their deep regret, but they were unable to change Weasel Bear's resolution, and none of them would dare to repeat the tradition.

<image-desc>A black and white photograph or detailed illustration of a traditional Indigenous bed structure. The bed of the prairie tribes is made of slender willow rods, peeled, straightened with the teeth, laid side by side, and fastened together into a type of mat using buckskin or rawhide strings passed through holes at the ends of the rods. The bed is stretched upon a platform raised about a foot above the ground; and one end of the mat is raised up in hammock fashion using a tripod and buckskin hanger. The rods laid across the platform, forming the bed proper, are usually about 3½ or 4 feet long (the width of the bed), while those forming the upright part suspended from the tripod are shorter as they

The hanging portion is distinct from the part resting upon the platform, and in some cases, there is a hanger at each end of the bed. Over the platform portion, buckskins and blankets are spread, which form a couch by day and a bed by night. A buckskin pillow, stuffed with buffalo hair and elaborately ornamented with beads or porcupine quills, is sometimes added. The bed is placed close against the side of the tipi. In the largest tipis, there are usually three beds: one being opposite the doorway and the others on each side; the fire is built in a hole scooped out of the ground in the center of the lodge. These are used as seats during waking hours, while the ground, with a rawhide spread upon it, constitutes the only table at mealtime (Plate CXXI; Figure 89). When going to bed, there is no undressing; as each person becomes sleepy, they simply stretch out and draw a blanket over themselves, head and all, while the other occupants of the tipi continue their talking, singing, or other business until they too lie down to pleasant dreams.

### 13. HA'TI NI'BÄT—E'HE'EYE'

->Ha'ti ni'bät—E'he'eye'!<-
->Ha'ti ni'bät—E'he'eye'!<-
->Nä'nibä'tawa',<-

->The cottonwood song—*E'he'eye'*!<-

->I am singing it,<-
->*He'yäya'ahe'ye'*!<-
->*He'yäya'ahe'ye'*!<-

The cottonwood (*Populus monilifera*) is the most characteristic tree of the plains and of the arid region between the Rockies and the Sierras. It is a species of poplar and takes its name from the white downy blossom fronds, resembling cotton, which come out upon it in the spring. The cottonwood and a species of stunted oak, with the mesquite in the south, are almost the only trees to be found upon the great plains extending from the Saskatchewan southward into Texas. As it never grows out in the open, but always close along the borders of the few streams, it is a reliable indicator of water either on or near the surface, in a region that is nearly waterless. Between the bark and the wood there is a sweet milky juice which the Indians are very fond of—as one who had been educated in the East said, "It is their ice cream"—and they frequently strip off the bark and scrape the trunk in order to obtain it. Horses also are fond of this sweet juice, and in seasons when the grass has been burned off or is otherwise scarce, the

Indian ponies sometimes resort to the small twigs and bark of the cottonwood to sustain life. In extreme cases, their owners have sometimes been driven to the same shift. In winter, the camps of the prairie tribes are moved from the open prairie to the shelter of the cottonwood timber along the streams. The tree is held almost sacred, and the sun-dance lodge is usually or always constructed of cottonwood saplings.

### 14. EYEHE'! A'NIE'SA'NA

> Eyehe'! A'nie'sa'na',
> Eyehe'! A'nie'sa'na',
> He'ee'ä'ehe'yuhe'yu!

->*Translation*<-

> *Eyehe'!* The young birds,
> *Eyehe'!* The young birds,
> *He'ee'ä'ehe'yuhe'yu!*
> *He'ee'ä'ehe'yuhe'yu!*
> The young Thunderbirds,
> The young Thunderbirds.

Among the Algonquian tribes of the east, the Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Kiowa, Comanche, and prairie tribes generally, as well as among those of the northwest coast and some parts of Mexico, thunder and lightning are produced by a great bird, whose shadow is the thundercloud, whose flapping wings make the sound of thunder, and whose flashing eyes, rapidly opening or closing, send forth the lightning. Among some tribes of the northwest, this being is not a bird, but a giant who puts on a dress of bird skin with head, wings, and all complete, by means of which he flies through the air when in search of his prey. The myth is not found among the Iroquois or the Cherokee, or, perhaps, among the Muskhogean tribes.

The Thunderbird usually has his dwelling on some high mountain or rocky elevation of difficult access. Within the territory of the myth, several places are thus designated as the Thunder's Nest. Thunder Bay of Lake Huron, in lower Michigan, derives its name in this way. Such a place, known to the Sioux as *Waqkiñ'a-oye'*, "The Thunder's Nest," is within the old territory of the Sisseton Sioux in eastern South Dakota in the neighborhood of Big Stone Lake. At another place, near the summit of the Coteau des Prairies, in eastern South Dakota, a number of large round boulders are pointed out as the eggs of the Thunderbird. According to the Comanche, there is a place on upper Red River where the Thunderbird once alighted on the ground, the spot being still identified by the fact that the grass remains burned off over a space having the outline of a large bird with outstretched wings. The same

<meta>This page continues the description of the Thunderbird myth among the Plains tribes, specifically focusing on a legend of a hunter's encounter and the physical representations of the bird in Cheyenne and Arapaho culture.</meta>

<page-num>969</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE THUNDERBIRD</header>

People tell how a hunter once shot and wounded a large bird which fell to the ground. Because he was afraid to attack it alone due to its size, he returned to camp for help, but when they approached the spot again, the hunters heard the thunder rolling and saw flashes of lightning shooting out from the ravine where the bird lay wounded. As they came closer, the lightning blinded them so they could not see the bird, and one flash struck and killed a hunter. His frightened companions then fled back to camp, for they knew it was the Thunderbird.

<image-desc>A black and white photograph of a rawhide cutout representing the Thunderbird (identified as Fig. 92). The figure has wide, outstretched wings and a broad tail. The entire silhouette is outlined with beadwork. A prominent zigzag line, representing lightning, runs vertically down the center of the body from the chest to the tail. The head is shown in profile, facing left, with a distinct crest or beak shape.</image-desc>

->FIG. 92—The Thunderbird.<-

To both the Cheyenne and Arapaho, the thunder (*ba'a'*) is a large bird with a brood of smaller ones; it carries a number of arrows in its talons with which it strikes the victims of lightning. For this reason, they call the eagle on our coins *baa*. When it thunders, they say *ba'a' nänitü'-hut*, "the thunder calls." In Indian <term>pictography</term>, the Thunderbird is depicted with zigzag lines running out from its heart to represent the lightning. A small figure of it (shown in figure 92), cut from rawhide and decorated with beads, is frequently worn on the heads of the dancers.

<meta>This page continues the transcription and translation of Arapaho Ghost Dance songs, moving from the symbolism of the whirlwind to the Thunderbird and the general Indian conception of the cosmos.</meta>

<page-num>971</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] INDIAN CONCEPTION OF THE COSMOS</header>

This song probably refers to the Thunderbird. There is an energetic swing to the tune that makes it a favorite. In Indian belief, the earth is a circular disk, usually surrounded on all sides by water, and the sky is a solid concave hemisphere coming down at the horizon to the level of the earth. In Cherokee and other Indian myths, the sky is continually lifting up and coming down again to the earth, like the upper blade of a pair of scissors. The sun, which lives on the outside of this hemisphere, comes through from the east in the morning while there is a momentary opening between the earth and the edge of the sky. It climbs along the underside of the sky from east to west and goes out at the western horizon in the evening to return during the night to its starting point in the east.

->*Translation*<-

> The *Hanahawuněn* gave to me,
> The *Hanahawuněn* gave to me,
> His paint—He made me clean,
> His paint—He made me clean.

The author of this song met a man from the now-extinct Arapaho band of the *Hanahawuněna* in the spirit world, who washed the visitor's face and then painted him afresh with some of the old-time mineral paint of the Indians. In accordance with Indian belief, all the extinct and forgotten tribes now have their home in the world of shades.

to be able to see and talk with him by joining the dance, Paul went to Sitting Bull, the leader of the dance, at the next gathering and asked him to help him see his dead brother. The result was that he was hypnotized by Sitting Bull, fell to the ground in a trance, and saw his brother. It was from Paul's statement, intelligently told in good English before I had yet seen the dance, that I was first led to suspect that hypnotism was the secret of the trances.

<header>MOONEY] THE HUMMER AND BULL-ROARER</header>

her trance, she made the toy and carried it with her to the next dance, twirling it in the air while singing the song. The *hätiku'tha*, or hummer, is used by the boys of the prairie tribes just as our boys use the "cut-water"—a circular tin disk suspended on two strings passed through holes in the middle and set into rapid rotation to produce a humming sound by alternately twisting the strings together and allowing them to untwist again. One of those I examined consists of a bone from a buffalo hoof, painted in different colors, with four buckskin strings tied around the middle. These strings extend out on each side and are fastened at each end to a small peg so they can be grasped more firmly by the fingers. It was carried in the dance in 1890 by an old Arapaho named Tall Bear, who had owned it for twenty years. Another specimen, shown in figure 93,*a*, now in the possession of the National Museum, is similar in construction but has only one string on each side.

A related toy—which can hardly be considered a musical instrument—is known among white people as the "bull-roarer." It is found among most of the western tribes, as well as among our own children and primitive peoples all over the world. It is usually a simple, flat piece of wood about 6 inches long, sometimes notched on the edges and decoratively painted, attached to a sinew or buckskin string of convenient length. It is held in one hand, and when twirled rapidly in the air, it produces a sound much like the roaring of a bull or distant thunder. For most tribes, it is simply a child's toy, but among the Hopi, according to Fewkes, and the Apache, according to Bourke, it has a sacred use in assisting the prayers of the medicine man to bring on storm clouds and rain.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the turtle as a mythological figure, specifically as the sustainer of the earth in Algonquian and Hindu traditions, transitioning from the previous page's introduction of the turtle in Arapaho creation stories to its broader cultural significance and the introduction of Song 27.</meta>

<language>English, Arapaho</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>976</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14]</header>

In the mythology of many primitive nations, from the ancient Hindus to our own Indian tribes, the turtle or tortoise is the supporter of the earth—the Atlas on whose back rests the burden of the whole living universe. A reason for this is found in the amphibious nature of the turtle, which makes it equally at home on land and in the water, and in its peculiar shape, which was held to be typical of the world. The world itself was conceived as a huge turtle swimming in a limitless ocean; the dome of the sky was its upper shell, and the flat surface of the earth was the bony breastplate of the animal, while enclosed between them was the living body—the human, animal, and vegetable creation. In Hindu mythology, when the gods are ready to destroy mankind, the turtle will grow weary and sink under his load, and then the waters will rise and a deluge will overwhelm the earth. (*Fiske.*)

The belief in the turtle as the sustainer of the earth was common to all the Algonquian tribes, to which the Arapaho and Cheyenne belong, and to the northern Iroquoian tribes. Earthquakes were caused by the turtle shifting his position from time to time. In their pictographs, the turtle was frequently the symbol of the earth, and in their prayers it was sometimes addressed as "mother." The most honored clan was the Turtle clan; the most sacred spot in the Algonquian territory was Mackinaw, the "Island of the Great Turtle"; the favorite medicine bowl of their doctors is the shell of a turtle; the turtle is pictured on the ghost shirts of the Arapaho; and farther south in Oklahoma, it is the recognized livestock brand by which it is known that a horse or cow belongs to the historic Delaware tribe.

This song evidently refers to the Thunderbird. It is one of the old favorites from the north and is sung to a sprightly tune in quick time. It differs from the others because only part of the line is repeated, rather than the entire line.

The meaning of this song is not clear. It may refer to the Thunderbird or to the Crow, the sacred bird of the Ghost Dance. The *ye'nis*, or wild rose, is highly valued among the prairie tribes for its red seed berries, which are pounded into a paste and dried for food. It is often mentioned in the Ghost songs and is sometimes pictured on the Ghost shirts. Although rather tasteless, the berries have nutritional value. They are gathered in winter and are sometimes eaten raw, but they are usually first boiled and strained to remove the seeds. This dough-like substance is sometimes mixed with marrow from broken bones, wrapped around sticks, and then roasted before the fire. It is never stored for future use. The Cherokee call the same plant by a name that means "rabbit food," because of the animal's fondness for the berries.

### 30. NIHA'NATA'YECHE'TI

> He'yoho'ho'! He'yoho'ho'!

> *He'yoho'ho'! He'yoho'ho'!*
> The yellow-hide, the white-skin (man).
> I have now put him aside—
> I have now put him aside—
> I have no more sympathy with him,
> I have no more sympathy with him.
> *He'yoho'ho'! He'yoho'ho'!*

This is another song about white people, who are referred to as "yellow hides" or "white skins." The proper Arapaho name for a white man is *Nia'tha*, meaning "skillful." Many different names are applied to white people by various Indian tribes. The Comanche, Shoshoni, and Paiute call them *Tai'vo*, or "easterners"; the Hopi, who are of the same ancestral stock as those three tribes, know them as *Paha'na*, or "eastern water people"; the Kiowa call them *Be'dǎlpago*, "hairy mouths," or *Ta'ka'-i*, "standing ears." It is very doubtful whether the "pale face" of romantic fiction ever existed in the Indian mind.

<header>MOONEY] SACRED REGARD FOR CEDAR</header>

### *Translation*

> The cedar tree, the cedar tree,
> We have it in the center,
> We have it in the center
> When we dance,
> When we dance.
> We have it in the center,
> We have it in the center.

The Kiowa, the Sioux, and perhaps some other tribes performed the Ghost Dance around a tree set up in the center of the circle. Among the Kiowa, this tree was a cedar, and this was probably the case with the other tribes whenever a cedar could be obtained, as it is always a sacred tree in Indigenous belief and ceremony. The southern Arapaho and Cheyenne never used a tree in connection with the Ghost Dance, so this song could not have originated among them. The cedar is held sacred for its evergreen foliage, its fragrant scent, its red heartwood, and the durable character of its timber. Because of its fine grain and enduring qualities, the prairie tribes make their tipi poles from its wood, which will not warp from heat or moisture. Their flageolets or flutes are also made of cedar, and in the mescal and other ceremonies, its dried and crumbled foliage is thrown upon the fire as incense. In Cherokee and Yuchi myth, the red color of the wood comes from the blood of a wizard who was killed and beheaded by a hero. The wizard's head was hung in the tops of several trees in succession but continued to live until, on the advice of a medicine man, the people hung it in the topmost branches of a cedar tree, where it finally died. The blood from the severed head trickled down the trunk of the tree, and thus the wood was stained.

### 33. A-NI'QANA'GA

> A-ni'qana'ga,
> A-ni'qana'ga,
> Ha'tăni'i'na'daně'na,
> Ha'tăni'i'na'daně'na.

->*Translation*<-

> There is a solitary bull,
> There is a solitary bull —
> I am going to use him to "make medicine,"
> I am going to use him to "make medicine."

From the buffalo, they obtained food, fuel, clothing, shelter, and domestic furniture, as well as shields for defense, points for their arrows, and strings for their bows. As the old Spanish chronicles of Coronado put it: "To be brief, they make as many things from them as they have need of, or as many as are sufficient for them in the conduct of this life."

Among Indigenous peoples, the professions of medicine and religion are inseparable. The doctor is always a priest, and the priest is always a doctor. Consequently, to the white people in Indian territory, the Indigenous priest-doctor has come to be known as the "medicine man," and anything sacred, mysterious, or of wonderful power or effectiveness in Indigenous life or belief is designated as "medicine." This term is the closest equivalent to the native expressions in various languages. To "make medicine" is to perform some sacred ceremony, ranging from the curing of a sick child to the consecration of the sun-dance lodge. Among the prairie tribes, the great annual tribal ceremony was commonly known as the "medicine dance," and the special guardian deity of every warrior was spoken of as his "medicine."

The buffalo was to the nomadic hunters of the plains what corn was to the more settled tribes of the east and south—the living, visible symbol of their support and existence, and the greatest gift of a higher being to his children. Something of the buffalo entered into every important ceremony. In the medicine dance—or sun dance, as it is frequently called—the head and skin of a buffalo hung from the center pole of the lodge. In the rigorous physical trials that accompanied this dance among some tribes, the dancers dragged buffalo skulls around the circle; these were tied to ropes fastened to skewers driven through incisions in their bodies and limbs. A buffalo skull is placed in front of the sacred sweat lodge, and on the battlefield of Wounded Knee, I have seen buffalo skulls and plates of dried meat placed at the head of the graves. The buffalo was the sign of the Creator on earth, just as the sun was his glorious manifestation in the heavens. Buffalo hair was an important element in the preparation of "medicine," whether for war, hunting, love, or healing itself, and for such

### 34. A-NĔX'THIBIWĂ'HANĂ

->A'-nĕä'thibiwă'hană,<-
->A'-nĕä'thibiwă'hană—<-
->Thi'äya'nĕ,<-

->*Translation*<-

> The place where crying begins,
> The place where crying begins—
> The <term>thi'äya</term>,
> The <term>thi'äya</term>.

This song refers to the sweat-lodge already described in the treatment of the Ghost dance among the Sioux. In preparing the sweat-lodge, a small hole, perhaps a foot deep, is dug out in the center of the floor space to serve as a receptacle for the heated stones over which the water is poured to produce the steam. The earth thus dug out is piled in a small hillock a few feet in front of the entrance to the sweat-lodge, which always faces the east. This small mound is called <term>thi'äya</term> in the Arapaho language; the same name is also applied to a memorial stone heap or to a stone monument. It is always surmounted by a buffalo skull, or in these days by the skull of a steer, placed so as to face the doorway of the lodge. The <term>thi'äya</term> is mentioned in several of the Ghost-dance songs, and usually, as here, in connection with crying or lamentation, as though the sight of these things in the trance vision brings up sad recollections.

### 36. A-HU'HU HA'GENI'STI'TI BA'HU

->*Translation*<-

The crow is making a road,

He has finished it,

His children,

Then he collected them (i.e., on the farther side).

(The crow (*ho*) is the sacred bird of the Ghost Dance, revered as the messenger from the spirit world because its color is symbolic of death and the shadow land. The raven, which is essentially a larger crow and lives in the mountains but occasionally comes down into the plains, is also held sacred and regarded as a bringer of omens by the prairie tribes, as well as by the Tlingit and others of the northwest coast and by the Cherokee in the east. The crow is depicted on the shirts, leggings, and moccasins of the Ghost dancers, and its feathers are worn on their heads. Whenever it is possible to kill one, the skin is stuffed as if alive and carried in the dance, as shown in the picture of Black Coyote (*plate cv*). At one time, the dancers in Left Hand's camp had a crow which was claimed to have the power of speech and prophetic utterance, and its hoarse, inarticulate cries were interpreted as inspired messages from the spirit world. Unfortunately, the bird did not thrive in captivity and soon departed for the land of spirits, leaving the Arapaho once more dependent on the guidance of trance revelations. The eagle, the magpie, and the sage-hen are also sacred in the Ghost Dance; the first is held in veneration by Indians, as well as by other peoples throughout the world, while the magpie and the sage-hen are revered for their connection with the country of the messiah and the mythology of his tribe.

The crow was probably held sacred by all the tribes of the Algonquian race. Roger Williams, speaking of the New England tribes, says that although the crows sometimes damaged the corn, scarcely one Indian in a hundred would kill one, because their tradition held that this bird had brought them their first grain and vegetables. It supposedly carried a grain of corn in one ear and a bean in the other from the field of their great god Cautantouwit in Sowwani'u, the southwest, the happy spirit world where the gods and the souls dwelt.

<summary>This page describes the sacred status of the crow as a messenger from the spirit world in the Ghost Dance and explains its symbolic presence on dance regalia. It also connects this reverence to broader Algonquian traditions and mentions other sacred birds like the eagle, magpie, and sage-hen.</summary>

of the great and good. The souls of the wicked were not permitted to enter this elysium after death, but were doomed to wander without rest or home. (Williams, *Key into the Language of America, 1643.*)

(In Arapaho belief, the spirit world is in the west, not on the same level as our earth, but higher up, and also separated from it by a body of water.) In their statement of the Ghost Dance mythology referred to in this song, the crow, as the messenger and leader of the spirits who had gone before, gathered their armies on the other side and advanced at their head to the near edge of the shadow land. Then, looking over, they saw far below them a sea, and far out beyond it toward the east was the boundary of the earth, where lived the friends they were marching to meet again. Taking up a pebble in his beak, the crow then dropped it into the water and it became a mountain towering up to the land of the dead. Down its rocky slope he brought his army until they halted at the edge of the water. Then, taking some dust in his beak, the crow flew out and dropped it into the water as he flew, and it became a solid arm of land stretching from the spirit world to the earth. He returned and flew out again, this time with some blades of grass, which he dropped upon the land thus made, and at once it was covered with a green sod. Again he returned, and again flew out, this time with some twigs in his beak, and dropping these also upon the new land, at once it was covered with a forest of trees. Again he flew back to the base of the mountain, and is now, for the fourth time, coming on at the head of all the countless host of spirits which has already passed over the sea and is assembling on the western boundary of the earth.

<header>MOONEY] THE COYOTE MEN 985</header>

->*Translation*<-

> Little boy, the coyote gun —
> Little boy, the coyote gun —
> I have uncovered it — *Ahe'e'ye'!*
> I have uncovered it — *Ahe'e'ye'!*
> There is the sheath lying there,
> There is the sheath lying there.

This song was composed by Nakash, or "Sage," one of the Northern Arapaho delegates to the Messiah. It clearly refers to one of his trance experiences in the other world and relates to an interesting feature in the social structure of the Arapaho and other prairie tribes. The *ga'ahinĕ'na* or *gaahi'na*, "coyote men," were an order of middle-aged men who acted as pickets or lookouts for the camp. When the band camped in a convenient location for hunting or other business, it was the duty of these men, usually four or six in a band, to take their positions on the nearest hills to keep watch and give timely warning if an enemy approached. It was a position of danger and responsibility, but it was held in corresponding respect. When on duty, the *gaahi'nĕn* wore a white buffalo robe, had his face painted with white clay, and carried in his hand the *ya'haga'ahi'na* or "coyote gun"—a club decorated with feathers and other ornaments and usually covered with a sheath of bear gut (*i'tha'q'*). He had to be unmarried and remain so while in office, finally choosing his own successor and delivering the "coyote gun" to him as a staff of authority. They were never all off duty at the same time; at least half were always on guard, with one or more coming down to the village at a time to eat or sleep. They built no shelters on the hills but slept there in their buffalo robes, though they sometimes returned in shifts to sleep in their own tipis. Usually, however, they preferred to sleep alone upon the hills to receive inspiration in dreams. If attacked or surprised by the enemy, they were expected to fight. The watcher was sometimes called *higa'ahi'na-it*, "the man with the coyote gun." The corresponding officer among the Cheyenne carried a bow and arrows instead of a club.

In his trance vision, the author of this song saw a large camp of Arapaho, and in the middle of the camp circle, as in the old days, were sitting the seven priests of the *Chĭnachichi'bät*, each wearing on his head the Thunderbird headdress, previously described and illustrated under song number 14. This vision of the old life of the tribe brought back sorrowful memories and caused him to weep. In the similar song that follows, the singer laments for the *Chĭnachichi'bät* and the *bä'qati* gaming wheel. The priests referred to here were seven in number and formed the highest order of the military and social organization that existed among the Blackfeet, Sioux, Cheyenne, Kiowa, and probably all the prairie tribes except for the Comanche in the south, among whom it seems to have been unknown. The society, as far as it has come to the attention of white men, has commonly been designated by them as the "Dog Soldier" society—a misunderstanding of a name belonging probably to only one of the six or eight orders of the organization. The corresponding Blackfoot organization, the *Ikunuhkatsi* or "All Comrades," is described by Grinnell in his "Blackfoot Lodge Tales." The Kiowa organization will be noted later.

Among the Arapaho, the organization was called *Běni'něna*, "Warriors," and consisted of eight degrees or orders, including nearly all the men of the tribe above the age of about seventeen. Those who were not enrolled in one of the eight orders were held in very little respect and were not allowed to take part in public ceremonies.

orders to accompany war expeditions. Each of the first six orders had its own unique dance, and the members of the principal warrior orders also had their specific staff or badge of rank.

First and lowest in rank were the *Nuhine'na* or Fox men, consisting of young men up to the age of about 25 years. They had no special duties or privileges, but had a dance called the *Nuha'wŭ* or fox dance.

Next came the *Hă'thahu'ha* or Star men, consisting of young warriors about 30 years of age. Their dance was called the *Ha'thahŭ*.

The third order was that of the *Hichăă'quthi* or Club men. Their dance was called *Hichăă'qawŭ*. They were an important part of the warrior organization, and were all men in the prime of life. The four leaders carried wooden clubs, bearing a general resemblance in shape to a gun, notched along the edges and variously ornamented. In an attack on the enemy, it was the duty of these leaders to dash on ahead and strike the enemy with these clubs, then to ride back again and take their places in the front of the charge. said that the position of leader of the *Hichää'quthi* was a dangerous honor, but the honor was in proportion to the danger itself, and there were always candidates for a vacancy. It was one of those offices where the holder sometimes died but never resigned. The other members of the order carried sticks carved at one end in the rough likeness of a horse's head and pointed at the other. In desperate encounters, they were expected to plant these sticks in the ground in a line in front of the body of warriors and to fight beside them to the death unless a retreat was ordered by the chief in command.

The fourth order was called *Bitahi'něna* or Spear men, and their dance was called *Bitaha'wǔ*. This order came originally from the Cheyenne. Their duties and unique symbols of office were about the same among all the tribes. They performed police duty in camp, when traveling, and during the hunt, and they were expected to see that the orders of the chief were obeyed by the tribe. For instance, if any person violated the tribal code or failed to attend a general dance or council, a party of *Bitahi'něna* was sent to kill his dogs, destroy his tipi, or in extreme cases to shoot his ponies. On hunting expeditions, it was their business to keep the party together and see that no one killed a buffalo until the proper ceremonies had been performed and the order was given by the chief. They were regarded as the representatives of the law and were never resisted in performing their duty or inflicting punishments. In war, they were fierce warriors, equaling or surpassing even the *Hichää'quthi*. Of the leaders of the order, two carried a sort of shepherd's crook called *nu'sa-icha'tha*, having a lance point at its lower end; two others carried lances wrapped with otter skin; four carried lances painted black; one carried a club shaped like a baseball bat, and one carried a rattle made of the scrotum of a buffalo and decorated with its hair. In battle, if the enemy took shelter behind defenses, it was this man's duty to lead the charge, throw his rattle among the enemy, and then follow it himself.

The fifth order was called *Aha'känä'na* or Crazy men. They were men more than 50 years of age and were not expected to go to war, but must have advanced through all the lower orders. Their duties were religious and ceremonial, and their symbols consisted of a bow and a bundle of blunt arrows. Their dance was the *Ahaka'wǔ* or crazy dance, which well deserved the name. It will be described in another place.

The sixth was the order of the *Hěthě'hině'na* or Dog men. Their dance was called *Hěthěwa'wǔ'*. They had four principal leaders and two lesser leaders. The four principal leaders were the generals and directors of the battle. Each carried a rattle and wore around his neck a buckskin strap (two being yellow, the other two black) which hung down to his feet. On approaching the enemy, they were obliged to go forward, shaking their rattles and chanting the war song, until some other warriors of the party took the rattles out of their hands. <header>MOONEY] ARAPAHO WARRIOR ORDERS</header>

the ground and tied themselves to them with straps, anchoring themselves at the front of the battle. There they remained until, if the battle appeared lost, they themselves gave the order to retreat. Even then, they waited until members of their own society released them by pulling the lances out of the ground and driving them away from the spot with a distinctive quirt <note>a short-handled riding whip</note> carried only by the private members of this division. No one was permitted to retreat without their permission, under penalty of disgrace, nor were they allowed to retire until they were released in this manner. If their followers forgot to release them during the confusion of a retreat, they were expected to die at their posts. They could only be released by someone from their own division, and anyone else who attempted to pull the lances from the ground was resisted as an enemy. When pursued during a retreat, they had to give up their horses to the women if necessary, and either find other horses or turn and face the enemy alone on foot. They rarely accompanied any but large war parties; and, although they did little actual fighting, their mere presence inspired the warriors with desperate courage. Driving their lances into the ground was always understood as a signal for a fight to the death.

The seventh order was the *Núnaha'wǔ*, a word whose meaning is now unknown. This was a secret order. They had no dance, and only they witnessed their ceremonies. They did not fight, but accompanied war parties and performed secret ceremonies and prayers for success every night.

The eighth and highest order was the *Chi'nachině'na*, or Water-pouring men, the "seven venerable priests" referred to in the song. They were the high priests and instructors of all the other orders, numbering seven individuals chosen from among the oldest warriors of the tribe. Their name refers to their practice of pouring water over heated stones in the sweat-lodge to produce steam. They had no dance and were not expected to go to war, though one of the seven could choose to accompany a war party if he wished. Their ceremonies were performed in a large sweat-lodge called a *chĭnachichi'bät*. When the entire tribe camped together, this lodge occupied the center of the circle, between the entrance and the lodge where the sacred medicine pipe was kept. Unlike the ordinary sweat-lodge, this one did not have a mound and buffalo skull in front of the entrance.

The warrior organization of the Kiowa is called *Yä'pähe* ("Soldiers") and consisted of six orders, each with its own dance, songs, and ceremonial dress. 1. *Poläñyup* or *Tsäñ'yui* ("Rabbits"). These were boys and young men between the ages of 8 and 15. Their dance, in which they were trained by certain old men, involves a unique step that imitates the jumping movement of a rabbit. 2. *Ädalto'yui* or *Te'ñbiyu'i* ("Young Mountain Sheep," literally "Herders" or "Corralers"). 3. *Tseñtä'nmo* ("Horse Head-dress (?) people"). 4. *Toñkoñ'ko* ("Black-leg people"). 5. *T'äñpe'ko* ("Skunkberry (?) people"). 6. *Kâ'itseñ'ko* ("Principal Dogs" or "Real Dogs"). These last were the highest warrior

### 46. NA'TÄNU'YA CHĔ'BI'NH

> Na'tǎnu'ya chě'bi'nh—
> Na'tǎnu'ya chě'bi'nh,
> Na'chicha'ba'n,
> Na'chicha'ba'n.

->*Translation*<-

> The pemmican that I am using—
> The pemmican that I am using,
> They are still making it,
> They are still making it.

This song refers to pemmican, a preparation of dried and pounded meat that was once a favorite food of the prairie tribes. The author of the song apparently tasted it while it was being prepared by the women in the spirit world. <note>See Sioux song 7.</note> One must be an Indian to understand the thrill of joy that would fill the hearts of the dancers when told that a dreamer had seen their departed friends in the spirit world still making and feasting on pemmican. During the first year or two of the movement, it happened several times at Ghost dances in the north and south—among the Sioux as well as among the Arapaho and others—that meat was displayed and tasted as genuine buffalo beef or pemmican brought back from the spirit world by one of the dancers. It is not necessary to explain how this deception was carried out or why it succeeded. It is enough to know that it was done, and that the dancers were in a state of mind to believe anything.

<page-num>992</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

Wherever found, the eagle was regarded as sacred among the Indian tribes of both the East and West. Its feathers were highly prized for ornamental and “medicine” purposes, and an elaborately detailed ritual of prayer and ceremony was the necessary accompaniment to its capture. Among all the tribes, the chief purpose of this ritual was to obtain the help of the gods in inducing the eagle to approach the hunter, and to turn aside the anger of the eagle spirits at the necessary sacrilege.

The feathers most valued were those of the tail and wings. These were used to ornament lances and shields, to be worn upon the head, and to decorate the magnificent war bonnets—the finest of which have a pendant or trail of eagle-tail feathers reaching from the warrior’s head to the ground when he stands erect. The whistle used in the sun dance and other great ceremonies is made of a bone from the leg or wing of the eagle. The fans carried by the warriors on parade, and also used to sprinkle holy water in the mescal ceremony of the southern prairie tribes, are commonly made of the entire tail or wing of that bird. Hawk feathers are sometimes used for these various purposes but are always considered far inferior to those of the eagle. The smaller feathers are used on arrows.

Eagle feathers and ponies were formerly the standard of value and the medium of exchange among the prairie tribes, just as wampum was for those on the Atlantic coast. The standard varied according to place and season, but in a general way, two to four eagles were rated as equal to a horse. In these times, eagle-feather war bonnets and eagle-tail fans are the most valuable parts of an Indian’s outfit and the most difficult to purchase from him.

Among the Pueblo tribes, eagles are sometimes taken from the nest when young, kept in cages, and regularly stripped of their best feathers. Among the Caddo, Cherokee, and other tribes of the timbered country in the East, they were shot with bows and arrows or with guns, but always according to certain ritual ceremonies. Among the prairie tribes along the entire extent of the plains, they were never shot; instead, they had to be captured alive in pitfalls and then strangled or crushed to death, if possible without shedding blood. A description of the Arapaho method will suffice, with slight modifications, for all the prairie tribes.

The hunter withdrew with his family away from the main camp to some rough, hilly country where eagles were abundant. After some preliminary prayers, he went alone to the top of the highest hill and there dug a pit large enough to sit or lie down in. He was careful to carry the earth taken out of the hole far enough away from the place that it would not attract the eagle's notice. The pit was roofed over with a covering of light willow twigs, above which earth and grass were placed to give it a natural appearance. The bait was a piece of fresh meat or—as appears from this song—a piece of tallow stripped from the ribs of the buffalo. This was tied to a rawhide string and laid upon the top of the pit, while the rope was passed down through the roof into the cavity below. A coyote skin, stuffed and set up erect as if alive, was

sometimes placed near the bait to add to the realistic effect. After sitting up all night singing the eagle songs and purifying himself for the ceremony, the hunter started before daylight without eating any breakfast or drinking water. He went up the hill to the pit and entered it. Having closed the opening again, he sat inside holding the end of the string in his hands to prevent a coyote or other animal from taking the bait while waiting for the eagles to come.

If other birds came, he drove them away or ignored them. When the eagle finally arrived, the other birds flew away immediately. The eagle swooped down, always landing to one side and then walking over onto the roof of the trap to reach the bait. At that moment, the hunter reached his hand up through the framework, grabbed the eagle by the legs, pulled it down, and quickly strangled it or broke its neck. He then reset the bait and the roof and sat down to wait for another eagle. He might be lucky enough to capture several during the day, or so unfortunate as to catch none at all. At night, but not before, he went back to his own tipi to eat, drink, and sleep, returning to the pit before daylight. While in the pit, he did not eat, drink, or sleep. The eagle hunt, if it can be called that, lasted four days and had to end then, regardless of the hunter's success.

At the end of four days, he returned home with the bodies of the eagles he had caught. A small lodge was set up outside his tipi, and the eagles were hung by their necks from a pole laid across two forked sticks driven into the ground. After further prayers and purifications, the feathers were stripped from the bodies as they hung.

The Blackfoot method, as described by Grinnell in his *Blackfoot Lodge Tales*, was essentially the same as that of the Arapaho. He adds several details that were likely common to both tribes and others, but which my Arapaho informants did not mention. While the hunter was away in the pit, his wife or daughters at home must not use an awl for sewing or other purposes; if they did, the eagle might scratch the hunter. He took a human skull with him into the pit so that he would be as invisible to the eagle as the spirit of the skull's former owner. He must not eat the berries of the wild rose during this period, or the eagle would not attack the bait, and he had to put a piece of <term>pemmican</term> into the mouth of the dead eagle to gain the goodwill of its fellows and encourage them to come and be caught.

The eagle-catching ceremony of the Caddo, Cherokee, and other eastern tribes will be discussed when treating the Caddo songs.

### 49. A-BÄ'QATI' HÄ'NICHÄ'BI'HINÄ'NA

> A-bä'qati' hä'nichä'bi'hinä'na,
> A-bä'qati' hä'nichä'bi'hinä'na.
> A-wa'täna'ni ani'ä'tähï'näna,
> A-wa'täna'ni ani'ä'tähï'näna.

->*Translation*<-

> With the <term>bä'qati</term> wheel I am gambling,
> With the <term>bä'qati</term> wheel I am gambling.
> With the black mark I win the game,
> With the black mark I win the game.

This song comes from the northern Arapaho. The author of it, during his visit to the spirit world, found his former friends playing the old game of the <term>bä'qati</term> wheel. This game was practically obsolete among the prairie tribes but has been revived since the beginning of the Ghost Dance. As it was a favorite game for men in the old days, many of the songs based on these trance visions refer to it; the wheel and sticks are made by the dreamer and carried in the dance while they sing.

The game is played with a wheel (<term>bä'qati</term>, "large wheel") and two pairs of throwing sticks (<term>qa'qa-u'nûtha</term>). The Cheyenne call the wheel <term>ä'ko'yo</term> or <term>äkwi'u</term>, and the sticks <term>hoo'isi'yonots</term>. It is a game for men involving three players: one rolls the wheel while the other two, each armed with a pair of throwing sticks, run after it and throw the sticks so as to cross the wheel in a certain position. The two throwers are the competitors, while the one who rolls the wheel is merely an assistant. Like most American Indian games, it is a form of gambling, and high stakes are sometimes wagered on the outcome. It is common to the Arapaho, Cheyenne, Sioux, and probably to all the northern prairie tribes, but is not found among the Kiowa or Comanche in the south.

The wheel is about 18 inches in diameter and consists of a flexible young tree branch, stripped of its bark and painted, with the two ends fastened together with sinew or buckskin string. At equal distances around the circumference of the wheel, four figures are cut. The two opposite each other form a pair but are distinguished by different colors—usually blue or black and red—and by lines or notches on the surface. These figures are identified simply by their colors. Figures of birds, crescents, and other designs are sometimes also cut or painted on the wheel, but these have nothing to do with the game. (See plate CXI.)

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the Arapaho wheel-and-stick game (bä'qati) and its associated songs as part of the Ghost Dance rituals, following the introduction of the game's equipment and basic rules.</meta>

<page-num>995</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE BÄ'QATI GAME</header>

The sticks are light rods, about 30 inches long, tied in pairs by a particular arrangement of buckskin strings and distinguished from one another by pieces of cloth of different colors fastened to the strings. There is also a pile of tally sticks—usually one hundred in number, about the size of lead pencils and painted green—for keeping score in the game. The sticks are held near the center in a particular way between the fingers of the closed hand. When the wheel is rolled, each player runs from the same side and tries to throw the sticks to strike the wheel so that, when it falls, both sticks in his pair are either over or under a certain figure. It requires dexterity to do this, as the string tends to strike the wheel in a way that makes one stick fall under and the other over, in which case the throw does not count. The players assign their own value to each figure; the usual value is five points for one and ten for the other figure, with double that number for a throw that crosses the two corresponding figures, and one hundred points to win the game.

The wheel-and-stick game, in one form or another, was almost universal among Indian tribes. Another game among the prairie tribes is played with a netted wheel and a single stick or arrow; the goal is to send the arrow through the netting as close as possible to the center or bull's-eye. This game is called *ana'wati'n-hati*, "playing wheel," by the Arapaho.

This song is unusual because it has two sharp yelps at the end, in the style of the ordinary songs of the warrior dances.

### 55. I'NITA'TA'-USÄ'NA

I'nita'ta'-usä'na,
I'nita'ta'-usä'na.

->*Translation*<-

Stand ready,
Stand ready.
(So that when) the crow calls you,
(So that when) the crow calls you.
You will see him,
You will see him.

This song was composed by Little Raven, one of the delegation of seven from the southern Arapaho and Cheyenne who visited the messiah in Nevada in August 1891. It is a message to the believers to be ready for the impending arrival of the new earth. The first line is sometimes sung *I'nita'ta-u'sä-hu'na*.

### 56. WA'WÄTHÄ'BI

Nä'nisa'na-ǔ', nä'nisa'na-ǔ',
Wa'wäthä'bichä'chini'nabä'nagu'wa-u'i'naga'thi—He'e'ye'!
Häthi'na ne'nahu',
Häthi'na ne'nahu'.

->*Translation*<-

My children, my children,
I have given you magpie feathers again to wear on your heads—*He'e'ye'*!
Thus says our mother,
Thus says our mother.

This song provides a good example of the possibilities of Indian word building. The second word might serve as a companion piece to Mark Twain's description of a complex word in German. It consists of seventeen syllables, all so interwoven to complete the meaning of the word-sentence that no part can be separated from the rest without destroying the whole. The main verbal part indicates that "I have given you (plural) a headdress again." The final syllables, <term>wa-u'i-naga'thi</term>, show that the headdress consists of the tail feathers (<term>wagathi</term>) of the magpie (<term>wa-u-i</term>). The syllable <term>cha</term> implies repetition or the return of an action, suggesting this was likely not the first time the messiah had given magpie feathers to his visitors.

The magpie (<term>Pica hudsonica</term> or <term>mittalii</term>) of the Rocky Mountains, the Sierra Nevada, and the intermediate region of Nevada and Utah is perhaps the most prominent bird in the Paiute country. It generally resembles a crow or blackbird, being about the size

<header>MOONEY] USE OF MAGPIE FEATHERS</header>

of the latter, being jet black except for the breast, which is white, and a white spot on each wing. Its tail has two long feathers with a beautiful, shifting metallic luster. It is a native bird, often found in small flocks near the Paiute camps. The Paiute hold it sacred and value the long tail feathers for decoration as highly as the Plains tribes value eagle feathers. In 1891, the standard price for these feathers was 25 cents a pair. The delegates who crossed the mountains to visit the messiah brought back many of these feathers, which from then on played an important role in the Ghost Dance ceremony. Indeed, they were in such high demand that traders tried to meet it—first by importing genuine magpie feathers from the mountains, but later by dishonestly substituting chosen crow feathers from the east at the same price.

The song is also unusual because it refers to the messiah as "my mother" (*nena*) instead of the usual "our father" (*hesûnanin*).

In this song, the dreamer tells of his trance visit to the spirit world, where he found his friends busily engaged in cutting up meat after a successful buffalo hunt, while the crows were hovering about the carrion. ### 59. AHU’NÄ HE’SÛNA’NIN
Ahu’n̈a he’sûna’nîn—
Ahu’n̈a he’sûna’nîn—
Ni’tabä’tanî’ bäta’hina’ni,
Ni’tabä’tanî’ bäta’hina’ni,
Ha’kä hä’sabinî’n̈a he’sûna’nîn,
Ha’kä hä’sabinî’n̈a he’sûna’nîn.

#### Translation
There is our father—
There is our father—
We are dancing as he wishes (makes) us to dance,
We are dancing as he wishes (makes) us to dance,
Because our father has so commanded us,
Because our father has so commanded us.

The literal meaning of the last line is “because our father has given it to us,” which is the prairie idiom for directing or commanding—being to “give a road” or to “make a road” for the one thus commanded. To disobey is to “break the road,” and to depart from a former custom is to “make a new road.” The idea is expressed in the same way both in the various spoken languages and in sign language.

The author of this song was a woman who, in her trance vision, saw her female friends in the other world playing the ball game, as described in song number 7. In this case, however, her partner is urged to *throw* the ball instead of striking it.

64. HISE'HI, HISE'HI
Hise'hi, hise'hi,
Hä'tine'bäku'tha'na,
Hä'tine'bäku'tha'na,
Häti'ta-u'seta'na,

->*Translation*<-
My comrade, my comrade,
Let us play the awl game,
Let us play the awl game,
Let us play the dice game,
Let us play the dice game.

The woman who composed this song tells how, on waking up in the spirit world, she met a party of her former girl companions and sat down with them to play the two games universally popular with the women of all the prairie tribes.

The first is called <term>ne'bäku'thana</term> by the Arapaho and <term>tsoñä</term> or “awl game” (from <term>tsoñ</term>, an awl) by the Kiowa, because an awl—the Indian woman’s substitute for a needle—is used to keep record of the score.

<image-desc>A square diagram with arcs in the four corners. Dots are placed along the edges between the arcs. On the top edge, "RIVER (Dangerous)" is written vertically on the right side and "RIVER" horizontally on the left side. On the left edge, "RIVER" is written horizontally near the center. On the right edge, "RIVER (Dangerous)" is written vertically near the bottom. In the center of the square is a circle labeled "STONE."</image-desc>

->FIG. 95—Diagram of awl game.<-

The game is becoming obsolete in the north, but is the everyday summer amusement of the women among the Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache in the southern plains. It is very amusing because of the unforeseen “rivers” and “whips” that are constantly turning up to disappoint the expectant winner; a party of women will frequently sit around the blanket for half a day at a time, with a constant ripple of laughter and good-humored jokes as they follow the chances of the play. It would make a very charming picnic game, or could readily be adapted to a modern parlor.

The players sit upon the ground around a blanket marked in charcoal with lines, dots, and quadrants in the corners, as shown in figure 95. In the center is a stone upon which the sticks are thrown. Each dot, except those between the parallels, counts a point, making twenty-four points for dots. Each of the parallel lines, and each end of the curved lines in the corners, also counts a point,

# MOONEY] THE AWL GAME

...making sixteen points for the lines or forty points in total. The players start from the bottom, with opposing players moving in opposite directions. With each throw of the sticks, the thrower moves her awl forward and sticks it into the blanket at the dot or line reached by her throw. The parallel lines on each of the four sides are called <term>“rivers,”</term> and the dots within these lines do not count in the game. The rivers at the top and bottom are <term>“dangerous”</term> and cannot be crossed. When a player is unlucky enough to make a throw that lands her on the edge of the river (that is, on the first line of either of these pairs of parallel lines), she <term>“falls into the river”</term> and must lose everything she has gained so far and begin again at the start. Similarly, when a player moving in one direction makes a throw that brings her awl to the spot occupied by the awl of an opponent coming from the other direction, that opponent is <term>“whipped back”</term> to the starting point and must begin all over again. Thus, there is a constant succession of unexpected events that provide endless amusement for the players.

<image-desc>Four vertically oriented wooden sticks used in the game. They are flat on one side and rounded on the other, featuring various geometric carvings such as chevrons, crosses, and diamonds. The stick on the far right is noticeably thinner than the others. Below the image is the caption: FIG. 96—Sticks used in awl game.</image-desc>

The game is played with four sticks, each between 6 and 10 inches long, flat on one side and rounded on the other (figure 96). One of these is the <term>trump stick</term>; it is marked distinctively in the center on both sides and is also distinguished

Fine lines at the end of the bundle suggest detail or movement. Below the image is the caption: FIG. 97—Trump sticks used in awl game.</image-desc>

by a green line along the flat side (figure 97), while the other sticks each have a red line. The <term>Kiowa</term> call this trump stick <term>sahe</term>, meaning “green,” because of the green stripe, while the others are called “red.” There are also several small green sticks, about the size of lead pencils, used for keeping score. <meta>This page continues the description of Indigenous games, moving from the awl game discussed on the previous page to a detailed explanation of the Arapaho dice game, including its equipment, scoring, and cultural context.</meta>

# MOONEY] THE DICE GAME

The requirements are a small wicker bowl or basket (*hatěchi'na*), five dice made of bone or plum stones, and a pile of tally sticks like those used in the awl game. The bowl is 6 or 8 inches in diameter and about 2 inches deep; it is woven like a basket from the tough fibers of the yucca (figure 98). The dice may be round, elliptical, or diamond-shaped and are marked on one side with various lines and figures; the turtle is a favorite design among the Arapaho (figure 99). Two of the five must be identical in shape and marking. The other three are marked with a different design and may also be a different shape. Any number of women or girls may play, with each throwing in turn, and sometimes one set of partners plays against another. The players toss the dice up from the basket, letting them drop back into it, and score points based on how the dice land in the basket. Each player's first throw is made from the hand instead of the basket. One hundred points usually constitute a game, and stakes are wagered on the result, as is the case in almost every other Indian contest of skill or chance. 

For the purpose of explanation, we shall designate two of the five dice as "rounds" and the other three as "diamonds." It should be understood that only the marked side counts in the game, except when the throw happens to turn up the three diamonds blank while the other two show the marked side, or, as sometimes happens, when all five dice land blank-side up. In every case, all of at least one kind must land face up to score a point. A successful throw entitles the player to another turn, while a failure obliges her to pass the basket to someone else. The scoring is as follows:

<image-desc>Six small dice or game pieces. Two are elongated, elliptical shapes with a vertical central line and horizontal cross-hatching. Four are circular, each marked with four lines meeting at the center in a cross-like or star-like pattern. Legend: FIG. 99—Dice used in dice game.</image-desc>

| Scoring Condition | Points |
|-------------------|:------:|
| Only 1 of either kind | 0 |
| 2 rounds | 3 |
| 3 diamonds (both rounds blank-side up) | 3 |
| 3 diamonds blank (both rounds marked-side up) | 3 |
| 4 marked sides up | 1 |
| 5 (all) blank sides up | 1 |
| 5 (all) marked sides up | 8 |

A game similar in principle, but played with six dice instead of five, is also played by Arapaho women, as well as by the women of the Comanche and likely other tribes.

> My children, my children,
> My top, my top—
> It will win the game,
> It will win the game.

The man who composed this song when he entered the spirit world in his vision met one of his childhood friends there who had died many years before; once more, he spun tops with him as they had in their youth.

Tops are used by all Indian boys and are made of wood or bone. They are not thrown or spun with a string, but are kept in motion by whipping them with a small quirt or buckskin whip. In winter, they are spun upon the ice. The younger children make tops to twirl with their fingers by running a stick through a small berry.

### 66. HE'NA'GA'NAWA'NEN

He'na'ga'nawa'nen näa'wu'nani'nä bi'gushi'shi He'sûna'nini'—Ahe'e'ye'!
He'na'ga'nawa'nen näa'wu'nani'nä bi'gushi'shi He'sûna'nini'—Ahe'e'ye'!
Nithi'na hesûna'nini'—Ahe'e'ye'!
Nithi'na hesûna'nini'—Ahe'e'ye'!

->Translation<-

> When we dance until daylight our father, the Moon, takes pity on us—*Ahe'e'ye'*!
> When we dance until daylight our father, the Moon, takes pity on us—*Ahe'e'ye'*!
> The father says so—*Ahe'e'ye'*!
> The father says so—*Ahe'e'ye'*!

Among the Arapaho, as with many other tribes, the moon is masculine and the sun is feminine. In mythology, the two are brother and sister. There are various myths to account for the spots on the moon's surface: some see a large frog in them, while to others, they look like a kettle hanging over a fire. The Arapaho name for the moon, *bi'gushish*, literally means "night sun," while the sun itself is called *hishinishish*, or "day sun." A similar naming convention exists among most other tribes.

In one Ghost Dance, seven different women carried these game sticks.

<meta>This page continues the description of the *bătĭqta'wa* game from the previous page and introduces song number 69, which describes the *ga'qutit* or "hunt the button" game.</meta>

<page-num>1008</page-num>
<header>THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETH. ANN. 14</header>

is a very simple game, the contestants merely throwing or sliding the sticks along the ground to see who can send them farthest. Two persons or two parties play against each other, with boys sometimes playing against girls or men against women. It is, however, more especially a girls' game. The game sticks (*bătĭqta'wa*) are slender willow rods about 4 feet long, peeled and painted and tipped with a point of buffalo horn to enable them to slide more easily along the ground. In throwing, the player holds the stick at the upper end with the thumb and fingers and, swinging it like a pendulum, throws it out with a sweeping motion. Young men throw arrows about in the same way, and small boys sometimes use ordinary reeds or weed stalks. Among the Omaha, according to Dorsey, unstrung bows are made to slide along the ground or ice in the same manner.

### 69. YI'HÄ'Ä'HI'HÍ'

->Yi'hä'ä'hi'hí', Yi'hä'ä'hi'hí',<-
->Hä'nänä'hi'gutha'-u ga'qaä'-hu'hu',<-
->Hä'nänä'hi'gutha'-u ga'qaä'-hu'hu'.<-

->*Translation*<-

->Yi'hä'ä'hi'hí', Yi'hä'ä'hi'hí',<-
->I throw the "button,"<-
->I throw the "button."<-

In his trance vision, the author of this song entered a tipi and found it filled with a circle of his old friends playing the *ga'qutit*, or "hunt the button" game. This is a favorite winter game among the prairie tribes and was probably common throughout the country. It is played by both men and women, but never by the two sexes together. It is the regular game during the long winter nights after the scattered families have left their exposed summer positions on the open prairie and moved near one another in the shelter of the timber along the streams. When hundreds of Indians are thus camped together, the sound of the drum, the rattle, and the gaming song resound through the air every night. To a stranger, there is a fascination to such a camp at night, with the conical tipis scattered about under the trees, the firelight from within shining through the white canvas and distinctly outlining on the cloth the figures of the occupants making merry inside with jest and story, while from half a dozen different directions comes the measured tap of the Indian drum or the weird chorus of the gaming songs. Frequently, there will be a party of twenty to thirty men gaming in one tipi and singing so that their voices can be heard far out from the camp, while from another tipi a few rods away comes a shrill chorus from a group of women engaged in another game of the same kind.

The players sit in a circle around the tipi fire, those on one side of the fire playing against those on the other. The only requirements are the "button" or *ga'qaä*, usually a small piece of wood around which is tied a piece of string or otter skin, with a pile of tally sticks, as has

<meta>This page continues the description of the "hunt the button" game, detailing the mechanics of play, the use of songs, and tribal variations in the lyrics.</meta>

<page-num>1009</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE "BUTTON" GAME</header>

has been already described. Each side has a "button"; the button for one side is painted black, and the other is red. The leader of one side takes the button and tries to move it from one hand to the other, or to pass it to a partner, while the opposing side keeps a sharp lookout and tries to guess which hand it is in. Those with the button try to deceive their opponents about its location by crossing one hand over the other, by folding their arms, or by putting their hands behind them to pass the <term>ga'qaä</term> to a partner, all while keeping time to the rhythm of a gambling chorus sung by the whole group at the top of their voices. The song is very strange and almost impossible to describe. It is usually—though not always or entirely—meaningless syllables; it jumps, halts, and staggers in a very surprising way, yet always remains in perfect time with the movements of the singers' hands and arms. A great deal of good-natured excitement prevails, and every few minutes an especially excited player claps his hands over his mouth or beats the ground with his palms and lets out a regular war whoop. Meanwhile, the opposing players watch the others' hands or look directly into their faces to catch any revealing movements of their features; when someone thinks he has discovered which hand holds the button, he points his thumb toward that hand with a loud, "*That!*" If he guesses correctly, his side scores a certain number of tallies and then takes the button and begins another song. If the guess is wrong, the losing side must give up an equal number of tally sticks. The play continues in this way until the early hours of the morning. It is always a gambling game, and the stakes are sometimes very high.

The first line of the song provided here is an imitation of one of these gambling songs. Among the prairie tribes, each song has one or perhaps two meaningful words related to the game, while the rest of the song consists of a series of meaningless syllables. Among some other tribes, particularly the Navaho, as described by Dr. Washington Matthews, the songs have meaning and are prayers to different animal or elemental gods to assist the player.

As examples of another variety of gambling songs, we provide two here that were heard among the Paiute of Nevada during a visit to the messiah in the winter of 1891–92. They have pleasant tunes, quite different from those of the prairie tribes, and were borrowed by the Paiute from the Mohave; they may have a meaning in the Mohave language, though they are unintelligible to the Paiute.

### *Translation*

> Father, the Morning Star!
> Father, the Morning Star!
> Look on us, we have danced until daylight,
> Look on us, we have danced until daylight.
> Take pity on us — *Hi'i'i'*!

This song is sung about daylight, just before the closing song, after the dancers have danced all night and are now ready to finish and go home. When the new doctrine arrived among the prairie tribes, the Ghost Dance was held at irregular and frequent intervals—almost every night, in fact—lasting sometimes until about midnight and sometimes until daylight, without any specific rule. As the ceremony became more structured, however, the Messiah gave instructions that the dance should be held only at intervals of six weeks and should then continue for four consecutive nights. It was to last until about midnight for the first three nights, but on the fourth night, it was to continue all night until the daylight of the next morning. The original letter containing these directions is given in chapter X. For a long time, these directions were strictly followed, but the current tendency is to return to the original style of one-night dances held at short intervals. This song to the morning star was sung just before daylight on the final morning of the dance.

Among all the prairie tribes, the morning star is held in great reverence and is the subject of much mythological belief and ceremony. It is universally represented in their pictographs as a cross, usually of the Maltese pattern. In this form, it is frequently pictured on the ghost shirts. The Arapaho name, <term>nagāq'</term>, means literally "a cross." The Kiowa know it as <term>t'aiñso</term>, "the cross," or sometimes as <term>dä-e'dal</term>, "the great star."

> Thus says our father, the Crow,

> Go around five times more—

This is the closing song of the dance used since the return of the great delegation of southern Arapaho and Cheyenne who visited the <term>messiah</term> in August 1891. Before 그 time, the closing song had been number 52, beginning with *Ni'nini'tubi'na hu'hu'*. The literal translation of the second part is "stop five times," the meaning and practice being that they must make five circuits while singing this song and then stop. As already stated, in accordance with the instructions of the <term>messiah</term>, the Ghost Dance is now held (theoretically) at intervals of six weeks and continues for four consecutive nights. It closes about midnight, except on the last night, when the believers dance until daylight. As daylight begins to appear in the east, they sing the song to the morning star, as previously given (number 72). Then, after a short rest, the leaders start this, the closing song, which is sung while the dancers make five circuits, resting a few moments between each circuit. Then they let go of each other's hands, wave their blankets in the air to fan away all evil influences, and go down to the river to bathe—the men in one place and the women in another. After bathing, they put their clothes back on and disperse to their various camps, and the Ghost Dance is over.

### ARAPAHO GLOSSARY

In this and the other glossaries provided here, it is intended only to give a concise definition of the meaning of each word without going into details of grammar or etymology. The Ghost Dance was studied for its mythology, psychology, ritual, and history; in this context, language was only a means to an end, as it was impossible in just a few months to devote close attention to the numerous languages spoken by the tribes represented in the dance.

The Arapaho language, as will be seen from the specimens provided, is eminently <term>vocalic</term>, with almost every syllable ending in a vowel and almost no double consonant sounds. Like the Cheyenne language, it lacks the sounds *l* and *r*. The most prominent vowel sounds are *a*, *ä*, and *i*, and in some instances, there are combinations of several vowel sounds without any intervening consonant. The soft *th* sound is also prominent. The *g* and *d* sounds frequently sound like *k* and *t*, respectively, and *b* in the standard dialect becomes *v* among the northern Arapaho. The only sound of the language (except for the medial *k* and *t*) not found in English is the <term>guttural</term> *q*, and the language is entirely devoid of the hissing effect of Cheyenne or the choking sounds of Kiowa.
