<header>MOONEY] ARAPAHO GLOSSARY</header>

In the songs, it is common to prefix *a*, and to add *i, hi, hu, huhu*, etc., to the ends of words in order to fill out the meter. In a few cases, changes are made in the body of the word for the same purpose. In the glossary, these meaningless syllables are not given where they occur at the end of words. Words beginning with a vowel sound may sometimes be written as beginning with the breathy *h*, and *s* is sometimes pronounced *sh*.

*Aä'ninĕ'na*—the name by which the Arapaho Grosventres of the Prairie, one of the five principal divisions of the Arapaho, call themselves. It is said to signify "white clay men," from *aäti*, "white clay," and *hinĕ'na*, "men." They are called *Hitu'nĕna*, or "beggars," by the rest of the tribe, and are commonly known to the whites under the French name of Grosventres, "big bellies."
*Aanû'hawa*—another name for the *Ha'nawunĕ'na* division of the Arapaho. The meaning of the word is unknown.
*Abää'thina'hu*—for *Bääthi'na*.

*Ächishini'qahi'na*—he was taking me around.
*A'gană'*—bed-covers made of buffalo skin; singular, *a'gă'*.
*Aha'känĕ'na*—"crazy men," one of the ranks of the Arapaho military organization. The word is derived from *aha'ka*, crazy, and *hinĕna*, men. The "fire moth," which flies around and into the fire, is called *aha'kăă'*, or "crazy," and the *Aha'känĕna* are supposed to imitate the action of this moth in the fire dance. See Arapaho song 43 and Cheyenne song 10.
*Aha'känithi'ĭ*—they are crazy. In the Indian view, "foolish" and "crazy" are generally synonymous. Compare *Aha'känen'a* and *Ahaka'wŭ*.
*Ahaka'wŭ*—the crazy dance. It is called *Psam* by the Cheyenne, from *psa*, crazy. See Arapaho song 43 and Cheyenne song 10.

*Bä'qätibä*—with the *bä'qäti* (see entry).

*Bäsawunë'na*—one of the five divisions of the Arapaho, and formerly a distinct tribe. The name is variously translated as "wood lodge men," "big lodge men," or "big lodge people"; the final part is derived from *hinë'na*, "men."

*Bäta'hina'ni*—he makes me dance. (In the songs, *when*, *where*, etc., are sometimes understood within the verbs). *Bäta't*, a dance; *nibä'tana*, I dance; *nitabä'tani*, we are dancing; *bätäna'ni*, when we dance; *Thi'gûnäwa't*, the Ghost dance. Compare also *Hena'gana'wanën*.

*Bätäna'ni*—when we dance. Compare *Bäta'hina'ni*.

*Bäti'qtawa*—the throwing-stick used in the *bäti'qtûba* game. See Arapaho song 68.

*Bäti'qtûba*—the game of the "throwing-stick" or "snow-snake" among the prairie tribes. See Arapaho song 68.

*Bena*—for *Bäë'na*.

*Běni'něna*—"warriors," the military organization of the Arapaho. See Arapaho song 43.
*Běni'nina*—he gave it to me. *Běni'na*, I gave it to him; *běnině'thin*, I gave it to you; *niibi'nu*, I gave it to them; *hǎsa-bini'na*, he has given it to us; *tabini'na*, he (she) gave it to me; *da'chi'bini'na*, he will give me a hawk feather.
*Bětiděĕ*—the Kiowa Apache name for the Arapaho.
*Beyi*—a (white) shell.
*Bi'ga*—night.
*Bi'gushish*—the moon, literally "night sun," from *bi'ga*, night, and *hishi'sh*, sun, or celestial body. The sun is distinguished as *hishi-nishi'sh*, or "day sun," from *hishi*, day, and *hishi'sh*. In many Native American languages the sun and moon have only one name, with an adjective prefix or suffix to distinguish between day and night. See Arapaho song 66. The morning star is called *naga'q*, "the cross"; the Milky Way is *hi'thina'na-ba*, "the buffalo road," or *thi'gûni-ba*, "the spirit or ghost road"; the Pleiades are *bä'nakûth*, "the group (sitting)."
*Biqǎna'kaye'na*—I am crying because of thirst. *Naka'yena*, I am thirsty.
*Bishiqa'wa*—coming into sight, approaching from a distance. (Third person, singular.)
*Bitaa'wu*—the earth.
*Bitaha'wǔ*—the dance of the *Bita'hiněna*. See Arapaho song 43.
*Bita'hiněna*—"spear men"; one of the degrees of the Arapaho military organization. The name comes from the Cheyenne word for spear, *bitahä'na*; the Arapaho word for spear is *qawä'*. See Arapaho song 43.
*Bi'täye*—captor, seizer; the name by which the Arapaho *Hänä'chäthi'ǎk*, "Sitting Bull," was called when he was a boy.
*Chǎna'ha't*—where there is none. *Iyahu'h*, it is all gone.
*Chänii'nagu'nĭt*—he wears them, he is wearing them.
*Cha'qtha* (singular, *Chaq*)—"enemies," the Arapaho name for the Comanche.
*Chǎ'säq*—another, another of them; from *chǎ'saiy'*, one. See *Yathûn*.
*Chěbi'nh*—greasy, something greasy; figuratively used for pemmican. See Arapaho song 46.

<column-break/>

*Chi'bät*—a sweat-house.
*Chi'chita'ně*—literally, a target, a mark to shoot at. A boy's game. See Arapaho song 4.
*Chǐnachi'chibä'iha*—venerable (memorable or ancient) priests of the *Chi'nachichi'bät*, or sacred sweat-lodge, from *chǐnachi'chibät*, the sacred sweat-lodge, and *bäiiä*, old man. See Arapaho song 43.
*Chi'nachichi'bät*—the sacred large sweat-house; from *chi'bät*, sweat-house. See Arapaho song 43.
*Chǐnachi'chibä'tina*—immortal, venerable, or never-to-be-forgotten priests of the sweat-house; from *chi'bät*, sweat-house. See Arapaho song 43.
*Chi'nachině'na*—water-pouring men; the highest degree of the Arapaho military organization. See Arapaho song 43.
*Dǎ'chäbi'hati'taniï*—where there is gambling; where they are gambling. In the Arapaho language there is no generic term for playing for amusement only. *Chäbi'hinä'na*, I am gambling; *hänĭ'chäbihinä'na*, I am gambling with it; *di'chäbihäti'tani'ĭ*, while or when they are gambling with it.
*Da'chǎ'-ihi'na*—in order to please me.
*Da'chi'bini'na*—he will give me a (chicken) hawk feather. Compare *Běni'nina*.
*Da'chinathi'na*—he having come for me (participle). *Nichĭnû'ti'hǎ*, I come for him.
*Da'naa'bäna'wa*—I moved it ("when" is sometimes understood).
*Dǎ'nasaku'tawa*—I am standing upon it.
*Dǎna'tiněnawa'ǔ*—because I longed, or wished, to see him; *da* in composition gives the idea of "because."
*De'tawuni'na*—he told me. Compare *Häthi'na*.
*Di'chäbihäti'tani'ĭ*—while or when they are gambling with it. Compare *Dǎ'chäbi'hati'taniï*.
*Di'chin*—because. *Haka* is also sometimes used.
*Diině'tita'niěg*—living people; human existence.
DOG SOLDIER—a popular but incorrect name given by white people to the military organizations of the prairie tribes. See Arapaho song 43.
*E'eye'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
*Ehe'eye'!*—the same.

*E'hihänakuwu'hunit*—he turned into a moose. *Naku'wu*, moose; *iwä'qu*, elk. *Ehihä'sina'kawu'hunit*—for *E'hihänakuwu'hunit*.

*Ehihä'siniëhi'nit*—he is beginning to be a bird, he is turning into a bird; *ni'ëhi*, a bird.

*E'yahe'eye'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*Eye'ae'yuhe'yu!*—the same.

*E'yehe'!*—the same.

**FORKS-OF-THE-RIVER MEN**—the main one of the three bands of the northern Arapaho. Their current chief is Black Coal.

*Gaahi'na*—another form of *Ga'ahinë'na*.

*Ga'ahinë'na*—"coyote men," from *ga'a*, coyote, and *hinë'na*, men; singular, *ga'ahinë'n*. The camp guards or sentries of the Arapaho. See Arapaho song 41.

*Ga'awä'*, or *ga'awäha*—a ball, used in the woman's game of *gü'gä'hawa't* or shinny. See Arapaho song 7.

*Gaäwa'tina*—canned goods, canned fruits.

*Ga'näni'na*—he wiped me off, he cleaned me. *Ganë'naa*, I wipe him off.

*Ga'qaä*—the "button" or small object hidden by the players in the *ga'qutit* game. See Arapaho song 69.

*Ga'qutina'ni*—when I play *ga'qutit*. See Arapaho song 69.

*Ga'qutit*—the "hunt the button" game of the Western tribes. See Arapaho song 69.

*Gasi'tu*—carrion.

*Ga'wunë'häna*—another form of *Gawunë'na*.

*Gawunë'na*—one of the five bands of the southern Arapaho. The name is the same as that applied by the Arapaho to the Blackfeet, from whom this band is said to be descended. It is also the Arapaho name for the Blackfoot band of the Sioux. The name is of foreign origin and cannot be explained by the Arapaho. The Blackfeet are sometimes also called *Watä'nità'si*, "black feet," by them.

**GREASY FACES**—one of the three bands of the northern Arapaho. Their current chief is Spotted Horse.

**GROSVENTRES (OF THE PRAIRIE)**—the name by which the *Aä'ninë'na* (an Arapaho division) are commonly known to white people.

<column-break/>

The correct French form is *Gros Ventres des Prairies*, "Big Bellies of the Prairie," to distinguish them from the Minitari, or Hidatsa, who were called *Gros Ventres du Missouri*. The term *Gros Ventres*, as applied to this division of the Arapaho, is derived from a misunderstanding of the Indian hand gesture for the tribe, which actually signifies "belly people," that is, "spongers" or "beggars."

*Gü'gä'hawa't*—the woman's game of shinny. See Arapaho song 7.

*Gun*—but.

*Gushi'nä*—throw it! (imperative singular). *Asegü'*, I throw it; *chegü'*, throw it here!

*Ha'änake'i*—rock, the rock.

*Ha'anünä*—forcibly, violently. *Habätä'nani'hi*—for *Bätäna'ni*.

*Ha'dä'wuha'na*—we have made them desolate; we have deprived them of all happiness.

*Hageni'stit*—he is making it across the water. Compare *Hani'stit*.

*Ha'hat*—the cottonwood tree (*Populus monilifera*).

*Ha-ina'tä*—it lies there, it lies upon it.

*Hä'inawa*—I know. *Ni'hawa*, I do not know.

*Ha'ka*—because. *Dichin* has the same meaning.

*Ha'nä*—for *Ha'änünä*.

*Hänä'chä-thi'ä'k*—Sitting Bull, the Arapaho apostle of the Ghost Dance; from *hänä'chä*, a buffalo bull, and *thi'äk*, he is sitting. In his early youth, before going to Wyoming, he was called *Bi'täye*, "Captor."

*Ha'naë'hi*—little boy (vocative).

*Ha'nahawu'nën* (singular).

*Ha'nahawunë'na*—one of the five divisions of the Arapaho, but now practically extinct. The meaning of the name is unknown, but the final syllables are from *hinë'na*, signifying "men," or "people."

*Hänai'säi*—at the boundaries.

*Hä'nänä'higu'tha-u*—for *Nä'higu'tha*.

*Hana'nawu'nänu*—those who have been taught (?).

*Hänä'tähinä'na*—I win the game (by means of something).

*Hä'nätä'hi'nät*—It will win the game.

*Ä'nätähi'nänä*, I win.

*Häni'*—for *Häni'ïni*.

*Hä'nibiwă'hĭnă'*—because of it, I am made to cry; I am crying for its sake. Compare *Bähibiwă'hĭna*.
*Hänĭ'chübihĭ'năna*—I am gambling with it. Compare *Dä'chäbi'hatĭ'taniĭ*.
*Hänĭ'ĭnĭ*—by this means, by its means; abbreviated to *hänĭĭ* or *hänĭ*.
*Hänĭ'niahu'na*—I fly around with it.

*Hänĭ'nihiga'huna'*—for *Hänĭ'ĭnĭ nĭhiga'huna*,—by its means I am running swiftly.
*Hani'stit*—he has finished it; now he has finished it. Compare *Hagenĭ'stit*.
*Hänĭta'quna'nĭ*—in the pitfall; from *ta'quna*, a pitfall. See Arapaho song 47.
*Ha'qihana*—"wolves," one of the five bands of the southern Arapaho.
*Hä'sabini'na*—he has given it to us. Compare *Bënĭ'nina*.
*Hä'tää'naku'ni*—you may have it. *Nänĭ'thana'na*, I have it.

*Hä'tani'i'bii'na*—for *Hä'tanbii'na*.
*Hatänĭ'ina'danë'na*—I am about to use him to "make medicine," that is, to perform a sacred ceremony (remote future). The immediate future is *hatänĭ'nadanë'na*; *inĭ* is the root of "to use"; *nadanë'na*, is to "make medicine," from the root *në'na*, to sing. The gesture signs for "song" and "medicine" are also nearly the same. See Arapaho song 33.
*Hatänĭ'niahu'hĭ'na*—he is going to make me fly around. *Hänĭ'niahu'na*, I am flying; *gaya'ahuha*, I make him fly.
*Ha'tani'nitani'na*—for *Hatnĭ'tani'na*.
*Hatĕchi'na*—the basket bowl used in the dice game. See Arapaho song 64.
*Hä'thäbë'na* (-wa)—I hand it to you.
*Ha'thahu'*—star dance; the dance of the *Hä'thahu'ha*. See Arapaho song 43.
*Hä'thahu'ha*—star people, from *hä'tha*, star; one of the ranks of the Arapaho military organization. See Arapaho song 43.
*Häthĭ'na*—he tells me, he says to me. Present, *häthĭ'na*; future, *nĭhiithi'na*; perfect, *hatnĭthĭ'na*; *he'itāwuni'na*, it tells me; *de'tawuni'na*, another form for "he told me."

*Ha'ti*—for *Ha'hat*.
*Hätiku'tha*—the humming toy used by boys of the prairie tribes. See Arapaho song 25.
*Hätina'hawa'bä*—you (plural) will see him; *nana'hawă*, I see him; *ni'nahawa'na*, we see them; *nahäbi'na*, he saw me; *na'hawú*, I saw him; *he'năă'awă*, when I see it; *tahu'naha'thihi'na*, to make me see them. *Nina'hawa*, I look at him.
*Hätině'bäku'thana*—let us play *në'bäku'thana*, the awl game. See Arapaho song 64.
*Hätini'tubi'bä*—he is calling you (plural); *ninĭ'tuwa*, I call him.
*Häti'ta-usĕta'na*—let us play *ta'-usĕta'na*. See Arapaho song 64.
*Hä'tnaa'waa'*—it is about to move (immediate future).
*Hätnaawaa-uhu'*—for *Hä'tnaa'waa'*.
*Hatnĭ'tani'na*—he will hear me. *Nänĭ'ta'nă*, I hear him; *nitabä'na*, I hear it; *ninĭ'dănă'û*, I heard him. In the form in Arapaho song 61, *Hatani'nitani'na*, the syllable *ni* is repeated in the body of the word to fill in the meter.
*Hatnĭ'thi'ăka'tana*—we have it in the center. *Nahĭ'thaä'ntană*, I am the center; *nähĭ'thiănĭ'na'ta*, it is in the center.

*He'ee'ä'che'yuhe'yu!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
*He'eye'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*Hesû'na*—the father. *Hesûna'nĭn*, our father; *nisû'na*, my father, from which comes *hi-nisû'na-hu* of the songs.

*Hëtabi'nuhu'ni'na*—I am poor; I am needy.

# THE GHOST-DANCE RELIGION [ETHNOLOGICAL ANNUAL 14]

*Hĕthĕ'hinĕ'na*—Dog men, from *hĕth*, dog, and *hinĕ'na*, men; one of the ranks of the Arapaho military organization. See Arapaho song 43.

*Hĕthĕwa'wŭ*—The dance of the *Hĕthĕ'hinĕ'na*. See Arapaho song 43.

*He'wa-u'sa*—you are a young crow, you are the offspring of the crow; *ho* or *hu*, crow; *hosa*, a young crow, a little crow. This was the Indian name of Little Raven, the famous Arapaho chief, who died several years ago.

*He'yahe'eye!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*He'yäya'ahe'ye!*—the same.

*He'yoho'ho!*—the same.

*Hi'a!*—the same.

*Hi'bithini'na*—they are flying about it. *Ninaä'niahu'tawa*, I am flying about it. Compare *Nänii'ahu'na*.

*Hichää'qawŭ*—the dance of the *Hichää'quthi*. See Arapaho song 43.

*Hichää'quthi*—Club men, from *chää'tha*, a club; one of the ranks of the Arapaho military organization. See Arapaho song 43.

*Hi'chäbä'-i*—high up, on high, that is, in heaven, in the sky, or in a tree top.

*Higa'ahina'-it*—"The man with the coyote gun;" from *gaahi'na*, the "coyote men;" a camp guard or lookout among the Arapaho. See Arapaho song 41.

*Hiii!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*Hi'nä*—here; here it is.

*Hinä'ähä'k*—it is! (strongly affirmative). Compare *Hi'nä*.

*Hinä'äthi*—the long wing-feather (referring to the longest wing pinion, worn on the head).

*Hina'wŭn*—his paint; *hĭnă'w'*, (red) paint, the Indian clay paint; *nina'w'*, my paint; *hena'w'*, your paint.

*Hi'ni* or *i'nĭ*—that, that one.

*Hi'nini!*—a meaningless song ending.

*Hi'niqa'aga'yetu'sa*—for *Hi'nĭ niqaqa'yätusă*.

*Hinisa'na*—his children. Compare *Nänisa'näŭ*.

*Hinisû'nahu*—for *Nisû'na*.

*Hĭsä'*—my female comrade, or companion (vocative).

*Hi'sähihi*—for *Hĭsä'*.

*Hise'hi*—the same.

<column-break/>

*Hitäsi'na*—(singular, *Hi'täsi*)—"scarred people," the Arapaho name for the Cheyenne. From *hitäshi'ni*, scarred or cut.

*Hiti'cha*—this pipe. Compare *Äti'cha-ni'na*.

*Hiticha'ni*—for *Hiti'cha*.

*Hitu'nena*—the name by which the *Aä'ninĕ'na* or Arapaho Grosventres of the Prairie are known to the rest of the tribe. Another form is *Hitu'nĕni'na*. It signifies "begging men," or more exactly "spongers," the ending part being from *hinĕ'na*, "men." The Arapaho call the Sioux *Natni*, and the Assiniboin *Tu-natni*, and "begging Sioux."

*Hi'yu*—here it is. *Näyu*, there it is; *häyu*, where is it? what is it?

*Ho*—crow; usually doubled as *Huhu* or *Ahuhu* in the songs. The crow is the sacred bird of the Ghost dance, and is also held sacred by the Algonquian tribes generally. See Arapaho song 36.

*Ho'sa*—"Little Crow," better known as "Little Raven," the celebrated chief of the southern Arapaho. He died several years ago and was succeeded by the present head chief *Na'wat* or Left Hand. The name is derived from *ho*, "crow," and *sa*, the diminutive.

*Hu!*—a meaningless exclamation sometimes used by devotees and priests in the Ghost dance when under strong excitement, such as *Hu! Hu! Hu!*

**HUBBUB**—the name given by early New England writers to the Indian dice game. See Arapaho song 68.

*Huhu*—for *Ho*.

*Hu'nä*—crows; plural of *ho* or *hu*; figuratively used in the songs for crow feathers worn on the head.

*Hu'naku'nithi*—wearers of the crow feathers; the name given to the seven leaders of the Ghost dance who wear crow feathers on their heads. *Ho*, crow; plural, *hona* or *huna*.

*Hu'wisä'na*—I go straight to it. *Huwi'sä*, you go, etc.; *qănu'wisät*, he goes, etc.

*Huyu*—another form of *Hi'yu*.

*Ih!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

**IKUNUHKATSI**—"All Comrades," the military society of the Blackfeet. See Arapaho song 43.

*Ina'habi'ä*—Look on us! *Nina'hawa*, I look at him. Compare *Achiga'häwa*.

*I'nĭt*—timber.

*Inita'ta-usä'na*—stand ready! (imperative plural). *Näni'tata'-usä'na*, I am ready.

*Inu'na-i'na*—the name used by the Arapaho to designate themselves. It signifies "our people," or "people of our kind."

*I'thaq*—a gut; a sheath or case made of bear gut. See Arapaho song 41.

*I'thetihi*—good.

*Iyahu'h*—gone, it is all gone.

*Iyehe'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*Iyehe'eye*—<note>the same as above</note>.

*Iyu*—another form of *Hi'yu*.

KANINAHOIC—the Ojibwa name for the Arapaho.

KANINA'VISH—<note>the same as above</note>.

*Kawinahan*—the form used by Hayden for *Gawunĕ'na* or *Gawunĕ'häna* <note>see entry</note>.

*Ku'niahu'na*—I fly with it on my head.

MAQPI'ATO—the Sioux name for the Arapaho. It signifies "blue cloud," that is, "a clear sky"; the reason is unknown.

MINNETAREES OF FORT DE PRAIRIE—The name given by Lewis and Clark to the *Aä'ninĕ'na* or Arapaho Gros Ventres. The *Aä'ninĕ'na* are known to French Canadians as the *Gros Ventres des Prairies*, while the Minitari are called by them *Gros Ventres du Missouri*, and the American explorers incorrectly combined the two names.

*Näa'wunani'nä*—he takes pity on us. Compare *Hatäna'wunäni'na*.

*Na'chichaba'n*—they are still making it. *Nü'nistină*, I make it; *Näsu'nistină*, I am still making it.

*Naga'q*—the morning star. See Arapaho songs 67 and 72. The word literally means "a cross."

*Nahäbi'na*—he saw me. Compare *Hätina'hawa'bä*.

*Nä'hänĭ*—here! look! Compare *Ächiqa'häwä*.

*Naha'ta*—look at it! (imperative singular). Compare *Ächiqa'häwä*.

*Na'hawaü'*—used for *Na'hawu'*.

*Na'hawüū'*—I saw him. Compare *Hätina'hawä'bä*.

*Nä'hibiwa'huna*—then I begin to cry or lament. Compare *Bähibiwä'hina*.

*Nü'hibi'wahuna'na*—then I wept. Compare *Bähibiwä'hina*.

*Nä'higu'tha*—I throw it. *Nina'gu'tha*, I throw it where it cannot be found.

<column-break/>

*Nä'hinä'n*—stop!

*Nä'inaha'tdäbä'naq*—I then saw the multitude plainly.

*Na'kash*—sage; the wild sage (*Artemisia*); the name of a prominent northern Arapaho.

*Na'kasinĕ'na*—the name by which the northern Arapaho call themselves. It signifies "sagebrush men," from *na'kash*, "sagebrush," and *hinĕ'na* or *hinĕ'nina*, the plural of *hinĕ'n*, "man." They are called *Ba'achinĕ'na* by the other Arapaho, and *Tägyä'ko* by the Kiowa.

*Nänä'*—it is that, that is the thing.

*Na'nagă'qănĕt*—white-skinned (singular); from *na'guă*, white (organic) and *wană'q*, skin. *Núna'chă*, white (inorganic); either *na'guă* or *núna'chă* may be used in speaking of a house. *Na'nagă'qănĕt* is one of the Arapaho names for white people, the ordinary term being *Nia'thn* <note>see entry</note>. See also *Niha'nätaye'chet*.

*Nanaha'thähi*—he showed me. *Nanaha'tha*, I show him.

*Nänä'nina*—it is I, I am he (emphatic).

*Nana'thina'ni*—he came to take me, he came for me. In the songs the adverb "when" or "where" is sometimes implied with the verb. See Arapaho song 38.

*Näne'th*—when I met him.

*Nä'niahu'na*—used for *Nänii'ahu'na*.

*Nänibä'tawa*—I am singing it; *Nänibina*, I sing; *ibä't*, a song.

*Nänibä'tia*—used for *Nänibä'tawa*.

*Nü'nihithätu'hŭna*—thus I shouted, or called. *Nä'ni* in composition signifies "thus."

*Näni'ibä*—it is spotted.

*Nani'nibinä'si*—the wind makes them sing. *Näni'bina*, I sing. Compare *Nänibä'tawä*.

*Nänisa'na*—used for *Nüni'sanăü'*.

*Nänisanăü'* or *Näni'sanăq*—my children. *Näni'sa*, my older child; *näni'sanĕ'äĕ*, my young child.

*Nänisa'taqi*—used for *Ni'sataq*, meaning seven.

*Nänisa'tăquthi*—used for *Ni'sataq*, meaning seven.

*Nä'nitha'tuhŭ'na*—used for *Nä'nihithatu'hŭna*.

*Näniwu'hună*—I carry it as I fly about in circles. Compare *Hi'bithini'na* with *Tahĕti'niahu'na*.

*Nasu'siyakunawa*—I am stripping it. I am unsheathing it. Compare *Sä'niyagu'nawa'*.

*Na'tănu'ya*—what I am using. *Tanu'năwa'*, I use it.

*Na'tenehi'na*—another form of *Natni* or *Na'tnihi'na*.

*Na'tni* or *Na'tnihi'na*—the Arapaho name for the Sioux. The origin of the word is unknown, but it may possibly be a form of *Na'dowe*, the general Algonquian name for Indians of a different tribe.

*Natu'wani'sa*—my top (a toy); from *uwani'sa*, a top. See Arapaho song 65.

*Na'waa'tănû*—I prayed to him; *ni'awăaa'tanû*, I am praying (to him).

*Na'wat*—"Left Hand," the current head chief of the Southern Arapaho.

*Na'wathin'ĕha*—the name by which the Southern Arapaho are known to the rest of the tribe. It means "southerners," and is said to be an old form of *Nawunĕ'na*, the name the Southern Arapaho call themselves.

*Na'wunĕ'na*—the proper name of the Southern Arapaho. It means "southern men," from *nawun* ("south") and *hinĕ'na* ("men"). They are called *Nawa'thinĕ'ha* ("southerners") by the Northern Arapaho, which is said to be the older form.

*Năya'qût*—the whirlwind. The powers and phenomena of nature are generally personified in Indian thought and language.

*Nă'yu*—there it is. Compare *Iyu*.

*Nea-i'qaha'ti*—for *Ne'ia-i'qahat*.

*Neă'thibiwa'na*—the place where crying begins. Compare *Bähibiwä'hina*.

*Nĕ'bäku'thana*—the "awl game" played by the women of the prairie tribes. See Arapaho song 64.

*Nĕ'chäi'hit*—he gave me this grateful gift; he gave me this, and I am thankful for it.

*Nĕ'cha'wu'nani*—have pity on me (singular command). Compare *Hatana'wunani'na*.

*Nehawa'wună'na*—I have no sympathy for him. Compare *Ti'awawu'nănu*.

*Nĕ'ia-i'qahat*—now he is collecting them; now he begins to gather them.

*Ne'na(-hu)*—my mother. *Nesû'na*, my father.

*Nesû'na*—another form of *Nisû'na*.

*Nĕti'qtawa*—my *ti'qtawa* or throwing-stick. The game is called *bătĭ'qtûba*, abbreviated to *ti'qtûp*. The throwing-stick is called *bătĭ'qtawa* or *ti'qtawa*. See Arapaho song 68.

<column-break/>

*Nĕ'tita'wahu*—for *Netĭ'qtawa*.

*Ni'ănĕ'thăhi'nani'na*—he did not recognize me. The negative meaning is contained in *ănĕ'th*; *ä'ninani'na* means he recognized me.

*Ni'ănita'wathi*—they push hard; that is, they persevere. *Năni'ăni'tawana* means "I push hard," "I do my best," or "I do what is right."

*Nia'rhari's-kûrikiwa's-hûski*—the proper Wichita name for the Arapaho.

*Ni'ăsa'kua'na*—I am looking on or watching. Compare *Hätina'hawa'bä* and *Ächiqa'hăwa*.

*Nia'thu* or *Nia'thuă*—the white people; the singular is *Nia'tha*. The word literally means expert, skillful, or wise, and is also the Arapaho name for the spider. The word for "white" is *nu'na'cha'ă*. Compare *Na'nagă'qănĕt* and *Niha'nătaye'chet*.

*Niathu'a-u*—for *Niathu'a*.

*Niati'biku'thahu*—for *Niati'biku'thathi*.

*Niati'biku'thathi*—they are rolling it.

*Nibăi'naku'nithi*—they all wear it on their heads. *Ninaku'na* means "I wear it on my head."

*Nibă't*—song. Compare *Nänibä'tawa*.

*Nibă'tia*—for *Nibă't*.

*Ni'binu*—for *Niibi'na*.

*Ni'bithi't*—I have nothing to eat.

*Ni'chiă*—river.

*Ni'chihinĕ'na*—"river men," the Arapaho name for the Kiowa. From *ni'chiă* (river) and *hinĕ'na* (men); they are so called because of the Kiowa's former residence on the upper Arkansas River, from which they were driven by the Arapaho and Sioux.

*Niesa'na*, or *Ni'ehisa'na*—the young birds. *Niĕ'hĕ* means bird; *niĕ'hisa* means a young bird.

*Niha'nătaye'chet*—yellow-hided (singular); from *niha'ne* (yellow) and *nata'yech* (a hide). This is one of the Arapaho names for white people. The ordinary term is *Nia'thu* <note>see that entry</note>.

*Nĭhiga'hu*—he is running. *Năniga'na* means "I run"; *năni'higa* means "he runs"; *nĭhiga'huna* means "I am running swiftly."

*Nĭhiga'huna*—I am running swiftly. Compare *Nĭhiga'hu*.

*Nihii'nă*—forcibly, swiftly.

*Niibi'na*—I gave it to them. Compare *Bĕni'nina*.

*Niitegu*—for *Nii'tĕhăg*.

*Nii'tĕhăg*—it was him; he was the one.

*Niitu'qawigû'niĕ*—where they were coming down; where they were descending toward us.

*Ninaä'niahu'na*—I fly in circles (habitually); I am constantly flying around in circles. Compare *Hi'bithini'na* and *Tahĕti'niahu'na*.
*Ninaä'niahu'tawa*—I am flying around it. Compare *Hi'bithini'na*.
*Ninaä'qäwa'*—I go around it.
*Ni'nagänawa'ni*—we have danced until daylight. Compare *He'nagana''wanĕn* and *Bäta'hina'ni*.
*Ni'nahawa'na*—we see them. Compare *Hätina'hawa'bä*.
*Ninä'ninati'nakuni'na*—It is I who have (wear) it on my head; I am the one who ties it on my head.
*Ninĕ'n*—tallow.
*Niniha'niahu'na*—I fly around yellow. *Niha'ne*, yellow. Compare *Hi'bithini'na* and *Nänii'ahu'na*.
*Ni'nini'tubi'na*—he has called me.
*Nini'tănă'û*—I heard him. Compare *Hatni'tăni'na*.
*Ninitu'sa*—making a sound, resounding.
*Ni'qa*—father (vocative; no possessive pronoun implied). A more respectful or affectionate form than *nisûna*.
*Niqaqa'yătusa*—the loudest sounding, the loudest of all. The idea of "loudest" is contained in *qaqa'y'*, and "sounding" in *tusa*. See *Ninitu'sa*.
*Ni'qahu'hu'*—for *Ni'qa*.
*Ni'qana'ga*—that one buffalo bull; there is a solitary bull. *Hänä'chä*, a buffalo bull, is changed in the song to *qana'ga*. *Ni* in composition means alone or single, from *nisi*, only one; *chäsaiy'*, one.
*Nisa'na*—the same as *nisû'na* or *nesûna*, my father.
*Ni'sataq*—seven. See *Yathûn*.
*Nisû'na*—my father. Compare *Hesû'na*.
*Ni'tabä'na*—I hear it. Compare *Hatni'tăni'na*.
*Nitabä'tani*—we are dancing. Compare *Bäta'hina'ni*.
*Nita-i'sa*—my relative.
*Ni'tawuna'na*—I take pity on them. Compare *Hatäna'wunani'na*.
*Nithi'na*—he said it, he has said it (immediate past). Compare *Häthi'na*.
*Nuha'wŭ*—Fox dance; the dance of the *Nuhinĕ'na*. See Arapaho song 43.
*Nuhinĕ'na*--Fox men, from *nu*, fox and *hinĕ'na*, men; one of the ranks of the Arapaho military organization. See Arapaho song 43.

<column-break/>

*Nu'nagûna''-u'ăt*—he came with it, he brought it with him.
*Núnaha'wŭ*—one of the ranks of the Arapaho military organization; the meaning of the word is unknown. See Arapaho song 43.
*Nû'nanû'naa'tăni'na*—he is circling above me. See Arapaho song 39.
*Nû'nanû'naku'ti*—I am circling it, I am waving it around in circles.
*Nu'sa-icha'tha*—the ceremonial crook or lance carried by the leader of the *Bita'hinĕna*. See Arapaho song 43.
*Qa'qa-u'nûtha*—the "throwing sticks" used in the game of the *bä'qati*. See Arapaho song 49.
SANI'TIKA—Pawnee name for the Arapaho; from the Comanche name *Sä'rĕtika*, "dog eaters."
*Sä'niyagu'nawa'*—I have stripped it, I have unsheathed it. *Nasu'siyakunawa*, I am stripping it, I am unsheathing it.
SÄ'PANI—the Shoshoni name for the *Aä'ninĕna* or Arapaho Grosventres. It means "belly people," from *säp*, belly, and *ni*, the tribal suffix.
SÄ'RĔTĔKA—Comanche and Shoshoni name for the Arapaho. It means "dog-eaters," from *sä're*, dog, and *tĕka*, a form of the verb "to eat," referring to their special fondness for dog meat. The name is also sometimes used by the Wichita.
*Säsa'bä-ithi*—looking around, that is, watchers or lookouts. One of the five bands of the southern Arapaho.
*Se'hiwûq*—"weasel bear," from *sea* weasel, and *wûq*, bear; also translated as "gray bear," from *se*, gray, and *wûq*, bear. The name of the keeper of the *sĕ'icha* or sacred pipe of the Arapaho. See Arapaho song 2.
*Sĕ'icha*—"flat pipe," from *sĕĭ*, flat, and *hicha*, pipe. The sacred pipe and tribal "medicine" of the Arapaho. See Arapaho song 2.
*Ta'ăwûn*—strike it (singular command).
*Tabini'na*—he (she) gave it to me. Compare *Bĕni'nĕna*.
*Ta'chawa'gŭna*—while I am carrying a load of (buffalo) beef on a horse. *Ha'gŭ'*, I carry a load of beef on a horse in motion; second person, *hagŭ'nĭ*; third person, *hagŭ'tĭ*; *ta'*, prefix in composition with the verb, implies "while."

*Tahëti'niahu'na*—I make the deep or loud thunder as I fly about in circles (habitual). Compare *Ninaä'niahu'na* and *Tahuna'änä'niahu'na*. See Arapaho song 27.

*Ta'huna'änä'niahu'na*—I make the thunder (or a loud resounding noise) as I fly about in circles (habitual). Compare *Ninaä'niahu'na* and *Tahëti'niahu'na*.

*Tahu'nahathihi'na*—to make me see them. Compare *Hätina'hawa'bä*.

*Ta'na-u'gahe'na*—he put me there. *Nita'-uqa'*, I put him there (present tense).

*Tani'bäthä*—"pierced noses," the <term>Arapaho</term> name for the <term>Caddo</term>; *tani*, nose.

*Ta'thiaku'tawa*—I stood upon it (?). The regular form for "I was standing upon it" is *Niqtä'saku'na*.

*Ta'-usëta'na* or *Ta'-usëta'tina*—literally "striking" or "throwing against" something; the dice game played by the women of the prairie tribes. See Arapaho song 64.

*Ta'wünä*—for *Ta'äwün*.

*Të'bë*—at first, the first time, in the beginning.

*Të'bë'tana'-isët*—when he first came; *të'bë*, the first time.

*Tha'kú'hinëna*—"whetstone men" or "knife-whetting men," the <term>Arapaho</term> name for the <term>Kiowa Apache</term> (Na-diisha-Dena), and for all other southern Athapascan tribes known to them, including the <term>Lipan</term>, <term>Mescalero</term>, <term>Jicarilla</term>, and <term>Apache</term> proper. The sign for Apache in the sign language of the plains also conveys the same idea, being made by briskly rubbing the left forefinger with the right, as though whetting a knife. *Gäta'ka*, the <term>Pawnee</term> name for the Kiowa Apache, seems to have a connection to this word.

*Thëni'ehi'nina*—I am a bird, from *nië'hë*, bird.

*Thi'aku*—they are there.

*Thi'äya*—the sweat-house mound. The name is also applied to a stone heap or monument. See Arapaho song 34.

*Thiäya'na*—on the *thi'äya* or sweat-house mound.

*Thiäya'në*—at the *thi'äya* or sweat-house mound.

*Thigûnâwa't*—the <term>Ghost dance</term>, from *thig*, ghost or spirit of a deceased person, and *bäta't*, a dance. Compare *Bäta'hina'ni*.

<column-break/>

*Ti'awawu'nănu*—when I sympathized with them, when I liked them. I sympathize with him, *tiäwu'nănă*. *Ti* or *tihi* when combined with verbs usually conveys the idea of "when." *Nehawa'wunăna*, I have no sympathy for him. Compare *Hatâna'wunăni'na*.

*Ti'naha'thihu*—I show it to them (habitual), or to show it to them. *Ni'naha'thihu*, I show it to him.

*Ti'qtûp*—the common abbreviated form of *Bätĭ'qtûbă*, which see.

*Uhiyeleyeheye!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*Ûtnitha'wuchä'wahănăni'na*—we shall surely be put again (with something understood). The idea of "surely" is contained in *ûtni'thawĭ*; *chä* is from *chä'i'hĭ*, "again."

*Wa'ku(-hu)*—a feather to wear on the head.

*Wa'ku'na*—feathers worn on the head; a feather headdress. They are usually painted and beaded, and sometimes mounted on a small stick. A single feather worn in this way is called *wa'ku*.

*WAKIÑYAN-OI*—Thunder's Track. The <term>Sioux</term> name of a locality in eastern South Dakota. See Arapaho song 14.

*Waqui'si*—Ugly Face Woman, an <term>Arapaho</term> man. *Hi'si*, woman, is frequently abbreviated to *si* in compound words.

*Wa'quithi*—Bad faces, or Ugly faces; the primary of the five bands of the southern Arapaho. Their chief, Nawat, or Left Hand, is also the principal chief of the southern branch of the tribe.

*Watäna'ni*—a black mark or picture, from *watä'yä*, black. See Arapaho song 49.

*Wa'tän-ga'a*—Black Coyote, from *watän*, black, and *ga'a*, coyote. A southern Arapaho, captain of the Indian police, and one of the principal leaders of the <term>Ghost dance</term> among the Arapaho.

*Wa'wa*—now; it also gives the idea of being done or completed.

*Wa'wagathä'na*—I have already put him aside, now I have put him aside. *Wawa* or *waw'*, "now," in composition, gives the idea of "already" or completed action.

*Wa'wăna'dană'diä*—I am about to hum (that is, with the *Hätiku'tha*). See Arapaho song 25.

*Wawäthäbichä chinïnabänaguwa-u-inagathi* — I have given you (plural) again, a headdress of magpie feathers; from *wa'-wäthä'bichä chinï'nabä'nak*, I have given it back again; *wa'-u-i*, magpie; *waga'thi*, a bird's tail feathers. In the verb the root is from *bini'na*, I give it to him; *waw* denotes completion, as "already" done; *chä* implies repetition or return of action. See Arapaho song 56.

*Wünayu'uhu* — for *Wä'nayu'ü*, they are new. *Wä'nayä'*, it is new.

*Ya'gaahi'na* — for *Ya'hagaahi'na*.

*Ya'hagaahi'na* — the "coyote gun" or ceremonial club of the *Ga'ahinë'na* or "Coyote men." See Arapaho song 41.

*Yahe'eye'!* — a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.

*Ya"na-u'si'ya* — how bright the moonlight is! *Na'-u'si'ya*, the moonlight is bright.

<column-break/>

*Ya'thäyü'na* — five places, in five places; from *ya'thûn*, five, and *yûna*, places.

*Ya'thûn* — five. Other numerals are: 1, *chü'saiy'*; 2, *hëni'si*; 3, *hënä'si*; 4, *yen*; 5, *ya'thûn* or *ya'thûn*; 6, *ni'tataq*; 7, *nï'sataq*; 8, *näsataq*; 9, *thi'ataq*; 10, *wëtätaq*; 20, *ni'sa*; 29, *ni'sa-thi'atäqu'n*; 30, *näsa*; 40, *ye'ya*; 50, *ya'thaiya*; 60, *nitatû'sa*; 70, *ni'satûsa*; 80, *nä'satû'sa*; 90, *thi'atû'sa*; 100, *wë tätû'sa*.

*Ye'nis* — the wild rose. The rosebush is *ye'nis*; the seed berry is *ye'nun*, literally "louse child," from the resemblance of the seeds to nits or lice. See Arapaho song 29.

*Ye'nisiti'na* — with the wild rose; from *ye'nis*, the wild rose, and *ti'naq*, with.

*Yï'hä'ä'ä'hi'hï'* — a meaningless word combination of syllables used in the gambling songs. See Arapaho song 69.

# THE CHEYENNE

## TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*Ba'hakosïn* — Caddo name; "striped arrows," *bäh*, arrow. The Caddo sometimes also call them *Siä'näbo*, from their Comanche name.

*Cheyenne* — popular name, a French spelling of their Sioux name. It has no connection with the French word *chien*, "dog."

*Dzïtsï'stäs* — proper tribal name; nearly equivalent to "our people."

*Gatsa'lghi* — Kiowa Apache name.

*Hitäsi'na* (singular *Hi'täsi*) — Arapaho name, signifying "scarred people," from *hitäshi'ni*, "scarred or cut." According to the Arapaho statement the Cheyenne were so called because they were more addicted than the other tribes to the practice of gashing themselves in religious ceremonies. The name may have more special reference to the tribal custom of cutting off the fingers and hands of their killed enemies. (See tribal sign, page 1024.)

*Itäsupuzi* — Hidatsa name, "spotted arrow quills" (Matthews).

*Ka'naheäwastsïk* — Cree name, "people with a language somewhat like Cree" (Grinnell).

*Niere'rikwats-kûni'ki* — Wichita name.

*Nanoni'ks-kare'niki* — Kichai name.

*Pägänävo* — Shoshoni and Comanche name; "striped arrows," from *päga*, "arrow," and *nävo*, "striped."

*Sük'o'ta* — Kiowa name; seems to refer to "biting."

*Sa-sis-e-tas* — proper tribal name according to Clark (Indian Sign Language, 99, 1885). The form should be *Dzïtsï'stäs* as given above.

*Shaiela* or *Shaiena* — Sioux name; "red," or decorated with red paint. According to Riggs, as quoted by Clark, the Sioux call a foreign language a "red" language, while they designate one of their own stock as "white," so that the name would be equivalent to "aliens." The Sioux apply the same name also to the Cree.

*Shiü'navo* — another Comanche name, probably a derivative from the word *Cheyenne*.

*Shië'da* — another Wichita name, derived from the word *Cheyenne*.

*Staitan* — unidentified tribal name, given by Lewis and Clark. Identical with the Cheyenne, from their own word *Histä'itän*, "I am a Cheyenne."

### TRIBAL SIGN

The Cheyenne tribal sign, made by drawing the right index finger several times across the left forefinger, is commonly interpreted as "cut fingers" or "cut wrists." It is said to be derived from their custom of cutting off the fingers and hands of slain enemies. Although the same practice was found among other tribes, the Cheyenne were particularly distinguished in this regard. In Mackenzie’s major battle with the Cheyenne in Wyoming in 1876, two necklaces made of human fingers were found in the captured Indian camp, together with a small bag filled with hands cut from the bodies of children of the Shoshoni tribe, who were their enemies. One of these necklaces was afterward placed in the National Museum at Washington. (See Bourke in the *Ninth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology*.) Some knowledgeable Indian authorities say, however, that the sign is intended to indicate "striped people," or "striped-arrow people," referring to the fact that the Cheyenne usually feathered their arrows with the striped feathers of the wild turkey. This agrees with the interpretation of the name for the Cheyenne in several different languages.

### SKETCH OF THE TRIBE

The Cheyenne are one of the westernmost tribes of the great Algonquian stock. In one of their ghost songs, they sing of the "turtle river," on which they say they once lived (*Cheyenne song 3*). From several pieces of evidence, this seems to be identical with the Saint Croix River, which forms the boundary between Wisconsin and Minnesota. This statement agrees with the opinion of Clark (*Indian Sign Language*), who locates their earliest tradition in the neighborhood of Saint Anthony Falls. They were driven out by the Sioux and forced toward the northwest, where they came in contact with the Assiniboine (called by them Hohe'), with whom they were never afterward at peace. At a later period, according to Lewis and Clark, they lived on the Cheyenne branch of the Red River in northern Minnesota, from where they were again driven by the Sioux into the prairie.

In 1805, they wandered about the head of the Cheyenne River of Dakota and in the Black Hills, and were at war with the Sioux, though at peace with most other tribes. Since then, they have pushed on to the west and south, always in close alliance with the Arapaho. These two tribes say they have never known a time when they were not associated. About forty years ago, in Wyoming, the band known since then as the Northern Cheyenne separated from the others (according to Clark) and have since lived chiefly in Montana or with the Sioux, with whom the Cheyenne made peace about sixty years ago. The other and larger portion of the tribe continued to range chiefly on the lands of the Arkansas and Canadian rivers in Colorado and the western part of

<header>MOONEY] DIVISIONS OF THE CHEYENNE</header>

Kansas and Oklahoma. In 1840, they and the <term>Arapaho</term> made peace with the <term>Kiowa</term> and <term>Comanche</term>. They participated in raids with these tribes into Texas and Mexico until 1869, when they were assigned to a reservation in what is now western Oklahoma. In 1874, they—along with the <term>Kiowa</term>, <term>Comanche</term>, and <term>Kiowa Apache</term>—went to war again due to the destruction caused by buffalo hunters, but the uprising was quickly suppressed. In 1890, they sold their reservation and accepted individual land allotments. The northern <term>Cheyenne</term> joined the <term>Sioux</term> in the "Custer war" of 1876–77. After the surrender of the hostile forces, they were moved to Oklahoma and placed with the southern <term>Cheyenne</term>. However, they were very unhappy with their location. This dissatisfaction led to an attempt by a large group under <term>Dull Knife</term> to escape to the north in September 1878. They were pursued, and some were captured and held at <term>Fort Robinson</term>, Nebraska. From there, they made a desperate escape attempt on the night of January 9, 1879, which resulted in the deaths of nearly all the prisoners. They were eventually granted a reservation in Montana, where they remain today, except for a few living among the <term>Sioux</term>. According to the official report for 1892, the southern <term>Cheyenne</term> in Oklahoma numbered 2,119; the northern <term>Cheyenne</term> in Montana numbered 1,200; and those with the <term>Sioux</term> at <term>Pine Ridge</term>, South Dakota, numbered 120, for a total of 3,439.

The <term>Cheyenne</term> have eleven tribal divisions. They have at least two dialects, but probably more. The tribal divisions in their order in the camping circle are—

1. *Evi'sts-unĭ' pahis* ("smoky lodges"—Grinnell, according to Clark).
2. *Sŭta'ya* or *Sŭ'tasi'na*. This is one of the most important divisions and previously formed a separate tribe, but was later merged with the <term>Cheyenne</term>. According to the shared <term>Cheyenne</term> and <term>Blackfoot</term> tradition recorded by <term>Grinnell</term>, they appear to have originally been part of the <term>Blackfeet</term> but became separated from the main tribe when ice suddenly broke while they were crossing a large river. They drifted south and eventually met and joined the <term>Cheyenne</term> in the Black Hills. Their name, spelled *Suti* by <term>Grinnell</term>, is said to mean "strange talkers." Today, they live on the upper Washita River in Oklahoma and speak a dialect that differs significantly from the rest of the tribe.
3. *Ĭ'sium-itä'niuw'*, ("ridge-people;" singular, *Ĭ'siumi-tän*—Grinnell, according to Clark).
4. *Hĕwă-tä'niuw'*, "hairy men." This name is also sometimes used as a group name for all the southern <term>Cheyenne</term> to distinguish them from the northern <term>Cheyenne</term>, who are collectively called *Hmĭ'sĭs*. The southern <term>Cheyenne</term> are also known collectively as *So'wăniă*, or "southerners."
5. *Ŏ'ivimă'na*, "scabby." This name is said to have been originally given to them because of an epidemic that once broke out among their horses, leaving them mangy.
6. *Wĭ'tapi'u* ("haters"—Grinnell, according to Clark).

<page-num>1027</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] CHARACTER OF THE CHEYENNE</header>

Following general Indian custom, the various divisions camp in the order shown in figure 100.

The <term>Cheyenne</term>, like the prairie tribes in general, are—or were until only a few years ago—a nation of nomads, living in skin <term>tipis</term> and depending almost entirely on the buffalo for food. Yet they have a faint memory of a time when they lived in permanent villages and planted corn. In their genesis tradition, which takes four "smokes" or nights to tell, they relate how they "lost" the corn a long time ago before they became wanderers on the plains. They place their dead on scaffolds in trees, unlike their allies, the <term>Arapaho</term>, who bury their dead in the ground. Their most sacred possession is the bundle of "<term>medicine arrows</term>," which is now held by the southern division of the tribe. They have a military organization similar to the one existing among the <term>Arapaho</term> and other prairie tribes, as described under number 43 of the <term>Arapaho</term> songs. Above all other tribes of the plains, they are distinguished for their desperate courage and pride; they are preeminently warriors among people whose primary trade is war. They are strongly conservative and have steadily resisted every advance of civilization. Here again they differ from the <term>Arapaho</term>, who have always shown a willingness to meet the white man halfway. In fact, no two peoples could exhibit more marked differences in characteristics on almost every point than these two allied tribes. The <term>Cheyenne</term> possess a quick and strong intelligence, but their fighting temperament sometimes makes them rather unmanageable subjects to deal with. Their conservatism and tribal pride tend to restrain them from following "strange gods," so they take a somewhat skeptical position toward the new messiah; however, they still conform to all the requirements of the dance code just to be on the safe side.

Clark, in his *Indian Sign Language*, summarizes the characteristics of the <term>Cheyenne</term> as follows:

> As a tribe they have been broken and scattered, but in their wild and savage way they fought well for their country, and their history during the past few years has been written in blood. The men of the <term>Cheyenne</term> Indians rank as high in honesty, energy, and determination as those of any other tribe I have ever met; in physique and intellect, they are superior to most tribes and the equal of any. Under the most demoralizing and trying circumstances, they have preserved to a remarkable degree that part of their moral code relating to chastity. Public sentiment regarding this matter has been so strong among them that they have been, and still are, noted among all the surrounding tribes for the virtue of their women.

The <term>Cheyenne</term> language lacks the liquid sounds *l* and *r*. It is full of hissing sounds and difficult combinations of consonants, so it does not lend itself easily to song composition. For this reason, among others, the <term>Cheyenne</term> in the south usually join the <term>Arapaho</term> in the <term>Ghost dance</term> and sing the <term>Arapaho</term> songs.

<summary>This page describes the Cheyenne as a courageous and conservative warrior tribe who transitioned from settled farming to a nomadic buffalo-hunting lifestyle. It highlights their cultural differences from the Arapaho, their high moral standards regarding chastity, and the linguistic difficulties that lead them to use Arapaho songs during the Ghost Dance.</summary>

<keywords>Cheyenne, Arapaho, medicine arrows, Indian Sign Language, Ghost dance, nomad, tipis, genesis tradition, buffalo, messiah, tribal character, linguistics</keywords>

## 1. O'TÄ NÄ'NISĬ'NÄSISTS

> O'tä nä'nisĭ'näsists—Ehe'e'ye'!
> O'tä nä'nisĭ'näsists—Ehe'e'ye'!

> Ho'ivitu'simo'moĭ'ts—E'ähe'e'ye'!

> Nitu'si'mitä'nun,

->*Translation*<-

> Well, my children—*Ehe'e'ye'*!
> Well, my children—*Ehe'e'ye'*!
> When you meet your friends again—*Ähe'e'ye'*!
> When you meet your friends again—*Ähe'e'ye'*!
> The earth will tremble—*E'ähe'e'ye'*!
> The earth will tremble—*E'ähe'e'ye'*!
> The summer cloud <note>The meaning here is uncertain</note>
> It will give it to us,
> It will give it to us.

The interpretation of this song is imperfect and the meaning is not clear. It evidently refers to the earthquake which it is believed will occur at the moment the spirit world contacts the old earth. The literal meaning of the second line, translated as "when you meet your friends again," is actually "when you are living together again."

### 3. NÄ'NISO'NÄSI'STSIHI'

->Are painted their different colors,<-

This song has a very beautiful tune. The Cheyenne claim to have lived originally in the north on a stream known to them as the "River of Turtles." Reverend H. R. Voth, a former missionary among the Cheyenne and Arapaho, states that the Indians say that along the banks of this stream were clays of different colors which they used for paint. In a letter dated October 1, 1891, he says: "I now have in my possession some red and some gray or drab paint that Black Coyote brought with him from the north, which he claims came from that ancient Turtle River, and which the Indians are now using to paint themselves. They say there are more than two kinds of colors at that river, or at least there used to be." According to Clark (*Indian Sign Language*, page 99), the oldest traditions of the Cheyenne locate their former home on the headwaters of the Mississippi in Minnesota, near where Saint Paul is now located. Other facts support this testimony, and the traditional "River of Turtles" would seem to be the same as the Saint Croix, which was described by Coxe in 1741:

> A little higher up is the river Chabadedą, above which the Meschacebe <note>Mississippi</note> forms a beautiful lake twenty miles long and eight or ten wide. Nine or ten miles above that lake, on the east side, is a large, pleasant river called the River of Tortoises. Once you have entered a short distance, it leads far into the country to the northeast and is navigable by the largest boats for forty miles. About the same distance further up, the Meschacebe falls from the rocks about fifty feet, but it is navigable for a significant distance by large ships—as it is also beyond that point, except for another waterfall eighty or ninety miles higher—by large vessels to its sources, which are in the country of the Sioux, not

It is hardly necessary to state that the idea of a devil is not indigenous, although it is now embodied in the Indian mythology and language through contact with white people. The "White Man Above" is understood to mean the ruler for whom the messiah is a precursor, equivalent to our idea of God.

A significant number of the Cheyenne ghost songs refer to rivers seen in the spirit world; these are frequently designated by colors, such as yellow, blue, and so on. It may be that certain rivers play a prominent part in their mythology, and as has been noted, they locate their earliest traditional home on the "Turtle River." The word translated here as "blue-green" might mean either blue or green, as in Cheyenne and many other Indian languages the two colors are not differentiated. Compare Cheyenne song number 16.

Although she is a young woman, she is regarded as a leader in the Cheyenne Ghost Dance, having frequently been in trances and having composed numerous songs. In this song, she relates her experience in one trance, during which she and her female companion played together the women's game of shinny (already described) and then went to look for their mothers, who had passed into the spirit world years before.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Cheyenne Ghost Dance songs, moving to song number 10, which describes the "Crazy Dance" and provides its cultural and ceremonial context among the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes.</meta>

<page-num>1033</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] THE CRAZY DANCE</header>

->*Translation*<-

->The buffalo head — *Yä'hä'yä'!*<-
->The half buffalo —<-
-><note>Repeated at will</note><-

This song refers to the Crazy Dance, which the song's author saw the former warriors of his tribe performing in the spirit world. The Crazy Dance, called *Psam* by the Cheyenne and *Ahaka'wŭ* by the Arapaho, belonged to one of the military orders already described in the section on Arapaho songs. (See Arapaho song 43.) The names in both languages are derived from their words for "crazy." Men, women, and children participated in the ceremony, dressing in skins or other costumes to represent various animals—such as buffaloes, panthers, deer, and birds—along with one bear, two foxes, and seven wolves, in addition to two "medicine wolves." Each dancer tried to imitate the animal they portrayed in both action and appearance.

The two foxes were responsible for constantly running and tripping over the others as they tried to escape from the crowd. The dance, whose essential feature was doing everything in reverse, had parallels among many eastern tribes, particularly the ancient Huron and Iroquois. It was considered the most colorful and entertaining dance among the prairie tribes. The "half buffalo" mentioned in the song refers to a robe worn by certain dancers; it consisted of the upper half of a buffalo skin, with the head and horns positioned over the dancer's own head.

The dance was a display of intentional madness in which the performers tried to outdo one another in absurd and frantic actions, specifically by constantly doing the exact opposite of what they were told to do. It was performed only to fulfill a vow made by someone for the recovery of a sick child, for a successful war expedition, or for some other traditional blessing. It lasted four days; the performers danced naked for the first three days and wore full dance costumes on the fourth.

The leaders of these antics were two performers whose bodies and cheeks were painted with white clay and whose ears were filled with hair shed by buffalo, which was believed to grant strong <term>medicine</term> powers. They carried whistles and shot at the spectators with blunt arrows. These two were allowed almost any freedom, and as a result, they were truly feared by the others. Among other customs, the crazy dancers used to dance through a fire until they trampled it out. This was done to imitate the fire-moth, called *aha'kăa'* ("crazy") by the Arapaho, which hovers around a flame and eventually flies into it. They also handled venomous snakes and, it is said, would sometimes even surround and kill a buffalo using only their physical strength. The Cheyenne version of the dance differed somewhat from the Arapaho version. It was last performed in the south about ten years ago.

<vocab>Crazy Dance, Psam, Ahaka'wŭ, Cheyenne, Arapaho, medicine wolves, contrary dance, fire-moth, aha'kăa'</vocab>

It details the specific roles of performers, such as the "foxes" and white-clay-painted leaders, and the symbolic imitation of the fire-moth.</summary>

->Translation<-

The crow—*Ehe'e'ye'*!
The crow—*Ehe'e'ye'*!
The grease paint—*He'e'ye'*!
The grease paint—*He'e'ye'*!
He brings it to me,

Red is a sacred color among all Indians and usually symbolizes strength and success. For this reason, it is a favorite color for painting the face and body for the dance or the warpath, and for painting the war pony, the lance, and so on. On all important occasions when painting the face or body, the skin is first anointed with grease to help the paint stick better and to avoid obscuring the sharp lines of the design.

This song was also composed by Mo'ki, "Little Woman," the wife of Grant Left-hand. Because of her frequent trances and resulting leadership in the Cheyenne Ghost Dance, she takes the title of the Crow Woman, that is, the woman messenger from the spirit world. The story of her and her husband's connection to the Ghost Dance is interesting for the light it sheds on the workings of the Indian mind, especially regarding religion.

Mo'ki is a young Cheyenne woman married to a young Arapaho, Grant Left-hand, who is about 30 years of age. He is a former Carlisle student and the son of Nawat, or Left-hand, the principal chief of the southern Arapaho. Despite several years of English education, Grant is a firm believer in the doctrine and the dance. He is the principal organizer and leader of the auxiliary "crow dance" in his own tribe, while his wife is just as prominent in the Ghost Dance among the Cheyenne. She has composed a series of a dozen or more songs describing her various trance experiences in the spirit world.

<meta>This page continues the biographical account of Mo'ki and Grant Left-hand, illustrating the personal grief that fueled participation in the Ghost Dance, and begins a glossary of Cheyenne terms used in the songs.</meta>

<page-num>1039</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] GRANT LEFT-HAND AND THE DANCE 1039</header>
<columns>2</columns>

Her first child died soon after birth, and the young mother was keenly affected by the loss. Afterward a boy was born to them, and he became the idol of his parents, especially of the father. He grew up into a bright and active little boy, but when he was about 4 years of age he was suddenly seized with a spasm in the night and died in a few minutes, almost before his father could reach his bed. This second loss brought deep sorrow to them both, and the mother brooded over it so much that there was serious fear for her own life. Then came the Ghost Dance and the new doctrine of a reunion with departed friends. The mother went to the dance, fell into a trance, met her children as if they were alive, and played with her little boy. On awaking and returning home, she told her husband. He could hardly believe it at first, but it required only a little persuasion to induce him to attend the next Ghost Dance with her because, as he said, "I want to see my little boy." He himself fell into a trance, saw his children, and rode with his little boy on the horse behind him over the green prairies of the spirit land. From that time, both became devoted followers and leaders of the Ghost Dance; their trances have been frequent, and every dance is welcomed as another opportunity for reunion with departed friends. The young man was deeply moved as he spoke of his love for his children, the sudden death of the little boy, and their second meeting in the other world. As his wife sat by his side looking up into our faces and listening intently to every word—although she understood very little English—it could not be doubted that their faith in the reality of the vision was real and earnest. Every Indian parent who has lost a child, every child who has lost a parent, and every young man and woman who has lost a brother, sister, or friend affirms a similar reason for belief in the Ghost Dance.

*Iyo'häĭ*—he (she, or it) is rising. *Nä'ohä*, I rise.

*Mä'ĭnoyo'hi*—Turtle river; from *mä-ĭ'nh*, turtle (plural, *mäĭno'nh*), and *o'hĭ*, river.
*Mäpĭ'vǎ*, water.
*Mä'noyo'h*—for *Mä'ĭnoyo'hi*.
*Mänoyu'hii*—for *Mä'ĭnoyo'hi*.
*Mäpĭ'vǎ*—water.
MARANSHOBISHGO—"cut-throats;" according to Long, the name applied by the Cheyenne to the Sioux. The form is incorrect, as there is no *r* in the Cheyenne language.

*O'go'ch* or *O'go'chi* or *O'go'ki*—the crow. In the Ghost dance, the crow is the messenger of the spirit world. The messiah and God are frequently referred to as "The Crow." See Arapaho song 36.

STAITAN—a name used by Lewis and Clark to designate a tribe identical with the Cheyenne. It is a corruption of the Cheyenne word *histä'itän*, "I am a Cheyenne."

<header>MOONEY] SKETCH OF THE COMANCHE</header>

# THE COMANCHE

## TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*Bo'dălk'iñago* — common Kiowa name, meaning "reptile people" or "snake men," from *bo'dal* (reptile, insect) and *k'iñago* (people).
*Cha'tha* — (singular *Cha'*) Arapaho name, meaning "enemies."
*Comanche* — popular name; of Mexican-Spanish origin and unknown meaning. It appears as early as 1757, and in the form *Cumanche* as early as 1720.
*Gyai'-ko* — the common name given by the Kiowa to the Comanche, meaning "enemies."
*Iatan* — the French spelling of the name applied by several of the plains tribes to the Ute Indians, and by extension to the related Comanche and Shoshoni. It is a derivative of the name Yuta or Ute, with the final *n* representing a nasalized vowel sound. The closest approximation is perhaps *Iätä-go*, the Kiowa (plural) name for the Ute. Variations are *L'Iatan, Aliatan, Halitane, Ayutan, Tetau* (for *Ietau* or *Ietan*), *Jetan, Yutan*, etc. The form *Läitanes* appears as early as 1740 (Margry, VII, 457).
*Idahi* — Kiowa Apache name; the meaning is unknown.
*Ietan* — a name applied by some of the prairie tribes to several Shoshonean tribes, particularly the Shoshoni and the Comanche. It appears in a number of forms and is found as *Läitanes* as early as 1740 (Margry, VII, 457).
*La Playe* — former French trader's name, perhaps a corruption of *Tête Pele'e*.
*Na''lani* — Navajo name, meaning "many aliens" or "many enemies," applied collectively to the southern plains tribes, but more specifically to the Comanche.
*Na'nita* — Kichai name.
*Na'tăa'* — Wichita name, interpreted in various ways as "snakes" (meaning "enemies") or "dandies."
*Nüma* — the tribe's own name for themselves, meaning "people." The Shoshoni and Paiute designate themselves by the same name.
*Pa'douca* — the name given to the Comanche by the Osage, Quapaw, Kansa, Oto, and other Siouan tribes. It has several dialectal forms and was used in this form by Pénicaut as early as 1719. It may perhaps be a contraction of *Pe'nä-tëka*, the name of the principal eastern division of the Comanche.
*Sänko* — obsolete Kiowa name; it may mean "snakes," from *säne* (snake).
*Sau'hto* — Caddo name.
*Shishino'wĭts-Itäniuw'* — Cheyenne name, meaning "snake people."
*Tête Pele'e* — a name said to have been applied to the Comanche by French traders, meaning "bald heads." This identification seems doubtful, as the Comanche only cut their hair when mourning.
*Yă'mpai-ni* or *Yă'mpai-Rĭ'kani* — Shoshoni name, meaning "yampa people" or "yampa eaters." It is specifically the name of only one division, but is used collectively for the whole tribe. The yampa plant is the *Carum gairdneri*.

## TRIBAL SIGN

The tribal sign for the Comanche is "snakes," the same as that for the Shoshoni, but with the finger drawn toward the rear instead of thrust forward.

## SKETCH OF THE TRIBE

The Comanche are one of the southern tribes of the great Shoshonean family, and the only one of that group living entirely on the plains. Their language and traditions show that they are a relatively recent offshoot from the Shoshoni of Wyoming; both tribes speak practically the same dialect and, until very recently, maintained

constant and friendly communication. Within the traditional period, the two tribes lived adjacent to each other in southern Wyoming; since that time, the Shoshoni have been forced back into the mountains by the Sioux and other prairie tribes, while the Comanche have been driven steadily southward by the same pressure. In this southern migration, the Pe'nätĕka seem to have preceded the rest of the tribe. The Kiowa say that when they moved southward from the Black Hills region, the Arkansas River was the northern boundary of the Comanche.

In 1719, the Comanche are mentioned under their Siouan name of Pa'douca as living in what is now western Kansas. It should be remembered that a range of 500 to 800 miles was an ordinary distance for a prairie tribe, and that the Comanche were equally at home on the Platte River and in the Mapimí Basin of Chihuahua. As late as 1805, the North Platte was still known as Padouca Fork. At that time, they roamed over the country near the headwaters of the Arkansas, Red, Trinity, and Brazos rivers in Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas. For nearly two hundred years, they were at war with the Spaniards of Mexico and extended their raids far down into Durango. They were generally friendly to Americans, but became bitter enemies of the Texans, who forced them off their best hunting grounds; the Comanche carried on an unrelenting war against them for nearly forty years. They have been close allies of the Kiowa for perhaps one hundred and fifty years. In 1835, they made their first treaty with the government, and by the Treaty of Medicine Lodge in 1867, they agreed to move to their current reservation, situated between the Washita and Red rivers in the southwestern part of Oklahoma. However, it was not until after the last outbreak of the southern prairie tribes in 1874–75 that they and their allies, the Kiowa and Apache, finally settled on it. They were probably never a large tribe, although they were thought to be populous because of their wide range. Within the last fifty years, they have been severely decimated by war and disease. They numbered 1,512 in 1893.

The <term>gentile system</term> <note>A social organization based on clans or kinship groups.</note> seems to be unknown among the Comanche. They have, or still remember, thirteen recognized divisions or bands, and they may have had others in former times. Of these, all but five are practically extinct. The Kwǎ'hǎri and Pe'nätĕka are the most important. Following in alphabetical order is the complete list as given by their leading chiefs:

1. *Detsǎna'yuka* or *No'koni*. This band, to which the current head chief Quanah Parker belongs, was formerly called *No'koni*, meaning "wanderers." However, upon the death of Quanah's father, whose name was also *No'koni*, the name was tabooed according to Comanche custom, and the division took the name *Detsǎna'yuka*, "bad campers," which was intended to convey the same idea of wandering.

2. *Ditsǎ'kǎna*, *Wĭ'dyu*, *Yäp'ä*, or *Yä'mpäri'ka*. This division was formerly known as *Wĭ'dyu*, "awl," but for a reason similar to that just

It was mentioned that the name was changed to *Ditsä'kăna*, "sewers," which conveys the same idea, as an awl was the substitute for a needle. They are equally well known as *Yäpä*, the Comanche name for the root of the *Carum gairdneri*, known to the Shoshoni and Bannock as *yampa*, or sometimes as *Yämpä-ri'ka*, a dialect form meaning "yampa eaters." The entire Comanche tribe is known to the Shoshoni by the name *Yü'mpaini* or *Yämpai-ri'kani*, "yampa people" or "yampa eaters." The *Yäpä* are also sometimes known as *Etsitü'biwat*, "northerners," or "people of the cold country," because they usually roamed along the northern frontier of the tribal territory; this fact may account for the Shoshoni having designated the whole tribe by their name.

3. *Kewa'tsăna*. "No ribs;" extinct.
4. *Kotsa'i*. Extinct.
5. *Ko'tso-tě'ka*. "Buffalo eaters," from *ko'tso*, buffalo, and *tě'ka*, the root of the verb "to eat."
6. *Kwa'hări* or *Kwa'hădi*. "Antelopes." This division was one of the most important of the tribe and was named because its members frequented the prairie country and the Staked Plains, while the *Pe'nätěka* and others roamed farther east on the edge of the timber region. They were the last to come in after the surrender in 1874. The *Kwa'hări*, *Ditsä'kăna*, and *Detsăna'yuka* were sometimes collectively referred to by white people as northern Comanche, as distinguished from the *Pe'nätěka*, who were known as eastern or southern Comanche.
7. *Motsai'*. Perhaps from *pä-motsan*, "a loop in a stream." These and the *Těna'wa* were almost entirely wiped out in a battle with the Mexicans around 1845.
8. *Pä'gatsû*. "Head of the stream" (*pä*, a stream); extinct.
9. *Pe'nätěka*, or *Penä'nde*. "Honey eaters." These and the *Kwa'hări* were the two most important divisions in the tribe. They lived on the edge of the timber country in eastern Texas, and therefore were frequently known to white people as eastern or southern Comanche. They had only a loose alliance with their western relatives and sometimes joined the Texans against them. Other Comanche names for them include *Te'yuwĭt*, "hospitable;" *Tě'kăpwai*, "no meat;" and *Ku'baratpat*, "steep climbers."
10. *Po'hoi*. "Wild-sage people," meaning the Shoshoni. This is not strictly the name of a Comanche division, but refers to some immigrant Shoshoni from the north who were integrated into the Comanche.
11. *Tänĭ'ma*. "Liver eaters," from *nĭm* or *nüm*, liver. This band is extinct; only one old man is known to still be alive.
12. *Těna'wa* or *Te'nähwĭt*. From *tě'näw'*, "downstream." Extinct. See *Motsai'* above.
13. *Wa-ai'h*. "Maggot." Extinct.

The Comanche were nomadic buffalo hunters, constantly on the move, cultivating nothing from the ground, and living in skin tipis. Except for the fact that they are now confined to a reservation and forced to depend on government rations, they have changed very little from their original

condition. They still mostly live in canvas tipis and dress in buckskin. They were long noted as the finest horsemen of the plains and had a reputation for dash and courage. They have a high sense of honor and consider themselves superior to the other tribes with which they are associated. Physically, they are well-built and rather stout. Their language is the trade language of the region and is more or less understood by all the neighboring tribes. It is sonorous and flowing; its chief characteristic is a rolling *r*, and it has no *l*. The language has several dialects and is practically the same as that of the Shoshoni in the north. Their current head chief is Quanah Parker, an able man whose mother was an American captive. His name, *Kwäna* or *Kwai'na*, means a sweet smell.

Because they have participated very little in the Ghost Dance, the Comanche have only a few songs in their own language; however, these are particularly pleasing for their martial ring or soothing softness. They call the dance *A'p-Anĕ'ka'ra*, "the father's dance" (from *a'pă*, father; *nĕ'ka'ra*, a dance), or by another name which means the "dance with joined hands."

# THE PAIUTE, WASHO, AND PIT RIVER TRIBES

## PAIUTE TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*Hogăpă'goni*—Shoshoni name, "rush arrow people" (*hogăp*, a small water reed; *pägă*, "arrow").
*Nüma*—proper tribal name, signifying "people" or "Indians;" the same name is also used for themselves by the Shoshoni and Comanche.
*Pai-yu'chimǔ*—Hopi name.
*Pai-yu'tsĭ*—Navaho name.
*Palǔ*—Washo name.
*Paiute* or *Piute*—popular name, variously interpreted as "true (*pai*) Ute" or "water (*pä*) Ute"—pronounced among themselves as *Paiuti*.

<note>The northern bands of the Paiute are frequently included with the Shoshoni and others under the name of Snakes, while the others are often included with various Californian tribes under the collective name of Diggers.</note>

## SKETCH OF THE PAIUTE

### CHARACTERISTICS

The Paiute belong to the great Shoshonean stock and occupy most of Nevada, along with adjacent portions of southwestern Utah, northwestern Arizona, and northwestern and southeastern California. The Pahvant and Gosiute on their eastern border are frequently, but improperly, classified as Paiute, while the Chemehuevi, associated with the Walapai in Arizona, are only a southern offshoot of the Paiute and speak the same language. Regarding the Indians of the Walker River and Pyramid Lake reservations, who constitute the main body of those commonly known as Paiute, Powell claims that they are not Paiute at all, but another tribe which he calls <term>Paviotso</term>. He says: "The names by which the tribes are known to white men and the department give no clue to the relationship of the Indians. For example, the Indians in the vicinity of the reservation on the Muddy River and the Indians on the Walker River and Pyramid Lake reservations are called Pai or Pah Utes, but the Indians know only those on the Muddy by that name, while those on the other two reservations are known as <term>Paviotsoes</term>, and speak a very different language, though it is closely allied to, if not identical with, that of the Bannocks." (*Comr., 45.*) The Ghost Dance originated among these Indians in the neighborhood of Walker River, from whom the songs given here were obtained; for convenience of reference, we shall speak of them under their popular title of Paiute, without asserting its correctness.

The different small bands have little political coherence, and there is no recognized head chief. The most influential chiefs among them in modern times have been Winnemucca, who died a few years ago, and Natchez. Wovoka's leadership is spiritual, not political. The Indians of Walker River and Pyramid Lake claim the Bannock as their cousins,

but they may be safely estimated at from 7,000 to 8,000 and are thought to be increasing. In 1893, those on reservations, all in Nevada, were reported to number 563 at Walker River; 494 at Pyramid Lake; and 209 at Duck Valley (Western Shoshone agency, in connection with the Shoshoni). Nevada Indians off the reservation were estimated to number 6,815, nearly all of whom were Paiute.

As a people, the Paiute are peaceable, moral, and industrious, and are highly praised for their good qualities by those who have had the best opportunities for judging. While apparently not as intellectually quick as the prairie tribes, they appear to possess more solidity of character. By their willingness and efficiency as workers, they have made themselves necessary to white farmers and have been able to supply themselves with good clothing and many of the comforts of life. On the other hand, they have steadily resisted the vices of civilization, so that they are described by one agent as presenting the "singular anomaly" of improvement through contact with white people. Another authority says: "To these habits and excellence of character may be attributed the fact that they are annually increasing in numbers, and that they are a strong, healthy, active people. Many of them are employed as laborers on the farms of white men in all seasons, but they are especially helpful during the time of harvesting and haymaking." (*Comr., 46.*) They would be the last Indians in the world to preach a crusade of extermination against white people, as the messiah religion has been portrayed. Aside from their earnings among the whites, they derive their livelihood from the fish of the lakes, jackrabbits and small game of the sage plains and mountains, and from piñon nuts and other seeds which they grind into flour for bread. Their ordinary dwelling is the *wikiup*, or small rounded hut of tule rushes over a framework of poles, with the ground for a floor and the fire in the center, and almost entirely open at the top. Strangely enough, although they appreciate the advantages of civilization regarding good clothing and such food as they can buy at the stores, they show no desire to live in permanent houses or to obtain the furniture of civilization, and their *wikiups* are almost bare of everything except for a few wicker or grass baskets of their own weaving.

The Paiute ghost songs have a monotonous, halting movement that makes them displeasing to the ear of a white man, and they are inferior in expression to those of the Arapaho and the Sioux. A number of words consisting only of meaningless syllables are inserted merely to fill in the meter. Like the related Shoshoni and Comanche, the language has a strong rolling *r*.

### GENESIS MYTH

At first the world was all water, and remained so for a long time. Then the water began to go down, and at last Kura'ngwa (Mount Grant) emerged from the water, near the southwest end of Walker Lake. There was fire on its top (it may have been a volcano), and when the wind blew hard, the water dashed over the fire and would have extinguished

it, but the sage-hen (*hutsi*—*Centrocercus urophasianus*) nestled down over it and fanned away the water with her wings. The heat scorched the feathers on the sage-hen's breast, and they remain black to this day. Afterward, the Paiute obtained their first fire from the mountain through the help of the rabbit, who is a great wonder-worker, "much like a god." As the water subsided, other mountains appeared until at last the earth was left as it is now.

Then the great ancestor of the Paiute, whom they call *Nümi'naă'*, "Our Father," came from the south from the direction of Mount Grant—where his footprints can still be seen—and journeyed across to the mountains east of Carson Sink and made his home there. A woman, *Ibidsĭi*, "Our Mother," followed him from the same direction; they met, and she became his wife. They dressed themselves in skins and lived on the meat of deer and mountain sheep, for there was plenty of game in those days. They had children—two boys and two girls. Their father made bows and arrows for the boys, and their mother fashioned sticks for the girls with which to dig roots. When the children grew up, each boy married his sister, but the two families quarreled until their father told them to separate. So, one family went to Walker Lake and became *Aga'ih-tĭka'ra*, "fish eaters" (the Paiute of Walker Lake), while the other family went farther north into Idaho and became *Kotso'-tĭkăra*, "buffalo eaters" (the Bannock); however, both are one people and have the same language. After their children had left them, the parents went to the mountains farther east; there, *Nüminaă'* ascended into the sky, and his wife followed him.

### THE WASHO

Associated with the Paiute are the Washo, or *Wâ'siu*, as they call themselves—a small tribe of about 400 souls who have no known affinity with any other Indians. They occupy the mountain region in the extreme western portion of Nevada, around Washo and Tahoe lakes and the towns of Carson and Virginia City. They formerly extended farther east and south but were driven back by the Paiute, who conquered them, reducing them to complete subjection and forbidding them from using horses—a prohibition that was rigidly enforced until within a few years. Broken in spirit, they became mere hangers-on of the white settlements following the opening of the mines and are now terribly demoralized. They have been utterly neglected by the government, have never been included in any treaty, and now have no home they can call their own. They are devoted adherents of the messiah but usually join in the dance with the nearest Paiute camp, whose songs they sing, and they probably have no Ghost songs in their own language. We quote a gloomy account of their condition in 1866. This description applies equally well today, except that their numbers have diminished:

> This is a small tribe of about 500 Indians living in the extreme western part of the state. They are usually a harmless people, with much less physical and mental

They show an almost uncontrollable appetite for intoxicating drinks. They are sensual and filthy, and are decreasing in numbers every year from the diseases contracted through their indulgences. A few have learned the English language and will do light work for reasonable pay. They spend the winter months around the villages and homes of white people, from whom they obtain adequate supplies of food and clothing. They spend the spring, summer, and autumn months fishing around Washo and Tahoe lakes and the streams which flow through their country. They also gather grass seed and pine nuts, and hunt rabbits, hares, and ducks. There is no suitable place for a reservation within the boundaries of their territory, and, in view of their rapidly decreasing numbers and the diseases to which they are subjected, none is needed. (*Comr., 47.*)

### THE PIT RIVER INDIANS

Another group of Indians closely associated with the Paiute on the northwest consists of a number of small tribes, known collectively to the whites as Pit River or Hot Springs Indians, who hold the basin of the Pit River in northeastern California from Goose Lake to the junction with the Sacramento River. Among their tribes or bands are the Achoma'wi, Huma'whi, Estakéwach, Hantéwa, Chumâ'wa, Atua'mih or Hamefku'ttelli, Ilma'wi, and Pa'kamalli. (*Powers, Tribes of California.*) They are at present supposed to constitute a distinct linguistic group, but it is probable that better information will show their connection with some of the neighboring Californian stocks. With the exception of a few at the Round Valley reservation in California, none of them are on reservations or have any official recognition by the government. They probably number between 1,000 and 1,500 people. The northern bands have suffered much from Modoc slave raids in former days, and are much inferior in physique and intellect to those lower down the river, who were the terror of northern California thirty years ago, and who were described by recent observers as good workers—intelligent, brave, and warlike. (*A. G. O., 9.*)
