<header>MOONEY] MYTH OF THE MILKY WAY</header>

This is one of the favorite songs of the Paiute Ghost Dance. The tune has a plaintive but rather pleasing effect, although it is inferior to the tunes of most ghost songs of the prairie tribes. The words, as they stand, are very simple, but they convey a great deal of meaning to the Indian. It must be remembered that the dance is held in the open air at night, with the stars shining down on the vast plain walled in by the giant Sierras, which are fringed at the base with dark pines and have peaks white with eternal snows. Under such circumstances, this song of the snow lying white upon the mountains and the Milky Way stretching across the clear sky evokes in the Paiute the same patriotic love of home that comes from lyrics about singing birds, leafy trees, and still waters to the people of more fertile regions. In the mythology of the Paiute, as in that of many other tribes, the Milky Way is the path of the dead to the spirit world. *Ro'rǎni'* serves merely to fill out the meter.

### 5. PÄGÜ'NÄVÄ'

This song is an invocation of the elemental forces. It was composed by an old woman who left the circle of dancers and stood in the center of the ring while singing it.

### PAIUTE GLOSSARY

*Agai'h-tïka'ra*—"fish eaters;" the distinctive name of the Paiute of Walker Lake, Nevada.
*Bai'-yo*—it is broken.
*Ba'wă*—going around in a circle.
*Dĕna*—for *Tï'na*.
*Do*—black.
*Dombi'na*—for *Tï'mbi* or *Tübi*.
*Do'roni*—rolling on the ground, wallowing.
*Do'yon* or *Do'yonji*—it is growing tall.
*Ga'yon* or *Ga'yoni*—slender, tall and slender.
*Gosi'pa*—the Milky Way, the road of the dead. See Paiute song 1.
*Hävi'gïnú*—it lies there, it lies there asleep; *hävi'kwă*, sleep.
*Hogăpä'goni*—"rush-arrow people;" the Shoshoni name for the Paiute; from *hogăp*, a small water reed; *pägă*, arrow, and *ni*, the tribal suffix.
*Hutsi*—the sage-hen (*Centrocercus urophasianus*).
*Ïbidsi'ï̆*—"our mother;" the mythic maternal ancestor of the Paiute.
JACK WILSON—see Wovoka.
*Ka*—the root of the verb "sit;" *yä'nakatü'*, I am sitting down.
*Kai-va*—mountain.
*Kosi*—for *Kosi'ba*.
*Kosi'ba*—dust.
*Kotso'-tïka'ra*—"buffalo eaters;" the Paiute name for the Bannock. Compare *Ko'tso-tĕ'ka*, a Comanche division.
*Kura'ngwa*—"very high peak;" applied to Mount Grant, the sacred mountain of the Paiute, west of Hawthorne and near the southwestern end of Walker Lake, Nevada.
*Kwohi'tsauq* or *K'wijau'h*—"big rumbling belly," one of the names assumed by Wovoka the messiah. It was originally the name of his paternal grandfather.
*Nänigü'kwa*—the Paiute name of the Ghost Dance. The word signifies the "dance in a circle;" *nüka*, a dance.
*Noyo'ä*—to come gliding or creeping; the verb is applied to the movement of a snake or of an object that progresses without the aid of feet.
*Noyo'wana*—for *Noyo'ä*.

<column-break/>

*Nümä*—"people," or "Indians," the name used by the Paiute, Shoshoni, and Comanche to designate themselves.
*Nümi'-naä'*—"our father;" the mythic ancestor of the Paiute.
*Nüvä'*—for *Nüvä'bi*.
*Nüvä'bi*—snow.
*Nüvä'-ri'pă*—snowy earth, snow-covered earth (compound word); from *nüvä'bi*, snow, and *ri'pă* or *ti'pă*, earth.
*Pägü'nävä*—fog.
Paiute or Piu'te—(*Pai-yu't*) the name by which the Nümä of Nevada and the adjacent region are popularly and officially known. It has been translated as "true (*pai*) Ute" or "water (*pä*) Ute." They themselves pronounce the word in three syllables, *Pai-u'-ti*.
PAI-YU'CHIMŪ—the Hopi name for the Paiute.
PAI-YU'TSÏ̆—the Navajo name for the Paiute.
PALŪ—the Washo name for the Paiute.
*Päsü'*—for *Päsü'bi*.
*Päsü'bi*—willow.
PAVIO'TSO—the proper tribal name of the Indians of Walker River and Pyramid Lake reservations in Nevada, according to Powell, who considers them distinct from the Paiute.
*Pu'i*—for *Pu'igai'-yu*.
*Pu'igai'-yu*—verdant, green (applied to growing plants).
*Ro'răni*—a word without meaning used to fill out the rhythm of the songs.
*Ro'yon* or *Ro'yonji*—other forms of *Do'yon*.
SNAKE INDIANS—a name loosely applied to various northern bands or tribes of Shoshonean stock, including Paiute, Bannock, Shoshoni, and sometimes even the Comanche.
*Sowi'na*—ringing like a bell, roaring.
*Sû'ng-ä*—for *Sû'ng-äbi*.
*Sû'ng-äbi*—cottonwood.
*Taivo*—the Paiute, Shoshoni, and Comanche name for a white man. See *Tä'vibo*.
*Täkwü'kwij*—lightning.
*Tä'vibo*—"white man," the father of Wovoka the messiah. The word is related to *täbi* or *tävi*, the sun; *tävä'năgwăt*, the east or sunrise place.

# THE SIOUX

## TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*Chahrarat*—Pawnee name (according to Grinnell).
*Dakota*, *Nakota*, or *Lakota*—the proper tribal name, depending on the dialect, meaning "allies" or "friends." Sometimes they also refer to themselves as *Oceti Sakowin*, the "seven council fires," in reference to their seven great divisions.
*Itahatski*—Hidatsa name, meaning "long arrows" (according to Matthews).
*K'odalpä-Kiñago*—Kiowa name, meaning "necklace people," which is perhaps a misunderstanding of "neck-cutting people," that is, beheaders.
*Maranshobishgo*—Cheyenne name, meaning "cut-throats" (according to Long). The name is clearly incorrect, as the Cheyenne language does not have the letter *r*.
*Nadowesi* or *Nadowesiu*—meaning "little snakes" or "little enemies." *Nadowe*, meaning "snake" and figuratively "enemy," was the common Algonquian term for all tribes of foreign lineage. The Ojibwa and other tribes designated the Iroquois, who lived east of them, as *Nadowe*, while the Sioux, who lived to the west, were distinguished as *Nadowesi* or *Nadowesiu*. From this term come the names Nadouessioux and Sioux.
*Natnihina* or *Natni*—Arapaho name; Hayden gives the form as *Natenehina*, which he translates as "cut-throats or beheaders," but it may be derived from *Nadowe*, as explained above.
*Niake'tsikûtk*—Kichai name.
*Pambizimina*—Shoshone name, "beheaders."
*Papitsinima*—Comanche name, "beheaders," from *papitsi*, meaning to behead, and *nima* or *nüma*, meaning people.
*Shahañ*—The name used by the Osage, Kansa, Oto, and other tribes (according to Dorsey).
*Sioux*—the popular name, abbreviated from Nadouessioux, which is the French form of their Ojibwa name.
*Tsâba'kosh*—Caddo name, "cut-throats."

## TRIBAL SIGN

A sweeping motion of the right hand in front of the neck. This is commonly interpreted as "cut-throats" or "beheaders," but the Kiowa claim it refers to a type of shell necklace that was formerly unique to the Sioux.

### SKETCH OF THE TRIBE

The Sioux constitute the largest tribe in the United States and are too well known to require an extended description here. Although they are now thought of primarily as a prairie tribe, their emergence onto the plains is comparatively recent; within the historical period, their range extended as far east as central Wisconsin. They were driven out of that region and most of Minnesota by the westward advance of the Ojibwa. There is reason to believe that the true home of the entire Siouan stock is not in the west, or even in the central region, but along the South Atlantic slope. (See the author’s *Siouan Tribes of the East*.)

The Sioux language has three well-marked dialects: the eastern or Santee, the middle or Yankton (including the Assiniboine in the north), and the western or Teton. The tribe consists of seven great divisions, each of which in turn has or had subdivisions. Dorsey lists over one hundred in all. Each grand division had its own camping circle, and when two or more such divisions camped together, they usually camped in concentric circles (*Dorsey*). The seven great divisions are: 1. *Mde-wakañ-toñwañ* (Medewacanton), “village of Spirit Lake;” 2. *Waqpekute* (Wahpacoota), “leaf shooters;” 3. *Waqpetoñwañ* (Wahpeton), “leaf village;” 4. *Sisitoñwañ* (Sisseton), variously interpreted as “slimy village” or “swamp village;” 5. *Ihañktoñwañ* (Yankton), “end village;” 6. *Ihañktoñwañna* (Yanktonais), “upper end village;” 7. *Titoñwañ* (Teton), “prairie village.”

The first four divisions are collectively known as the Isañati or Santee Sioux. The name is believed to be derived from *isañ*, the dialect word for “knife.” They formerly occupied the Mississippi, Minnesota, and upper Red rivers in Minnesota and were afterward gathered on reservations at Devil's Lake, North Dakota; Lake Traverse (Sisseton Agency) and Flandreau, South Dakota; and Santee Agency, Nebraska. Those at Lake Traverse and Flandreau have now taken land allotments as citizens.

The Yankton and Yanktonais, who together speak the middle dialect, primarily occupied the country along the James River, east of the Missouri in North Dakota and South Dakota, extending into Iowa. They are now on the Yankton and Crow Creek reservations in South Dakota and the Fort Peck reservation in Montana.

The Teton constitute more than two-thirds of the entire Sioux tribe and held nearly the whole country southwest of the Missouri from the Cannonball River to the South Platte, extending westward beyond the Black Hills. They are all now on reservations in South and North Dakota. They are further subdivided into seven principal divisions: 1. *Sichañgu*, “burnt thighs” (Brulés), now on the Rosebud reservation; 2. *Ogalala*, referring to the “scattering” of dust in the face (Clark), now on the Pine Ridge reservation under the celebrated chief Red Cloud (*Maqpe-Luta*); 3. *Hunkpapa*, “those who camp at the end (or opening)

<header>MOONEY] SKETCH OF THE SIOUX</header>

of the camping circle" (Clark), on the Standing Rock reservation; 4. *Minikañzu*, "those who plant by the water," on the Cheyenne River reservation; 5. *Itazipko*, "without bows" (Sans Arcs), on the Cheyenne River reservation; 6. *Sihasapa*, "black feet" (not to be confused with the Blackfoot tribe), on the Cheyenne River and Standing Rock reservations; 7. *Ohenoñpa*, "two kettles," on the Cheyenne River and Rosebud reservations. According to the official report for 1893, the Sioux within the United States number about 23,410, which, with 600 permanently settled in Manitoba, makes the total population about 24,000 souls.

The Sioux, under the name of Nadouessi, are mentioned by Jesuit missionaries as early as 1632. They made their first treaties with our government in 1815. The most prominent events in their history since that date have been the treaty of Prairie du Chien in 1825, which defined their eastern boundary and stopped the westward advance of the Ojibwa; the Minnesota massacre of 1862, which resulted in the expulsion of the Sioux from Minnesota; the Sioux war of 1876–77, largely following the unauthorized invasion of the Black Hills by miners, and the chief incident of which was the defeat and massacre of an entire detachment under General Custer; the treaty by which the great reservation was broken up in 1889; and the outbreak of 1890, including the massacre of Wounded Knee.

Because of their superior numbers, the Sioux have always assumed, if not exercised, lordship over all the neighboring tribes with the exception of the Ojibwa. The Ojibwa, having acquired firearms before the Sioux, were able to drive the latter from the headwaters of the Mississippi and were steadily pressing them westward until stopped by the intervention of the United States government. The Sioux, in turn, drove the Cheyenne, Crow, Kiowa, and others before them, forcing them into the mountains or down onto the southern prairies. The eastern bands were sedentary and largely agricultural, but the Teton were solely and preeminently wandering buffalo hunters. All lived in *tipis*—the word comes from the Sioux language—which were made of bark in the timber country and of buffalo skins on the plains. In warlike character, they are probably second only to the Cheyenne and have an air of proud superiority rather unusual among Indians. Clark says of them, "In mental, moral, and physical qualities I consider the Sioux a little lower but still nearly equal to the Cheyenne, and the Teton are the superior branch of the family." (*Indian Sign Language*, 345.) The eastern Sioux are now far advanced toward civilization through the efforts of teachers and missionaries for over a generation, and the same is true to a lesser degree of the Yankton, while the majority of the Teton are still nearly in their original condition.

I found the Sioux very difficult to approach on the subject of the Ghost Dance. This was natural, considering the trouble that had come to them because of it. When I was first at Pine Ridge, the troops still camped there served as a reminder of the conflict, while in

In the little cemetery at the agency were the fresh graves of the slain soldiers, and only a few miles away was the Wounded Knee battlefield and the trench where the bodies of nearly three hundred of their people had been thrown. To my questions, the answer was almost invariably, "The dance was our religion, but the government sent soldiers to kill us because of it. We will not talk any more about it." Another reason for their unwillingness was the fact that most of the interpreters were from the eastern or Santee portion of the tribe and looked with contempt on the beliefs and customs of their more primitive western brothers; between these groups, there was, in consequence, very little friendly feeling. On one occasion, while endeavoring to break

->FIG. 102—Native drawings of Ghost dance—A, Comanche; B, Sioux<-

the ice with one of the initiates of the dance, I told him how willingly the Arapaho had given me information and even invited me to join in the dance. "Then," said he, "don't you find that the religion of the Ghost dance is better than the religion of the churches?" I could not easily say yes, and I hesitated a moment to frame an answer. He noticed it at once and said very deliberately, "Well, then, if you have not learned that, you have not learned anything about it," and he refused to continue the conversation.

### SONGS OF THE SIOUX

#### 1. A'TE HE'YE E'YAYO

->*Opening song*<-

A'te he'ye e'yayo!
A'te he'ye e'yayo!
A'te he'ye lo,
A'te he'ye lo.
Nitu'ñkañshi'la wa'ñyegala/ke—kta' e'yayo'!
Nitu'ñkañshi'la wa'ñyegala/ke—kta' e'yayo'!
A'te he'ye lo,
A'te he'ye lo.
Ni'takuye wañye'găla/ke—kta' e'yayo'!
Ni'takuye wañye'găla/ke—kta' e'yayo'!
A'te he'ye lo,
A'te he'ye lo.

->*Translation*<-

The father says so—*E'yayo!*
The father says so—*E'yayo!*
The father says so,
The father says so.
You will see your grandfather—*E'yayo!*
You will see your grandfather—*E'yayo!*
The father says so,
The father says so.
You will see your relatives—*E'yayo!*
You will see your relatives—*E'yayo!*
The father says so,
The father says so.

This is the opening song of the dance. While singing it, all the dancers stand motionless with hands stretched out toward the west, the country of the messiah and the direction from which the new spirit world is to come. When it is ended, all cry together, after which they join hands and begin to circle around to the left. “Grandfather,” as well as “father,” is a respectful term applied to the messiah.

Michi'nkshi nañpe ma'yuzaye,
Michi'nkshi nañpe ma'yuzaye,
A'te he'ye lo,
A'te he'ye lo.
Ini'chaghe-kte,
Ini'chaghe-kte,
A'te he'ye lo,
A'te he'ye lo.
Chăno'ñpa wa'ñ chi'cha-u'pi,

This song refers to the sacred pipe which, according to Sioux tradition, was brought to them by a mysterious young woman from the spirit world. The story, as outlined by Captain J. M. Lee, is as follows: In ancient times, the Sioux were always at war, not only with other tribes but also among themselves. On one occasion, two young men were out hunting when they saw a young woman approaching them with her arms folded. Seeing that she was not from their own tribe, one hunter proposed to the other that they should kill her, but the other refused and urged that they wait until they learned what she wanted. The first speaker, however, was about to kill her as she drew near, when she suddenly stooped down and took something resembling an anklet from around her ankle, which she waved about her head. The motion was so rapid that it seemed as though a cloud encircled her for a few moments; when she stopped, the snake she had taken from her ankle glided away through the grass. But the young warrior who had intended to kill her had disappeared, swept from the face of the earth.

Turning then to his companion, she said, “I come to you as a friend and helper. Your people have been killing each other. I bring you a pipe, which is a token of peace,” and she held out a pipe as she spoke. “When you smoke it, your thoughts will be of peace, and no murderer <note>that is, no one who kills a member of his own tribe</note> must be allowed to smoke it.” She returned with him to his village, where the women prepared a large tipi for her reception, to which the chiefs of the tribe came to listen to her instructions. She taught them to be at peace with one another.

The narrative describes her encounter with two hunters and the divine punishment of one who intended to harm her.</summary>

<header>MOONEY] SACRED PIPE OF THE SIOUX</header>

one another, if they would be happy, and when they listened to her words and accepted her teachings, she gave them the sacred medicine pipe to smoke from then on in their councils as a constant reminder of the peace covenant of the Lakota. Her mission now ended, she said she must leave them, and although they pleaded with her earnestly to stay with them, she could not linger longer, but disappeared as suddenly and mysteriously as she had come.

A variation of this legend is given by Colonel Mallery in his paper in the Tenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, where it is illustrated by a colored plate from a picture by the Indian storyteller. According to this version, the pipe maiden was the mysterious white Buffalo Cow, and brought, with the pipe, a package of four grains of corn of different colors. This corn sprang from the milk which dropped from her udder, and was thus, along with the flesh of the buffalo itself, appointed from the beginning to be the food of all the red tribes. The seeming snakes about her waist and ankles were really blades of grass (corn?). She taught the people to call her "grandmother," a respectful title among Indians, and after leading them to her relatives, the buffalo, she faded from their sight as they stood gazing at her.

The pipe holds an important part in the mythology and ritual of almost all our tribes, east and west, and no great ceremony is complete and no treaty was ever confirmed without it. It is generally symbolic of peace and truth. As a peace emblem, it was formerly carried by every bearer of a friendly message from one tribe to another and was smoked in solemn ratification of treaties, the act of smoking being itself in the nature of an oath. Among the prairie tribes, an individual accused of a crime is offered the sacred pipe, and if he accepts it and smokes, he is declared innocent, as no Indian would dare to smoke it if guilty. The ordinary ceremonial pipe of the prairie tribes is made of the red stone, known as <term>catlinite</term>, from the famous pipestone quarry in Minnesota in the old country of the Sioux. The peace pipe of the Cherokee was made of a white stone, somewhat resembling talc, from a quarry near Knoxville, Tennessee. It is said to have had seven stem holes, symbolic of the seven clans of the Cherokee, and was smoked by seven counselors at the same time. In every case, the tribe has a legend to account for the origin of the pipe. A flat pipe is the tribal "medicine" of the Arapaho, and is still preserved with the northern band in Wyoming. (See Arapaho songs 1 and 2.) Besides the stone pipe, there are also in use pipes of clay or bone, as well as cigarettes, but as a rule no ceremonial character attaches to these. In ceremonial smoking, the pipe is passed around the circle of counselors, each of whom takes only a few puffs and then hands it to his neighbor. Each one as he receives the pipe offers it first to the sun, holding the bowl up toward the sky and saying, "Grandfather, smoke;" then to the earth, the fire, and perhaps also to each of the four cardinal points and to one or another of their mythological heroes. Among the Kiowa

I have seen a man hold up the pipe to the sky, saying, “Smoke, Sinti” (Sinti being their great mythological trickster), and then in the same way, “Smoke, Jesus.”

In the Ghost Dance at Rosebud and Pine Ridge, as it was usually performed, a young woman stood in the center of the circle holding out a pipe toward the Messiah in the west, and she remained there throughout the dance. Another young woman usually stood beside her holding out a <term>bägati</term> wheel (see Arapaho song 49) in the same way. This feature of the dance is said to have been introduced by Short Bull.

In the old days, an Indian camp during the cutting up of the meat after a buffalo hunt was a scene of the most joyous activity, some faint recollection of which still lingers around ration day at the agency. Thirty years ago, when a grand hunt was planned, preparations were made for days and weeks ahead. Couriers were sent out to collect the neighboring bands at a common meeting place, medicine men began their prayers and ceremonies to attract the herd, the buffalo songs were sung, and finally, when all was ready, the allied bands—or sometimes the whole tribe—men, women, children, horses, dogs, and <term>travois</term>—moved out into the buffalo grounds. Here the immense camp of hundreds of tipis was set up, more ceremonies were performed,

<meta>This page continues the description of the traditional buffalo hunt, moving from the preparations mentioned on the previous page to the actual slaughter and the communal processing of the meat.</meta>

<page-num>1067</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] JERKED MEAT AND PEMMICAN</header>

The mounted warriors rode out as a group to surround and kill the herd. The women followed closely after them to strip the hides from the fresh carcasses, cut out the best portions of the meat and tallow, and bring them into camp. Here, the meat was cut into thin strips and hung upon frames of horizontal poles to dry, while the tallow was stripped off in flakes. In the dry prairie atmosphere, one day is usually enough to cure the meat without the help of salt or smoke. When dried this way, it is known as “jerked beef.” While the meat is fresh, for the first day or two, the camp is a scene of constant feasting; the juicy steaks or the sweet ribs are kept broiling over the coals in one tipi or another until far into the night. It is the harvest celebration of the prairie tribes. As soon as the meat is dry, the tipis are taken down and packed into the wagons along with the meat, and one family after another starts for home until, in a short time, the great camp is a thing of the past.

The jerked beef or venison is commonly prepared for eating by being boiled until it is reasonably tender. In eating, the Indian takes a strip cooked this way, dips one end into a soup made by dissolving some salt in warm water, takes the salted portion between his teeth, and saws off enough for a mouthful with a knife held in his other hand. Between mouthfuls, he takes bites from a strip of dried tallow placed in the dish with the meat.

For pemmican, the jerked beef or other meat is toasted over a fire until it is crisp and is then pounded into a hash with a stone hammer. In the old times, a hole was dug in the ground and a buffalo hide was staked over it to form a skin basin, into which the meat was thrown to be pounded. The hide used was from the neck of the buffalo—the toughest part of the skin and the same used for shields—and the only part which would withstand the wear and tear of the hammers. In the meantime, the marrow bones are cracked open and boiled in water until all the grease and oil rise to the top, where they are skimmed off and poured over the pounded beef. As soon as the mixture cools, it is sewn up into skin bags (not the ordinary painted parfléche <note>A parfléche is a container or case made of untanned animal hide.</note> cases) and stored away until needed. It was sometimes buried or otherwise cached <note>Stored in a hidden place for future use.</note>. Pemmican prepared this way will keep indefinitely. When prepared for immediate use, it is usually sweetened with sugar, mesquite pods, or some wild fruit mixed and beaten up with it during the pounding. It is extremely nourishing and has a very pleasant taste to one accustomed to it. On the march, it was to the prairie Indian what parched corn was to the hunter of the forest tribes, and it has been found so valuable as a concentrated food that it is used extensively by Arctic travelers and explorers. A similar preparation is used on the pampas of South America and in the desert regions of South Africa, while the canned beef of modern commerce is an adaptation of the Indian idea. The name comes from the Cree language and indicates something mixed with grease or fat. (Lacombe.)

<vocab>jerked meat, pemmican, tallow, prairie tribes, tipi, buffalo hide, parfléche, Cree language, Lacombe</vocab>

### 8. LE HE'YAHE'

->*Translation*<-

> This one says— *Ye'ye!*

This song might be better translated as, "I am a Crow nation," that is, I represent the nation of Crows. The Crow nation probably represents the spirits of the dead in the other world, as explained in Arapaho song 36. In several of the Ghost Dance songs, expressions occur such as "I am a Crow," or "the Crow woman is going home," and so on. Compare this with Sioux song 18.

<header>MOONEY] BUFFALO HUNTING</header>

The phrase "give it back to me" is intended to show how remote the old life of the Indians has become—the life they led before they used guns and other items from the white man. The last line has no particular connection with the rest, except as a common refrain in the ghost songs.

### 17. HE'! KII'ÑYAÑKA A'GALI'-YE

*He'! kii'ñyañka a'gali'-ye,*
*He'! kii'ñyañka a'gali'-ye,*
*Wañ! le'chiya wanasa'pi-kta' keya'pi lo,*
*Wañ! le'chiya wanasa'pi-kta' keya'pi lo,*
*Wañhi'ñkpe ka'gha-yo!*
*Wañhi'ñkpe ka'gha-yo!*
*A'te he'ye lo, A'te he'ye lo.*

->Translation<-

*He! They have come back racing,*
*He! They have come back racing,*
*Look! They say there is going to be a buffalo hunt over here,*
*Look! They say there is going to be a buffalo hunt over here,*
*Make arrows! Make arrows!*
*The father says so, the father says so.*

This song may be considered a supplement to the previous one. In the old days, when going on a buffalo hunt, it was the custom among the Sioux to send out a small scouting party to locate the herd. Upon finding it, these men immediately returned at a full gallop to the main body of hunters; however, instead of stopping when they reached them, they dashed past and then turned to fall in behind. The first line refers to this custom. The song’s author, upon waking up in the spirit world, sees the scouting party just dashing in with news of the buffalo's presence. Everyone immediately prepares to join the hunt, and “the father” commands him to make (or get ready) his arrows and go with them.

### 18. MI'YE WAÑMA'YAÑKA-YO

*Mi'ye wañma'yañka-yo!*
*Mi'ye wañma'yañka-yo!*
*Ka'ñghi oya'te wañ chañku' waka'ghe lo,*
*Ka'ñghi oya'te wañ chañku' waka'ghe lo,*
*Yani'pi-kta'-cha, yani'pi-kta'-cha.*
*Kola he'ye lo, kola he'ye lo.*

->Translation<-

*Look at me! Look at me!*
*I am making a road for one of the Crow nation (?),*
*I am making a road for one of the Crow nation (?),*
*You will surely live, you will surely live.*
*Our friend says so, our friend says so.*

The idea of this song is somewhat similar to that of number 8. It does not refer to the Crow Indians. As has already been explained,

### 19. MAKA' SITO'MANIYAÑ

->Maka' sito'maniyañ ukiye,<-
->Oya'te uki'ye, oya'te uki'ye,<-

->*Translation*<-

->The whole world is coming,<-
->A nation is coming, a nation is coming,<-
->The Eagle has brought the message to the tribe.<-
->The father says so, the father says so.<-
->Over the whole earth they are coming.<-
->The buffalo are coming, the buffalo are coming,<-
->The Crow has brought the message to the tribe,<-
->The father says so, the father says so.<-

This fine song summarizes the entire hope of the Ghost Dance—the return of the buffalo and the departed dead, with the message being brought to the people by the sacred birds, the Eagle and the Crow. The eagle known as *wañ'bali* is the war eagle, from which feathers are obtained for war bonnets.

### 22. MICHĬ'NKSHI TAHE'NA

->*Translation*<-

> My child, come this way,

> You will take home with you a good country,

This song may refer to the vision of the new earth, which the messiah showed to the Sioux delegates when they visited him. (See page 797.) The first line means literally "return in this direction"; the imperative form used is somewhere between a command and a plea.

### 23. WANA WICHĚ'SHKA

> Wana wichě'shka a'ti-ye,
> Wana wichě'shka a'ti-ye.
> Wihu'ta oho'măni, wihu'ta oho'măni,
> Oka'tañna, oka'tañna,
> Koyañ wowa'hiñ-kte,
> Koyañ wowa'hiñ-kte.

->*Translation*<-

> Now set up the tipi,
> Now set up the tipi.
> Around the bottom,
> Around the bottom,
> Drive in the pegs,
> Drive in the pegs.
> In the meantime, I shall cook,
> In the meantime, I shall cook.

The form of the verb *oka'tañna* shows that it is a woman speaking, even if we did not learn this from the context. To those who know Indian life, it brings up a vivid picture of a prairie band on the march, stopping at noon or in the evening. > Soon I shall see my child,
> Soon I shall see my child,
> Says your mother,
> Says your mother.

This song clearly describes the trance vision of a mother who saw her child in the spirit world and expresses the hope that she may soon be reunited with him. According to the custom of the Ghost Dance, it is likely that she made a pair of moccasins to give him when they next met, and that she carried them in the dance as she sang.

### 26. WAKA'ÑYAÑ IÑYA'ÑKIÑ-KTE

> Waka'ñyañ iñya'ñkiñ-kte,
> Waka'ñyañ iñya'ñkiñ-kte,
> Chañgäle'shka wañ luza'hañ iñya'ñkiñ-kte,
> Chañgäle'shka wañ luza'hañ iñya'ñkiñ-kte,
> Wañwa'yag upo, wañwa'yag upo,
> A'te he'ye lo, a'te he'ye lo.

->*Translation*<-

> The holy (hoop) shall run,
> The holy (hoop) shall run,
> The swift hoop shall run,
> The swift hoop shall run.
> Come and see it,
> Come and see it,
> Says the father,
> Says the father.

This song refers to the game of the wheel and sticks (*bä'qati* in Arapaho) already described in the Arapaho songs. It is said that the medicine man of Big Foot's band carried such a hoop with him during their flight from the north and displayed it in every dance held by the band until the fatal day of Wounded Knee. A similar hoop was carried and hung upon the center tree at the dance at No Water's camp near Pine Ridge. To the Indian, it symbolizes the revival of traditional games.

### SIOUX GLOSSARY

*A'gäli (-ye)*—they have returned; *waku*, I am returning or coming home; *wagali'*, I have returned.
*Ahi' (-ye)*—they have come; *wa-u'*, I come; *hi*, he has come.
*A-icha'gha*—growing upon; from *kagha*, to grow or spring up.
*A'te* or *Ate-ye*—father; *ate kiñ*, the father; *ate-mita*, my father; *ni'-ate*, your father; *at-kuku*, his or her father. *Ye* is a syllable sometimes added to complete the meter.
*Ati'-ye*—set up the tipi; here *ye* is the imperative suffix.

<column-break/>

*Aya'gäli'pi-kte*—you (plural) will take home with you, you will bring back with you; from *awa'gäle*, I take it home.
*Chañgäle'shka*—a hoop; the *bä'qati* hoop. See Sioux song 26 and the Arapaho songs.
*Chañku'*—road, trail.
*Chäño'ñpa*—pipe; *o'ñpa*, to smoke; *cha'ñli*, tobacco.
*Cha-yani'pi-kta*—you (plural) will live; from *ni'wa-ŭñ*, I live, I go about alive; the regular form is *Yanipi-kta* (see that entry).
*Cheya'ya*—he is constantly crying. *Wa-che'yă*, I cry; the final *ya* implies repetition or habit.

*Chi'cha-u'pi*—I bring it to you (plural). *Chicha* implies "I to you," or "I mean you"; *u* implies "come," from *wa-u*, "I come"; *pi* is the plural participle, and with *chi-cha* implies "I bring it to you," or "I come with it to you."
*Chichu'-chĕ*—I give it to you, indeed; *waku'*, I give it to him; *chĕ* conveys the idea of "verily" or "indeed." Compare *Maqu'-we*.
*Chiñyi*—for *Kiñhiñ*, "when," or "when it is so."
*Echani*—you think so about it; *echa'mi*, I think; *echa'ni hwo*, "who do you think?"
*Eya!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs.
*Eya*—he says; *epa*, I say. *Eya'ya*, he reiterates, he says again; *e'yahe*, *eya'pi*, they say.
*E'yahe*—another form of *eya*, he says; see above.
*Eya'pi*—they say. Compare *Eya*.
*Eya'ya*—he reiterates, he says again. The final *ya* implies repetition. Compare *Eya*.
*E'yaye'ye!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs.
*E'yayo'!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs to fill in the measure.
*E'yeye'yeye!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs.
*Găle'shka*—spotted.
*Ha'eye'ya!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs.
*Hañpa*—moccasin.
*Ha'yeye!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs.
*He*—(1) an exclamation, "look!" or "look here!"; (2) an interrogative particle, placed after the sentence; (3) the demonstrative "that."
*Hĕku'wo*—come home now, return home at once; *wa-u*, I come; *he*, a prefix implying "now," or "directly."
*He'na*—those, plural of *he*, "that."
*He'uwĕ*—that is he coming; from *he*, "that"; *u*, "coming"; and *wĕ*, the feminine particle.
*Heyahe* (-ye)—he says that, he says this; *ye* is usually the female suffix. Compare *He'ye*.
*He'ye*—he says.
*He'yeye'!*—an unmeaning exclamation used in the songs.
*Hiyumichi'chiya'na*—hand me my own; *na*, the female imperative particle.

<column-break/>

*Hoshi'hi* (-ye)—he has arrived with a message; he has brought a message; from *hoshi'*, to tell news, to carry a message.
*Hûñku*—his mother; *inû'ñ*, mother.
*Hwo*—an interrogative sign, used by a man; a woman says *wi*.
*Ina'*—mother; my mother.
*Ini'chaghapi-kte*—you (plural) will grow or live. Compare *Inichaghe-kte*.
*Inichaghe-kte*—you (singular) will grow, that is, you will live; *icha'ghehe*, it is growing.
*Iñyañkiñ-kte*—it shall run; from *iñyañka*, to run.
*Ita'zipa*—a bow (to shoot with).
*Ka'gha-yo*—make them; *waka'ghe*, I make it; *yo*, an imperative particle.
*Kañghi'*—a crow.
*Kaye*—another form of *kaya*, to take to one.
*Keya'pi*—they say that, they say it; *epa*, to say.
*Kii'ñyañka*—racing; from *iñyañka*, to run; the prefix *ki* implies a contest or emulation.
*Kiñ*—the.
*Kiñhañ*—explained as another form of *kiñ*; the ordinary meaning is *when* or *if*.
*Ko'la*—friend.
*Koñ*—that (demonstrative); it sometimes conveys the idea of "aforesaid."
*Ko'yañ*—in the meantime.
*Ku'pi-ye*—you will return.
*Lechel*—thus, in this way; from *le*, "this."
*Lechi'ya*—over here in this place; from *le*, "this."
*Lena*—these things; from *le*, "this."
*Lo*—an emphatic or euphonic particle used at the end of a phrase or sentence; it may be described as an emphatic or euphonic period. *Lo* is used by men, *ye* by women.
*Lu'zahañ*—swift.
*Maka'*—earth, the earth.
*Mako'che*—a country.
*Mani'ye*—he walks (habitual); *mawani*, I walk; the suffix *ye* usually denotes a female speaker.
*Maq'pe-Luta*—Red Cloud, the noted chief of the Ogalala Teton Sioux at Pine Ridge; from *maqpi'ya*, a cloud, and *luta*, red.
*Maqu'-we*—he gave to me, indeed; from *waku'*, I give it; *we* is an emphatic particle. Compare *Chichu'-chĕ*.

# THE KIOWA AND KIOWA APACHE

## KIOWA TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*   *Be'shiltchă*—Kiowa Apache name, meaning unknown.
*   *Caygua*—Spanish form, from their proper name, *Kaijwu*.
*   *Gahe'wa*—Wichita and Kichai name; another form of Kiowa.
*   *Kâ'igwŭ*—"real or principal people," the proper tribal name.
*   *Kai-wă*—Comanche and Caddo name; from their proper name, *Kaigwu*.
*   *Kiowa*—popular name, a corruption of the name used by themselves.
*   *Kwŭ'da*—"going out"; an old name formerly used by the Kiowa for themselves.
*   *Nǐ'chihině'na*—"river men," the Arapaho name; so called because they formerly lived on the upper Arkansas River, from which the Arapaho claim to have driven them.
*   *Tepda*—"coming out," "issuing"; another old name formerly used by the Kiowa for themselves.
*   *Witapäh'at* or *Witapäh'tu*—Cheyenne name, from their Sioux name, *Witapähä'tu*.
*   *Wi'tapähä'tu*—"island butte people" (?), the Sioux name.

## KIOWA TRIBAL SIGN

The Kiowa tribal sign indicates "hair cut off at the right ear," referring to a former custom of the warriors. From a careless habit in making this sign, it has sometimes been wrongly interpreted to mean "foolish" or "rattle-brained."

## SKETCH OF THE KIOWA

As far as current knowledge goes, the Kiowa constitute a distinct linguistic stock; however, it is likely that more material will allow us to prove their connection with some tribes farther north, from which direction they came. They are mentioned in Spanish records at least as early as 1732. Their oldest tradition, which agrees with the combined testimony of the Shoshoni and Arapaho, places them near the junction of the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin forks, at the extreme head of the Missouri River, in the neighborhood of the present Virginia

<summary>This page concludes the Sioux glossary and provides a synonymy of names for the Kiowa tribe. It also describes the Kiowa tribal sign and begins a historical sketch of the tribe's origins at the headwaters of the Missouri River.</summary>
<keywords>Sioux glossary, Kiowa, Kiowa Apache, tribal synonymy, sign language, tribal history, Missouri River, Arapaho, Shoshoni</keywords>

--- Page 529 ---
<meta>This page continues the historical sketch of the Kiowa tribe, detailing their migrations, alliances with the Crow and Comanche, and their eventual settlement on a reservation in Oklahoma.</meta>

City, Montana. They afterward moved down from the mountains and formed an alliance with the Crow, with whom they have since remained on friendly terms. From there, they drifted southward along the base of the mountains, driven by the Cheyenne and Arapaho. Around 1840, they made peace with these latter tribes, with whom they have since commonly acted in coordination. The Sioux claim to have driven them out of the Black Hills, and in 1805, they were reported to be living on the North Platte. According to the Kiowa account, when they first reached the Arkansas River, they found their passage opposed by the Comanche, who claimed all the territory to the south. A war followed, but peace was finally established; at that time, the Kiowa crossed to the south side of the Arkansas and formed a confederation with the Comanche that continues to this day. In league with the Comanche, they carried on a constant war against the frontier settlements of Mexico and Texas, extending their raids at least as far south as Durango. Among all the prairie tribes, they were noted as the most predatory and bloodthirsty, and they have likely killed more white men in proportion to their population than any of the others. They made their first treaty with the government in 1837 and were placed on their current reservation jointly with the Comanche and Apache in 1868. Their last outbreak was in 1874–75, in conjunction with the Comanche, Apache, and Cheyenne. While they were probably never very numerous, they have been greatly reduced by war and disease. Their most recent terrible blow came in the spring of 1892, when measles killed over 300 members of the three confederated tribes. Their current chief is *Gu'i-pä'go*, or Lone Wolf. They occupy the same reservation as the Comanche and Apache, between the Washita and Red rivers in southwestern Oklahoma, and numbered 1,017 in 1893.

The Kiowa do not have a clan system, and there are no restrictions regarding intermarriage between the divisions. They have six tribal divisions, including the associated Apache, who form an integral part of the Kiowa camping circle. A seventh division, the *K uăto*, is now extinct. The tribal divisions in the order of the camping circle are:

1. *K'a't'a* — "biters," i.e., Arikara or Ree; so called, not because of Arikara origin, but because they were more closely associated with that tribe in trade and other matters when the Kiowa lived in the north.
2. *Ko'gu'i* — "elks."
3. *Kâ'igwŭ* — "Kiowa proper." This is the oldest division, which holds the responsibility of keeping the medicine tipi, where the grand medicine of the tribe is kept.
4. *Kĭñep* — "big shields." This is the largest division in the tribe and is of corresponding importance.
5. *Semät* — "thieves," the Apache.
6. *Koñtä'lyui* — "black boys." Sometimes also called *Si'ndiyu'i*, "Sindi's children." They are said to be of a darker color than the rest of the

# THE KIOWA APACHE

A small tribe of Athapascan origin, who call themselves *Na'-isha* or *Na-di'isha-de'na* and are popularly known as the Apache or Kiowa Apache, has been associated with the Kiowa for as long as the traditions of either tribe record. While they retain their own distinct language, nearly all of them speak and understand Kiowa, and they form an essential part of the Kiowa camping circle. They are indistinguishable in their dress and general way of life. They came from the north with the Kiowa and were mentioned under the name Cataka as living in the Black Hills region in 1805. La Salle spoke of them as the Gattacka as early as 1681. There is no reason to believe that they were ever part of the Apache people of Arizona and New Mexico; instead, like the Sarsi, they are probably a distinct Athapascan group that has always lived east of the mountains. Having been forced by their small numbers to unite with a stronger tribe, they have since shared the Kiowa's migrations southward along the plains. The *Na-isha* are called *Ga'taqka* by the Pawnee and sometimes by the Wichita; *Cataka* by Lewis and Clark in 1805; and *Kataka* in their first treaty with the government, made alongside the Kiowa in 1837. They are known as *Ta'shiñ* by the Comanche; *Gïnä's* by the Wichita; *Ka'ntsi* ("deceivers") by the Caddo; *Kiri'nähïs* by the Kichais; *Tha'kahinë'na* ("knife-whetting men"?) by the Arapaho; and *Mûtsiănätä'niuw'* ("whetstone people") by the Cheyenne. They have several names among the Kiowa but are commonly called *Semät*, meaning "thieves." Other Kiowa names for them include *Tagu'i* (of unknown meaning) and *Sa'dălso'mte-k'iñ-ago* ("weasel people"). The tribal sign for them—as for the Apache, Lipan, and Navajo—conveys the idea of "knife whetters." In 1891, they numbered 325 people. By 1893, they had been reduced to 224, primarily due to a measles epidemic.

More extensive information regarding the Kiowa and Kiowa Apache will be provided in the author's memoir, *Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians*, which is currently being prepared for the Bureau of Ethnology.

->I scream because I am a bird,<-
->I scream because I am a bird,<-
->I bellow like a buffalo,<-
->I bellow like a buffalo.<-
->The boy will rise up,<-
->The boy will rise up.<-

This song was composed by Pa-guadal, or "Red Buffalo," at a Ghost Dance held on Walnut Creek in the summer of 1893, under the direction of the prophet Pa-iñgya (see page 907), for the purpose of resurrecting Red Buffalo's son, who had recently died. Pa-iñgya assured the people that if they held the dance as he directed, the dead boy would rise up alive from the ground before their eyes. During the dance, Red Buffalo became "crazy" <note>The term "crazy" here refers to the state of entering a trance or spiritual ecstasy.</note> and composed this song. In his trance, he evidently imagined himself to be a bird. His father was one of the "buffalo doctors," or surgeons of the tribe, who are under the special protection of the buffalo and whose war cry is an imitation of the bellowing of a buffalo bull. Red Buffalo claims to have inherited his father's knowledge; hence his assertion that he bellows like a bull. However, the boy was not resurrected.

<header>MOONEY] SONGS OF THE KIOWA</header>
<sig>14 ETH—PT 2——29</sig>

->*Translation*<-

->I am mashing the berries,<-
->I am mashing the berries.<-
->They say travelers are coming on the march,<-
->They say travelers are coming on the march.<-
->I stir (the berries) around, I stir them around;<-
->I take them up with a spoon of buffalo horn,<-
->I take them up with a spoon of buffalo horn,<-
->And I carry them, I carry them (to the strangers),<-
->And I carry them, I carry them (to the strangers).<-

This song provides a vivid picture of traditional Indian home life and hospitality. In her dream, the woman who composed it imagines herself preparing fruit when news arrives that travelers are approaching; the verb implies that they are on the move with their children, dogs, and household property. She stirs the berries around a few more times, lifts them out with a spoon of buffalo horn, and goes to offer them to the strangers. The translation is an exact paraphrase of the rhythmic repetition of the original. The berry called <term>ehyuñ'i</term>, <gloss>"principal or best fruit,"</gloss> is not found in the current territory of the Kiowa, but is remembered as one of the pleasant things of their old home in the north. It is described as a species of cherry.

->That wind, that wind<-
->Shakes my tipi, shakes my tipi,<-
->And sings a song for me,<-
->And sings a song for me.<-

To those familiar with it, this short song evokes pleasant memories of the prairie camp when the wind is whistling through the tipi poles and blowing the flaps about, while inside the fire burns bright and the songs and games continue.

*Äguănpo'nbä*—I went to see dancing; *ägu'anponbä'ta*, I am going to see a dance; *guan*, a dance.
*Ähäyä'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
*Ä'hiñ-aih*—in the tops of the cottonwoods; from *ä'hiñ*, cottonwood, and *aih*, in or on the tree tops.
*Aho'ähe'dal*—they are approaching, it is said (such as a family on the move, or an army on the march, with household goods, etc.); the suffix *hedal* implies a report or rumor. *Äho'ä*, I am coming on, with my family and possessions. Compare *Imzä'nteähe'dal*.
*Aho'ho'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
*Ähyä'to*—the Kiowa name for the Arapaho, meaning unknown. The Kiowa call the wild plum by the same name.
*Äka'na*—for *Äka'on*, <note>see that entry</note>.
*Äka'on*—I am poor. The words for "rich" and "poor" refer to reputation and mental and moral qualities rather than to material possessions. A man may own many horses, but if he has no war record, he is considered poor.
*Änimhä'go*—he gets up again, he rises again. *Dehä'go*, I rise; *behä'*, get up; *ïmhä'go*, he will get up.
*Ankañ'yona*—he pities us much; *gyäkañ'ti*, it is a pity. Compare *Iñkañ'tähe'dal*.
*Anso*—feet; *anso'i*, foot.
*Ä'nyägälo'nte*—I bellow like a buffalo (habitually); *nyäo'nto*, I am bellowing like a buffalo.
*Äomhe'dal*—he was made so; *äo'mdatso'-ha*, I am made so, I am rendered thus.
*Ä'piatañ*—"wooden stabber, or lance"; the name of a Kiowa sent by his tribe as a delegate to the messiah in 1890.
*Asa'tito'la*—"he whom we send to work," that is, "the messenger"; the name by which the Kiowa prophet, *Bi'änk'i*, is now known.
*Äto'tl-e'dal*—he was sent; *gyätö'*, I send him.
*Ätso'dalsä'dal*—I have wings (attached); from *tsodal*, wing.
*Bä'atcñ'yi*—we cry and hold fast to him; *gyäten'ta*, I cry and hold fast to him.
*Bate'yä*—he is approaching; *äba'teyä*, I am approaching. Compare *Imzä'nteähe'dal*.
*Be'a'mâ'nhäyi*—stretch out your (plural) hands in entreaty. *Dea'mânhä'go*, I

<column-break/>

stretch out, etc.; *bea'mânhä*, stretch out your (singular <note>direct address</note>), etc.
*Be'dälgu'at*—another Kiowa name for the Wichita; meaning "painted or tattooed lips"; from *bedal*, lips or mouth, and *guat*, painted, tattooed, or written. See *Do'gu'at*.
*Be'dälpago*—"hairy mouths"; one of the Kiowa names for the white people; from *bedal*, lips or mouth, *pa*, downy hair or fuzz, and *go* or *gua*, the tribal suffix. Compare *Ta'ka'-i*.
*Beta'!*—an exclamation roughly equivalent to "I see" or "I understand."
*Bi'änk'i*—"eating man," "eater," a Kiowa prophet and medicine-man; also known as *Asa'tito'la*, "the messenger."
*Botk'iñ'ago*—the Kiowa name for the *Aä'nině'na* or Arapaho Gros Ventres. The name means "belly people"; from *bot*, belly or stomach, and *k'iñago*, people, from *k'iñahi*, "man."
*Dä-e'dal*—"great star"; from *dä*, star, and *e'dal*, great; one of the Kiowa names for the morning star. It is more commonly called *T'aiñso*, "the cross." (See Arapaho song 72.)
*Da'gya*—a song.
*Dakañ'äthe'dal*—another form of *Iñkañ'tähe'dal*, <note>see that entry</note>.
*Dak'iñ'a*—spirit, God; plural *dak'iñ'ago*; from *da-i*, medicine or mystery, and *k'iña* or *k'iñahi*, man.
*Dak'iñ'ago*—spirits, the spirits; spirit, God, *dak'iñ'a*.
*Da'mânhägo*—for *Dea'mânhä'go*.
*Däsa*—I have eyes; *dä*, *t'ä*, eye.
*Da'ta-i*—father.
*Da'te*—a long time.
*Da'tekañ*—"keeps his name always," a Kiowa prophet about 1881, who undertook to bring back the buffalo.
*Datsä'to*—I pray for them; *ni'ndatsä'to*, I pray for him.
*Dea'mânhä'go*—I hold out my hands toward him in entreaty. Compare *Be'a'mâ'nhäyi*.
*De'beko'datsä*—let us all pray or worship, we must all pray or worship; *deda'tsäto*, I pray.
*De'dom*—all the world; from *dom*, the earth, and *de*, all or complete.
*Degi'äta*—I am mashing or pounding it.
*De'gu'änta*—I stir it around.

*De'gyägo'mga*—every living creature; the prefix *de* conveys the idea of "every" or "all."
*Dehi'äta*—I take it.
*De'ïmgo*—look, everybody! See, everybody around! The prefix *de* gives the idea of "everybody" or "all."
*De'ïmhä'date*—everybody will arise; from *dehä*, "I rose up from a reclining position." The prefix *de* gives the idea of "everybody," "all," or "completeness," depending on the context.
*Deo'ta*—I lift it up, I raise it.
*Do'*—tipi.
*Do'gu'at*—the Kiowa name for the Wichita, meaning "painted or tattooed faces," from *dobä*, "face," and *gu'at*, "painted," "engraved," or "written."
*Dom*—the earth.
*Dom-gäga*—with the earth; *gäga*, "with," in composition.
*Ehä'eho'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
*E'häyä!*—same as above.
*E'hyuñi*—"principal, real, or best fruit;" a berry, probably a dwarf cherry, described as a black grape-like fruit growing in clusters on bushes from 4 to 6 feet high, in the Sioux country. It was eaten raw or mixed with pemmican.
*E'manki'na*—"can't hold it," a Kiowa policeman, now dead, seen by Asatitola in a vision.
*E'peya*—"afraid of him," a Kiowa warrior who died while a prisoner at Fort Marion, Florida, about 1875.
*Ezä'nteähe'dal*—it is approaching, they say. Compare *Imzä'nteähe'dal*.
*Ezä'nteda'te*—it will shake, or tremble (impersonal).
*Gâ'dal-gâ'ga*—with the buffalo; *gäga*, "with," in composition; *gâdal*, buffalo, generic; *pa*, a buffalo bull.
*Gâ'dal-guñ*—a buffalo horn; from *gâdal*, "buffalo," and *gu'ñti*, "horn."
*Gatä'dalto*—I shall cut it off, or I am cutting it off (the present and future are the same).
*Go*—and.
*Go'mgyä-da'ga*—that wind; from *gomgyä*, "wind," and *daga*, "that" or "the," in composition.
*Go'mtäyä*—on (my) back; from *gomtä* or *gombă*, "back."
*Guadal*—red.

<column-break/>

*Guăñ*—a dance.
*Guan-â'dalka-i*—"dance frenzy;" from *guan*, "a dance," and *â'daika-i*, "crazy" or "foolish"; the Kiowa name for the Ghost-dance ecstasy.
*Gu'ato*—bird.
*Gyäko'm*—life, living; *hita' ägyä' komta'yä*, I am alive.
*Gyätä'to*—I shall cut them off; *gatä'dalto*, I cut it off.
*Häoñ'yo*, or *Äoñ'yo*—a cry of grief, especially at funerals.
*Heye'heye'heye'heye'!*—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
*Imhä'go*—he would get up, he would arise. Compare *Äñïmhä'go*.
*Imzä'nteähe'dal*—they are approaching, it is said; from *dezä'nteä*, "I move about"; the ending *hedal* makes it a matter of report or common belief, equivalent to "they say." Compare *Ezä'nteähe'dal*. The verb implies coming on like a herd, a company, or like people on a march. The simple verb for approaching is *äba'teä*. Compare *Bate'yä* and *Äho'ähe'dal*.
*Iñatä'gyi*—it is a good one; from *tägya* or *gyätä'gya*, "good."
*Iñhä'po* or *Iñhäpa'de*—he sings for me (as if to teach me); *dagya gehäpo*, I sing a song for him.
*Iñkañ'tähe'dal*—he has had pity on me; from *gyäkañ'ti*, "(it is a) pity." Compare *Ankañ'gona*.
*Ka'ante*—another form of *Ka'on*, "poor." Compare *Äka'on*.
*Kâitseñ'ko*—"principal, or real dogs;" the highest degree of the Kiowa military organization. (See Arapaho song 43.)
*Komse'ka-k'iñ'ahyup*—the former Kiowa name for the Arapaho. It means "men of the worn-out leggings;" from *komse*, "smoky, soiled, or worn-out," *kati*, "leggings," and *k'iñ'ahyup*, "men."
*Mânsâ'dal*—I have hands or arms; *mânto*, "hand" or "arm."
*Ma'sep*—the Kiowa name for the Caddo, meaning "pierced noses;" from *mak'on*, "nose," and *sep*, the root of a verb meaning to pierce or sew with an awl.
*Na*—I, my; sometimes placed before the verb to make it emphatic.
*Na ädâ'ga*—because I am (emphatic); from *na*, "I," "my," and *ädâ'ga* <note>see entry on page 1089</note>, "because I am."

*Nada'g* — for *Na ädă'ga*, which see.
*Nyää'mo* — he will give it to me; *nyänä'mo*, I will give it to him. There are several verbs for *give*, depending on the nature of the object being given.
*Nyä'hoänga'mo* — he shows or tells me the way; *nyän'hoänga'mo*, I show him the way; *hoăn*, road or way.
*Nyäo'ngum* — I scream; from *äno'nde*, it screams, or makes a sound with the mouth.

*Nyäzä'ngo* — it shakes mine; *änzä'ngo*, it shakes his.
*O'mda* — I have a shape or form (implying a likeness, such as *ädăta'-i o'mda*, I have a form like my father's).
*Pa-gu'adal* — "red buffalo"; from *pa*, a buffalo bull, and *gu'adal*, red. A Kiowa man who composed one of the Ghost Dance songs.
*Pa'-iñgyä* — "standing in the middle"; a Kiowa prophet who, in 1887, preached the rapid destruction of the white people and the return of the buffalo.
*Poläñ'yup* — "rabbits"; the lowest rank of the Kiowa military organization. (See Arapaho song 43.)
*Sa'he* — green. (See Arapaho song 64.)
*Säk'o'ta* — the Kiowa name for the Cheyenne; the word seems to refer to "biting."
*Set-t'ain'ti* — "white bear," a famous Kiowa chief, active around 1865–1875. The name comes from *set*, bear, *t'aiñ*, white, and *ti*, the personal suffix.
*Soda'te* — he will descend; *äso'ta*, I descend.
*Tägyä'ko* — the Kiowa name for the Na'-kasinĕ'na or northern Arapaho. The word has the same meaning, "sagebrush people," from *tägyi*, "sagebrush," and *ko*, the tribal suffix.
*T'aiñ'so* — the morning star; literally "the cross"; it is sometimes also called *Dä-e'dal*, the "great star." (See Arapaho song 43.)

<column-break/>

*Ta'ka'-i* — one of the Kiowa names for white people; the word literally means "prominent ears" or "ears sticking out," as compared with the ears of Indians, which are partly hidden by their long hair. The same name is also applied to a mule or donkey. Compare *Be'dalpa'go*.
*Tälyi* — a boy.
*T'añgya* — a spoon; in certain circumstances the suffix *gyä* is dropped and the word becomes *t'a*.
*T'añ'peko* — skunkberry (?) people; one of the ranks of the Kiowa military organization. (See Arapaho song 43.)
*Teñ'beyui* — "young mountain sheep," another name for the *Ädalto'yui*, which see.
*Ton* — tail; *gu'ato-ton*, bird tail; frequently used to denote a fan or headdress made from the tail feathers of an eagle, hawk, or other bird.
*Tongyä-gu'adal* — "red tail"; the name of a Kiowa man; from *ton* or *tongyä*, tail, and *gu'adal*, red.
*Toñkoñ'go* — "black legs," one of the ranks of the Kiowa military organization. (See Arapaho song 43.)
*To'ñsâdal* — I have legs; from *toñti*, leg.
*Tsä'hop* — movers, emigrants (those moving with household goods, etc.). The word has no singular form.
*Tsäñ'yui* — "rabbits"; another name for the *Poläñ'yup* rank of the Kiowa military organization. (See Arapaho song 43.)
*Tseñtän'mo* — horse headdress people (?), one of the ranks of the Kiowa military organization. (See Arapaho song 43.)
*Tsi'sûs* (*Tsi'sûs-ä*) — Jesus.
*Tsoñ* — an awl.
*Tsoñ'-ä* — the awl game. (See Arapaho song 64.)
*Yä''pähe* — soldiers; the military organization of the Kiowa. (See Arapaho song 43.)

# THE CADDO AND ASSOCIATED TRIBES

## CADDO TRIBAL SYNONYMY

*Asinais*—an old French name, derived from *Hasinai*.
*Caddo*—the popular name, from *Kä'dohadä'cho*.
*Caddodaquio*—Joutel (1687), another form of *Kä'dohadä'cho*.
*Cenis*—an old French name used by Joutel in 1687; from *Hasinai*.
*Dä'sha-i*—Wichita name.
*Dĕ'sa*—another form of *Dä'sha-i*.
*Hasi'nai* or *Hasi'ni*—the correct generic term for at least the main Caddo divisions, and perhaps for all of them. They also use it as a synonym for “Indians.”
*Kä'dohadä'cho*—the name of the Caddo proper, as they use it themselves.
*Ma'se'p*—Kiowa name; “pierced nose,” from *mak'on*, nose, and *sep*, the root of a verb meaning to pierce or sew with an awl.
*Na'shonït* or *Na'shoni*—Comanche name, frequently used also by neighboring tribes to designate the Caddo; the Nassonite mentioned by early French writers on Texas.
*Nez Percé*—French traders’ name; “pierced nose.”
*Ni'rïs-hä'ri's-ki'riki*—another Wichita name.
*Otä's-itä'niuw'*—Cheyenne name; “pierced nose people.”
*Tani'bänĕn, Tani'bänĕnina, Tani'bätha*—Arapaho name; “pierced nose people,” from <term>tani</term>, nose.

## CADDO TRIBAL SIGN

->“Pierced nose,” referring to their former custom of piercing the nose to insert a ring.<-

## SKETCH OF THE CADDO

The Caddo are the primary southern representatives of the Caddoan stock, which also includes the Wichita, Kichai, Pawnee, and Arikara. Their confederacy consisted of about a dozen tribes or divisions, who claimed the entire lower Red River and the surrounding territory in Louisiana, eastern Texas, and southern Arkansas as their original lands. The names of these twelve divisions, including two of foreign origin, have been preserved as follows:
*Kä'dohadä'cho* (Caddo proper).
*Nädä'ko* (Anadarko).
*Hai'-nai* (Ioni).
*Nä'bai-dä'cho* (Nabedache).
*Nä'kohodo'tsi* (Nacogdoches).
*Näshi'tosh* (Natchitoches).
*Nä'ka'na'wan*.
*Hädai'-i* (Adai, Adaize).
*Hai'-ĭsh* (Eyeish, Aliche, Aes).
*Yä'tăsi*.
*I'măha*—a band of Omaha, or perhaps more likely Kwâpâ <note>Quapaw</note>, who lived with the *Kä'dohadä'cho* but kept their own distinct language.

It also provides a historical overview of the Caddoan confederacy, listing its eleven surviving tribal divisions along the Red River.</summary>

<header>MOONEY] SKETCH OF THE CADDO</header>

A few members of the *Imaha'may* still live among the Caddo, though they retain only the name. It will be remembered that when the Caddo lived in eastern Louisiana, the Arkansas or *Kwâpâ* were their closest neighbors to the north; these *Imaha'may* may have been a part of the *Kwâpâ* who lived "upstream" (*U'mañhañ*) on the Arkansas River. The Caddo call the Omaha tribe by this same name.

*Yowa'ni*—This group was originally a band of the Heyowani division of the Choctaw. They joined the Caddo a long time ago, likely around the time the Choctaw began to retreat across the Mississippi River to escape the whites. A few are still living with the Caddo and retain their distinct language. Evidence suggests that some *Koasati* (*Cooshatties*) were mixed with them.

The Kä'dohadä'cho seem to be recognized as the principal Caddo division. The general term *Hasi'nai*, by which the confederates designate themselves, is sometimes regarded as belonging more properly to the three divisions named first. According to their own statements, some of the dialects spoken by the various divisions were mutually unintelligible. Currently, the Kä'dohadä'cho and Näda'ko are the dominant dialects, while *Näbaidächo*, *Näkohodotsi*, *Hădai'-i*, and *Hai'-ish* are practically extinct. The *Kichai*, *Bidai*, and *Akokisa*, who formerly lived near the Caddo on the eastern border of Texas, did not belong to the confederacy, although at least one of these tribes, the *Kichai*, is of the same linguistic stock and is now on the same reservation.

The Caddo have ten gentes <note>clans</note>: *Na'wotsi* (Bear); *Tasha* (Wolf); *Ta'năhă* (Buffalo); *Ta'o* (Beaver); *Iwi* (Eagle); *Oăt* (Raccoon); *Ka'g'aih* (Crow); *Ka'gă-hănĭn* (Thunder); *Kǐshi* (Panther); and *Sûko* (Sun). The Bear clan is the most numerous. The Buffalo clan is also sometimes called *Koho'* or Alligator, because both animals bellow in the same way. Members of a particular clan will not kill the animal from which the clan takes its name. In the old times, no Caddo would kill either an eagle or a panther, although they were not afraid to kill bears, unlike many of the western tribes. However, an eagle might be killed for its feathers by a hunter who was regularly initiated and consecrated for that purpose.

The original home of the Caddo was on the lower Red River in Louisiana. According to their own tradition, which has parallels among several other tribes, they emerged from underground through the mouth of a cave in a hill they call *Cha'kanĭ'nă*, "The place of crying." This hill is on a lake close to the south bank of the Red River, exactly at its junction with the Mississippi. In those days, humans and animals were all brothers and lived together under the ground. But at last, they discovered the entrance to the cave leading up to the surface of the earth, and so they decided to ascend and come out. First, an old man climbed up, carrying fire and a pipe in one hand and a drum in the other. After him came his wife, with corn and pumpkin seeds. Then followed the rest of the people and the animals. All intended to come out, but as soon as the wolf had climbed up, he closed the hole and shut up the

...rest of the people and animals under the ground, where they still remain. Those who had come out sat down and cried a long time for their friends below; this is the reason for the name of that place. Because the Caddo came out of the ground, they call it *ină'*, "mother," and they return to it when they die. Because they have possessed the pipe, the drum, the corn, and pumpkins since they became a people, they hold fast to these things and have never thrown them away.

From this place they spread out toward the west, following the course of the Red River, along which they established their primary settlements. For a long time they lived on Caddo Lake, on the boundary between Louisiana and Texas; their main village on the lake was called *Sha'chidǐ'ni*, or "Timber Hill." Their acquaintance with white people began at a very early period. One of their tribes, the *Näďäko*, is mentioned under the name *Nandacao* in the narrative of De Soto's expedition as early as 1540. The *Kädohadächo* were known to the French as early as 1687. The relations of the Caddo with the French and Spaniards were intimate and friendly. Catholic missions were established among them around the year 1700 and continued to exist until 1812, when the missions were suppressed by the Spanish government and the Indians were scattered. In the meantime, Louisiana had been purchased by the United States, and the Caddo soon began to be pushed away from their ancient villages into the western territory, where they were exposed to constant raids by the prairie tribes. From this time their decline was rapid, and the events of the Texan and Mexican wars aided still further in their social breakdown. They made their first treaty with the United States in 1835, at which time they were located chiefly in Louisiana, southwest of the Red River and adjoining Texas. They afterward moved to the Brazos River in Texas, and then to the Washita River in Indian Territory in 1859. When the American Civil War broke out, the Caddo, not wishing to take up arms against the government, fled north into Kansas and remained there until the close of the war, when they returned to the Washita. Their present reservation, which they hold only by executive order and jointly with the Wichita, lies between the Washita and Canadian rivers in western Oklahoma, with the Cheyenne and Arapaho to the north and west and the Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache to the south. In 1893, they numbered 507 people.

In person, the Caddo are rather smaller and darker than the neighboring prairie tribes, and from their long residence in Louisiana, they have a considerable amount of French ancestry. They are an agricultural tribe, raising large crops of corn, pumpkins, and melons, and they still maintain industrious habits despite their many changes of fortune. They were never buffalo hunters until they moved out onto the plains. They formerly lived in conical grass houses like the Wichita, but now they live in log houses and generally wear <term>citizen's dress</term> <note>Western-style clothing as opposed to traditional tribal attire</note> except during dances. The old custom which gave rise to the name and tribal sign of "Pierced Nose" is now obsolete. In 1806, Sibley said of them, "They are brave, despise danger or death, and boast that they have..."

never shed white man's blood." Their former enemies, the prairie tribes, bear witness to their bravery, and their friendship toward the whites is a part of their history, but it has resulted in no great advantage to themselves, as they have been dispossessed from their own country and are recognized only as tenants at will in their present location.
   They and the Wichita received the new doctrine from the Arapaho, and were soon among its most earnest adherents, notwithstanding the fact that they were regarded as the most advanced of all the tribes in that part of the country. It may be that their history had led them to feel a special need of a messiah. They have been hard and constant dancers, at one time even dancing in winter when there was nearly a foot of snow upon the ground. Their first songs were those which they had heard from the Arapaho and sang in a corrupted form, with only a general idea of their meaning, but they now have a number of songs in their own language, some of which are singularly pleasing in melody and sentiment.

### THE WICHITA, KICHAI, AND DELAWARE

   Closely associated with the Caddo on the same reservation are the Wichita, with their subtribes, the Tawakoni and Waco, numbering together 316 in 1893; the Delaware, numbering 94, and the Kichai (Keechies), numbering only 52. Of these, all but the Delaware, who are <term>Algonquian</term>, belong to the <term>Caddoan</term> stock. The Wichita and their subtribes, although retaining in indistinct form the common Caddoan tradition, claim as their proper home the Wichita mountains, near which they still remain. Sixty years ago their principal village was on the north side of the north fork of Red river, a short distance below the mouth of Elm creek, in Oklahoma. They live in conical grass houses and, like the other tribes of the stock, are agricultural. They call themselves *Ki'tikiti'sh*—they are called *Tawe'hash* by the Caddo and Kichai—and are known to most of their other neighbors and in the sign language as the "Tattooed People" (*Do'kănă*, Comanche; *Do'gu'at*, Kiowa), from an old custom now nearly obsolete. For the same reason and from their resemblance to the Pawnee, with whose language their own has a close connection, the French called them *Pani Piqué's*.
   The Kichai or Keechie, or *Ki'tsäsh*, as they call themselves, are a small tribe of the same stock, and claim to have moved up Red river in company with the Caddo. Their language is different from that of any of their neighbors, but approaches the Pawnee.
   The Delaware are a small band of the celebrated tribe of that name. They removed from the east and settled with the main body in Kansas, but drifted south into Texas while it was still Spanish territory. After a long series of conflicts with the American settlers of Texas, before and after the Mexican war, they were finally taken under the protection of the United States government and assigned to their present reservation along with other emigrant tribes from that state.

These tribes, sharing a reservation, have distinct linguistic roots and histories of migration through Oklahoma and Texas.</summary>

This is another song composed by Nyu'taa, who explained it herself. While singing this song, Nyu'taa was sitting near me when she suddenly cried out and went into a spasm of trembling and crying that lasted for several minutes, lifting her right hand toward the west at the same time. Such attacks were so common among the women at song rehearsals that they frequently interfered with the work, although the bystanders regarded them as a matter of course and took only passing notice of these incidents.

### 12. NA' IWI' O'WI'TA'

<image-desc>Musical notation for the song "Na' iwi' o'wi'ta'". It consists of two lines of staff with a G-clef, a key signature of F# (G major/E minor), and changing time signatures: 5/4, 3/4, 7/4, 5/4. Phonetic lyrics are printed beneath the notes.</image-desc>

->Na' i - wi' o' - wi' - ta', na' i - wi' - o' - wi' - ta'; do'-hya di'-wa - bo'n na' na' i - wi' o' - wi' - ta',<-
->do'-hya di'-wa - bo'n na' na' i - wi' o' - wi' - ta'; na'-ha' na'-da-ka-'a', na'-ha' na'-da-ka-'a'.<-

->Na' iwi' o'wi'ta',<-
->Na' iwi' o'wi'ta';<-
->Do'hya di'wabo'n na' na' iwi' o'wi'ta',<-
->Do'hya di'wabo'n na' na' iwi' o'wi'ta';<-
->Na'ha' na'daka'a', Na'ha' na'daka'a'.<-

->*Translation*<-

->See! the eagle comes,<-
->See! the eagle comes;<-
->Now at last we see him—look! look! the eagle comes,<-
->Now at last we see him—look! look! the eagle comes;<-
->Now we see him with the people,<-
->Now we see him with the people.<-

This refers to what the Caddo call the "return of the eagle feathers" in the Ghost Dance. Among the Caddo, as with other tribes, the eagle is a sacred bird, and in the old days only the few medicine men who knew the sacred formula dared to kill one for its feathers. If anyone else should kill an eagle, his family would die or some other great misfortune would come upon him. The formula consisted of certain secret prayers and ritual performances. Among the Cherokee, the eagle killer's prayer was a petition to the eagle not to seek revenge upon the tribe, because it was not an Indian, but a Spaniard, who had killed him—an indication of the vivid memory of the cruelty of the early Spaniards held among the southern tribes. To further guard against the anger of the eagles, the Cherokee eagle killer, upon his return to the village, announced that he had killed, not an eagle, but a snowbird, the latter being too small and insignificant to be feared. The eagle-killing ceremony among the northern prairie tribes has already been described under Arapaho song 47. The Caddo eagle killer always took with him a robe or some other valuable offering; after shooting the eagle, saying the prayer, and pulling out the tail and wing feathers, he covered the body with the robe and left it there as a peace offering to the spirit of the eagle. The dead eagle was never brought home, as was the custom among the Cherokee. The last Caddo man who knew the eagle-killing ritual died some years ago, and since then they have had to go without eagle feathers or buy them from the Kiowa and other tribes. Since Sitting Bull came down and "gave the feather"

This song also refers to the use of eagle feathers in the dance.

#### Translation

->E'yehe'! Nä'nisa'na,<-
->E'yehe'! Nä'nisa'na.<-
->Come on, Caddo, we are all going up,<-
->Come on, Caddo, we are all going up<-
->To the great village — He'e'ye'!<-
->To the great village — He'e'ye'!<-
->With our father above,<-
->With our father above where he dwells on high — He'e'ye'!<-
->Where our mother dwells — He'e'ye'!<-
->Where our mother dwells — He'e'ye'!<-

The sentiment and swinging tune of this spirited song make it one of the favorites. It encourages the dancers with the hope of a speedy reunion of the entire Caddo nation, both living and dead, in the "great village" of their father above, and requires no further explanation.

### CADDO GLOSSARY

Ăă—Father.
Ăă Kakĭ'mbawiŭt—"the prayer of all to the Father"; from *aa*, the Father (i.e., God), and *tsĭmba'dikû*, I pray; the Ghost Dance, also called *Nä'nisa'na Gao'shăn*, or the Nä'nisa'na dance.
A'nana—for Nänä.
A'nanasa'na—for Nana'sana.
Ba'hakosĭn—"striped arrows," from *bah*, arrow; the Caddo name for the Cheyenne. They sometimes call them *Siä'-näbo*, from their Comanche name.
Cha'kani'na—"the place of crying"; the traditional first settlement of the Caddo tribes, where they emerged from the

<column-break/>

ground, at the mouth of the Red River, on the south bank in Louisiana.
Detse-ka'yăă—"dog eaters"; the Caddo name for the Arapaho.
Di'wabon—we see him; *tsibo'nä*, I see him.
Di'wĭti'ă—we are all going up, we shall all ascend; *tsidiû'*, I ascend.
Do'hya—now, at once.
E'yahe'ya!—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
E'yehe'!—*ibid.*
Ganio'sĭt—he (or she) is painted; *atsĭno'sĭt*, I paint myself.
Gao'shăn—a dance; *ga'tsioshăn*, I dance.

<page-num>1103</page-num>
<header>MOONEY] CADDO GLOSSARY</header>

<image-desc>Circular purple ink stamp at the top center of the page reads "UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA".</image-desc>

**Gû'kwûts**—my (plural); **gûkwû'nda**, my (singular); **ha'nĭn gû'kwûts**, my children.
**Hǎ'-iă**—he (she) dwells there below. Compare *Ko'iă*.
**Ha'-imi**—large.
**Ha'-nai**—a tribe of the Caddo confederacy.
**Hǎ'naǎ** or **Hǎ'nǎ**—there he is! that is he!
**Ha'nani'to**—this feather, the feather; *ni'toh*, feather; *ha'taha*, feather (generic).
**Ha'natobi'na**—a feather headdress; feathers prepared to wear on the head.
**Ha'nĭn**—children.
**Ha'nitu**—for *Ni'toh*.
**Hasi'ni** or **Hasi'nai**—the Caddo; the generic name used by themselves.
**Ha'taha**—feather (generic); *nitoh*, feather (specific).
**Ha'wano**—paint.
**Ha'yano**—people.
**Ha'yo**—above, on high. Compare *Naha'yo*.
**He'eye'!**—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
**He'yahe'eye'!**—the same.
**He'yawe'ya!**—the same.
**He'yoi'ya!**—the same.
**Hi'na**—eagle feathers.
**Ika**—grandmother; a term sometimes applied to the thunder or storm spirit.
**Inǎ'**—mother; *na inǎ'*, mother above.
**I'tsiya**—I have come; *hatsi'ûs*, I come.
**I'wi**—eagle; also the name of a Caddo clan.
**Ka'gǎhǎnĭn**—thunder; a Caddo clan.
**Ka'g'aih**—crow; a Caddo clan.
**Kaka'na**—they cried; *ha'tsikaka's*, I cry.
**Ka'ntsi**—"cheats;" the Caddo name for the Kiowa Apache, Lipan, and Mescalero.
**Kǐ'shi**—panther; a Caddo clan.
**Kiwa't**—village, town, settlement.
**Koho'**—alligator; another name for the **Ta'nǎhǎ** or Buffalo clan of the Caddo.
**Ko'iă**—where he dwells above; *tǎ'-iă*, he dwells above; *datsii'ǎ*, I dwell above.
**Na**—see! look! now!—also coming down from above, as *iwi-na*, the eagle coming down from above.
**Nǎǎ'**—father above, that is, God; from *ǎǎ'*, father, and *na*, above, on high.
**Na'daka**—with the people.
**Nahǎ'**—that's all! now you see! there now!

<column-break/>

**Naha'yo**—up, above, the plural of *Ha'yo*.
> *Hasi'ni diwĭti'a na'hayo*, all the Caddo are going up, everyone of the Caddo is going up.

**Na-iye'**—sister above; from *na*, above, in composition, and *iye'*, sister.
**Nǎnǎ'** or **Nǎ'nǎnǎ'**—that one (demonstrative).
**Nana'sana**—is he making it?
**Na'ni'asa**—they are using it; *ha'tsĭna'sa*, I use it.
**Na'nia'sana**—for *Na'ni'asa*.
**Nü'nisa'na**—an Arapaho word, adopted by the Caddo in the Ghost-dance songs and meaning "my children."
**Nü'nisa'na gao'shăn**—"Nünisana dance," one of the Caddo names for the Ghost dance, from *gao'shăn*, a dance, and *nünisa'na* (which see), an Arapaho word which forms the refrain of so many Arapaho Ghost-dance songs. It is also called **Ǎǎ Kaki'mbawiút**, "the prayer of all to the Father."
**Na'tsiwa'ya**—I am coming.
**Na'wi**—below; *ha'yo*, above.
**Nawotsi**—bear; a Caddo clan.
**Ni**—a syllable prefixed merely to fill in the meter.
**Niahu'na**—for *Ni'tahǔ'nt*.
**Ni'tahǔ'nt**—it has returned. It has come back; *tsǐtsihǔ'nǎ*, I return; *Ni'tsiho*, when I returned.
**Ni'toh**—feather (specific); *ha'taha*, feather (generic).
**Ni'tsiho**—when I returned. Compare *Ni'tahǔ'nt*.
**Nû'na**—because.
**O'ǎt**—raccoon; a Caddo clan.
**O'wita**—he comes; *a'tsiús*, I come.
**Sha''chadǐ'ni**—"Timber hill," a former Caddo settlement on Caddo lake, Louisiana.
**Si'bocha'ha**—I want to see them; *hatsi'bos*, I see.
**Sûko**—sun; a Caddo clan.
**Tǎ'-iă**—he dwells above. Compare *Ko'iă*.
**Ta'nǎhǎ**—buffalo; a Caddo clan.
**Ta'o**—beaver; a Caddo clan.
**Tasha**—wolf; a Caddo clan.
**Tsaba'kosh**—cut-throats; the Caddo name for the Sioux.
**Wa'hiya'ne!**—a meaningless exclamation used in the songs.
**Wi'ahe'eye'!**—the same.
**Wi'tǔ!**—come on! get ready.
**Wû'nti**—all of them.

**Keam, Thomas V.** Letters and oral information.

Mr. Keam, of Keams Canyon, Arizona, has been a trader among the Navajo and Hopi (Moki) for a number of years. He speaks the Navajo language fluently and takes an informed interest in everything relating to these tribes. He has provided valuable information orally and by letter, along with much kind assistance while the author was in that region.

<meta>This page serves as an erratum, correcting information regarding Shaker religious figures mentioned previously in the text, following the alphabetical list of authorities.</meta>

### ERRATUM

From a letter by Judge James Wickersham, who has already been cited as an authority on the Shaker religion of the Columbia River tribes, it appears that Aiyal is not the same person as Yowaluch, as was stated by our Yakima informants, who were undoubtedly misled by the similarity of the sounds of their names. Judge Wickersham writes: “I know this man Aiyal, and he and Yowaluch, while great friends, are not the same person. Aiyal is a Cowlitz, and was sent by Yowaluch to the Yakima, along with John W. Simmons, to convert that tribe.”

<summary>This erratum clarifies that Aiyal and Yowaluch are two distinct individuals, correcting an earlier error caused by the similarity of their names. It specifies that Aiyal is a member of the Cowlitz tribe who helped spread the Shaker religion to the Yakima people.</summary>
<keywords>James Wickersham, Shaker religion, Columbia River tribes, Aiyal, Yowaluch, Yakima, Cowlitz, John W. Simmons, religious conversion</keywords>
